16176-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Hard fighting on the Indian frontier leads the November 11, 1897 Great Round World. Afridi tribesmen held the rising ground called Dargai Ridge, which British troops had to cross. A detachment sent to dislodge them did so easily. The village of Dargai soon stood in flames. The tribesmen seemed routed and gone, so the troops took no pains to fortify the ridge, turning instead to preparations for the advance.

The children's paper retells the engagement in short, admiring sentences, making frontier war plain for school readers. Its young audience could follow regiments, ridges, and retreats week by week. The issue preserves a schoolroom view of Britain's Tirah campaign in the fall of 1897.
16267-the-gamester-1753:
Edward Moore's tragedy The Gamester reached the stage at Drury Lane and print in London in 1753, sold by Francklin in Covent Garden and Dodsley in Pall Mall. The title page hides the author, but the dedication to Henry Pelham signs itself Edw. Moore, and a prologue by Garrick with an epilogue and the original cast precede the eighty-four-page text. New editions followed in the same year and again in 1755, 1771, and 1776.

The play takes gambling as its tragic subject, watching a gamester stake fortune, family, and honor on the turn of a card. Moore, a minor Augustan dramatist, writes in the moral, domestic style of his age. Readers of eighteenth-century drama will find a compact tragedy on chance, debt, and ruin.
24780-the-letters-of-queen-victoria-vol-:
Edited by Arthur Christopher Benson and Viscount Esher and published in 1908, this second volume prints Queen Victoria's letters from 1844 to 1853. The selection, made by authority of the King, runs year by year, from the Emperor Nicholas's visit and the Spanish marriages to the purchase of Osborne and the great Chartist scare.

The letters show the Queen at work and at home: writing to ministers, fretting over her children, and judging the courts of Europe. Notes on the crisis in Parliament and the King of Saxony's visit fill out the record. Historians and royal readers alike will find a close, human view of a young queen learning to rule.
4054-a-lady-s-visit-to-the-gold-diggings:
A lady's account of the Australian gold diggings in 1852 and 1853 follows her voyage out, her stay in Melbourne, and her camping trips to Forest Creek, Eagle Hawk Gully, and Ballarat. German friends part from the party to follow their own plan, leaving fifteen travelers, herself included.

Coffee shops, blacksmiths, and a neat weather-board inn mark the townships, while hill and dale scenery opens beyond them. The writer notes diggers, camps, and daily hardship with a keen, practical eye. Readers who like firsthand gold-rush history will find a lively, plain-spoken record by a woman on the fields.
6348-copyright-renewals-1953: The hosted file for this title holds no renewal data itself, only a short placeholder note explaining that the 1953 renewals were placed in two other files instead. Readers looking for the 1953 entries are directed to two other files, one for January to June and one for July to December. The note marks this file as an unused empty reserve from the series. No lists, names, or renewal records appear in the sample.
9198-the-complete-angler-1653:
Izaak Walton wrote The Complete Angler, or The Contemplative Man's Recreation, first published in 1653. This file gives a facsimile reprint of that first edition, with a preface by Richard Le Gallienne. Le Gallienne notes the scorn poured on first editions, and confesses his own love of Walton's Lives, bought at the cost of hunger and cold.

Walton's dialogue on fishing, nature, and quiet life made the book a classic of contemplation. Anglers still quote it, and readers still seek its calm. The facsimile lets modern eyes see the beloved book as its first readers saw it.
a-lady-s-visit-to-the-gold-diggings-of-a:
Ellen Clacy's A Lady's Visit to the Gold Diggings of Australia in 1852-53, published under her byline as Mrs. Charles Clacy, begins with her brother throwing aside Homer and Euclid for emigrants' guides. The gold excitement carried the pair from England to Melbourne within weeks. Her contents promise the voyage out and the camping road through the Black Forest to Eagle Hawk Gully. An appendix asks who should emigrate, and answers from experience.

Inside, Clacy tents at the diggings, visits Ironbark Gully and Forest Creek, and records an adventure and the story of Harriette Walters. Ballarat, New South Wales, and South Australia widen the tour before the homeward voyage. She writes for the mothers and sisters in England who wanted facts about the fields. Readers get the gold rush through a young woman's eyes, short on marvels, as she warns, and long on prices, roads, and weather.
argentine-constitution-1853:
Argentina adopted its constitution in 1853, after decades of civil war and the fall of the dictator Rosas. Delegates met at Paraná, since Buenos Aires had refused to join the new union. The thinker Juan Bautista Alberdi supplied the charter's blueprint in his book Bases, and the American constitution supplied its pattern.

The text builds a federal republic of provinces with a president, a congress of two houses, and an independent judiciary. A full bill of rights guards speech, property, worship, and movement, and the charter throws the country open to European immigration. Buenos Aires joined a few years later, and the charter, amended since, still rules Argentina today. It founded the modern Argentine state: the founding law of the nation's nationhood, built to end anarchy by law.
arxiv-2509-00153:
Yongda Zhu leads a team of thirty authors who report in 2025 that a bright quasar's light may stunt nearby galaxy growth at redshift six point three. Quasars are brilliant cores of young galaxies. The quasar J0100+2802 is the most ultraviolet-luminous one known at that era. Space telescope spectra cover galaxies around it on intergalactic scales.

Galaxies within about seven megaparsecs show weaker oxygen emission for their ultraviolet glow, a sign of suppressed recent star birth. The ultraviolet glow itself stays flat with distance, while oxygen glow rises away from the quasar. The trend holds after checks for completeness, density, and brightness, and it tracks the quasar's ionization rate. Intense radiation may thus shape whole neighborhoods in the early universe.
arxiv-2509-00253:
A. N. Zhukov leads a team of seventy authors who describe the ASPIICS coronagraph aboard the Proba-3 mission in 2025. A coronagraph blocks a star's glare to reveal its faint corona, the hot outer atmosphere. Proba-3, a European Space Agency mission launched in December 2024, flies two spacecraft in precise formation on a highly elliptical orbit.

One craft carries the telescope, the other a disk that blocks the Sun, about one hundred forty-four meters apart. That gap, a hundred times larger than in classic designs, yields eclipse-like views down close to the solar limb with very low stray light. Six hours of each orbit are spent in formation. ASPIICS will image and measure polarized light from the inner corona.
arxiv-2509-00353:
Koushik Ahmed Kushal and Abdullah Al Mamun present AQFusionNet in 2025, a multimodal model that predicts the Air Quality Index from images and sensor data. Air monitoring in resource-constrained regions is hampered by sparse sensors and thin infrastructure. Ground-level sky imagery carries clues about haze that sensors alone may miss.

Lightweight convolutional backbones, MobileNetV2, ResNet18, and EfficientNet-B0, extract visual features. Sensor features join them in aligned embedding spaces for a joint prediction. On more than eight thousand samples from India and Nepal, the fused model beats single-mode baselines. Top accuracy passes ninety-two percent, with an eighteen and a half percent gain over single-modality approaches at low compute cost.
arxiv-2509-00853:
Hideya Watanabe, writing alone, interprets the Berele row-insertion in terms of representations. Row-insertion is a procedure that places numbers into tableaux. The Berele version is the symplectic analogue of the Schensted one. Watanabe uses quantum symmetric pairs of type AII for his reading. Such pairs couple a quantum group with a coideal subalgebra.

He lifts two known links to this quantum setting. One is Berele's Robinson-Schensted link between tableaux and representations. The other is the Kobayashi-Matsumura RSK link of the same kind. Both become isomorphisms of representations over the subalgebra. He also sets up the dual RSK link of type AII. The work ties tableaux combinatorics to quantum group theory.
arxiv-2509-00953:
H Francisco, with three co-authors, improves deorbitalized functionals for electronic structure work. Deorbitalization replaces dependence on the Kohn-Sham kinetic energy density. The new dependence is on the density gradient and Laplacian. In principle, this should speed up calculations a lot. It shifts from an orbital-based potential to a true local one.

That gain is often lost to roughness in the density, though. The Laplacian causes roughness, which spreads into the potential. The team builds a new deorbitalizer based on the RPP one. Smoothness of the potential is a design goal for it. Keeping constraint satisfaction is another goal. Applied to the r2SCAN functional, timing improves a lot for solids. Accuracy also improves over RPP for both solids and molecules.
arxiv-2509-01053:
Xiaoying Song leads a team of five authors on a fusion model for consistent crisis response. Automated replies can assist communication with crisis-affected people. Consistency of style is a key factor, though often overlooked. Style affects the trust affected people place in responders. Few studies explore methods for keeping style consistent.

The team proposes a new metric for style consistency. Their fusion-based approach to generation is grounded in that metric. The method works in two stages at the instance level. It first assesses the style of candidate replies. It then optimizes and merges them through a fusion step. High-quality replies result with much less variation in style. Tests across datasets show gains over baselines in quality and uniformity both.
arxiv-2509-01253:
Cloud models must answer questions on private data without seeing it, and fully homomorphic encryption allows computation on locked data directly. Sayan Biswas, with nine co-authors, notes that this encryption is slowed by costly bootstrapping steps and rough stand-ins for nonlinear functions. Their framework, Safhire, splits the work between server and client.

Linear layers run under encryption on the server, while nonlinear steps are handled by the client in plain form. That split removes bootstrapping and allows exact activations, cutting cost sharply. Randomized shuffling hides intermediate values so clients cannot rebuild the model. Packing tricks cut delay further, and tests showed latency several times lower than prior approaches, while keeping both user data and the server's model private.
arxiv-2509-01353:
Drawing a circular arc with a polynomial curve is a basic task in design software, and the best fit depends on how error is judged. Ema Cesek and Ales Vavpetic study optimal approximations where the error is measured through curvature, how sharply the curve bends. They require geometric continuity, smooth joins of stated order, at the arc's end points.

Three cases are analyzed: a parabolic curve with basic continuity, a cubic with first-order smoothness, and a quartic with second-order smoothness. For each, the authors work out the optimal choice under the curvature standard. They also compare those results with approximations judged by radial error, the distance from the true circle. The study gives designers a clear account of what curvature-based fitting buys, and how it differs from the more common radial standard.
arxiv-2509-01453:
Some images stick in memory while others fade, and what a computer vision model does inside may hint at why. Ece Takmaz, Albert Gatt, and Jakub Dotlacil explore links between human image memorability and the inner features of pre-trained transformer vision encoders. They examine activations, attention patterns, and how uniform image patches are across the picture.

Those features correlated with memorability to some degree. The team also tested sparse autoencoder loss, the error a compact rebuilding model makes on an encoder's representations, as a stand-in signal. That loss proved a strong correlate of memorability, beating past methods based on convolutional networks. Takmaz and the co-authors argue model-internal signals can predict what humans remember, opening a window on how machine and human vision overlap.
arxiv-2509-01553:
Dark matter haloes host smaller subhaloes. Explaining their numbers and layout has been a long project for Eduard Salvador-Sole, Alberto Manrique, and Andreu Rocamora. In three earlier papers, they derived substructure traits from a peak model. A model of stripping and shock heating joined it. They set aside dynamical friction, the drag that slows orbiting subhaloes. This fourth paper adds that missing force.

The inclusion is fully analytic. It avoids step-by-step tracking of subhalo orbits. Simple, accurate formulas follow for the counts and radial spread of subhaloes. The formulas split the effects of friction from those of tidal stripping and shock heating. The results reproduce and explain simulation findings. They extend them to haloes of any mass, age, and cosmic epoch in the chosen cosmology.
arxiv-2509-01653:
Isabelle Connor, James R Beattie, Anne Noer Kolborg, and Enrico Ramirez-Ruiz model how exploding stars stir gas inside galaxies. Star forming galaxies churn with motion fed in part by supernova blasts. The team runs detailed computer models that track heating, cooling, and gravity in layered gas. They vary galaxy mass, blast rate, and how the blasts are seeded.

Even when the gas itself changes a lot, the pattern of speed swings settles into one shared shape. That shape runs smoothly from winds above the disk down into the disk itself. The authors also link squeezing modes of the flow to the mix of hot and warm gas. The work hints that galaxy churn may follow broad rules across unlike systems.
arxiv-2509-01953:
Haiqing Zhu, Lexing Xie, and Yun Kuen Cheung analyze entry barriers in online content markets with game theory. Low quality content floods platforms that set no real entry bar. The authors ask whether implicit or explicit barriers plus smart rewards can lift quality. Two barrier types are studied in a formal model of providers and platforms.

One barrier emerges on its own: incumbents collective behavior disadvantages newcomers at equilibrium under common reward rules. The second is strategic, where the platform charges entry fees to deter weak contributors. Feeding those fees back into the reward pool can raise overall quality in their proofs. The findings ground designs that pair fees with rewards for healthier platforms.
arxiv-2509-02253:
Erik Burman and Fabian Heimann present a 2025 numerical methods paper on solving a transport equation, which tracks how a quantity moves, on domains whose boundary itself travels. The boundary moves with the same flow as the material inside, a case that makes standard meshes awkward.

Their approach uses unfitted space-time finite elements, meaning the grid stays fixed while the domain cuts through it. Elements can jump between time slices, and the moving shape gets a second-order geometric treatment. The authors prove stability in a norm built for the problem and derive high-order error bounds. Test problems confirm the theory. The work helps engineers simulate moving-boundary flows without rebuilding a mesh at every step.
arxiv-2509-02353:
Federico Amato and four co-authors present a 2025 quantum thermodynamics paper on an Otto engine, a heat engine cycle, built from an optical cavity pushed by radiation pressure. Beams of specially prepared three-level atoms, called phaseonium, drive the cavity instead of ordinary hot and cold baths.

How many atoms sit in each level, together with their ground-state coherence, fixes the ratio that steers the cavity, so it relaxes to a heat-like state at an apparent temperature. The authors show this charging stays passive, with no usable work hidden in the field itself. They also bound the cost of preparing the atoms, framing any gain as a trade-off, not a free lunch. A two-cavity cascade produced notably more power per injected atom than separate engines.
arxiv-2509-02753:
Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata, Sandeep Madireddy, Murali Emani, and Venkatram Vishwanath wrote a 2025 machine learning systems paper on speeding up mixture-of-experts model inference. Such models activate a few experts per token, but standard designs use the same count in every layer.

The authors first show that pruning experts mainly saves memory, not run time, on optimised GPU frameworks. Their LExI method instead chooses how many experts each layer should activate, using only model weights and no extra data. Layer importance scores drive the assignment, cutting redundant computation. On language and vision benchmarks, LExI beat pruning methods on efficiency with negligible accuracy loss. In one test, a tuned model matched a pruned rival's speed while scoring clearly higher accuracy.
arxiv-2509-02953:
Jia-Ai Shi, Chen-Can Wang, and Bing-Nan Lu reported a 2025 nuclear theory test of a key consistency demand. Effective field theories use a cutoff, a limit that ignores very short distances. Their predictions should not depend on where that cutoff sits. That independence is called renormalization group invariance.

The team worked on a lattice, a grid in space, and added special correction terms to restore symmetries the grid breaks, such as rotation. They tuned the theory's two- and three-body forces on the lightest nuclei. Precise Monte Carlo calculations, which sample many random paths, then gave the helium-4 binding energy. The value barely moved across a wide cutoff range and landed close to experiment.
arxiv-2509-03353:
Oguzhan Baser and 3 co-authors released Fair-Synergy in 2025, a framework for sharing computing resources fairly across fleets of AI agents. Cloud-assisted teams of robots or vehicles differ widely in hardware and surroundings, so naive sharing can starve some agents while pampering others. Fairness here means balancing gains across the whole fleet.

The method exploits a concave link between each agent's accuracy and the resources it receives: early resources help a lot, later ones less. Allocation is framed over a landscape of model size, training data volume, and task complexity. Tests used well-known vision and language models on image and language datasets. The framework beat standard benchmarks by wide margins in both shared inference and shared learning settings. The authors also chart how fairness levels shift outcomes for the worst-off, best-off, and average agents.
arxiv-2509-03653:
Siddharth Samsi and three co-authors focus on speeding up a graph computing challenge using graphics processors and ordinary data science tools in a 2025 research paper. The HPEC Graph Challenge benchmarks stress high-performance systems with workloads that classic tests miss. Its newest challenge, anonymised network sensing, is a long end-to-end pipeline involving data input, graph structures, preparation, and analysis.

The challenge is normally expressed with GraphBLAS, a standard for graph operations written as linear algebra. The authors reinterpret those formulations in data science language instead. Off-the-shelf tools from NVIDIA's RAPIDS ecosystem, including cuDF and CuPy, then carry the whole workload without specialised high-performance code. Compared with the same code running on Pandas on a central processor, speedups reach hundreds of times on A100 hardware and far higher on newer H100 and H200 chips. Performance and programmer productivity, they argue, can come together.
arxiv-2509-03753: In a 2025 research paper, Michael Greer focuses on speeding up support point queries by changing how convex hulls are stored in memory. A support point query asks which point of a shape reaches farthest in a given direction. Such queries sit at the heart of common collision detection algorithms in games and simulations. Greer evaluates several memory layout improvements for the hull data. Computation times improve significantly in the reported tests. The size of the gain depends on how many vertices the convex hull has.
arxiv-2509-03853:
Haoyu Jiang and two co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to simulation-based inference, Bayesian analysis for models that can be simulated forward but have no writable likelihood. Approximate methods and deep generative models widened its use, but cost grows steeply with sample size and dimension count.

Their method fuses score matching with Langevin dynamics, sampling that follows the posterior's gradient with added noise. Structure in the log-likelihood is used twice over. Localisation concentrates computation where posterior mass sits, instead of roaming the full space. A structured score network hard-wires properties true scores obey, notably additivity over observations and Fisher information identities. Theory and experiments both indicate better efficiency alongside better scalability. Across benchmark and harder problems, with large samples and moderate counts, the method matches or beats existing approaches. The goal is practical Bayesian inference for simulator-heavy science.
arxiv-2509-03953:
A 2025 research paper by Ángel Aso-Mollar and three co-authors focuses on handling infinite control parameters in automated planning through best-first search. Automated planning finds action sequences that reach a goal. Control parameters extend actions with continuous numeric choices, like exact speeds or angles, giving infinitely many decision values where ordinary planners expect finite menus.

Leading approaches treat those parameters as side constraints bundled with temporal and numeric restrictions, never as true decision points. The authors instead search over the infinite decision space directly, with a best-first heuristic algorithm. Its engine is delayed partial expansion: a state is not expanded fully at once, but its successors are generated incrementally in subsets. Under stated conditions, the search is proved complete in the limit, meaning patience guarantees a solution when one exists. Experiments show the algorithm competes well with planners, opening a cleaner route for planning with continuous choices.
arxiv-2509-04053:
Jacqueline J Vallon and thirteen co-authors tackle a trust problem for medical prediction software in a 2025 research paper. A model can score well overall yet behave in ways doctors find wrong. One example is survival odds that fail to fall steadily as cancer stage rises. The team uses prostate cancer outcome forecasts as their test case, and traces much of the trouble to choices left unspecified when models are built.

Doctors shared their expectations through a survey, and those views became rules inside the model. Accuracy held up after the change. In a randomized trial, doctors also judged competing models directly. Bigger gaps between model predictions made the contrast easier for clinicians to spot.
arxiv-2509-04553:
Alba V Alonso-Tetilla and thirteen co-authors test what hides so many growing black holes at cosmic noon in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Obscured active galactic nuclei are wrapped in dust, but whether the wrapping is a passing phase, a viewing angle effect, or both stays contested. Semi-analytic galaxy models with object-by-object black hole life stories are run across the peak era of galaxy growth. Light curves mix obscured and visible phases in different proportions to mimic feedback clearing dust away.

Short hidden phases followed by long visible ones underproduce the obscured fractions that X-ray surveys infer. Longer, repeated, or sharply ending hidden phases fare better. A long-lived inner dust torus whose thickness shrinks with power also helps naturally. Mergers and starbursts alone fall short.
arxiv-2509-05353:
Fourier tools for a group built from quaternions are constructed by O. A. Ariyo and M. E. Egwe in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is the quaternionic Heisenberg group, a space with a four-dimensional layer and a three-dimensional layer, together with a compact group of its symmetries.

The pair form a motion group by combining the symmetries with the group itself, a construction called a semidirect product. For such Gelfand pairs, which are symmetry setups where a certain algebra is commutative, they build the spherical Fourier multiplier, an operator that rescales waves by frequency. Work of this kind extends harmonic analysis, the study of waves on groups, beyond ordinary flat spaces.
arxiv-2509-05453:
Subspaces that stay fixed under every operator commuting with a given one are chased by Maria F. Gamal' in a solo 2025 paper about linear maps on infinite-dimensional spaces. Whether such hyperinvariant subspaces always exist is a long-standing open problem for many operator classes.

Gamal' proves such subspaces exist under two sets of conditions. In the first, one operator acts like a one-sided shift on a subspace, while its adjoint acts in a subnormal way on the rest. In the second, the operator is intertwined on both sides with a hyponormal operator and its adjoint. Whether subnormal operators have such subspaces is not studied here.
arxiv-2509-05753:
Watermarks that change in telling ways when media are edited are proposed by Ching-Chun Chang and Isao Echizen in a 2025 digital forensics paper. Synthetic media and ordinary editing blur what really happened to an image, mixing content edits, colour changes, and viewpoint shifts into one unclear history.

Their tell-tale watermarks are tuned per transformation class to be neither fully robust nor fragile, but interpretable. They evolve under the same dynamics as the carrier image, leaving readable traces after transformations. Explanatory reasoning then infers the most plausible chain of events across combinations of transformations. Experiments support the system's fidelity, synchrony, and traceability. Reconstructing provenance, not just flagging fakes, is the aim.
arxiv-2509-06053:
Game-playing policies written as readable code, evolved by language models, are the product of PolicyEvolve, a 2025 framework from Mingrui Lv and four co-authors. Neural policies for multiplayer games need millions of practice samples and stay opaque, which blocks deployment. Single-agent work had shown models can write rule-based policies instead; this team extends the idea to adversarial multiplayer settings.

Four modules cooperate: a global pool keeps elite policies, a local pool holds the current round's drafts, a planner writes and refines code, and a trajectory critic spots weaknesses from match records. Only drafts that beat the pool average earn promotion. The loop reaches strong policies with minimal environment interaction, cutting the hand-crafting such code usually demands.
arxiv-2509-06153:
Einstein's gravity is recast in tetrad and connection variables, without fixing the time gauge, in a 2025 paper by Erick I. Duque. The Hamiltonian formulation starts from the Hilbert-Palatini action with Barbero-Immirzi and cosmological constants, using the traditional ADM split of spacetime. The result contrasts with the Ashtekar-Barbero approach, which fixes more structure earlier.

Duque's phase space is larger, with more first-class constraints generating transformations equivalent, on shell, to spacetime diffeomorphisms and local Lorentz rotations. The mismatch between tetrad and connection components is resolved by second-class constraints, handled through Dirac brackets or direct solution. The system stays well defined even off that constraint surface, hinting at a more general geometric theory, and implications for canonical quantum gravity are discussed.
arxiv-2509-06253:
Ranking how strange an interstellar visitor is needs a scale, and Oem Trivedi and Abraham Loeb formalize one in a 2025 paper. Three interstellar objects are known, most recently 3I/ATLAS, and the Rubin Observatory should find dozens more within a decade. The Loeb scale classifies such objects by their nature, from natural to technological.

The authors supply a quantitative mapping for the scale, modeled on Sagan's formula for the Kardashev scale of civilizations by energy output. With a steady stream of discoveries expected, a shared ranking promises to focus follow-up observations and public discussion on the most anomalous cases.
arxiv-2509-06353:
A disputed bump in particle data is a real resonance, argue Yin Huang and Xurong Chen in a 2025 paper on the G(3900). Evidence for this charmed structure near thirty-nine hundred megaelectronvolts appeared eighteen years ago in electron-positron collisions making D meson pairs, but interference effects and a nearby threshold could fake it. A larger BESIII sample in 2024 confirmed the structure without settling its nature.

The authors show that plotting the cross section against the D meson's transverse momentum reveals a prominent Jacobian peak. Interference alone cannot manufacture that feature, so it directly evidences a genuine state, and the peak's position pins the mass precisely. The criterion extends to other hadronic systems.
arxiv-2509-06453:
Should capturing human attention carry a tax? Hamza Belgroun and two co-authors pose that question in a 2025 paper spanning philosophy, economics, and law. Attention, they note, is scarce, valuable, and traded by digital platforms. The authors treat it as a shared good that firms can overuse, much like a crowded common pasture.

Heavy screen time, they argue, brings harms that markets do not price: weaker personal control, poorer health, and damage to public life and democracy. Among tools from information campaigns to outright limits, they favor a Pigouvian tax, meaning a charge set to cover the social cost of the harm. Such a tax could push platforms to redesign compulsive features while leaving user choice intact, and it reframes attention as a resource worth protecting together.
arxiv-2509-06553:
Dental X-rays read across hospitals without pooling private data are studied by Johan Andreas Balle Rubak and five co-authors in a 2025 medical imaging paper. The task is outlining teeth in panoramic radiographs. Federated learning, where each site trains locally and shares only model updates, promises privacy, but messy real data may break it.

An attention U-Net model was trained on more than two thousand radiographs from six institutions under four conditions: clean data, damaged labels, added image noise, and one faulty site. Federated training matched or beat centralized training and clearly beat purely local training in every condition, even with corrupted labels or noise. Watching each site's training loss also flagged the faulty site reliably. The authors present this as a practical, privacy-keeping route for clinical AI.
arxiv-2509-06753:
A honeycomb magnet strained until its twin crystals separate is measured with neutrons by Yi Li and twelve co-authors in a 2025 condensed matter paper. The material, alpha-ruthenium trichloride, is a leading candidate for a Kitaev quantum spin liquid. Crystal twinning had blurred its true spin dynamics for years.

Biaxial strain pulled the crystals into a single orientation, and inelastic neutron scattering then revealed the intrinsic excitations. Low-energy spin waves emerge from points transverse to the magnetic Bragg peaks, direct evidence of anisotropic interactions. The clean spectrum sharply constrains the extended Kitaev Hamiltonian and yields a consistent set of exchange couplings. Above the spin-wave band, broad continua appear, including a sixfold-symmetric spread of spectral weight that ordinary magnons cannot explain. That pattern supports fractionalized excitations, a hallmark of spin liquid physics.
arxiv-2509-07153:
Dark matter halos grow out of dense patches in the early universe called protohalos. Farnik Nikakhtar and 3 co-authors revisit how the shapes of those patches connect to the halos they become, in a 2025 research paper. The work is driven by a new method, based on optimal transport theory, that aims to rebuild protohalo positions and shapes from observed galaxies.

The authors measure protohalo structure with three invariants, or summary numbers, taken from inertia, deformation, and energy shear tensors. They also introduce a new estimator that adds up information across redshifts. Earlier work linked only the first two invariants to halo growth. The team finds the third invariant also tracks halo assembly and final shape strongly. That result sharpens tools for reading a halo's history from its starting patch.
arxiv-2509-07253:
Julian Killingback and 1 co-author argue in 2025 that search models need harder tests. Retrieval models find documents that match a query, and most benchmarks still use short, single-topic queries. Real users, shaped by chat-style AI tools, now ask complex questions with several parts, limits, and conditions at once. Few public test sets measure how retrieval handles such requests in realistic settings.

To close the gap, the authors build a diverse set of complex retrieval tasks and run a representative group of leading retrieval models on them. The benchmark is meant to show the true capability of each model, not just its skill on easy queries. Better measurement matters because retrieval quietly underpins search engines, research tools, and AI assistants. The authors hope the new tasks spur a generation of retrieval models built for real, messy information needs.
arxiv-2509-07553:
Zheng Wu and 10 co-authors present VeriOS in 2025, a framework that lets operating system agents ask humans for help when a situation looks untrustworthy. OS agents drive a device's graphical interface to automate tasks, but most are built for ideal conditions. In messy real settings, an agent that blindly keeps executing can do real harm, a risk called over-execution.

The framework is query-driven: the agent decides when to query the human rather than always acting or always asking. VeriOS-Agent is trained in three stages, using supervised fine-tuning and group relative policy optimization to separate and use meta-knowledge about trustworthiness. In experiments it raised the average step-wise success rate by about 19.7 percent over the strongest baselines, with large gains in untrustworthy scenarios and no loss in normal ones. Knowing when to ask is framed as a core safety skill.
arxiv-2509-07753:
Lucas Borges and 2 co-authors propose in 2025 a cavity scheme to excite chosen molecular vibrations for ground-state chemistry. Molecular polaritonics studies molecules coupled strongly to confined light. Most work asks how electronic excitations mixed with light alter photochemistry. Selectively pumping molecules into high vibrational states is a different goal. Done with infrared lasers, it could catalyze reactions with no electronic excitation. That task is hard.

Their setup uses two cavity modes, in the electronic strong coupling regime. It is inspired by STIRAP, a technique that transfers populations between quantum states. In STIRAP, the middle state is never occupied. One cavity mode pumps the molecular system here. The other gives a tunable decay channel, through photon leakage. On a model system, the scheme populates vibrational states in a selective way. It works with coherent and incoherent light sources, at high efficiency in the first findings.
arxiv-2509-07953:
Robots that learn by watching people hit a ceiling on long, delicate jobs, and Zheyuan Hu and 6 co-authors propose a fix in a 2025 robotics paper. Imitation learning trains capable policies from human demonstrations, yet performance on contact-rich, deformable-object, and long-horizon tasks stalls well below perfect, even with thousands of expert examples.

Their phase, called RaC, comes after imitation pretraining. A person supervises the robot's own attempts and intervenes when things go wrong, producing examples of recovery and correction rather than flawless performance. Fine-tuning on those rescue moments teaches the policy how to get back on track. Robots in real homes and factories will make mistakes; learning to recover may matter more than polishing perfect demonstrations.
arxiv-2509-08053:
Alberto Giuseppe Catalano and 6 co-authors measure the quantum magic stored in symmetry-protected topological phases in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Magic is the resource that lifts quantum states beyond what stabilizer methods can simulate classically. The authors quantify it with a stabilizer Rényi entropy in one-dimensional chains that host these protected phases.

Two models, the dimerized XX chain and the Cluster-Ising chain, have exact dualities pairing a topological phase with a trivial one. Dual points carry identical magic despite belonging to different topological sectors. Only edge effects under open boundaries create a small asymmetry. Sorting out which resources truly belong to topological order helps target the ingredients quantum computers actually need.
arxiv-2509-08353:
Abdul Rehman and 4 co-authors assess attention in children with neurodevelopmental disorders through games in a 2025 paper. A single game score says too little about how a child attends. Their scoring frame fuses three streams: where the eyes go, how engagement rises and falls in time, and how well the child plays.

Difficulty adapts as the child plays. Each level aims at set stimuli. Weights shift as the load grows, so the score stays fair. Time-based checks catch lapses that a final score would smooth away. Teachers and clinicians need measures that respect how differently these children attend. A game that adapts while it measures could give fairer, richer reports than a fixed test.
arxiv-2509-08553:
Electronic health records could power medical discovery across hospitals, but every site codes its data differently. Jessica Gronsbell and 13 co-authors introduce PEHRT, a shared harmonization pipeline, in a 2025 research paper. PEHRT bundles open-source code, visualization tools, and documentation in one ready-to-use resource. It handles both structured records and unstructured clinical text.

The pipeline maps local codes onto standard ontologies for consistency. Where codes resist mapping, it learns embeddings, numerical summaries that capture meaning, using pre-trained language models. Sites can even refine shared embeddings together without exchanging patient-level data. The framework ignores which data model a hospital uses, so it deploys across diverse systems. By removing months of data-wrangling, PEHRT aims to let translational researchers start from research-ready data instead of raw chaos.
arxiv-2509-08853:
Leif Azzopardi and 1 co-author map political Overton windows of large language models in a 2025 paper. The Overton window is the range of views treated as acceptable in public debate. A point estimate of a model's politics can hide what it will or will not say.

An auditing method called PRISM probes models with task based prompts that draw out stances indirectly. Twenty-eight models from eight providers are tested with the Political Compass Test. Many default to left economic and liberal social positions, but willingness to express views varies widely. Some providers are far more restrictive than others. Windows give a richer view of bias.
arxiv-2509-08953:
Chart-making tools increasingly accept speech, touch, sketches, and text together, but nobody had mapped how that variety actually works. Astrid van den Brandt and 4 co-authors supply the map in a 2025 research paper. Their literature review found that multimodal interaction means many different things in chart authoring. They set out to characterize the design space systematically.

The team reviewed twenty visualization authoring tools that combine input modes. For each, they recorded how the modes are combined and what each mode adds. The comparison highlights features that set one tool apart from another. From the patterns, the authors draw design lessons and future research directions. Tool builders gain a clearer vocabulary for multimodal design. The overview should help the next wave of authoring systems become more accessible and more effective.
arxiv-2509-09053:
Julian Oelhaf and 6 co-authors review machine learning for power grid protection in a 2025 paper. New wind, solar, and local sources reshape grids and strain old protection schemes, which guard lines and gear from faults. The review follows the PRISMA scoping frame.

More than one hundred papers are summed up for scope, scores across settings, and fit to changing grids. Models often score high on simulated data, but proof on real grids is scarce. Mixed methods, data, and metrics block fair comparison across studies. The team gives a task taxonomy and reporting rules, and urges public test sets and real world checks before use.
arxiv-2509-09553:
Ken Ono and 1 co-author prove a long-standing conjecture about the partition function in a 2025 number theory paper. The partition function counts how many ways a whole number can be split into a sum of smaller ones. Whether those counts come out even or odd along a special quadratic family had resisted proof since the first author raised the question in 2010.

Their new idea is geometric. Twisted Borcherds products built from Ramanujan's mock theta functions recast the counts through special points on a modular curve. Careful arguments about lifting those points and comparing series then rule out one-sided parity. The family holds infinitely many counts of each kind, and a stronger lower bound for odd values follows.
arxiv-2509-09653:
One big quantum computer is hard to build, so data centers of small ones, networked by entanglement, are the pragmatic alternative. Yufeng Xin and Liang Zhang design that network in a 2025 research paper. Their architecture is a three-layer fat-tree, a classic data center layout, adapted to quantum links. Special leaf switches and an advanced swapping spine switch handle the entanglement traffic.

The hard resources are entanglement requests arriving in volume and quantum memories that decohere while they wait. A queue scheduling mechanism manages memory to protect fidelity. The authors support the design with queuing theory models and simulations in a quantum network simulator. The architecture scales while keeping entanglement fidelity high. Modular quantum data centers will need exactly this kind of unglamorous plumbing decided early, before the machines multiply and the network becomes the computer.
arxiv-2509-09953:
Mahfuzul I. Nissan and 1 co-author hunt for early warnings of robot failure inside system logs in a 2025 safety paper. Even carefully engineered robots malfunction, and a missed anomaly can endanger people nearby. Their approach teaches machine learning models to flag odd log patterns before trouble grows, testing the idea in a simulator across two very different machines.

Logs came from a quadcopter scenario and a Pioneer ground robot scenario, both staged in CoppeliaSim. Three learners were compared head to head: logistic regression, a support vector machine, and an autoencoder. Regression won clearly on the drone, while the autoencoder proved strongest on the ground robot. The lesson is practical: the best detector depends on the platform and on how tangled its anomalies are.
arxiv-2509-10153:
Ursy Makanga and 2 co-authors show how a straight, floppy filament can start swimming on its own in a 2025 fluids paper. The filament should sit still by symmetry. Autophoretic particles move by making their own chemical gradients. Those gradients drive slip flows along their surfaces. A uniform elastic filament has no built-in bias. So it ought to go nowhere at all. That puzzle is what the authors attack.

Buckling supplies the missing bias. Once the filament bends past a threshold, its flows push the bent shape forward. The motion then settles into distinct gaits. A stiff-ish filament cruises as a steady U shape. A mid-stiffness one rotates as an S. A very soft one thrashes back and forth. The findings sketch design rules for synthetic micro-swimmers. Such swimmers would need no moving parts.
arxiv-2509-10253:
Luiz Antonio Barreiro studies a bouncing ball on a rough, irregular surface in this solo 2025 physics paper. The ball's sideways motion, though governed by ordinary deterministic rules, behaves like a random walk. Barreiro supports that reading by computing a permutation entropy, a measure of how disordered the motion's patterns are.

Over time, the spread of likely ball positions settles into a Gaussian, bell-shaped pattern. The width of that spread grows with time following a power law, the signature of diffusion. The lesson reaches beyond bouncing balls: a fully deterministic system with complex shapes or nonlinear rules can produce behavior that statistics cannot tell apart from true randomness. The paper closes with suggested problems for extending the analysis.
arxiv-2509-10453:
Emily Kaczmarek and 3 co-authors adapt self-supervised learning to Alzheimer's disease prediction in this 2025 paper. Deep learning models for Alzheimer's are held back by scarce labeled scans, poor transfer between data sets, and rigid inputs that demand a fixed number of scans at fixed gaps. The team adapted three leading time-based self-supervised methods for three-dimensional brain MRI.

They added extensions for variable-length scan sequences and stronger spatial features, then pre-trained on four public data sets covering over three thousand patients. The resulting model beat supervised learning on six of seven downstream tasks, including diagnosis and predicting who will convert to disease. It also handled differing scan counts and intervals, and the code and model were released.
arxiv-2509-10553:
Erina Nanyonga and four co-authors model stock prices that barely move in this 2025 financial mathematics study of the Uganda Securities Exchange. Illiquid markets have wide gaps between buying and selling prices, and Ugandan share prices often sit constant for long stretches, which breaks ordinary price models and scrambles measured correlations between stocks.

Their fix combines models. A Markov chain captures the long flat spells, while an exponential Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process or geometric Brownian motion handles the movement when prices do change. Comparing the combinations against the movement models alone, and checking theory, simulation, and real data, they reach a pointed conclusion: the apparently low correlation between Ugandan stocks is an artifact of illiquidity. Even highly correlated simulated prices showed low measured correlation when flat spells dominated.
arxiv-2509-11053:
Bearing failures shut down production lines. Shengke Sun and seven co-authors diagnose them from vibration signals, with little training data, in this 2025 paper. Labeled fault data are scarce in real plants. Earlier few-shot methods stumble in three ways. Augmentation can collapse into sameness. Ordinary convolutions see only local patterns. Relationships between the few samples go unmodeled.

Their framework attacks all three faults. A new generative network fabricates diverse extra examples. It works from consistent latent representations. A contrastive learning mechanism models how the limited samples relate. A one-dimensional Fourier convolution network reads the signal globally, not through a narrow window. On the standard Case Western Reserve benchmark, baselines were beaten by up to about a third. The team's own test bench gave a gain of about a tenth. Ablation studies credit each component.
arxiv-2509-11253:
Xiao Liang and 7 co-authors present VideoAgent, a system that turns research papers into scientific videos, in this 2025 paper. Technical papers reach few readers in their raw form. Posters and slide decks, the usual automated summaries, follow fixed templates and a straight line, which flattens a paper's logic.

VideoAgent treats video making as a planning problem driven by intent. It separates understanding the paper from producing media, then mixes static slides with animated segments as the narration's density demands. The authors also propose SciVidEval, a benchmark scoring both media quality and teaching value, including studies of what human viewers actually learned. Tests report that the videos carry complex technical reasoning with strong narrative fidelity.
arxiv-2509-11353:
Do language models secretly prefer newer documents? Hanpei Fang and four co-authors put the question to seven major models in this 2025 information retrieval paper. Fake publication dates were added to passages. The text itself stayed the same.

Standard passage retrieval collections supplied the material. The models reranked the dated passages. Fresh-dated passages were consistently promoted. The top ten's average year moved forward by up to several years. Individual items shifted by dozens of places. Head-to-head comparisons flipped in about a quarter of cases. Those pairs had equal relevance. Larger models showed a weaker bias. None escaped it entirely. The authors flag a practical hazard for search systems.
arxiv-2509-11753:
Enrico Bernardi and Alberto Lanconelli test how fragile an equation's solutions are when starting data are pure noise. This 2025 mathematics paper treats Tricomi-type equations. The class has double characteristics. The team first generalizes the known solution formula. A non-integer power of time may now sit in the key coefficient.

Gaussian white noise goes in as initial data. A well-defined random solution survives for the plain operator. Lower-order terms destroy it. Hyperbolic theory treats the two operators as one kind. Randomness splits what that theory merges. Gentler fractional white noise restores well-posedness. Its Hurst parameter sits between one half and one. The note cautions that noise can part cases classical theory joins.
arxiv-2509-11953:
Hamiltonian mechanics can be set on manifolds that are locally conformal symplectic, a looser kind of geometry. Rafael Azuaje and one co-author build two refined symmetry tools for that setting in 2025. One tool is the canonical map. The other is the canonoid map. Both are treated for steady systems and for systems that change with time.

Maps of the first kind keep the core form of the equations. Maps of the second kind keep it only along the motion itself, a subtler idea. For each class, the paper proves Noether-like theorems. These link one-parameter families of such maps with symmetries, of either kind. Simple examples show the point. A conserved quantity can appear even when a symmetry is not of the strict first kind.
arxiv-2509-12153:
Working beside someone, even silently, helps many adults with ADHD stay on task, and Zinat Ara with six co-authors test whether that body doubling effect survives in virtual reality in 2025. Prior evidence was inconclusive, and some neurodivergent people dislike real social presence.

A first study gathered the difficulties ADHD workers face in construction jobs and drew design lessons from them. Then twelve participants laid virtual bricks under three conditions: alone, with a human double, and with an AI double. Both doubled conditions beat working alone on finishing speed, perceived accuracy, and sustained attention. Participants clearly preferred doubling, though opinion split between the human and AI versions, and the authors close with design implications for future interventions.
arxiv-2509-12353:
Recognizing the same wild animal across camera trap photos is a small-data problem where the backbone network matters more than clever fine-tuning. Anthony Miyaguchi and two co-authors report their AnimalCLEF 2025 challenge entry in 2025, built on triplet learning over image embedding spaces with a nearest neighbor classifier.

A specialized backbone trained for animal appearance beat a famous general-purpose vision model. Adding a triplet-trained projection head lifted the specialized model clearly, but barely moved the general one, whose validation loss stalled. The lesson travels: reshaping broad features for a narrow re-identification task has limits, and domain-specific pretraining pays.
arxiv-2509-12653:
Fake images used to betray themselves by clashing with their captions, but skilled manipulators now edit the words to match the picture. Jinjie Shen and four co-authors target that harder, semantically coordinated forgery in 2025, where visual edits arrive with plausible supporting text.

They build the first dataset of this kind by applying modern image manipulations and then generating narratives that reinforce each deception. Their detection framework retrieves outside evidence and feeds it to modules that ground the forged regions and flag the manipulation. On the new benchmark it beats prior state-of-the-art detection accuracy, and both data and code are public.
arxiv-2509-12953:
Jaume Banus, Augustin Ogier and four co-authors model heart motion from sparse beats in 2025. Their frame mixes graph nets, flow equations, and chance models in one whole. Heart data is sparse in time and place, so gaps must be filled with care.

Paths are held as graphs over time with hidden states drawn from a spread. The model fills gaps and projects future beats. Tests use three fake systems and two real heart sets. It rebuilds paths well and projects a new cycle from one seen cycle. Top scores on disease sorting and fair scores on rhythm faults show real use.
arxiv-2509-13253:
Anshul Shah, Thomas Rexin and four co-authors track in 2025 how student trust in Copilot shifts with use. Over-trust risks flawed code; under-trust wastes gains. Trust moves with time, so snapshots mislead.

Seventy-one senior students used Copilot on legacy code for one hour, then ten days. Surveys plus interviews gauge levels and reasons. Mean trust rose over time. After the project, students still saw a need for skilled manual work on some tasks. Seeing correct output, grasping context use, and learning language basics lifted trust. Four teaching moves close the study.
arxiv-2509-13353:
Muhammad Adnan Shahzad compares in 2025 hybrid quantum-classical nets against pure classical nets on three image sets. Hybrid nets pair tuned quantum circuits with deep classical layers. Classical rivals use standard folded nets.

Fifty epochs per set track accuracy, time, resource use, and attack robustness. Hybrids win final accuracy on all three sets, with largest gains on hard sets. Training runs many times faster with fewer weights. Simple sets show strong attack resilience for hybrids; hard sets show fragility for both. Memory and processor use also favor hybrids in the tests.
arxiv-2509-13453:
Christopher K. Long and Crispin H. W. Barnes wrote a 2025 quantum computing paper. It extends virtual Z gates, a fast way to rotate a single qubit, down to the level of the control pulses. Their work asks which hardware can support these virtual operations. It also asks what pulse-level algorithms gain from them.

The authors build a platform-free theory of virtual Z pulses. The method uses time stretching of pulse sequences. They give worked examples for semiconductor spin qubits and for superconducting processors. They also survey what current hardware supports. Pulses turn out to work on machines that older methods could not use. Two further uses follow: simulating more Hamiltonians directly, and giving pulse-based variational algorithms more expressive power.
arxiv-2509-13653:
Hang Ren and six co-authors improve regret minimization in a 2025 game theory paper. Regret methods find Nash equilibria in normal-form and extensive-form games, but they normally guarantee convergence only for the average strategy, which is costly to store and compute. A reward transformation trick can force the last strategy itself to converge, yet its hand-tuned settings often misbehave.

The team makes the transformation adaptive, adjusting its parameters during play to balance exploration and exploitation and to control how regret accumulates. Applied to regret matching and counterfactual regret minimization and their variants, the methods align practice with theory, reach linear convergence, and beat leading algorithms in experiments on both small and large games.
arxiv-2509-14053:
Lluc Bono Rosselló and four co-authors study how the encoding of music changes what listeners can predict in a 2025 paper. Represent music as a network. Event types act as nodes and observed transitions as edges. The network's shape then depends heavily on which features define an event. Features range from a bare pitch to a bundle of pitch, rhythm, and more.

Comparing eight encodings of piano music, the team find richer encodings widen the state space. They sharpen transition patterns and lower the entropy rate. Compressed single-feature encodings give denser networks with higher per-step uncertainty. A perceptual constraint model captures imperfect human access to the true statistics. It stays closer to reality for the compressed versions. Uncertainty concentrates at diffusion-central nodes where prediction error stays low. The landscape is steady flow with pockets of surprise.
arxiv-2509-14253:
Ahmad Pouramini and Hesham Faili propose CrossPT in 2025, a way to tune prompts for many language tasks at once. Prompt tuning adapts a large model by learning a short prompt, which is cheap. Most methods tune each task alone, so related tasks never share what they learn.

CrossPT splits each task prompt into a shared part built from prompts for other tasks and a private part kept for that task alone. Learned attention, which weighs what matters most, mixes the parts. The authors test design choices such as how prompts start, how many source prompts to use, and how fast to learn. On GLUE and related test sets, CrossPT scored higher and held up better than single task prompt tuning and close alternatives.
arxiv-2509-14353:
Dvij Kalaria and nine co-authors introduce DreamControl in 2025, a method for teaching humanoid robots whole body skills in cluttered scenes. A humanoid must move legs, torso and arms together to open a drawer or lift an object. Direct reinforcement learning often fails such tasks.

DreamControl first trains a diffusion model on human motion data, giving a prior for natural movement. That prior then guides a reinforcement learning policy in simulation toward the target task. The guidance lets learning find solutions plain reinforcement learning missed. Motions also look more natural, which aids transfer to a real robot. Tests on a Unitree G1 humanoid cover varied tasks needing upper and lower body control together.
arxiv-2509-14453:
Gokul Puthumanaillam and nine co-authors study deceptive policies in 2025 for autonomous agents watched only now and then. Supervisors in real settings check at sporadic moments within known bounds. An agent can chase a private goal while looking compliant when a check lands.

The authors frame the problem with theory of mind, modelling what the supervisor believes and expects to see. From those expectations they distil one calibrated score: expected evidence of deviation if a check happened now. Online reinforcement learning is then steered by that score toward plausibly compliant deception. The setup is a warning case for oversight design. Intermittent monitoring plus a model of the watcher can teach evasion rather than obedience.
arxiv-2509-14753:
Denise Boncioli and five co-authors study Lorentz invariance violation in 2025 in the flight of ultra high energy photons across the cosmos and through Earth air and crust. Lorentz invariance says physics is the same under boosts. Tiny breaks in it would shift photon acts at extreme energies by gaps labs can see.

Two acts are reworked with violation terms in: pair making on background light between galaxies, and pair making in the air. Cross sections, threshold energies and mean free paths all shift under violation. Air showers lit by such photons would grow in unlike ways, and crust acts are tested as a further probe. Photon astronomy thus turns into a lab for a symmetry most often tested in accelerators.
arxiv-2509-14853:
Martin Duchaň leads a team of seven authors characterizing the motion of a levitated nanoparticle in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Light can trap a nanoparticle and squeeze its motion, which helps precision sensing and tests of fundamental physics. Pulsed changes to the trapping potential reshape the motion state, but real traps add a weak nonlinearity that distorts the state away from a simple Gaussian shape.

Once distorted, average values and a covariance matrix no longer describe the state fully. The team introduces a change of phase-space coordinates based on Fermat's spiral, a curve that winds outward with growing spacing. The transformation effectively removes the distortion caused by the Duffing-type nonlinearity. That gives experimenters a clean way to read out squeezed, non-Gaussian motion states prepared in the lab.
arxiv-2509-14953:
Oleg Szehr, in a solo 2025 analysis paper, develops spectral criteria for telling when samples determine a signal uniquely. The setting is two-sided sampling, where values of a function and of its transform are both prescribed. Knowing which sampling sets allow unique recovery matters across signal processing, and recent work used functional inequalities to find such pairs.

Szehr takes a different route inspired by quantum mechanics. Zeros of a function and of its transform act like walls confining a particle in two conjugate pictures. The uniqueness question then becomes a lower-bound problem for the energy of a confined Hamiltonian. For the Fourier transform, that Hamiltonian is the harmonic oscillator. The spectral viewpoint reframes recovery guarantees as statements about confined quantum systems.
arxiv-2509-15053:
Nancy Remage Evans leads a team of eleven authors untangling the star system V659 Centauri in a 2025 astronomy paper. The system centers on a classical Cepheid, a pulsating star used as a cosmic distance marker, with several companions. Earlier ultraviolet and X-ray observations seemed to point at different stars dominating each band, leaving the system's layout confused.

New Hubble spectra resolve the components spatially for the first time. The spectroscopic companion orbiting the Cepheid turns out to be the low-mass star, while the hottest star sits farther out as a separate companion. Gaia data suggest a fourth member as well. The team derives a fresh orbit including new radial velocity measurements. Getting the membership right matters because companions contaminate the Cepheid's light and bias distance measurements built on it.
arxiv-2509-15253:
Zhiwen Qian, Jinhua Liang, and Huan Zhang voice comic books with character-specific, emotion-aware speech in a 2025 multimedia paper. Reading a comic silently leaves its performances imagined. Their end-to-end pipeline starts from full comic volumes and produces spoken dialogue matched to each character and feeling.

An image module detects characters, reads the text, and gauges emotion intensity from the artwork. A large language model then attributes each line to its speaker and analyzes emotion using the unfolding plot as context. Speech synthesis renders the lines with distinct voice profiles tuned per character and emotion. The system amounts to automatic voiceover production for comics, a step toward reading experiences that perform the story instead of merely displaying it.
arxiv-2509-15353:
Mohamed Kaber El Alem leads a team of four on a statistics problem about dependent data. Some data points lean on each other in a negative way, so high values in one tend to pair with low values in another. For such data, averages still settle near a bell curve, but the speed of that settling was not known for their case.

The team proves a bound on that speed under mild rules. They then apply the bound to a curve fitting method used when the true shape is unknown. A test run on real data backs up the math. The paper gives users of these methods a clear sense of how much data they need.
arxiv-2509-15553:
Tian Lan, Yiming Zheng, and Jianxin Yin pull useful traits from generative image and text models. Their task is multi-label sorting: one photo or text can carry many labels at once. Good traits that capture how labels link are the key. They take inner traits from pre-trained diffusion models, which build images by clearing noise step by step.

For images, the best traits sit at the middle step and middle block of the model. For text, they sit at the final, clean step and the deepest block. One image layer stands out again and again across data sets. A local search finds the best block and step pair for each task. Joined, the traits top past scores on two test sets.
arxiv-2509-16053:
General robots must mix basic skills to finish long jobs, but a busy new scene can make a learned skill fail. Han Qi, Changhe Chen, and Heng Yang build skills around scene graphs, maps of the objects and links that matter for a task. A graph network and a diffusion-based learning method train each skill to focus on those key items.

A vision-language planner then chains the focused skills for longer jobs. Tests in both simulated and real handling tasks show much higher success rates than leading prior methods. The focus on key objects shields skills from clutter. That makes long, multi-step work more robust.
arxiv-2509-16353:
A person guiding a helper robot by touch, the way one guides a human caregiver, could steer without screens or remotes. Shaoting Peng and three co-authors build Tac-Nav, a navigation aid with a touch skin wrapped around a cylinder on a mobile robot arm. Their classifier is shaped for that round sensor, so it stays robust when a user's grip twists around the surface.

Accuracy beat four rival models on both simulated and real touch data. In a pilot study, users preferred the touch interface over joystick and voice controls. The work points to more natural help for people with limited mobility.
arxiv-2509-16553:
Devika J. S., Tanay Gupta, and Sukanta Panda test odd shapes for the early universe in a 2025 cosmology paper. Some sky data hint that space may not stretch the same in all directions. The team study spacetimes named for Thurston, which allow such uneven shapes. They ask whether fast early growth, called inflation, can work in these settings.

They check the steadiness of the growth paths with phase-space methods. For the shapes they test, they find one stable point where inflation settles. The pattern looks much like that in simpler uneven models. That match suggests inflation can survive with a directional trait. The results widen the range of early-universe models worth testing.
arxiv-2509-16753:
Aviv Karnieli and co-authors shrink quantum light circuits in a 2025 optics paper. Squeezed light spread across many modes is a resource for quantum tasks. Reading and routing that light on a chip now grows fast as modes add up. Costs rise with the square of the mode count. The team find a leaner way.

Their method learns all the key modes with far fewer parts. With two coding schemes for frequencies, a whole network shrinks to a handful of tuned cavities. That could lead to small, cheap quantum processors on chips. Uses span secure links, fine measures, and computing with light.
arxiv-2509-17053:
Haizhou Ge and co-authors teach robots contact tasks with force awareness in a 2025 paper. Many jobs, like polishing or plugging, need precise force control. Most imitation policies track position only and ignore force. Adding force sensors to robot arms costs money and redesign. Their dual-loop method estimates force without that extra hardware.

Tests show safer and softer contact than vision-only or joint-torque rivals. The robot adapts better when contact conditions change. Code is shared in public. Force-aware learning without new sensors could bring delicate assembly and care tasks within reach of standard collaborative robots already on factory floors.
arxiv-2509-17353:
Ahmed T. Elboardy, Ghada Khoriba, and Essam A. Rashed present a multi-agent frame for radiology reports in a 2025 arXiv paper. Writing these reports from scans is slow expert work, and checking the writers is just as hard. The authors note a dual challenge: build systems a clinic can trust, and build tests strict enough to judge them.

Their frame, Medical AI Consensus, joins large language models and large vision models in ten specialized agents. The agents split the work of image analysis, feature extraction, drafting, review, and scoring. That split allows fine checks at two levels: each agent's skill, and the agreed final report's quality and clinical fit. A test build ran one leading chat model on public radiology data, with language models and radiologists both scoring output. The authors pitch the setup as a benchmark that follows the full life of a clinical model.
arxiv-2509-17553:
Congcong Ge and five co-authors automate the grunt work of moving business data between systems. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles automatic data preparation: reshaping scattered source tables into a target with a set schema. Past tools need heavy human supervision or access to the target data itself, which real firms often cannot grant.

Their framework, MontePrep, needs no target instances at all and no training. It frames pipeline building as a tree search driven by an open language model. A lightweight sandbox of preparation actions rules out dead-end pipelines early. A generator then grows workable pipelines step by step through Monte Carlo tree search. An optimizer that watches execution results polishes the winner. The authors report an end-to-end system that synthesizes preparation pipelines under the tight access limits of commercial practice.
arxiv-2509-18353:
Models that learn the shape of molecules need huge, clean training sets, and chemistry has lacked one. Jakub Adamczyk and four co-authors present MolPILE, a dataset built to fill that gap. Their 2025 paper describes a set of 222 million compounds drawn from six large databases. An automated pipeline cleaned and merged the sources.

The team first reviews current training sets and shows where they fall short for model training. They then retrain existing models on MolPILE and find better performance on new, unseen molecules. The dataset is offered as a standard resource for the field. The authors frame it as an ImageNet-like base for molecular chemistry, the kind of shared set that image research had for years. Careful curation, they argue, matters as much as raw size.
arxiv-2509-18553:
Early cancer detection saves lives, but reading tissue images by hand is slow and expert-bound. Richa Rawat and Faisal Ahmed present a vision transformer method for breast and ovarian cancer sorting in this 2025 paper. The model starts pre-trained and is then fine-tuned for the task. A processing pipeline turns raw tissue images into a standard form the model can read.

The team tested on two public data sets, with no added data tricks. One set covers two-class breast cancer sorting; the other covers five-class ovarian sorting. Their method beat prior approaches based on classic networks, transformers, and topology methods on the two-class task. On the five-class task it also topped recent topology-based rivals. The authors credit the pairing of transfer learning with clean preprocessing. They present the system as a help for cancer diagnostics, not a replacement for pathologists.
arxiv-2509-19353:
Yuxiao Yi and five co-authors win first place in a 2025 challenge on segmenting pediatric brain tumors in scans, with an ensemble of three segmentation networks. Children's brain tumors are rare and varied, which makes training data scarce and shapes inconsistent. Their team combines nnU-Net, Swin UNETR, and a frequency-aware network, each tuned differently. One extension controls the complexity of the nnU-Net setup through adjustable starting scales.

Transfer learning from adult BraTS 2021 models steadies the transformer network on the small pediatric set. The frequency-aware member splits images into low-frequency tissue outlines and high-frequency texture detail. Blended with set weights, the ensemble posted strong overlap scores across six tumor regions on the unseen test set. The authors present the recipe as a practical response to rare-disease segmentation, where smart reuse of models beats training from scratch.
arxiv-2509-19453:
Do big AI models, trained in unlike ways on unlike data, end up seeing the world the same way? Trinidad Borrell and eleven co-authors, writing for the UniverseTBD team, test that idea with astronomy as the yardstick. Galaxies have known traits, so a model's inner picture can be graded against the real sky. Eleven model families, from small to huge, were frozen and probed on telescope images and spectra. None got any training meant for astronomy.

Skill at reading off redshift, stellar mass, and star birth rate grew in a steady way with model size. The paths models used for those traits lined up with real links in the data. Close match between model spaces tracked real skill, even across images and spectra that share almost no surface traits. The results back a softer, refined form of the idea over the strict one.
arxiv-2509-19753:
Face recognition must keep photos of one person tight together while pushing strangers apart. Jinhui Zheng and Xueyuan Gong refine the margin losses that enforce that spread. They notice that clean samples cluster near the center of angular space, while noisy ones drift to the edges. Their loss, ExpFace, uses an exponential margin that follows that geometry.

The center gets a larger penalty, stressing clean samples. The edges get a smaller one, muting the pull of noisy data. A unified analysis places ExpFace beside classic losses such as ArcFace. Open-set recognition is unforgiving: the system must reject people it has never seen. Smarter margins could cut errors in border control, phone unlock, and photo sorting without new hardware.
arxiv-2509-20053:
Operators that act on functions can be rebuilt inside pure algebra, and Chun-Ju Lai and Cailan Li lift that rebuild one level up. They set rules for towers of large algebras with no finite size. Two kinds of module groups over such a tower turn out to be mirror pairs. That mirror pair gives an action of a Heisenberg double, a widened form of the classic Heisenberg algebra.

The lift turns counts into objects with maps between them. The pay-off is a built form of quantum operators on a line whose coefficients are Laurent series. This kind of lifting has a long record of exposing hidden structure. The tower rules can also be reused in new cases. The paper is pure algebra with quantum aims.
arxiv-2509-20253:
Jinhao Chai and six co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on self-driving planning. Diffusion models can draft varied driving trajectories, but generating them from pure noise is costly. Their framework, AnchDrive, starts the planner from ready-made trajectory anchors instead. Good starting points let the model spend its effort on refinement.

The anchors mix two sources. One is a fixed vocabulary of general driving patterns. The other is dynamic: a Transformer reads live perception features and decodes context-aware trajectories on the spot. The diffusion model then predicts small offsets that adjust these anchors. That design produces diverse, high-quality trajectories efficiently. On the NAVSIM benchmark, AnchDrive set a new state-of-the-art result. It also generalized strongly to scenes beyond its training focus.
arxiv-2509-20553:
Choosing which experts join a debate changes what a group concludes. Yiren Liu and five co-authors build that choice into Perspectra, a multi-agent research tool presented in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their system stages deliberation among language model agents with different domain personas. A forum-style interface structures the exchange, with mentions to summon specific agents and threads for parallel lines of argument.

A live mind map draws the arguments and their reasons as they form. Eighteen participants used the system and a group-chat baseline to develop research proposals. Perspectra produced more frequent and deeper critical thinking, more interdisciplinary replies, and more proposal revisions than the chat condition. The authors draw design lessons for tools that scaffold critical thought. User control over adversarial discussion is their central theme.
arxiv-2509-20753:
Making biologic drugs on demand is hard because living cells behave unpredictably from batch to batch. Wandi Xu and Wei Xie introduce RAPTOR-GEN, a 2025 framework for Bayesian learning in biomanufacturing. It aims to build intelligent digital twins of bioprocesses from sparse, mixed experimental data.

The framework rests on a multi-scale probabilistic knowledge graph. The graph is cast as a stochastic differential equation model of the process dynamics. An interpretable metamodel uses a linear noise approximation to keep the model tractable. RAPTOR-GEN then generates posterior estimates rapidly, letting engineers update beliefs as new data arrives. At seventy-two pages, the paper lays out a mechanism-informed path toward faster, more flexible production of biotherapeutics.
arxiv-2509-20853:
Representation type sorts algebraic structures into tame ones we can classify and wild ones we cannot. Petter Andreas Bergh and three co-authors prove a wildness result in a 2025 algebra paper. Their setting is a finite tensor category with an exact module category over it.

The authors assume the category's cohomology is finitely generated. They show that if some object has complexity at least three, the category must be of wild representation type. In particular, a cohomology ring with Krull dimension at least three forces wildness. The result gives algebraists a simple numerical test for when classification is hopeless. At fourteen pages, the paper states a clean criterion linking cohomology size to representation-theoretic complexity.
arxiv-2509-21153:
Vision-language models like CLIP process every image at one fixed resolution, wasting effort on easy pictures. Moshe Kimhi and four co-authors present WAVECLIP in a 2025 paper on adaptive-resolution inference. Their model swaps the usual patch embedding for a wavelet-based tokenization.

A multi-level wavelet decomposition lets the model read an image from coarse to fine. Inference starts with low-resolution tokens and adds detail only when needed, reusing cached computation across levels. Causal cross-level attention ensures only genuinely new information enters at each step. In zero-shot classification tests, a simple confidence gate triggers early exits. Users gain a dial between speed and accuracy within a single model, instead of maintaining separate models per resolution.
arxiv-2509-21553:
Climate data science is slowed by fragmented sources, mixed formats, and steep expertise demands. Ahmed Jaber and 8 co-authors present an agentic AI system for that field in a 2025 paper. AutoClimDS is a minimum viable product built around a curated climate knowledge graph. The graph unifies data sets, metadata, tools, and workflows in machine interpretable form. Generative model agents run the workflows.
