Agents interpret natural language queries and discover data automatically. They acquire data programmatically and run end to end climate analyses in the cloud. A key result reproduces published figures and analyses from natural language instructions alone. The full workflow, from dataset selection to modelling, completes automatically. The authors aim to widen participation and improve reproducibility.
arxiv-2509-22053:
Knowledge distillation trains a small student model on the soft labels of a large teacher, and those soft labels carry more than the right answer. Hua Yuan, Ning Xu, Xin Geng, and Yong Rui examine what makes that extra information rich in this 2025 paper. Samples of the same class vary in appearance, and that variety helps the student generalize. Yet teachers are usually trained to hit the plain labels, ignoring the variety inside each class.

The authors add a contrastive loss inside each class during teacher training, so the teacher's soft labels preserve more of that inner variety. Used plainly, the loss destabilized training and slowed it down, so they blend in a margin loss to steady it. Their theory shows the loss provably widens the spread within classes in the right way. Experiments confirm the method improves distillation.
arxiv-2509-22353:
Can a world model learn a new setting just from context, with no retraining? Fan Wang and 10 co-authors study that skill in models that predict how a scene will change. They split the skill into two parts. One part spots which setting the model faces. The other part learns the rules of that setting from the prompt.

The team derives error bounds for both parts. Tests then confirm that both parts do occur in practice. Long context and varied training settings help the skill grow. The bounds show why those two factors matter most for models that adapt on the fly.
arxiv-2509-22453:
Alessio Traficante and 3 co-authors present Hyper, a Python tool that measures faint compact sources in sky maps. The tool works on far-infrared, submillimeter, and millimeter images, where sources often overlap. It finds sources by filtering out slow background trends. It then fits the local background with smooth curves and models each source with a two-dimensional Gaussian shape.

Several sources can be fit at once, which separates blended ones. This Python version keeps the logic of the older IDL tool but runs faster and is easier to configure. It can also clean the background slice by slice in three-dimensional data cubes. That helps studies of spectral lines and continuum emission.
arxiv-2509-22653:
Chih Yao Hu and 9 co-authors steer drones by pointing at pictures, not by predicting actions as text. Their framework, See Point Fly, is training-free and builds on vision-language models. It can follow any free-form instruction in any setting. The key shift is to treat action choice as a two-dimensional grounding task on the camera image.

The model breaks a vague command into steps, marking waypoints on the image each round. Waypoint plus travel distance becomes a three-dimensional move command. The system adjusts distance on the fly and runs in closed loop, so it can chase moving targets. It set a new record on a drone navigation benchmark and beat baselines in real-world tests.
arxiv-2509-22753:
Nicolae Cotfas maps the states for which a discrete position-momentum rule holds. In continuous quantum systems, position and momentum obey a famous commutation relation. For a qudit, a system with a finite but large number of levels, a discrete version holds approximately for a large part of the pure states. Cotfas explores that set of states in detail.

He shows it contains a family of discrete Gaussian states indexed by a continuous parameter. It also holds certain discrete coherent states. Various discrete Hermite-Gauss states belong as well, defined either as eigenstates of a discrete harmonic oscillator or via discrete creation and annihilation operators. The results suggest routes to prepare some of these states in experiments.
arxiv-2509-22853:
Irsyad Adam and 5 co-authors tune language models on the protein profiles of single cancer patients. Protein data shows the molecular marks that drive how each tumor grows, resists drugs, and varies. Large language models can reason across data types, but this task lacked both training data and a fitting design. The team built a data set with hundreds of thousands of open-ended examples drawn from the largest national cancer proteomics study.

Their model, KRONOS, lays out each patient's network of molecular links as a graph for the language model to read. It did well on sorting tumors by type, tracing how they change over time, and calling tumor stage from protein data alone.
arxiv-2509-23253:
Deep spiking networks usually lean on normalization, a scaling step brains do not use in that form. Peiyu Liu, Jianhao Ding, and Zhaofei Yu swap it for lateral inhibition, a circuit trait from the cortex. Their layers split into two neuron groups, one that excites and one that calms. The calm side sets how lively cells are and how much they gain. Two tricks steady the training.

One balances the two inputs at the start, with gain control built in. The other splits the training signal flow from the forward pass. Across data sets and designs, deep spiking nets trained in a stable way. Scores stayed close to rivals. The setup also serves as a test bed for cortex study.
arxiv-2509-23653:
Diffusion language models write by unmasking tokens, but a wrong token, once placed, usually stays forever. Zemin Huang and 3 co-authors give their model, RemeDi, a way to take tokens back. At each step it predicts both token distributions and a confidence score per token. Low-confidence tokens get remasked and can be resampled later with richer context around them.

Training teaches the skill in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on detecting and remasking errors, then reinforcement learning over full generation paths. On several data sets, RemeDi reached the best results among open-source diffusion language models. The authors present remasking as a core mechanism, not a patch.
arxiv-2509-24253:
Systems that answer questions from both images and text can fail in ways that flat accuracy scores hide. Yuelyu Ji and 2 co-authors built MRAG-Suite, a diagnostic platform for visual retrieval-augmented generation. It unites several multimodal benchmarks and filters questions by difficulty and ambiguity, two factors past evaluations ignored.

Under hard or ambiguous queries, accuracy dropped sharply and hallucinations stood out. A companion tool, MM-RAGChecker, checks claims one by one to locate the faults. The platform thus points builders to the exact stage where a system breaks. The authors offer it as a guide for improving visual question answering with retrieved evidence.
arxiv-2509-24353:
Video generation usually treats a clip as a stack of frame features, which forces heavy attention across time. Yixuan Ren and 4 co-authors built NeRV-Diffusion, which instead generates the weights of a network that represents the whole video. A hypernetwork tokenizer first encodes raw video into a latent that serves as those weights. A diffusion transformer then denoises in that weight space.

Tricks to keep the weights well-shaped include sharing the bottleneck latent across layers and reworking how weights are assigned. Training adds noise-aware loss weighting and scheduled sampling. Quality topped prior representation-based models and neared leading standard models on two real benchmarks. The smooth weight space also allows clean blends between frames and videos.
arxiv-2509-24553:
Axion dark matter may push on fermion spins like a faint oscillating magnetic field, far too weak for standard sensors. Christina Gao and 3 co-authors propose to focus that axion wind with ferrimagnetic flux concentrators. The concentrators amplify the fake field into a genuine magnetic field that precision magnetometers can measure.

Their sensor uses a levitated ferromagnet in its libration mode, reaching sub-femtotesla sensitivity. That setup could detect axion-electron couplings below the reach implied by current spin-precession methods, across a wide band of low frequencies. The scheme widens the experimental options for a hunt that has been limited by the signal's extreme weakness.
arxiv-2510-00453:
Xia Huang and Dong Ye wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on sharp forms of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and their stability. The principle limits how sharply a function's position and momentum can both be known. Sharp versions come with best constants and known equality cases. The authors summarize a linearization method for proving such inequalities and judging their stability.

Stability asks how near a function must sit to the extremal shape when the bound nearly binds. Combining their method with spherical harmonics and Hardy bounds, they revisit two families of estimates. In dimension four they settle a conjecture of Cazacu, Flynn, and Lam on the hydrogen uncertainty principle. They also improve recent two- and three-dimensional estimates from other authors. For a related pair of stability estimates, they identify the best constants and the extremal functions exactly.
arxiv-2510-00553:
Yuchen Cai and eight colleagues published this 2025 paper on a hidden simplicity inside reinforcement learning for language models. Training runs are long and expensive, and nobody knew how the model's weights actually move. The team tracked parameter updates across eight models and seven training algorithms. Two striking patterns emerged from the measurements.

First, nearly all reasoning gains live in a single dominant direction of the update matrix. Keeping just that rank-one subspace recovers over ninety-nine percent of the improvement. Second, that direction drifts linearly through training, making it predictable from early checkpoints. Their plug-in, AlphaRL, extrapolates the final update from a short early window. It sped training by up to two and a half times in tests. Over ninety-six percent of the reasoning performance survived the shortcut, with no extra tuning required.
arxiv-2510-00753:
Nde and six co-authors quantify a projection-driven selection bias in galaxy cluster mass calibration in this 2025 arXiv paper on cosmology. Optical surveys find clusters by galaxy richness and weigh them with weak gravitational lensing. Halo shape and unrelated structure along the line of sight can boost both the richness and the lensing signal together. A richness-selected sample shows more lensing than its true mean mass warrants, and masses come out biased high.

Using two simulations, MiniUchuu and Cardinal, with galaxy models and cluster finders, the team ran mock calibrations. The bias overestimated lensing mass by roughly twenty to fifty percent, and it grew to twenty to eighty percent for large-scale lensing. High-redshift and low-richness clusters suffered most in the Cardinal runs. The authors call this the most damaging known systematic in optical cluster cosmology and urge every future analysis to model it.
arxiv-2510-00853:
March-Pons, Pastor-Satorras, and Miguel model collective decision-making with higher-order interactions in this 2025 arXiv paper on complex systems. Groups from insect colonies to robot swarms must converge on one of several equally good options. Classical contagion models let agents influence each other only in pairs, plus a dose of autonomous exploration. The authors ask whether group-level influence changes the outcome when no option is objectively better.

Simulations and mean-field analysis give a sharp answer. Pairwise communication alone can deadlock the group, split forever between the options. Adding higher-order interactions breaks the symmetry and lets consensus form. Autonomous behaviour matters alongside, since uncommitted agents who explore independently keep feeding the process fresh commitments. The balance among the three ingredients decides whether a stalemate or a decision emerges. The authors suggest the same logic should inform decision protocols for artificial swarms.
arxiv-2510-00953:
Oliva and Tinjala model financial markets as an interpretable probabilistic state machine in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantitative finance. Market behaviour cycles through regimes such as expansion, contraction, crisis, and recovery, and one bell curve describes none of them well. The authors cluster historical returns using momentum and risk features measured over several time horizons. The clusters become the market states, labelled by the regime they resemble.

A transition matrix between states turns the clustering into a state machine that evolves day by day. Sampling from it generates a return distribution built as a mixture of Gaussians, one per state, weighted by state frequency. Across random assets and periods the benchmark beat the traditional normal model at matching real return statistics, including skewness and kurtosis. Traders can also watch state probabilities as live indicators. The authors stress the framework's interpretability alongside its accuracy.
arxiv-2510-01053:
Klemm and a large team use neutron scattering to untangle overlapping orders in the kagome metal FeGe, in this 2025 arXiv preprint on condensed matter physics. FeGe hosts a charge density wave inside an antiferromagnetic phase, and annealing can switch that charge order from strong to nearly absent. Below about sixty kelvin a spin density wave also appears, and how the three orders interact was unclear.

Inelastic neutron scattering found two distinct kinds of spin excitation below that temperature in both annealed sample types. Gapless excitations come from the incommensurate spin density wave, while gapped spin waves come from the antiferromagnetic order, and the two coexist. Charge order strongly shifts the magnetic onset temperature but affects the low-energy fluctuations only modestly. In the charge-ordered sample alone, the spin order also slightly distorts the kagome lattice in-plane.
arxiv-2510-01153:
Park, Liu, Zhou, and Osher solve optimal transport problems through the Hamilton-Jacobi equation in this 2025 arXiv paper on applied mathematics and machine learning. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to reshape one probability distribution into another, and it underlies tools from generative modelling to biomedical data analysis. Many neural solvers need adversarial training or numerical integration along the way, which adds cost and instability. The Hamilton-Jacobi viewpoint instead characterizes the optimal map through a single viscosity solution.

Using the method of characteristics, the authors derive closed-form transport maps in both directions, removing integration entirely. One neural network trains with a pure minimization loss built from those characteristics, so no adversarial stage remains. The framework covers a broad class of cost functions and supports class-conditional transport. Experiments on synthetic data and tasks such as colour transfer showed accuracy, scalability, and efficiency together.
arxiv-2510-01253:
Zhang, Zhou, and Liu teach an open language model to model and solve operations research problems with real solver tools. Optimization workflows demand translating word problems into mathematics, then computing exact answers. Closed commercial models raise privacy worries, and training from scratch is unaffordable.

A semi-automatic pipeline synthesizes diverse problem-and-answer pairs for fine-tuning. The tuned model writes solver calls instead of improvising arithmetic. On standard benchmarks it reached strong execution accuracy, beating same-size rivals. Unseen problem types still scored far above the strongest baseline, showing genuine generalization. Execution accuracy grades the solver's answer, not the model's prose. Semi-automatic synthesis keeps data costs far below hand-labeling. Privacy improves because an open model can run on premises. Tool augmentation converts reasoning into verifiable computation. Twenty-one points of zero-shot gain headline the result. Optimization leaves the textbook and enters chat.
arxiv-2510-01353:
Deshpande and co-authors at Patronus AI benchmark whether AI agents can remember and track state across the messy multi-platform life of a real organization. Conversation memory tests miss the enterprise reality of events scattered across chat, issue trackers, and code hosts. Their benchmark, Memtrack, interleaves asynchronous events from several platforms into one chronological timeline.

The streams carry noise, conflicts, and cross-references, plus code and file-system exploration. Metrics score correctness, efficiency, and redundancy of the agent's answers. Frontier models reasoned across large histories but faded on follow-up queries. Bolt-on memory systems brought only limited gains. Slack, Linear, and Git name the platforms braided together. Acquisition, selection, and conflict resolution are the memory skills tested. Expert design and agent synthesis jointly curated the scenarios. Tool-based memory access proved inefficient in the trials. Follow-up questions are where agent memory quietly dies.
arxiv-2510-01453:
Kasibatla and co-authors at UC San Diego generate graphical interfaces for command-line tools automatically, using the tools' own manuals as the blueprint. Shells expose power that menus hide, but syntax must be memorized and documentation scoured. Their system, GUIde, asks a language model to translate man pages into interface specifications.

An annotated grammar forms the bridge between manual text and widgets. The generated front ends present each command's options for discovery instead of recall. A corpus of real commands measured how completely the interfaces covered everyday tasks. Configuration files and other structured texts could follow the same route. Teletypes birthed the shell, and the shell outlived the revolution against it. Widgets and menus replace memorized flags with visible choices. Grammar generation by the model does the heavy translation work. A video demo and source code accompany the system description.
arxiv-2510-01953:
Buhrman, Galke, and Meichanetzidis define quantum advantage one instance at a time in this 2025 theory paper. Most comparisons ask whether quantum computers beat classical ones on whole problem classes. Real practice cares about single hard instances, where heuristics and average cases dominate. The authors adapt Kolmogorov complexity and instance complexity into quantum versions for that finer view.

An instance is queasy when its quantum instance complexity sits far below its classical one. Queasy instances are exactly where a quantum machine wins while classical methods struggle. A reduction from factoring proves that maximally queasy satisfiability instances exist, under standard assumptions. The team also shows that queasiness carries exponential algorithmic utility. The framework aims to guide the practical hunt for quantum advantage. It may also inspire new algorithm designs that target instance structure rather than worst cases.
arxiv-2510-02453:
Asawa and co-authors train a small advisor model that steers a giant black-box model per request. Their 2025 machine learning paper starts from a deployment reality. Hosted foundation models cannot be retrained by users. One fixed optimized prompt must serve every input and person. Advisor Models replace that fixed prompt with live guidance. A lightweight second model reads each new input first. It then issues steering instructions in plain language. Reinforcement learning trains the advisor from task rewards. The big model itself stays untouched behind its interface.

Tests covered reasoning tasks and personalization settings. Advisors beat static prompt optimizers across those domains. They learned quirks of each environment on their own. Trained advisors also transferred to other black-box models. Specialization did not destroy robustness on odd inputs. Learnable steering layers may sit atop many hosted services. Custom behavior no longer needs model ownership.
arxiv-2510-02753:
Retana-Montenegro images the fields around three X-shaped radio galaxies with a wide field technique. His astronomy paper uses the upgraded GMRT telescope in India. X-shaped galaxies sprout two pairs of radio lobes. One pair runs bright, the other faint like wings. Imaging ran at four hundred megahertz in Band-3. A modified extreme peeling calibration cleaned the wide views. That method corrects direction dependent distortions facet by facet. Other radio sources across the fields came out sharply too. Archival data at other frequencies joined the analysis.

Spectral ages dated the lobes and wings. The wings came out oldest in both dated galaxies. Past radio activity, not jets, built the wings. Spectral index maps steepened from lobes toward wings. That gradient matches aging electron populations. The calibration proved robust far from field centers. Other GMRT bands could reuse the approach. X shapes record a galaxy's radio history book.
arxiv-2510-02853:
Xu and co-authors propose a rule that links brain activity to the tasks it serves. It says population activity keeps the core math shape of its task. Their test case is the grid cell system. Grid cells help animals track position in space. Each cell fires on a hexagonal grid of spots. Together, the population traces a torus, a donut-shaped surface.

Two tasks explain that shape, the authors argue. Measuring distance calls for a flat geometric surface. Tracking a path calls for a group with a simple swap rule. Each demand on its own forces a torus layout. A small network built to hold that layout produced hexagonal firing fields. One popular guess failed the test. Matching shapes at every scale was not enough to make hexagons. The rule may guide both brain theory and machine learning design.
arxiv-2510-03053:
Chen, Jiang, and Wang prove limit theorems for a numerical scheme for random equations. The Milstein scheme samples a stochastic differential equation in small steps. Long runs of it settle toward a steady distribution. That discrete steady state differs slightly from the true one. Those averages serve as estimates of the steady state. A central limit theorem describes their random spread.

The spread forms a bell curve as runs grow long. Multiplicative noise drives the equation in their setup. Standard conditions on the coefficients keep things well behaved. Cramér-type bounds then grade medium-sized errors. Both plain and self-normalized versions are derived. Such bounds matter when samples are costly and runs are short. They tell users how much to trust a finite average. The results extend classic theory to this higher-order scheme. Milstein steps capture noise effects that Euler steps miss.
arxiv-2510-03153:
Suprabha and a large Heriot-Watt team improve teamwork among embodied AI agents. CoELA builds agents that share virtual spaces and talk to cooperate. Language models drive their reasoning and their messages. Raw prompting, though, breeds chatter, wasted moves, and garbled outputs. The team tested many models against many prompt designs. They sought the pairing that maximized joint task success. A speech layer was added to the system as well.

One pairing stood clearly above the rest. Explicit instructions joined with a structured prompt variant won. Redundant actions and fuzzy outputs both dropped sharply. Communication between agents grew shorter and cleaner. The best combo lifted efficiency notably for one model family. Gains reached about a fifth over the original system. A voice chat window now speaks the agents' dialogue aloud. Developers can hear turn-taking and alignment problems directly.
arxiv-2510-03353:
Gomes and colleagues present a 2025 survey paper on data sets of sonar images for underwater research. Sonar lets robots and scientists see where light and cameras fail. Progress in learning from sonar images stalls when good labeled data are scarce. The team mapped sets across five sonar types, from side scan to synthetic aperture systems. They also tracked which tasks each set supports, such as sorting, detection, and 3D rebuilding.

Their findings land in a master table and a timeline of releases. The survey shows data availability growing over the past five years. It also flags stubborn gaps, including clashing formats across sonar types and heavy acoustic noise. The authors do not rank set quality, since key calibration facts often go unreported. Instead, newcomers get a map of what exists and where new data would help most. That map should speed entry into underwater robotics and ocean monitoring work.
arxiv-2510-03553:
Rahman and Salam present a 2025 arXiv paper testing how language models decide when cultural values collide. Their benchmark, CCD-Bench, holds over two thousand dilemmas across seven life domains. Each dilemma offers ten anonymized answers, one for each of the ten GLOBE cultural clusters covering sixty two societies. A Latin square layout guards against order effects in the prompts. The team ran seventeen non reasoning models through the set and tallied their choices and reasons.

Models leaned hard toward Nordic and Germanic European answers, which drew about a fifth and an eighth of picks in the study. Eastern European and Middle Eastern options sat near the bottom. Although most rationales cited several value dimensions, they recycled a narrow pair again and again. Assertiveness and gender equality themes appeared in under three percent of rationales. The authors read this as a consensus seeking, progress centered outlook baked in by training.
arxiv-2510-03753:
Harland-Lang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper reassessing how high momentum fraction data shape the MSHT fit of proton structure. Parton distribution functions describe how a proton's momentum divides among its quarks and gluons, and every collider prediction leans on them. The high x region, where one parton carries most of the momentum, is constrained and sensitive. The team revisits target mass and higher twist corrections at approximate next to next to next to leading order for the first time in a fit.

Those corrections proved moderate but not negligible, shifting the distributions and the strong coupling value. Results grew stable at that order than at lower ones. Among updates, SeaQuest Drell Yan measurements had the largest effect, sharpening the separation between light quark types at high x. Updated fixed target treatments and ZEUS data mattered. Precision at the LHC is limited by these corners of the fit.
arxiv-2510-04353:
McCrory and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on keeping a teleoperated humanoid robot stable when it leans on its hands across uneven surfaces. Multi-contact tasks push robots to their torque and friction limits, so tracking the operator's motion exactly can cause slipping or saturation. Their retargeting method adjusts contact points and posture in real time to protect the stability margin. The scheme activates only when stability actually depends on the commanded setpoints, leaving the operator full control otherwise.

The core tool is an efficient analytical gradient of the centroidal stability margin, fast enough for kilohertz control rates. That gradient flags moments when small setpoint changes buy large stability gains. Simulation and hardware teleoperation trials showed increased stability margins during manipulation tasks. Higher margins also correlated empirically with better impulse resilience and joint torque headroom. Shared control of this kind matters because teleoperation demonstrations increasingly train learning systems.
arxiv-2510-04553:
Jorge Ruiz Williams wrote this 2025 paper on a fast way to map the shape of brain scan data. Topological data analysis reads MRI volumes for loops, tunnels, and connected parts across scales. Exact methods for that summary are far too slow on a brain volume. Williams built a witness based pipeline that samples the volume with care instead.

The pipeline picks landmark points with a hybrid score that balances spread against local density. Those landmarks shrink typical point distances by a third to over half against random picks. A witness filtration then reads the topology from the landmarks at a fraction of the cost. Benchmarks on public brain data and synthetic shapes ran in under ten seconds on a single graphics card. The topological features survived the shortcut in his tests. The code ships on PyPI as a package named whale tda, with scripts for direct use in imaging work.
arxiv-2510-04653:
Ryota Kojima and Corina Cîrstea wrote this 2025 paper on a new semantics for logics of system behavior. Modal logics describe what a reactive system may do next, and fixpoint logics add claims about the run. Coalgebra gives one semantics for such logics across many system types. The team defines a semantics built on continuations, the programming idea of the rest of a computation. Predicates and continuations turn out to be two views of one thing.

Their result is that the continuation semantics matches the coalgebraic one for fixpoint modal logic. The match holds for every branching type the framework allows. They then rebuild coalgebraic models of the tree logic CTL star under the same idea. Those models may use non maximal execution maps, a freedom the setup denied. A transfer result moves execution maps along maps between monads. From it, the equivalence extends to the tree logic as well.
arxiv-2510-04953:
The Euclid Collaboration prepares a sharper way to weigh the universe in this 2025 arXiv paper. Euclid is a European space telescope that maps how gravity bends light from distant galaxies. That bending, called weak lensing, traces the spread of dark matter. The paper readies advanced lensing statistics for the mission's first data release.

Standard analyses use only simple pair correlations between galaxy shapes. The team adds five higher-order statistics that capture richer patterns in the maps. They test the full pipeline on about ten thousand mock catalogs built from large simulations. The mocks mimic real Euclid redshift data and survey layout. Their forecasts show a 2.5-fold improvement from adding the extra statistics.
arxiv-2510-05053:
Mohammad-Ali Mahmoudpour and Saeed Mahmoudpour tackle a neglected kind of image damage in this 2025 arXiv paper. Poor lighting often ruins a photo's contrast. Quality scoring tools exist for blur and noise, but contrast damage behaves differently. Their goal is to grade contrast-distorted images without seeing the clean original.

Their method first manufactures a stand-in reference image. Several contrast enhancement algorithms compete to restore the photo. A trained classification network picks the best restorer for each image, using a purpose-built set of 49,500 examples. The restored image then serves as a pseudo-reference for a standard full-reference comparison. Tests on three public databases showed promising accuracy across varied contrast distortions.
arxiv-2510-05153:
Zhangchi Liu gives the symbol grounding problem a unified mathematical treatment in this 2025 arXiv paper. The problem asks how words or symbols ever gain real meaning. Liu models a symbolic system as a program and a world as a data string. Grounding then means compressing that string into a shorter description.

Four results follow from algorithmic information theory. Most worlds are random and incompressible, so no purely symbolic system can ground them. Any system specialized for one world can be defeated by another world built against it. Adapting to a new world needs fresh information that the system cannot deduce internally. Chaitin's theorem finally caps what any finite learner can comprehend. Meaning, Liu concludes, is an endless compression process, not a final state.
arxiv-2510-05353:
Abid Hussain and Touqeer Ahmad design a safer way to compare survival between two groups in this 2025 arXiv paper. Clinical data are right-censored, so many patients' event times stay unknown. Standard tests like log-rank and Wilcoxon gain or lose power depending on the unknown pattern of difference. Picking the wrong test can sink a study.

Their composite test splits the data into uncensored and censored subsets. It sums two independent Mann-Whitney statistics built from those subsets. The design adapts automatically to early, late, and crossing hazard patterns without preset weights. Extensive simulations showed the nominal error rate held throughout. Power matched the better of the classic tests in standard cases and beat both when survival curves crossed.
arxiv-2510-05453:
Kapoor and Chandra work on a core task in water science, predicting how much water will flow in rivers. Planners use such forecasts to manage water supplies and to warn towns about floods. Their 2025 paper builds QDeepGR4J, a model that joins a classic rainfall-runoff model with deep learning. The design aims at extreme flows, where plain forecasts often fail.

The model predicts a range of flows instead of one fixed number. That range shows how unsure the forecast is, and wide ranges can flag flood risk early. Tests used river records from the CAMELS-Aus dataset across many Australian catchments. The team also extended the forecasts several steps ahead in time. The new model beat deep learning baselines on accuracy and on the quality of its ranges. It also spotted flood events well, which supports its use as a warning tool.
arxiv-2510-05553:
Tan and colleagues teach drone teams to flock through cluttered forests. Flocking control often uses artificial potential fields, which pull drones together and push them off obstacles. Those fields can trap a flock in dead ends, especially in three-dimensional settings. Their 2025 system, GO-Flock, pairs the reactive control with an active planning layer.

An upstream module reads depth maps and picks waypoints plus virtual agents for avoidance. A downstream module then steers the flock with cohesion, goal pull, and obstacle push. Earlier field methods had mostly been proven in empty or simplified spaces. Tests compare the system against passive field-based rivals on flock quality and trap escape. Final trials flocked nine drones through a forest scene, six real and three virtual. This trial used hardware in the loop for realism. The hybrid design reached goals faster while keeping the flock together.
arxiv-2510-05753:
Bai and colleagues benchmark privacy attacks against transfer-learned models. Fine-tuning foundation models on small sensitive datasets is now standard practice. Membership inference attacks estimate how much those models leak their fine-tuning data. Their 2025 comparison runs many attacks across transfer settings.

No single attack captures all privacy risks in this setting. The likelihood ratio attack performs best across most scenarios tested. The inverse Hessian attack wins instead on PatchCamelyon in the high-data regime. Score-based attacks weaken as fine-tuning data grows, following a power law. Head-only and FiLM fine-tuning show no significant difference for most attacks. Attack strength also depends on choices like shadow model counts. Practitioners should pick attacks per regime rather than trusting one default. Parameterization can then be chosen utility-first, since privacy barely changes. From-scratch results do not transfer, so evaluations must be redone per paradigm.
arxiv-2510-05953:
Heßberger reviews low-lying isomeric states in the heaviest nuclei. Isomers are nuclei with identical charge and mass but different structure and decay behavior. Superheavy nuclei host long-lived examples whose properties often remain disputed. His 2025 review compiles their decay probabilities and structures systematically.

Coverage is restricted to isomers with half-lives typically above one microsecond. Four kinds are distinguished: spin, seniority, K, and shape isomers. Early history of the field opens the review before the catalogue. Cases still unclear or under discussion receive special emphasis. The author offers hints for further work rather than final verdicts. The review presents itself explicitly as a snapshot of present knowledge. Some statements will likely change as better data arrive. Appendix tables compile claims, including uncertain or even dubious ones. Proving or disproving the dubious cases is left to future experiments.
arxiv-2510-06053:
Rusnáková, Chovanec, and Gazda route city traffic with help from quantum annealing in a 2025 paper. Choosing routes for thousands of vehicles at once is too hard for exact methods. The team restates the task as a QUBO problem, a binary puzzle form that quantum annealers can attack.

Their model penalizes pairs of vehicles that would crowd the same road segment at the same time, while also charging for travel time. Leiden clustering splits big instances into smaller ones without losing the worst congestion patterns. In benchmarks with up to 25,000 vehicles, the hybrid quantum solver landed within 1 percent of the classical Gurobi solver's quality. Its routes cut congestion by up to 25 percent compared with shortest-path routing. The workflow runs on maps of any city, which makes it an add-on for navigation platforms.
arxiv-2510-06353:
Tu and six co-authors assess face image recognizability by grounding the judgment in embedding space in a 2025 computer vision paper. Surveillance and web imagery vary wildly in pose, blur, lighting, and occlusion. Conventional quality metrics fail to predict what the deployed encoder can actually use.

Their framework, TransFIRA, is lightweight and annotation-free. It defines recognizability through class-center similarity and class-center angular separation. Both align with the encoder's decision boundaries. A recognizability-informed aggregation strategy then weights images during verification. On BRIAR and IJB-C, it achieved state-of-the-art verification accuracy. Its scores correlated with true recognizability nearly twice as strongly as prior approaches. They add encoder-grounded explanations of how degradations hurt recognizability. They present the first body recognizability assessment method. Robustness held under cross-dataset and out-of-distribution tests.
arxiv-2510-06553:
Chad Berner works in frame theory, a branch of mathematics tied to signal recovery. His 2025 paper starts from a neat fact about frames. A frame is a set of vectors that lets any signal in a space be rebuilt from simple measurements, in a stable way. Berner asks what happens when that definition is loosened.

His loosened version allows the rebuilding operator to be non-invertible, a real weakening of the usual rules. He then gives a complete classification of the sequences that still allow this kind of reconstruction. Several examples show sequences that qualify yet fail to be true frames. He also proves a stability result in the style of Paley and Wiener for these sequences. Certain well-known bases, including unconditional and exponential bases, are classified under the new condition too. The work maps exactly how far the frame idea can stretch before it breaks.
arxiv-2510-06653:
Paulo Enabe and Rodrigo Provasi build a faster numerical method for heat-like problems. Their 2025 paper works in two dimensions on meshes made of general polygons. Such problems, called parabolic, describe how heat or chemicals spread over time. The virtual element method handles odd polygon shapes well, but its standard form is costly to step forward in time.

Their version lumps the mass matrix into a simple diagonal form. Row sums plus a flooring step keep every diagonal entry positive. A neat finding simplifies the construction a great deal. The stabilization terms vanish exactly under row summation, so weights come only from a small polynomial system. The authors prove the lumped form stays equivalent to the true energy measure. They also bound the largest eigenvalue in a way that survives mesh changes. Paired with stability-preserving Runge-Kutta steps, the method stays both efficient and provably stable.
arxiv-2510-06753:
Wen-Tao Lu and Jun-Xian Wang hunt quasars whose light output changes dramatically over time. Their 2025 paper reports the first systematic search for changing-look behavior in an emission line. The line comes from helium gas ionized by extreme ultraviolet light near a supermassive black hole. It reacts sensitively when the quasar's ionizing glow changes.

The team mined repeated spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. From over nine thousand quasars with multiple spectra, strict checks and visual inspection left thirty-four cases. In each case, the helium line appeared or vanished between observations. Twenty-nine of them swung in brightness by more than a magnitude at their peak. Compared with known hydrogen-line changing-look quasars, this sample behaves similarly. It prefers higher feeding rates relative to the black hole's limit, though. Host galaxy light also contaminates this sample less, which makes the line easier to trust.
arxiv-2510-06853:
Anatole Storck leads a team simulating the first stars that ever formed. Their 2025 paper presents results from the MEGATRON simulation suite. Population III stars were the universe's first generation, born from pristine gas. The simulations follow radiation and chemistry together inside a Milky Way-mass halo at cosmic dawn.

The very first such stars ignite in small halos that cool through molecular hydrogen. Most later ones form in bigger halos above the atomic cooling threshold. That shift happens within about a hundred million years of the first star. A rising ultraviolet background drives the change by suppressing the hydrogen cooling. The overall formation rate then settles to a steadier value. The team also traced where the remnants of these stars end up today. Roughly three quarters to four fifths land in the stellar halo of the galaxy. The rest stay bound to smaller satellite systems.
arxiv-2510-06953:
Minju Gwak, Guijin Son, and Jaehyung Kim test whether smooth information flow marks good reasoning in language models. Their 2025 paper revisits the Uniform Information Density hypothesis from linguistics. The hypothesis says effective communication spreads information evenly rather than in bursts. The team asks whether that holds inside a model's reasoning traces.

They built an entropy-based measure of information density for each reasoning step. Two uniformity scores capture smoothness locally and across the whole trace. Across six reasoning benchmarks, smoother traces predicted correct answers. Picking the uniform trace improved accuracy sharply on a contest benchmark. Gains there ran from ten to thirty-two percent over baselines. Wrong traces showed bursts and sharp spikes of information. Correct traces avoided those spikes, staying locally smooth. Curiously, global unevenness paired with local smoothness still correlated with success on hard math. The signal beats internal measures for judging reasoning quality.
arxiv-2510-07653:
Chen and a large team of coauthors wrote this 2025 genomics paper on spatial transcriptomics. This technology measures gene activity while keeping each measurement's place in the tissue. Genes that vary across space reveal tissue structure and cell interactions. Many methods claim to find such spatial variable genes. The authors set out to compare those methods at large scale and to build a shared reference from the results.

They benchmarked twenty detection methods on hundreds of tissue slides from a public resource. Performance differed sharply by tissue type, image resolution, and study design. Beyond the contest, they built the first cross-tissue atlas of spatial variable genes. The atlas showed strong overlap between tissues, such as thymus and lymph node. In cancer samples, it exposed gene programs tied to spread, immune entry, and tissue identity. The atlas now serves as a reference for the field.
arxiv-2510-07953:
Yin and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on precipitation nowcasting, the short-range forecasting of rainfall from radar. Storms evolve fast, and the next two hours matter for floods, farming, and transport. Models that predict step by step accumulate errors over longer horizons. The authors first train a short-term model to generate extra synthetic radar sequences. Those synthetic sequences enrich training for the long-term model that follows.

Their method, SimCast, distills knowledge from the short-term teacher into the long-term student. A weighted loss pushes the student to care about heavy rainfall regions, where errors hurt most. The pipeline adds no cost at forecast time. On three benchmarks, SimCast beat existing approaches by a margin in mean skill scores. Heavy-rain performance improved most. The authors also plug SimCast into a diffusion framework to sharpen its outputs. Better near-term rain forecasts buy cities minutes of warning.
arxiv-2510-08153:
Eichenseher, Franz, Wolff, and Mauerer wrote this 2025 paper testing whether the best parameters of a leading variational quantum algorithm follow predictable patterns as circuits deepen. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm alternates problem and mixing steps, each with a tunable angle. Folklore said optimal angles drift smoothly with depth. Finding true optima is NP-hard, so the folklore mattered. The authors ran extensive simulations across instances and depths.

The patterns hold only at shallow depth. Optimal parameters often deviate substantially from expected trends. As depth grows, performance grows less sensitive to exact parameter choices anyway. A simple alternative, iteratively fixing components one at a time, matched established strategies and sometimes beat them at low depth. It tunes only two parameters per iteration. The study tells practitioners where pattern-based shortcuts are safe and where they mislead.
arxiv-2510-08353:
Alexus Annika Kumwembe and the DESI collaboration show in a 2025 arXiv paper that imaging data can sharpen a cosmic measurement. Small galaxy groups, called multiplets, tend to align with the large-scale tidal field around them. That alignment reveals the direction of tidal forces shaping cosmic structure. Past multiplet work in DESI relied on galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts, which give precise distances.

The team adds galaxy positions from the DESI Legacy Imaging catalog, which covers far more galaxies. Imaging lacks precise distances but adds sheer numbers and sky coverage. They find the imaging-based catalog yields alignment measurements similar to the spectroscopy-only ones. That match shows imaging can raise the signal-to-noise ratio of multiplet alignment in DESI. Stronger alignment signals help cosmologists probe how matter clumps and how galaxies respond to their surroundings.
arxiv-2510-08453:
Kiri Sakahara and Takashi Sato rethink endless games using an alternative set theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. Game theory gives paradoxical advice for long finite games, like the centipede game and the chain store paradox. Backward reasoning says players should defect or enter immediately, against intuition. The authors blame standard number systems for mis-modeling how people perceive huge horizons.

Their framework builds on Alternative Set Theory, which treats some huge quantities as indiscernible. Distinct topologies encode how a mind might view one long run of events. An equivalence relation then formally identifies quantities that a given perspective cannot tell apart. Within this setup, new intuitive subgame perfect equilibria appear. Which equilibrium arises depends on the temporal perspective and the payoff rule that were chosen. The authors say this grounds game theory in modes of human cognition.
arxiv-2510-08553:
Yunzhe Xu, Yiyuan Pan, and Zhe Liu give navigation agents an imagination-driven memory in a 2025 arXiv paper. Vision-and-language navigation asks agents to follow written instructions through buildings and streets. Memory-persistent versions demand that agents improve by accumulating experience over repeated episodes. Prior systems dumped whole memories into context or looked up a fixed window, and stored observations but not behavior.

Their system, Memoir, uses a world model, conditioned on language, that imagines future states along the route. Those imagined states serve as queries to retrieve relevant past observations and behavioral histories. A hybrid viewpoint-level memory anchors both observations and decision patterns to specific viewpoints. Specialized encoders then feed retrieved experience into the navigation model. Across ten testing scenarios, Memoir improved results throughout. It gained 5.4 percent in success weighted by path length on the IR2R benchmark over the best memory baseline.
arxiv-2510-09353:
Emerson de Melo and Júlia Kato settle a counting question in group theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. For any group, the symmetries of the group itself, called automorphisms, move elements around. The paths elements can take under all these symmetries form orbits, and the authors ask how many orbits a certain matrix group has.

The group in question consists of unitriangular matrices, square arrays with ones on the diagonal and zeros below it, taken over an infinite field. The authors prove the orbit count is finite whenever the matrices have size five or smaller. Once the size reaches six or more, the count becomes infinite. The result draws a sharp line between small cases that can in principle be listed and larger cases that cannot.
arxiv-2510-09453:
Nicholas King, Eugene Pashkovski, Reid Patterson, Paige Rockwell, and Gareth McKinley study how elastic materials respond to strong shaking in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is large amplitude oscillatory shear, a test that wiggles a material back and forth with growing force. Most work tracks the shear stress, but for very elastic materials the first normal stress difference can grow far larger and reveal more about nonlinear behaviour.

The authors build a Fourier-Tschebyshev framework that decomposes that normal stress signal into its higher-order spectral parts. They demonstrate it on two models, the quasilinear Upper Convected Maxwell model and, in turn, the fully nonlinear Giesekus model. They apply it to experiments on a silicone polymer and a polyurethane melt, pairing it with a fast strain sweep method to extract the material function in one sweep. Checks confirm consistency with the known links between shear and normal stresses.
arxiv-2510-09653:
Ranjan Sapkota and Manoj Karkee review the YOLO family of object detectors in a 2025 arXiv paper. YOLO models detect objects in images in a single pass and power much applied computer vision. The review spans five generations, from YOLOv5 to a preliminary YOLO27, tracing architecture, benchmarking, deployment, and future directions.

YOLO27 uses a scale-adaptive dual design. Small versions pair streamlined convolutional networks with dual-scale prediction. Larger ones use query-based transformer decoding that needs no non-maximum suppression. The largest adds a vision transformer backbone for global context. Earlier generations contribute their own ideas, such as YOLO26 dropping distribution focal loss and YOLOv8 introducing decoupled anchor-free detection. Preliminary YOLO27 scores range from about forty-two to sixty accuracy points, with latencies under two and a half milliseconds. The authors also compare the family against contemporary detectors across detection, segmentation, pose, tracking, and other tasks.
arxiv-2510-10353:
Jin and co-authors time the X-ray flicker of a black hole binary in this 2025 arXiv paper in astrophysics. The system, Swift J1727.8-1613, pairs a black hole with a normal star. The team analyzes Insight-HXMT observations taken during a bright soft X-ray flare on 19 September 2023.

They find type-B quasi-periodic oscillations, rhythmic brightness modulations, spanning the hard-intermediate and soft-intermediate states of the outburst. These states mark stages in how the accretion flow around the black hole is organized. Tracking the oscillations across the transition constrains models of the inner flow and any jet it launches. Each well-timed state change sharpens the picture of how black holes feed and flare.
arxiv-2510-10953:
Qing Zhu, Xian Yu, and Yu-Li Huang design chemotherapy schedules that stay good even when treatment times are unpredictable, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Clinics group patient types and assign each group one representative slot length, aiming to cut idle time and overtime. Real data from Mayo Clinic show treatment durations are lopsided and multi peaked. The team builds a distributionally robust model, planning against the worst plausible distribution inside an ambiguity set that mixes patient type distributions.

The model resists standard solvers, so they derive a closed form for the worst case expected cost, plus lower and upper bounds. The bounds grow with the variability inside each group, which proves a practical rule: group patient types with similar treatment times. Exact algorithms and fast clustering heuristics follow. Tests on synthetic data and Mayo Clinic records show the methods work.
arxiv-2510-11053:
Maurizio Palesi and ten co-authors measure a hidden cost of modular quantum computers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Single quantum processors hit physical limits, so future machines may link many quantum cores together. Cores must constantly exchange classical messages: measurement outcomes and timing signals that steer the quantum operations. The team built qcomm, an open source simulator that times the whole system, modeling gate execution, entanglement distribution, teleportation, and classical message delays together.

Their experiments vary classical bandwidth, link types, and how circuits are mapped onto cores, including runs of real quantum benchmarks on a cryogenic multi core design. These classical exchanges, they find, are generally not the main driver of run time. But their share grows exactly in the scenarios designers are aiming for: better quantum hardware, large scale links, and message aware mappings. Planning scalable machines without modeling these classical delays, they argue, risks building the bottleneck in.
arxiv-2510-11553:
Labeling medical images is expensive, so a hospital adopting a foundation model needs to know how many labeled examples are actually enough. Nikolay Nechaev and co-authors answer that question for chest X-ray classification in this 2025 arXiv medical imaging paper. Their approach fits power laws to learning curves, the predictable relationship between training set size and performance, to forecast how much data a target accuracy will require.

Testing several pathologies and foundation models, they found that XrayCLIP and XraySigLIP reach strong performance with significantly fewer labeled examples than a ResNet-50 baseline. The practical surprise is how early the forecast becomes reliable: learning curve slopes estimated from just fifty labeled cases accurately predicted the final performance plateaus. That means practitioners can label a small pilot batch, fit the curve, and order only the annotations needed to hit a chosen ROC-AUC threshold.
arxiv-2510-11653:
Reinforcement learning is supposed to teach models new skills, but on standard math benchmarks the base models solve nearly everything if sampled enough times, so fine-tuning mostly sharpens what exists. Prasanna Mayilvahanan and co-authors build a benchmark that cannot be beaten that way in this 2025 arXiv paper. MATH-Beyond collects problems that defeat common open-source models of up to eight billion parameters even at a sampling budget of a thousand attempts per problem.

The problems come from the DAPO-Math-17K and DeepScaleR datasets, so they remain standard high-school mathematics. They were filtered for verified answers, then run through a gauntlet of base models to keep only the unsolved ones. A forty-one-problem set stayed unsolved by all. When reinforcement-learning-tuned models such as Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen and DeepScaleR were tested, they still performed poorly. They release it to force exploration-driven methods.
arxiv-2510-11753:
Zeyu Cai studies a family of number puzzles in this 2025 arXiv paper. The equations set a power plus a fixed number equal to another power, with whole-number answers sought. Mathematicians call such problems exponential Diophantine equations. No general solution method is known for the whole family. The famous ABC conjecture implies each equation has only finitely many solutions, but that alone does not find them.

Cai builds an algorithm that settles individual cases completely. It first computes a strict upper bound on any possible solution for the given parameters. Then it checks every candidate below that bound by finite enumeration. The algorithm's termination is not proven for all inputs, so its design leans on heuristics. Even so, it proved reliable in large-scale numerical experiments. For each case it solves, the method also produces a rigorous proof that no solution was missed.
arxiv-2510-12053:
Ty Trusty accelerates the solvers behind cloth, muscle, and soft-body simulation. Physics animation often uses coordinate descent, updating one variable at a time: fast, but slow when everything is coupled. Newton's method converges quickly but costs far more per step. Trusty's 2025 arXiv paper, Coordinate Condensation, grafts a global correction onto the local updates.

The correction lives in a low-dimensional subspace built from a Schur complement, a standard algebraic compression. Recent work by Lan and colleagues used a similar subspace but paid for it with damping that degraded convergence. Trusty solves for the local and subspace displacements independently, deleting that damping. When the subspace captures the global coupling, the method converges at nearly Newton's rate while keeping coordinate descent's efficiency. Experiments across material stiffnesses and mesh resolutions show it beating both plain coordinate descent and the damped rival. The paper also maps where the trick fails.
arxiv-2510-12153:
Minhao Qiao, Hai Dong, and Iqbal Gondal balance blockchain privacy against accountability. Cross-chain systems force an all-or-nothing choice between staying fully unnamed and forced identity disclosure, blocking uptake in regulated finance. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes VeilAudit, a cross-chain auditing system built on Auditor-Only Linkability.

Users create linkable audit tags carrying zero-knowledge proofs of validity, never exposing their master wallet address. A special ciphertext lets named auditors test whether transfers across chains share one unnamed author, without learning who it is. When due process demands more, threshold-gated identity revelation unlocks the name only when a quorum agrees. The same machinery supports reputation building in pseudonymous settings, enabling cross-chain credit scoring from checkable behavioral history. The authors spell out the security guarantees and show a working prototype spanning multiple Ethereum-compatible chains. Their tests find the system practical for today's multi-chain world.
arxiv-2510-12553:
Roper, Cai, and Peacock weigh the gas in galaxy groups by detecting the faint shadow their motion casts on the cosmic microwave background, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. The kinetic Sunyaev Zeldovich effect is a tiny temperature shift where moving ionized gas scatters the background radiation. Stacking many groups can reveal how much baryonic matter their halos actually hold.

The team built a forward model from large cosmological simulations. It generates mock group catalogues and synthetic effect maps with a reconstructed velocity field, photometric redshift errors, and survey masks. Contamination from the cosmic infrared background was small. Comparing stacked observations with the model, they find the baryon fraction depends on halo mass. Massive groups hold the universal fraction, but low mass groups are depleted well below it within the virial radius. Their gas appears spread further out, reaching the universal share only beyond that radius, plausibly due to energetic feedback.
arxiv-2510-12653:
Hancart studies how two identical firms competing for the same candidates should design their hiring tests, in a 2025 arXiv economics paper. Each firm posts a selection procedure: a test plus an acceptance probability for each test outcome. Candidates then choose one firm to apply to, so a firm's procedure affects both what it learns and who shows up.

Two features of a test matter: its accuracy, in a classical statistical ordering, and its hardness. Hancart shows that in any symmetric equilibrium the chosen test must be maximal in the accuracy ranking and minimal in the difficulty order. Competition thus produces maximal but misguided learning. Firms end up with precise knowledge that is not relevant to payoffs, because the test also steers candidate self selection. The paper also examines capacity constraints, wage offers, and asymmetric equilibria where one firm is more picky than the other, mapping how competition reshapes screening.
arxiv-2510-13153:
Chen, Kataria, Shen, and Guo add dark matter halo spin to the bar formation story in this 2025 arXiv paper, a companion to their work on disk properties. Galactic bars form on a timescale already known to depend exponentially on disk mass fraction and to grow with disk hotness and thickness. Whether the halo's rotation, its spin, changes that picture had not been systematically tested.

The authors built N-body disk-halo models varying disk mass fraction and random motions, then introduced prograde halo spin, rotating with the disk, and retrograde spin against it. The established empirical relations survived in both cases. For rapid bar formation, halo spin barely mattered. For moderately slow formation, prograde spin hastened bar onset while retrograde spin delayed it. For extremely slow formation, spin's influence grew stronger but more stochastic, which the authors attribute to angular momentum exchange between disk and halo.
arxiv-2510-13453:
Thomas and Johal study bead-spring models held in nonequilibrium steady states between two heat baths. Their 2025 arXiv paper examines beads joined by springs, each bath kept at a different temperature. Such minimal models are simple enough to solve yet rich enough to show irreversibility. They serve as workhorses for probing heat flow at small scales. The model descends from polymer physics, where it described chain molecules.

For a single bead, the authors derive the steady probability distribution of its position. They use a recent effective temperature technique alongside numerical simulations of the motion equations. The position distribution turns out not to depend on the bead's mass. They also compute the entropy production rate for the one-bead system, by theory and simulation. For two beads, they obtain position distributions in both damping regimes. They close by testing ergodicity, whether time averages match ensemble averages.
arxiv-2510-13753:
Mensah constructs a strong solution for a three-way coupled system of polymeric fluid, solvent, and flexible structure. His 2025 arXiv paper models an Oldroyd-B fluid, a standard description of polymer solutions, flowing against a moving structure. Solute, solvent, and structure each evolve in their own dimension, then couple at the interfaces. Earlier theory rarely handled this triple coupling with high regularity.

The strategy splits the system apart before solving it. First the solute decouples from the solvent-structure pair, and each piece gets solved on its own. A fixed-point argument then glues the pieces back into one solution. The construction assumes only small initial acceleration from the moving boundary. A maximal regularity result for the Stokes problem on moving domains powers the estimates. That Stokes result, proved along the way, stands as an independent contribution. The final solution is unique within its higher-order regularity class.
arxiv-2510-13953:
Luigi C. Bresciani, Gabriele Levati, and Paride Paradisi map out the allowed interactions of axion-like particles using consistency rules from scattering theory, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Axion-like particles are light particles predicted by many extensions of the Standard Model, and they are hunted at colliders and in rare decay processes. Their interactions are usually listed in an effective theory sorted by operator dimension.

Using spinor-helicity techniques, a compact modern language for scattering amplitudes. With them, the authors derive the full set of partial wave unitarity bounds for the most general axion-like interactions up to dimension eight at high energy. These bounds are limits that keep collision chances physically sensible. They also compute positivity bounds, a second family of such limits, and stress that the two families complete each other. As a byproduct, their methods yield new positivity constraints for the Standard Model's own effective theory.
arxiv-2510-14053:
Shriyash Upadhyay and co-authors propose a regulation for frontier AI: require laboratories to release small 'analog' models alongside their flagship systems, in this 2025 arXiv position paper. Analog models are scaled-down versions, trained much like the proprietary giants and distilled from them, serving as stand-ins that outsiders can inspect.

The authors argue this sidesteps the usual safety-versus-innovation tradeoff that has shelved most frontier regulation. Safety and interpretability methods developed on smaller models generalize effectively to frontier-scale systems. So the wider research community could verify safety claims, study interpretability, and check algorithmic transparency. Labs would not have to disclose their full models. The mandate would cost labs little, since it reuses existing data and infrastructure, while serving the public good. Beyond the policy, they offer it as evidence that deeper understanding of models can relax the tradeoff and deliver more safety and more innovation.
arxiv-2510-14553:
Tang and colleagues, in a 2025 arXiv paper, address a glitch in text-to-image generation: the same character changes appearance from scene to scene. This identity shift makes it hard to illustrate a story with one consistent subject. Earlier fixes often assumed that every target scene is known in advance, which rarely holds in practice. The authors trace the shift to a learned link between a subject and its usual surroundings.

They prove this link between scene and identity is nearly universal in such models, and they bound its strength. Their method, Scene De-Contextualization, edits the prompt's internal representation to weaken that link. It finds the unstable directions in the representation and reweights them, with no retraining and no need to know future scenes. Experiments show that identity is preserved much better across images. Scene variety, meanwhile, stays largely intact.
arxiv-2510-15153:
Maryna Kachanovska and Étienne Peillon study a tricky boundary-value problem from plasma physics in this 2025 arXiv paper. The problem describes a hybrid plasma resonance, where waves in a cold plasma grow sharply near a certain curve. Along that curve the main coefficient of the equation vanishes and flips sign, which breaks the standard theory for solving such problems.

The pair prove a limiting absorption principle, a guarantee that solutions stay controlled as a small damping term fades away. They first establish bounds on the solution in weighted Sobolev spaces, which are function spaces tuned to the problem's singular curve. They then split the solution into a smooth regular part and an explicit singular part. That split has a useful payoff: it lets them state a radiation-like condition inside a bounded domain, turning the resonance problem into a well-posed one with a definite answer.
arxiv-2510-15353:
Marvin Nabroth reports measurements from the HADES experiment for its collaboration in this 2025 arXiv paper. HADES studies what flies out when heavy atomic nuclei collide at a few billion electron volts. Those collisions briefly create matter at very high baryon density, a regime where physicists hunt for signs of a critical point in quantum chromodynamics.

The analysis tracks how the counts of protons and light nuclei fluctuate from one collision to the next. New methods identify particles probabilistically rather than event by event, correct for detector efficiency, and remove distortions from uneven collision centrality. The corrected fluctuation ratios extend trends seen by the STAR experiment down to lower collision energies. Nabroth also shows how the ratios change with rapidity, a measure of particle direction, and compares them with baseline models that include local attractive interactions between particles.
arxiv-2510-15453:
J. Poyatos, O. Fors, and J. M. Gómez Cama ask what mathematical curve best describes how often stars flare at each energy. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies M dwarfs, small stars whose flares can batter the atmospheres of orbiting planets. Textbooks model flare frequency distributions as power laws, but recent work has argued for lognormal curves instead.

The team analyzed one hundred ten M dwarfs watched by two space telescopes, TESS and CHEOPS, and catalogued more than five and a half thousand flares. After correcting detection biases and merging both datasets, their combined distribution spanned nearly ten orders of magnitude in energy. Measured by duration, flares followed a clean power law. Measured by total energy, they bent away from it, fitting a truncated power law with a break near the superflare threshold. The authors conclude a change in flare physics explains the pattern.
arxiv-2510-15553:
Linda Cook, Ross J. Kang, Eileen Robinson, and Gabriëlle Zwaneveld prove a coloring conjecture for a special family of graphs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The conjecture, from Vu in 2002, links a graph's chromatic number, the fewest colors that color it properly, to how many common neighbors two vertices can share. Cook and colleagues tackle the case of claw-free graphs, which contain no induced three-pronged claw.

They show the chromatic number is at most the codegree parameter plus three. The bound is tight, since the line graph of the Petersen graph meets it exactly. A stronger version of the proof uses a parameter defined only over edges, counting common neighbors of adjacent pairs. The authors note the result generalizes Vizing's classic 1964 bound for edge coloring. Their structural approach is presented as a first step toward the full conjecture, which remains open for general graphs.
arxiv-2510-15753:
Ignacio Repiso, Salvador Pineda, and Juan Miguel Morales compare two method families in a 2025 paper. The problem is AC optimal power flow. It decides how electricity should flow through a grid. The flow must be cheap and safe. Interior-point methods are fast. But they can settle for local answers. Spatial branching methods guarantee the global optimum. They cost far more computing time.

The team tested networks of different sizes. Some test cases were rigged to contain local optima. They also tried versions boosted with past operating data. Those variants improved convergence for both families. They also cut computation times. The study maps where each approach wins in practice.
arxiv-2510-15853:
David Porlles and Wei Chen map quantum geometry in a 2025 paper. The materials are well-known semiconductors. They include silicon, germanium, and carbon. Gallium arsenide is covered too. Quantum geometry tells how electron states twist through momentum space. It drives several optical and transport traits. Yet it had not been charted for these standard materials.

The authors used a tight-binding model. They worked out the quantum metric of the valence bands. The metric covers the whole momentum space. It peaks at the centre point. Its curvature values vary strongly elsewhere. The momentum space is thus highly warped. Adding up the metric gives back a measured value. It matches the spread of the electron wavefunctions. Its link to the energy gap may gauge quantum criticality.
arxiv-2510-16153:
Robert Dougherty-Bliss and two co-authors count the ways to cut a four-by-n grid into two connected pieces that are exact mirror copies of each other in shape and size. The problem follows a puzzle in the French magazine Pour la Science, where Jean-Paul Delahaye had showcased the count for skinnier three-by-two-n rectangles.

The authors solve the wider case with the transfer matrix method, a bookkeeping technique that builds the grid column by column while tracking how the cut edge evolves. From that machinery they compute a generating function, a single formula whose coefficients give the number of valid cuts for every length n. The result turns a hands-on tiling puzzle into exact enumeration.
arxiv-2510-16253:
Arielle Sanford, Shuo Sun, and Christian B Mendl rebuild a protein folding model as a smooth flow instead of a tall stack. Tools like AlphaFold predict a protein's shape from its sequence using a block called the Evoformer, stacked forty-eight deep. That depth costs heavy compute and locks the design into fixed steps.

Their version swaps the stack for a neural ordinary differential equation, a model whose depth flows like time. Memory cost stays flat no matter how deep the flow runs, and solvers can trade speed against accuracy. The model trains in about seventeen hours on a single graphics card, far less than the original demands. Its shapes look plausible and catch features like alpha-helices, though they fall short of AlphaFold's accuracy. The trade shows lean, flexible folding models are within reach.
arxiv-2510-16753:
Wei Huang and nine co-authors present ELMM, a lightweight multimodal language model built to complete knowledge graphs that carry both images and text. Such graphs often miss facts, which weakens tools built on them. Large models could help fill the gaps, but each entity may bring many image tokens, adding noise and heavy compute costs.

ELMM answers with a visual token compressor that uses multi-head attention. It squeezes image tokens from both text and image viewpoints, cutting repeats while keeping needed detail. The full design aims to keep the strengths of large multimodal models at a fraction of the cost. The authors frame the work around two hurdles: semantic noise from token overload, and raw expense.
arxiv-2510-16853:
Matthew Sharp and three co-authors name and frame agentic inequality: the gaps in power and opportunity that open when access to capable AI agents is uneven. Agents plan and act on their own, unlike passive tools. Who gets them, how strong they are, and how many a person or firm can run will shape economic and political life.

The paper builds a framework with three dimensions: availability, quality, and quantity. It argues agents differ from past technology divides because they act as autonomous delegates that can be scaled and can compete with each other directly. Drivers range from model release choices to market incentives. A research agenda for governance closes the study.
arxiv-2510-16953:
Ersin Das leads sixteen co-authors in making ship crane transfers safer in a 2025 paper. Ship-mounted cranes move loads while the deck rolls with waves. That motion constantly disturbs the swinging payload. Controllers must avoid obstacles and land loads inside a target zone.

The team built a robust predictive controller with built-in safety barriers. Predictive control plans moves ahead while respecting stated limits. A special barrier rule keeps the payload inside safe bounds. Moving boxes around the load handle collision avoidance in real time. An online adjustment reduces how cautious the barrier must be. Trials used a five-axis crane on a motion platform mimicking the sea. The setup showed safe, accurate transfers under realistic disturbance.
arxiv-2510-17053:
Dongjin Lee leads eight co-authors in improving fake-versus-real sky event sorting in a 2025 paper. Telescope surveys must separate real cosmic events from image artifacts. Machine classifiers do this sorting, called real-bogus classification. Real events are rare, so labeled training examples are scarce.

One fix injects simulated point sources into real telescope images. The authors compare injection strategies for the first time in detail. Random injection scatters sources anywhere in the frame. Near-galaxy injection places them beside galaxies instead. A third dataset combined both strategies. Networks trained on these sets faced real gravitational-wave follow-up data. Random injection excelled at spotting asteroids and filtering artifacts. It underperformed, though, on genuine transient events.
arxiv-2510-17153:
Hyunjin Choo and four co-authors hunt for missing group links in tangled data in this 2025 paper. Groups that link many nodes at once form hyperedges in a hypergraph. Guessing which new groups will form helps in science, health, and social work. The full set of groups to check is far too vast to scan.

Their method scores groups with a rule drawn from real group data. A bound lets the search drop weak groups with no loss of the best. Proofs show dropped groups can never beat the kept ones. Tests on ten real hypergraphs beat top rival methods. The gains hold across five fields, from teams to cell groups.
arxiv-2510-17953:
Avik Chakraborty and three co-authors build string-like states in a three-dimensional expanding universe from gravitational memory alone. Memory here means a lasting shift left by passing gravity effects. The team glues two halves of space along a junction and asks what can live on that seam.

The string equations follow from the gluing rules themselves, with no extra input. A closed string can pulse for a while, born from past memory and fading into future memory. A clock-like measure also appears on its own at the junction. The work extends to junctions joining three or more parts, widening the picture.
arxiv-2510-18053:
Jiajun Fan, with four co-authors, makes the safety leash on fine-tuning generative models adjust itself. A fixed leash creates a bind: tight control guards skill but caps reward, while loose control invites cheating and collapse. Their ADRPO method loosens the leash for high-value samples and tightens it for poor ones.

Strength is set from advantage estimates, so the model explores hard where the payoff looks real. Applied with a distance-based leash to flow matching models, the method improved text-to-image fit in their tests. Trainers of image models get a tuning rule that follows data quality instead of a fixed schedule.
arxiv-2510-18153:
Ajay S Gill, with twenty-one co-authors, measures both the hot gas and the motion of a famous galaxy cluster pair through the microwave background. Hot gas leaves a thermal shadow, and moving gas adds a smaller kinematic shift. Fitting both at once across many frequencies and instruments avoids the shortcuts of a single processed map.

Data span eleven frequencies from two major observatories for the Abell 399 and Abell 401 pair and the filament between them. Dust and other foregrounds are modeled inside the fit. The thermal results match earlier work. Cosmologists get a fuller method for weighing and timing the largest structures.
arxiv-2510-18553:
Abdullah Al-Khatib and his five co-authors address how vehicles can reserve network bandwidth ahead of a trip when several mobile operators compete along the road.
