Safety and time-sensitive vehicle applications need guaranteed connections, but future travel times and prices are uncertain, so vehicles can easily book too much or too little. Their approach updates reservations along the driving path using a learning method built on Double Deep Q-Networks.

The strategy pursues two goals at once: lowering reservation cost across operators and keeping supply reliable when plans shift. It explicitly handles both underbooked and overbooked cases that arise as a journey unfolds. In extensive experiments against greedy updating and other learning methods, the approach cut bandwidth costs by about forty percent across all scenarios studied, while resolving the uncertain cases in a cost-effective way.
arxiv-2510-18653:
Pavel Mnev and Konstantin Wernli carry out a construction in Chern-Simons theory, a quantum field theory tied closely to the shape of three-dimensional spaces. They study the theory's perturbative path integral, computed in a chosen gauge around a flat connection, and view the whole computation as varying over the space of all flat connections. The goal is a truly global object, one that does not depend on arbitrary local choices.

The authors prove the integral stays consistent as it moves across that space, up to a term that does not affect its meaning in their formalism. From it they build a volume form on the space of flat connections whose class does not depend on the chosen metric, making it an invariant of the underlying three-dimensional manifold. Along the way, they extend the partition function to a broader setting mixing two connections and a metric.
arxiv-2510-18853:
Malena Sabaté Landman, writing alone, develops new iterative solvers for inverse problems, the task of reconstructing an unknown quantity from indirect measurements. Flexible Krylov methods are a standard tool here, especially when the penalty used to stabilize the reconstruction goes beyond the simple two-norm, for instance favoring sparse solutions. A related family avoids inner products altogether, which speeds computation and saves memory when working in low precision.

Landman presents flexible, inner-product-free methods, including a new flexible generalized Hessenberg method that allows the preconditioner, a helper that makes each step easier, to change from iteration to iteration. Randomized versions built on a sketch-and-solve idea aim to improve result quality cheaply. Theory accompanies the algorithms, and numerical experiments across different regularization terms show how the new methods perform.
arxiv-2510-18953:
Merna Abumusabh and four co-authors recast a rare B meson decay as a search for the QCD axion. The decay of a charged B meson into a kaon and invisible neutrinos is already measured, and the same final state could hide a light invisible particle instead.

Using only public Belle II data, the team rebuilds the link between true and measured motion without internal simulations. Their limit on the decay with an axion is about nine times stronger than before, and it constrains how the axion couples to bottom and strange quarks. The method turns one measurement into two probes at once.
arxiv-2510-19053:
Leandro Nery studies invariant theory for group actions that are not reductive, where the classical theorems of Hilbert and Schwarz may fail. For compact and reductive groups, polynomial invariants and smooth invariants line up neatly, but outside that safe zone the two kinds of invariants can split apart.

In two settings, discrete Lorentz groups acting on spacetime and cocompact actions on manifolds, Nery proves sharp contrasts. Polynomial invariants can be finitely generated while smooth ones are not generated by them, or the polynomial ring can shrink to constants alone while smooth invariants remain rich.
arxiv-2510-19753:
Qilin Ye and three co-authors explain when transformers truly learn an algorithm instead of memorizing a shortcut. Graph connectivity serves as the test problem. Working with a simplified disentangled transformer, they prove one thing first. A model with a given depth can compute connectivity for graphs whose diameter fits a bound tied to that depth. It does so, in effect, by powering the adjacency matrix.

Training dynamics then decide which strategy the model picks up. When most training graphs fit within capacity, the model learns the true algorithm. When too many exceed it, the model falls back on a node-degree shortcut. Tests confirm the theory: keeping training data within a model's capacity makes even standard transformers learn the exact algorithm.
arxiv-2510-19953:
Shaocong Ma and Heng Huang tackle zeroth-order optimization, where a method must improve a function using only function values and no gradients. Most gradient estimates in that setting carry bias unless the step size shrinks toward zero. The pair propose a new family of estimates designed to remove that bias entirely.

Their construction rewrites directional derivatives as a telescoping series and samples from carefully chosen distributions. They work out the best scaling and step sizes for four versions and prove that gradient descent with their estimates reaches optimal complexity for smooth non-convex problems. Experiments on synthetic tasks and language model fine-tuning support the theory.
arxiv-2510-20153:
Tristan Pollner, Amin Saberi, and Anders Wikum study two-stage bipartite matching, where edges arrive in two batches and a matching must be chosen after each one. Vertices matched in the first stage are gone when the second batch of edges is sampled from a known distribution. The goal is to maximize the total weight of the combined matching chosen across both stages.

The authors design polynomial-time approximations to the best possible online algorithm, with guarantees for both vertex-weighted and edge-weighted graphs under arbitrary distributions. Both ratios match known limits for the natural fractional relaxation and improve on the best earlier guarantee. Their rounding method matches offline vertices with probability tied to their fractional weights, using negative association to bound performance.
arxiv-2510-20653:
Jack Butler and four co-authors compare two ways to get better answers from large language models at run time without retraining them. One path lets a model reflect on its own answer and try again, while the other simply gives it a larger budget of steps or tokens to work with.

Tests span maths reasoning and translation across model families from three major makers, under varied depths of reflection and budgets. Reflection helps most in maths, in some cases more than tripling scores, while results in translation depend more on the market and language pair. A live marketing system built for an online fashion shop confirms that gains differ by setting, so teams should test before they spend.
arxiv-2510-20853:
Hyungjun Yoon leads thirteen co-authors on learning general body signal representations from earphones worn in daily life. Electrical body signals reveal much about health, yet most recordings come from bulky lab gear, and most models are built for one task with narrow filters.

The team gathered fifty hours of free living recordings with an earphone prototype and built DailySense, a data set spanning five human senses. Their token method splits signals into twelve bands guided by physiology, then learns by reconstruction so features adapt across the full spectrum. Tests on DailySense and four public sets show broad transfer, a step toward quiet everyday health sensing.
arxiv-2510-20953:
Francisco J Cruz-Zamorano and one co-author study semigroups of holomorphic self maps of the upper half plane that converge as slowly as possible to their Denjoy Wolff point. The slowest, or extremal, rate marks the edge of what continuous dynamics on this domain can do.

The main novelty lies in the parabolic case with zero hyperbolic step. Several characterizations are given, through the Herglotz form of the generator, through conformality of a modified Koenigs function at the fixed point, and more. The results complete a corner of iteration theory where convergence nearly stalls yet never stops.
arxiv-2510-21053:
Li An leads five co-authors on a reinforcement learning framework for watermarking language model text that must stay detectable, readable, robust to removal attacks, and secure at once. Green and red token list schemes bias word choice to hide a signal, but hand designed lists balance those goals poorly.

Direct optimization of list design is hard because several criteria pull in different directions and removal attacks adapt. Reinforcement learning searches the design space against all criteria jointly. Stronger watermarks support tracing and authentication of machine text, a growing need as generated content floods public channels.
arxiv-2510-21153:
Lianghong Chen leads three co-authors on doubt aware multi goal reward based learning that guides three sized molecule spread models toward molecules with several desired properties at once. Diffusion generators make high quality structures but struggle to control complex competing trait constraints that real drug design demands.

Surrogate trait models carry doubt estimates, and the reward based signal uses them so the generator favors molecules whose predicted virtues are trustworthy, not just optimistic. Multi goal guidance balances potency, safety, and form together. Better controlled de novo design could shorten the search for candidate compounds in drug discovery pipelines.
arxiv-2510-21253:
Boaz Moav, Ryan Gabrys, and Eitan Yaakobi study how to store data in DNA, which packs information densely and lasts a long time. The bottleneck is synthesis, the step that builds many DNA strands in parallel, and current methods restrict which building blocks can be added at each cycle.

They propose a hybrid model where each cycle adds one block chosen from a limited set, covering both older methods as special cases. For that model they define complex synthesis sequences, work out the best possible information rate in tight form, and describe its long-run behavior. Algorithms find optimal sequences both for known strands and for a two-dimensional array version, giving the field a fuller theoretical base for large-scale DNA storage.
arxiv-2510-21653:
Xingyu Cheng and three co-authors solve a quantum difference equation governing the K-theory of Grassmannians. Grassmannians parametrize flat subspaces of a fixed dimension. Such equations encode how quantum symmetries deform classical geometry. Their solutions are expected to reveal hidden integrable structures. Those are the rare systems that can be solved exactly.

From their solution, the authors extract the Bethe ansatz equations in a large-scale limit. Those equations govern the integrable systems. Parallel results hold for the matching version of the theory. Solutions without the symmetry weighting are described too. As the payoff use, they match the quantum K-theory ring of the Grassmannian with a quantum five-vertex model. That is a spin chain of XXZ type. It gives readers a concrete spin system whose algebra mirrors the geometry.
arxiv-2510-21953:
Adrián P. Bustamante, Alessandra Celletti, and Christoph Lhotka study two ellipsoidal bodies that spin while orbiting each other under their own gravity, a setup found in binary asteroids and double planets. The question is how the two rotations talk to each other, and when they stay stable or fall into resonant lockstep.

The analysis climbs a ladder of models. With orbits treated as fixed Keplerian paths and only the strongest gravity terms kept, each spin evolves alone. Adding finer terms couples the rotations into the spin-spin problem, and finally letting the orbit itself respond gives the full problem. The authors check linear stability and numerically chase the main resonances. Work like this helps explain the tidy spin states seen in real double systems.
arxiv-2510-22053:
Paul C. Parsons argues that keeping science gateways alive depends on user experience in a much wider sense than tidy screens. Gateways are the web portals through which researchers reach shared instruments and data, and as they mature, funders and host institutions worry about whether they will last.

Drawing on interviews and consulting work with more than sixty-five gateway projects, Parsons finds three stances toward user experience: ad hoc, project-based, and strategic. In the narrow view, design arrives late as a usability check; in the wider view he advocates, staffing, infrastructure, community ties, and timelines all shape how a gateway is experienced and maintained. The paper offers gateway teams a practice-based vocabulary for treating design as a sustainability strategy rather than a final polish.
arxiv-2510-22253:
Daniele Iannotti, Lorenzo Campos Venuti, and Alioscia Hamma study how magic is spread across random quantum states. Magic, formally called non-stabilizerness, measures distance from the classically tame stabilizer states. It is the resource that makes quantum computation hard to fake on a laptop.

For states drawn uniformly at random, the authors study the stabilizer Rényi entropies. Their probability distribution is not smooth. It carries sharp features modeled on Van Hove singularities. Those are kinks known from the density of states in crystals. For a single qubit, the distribution of stabilizer purity diverges at a critical value. The value ties to a saddle point on the Bloch sphere, at the H-type magic states. An exact formula for one case matches simulations. The divergence vanishes in dimension three and above.
arxiv-2510-22753:
Charged particle clouds in a magnetic field raise a basic question. Will their velocity moments stay finite for all time? Immanuel Ben Porat leads a team with three co-authors. In 2025 they answer yes for two Vlasov-Poisson systems. These systems model plasma with self consistent electric fields.

One system is two dimensional and magnetized. The other is three dimensional with screening. The outside magnetic field may vary in space and time. If moments start finite, they stay finite. That yields global classical solutions. The team also proves sharp stability bounds. Their distance measure matches the unmagnetized case in strength.
arxiv-2510-22853:
Compositional data are shares that sum to a whole. Some zeros in such data are structural, not random. Francesco Porro, Fabio Rapallo, and Sara Sommariva test shared structure in 2025. They compare two groups of such data. Each group has its own zero pattern.

Different zero patterns block standard logratio methods. Logratios compare parts on a log scale. Their test checks for a common principal subspace. It fits Aitchison geometry and logratio analysis. Under logratio normality, they derive a null distribution. A bootstrap version avoids distribution assumptions. Bootstrap means resampling the data. Simulations check small sample behavior. A microbiome dataset illustrates the method.
arxiv-2510-23053:
Zhiyu Wang, Suman Raj, and Rajkumar Buyya propose AirFed, a framework for fleets of drones that share edge computing work. Many drones must plan paths, offload tasks, and split resources while meeting strict deadlines for ground devices. Older methods scale poorly, converge slowly, and share knowledge badly among drones.

AirFed joins federated learning, graph models of the fleet, and multi-agent reinforcement learning. Drones learn together without pooling all raw data, and graph links capture who can help whom. The design targets large Internet of Things deployments where fast, coordinated offloading decides service quality.
arxiv-2510-23253:
Sam Pollard and Michael Wray question whether video question answering benchmarks truly test video understanding, under the title that a video is not worth a thousand words. Benchmarks keep getting harder and models keep using longer contexts, often with large language model backbones. That raises a worry: models may lean on text and barely use the moving image.

The authors probe interactions between modalities and ask how to measure real progress. If a model answers from language priors alone, high scores mislead. Their critique pushes the field to design tests where watching the video is genuinely required.
arxiv-2510-23553:
Alexis Ellis and four co-authors present OntoPret, a formal framework that helps machines interpret what people are doing. As humans and robots team up in settings like modern factories, a machine has to judge complex behavior safely and in real time. Robot software often lacks a rich model of human action, while behavior catalogs built by psychologists are not made for live teamwork.

OntoPret is an ontology, a structured set of categories and rules that a computer can process. Rooted in cognitive science and built with a modular method, it classifies behaviors such as straying from a task or acting deceptively. The authors show it flexes across two very different settings, factory work and gameplay. Their aim is to lay the groundwork for machines that can reason about human intentions, not just motions.
arxiv-2510-23653:
Santiago Torres simulates how debris disks around young solar-system-like setups evolve inside dense star clusters, where close flybys can reshape a planetary system. Most stars are born in such crowds, and our own system's far comet cloud may be a scar of that era. Using the LonelyPlanets framework, which pairs two established simulation codes, he follows four giant planets plus either a compact or an extended debris disk.

Compact disks mostly built Kuiper belt and scattered disk populations through their own planets' gravity. Extended disks were sculpted by passing stars instead, forming Oort cloud-like reservoirs and flinging out interstellar comets at one to three kilometers per second. Flybys at shallow angles worked best, creating Sedna-like bodies and inner cloud analogues, while polar flybys puffed the outer disk toward a round cloud. The results tie comet reservoirs to the birthplaces of their stars.
arxiv-2510-23853:
Yize Cheng and seven co-authors show that language model agents are temporally blind: they act as if no time passes between messages. In real deployments, hours may elapse while an agent assumes a frozen context. That blindness distorts tool use — the agent either trusts stale context and skips needed tool calls, or distrusts it and repeats calls it already made.

To measure the problem, the team built TicToc, a dataset of multi-turn conversations across seventy-six scenarios with high, medium, and low time sensitivity. Human judges marked whether a tool call or a direct answer was right at each step. Even with timestamps shown, no model matched human time perception better than sixty-five percent in normalized alignment. Simple prompting fixes helped little for most models. Targeted post-training did align decisions better, marking a path toward agents that understand elapsed time the way people do.
arxiv-2510-24053:
Jacob B. Roberts and fifteen co-authors present FolDE, a method for optimizing proteins with very few experiments. Improving a protein means building and measuring mutants, which is slow and expensive. Active learning-guided directed evolution cuts the cost by predicting winners and testing in rounds, but naive rounds pick the top predictions, yielding look-alike training data that starves later rounds.

FolDE is designed to maximize campaign success. Its engine is naturalness-based warm-starting: outputs from a protein language model augment the activity measurements and sharpen predictions from the start. A constant-liar batch selector adds diversity, which matters in multi-mutation campaigns. Across simulations on twenty protein targets, FolDE found twenty-three percent more top-decile mutants than the baseline and was fifty-five percent likelier to land a top one percent mutant. The workflow is open source, putting the savings within any lab's reach.
arxiv-2510-24253:
Marcin Łobejko and two co-authors prove that discrete and continuous heat engines assisted by a catalyst behave equivalently. In a discrete two stroke engine, a catalyst is an auxiliary system that returns to its start, does no work, and never touches the heat baths, yet boosts power and efficiency. Such engines are easy to analyze but hard to build, since each stroke needs precise control.

Continuous engines, driven externally while coupled to both baths at once, are easier to realize in the lab. The authors map the discrete strokes onto continuous processes, with and without a catalyst. The equivalence carries catalytic advantages from the discrete framework into the continuous one, guiding real designs.
arxiv-2510-24353:
Hannes Schulze and two co-authors build graded meanings for nominal systems, which are models of languages and processes that carry data. Name allocation in these systems eases the known hardness of register based models. There is a trade off between how much the model can express and how fast it can be checked. One class, regular nondeterministic nominal automata, matches a lossy form of register automata when names must be fresh locally.

Full register automata are much harder to check. The nominal class, by contrast, allows inclusion tests in a bounded space class. Trace inclusion in the base systems shares that bound. The graded meanings refine how these systems are read. The aim is to keep the speed gains while drawing finer lines between data carrying processes.
arxiv-2510-24553:
Piotr Borodako and Adam Sawicki study the high dimension limit of characters of compact reductive Lie groups and what it means for quantum randomness. For a group element, they examine the normalized irreducible character as the representation dimension grows. When the group is simple, the limit vanishes except at the identity element.

For semisimple groups, the same result holds when the dimensions of all simple components grow without bound. Using approximate t-designs, the authors connect this vanishing to bounds on how much quantum randomness large quantum systems can produce. The work links representation theory to limits on random state generation in quantum information.
arxiv-2510-24653:
Veronica Thai and nine co-authors share a rich data set on how eye doctors read huge slide shots of tissue. Reading these shots is slow and hard, and right calls average about seventy in a hundred. A second reader does not fix the lack of match by much, so the field needs proof of where reads go wrong.

Their set, PathoGaze1.0, holds close to nineteen hours of eye, mouse, and screen track data from nineteen readers. In all it logs more than one hundred seventy thousand gaze stops and far more mouse moves. The data may help train both new doctors and AI aids.
arxiv-2510-24753:
M Malnou, the sole author, builds a math frame for lines that carry waves in high grade sound like amps. Such fake lines use small coils and charge stores in a chain, plus parts that bend with the wave. To work well, the tones in the line must keep set ties of energy and push.

No shared frame yet tells which spread curves such a line can reach, the author notes. Two views are drawn on: one shapes the line in space with fixed parts, the other shapes it in tone with parts that shift by tone. That split shows core limits and leads to new amp forms. One new form is laid out in the work.
arxiv-2510-25153:
Hannah Comiskey, Niamh Cahill, Leontine Alkema, David Fraizer, and Worapree Maneesoonthorn project shares of birth control supply by zone when local data are thin. Where women get their birth control, from state or shop sources, shapes fair and green care plans. Land wide reads hide how shares shift from zone to zone.

As states push care calls down to zones, zone reads are now a must, yet they are logged on no set beat. The team's Bayes plan draws hid traits from a known health poll to fill the gap. It gives zone shares with odds based bands, not just point reads. That lets zone staff plan with doubt in view.
arxiv-2510-25353:
Zheng-Cheng Liang, Zhi-Yuan Li, and Yi-Ming Hu study gravitational waves. Their 2025 paper concerns a stochastic background signal. That background comes from eccentric stellar-mass binary black holes. Eccentric means their orbits are not circular. Such systems may reveal clues about their origins. Spaceborne detectors could observe this background signal.

The authors use a Bayesian framework for assessment. They account for contamination from the Galactic foreground. Three formation channels for binaries are covered. Isolated binary evolution is the first channel. Dynamical assembly in globular clusters is second. Assembly in active galactic nuclei is third. TianQin, LISA, and Taiji could detect some backgrounds. Four years of operation would be enough, they find. Signal strengths differ strongly by detector choice. Backgrounds from galactic nuclei show a spectral turnover. That feature could distinguish them from power-law backgrounds.
arxiv-2510-25953:
Prathamesh Tamhane, working alone, builds a plain language front end for a major astronomy database. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey holds vast data on stars and galaxies, but users must write SQL, a database query language, and know the schema to retrieve it. That barrier blocks many non experts who could use the data.

Tamhane fine tunes Microsoft Phi-2, a compact transformer model, on pairs of plain questions and matching SQL taken from survey examples. The interface turns a user request into a query that the SkyServer archive can run. Early tests show the model produces valid queries that are largely correct in meaning across varied astronomy requests, which suggests small models can serve specialized archives well.
arxiv-2510-26253:
Takuma Sato, Seiya Kawano, and Koichiro Yoshino show that teaching a language model a little pragmatics helps it read implied meanings. Pragmatics is the study of how context shapes meaning beyond literal words, and grasping implication is central to human communication. Their approach places an overview of pragmatic theories, such as Gricean pragmatics and Relevance Theory, into the prompt as in context guidance.

The model then reasons step by step toward an interpretation, guided by the theory. Compared with a baseline that prompts intermediate reasoning without theory, their method scored up to nine point six percent higher on pragmatic reasoning tasks in their experiments. Even naming the theories without detail gave larger models a small gain of about one to three percent.
arxiv-2510-26353:
Albi Isufaj, Pablo Molla, and Helmut Prendinger present methods for money prediction that is both clear and reliable. Large neural models call markets well but are opaque, which challenges trust and rule based compliance. Their first approach uses a prompt with a time series base model, Time-LLM, to avoid a wrong direction call. Their second pairs base model calls with a trust checks scorer that filters out weak calls.

A third strand argues for rule based reasoning that encodes domain rules, giving open grounds for each call. Experiments on equity and crypto coins data show the combined design reduces false positives and supports chosen execution. Only calls that pass both trust checks and clarity checks are acted on. The goal is checkable money AI.
arxiv-2510-26653:
Daniela Martin and Joseph Gallego test deep learning for tracking sea ice drift in the Arctic. Knowing how ice moves matters for navigation, climate research, and forecasting. Optical flow, a vision method that estimates motion between images pixel by pixel, is standard in computer vision but little tried on satellite radar images of ice.

Martin and Gallego run the first large benchmark of forty-eight deep learning optical flow models on RADARSAT-2 radar imagery, scored against GNSS-tracked buoys. Several models reached sub-kilometre accuracy, with errors of a few hundred metres. That is small next to the scales of ice motion and the needs of Arctic navigation. Unlike sparse buoy readings, flow gives a drift estimate for every pixel, which opens new options for navigation and climate modelling.
arxiv-2510-26753:
Niccolò Preti, with eight co-authors, simplifies the theory of rotating supersolids. A supersolid flows without friction yet keeps a crystal-like pattern, and a recent two-fluid model describes its mixed classical and superfluid motion at finite temperature. For a rigidly rotating supersolid, the team derives a single-fluid model instead.

Preti and the team show the seemingly separate contributions emerge from one global wavefunction whose phase varies in space. That view lets them design experiments to excite and detect the odd rotation dynamics of annular, ring-shaped supersolids. Those include partially quantized supercurrents, where each atom carries less than one standard unit of angular momentum. The results extend to a wider class of density-modulated superfluids.
arxiv-2510-27053:
Manohar Kalluri and Andrew Hillier compare a plasma instability in flat simulations versus full three-dimensional ones. The magnetic Rayleigh-Taylor instability drives mixing when a heavy fluid rests on a lighter one under a magnetic field. It shapes behavior in space plasmas and lab experiments alike, yet computing limits often force two-dimensional studies.

Running direct simulations in both settings across weak to strong fields, the pair find richer mode mixing in three dimensions. The three-dimensional layer mixes at small scales with less bulk spread, releases less stored energy, and dissipates more through small vortices. Growth rises steadily with field strength in three dimensions but not in two. Two-dimensional runs still track magnetic-to-kinetic energy conversion fairly, but not the full turbulence.
arxiv-2510-27253:
Qiyan Deng leads five co-authors in influence-weighted dataset distillation, a way to shrink training data without treating every example as equal. Distillation condenses a large dataset into a small synthetic subset that trains models nearly as well. Most methods assume all real instances contribute equally, yet real data mix informative examples with redundant or harmful ones.

Their framework, IWD, uses influence functions to estimate each instance effect on the distillation goal, then weights instances adaptively. Helpful data gain priority while weak or harmful data are downweighted. The modular design plugs into diverse existing distillation frameworks. Empirical results suggest consistent quality gains for distilled sets and model accuracy improvements up to several percent, arguing data quality should guide compression.
arxiv-2510-27353:
Julien Herrmann and Guillaume Pallez recheck a bold claim about AI and math in this 2025 paper. The claim: language models helped find new tricks for online bin packing, the task of filling bins as items arrive one by one. Reports said model-bred rules gave fresh insight for two standard item patterns. The pair take the rules apart piece by piece.

They find the rules stay opaque, hard to read even for experts in the field. From the wreckage they build a new class of rules that are simpler, faster, and clearer. The new rules also travel better to fresh cases. That hints the test cases were fairly simple all along. Their moral: claims for AI-found math need hard checks and full context.
arxiv-2510-27553:
M. McMurdo, T. Van Doorsselaere, N. Magyar, L. Banovic, and D. Lim compare kink-wave and Alfven-wave heating in a solar atmosphere model inside the MPI-AMRVAC simulation code. The coronal heating problem remains fundamental: standard Alfven wave solar models reproduce large-scale corona structure but neglect extra wave modes arising from transverse structuring. The team extends the physics module with both wave energy contributions plus radiative cooling.

Parameter studies vary Alfven reflection rates and the relative injection of the two wave energies, validated against Python-based simulations. Kink-wave-driven models sustain a stable atmosphere with realistic coronal temperature and density without artificial background heating, unlike Alfven-only models needing ad hoc terms. The higher kink heating rate at equal injected energy explains the difference, also shown on a larger-scale domain sustained entirely by kink heating.
arxiv-2510-27653:
Nathanael S. Schwindt, Anthony P. Straub, Michael F. Toney, and Michael R. Shirts probe how ions sit inside water-cleaning membranes in 2025 using computer models of moving atoms. Reverse osmosis and fine filters use polyamide films, whose inner build governs what passes and what is blocked. How ions bind inside the wet film was not fully known.

The model film was built to match how real films are made, then ions were tracked for long runs. Nearest oxygen gaps around ions match those in plain water. Counts of nearby partners drop, though, since outer partners shift past a cutoff rather than vanish. Positively charged ions bind tight to two kinds of oxygen sites in the film. Such detail can guide films that block salt better.
arxiv-2511-00153:
Justin Yu, Yide Shentu, and Di Wu present EgoMI, a framework for teaching robots active vision and whole-body manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations. Humans coordinate head and hand movement while manipulating, fixating visually before acting, which creates dynamic head motion that static robot sensors cannot copy, causing distribution shift. Their interface captures synchronized end-effector and active head trajectories from human demonstrators.

Robots can then learn policies that include where to look, not just how to move. Robotics readers get a way to transfer a subtle human skill: viewpoint control as part of manipulation. Closing the embodiment gap on vision may matter as much as matching arm motions.
arxiv-2511-00753:
Rankeya Datta, Jack Garzella, and Kevin Tucker work in algebra on rings that arise in the geometry of Berkovich. Their paper concerns dagger algebras and Tate algebras in prime characteristic, a setting where a special map called Frobenius plays a central role.

Using methods from two recent works, they prove that these algebras have a property named intersection flat Frobenius. In plain terms, taking p-th roots over such a ring behaves well with respect to flatness, a basic exactness condition in algebra. A further result follows for tight closure theory: certain completed rings built from these algebras contain the test elements that theory needs.
arxiv-2511-01553:
Elvin Hajizada and seven colleagues put a continually learning system onto Intel's Loihi 2 neuromorphic chip, hardware that computes with spikes like neurons do. The target is edge artificial intelligence that must learn new classes from single examples, one at a time, on a tight power budget, where ordinary processors waste energy on every small update.

Their network, CLP-SNN, reworks the Continually Learning Prototypes algorithm into event-driven dynamics: a local self-normalizing rule, new prototypes grown when novelty appears, and reward-gated plasticity in each neuron. It is the first online continual learner deployed on Loihi 2. On the OpenLORIS benchmark it matched standard baselines at one-shot learning, and each prediction-plus-update step took 0.33 milliseconds at a tiny fraction of the energy of a Jetson-based rival.
arxiv-2511-01753:
Zachary Hansen and Yuliya Lierler give a formal semantics for a modern feature of answer set programming, the logic programming paradigm behind the CLINGO solver. The feature is conditional literals, subformulas that act like nested implications inside rule bodies and let programs read almost like first-order logic.

Established semantics for programs using conditional literals, and arithmetic along with them, works only through a translation into infinitary propositional logic, which forces grounding. Hansen and Lierler instead build a semantics directly on the SM operator, requiring no grounding at all. Their main theorem proves the new semantics and the established one match in full. So programmers can trust that the cleaner definition captures the same programs' meanings.
arxiv-2511-01853:
Eric Heller and thirteen colleagues argue that a whole class of materials has been misunderstood because physicists treated lattice vibrations too statically. Strange metals show resistivities that grow linearly with temperature, at the so-called Planckian rate, over thousands of degrees. Phonons were long dismissed as incapable of explaining that. The authors contend the dismissal rested on perturbative methods that missed time-dependent, nonperturbative electron-lattice physics.

Their lens is quantum acoustics, a framework parallel to the quantum optics Glauber built for light sixty years ago. The team treats the standard Fröhlich model nonperturbatively, in the right parameter regime. From it they derive Planckian transport, polarons, charge density waves, and pseudogaps. They also account for the Drude peak anomaly and the missing low-temperature resistivity behaviors. The new physics, they claim, was hiding in the old model all along.
arxiv-2511-02053:
Jinchao Feng, Charles Kulick, and Sui Tang build statistical tools for learning how particles in mixed populations push and pull on each other, using only their recorded paths. Flocks, swarms, and cell colonies all follow this pattern: simple microscopic rules generate complex collective behaviour. With several species, the number of unknown kernels multiplies, and asymmetric relations such as predator and prey must be allowed.

Their Gaussian process framework treats the learning problem in a nonparametric Bayesian way. The analysis proves the kernels can be recovered from data, gives quantitative error bounds, and shows the posterior estimates are statistically optimal, building on earlier single-species theory. Numerical experiments confirm the predictions and show advantages over current kernel-based methods, offering a full inference pipeline from recorded paths to the laws behind them.
arxiv-2511-02453:
Thomas Sanchez, Pedro Gordaliza, and Meritxell Bach Cuadra warn that many claimed improvements of medical imaging AI over rivals may be statistical mirages, and that the mirage is worse than previously calculated. Small performance gains are already likely to be false positives. The missing ingredient in earlier analyses is underspecification: models with nearly identical validation scores can behave differently on new data simply because of random initialisation or training dynamics.

The authors extend a recent statistical framework for false outperformance claims by adding underspecification as an extra source of variance. Their simulations show that even modest seed-to-seed variability, around one percent, substantially raises the amount of evidence needed before a superiority claim is justified. The practical message for medical imaging is blunt: report and model your training variance, or small winning margins mean little.
arxiv-2511-02553:
Kristian Moring, Christoph Scheven, and Leah Schätzler prove a regularity result for a class of parabolic equations whose domain moves in time. The systems have p-growth structure, modelled on the parabolic p-Laplace equation, and are posed with Cauchy-Dirichlet data in a bounded noncylindrical domain. Such a region is one in space-time whose spatial slice can change shape as time advances. The question is whether the gradient of a solution is more integrable than the equation alone guarantees.

The result needs growth exponents above an explicit dimension-dependent threshold. The domains must satisfy regularity conditions and neither grow nor shrink too fast. Then the authors prove global higher integrability of the gradient, up to the boundary and the initial time. The conclusion is new even in the linear-flavoured case where the exponent equals two, the borderline that classical theory left open in this generality.
arxiv-2511-02653:
Neutron stars pack more than a sun's mass into a ball the size of a city, and their cores may hold quark matter. Milena Albino, Tuhin Malik, Marcio Ferreira, and Constanca Providencia weigh that idea in a 2025 Bayesian study. They model the outer layers with a relativistic mean field theory and the core with two quark models, then test each mix against real data.

The tests use nuclear lab facts, X-ray data from NICER, and gravitational waves from the merger GW170817. One quark model lets quarks appear just above normal nuclear density, even in light stars. The other holds off until twice that density, so light stars likely stay quark free. Both allow quark cores in heavy stars near two solar masses.
arxiv-2511-03053:
Ziyang Xu, Olaf Wysocki, and Christoph Holst predict the uncertainty of mobile laser scanning point clouds without leaning on costly ground truth. Such scans feed precise work like building models and deformation checks, but knowing each point's error usually needs a reference scan that is expensive or impossible to get. Their 2025 framework learns the error from the cloud's own geometry.

The method picks the best neighborhood for each point and extracts geometric features from it. On real data, a gradient boosting model matched a random forest's accuracy while running about three times faster. The predicted uncertainty tracks the cloud-to-cloud distance used as the error measure. The result is early proof that point-level scanning error is learnable from shape alone.
arxiv-2511-03253:
Hajime Fukuda, Takeo Moroi, and Thanaporn Sichanugrist suggest borrowing an error control trick to sharpen hunts for wave-like dark matter. Quantum sensors looking for that faint, wavy signal lose ground to noise that points the same way as the signal itself. Their plan links several sensors so noise in each one can be checked against the others, much like error correction in quantum computing.

For small sensor counts, the gain grows with the square root of the number used. With enough sensors, the setup matches the best limit set by ideal measuring, a bar that plain unlinked sensors cannot reach here because the wave phase is unknown. The idea fits many sensor kinds, including arrays of tuned cavities. It could widen the reach of future dark matter searches.
arxiv-2511-03353: Thomas Leble proves that the hexagonal lattice is locally best among all point layouts for a wide family of pair interactions. Energy per unit volume is the score, and the interactions allowed are fully monotone functions of squared distance, covering Gaussian pulls and power laws. Locally best means no small rearrangement of points can lower the energy further. Hexagonal order appears across nature, from honeycomb to crystal planes, and such proofs explain why one pattern keeps winning under many different force laws.
arxiv-2511-03453:
Davor Dragicevic extends a recent characterization of generalized splitting behavior in evolving systems to far wider settings. A dichotomy splits motion into parts that grow and parts that shrink under a chosen rate function. Recent work tied that split to two test traits, expansiveness and noncriticality, for ordinary equations in finite dimensions.

Dragicevic carries the tie to arbitrary invertible evolution families on Banach spaces, which include many partial differential settings. The proof runs on a time-rescaling trick and is, by the author's account, much simpler than the earlier route. Clean characterizations matter because they let researchers verify a hard global trait by checking two more concrete ones.
arxiv-2511-03553:
Sofie Helene Bruun and Dan Saattrup Smart build MultiZebraLogic, a benchmark of logic puzzles in nine languages checked by fluent speakers. Zebra puzzles hide a unique arrangement behind a trail of clues, making them a clean test of step-by-step reasoning. Puzzle size and clue counts tune the challenge, and a fresh twist adds red herring clues that say nothing useful.

Red herrings do make modern models stumble far more, the tests show. Modest grids already strain a plain model, while larger grids challenge a reasoning model. Scores also shift with language and with how culturally tuned the puzzle theme feels. Careful multilingual checks like this expose reasoning gaps that English-only tests hide.
arxiv-2511-03853:
Joong M Park is the lead author among fourteen authors reporting direct evidence that vortices in superconductors can multiply quasiparticles, the broken-pair excitations that spoil quantum states in transmon qubits. A fast quasiparticle relaxing inside a vortex core can break more Cooper pairs, because the excitation gap there is reduced and confinement is stronger.

Using femtosecond magneto-reflection spectroscopy at low excitation levels, the team watched quasiparticle numbers keep rising before the usual phonon bottleneck. The growth depended strongly on magnetic-field-tuned vortex density and vanished at higher fluence. Estimated density rose by about thirty-four percent at the highest vortex densities studied. The finding names a concrete poisoning route circuit designers must manage.
arxiv-2511-03953:
Wuxia Chen, Taposh Banerjee, and Vahid Tarokh address quickest change detection for Markov processes whose transition rules are unknown. Instead of estimating full likelihoods, they learn the conditional score, the gradient of the log density of the next state given the current one, directly from sample pairs.

A score-based CUSUM procedure uses differences of conditional Hyvarinen scores to flag kernel changes, with a truncated version keeping increments bounded. For uniformly ergodic chains, exponential lower bounds on mean time to false alarm and asymptotic upper bounds on detection delay are proved. High-dimensional settings, where explicit likelihoods are impractical, are the main target for this detection route.
arxiv-2511-04053:
Hirohane Takagi, Gouki Minegishi, Shota Kizawa, Issey Sukeda, and Hitomi Yanaka investigate how large language models internally handle several number attributes of one entity at once. Behavioural studies show number reasoning errors, but the inner cause has stayed unclear, and shared latent subspaces for numbers are their hypothesis.

Linear probing with partial correlation analysis, plus prompt-based weakness tests across model sizes, show models encode real-world numerical correlations yet steadily amplify them. Irrelevant number context shifts magnitude representations in consistent ways, with downstream effects that vary by model size. The findings expose a decision-making weakness and point toward fairer, representation-aware controls when attributes are tangled.
arxiv-2511-04153:
Fahim Ahmed is the lead author among seven authors benchmarking multi-agent pipelines that turn natural language questions into SQL queries. Text-to-SQL could let non-specialists query databases directly, but language models struggle with large schemas and complex reasoning, and prior work favours elaborate pipelines on flagship models over smaller, efficient ones.

Three designs compete: agents that discuss and refine queries before a judge decides, a planner-coder split, and several coders whose outputs a reasoning agent ranks. On a Bird-Bench development set, discussion lifted a small model's execution accuracy by up to about eleven percent after three rounds. Systematic comparison across model sizes guides cheaper system design.
arxiv-2511-04253:
J Z Kaminski and K Krajewska study ionization by a train of extreme ultraviolet pulses, solving the time-dependent Schroedinger equation with care, with the laser field treated exactly. Most work stops at a first-order nondipole approximation, which understates radiation pressure as field strength grows.

Photoelectron momentum and energy distributions show comb structures, with peaks shifted by emission angle. Exact results diverge from the first-order form more strongly at higher field strength. Angle-integrated spectra reveal extra fine structure inside comb peaks. Because the atomic potential is kept across the whole interaction region, loss of comb coherence with more pulses appears and is blamed on rescattering of the freed electrons.
arxiv-2511-04453:
Obada Kraishan, writing alone, tracks what a Hacker News launch does to GitHub stars. Hacker News is a key launch spot for open-source AI tools, yet its instant effect is rarely measured. His system runs only on public data feeds, so anyone can repeat the study.

The study covers one hundred thirty-eight launches of AI and language model tools from 2024 and 2025. Repositories gained on average one hundred twenty-one stars in a day and two hundred eighty-nine in a week. Models from simple elastic nets to gradient boosting find posting time a key predictor. Well-timed launches can gain hundreds of extra stars.
arxiv-2511-04553:
Alejandro Gomez Cadavid leads seven authors pairing quantum seeds with classical search for the LABS problem. LABS asks for binary sequences with very low autocorrelation, a hard combinatorial search. Their hybrid, QE-MTS, starts a memetic tabu search from quantum-prepared states.

Digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization supplies those strong starting points. For lengths from twenty-seven to thirty-seven, solution time scales far better than the best classical heuristic. It also beats the quantum approximate optimization algorithm while using six times less circuit depth. A bootstrap analysis projects a crossover near length forty-seven, where the hybrid pulls ahead.
arxiv-2511-04753:
Zonglin Lyu and three colleagues propose Condition Preference Optimization for controllable image generation. ControlNet lets users steer text-to-image models with image-based signals like edges. Follow-up work improved consistency but only optimized low-noise steps cheaply.

That shortcut ignores high-noise steps and adds approximation error, they argue. Direct preference optimization across all steps looks natural, yet uncertainty undermines it. Their condition-focused variant reshapes the preference training for control fidelity. Better control across the whole sampling path would make guided generation more faithful to sketches, poses, and layouts that users supply. The work targets practical control without retraining the base generator.
arxiv-2511-04953:
Kristóf Bérczi and co-authors prove a case of the rainbow arborescence guess, a claim about directed graphs whose arcs are painted in many colors. In the set-up, each color class by itself forms a spanning tree shape that fans out from a root.

The guess says a spanning tree exists that uses each color once and only once. The authors prove it when the base undirected graph is a simple cycle. Their proof adds one firm case to a broad open claim in graph theory, where most graph shapes still lack a proof.
arxiv-2511-05053:
Wakuto Matsumi and Riaz-Ul-Haque Mian add custom commands to a RISC-V graphics chip to speed mixed models that join hyperdimensional computing with neural nets. Hyperdimensional methods are light and parallel but weak on hard image tasks, while neural nets are strong yet costly.

RISC-V chips are open and can be reshaped for niche work, unlike locked designs. The authors built four custom commands tuned for hyperdimensional steps and ran hybrid image workloads on them. Their tests check how far such tailored hardware can cut the cost of running these mixed models.
arxiv-2511-05553:
Xinyan Cai and co-authors present EVLP, a planner meant to help robots carry out long tasks that need both words and images. A robot must break a job into steps and picture each stage to act well. Past methods planned text and vision apart, which led to clashes between the two streams.

EVLP joins both in one generation framework. It learns language reasoning and image creation together, with cross-modal attention linking them. Training adds forward and inverse dynamics tasks so the model ties actions to their visual effects. The authors say this unified planning makes long manipulation jobs more consistent and more accurate than split approaches.
arxiv-2511-05653:
Julius Adolff, Selim Hotinli, and Neal Dalal ask whether a microwave-background effect can reveal what dark energy is made of. Dark energy drives the universe's speeding expansion, but most tests only track the expansion history. The kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, from electrons moving in bulk, can probe how dark energy behaves on smaller scales.

Combining that signal with galaxy clustering, the authors forecast results for planned surveys. Adding the new data tightens limits on two key dark energy parameters and breaks ties that older probes leave. For a standard sound speed, the direct effects of dark energy clumping are tiny. With slower sound speeds they move into reach, so near-term surveys mainly test consistency.
arxiv-2511-05853:
Bingyang Guo, Qiang Zuo, and Ruiyun Yu build the first public 3D data set for finding surface defects on ceramic chip-package substrates. These substrates are key parts in integrated circuit packaging, but their complex shapes and tiny flaws, plus the lack of any public data set, have held back automated inspection.

Their data set, CPS3D-Seg, holds thirteen hundred point-cloud samples across twenty product types, each with point-level labels and, they report, the best resolution among industrial 3D data sets. They benchmark leading segmentation methods on it. They also propose CINet, a method using causal reasoning to discount confounders in the clouds. In tests CINet clearly beat existing algorithms on overlap and accuracy.
arxiv-2511-05953:
Atharva Mehta and co-authors raise a fairness alarm for AI music systems: whose music gets heard, and whose gets distorted. The field has worried about copyright, deepfakes, and transparency in generative music. This team points at cultural and genre bias, which shapes what creators, distributors, and listeners experience.

Bias can garble traditions from the Global South, producing outputs like distorted ragas that feel false to their own communities. That erodes creator trust, narrows what gets made, and risks erasing cultures from the record. The authors do not present a new model. They offer fixes at three levels: the data sets used for training, the models themselves, and the interfaces people meet, so music AI represents more traditions faithfully.
arxiv-2511-06053:
Yan He and Adetunmise Dada design a flat metalens that focuses infrared light of many colors to the same point. The short-wave infrared band they target serves quantum sensing, molecular spectroscopy, and free-space communication. Lenses there suffer color blur and are bulky to integrate.

Their lens is a pattern of silicon bars on a calcium fluoride base, each cell smaller than the wavelength. Tuning bar length and width controls both phase and delay, canceling dispersion while shaping the wavefront. Simulations showed the focal length stayed within a few percent of target across the whole band. Polarization across the focal spot varied only weakly with wavelength. The design promises compact infrared optics for small devices.
arxiv-2511-06153:
Sixtus Dakurah introduces a statistical test for comparing the shapes of functional brain networks. Brain networks carry patterns that reflect how the brain is organized, yet standard tests struggle to compare those patterns fairly. The new test checks whether two groups of networks are topologically equivalent, meaning their shapes match.

Under equivalence, shape features can be swapped between groups without warping either network, which grounds the permutation test. Distances between persistence diagrams supply the test statistic, and heat diffusion smooths noisy connections while keeping shape intact. Simulations favor the test over standard two-sample tests, and applied to ADHD study brain scans it finds real shape differences tied to cannabis use.
arxiv-2511-06453:
Biswajit Deb and Atri Deshamukhya test three inflation models inside a modified gravity theory against the newest sky data. Precise cosmic microwave background results have already ruled out many classic models of the universe's early rapid expansion by tightening limits on gravitational waves. Modified gravity offers room to rescue models that standard gravity cannot save.

The models studied are mutated hilltop, D-brane, and Woods-Saxon inflation, all placed in a minimal f(R,T) gravity where the function mixes curvature with the trace of the energy-momentum tensor. Predicted values for the spectral tilt, tensor ratio, and its running were charted and compared with several major datasets. Parts of the parameter space survive all current bounds.
arxiv-2511-06553:
Mario Bukal sharpens the predicted speed at which solutions of a thin-film equation settle into their final shape. The equation governs how a thin liquid layer spreads, pushing material through a fourth-order flow. Related equations, including the DLSS equation from semiconductor physics, share the same family structure.

Bukal rescales time in a way that preserves the solution's second moment, then measures distance to the steady state with a relative Rényi entropy. The resulting convergence rates beat those from the classical relative entropy, especially at early and middle times, and imply tighter control in the plain integral norm. The argument is formal for the family but can be made rigorous for strong thin-film solutions.
arxiv-2511-07253:
Umberto Cappellazzo and four co-authors unify speech recognition across hearing, lip-reading, and both together inside one large language model. Systems for automatic, visual, and audio-visual speech recognition are usually trained separately, wasting resources and missing cross-task synergies, and their fixed-rate token compression cannot trade accuracy against efficiency. Omni-AVSR instead trains a single model across multiple audio and visual granularities, adapting the matryoshka representation idea so one model supports elastic inference.

Three LoRA-based adaptation plans are compared for balancing shared knowledge against task-certain specialization in the backbone model. On the LRS2 and LRS3 benchmarks the unified model matched or beat state-of-the-art baselines while using greatly fewer training and deployment resources. It stayed robust under acoustic noise, and the authors analyze how performance scales with model size.
arxiv-2511-07453:
Guillermo Umbricht, Diana Rubio, and Domingo Tarzia analyze heat flow through a two-layer slab. Each layer conducts, carries, and makes or soaks up heat as it warms or cools. Outside faces exchange heat with surroundings, and the joint between layers resists flow.

An exact solution built with Fourier methods describes the heat field in two dimensions. A stable finite difference scheme then handles chosen cases numerically. Checks against known solutions and simulations match expected behavior. Engineers modeling layered walls, coatings, or devices gain a tested reference. The analysis shows how interface resistance and internal sources reshape heating and cooling.
arxiv-2511-07553:
Swadesh Vhakta, Denis Osipov, and Reetam Sen Biswas diagnose power grid collapse risk without running heavy time simulations. After a disturbance, governors respond and frequency settles somewhere new. Operators need to know whether that resting point is healthy, and if not, which weakness caused failure.

Governor behavior is folded into steady-state power flow equations, adding frequency as a solved variable. Sparse optimization then finds the smallest dangerous weaknesses. The method answers survivability and vulnerability questions from a static snapshot. Grid planners gain a fast screening tool for instability, useful as renewable swings make frequency control harder to guarantee.
arxiv-2511-07753: Viqar Husain and Irfan Javed report an inconsistency in one approach to quantum gravity. Semiclassical gravity keeps spacetime classical while matter follows quantum rules, replacing matter terms in the Einstein constraints with expectation values from quantum states. In the canonical formulation, those constraints must close into a consistent algebra. Husain and Javed show the algebra does not close, so the formulation contradicts itself. The short result warns that expectation-value sourcing, at least in canonical form, cannot serve as a consistent halfway house between classical geometry and quantum matter.
arxiv-2511-07953:
Francesco Battistoni, Aris Daniilidis, Carlo Alberto De Bernardi, and Enrico Miglierina revisit alternating projections in Hilbert spaces. The method bounces between two closed convex sets to find a best approximation point. Borwein and Bauschke introduced regular pairs in 1993 to guarantee that this process converges in norm.

Later work showed regular pairs also survive small variational changes to the method, under some boundedness conditions. These authors prove the converse: stability under such changes forces the pair to be regular. Their converse needs no boundedness assumption on the best approximation sets, which sharpens the known characterization.
arxiv-2511-08053:
Suparna Sarkar, Soumya Satpathi, and Swapan Pati examine localization in an open quasiperiodic ladder with dissipation. Particles in quasiperiodic potentials can spread out, stay localized, or mix both behaviors in varied energy ranges. Earlier routes to a mixed phase needed special hopping patterns or constrained potentials in one dimension.

Here usual nearest neighbor hopping suffices once energy loss and gain enter the system. An exact link between the open system spectrum and a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian guides the analysis. Balanced and imbalanced dissipation patterns produce varied phase maps, and changing dissipation strength tunes the critical points and the width of the mixed phase window.
arxiv-2511-08153:
Swaraj Pratim Sarmah and Umananda Dev Goswami ask whether two classes of active galaxies can supply the diffuse ultra high energy cosmic rays seen on Earth. Flat spectrum radio quasars and BL Lacertae objects are both plausible accelerators. The authors model their populations using luminosity dependent density evolution taken from observed gamma ray luminosity functions.

Cosmic ray nuclei are then propagated through space with energy losses from background photons. Resulting spectra are compared with Pierre Auger and Telescope Array data, and sky maps include magnetic diffusion effects. Both source types can match the flux, but anisotropy and source density disfavor quasars, while BL Lac objects stay consistent.
arxiv-2511-08553:
Mohamed Siala and two co-authors propose a new modulation family for future wireless systems, called Nyquist Signaling Modulation. Inspired by faster-than-Nyquist signaling, it deliberately allows controlled overlap between symbols, shaped by finite-impulse-response filters designed for the purpose.

The scheme works in any number of dimensions, including mixed setups, and can balance energy while preserving the key distance property of simple two-level signaling. For the one-dimensional case the authors derive closed-form optimal filters, and simulations track the theory across wide signal-to-noise ranges. An analog generator-matrix version merges modulation with coding in one structure. Paired with LDPC codes, or used for joint source and channel coding, the design aims at flexible, low-complexity physical layers for 6G.
arxiv-2511-08653:
Kaleem Ullah Qasim and Jiashu Zhang speed up tiny recursive reasoning models, small networks that refine their answers over repeated steps and can rival much larger models. Training them is slow, though, partly because every run uses full recursion depth and equal supervision weight from the start.

Their method, CGAR, treats depth as a curriculum: training begins with shallow recursion and deepens in three stages, cutting floating-point work by about forty percent. A second piece weights early supervision steps more heavily, with importance decaying exponentially, which lowers gradient variance. On Sudoku-Extreme the combined method trains about one point seven times faster with a tiny accuracy cost. Models also halt reliably at test time using fewer reasoning steps.
arxiv-2511-08953:
Phil Attard reviews the modern theory of three linked quantum effects: Bose-Einstein condensation, superfluidity, and superconductivity. The review sets out the rule that drives superfluid flow and the equation of motion for the condensed bosons.

Computer runs on Lennard-Jones helium-4 give the lambda point and the superfluid viscosity. The account of high-temperature superconductivity is presented in full. Attard also compares the modern approach with older ones: ground-state condensation, irrotational flow, and the macroscopic wavefunction. The piece serves as an entry point for newcomers to a field with several rival schools.
arxiv-2511-09153:
M. A. Probst and eight co-authors report the first spectroscopic reverberation mapping of WPVS 48, a nearby narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy. Reverberation mapping times how long light from the bright center takes to echo off surrounding gas. Their campaign used the ten-metre Southern African Large Telescope at 24 epochs over seven months in 2013 and 2014.

The team found a layered broad-line region, with hydrogen and helium lines responding from about 12 to 16 light-days out. From line widths and distances they estimate a central black hole near thirteen million solar masses. It appears to feed at about 39 percent of its Eddington limit. Continuum delays of up to eight days point to extra diffuse light from the same zone.
arxiv-2511-09753:
Nicolas Venkovic and Hartwig Anzt study how to compute sparse approximate inverses for symmetric positive definite matrices, a step that makes large linear systems faster to solve. A fixed sparsity pattern can miss key features of the true inverse, such as definiteness. The authors instead examine iterative methods whose sparse steps update their nonzero structure globally at each step through short recurrences.

They analyze the minimal residual method, a new locally optimal variant, and a conjugate gradient version with sparse matrix steps. For these matrices the minimal residual method is shown to converge steadily regardless of the starting guess. Practical dropping rules keep the inverses sparse, and numerical tests measure how well each resulting approximation works as a preconditioner.
arxiv-2511-10053:
Z. Rajabi Najjar and K. Azizi compute the masses of bound states made entirely of top quarks, motivated by a recent experimental hint. The CMS and ATLAS collaborations reported a pseudoscalar enhancement near the top-antitop threshold with significance above five sigma, suggesting a short-lived bound state nicknamed toponium. The authors study the pseudoscalar and vector toponium states plus the triply-top baryon using QCD sum rules.

Their calculation includes perturbative terms and nonperturbative operators up to dimension eight. The pseudoscalar mass estimate agrees with the near-threshold events, and both toponium states show negative binding energy, consistent with genuine bound states. The triply-top baryon's mass lands slightly above the sum of three top masses. The results give targets for searches at the LHC and future colliders.
arxiv-2511-10453:
Irina Saparina and Mirella Lapata address a common frustration with large language models: ambiguous requests. Models usually pick one reading of a vague request silently, which can annoy users or create safety risks. Their alternative is a single structured reply that lists the plausible readings of the request, each paired with its own answer.

Training uses reinforcement learning with a double goal. On ambiguous inputs it must cover as many valid readings as possible, and on clear inputs it must avoid inventing extra ones. The only supervision needed is several valid answers per input, with no clarification dialogues. Tests on conversational question answering and semantic parsing beat baseline coverage. Human judges also found the stated readings meaningful and well matched to their answers.
arxiv-2511-10553:
Mónica Clapp, Benedetta Pellacci, and Angela Pistoia study the Yamabe problem on compact Riemannian manifolds that have a boundary. The question asks for a metric, conformal to the given one, with constant scalar curvature inside and constant mean curvature on the boundary. It reduces to a nonlinear boundary-value problem with critical growth.

For positive solutions, the theory is by now complete, but sign-changing, or nodal, solutions are still largely open. The authors prove that least-energy sign-changing solutions exist when the manifold is positive and the boundary mean curvature is a non-negative constant. The dimension must be at least seven, and the boundary must have a nonumbilic point. Their proof is based on energy methods, built on conformal invariants and sharp energy bounds.
arxiv-2511-10953:
Wenrui Li, Wei Han, and their colleagues present a network that sums up videos with help from written prompts. Good summaries must catch links across a whole video, not just nearby frames, since frames close in time are not always close in meaning. Users may also want a summary built around a stated topic or request.

Their system first turns frames into a graph that keeps time order and context, with links running forward, backward, and both ways. A reasoning step then sorts frames that truly belong together from those that do not. A final step uses the text prompt to shape the summary that the system outputs.
arxiv-2511-11053:
Martina Alutto, Sofia Bellotti, and their colleagues model how green habits spread through a society where people differ by age and travel needs. Each group in their network stands for a community with a stated age band and mobility level, drawn from large surveys on electric car uptake in Northern Europe. Habit spread, dropout from discontent, and feedback between views and uptake all interact.

The authors find the balance points of that joint system and the conditions that allow wide uptake. They build synthetic populations and likeness networks from survey data to test targeted policies. One policy type acts on social views; the other aims to improve the offer itself.
arxiv-2511-11153:
Hazem Daoud, Sarvesh Kumar, and their colleagues present SCULPT, an interactive platform for studying multi-particle coincidence data from cold-target recoil ion experiments. Such experiments record many linked values per event, and patterns hide in that high-dimensional mass. The platform pairs machine learning with physics-aware analysis inside a web tool that users can explore directly.

A projection method squeezes the data into maps that reveal linked structure. A scoring system rates cluster quality with weighted metrics, giving users a reliability check on what they select. Molecule profiles, filters, and selection tools round out the platform, with extensions to autoencoders and automated observable search discussed.
arxiv-2511-11253:
Hyemin Boo, Hyoryung Kim, and their colleagues present CountSteer, a training-free method that helps image generators draw the exact number of objects a prompt asks for. Diffusion models make realistic images but often miscount, which shows a gap between words and pictures. The authors found the models are not blind to counts: internal signals shift in steady ways when the output count is right or wrong.

CountSteer steers the model's cross-attention states during generation to use that latent count sense. In experiments, object-count accuracy rose by about four percent with no loss of visual quality. The authors present it as a simple step toward more controllable, reliable generation.
arxiv-2511-11653:
Meixiu Long and fourteen co-authors propose GroupRank, a middle path for using large language models to rerank search results. Scoring passages one by one is fast but blind to comparisons, while feeding whole lists captures context at punishing cost and latency.

Groupwise reranking scores passages in small groups, balancing comparison against efficiency. An answer-free data synthesis pipeline fuses local signals to train the reranker without costly labels. The paradigm is presented as both effective and efficient across retrieval tests. Search systems live or die on this trade-off, and a groupwise compromise could bring language model judgment into production reranking.
arxiv-2511-11853:
The CMS Collaboration searches for a new neutral gauge boson, called Z prime. It would show up with one or two jets, at least one from a bottom quark. It would decay into a pair of muons. Such a particle would signal a new fundamental force. This channel had never been covered at lower masses.

The data are proton-proton collisions at thirteen tera-electronvolts. They total one hundred thirty-eight inverse femtobarns. No clear excess over background is seen. Upper limits are set for boson masses from one hundred twenty-five to three hundred fifty giga-electronvolts. The results are the first in the lower mass range. They are also the strongest above it. Null results of this precision shrink where new forces can hide.
arxiv-2511-11953:
Yemko Pryor and five co-authors assemble aligned datasets on forensic DNA databases in the United States. The span is 2001 to 2025. These databases grew a lot over two decades. Public, comparable records lagged far behind that growth. Three linked datasets cover national, state, and demographic views.

Monthly National DNA Index System statistics are rebuilt from FBI archives. They track offender, arrestee, and forensic profiles. Laboratory counts and investigations aided are included. State data add collection laws and familial search practices for all fifty states. Uniform breakdowns by group complete the set. Forensic DNA policy is debated fiercely. A quarter-century of consistent numbers gives all sides a common factual base.
arxiv-2511-12253:
Harrison Goldstein and five co-authors address a central problem in property-based testing: how to generate random inputs that satisfy a given condition, and only those inputs. Valid cases can be rare, so naive random sampling wastes most of its effort. Efficient generation is vital for testing with rich preconditions.

Their approach borrows from deductive program synthesis. Rules based on the meaning of generators give an automatic procedure that builds a correct generator for a predicate. Recursive conditions are handled by rewriting them in a form that matches a known building pattern. The system, Palamedes, is a library for the Lean theorem prover and builds on standard proof search tools.
arxiv-2511-13453:
Iulius Gherasim and Carlos García Sánchez search for the best way to run AI models on Android phones. Phones now handle tasks from voice help to advanced photo work, but speed depends on squeezing varied hardware well. Their study covers object detection with YOLO models and image classification with ResNet.

They compare quantization schemes, which shrink model numbers for speed, and the use of on-device graphics and neural accelerators. Each setup is judged by how much accuracy it loses against how much speed it gains. The goal is a practical recipe for minimal delay and strong responsiveness without giving up more accuracy than the task can afford.
arxiv-2511-13653:
Leo Gao and 5 co-authors train weight-sparse transformers so their internal circuits stay readable to humans. Mechanistic interpretability seeks circuits that people can follow, and forcing most weights to zero leaves each neuron with few links. Pruning then isolates the small subnetwork that carries a chosen hand-crafted task.

The recovered circuits often use neurons and channels that match natural concepts, joined by a handful of clear connections. Making weights sparser trades raw capability for clarity, while larger models push that frontier outward, though scaling past tens of millions of active weights stays hard. Early results also suggest the method can help explain existing dense models, not just new sparse ones.
arxiv-2511-14053:
Fabio L. Braghin, Marcelo Loewe, and Cristian Villavicencio calculate how a magnetic field switches on pion couplings that vanish in empty space. Working in Weinberg's large-color-number effective field theory, they study relatively weak fields and the pion's coupling to constituent quark currents. Two channels are examined: a scalar current and a vector current.

The induced couplings, or form factors, are zero in vacuum and appear only because the field is present. Physically they may describe a neutral pion fluctuating into a scalar quark-antiquark meson or into a vector meson. The authors discuss possible observable consequences for hadron physics in magnetized settings, such as heavy-ion collisions and magnetized stars.
arxiv-2511-14153:
Fatima Kazi, Alex Young, Yash Inani, and one co-author survey and measure bias inside large language models. Models absorb explicit and implicit biases from training text, risking stereotypes and misinformation in their outputs. The team evaluated several generative models, including BERT and GPT-3.5, on the StereoSet and CrowSPairs benchmarks.

They built an automated framework to flag social biases across gender, race, profession, and religion, using separate routes for explicit and implicit bias. Fine-tuned models handled racial bias well but struggled with gender bias, and many leaned too hard on keywords. A bag-of-words analysis exposed implicit stereotyping in vocabularies, and prompt-based fine-tuning with augmented data improved performance.
arxiv-2511-14653:
Boris Alexeev, John Jasper, and Dustin G. Mixon study matrices whose entries are all plus or minus one and whose shape is nearly as well behaved as possible. Quality is measured by the condition number, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value. An exact Hadamard matrix would score one, but such matrices do not exist in most sizes.

The authors prove the best possible score still tends toward one as the size grows, and they give matching lower bounds in most sizes. Along the way they settle an open problem about flat orthogonal matrices. They also describe explicit endless families of good matrices, which are useful in signal processing and coding.
arxiv-2511-14953:
Joey Velez-Ginorio, Nada Amin, and two co-authors show that loops can be compiled into recurrent neurons without losing the ability to train by gradient descent. Differentiable programming struggles with discrete tools: branches and loops have no obvious derivatives, so they are banned from parts of a program where learning must flow. Earlier work freed branches by compiling them into linear neurons.

This work does the same for iteration, turning loops into linear recurrent neurons that still pass gradients. That makes looping algorithms first-class citizens inside differentiable programs and neural networks. The wider payoff is freedom in how learning systems are built, since control flow no longer has to stop where training begins.
arxiv-2511-15253:
Sirui Chen, Jinsong Zhou, and four co-authors present PresentCoach, a two-agent system that teaches presentation skills the way a good mentor does: show, then critique. Learners rarely get both a strong example to imitate and personal feedback on their own attempt. Earlier tools score a speech or draft a script in isolation, leaving the learner to connect the dots.

One agent turns the user's slides into a model presentation video, with narration written, voiced in a personalized synthetic voice, and synced to the visuals. The second agent then grades the user's recorded rehearsal against that exemplar. Pairing a target performance with interactive coaching closes the practice loop that single-purpose tools leave open.
arxiv-2511-15653:
