Guy Boyde studies a pictorial chain complex built from planar loops, called the dga of planar loops, in its first nontrivial case where a size parameter satisfies a simple doubling relation. A chain complex is a sequence of algebraic objects linked by maps, used to extract shape information. This example was introduced in an earlier paper by Boyde with Boyd, Randal-Williams, and Sroka, where a minimal model was given.

For the first nontrivial case, Boyde gives a new model that incorporates two natural reflection symmetries, which flip the pictures in structured ways. He also provides a more explicit description of the existing model. The work is a focused algebraic study of one small but foundational case.
arxiv-2511-15853:
Rebecca Gjini, Matthias Morzfeld, Oliver R. A. Dunbar, and Tapio Schneider race competing ensemble Kalman methods against each other for climate model calibration. Ensemble Kalman methods update a set of runs to fit observations without needing derivatives. They scale well and tolerate noisy statistics. Calibration matters more as hybrid physics and machine learning models gain parameters that hand-tuning cannot keep up with.

The authors ask which variant deserves use for learning climate parameters by matching modeled and observed climate statistics. Systematic numerical experiments use Lorenz-type models of rising complexity. Those models are common simplified stand-ins for climate dynamics. The race compares relative computing efficiency across the variants in this idealized setting, guiding faster cycles for calibration-driven model work.
arxiv-2511-15953:
Arif Er and Meng-Chwan Tan explain a duality between two twists of five-dimensional gauge theory. On certain five-manifolds, the Haydys-Witten twist with a gauge group is dual to the Geyer-Mülsch twist with the Langlands dual group. That swap exchanges electric and magnetic data. Both theories also admit lower-dimensional readings through gauged Landau-Ginzburg models.

Through those readings, categories built from instanton Floer homology of two- and three-manifolds are dual to new holomorphic flat Floer categories for the dual group. Atiyah-Floer style links to symplectic categories also follow. The physics argument gives gauge-based extensions of math conjectures about mirror symmetry and Langlands duality for these higher categories.
arxiv-2511-16053:
Connor Walsh, Ian MacPherson, and five co-authors present a teaching-friendly quantum mechanics problem: a quantum dot made from two crossed troughs. Each trough is a two-dimensional channel, and there is no potential well anywhere. Surprisingly, the crossing point still supports a bound state, a particle state trapped near the intersection with energy below the free continuum.

Several solution methods are compared, including matrix mechanics, finite differences, and mode matching. Mode matching proves most accurate here and also yields a simple trial wave function. That variational function gives the lowest energy obtained so far from an analytical variational solution, making the system a useful showcase of complementary computational techniques.
arxiv-2511-16353:
Jonathan Kamp, Lisa Beinborn, and Antske Fokkens examine human-written rationales, the highlighted words that explain a text label, and ask what the common sufficiency metric really measures. Sufficiency scores how well the rationale alone supports the label, and it is widely used to judge explanation quality.

Comparing the metric with token classification and with attention regularization, the authors find surprises. Highly informative rationales were not likely to help a model classify correctly, and sufficiency instead reflects the pull of the non-rationale context in the same input. Feeding rationales into the model did help cross-domain classification at times, but unevenly across tasks and model types. The metric and token classification also appeared unrelated, showing that such metrics need deeper study.
arxiv-2511-16653:
Md. Samiul Alim and five co-authors prune neural networks in one shot, guided by a teacher model, instead of the usual slow cycle of training, pruning, and retraining. Their trick is to let the teacher shape the importance scores themselves, so the weights kept are those that matter both for the task and for knowledge transfer.

After the one-shot global pruning, sparsity-aware retraining, with or without distillation, restores accuracy without reviving pruned connections. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet the method reached high sparsity with minimal accuracy loss. It beat strong baselines such as EPG and EPSD at high sparsity and costs far less computation than iterative schemes, making it attractive for deploying models on constrained hardware.
arxiv-2511-16853:
Xizhe Xue and Xiao Xiang Zhu present REO-Instruct, a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models can do quantitative science on satellite imagery, not just describe it. Earth observation models are usually graded on captioning or classification, while the field's real needs include regressing measurable quantities such as forest biomass.

The benchmark chains tasks in a forest setting: human activity, land-cover classification, ecological patch counting, and above-ground biomass regression. It pairs co-registered Sentinel-2 and radar imagery with structured text annotations built by a hybrid human-AI pipeline. Baseline tests across generic vision-language models show current systems struggle with numeric reasoning even when their descriptions are sound. REO-Instruct gives developers a standard yardstick for models that must both describe a landscape and measure it.
arxiv-2511-17053:
Teng Fu and four co-authors build a single system, OmniPT, that tracks pedestrians in video and also answers language-based requests about them. Large vision-language models excel at describing whole images but lag expert models at pinpointing individual objects. New tracking tasks, meanwhile, ask for exactly that mix: follow a person named in words, across views, and explain what they are doing.

OmniPT reshapes tracking into tasks a foundation model can perform, with answers in a fixed, checkable format. Training alternates reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning, passing through a stage fed by many pedestrian datasets. Tests on tracking benchmarks show the unified model outperforming earlier methods. The work points toward trackers that a user can question and direct in plain language.
arxiv-2511-17153:
Diego Velazquez and six co-authors release LangMark, a dataset for automatic post-editing, the task of fixing machine translation errors without redoing the translation by hand. Good post-editing systems were held back by a lack of large, multilingual training data based on real machine output. LangMark fills that gap for translations from English into seven languages, including French, German, Japanese, Russian, and Spanish.

The dataset holds nearly 207,000 triplets: a source segment, the machine translation, and a human expert's corrected version. Using it, the authors show that large language models with few-shot prompting can post-edit effectively, beating leading commercial translation systems on their tests. Because expert linguists produced the corrections, the data offers both scale and quality. The release should spur better post-editing research.
arxiv-2511-17453:
Ivan Proskurnin proves a lower bound for the Milnor number of a function germ that stays unchanged under the action of a finite abelian group. The Milnor number is a standard measure of how complex a singular point is, and earlier work by Chulkov gave an inequality of this kind. Proskurnin's result extends that inequality to the invariant setting, where the group action restricts which functions may appear.

He also shows the bound cannot be improved in general, since functions with any number of variables can reach it exactly. The functions that do reach it turn out to be stable in a group-aware sense, acting as the invariant counterparts of the simplest stable singularities. The paper is a compact piece of pure maths that sharpens what is known about symmetric singularities.
arxiv-2511-17653:
Mazyar Taghavi and Javad Vahidi propose MARL-CC, a mathematical framework for multi-agent reinforcement learning in connected autonomous vehicles. Their dynamics are nonlinear, each vehicle sees only part of the world, and credit for joint outcomes is hard to assign. Few learning approaches guarantee stability in that setting. MARL-CC answers by joining differential geometric control, Bayesian inference, and Shapley-value credit assignment in one optimization design.

Bounded policy updates keep learning safe. Decentralized belief estimation lets each vehicle reason from its own view, and the Shapley logic spreads rewards fairly. The theory gives convergence and stability guarantees under stochastic disturbances and message delays. In simulation and real-world testbeds, the authors report up to forty percent faster convergence and better cooperative gains than leading baselines, including PPO, DDPG, and QMIX. They frame MARL-CC as a scalable base for intelligent transport, drone coordination, and distributed robotics.
arxiv-2511-17753:
Austin Wallace, C. David Sherrill, and Giri Krishnan address a practical choice in quantum chemistry: which method gives good accuracy for forces between molecules without wasting computer time. Methods range widely in cost and in error, and the best pick changes by case.

Their framework trains a group of machine learning models to predict the error of each method against a high level gold standard. Tests on fragments of biological molecules and small organic pairs give very small errors in those forecasts. The approach also groups methods in ways that match theory, helping users pick a cheaper route safely.
arxiv-2511-18153:
Shreyas Kumar, Barat S, Debojit Das, and four co-authors coordinate two robot arms for delicate snap fit assembly, such as pressing a lens into an eyewear frame. The snap must be detected instantly, and force eased off before overshoot damages parts. External sensors are not always available for that timing.

Their SnapNet network detects the engagement moment from joint velocity transients alone, using only the robot's own proprioceptive signals, with high recall across geometries. A coordination framework then modulates impedance when that event fires, aligning parts and inserting compliantly. On a mixed bimanual platform, peak impact forces fall by up to about thirty percent versus standard control.
arxiv-2511-18553:
Ernesto Araya and Hemant Tyagi tackle matching two sets of time series that hide the same signals in shuffled, noisy form. Each series follows a vector autoregressive rule, where the next step leans on the last. One set is a permuted, noise added copy of the other, and the hidden shuffle is the prize.

The task extends the classic point cloud match to series with time links. The team derive the most likely shuffle estimator, which lands as a quadratic search over permutations. They study when that search can be solved and when the true match can be found at all. Such matching aids data linkage where series arrive scrambled. Time structure, they show, both helps and binds the hunt.
arxiv-2511-18753:
Canon Sun, Marcel Franz, and Joseph Maciejko show that strain can stamp a Berry phase on a chiral superconductor. Between the point where superconductivity starts and the point where time reversal breaks, a strained p-wave superconductor sits in an in between phase. In plane strain splits the start points of its two orbital parts, which opens a Dirac cone in the phase map.

Vary the strain slowly around a loop that rings that cone, and the order parameter gains a phase of half a turn. The turn comes from a half rotation of the gap function. That half rotation leaves a mark in the superfluid stiffness, seen through vortex shapes and the upper critical field. A hidden phase thus turns visible.
arxiv-2511-18953:
Vasudevarao Allu, Raju Biswas, and Rajib Mandal extend Bohr inequalities to holomorphic maps between high dimensional balls. The classic Bohr result bounds how a bounded analytic function's coefficients can add up near the center. Their maps run from the unit ball of a complex Banach space into the closure of a unit polydisc.

First comes a sharper bound that joins squared norms of the map and of its homogeneous parts. A second refined bound mixes coefficient norms with their squares. A third covers compositions with a Schwarz map that has a zero of set order at the origin. Each Bohr radius is shown sharp, so no larger safe radius exists. Coefficient control of this kind anchors complex analysis in many variables.
arxiv-2511-19153:
Francisco Sena and Alexandru I. Tomescu solve flow decomposition on general graphs, a problem at the heart of genome assembly methods. Decomposition splits a weighted graph into weighted paths or walks, but most past results covered only graphs without cycles. Workarounds forced cyclic graphs into acyclic form with heuristic preprocessing.

Their framework uses dominator trees, a classic tool from compiler theory, to find safe edge sequences that must appear in some walk of any solution. They show the longest safe sequences come from shared leaves of two dominator trees and can be listed in linear time. Those sequences speed up integer programming formulations for any such decomposition task.
arxiv-2511-19253:
Boyuan Wu addresses two chores that slow cooperative multi-agent learning: writing good reward functions and building a training curriculum that avoids dead ends. Fixed rules are brittle, and putting a large language model inside the live control loop is costly. His framework, MAESTRO, moves the language model offline and uses it as a training architect instead.

One part generates varied traffic scenarios matched to current skill, while another writes reward functions as runnable Python code that adapts as tasks get harder. These guide a standard MADDPG learner without adding cost at run time. On large traffic signal control in Hangzhou, with sixteen intersections, the full system improves both performance and stability.
arxiv-2511-19653:
Mahmud Suhaimi Ibrahim, Shantanu Rahman, Muhammad Samin Hasan, Minhaj Uddin Ahmad, and Abdullah Abrar plan collision-free routes for fleets of identical drones flying in formation outdoors. Avoiding mid-air collisions between fleet members is the central problem of formation flying. Their method borrows from network flow theory: the fleet's airspace becomes a flow graph built from real GPS coordinates, a shortest-path algorithm finds the cheapest route. And a classic max-flow method then assigns paths so no two drones ever claim the same space at once.

Simulations cover up to sixty-four drones in several formations, and a live experiment with three quadcopters checks that the plans work physically, not just on screen. The authors report the method reliably produces safe, complete, collision-free path sets, a building block for drone shows, delivery fleets, and survey teams.
arxiv-2511-19753:
Xian Xu and Diana Y. Qiu build a first-principles method to compute circular dichroism in solids, the uneven absorption of left and right circular light. Such spectra probe chirality and momentum-space geometry, but periodic systems with strong exciton effects resist standard methods, which converge slowly and suffer gauge and origin ambiguities.

Their framework couples the GW method with the Bethe-Salpeter equation under full minimal coupling, judging optical elements directly at finite photon momentum. Dipole, magnetic, and quadrupole channels enter on equal footing. On two chiral two-dimensional perovskites, magnetic and quadrupole parts contribute equally, and transitions missed by older methods reshape the spectra.
arxiv-2511-19953:
Wen Zhang, Qin Ren, Wenjing Liu, Haibin Ling, and Chenyu You present SPROUT, a training-free method for outlining cell nuclei in pathology slides. Accurate nuclear segmentation supports clinical insight, but most strong methods need dense labels and costly fine-tuning. Vision foundation models promise zero-shot help, yet training-free routes for this task remain little explored.

SPROUT builds slide-specific reference prototypes from histology-informed priors to bridge domain gaps. A partial optimal transport scheme then guides feature alignment step by step. The aligned foreground and background features become positive and negative point prompts for the Segment Anything Model, which draws the nuclear outlines with no parameter updates. Across several histopathology benchmarks, SPROUT performs competitively without any supervision or retraining.
arxiv-2511-20053:
Sandipan Dutta, Krishnendu Gongopadhyay, and Rahul Mondal classify quaternionic projective transformations by the calm regions of their action. For a cyclic group built from one map of quaternionic projective space, the equicontinuity region is the set where the group's action stays uniform. The authors describe these regions for the full linear group over the quaternions.

They show the region depends only on the generator's dynamical type: elliptic, parabolic, loxodromic, or loxoparabolic. Elliptic cyclic groups act with equicontinuity on the whole space. For the other three types, the region is fixed by explicit subspaces read off its Jordan form. The result gives a plain reading of how these maps sort into kinds.
arxiv-2511-20153:
Salamone, Martinez Diaz, Li, Cvitkovich, and Niquet sharpen a cheap model for silicon spin qubits. Their 2025 paper refines the two-band k·p model for SiGe structures. Silicon's conduction band has six equivalent valleys. Splitting between opposite valleys affects qubit quality deeply. Small splittings leak spin information and hurt fidelity.

Atomistic tight-binding computes splittings accurately but expensively. The two-band model promises the same answers far cheaper. Inter-valley potentials are the model's delicate ingredient. The team sets rules for choosing and placing them. A fine grid along the valley axis is required. Coarser grids suffice across the other directions. Valley splittings matched tight-binding in test structures. SiGe spikes and wiggle wells were both reproduced. Valley-orbit mixing effects came out correctly too. Inter-valley dipole elements matched as well. Those elements govern qubit control and dephasing rates. A realistic qubit device simulation illustrates the method.
arxiv-2511-20353:
Sportich, Boubakri, Simonin, and Renzaglia let drones choose viewpoints by the map quality users actually want. Their 2025 paper presents a quality-guided exploration framework. Next-best-view planning usually chases raw information gain. A fast survey and a precise survey need different flights. One objective cannot serve both goals well.

Their planner takes user quality requirements as input. A truncated signed distance field stores map uncertainty. View candidates are generated adaptively from that field. Selection scores views by expected quality contribution. The framework is modular across its pipeline stages. Simulations in realistic scenes validated the approach. Behavior shifted sensibly with the stated goal. Coverage beat conventional next-best-view strategies overall. Final map quality and path efficiency also improved. Small drones' tight compute budgets shaped the design. Inspection and rescue missions have differing fidelity needs. Multi-drone teamwork is the stated next step. Exploration becomes a goal-driven service.
arxiv-2511-20653:
Claudinei Daitx and Haitham Amar tested in 2025 how well large language models answer study-abroad questions, the kind students ask about admissions, visas, scholarships, and eligibility. Their questions came from the real advising work of ApplyBoard, a company that guides students from first search through enrolment. A wrong answer can cost a student a visa or a place, so the pair graded each reply for correctness and for invented content.

Each answer was marked correct, partial, or wrong, with partial credit tracking whether the reply covered every area the question touched. The team also scored faithfulness, meaning whether the answer stuck to the evidence, plus answer relevance and an overall hallucination score called ANAH v2. Models that reason step by step behaved measurably differently from direct answerers. GPT-5 stood out for short, on-target checklists that stayed close to the main topic instead of wandering into extra areas.
arxiv-2511-20753:
Aranya Bhattacharya and colleagues explore in 2025 whether geometry should be measured by areas rather than lengths. Their arena is the AdS/CFT correspondence, a duality linking gravity in a curved bulk space to a quantum theory on its boundary. Area metrics generalise ordinary metrics: any length-based geometry defines one, but not vice versa. The idea tempts because black hole entropy and holographic entanglement entropy are both computed from areas.

Working around a four-dimensional anti-de Sitter background, the team uses the Ryu-Takayanagi formula, which ties entanglement to a minimal area. With the first law of entanglement, they derive a holographic dictionary entry for area metrics and an equation of motion for their small fluctuations. They then hunt for bulk action principles that would produce that equation. Writing the fluctuations through Lanczos-like potentials yields an especially elegant model, and the team supplies a 15-minute video abstract.
arxiv-2511-20953:
Tianyue Liu and four co-authors complete in 2025 a study of how quantum 6j symbols behave at large values, and find a new geometry hiding inside them. These symbols, from the modular double of a quantum group, are building blocks of three-dimensional quantum gravity models. Earlier work tied their semiclassical limit to volumes of hyperbolic tetrahedra. The authors extend the symbols analytically into b-6j symbols and examine the remaining parameter cases.

Those cases correspond, they prove, to truncated hyperideal tetrahedra in anti-de Sitter geometry, and the symbols' asymptotics give the tetrahedra's AdS volumes. It is the first appearance of anti-de Sitter geometry in the asymptotics of quantum invariants. Via conformal field theory, the tetrahedra's edge lengths and dihedral angles match Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates on four-holed spheres. The result also supplies a concrete instance of 3D/2D holography in the AdS/CFT spirit.
arxiv-2511-21053:
Chenglizhao Chen and colleagues introduce in 2025 AerialMind, the first benchmark of its scale for referring multi-object tracking from drones. The task: given a spoken-style instruction, find and follow the matching objects through video. Existing datasets cover ground-level views, but drone footage adds fast motion, camera rotation, tiny objects, and wide scenes. AerialMind contains 48,485 frames with an average of 247.4 language expressions per sequence, second-highest among benchmarks.

Building it by hand would have been prohibitively slow, so the team created COALA, a semi-automated labelling assistant where AI agents draft annotations for human checking. They also propose HawkEyeTrack, a tracking method tuned for aerial perception, and two new metrics isolating scene-induced and motion-induced failures. The benchmark bites: an established transformer tracker scored a HOTA of 19.51 in-domain, where higher means better tracking. Experiments, the authors report, confirm both the dataset's difficulty and HawkEyeTrack's effectiveness.
arxiv-2511-21353:
V. V. Bavula completes a two-century-old program in algebra in a 2025 paper on Galois theory. Classical Galois theory links the intermediate fields inside a field extension to subgroups of its symmetry group, but only when the extension is Galois, a well-behaved special case. Bavula's earlier work replaced symmetry groups with a larger ring built from the extension's automorphisms together with its differential operators, under a principle he calls maximal symmetry.

Bavula now obtains an analogue of Galois theory for arbitrary finite field extensions, with no normality or separability assumptions. Subfields in between are described through invariants of the natural algebraic objects attached to each one, through two Galois-type matchings. For normal extensions, the maximal symmetry equality characterizes the class exactly. The result closes the gap between the classical theory and the general case that textbooks leave open.
arxiv-2511-21453:
Thomas Jackson extends a landmark quantum magnetism result to branching lattices in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. The AKLT model, a chain of interacting quantum spins, was the first proven example of the Haldane phase and of a matrix product state, the workhorse description of one-dimensional quantum matter. One open question is whether its ground state keeps long-range antiferromagnetic order, spins alternating direction coherently across the whole system. That was known mainly for special tree-like lattices called Bethe lattices.

Jackson proves the ordering result for a wider family of trees and treelike graphs satisfying stated conditions. His construction builds the ground state of the AKLT model on an arbitrary graph, following the Weyl representation approach. It exploits the model's odd feature: quantum expectation values reduce to a classical partition function in the same number of variables. The advance clarifies how this solvable state behaves beyond one dimension.
arxiv-2511-21553:
Idir Mohamed Yacine and Thomas Romary make flexible spatial statistics fast enough for messy real data, in 2025. Spatially varying coefficient models let each predictor's effect change across a map, useful for soil pollution, where a contaminant's behavior depends on local conditions. The Bayesian version is rigorous but slow, inverting huge matrices at every sampling step. Their test case is punishing: a Toulouse soil dataset where two-thirds of observations are censored, known only to fall below a detection limit.

Yacine and Romary accelerate the model with the Vecchia approximation, which replaces the full spatial dependence with small conditioning sets. Their latent-free variant removes a hidden field from the parameter space while keeping accuracy. Validation studies show the approximation holds up even at 75 percent censoring, well beyond the Toulouse data's level. The result is a practical route to mapping how pollution drivers vary across a region, with uncertainty attached.
arxiv-2511-21753:
Sameeah Noreen Hameed and four coauthors teach language models to pull disaster impacts and their exact locations out of social media posts, in 2025. During disasters, sensors and satellites leave gaps: clouds block views and satellites revisit slowly. People's posts act as ground-level geo-sensors, but a post may name several places while only some were actually hit.

The key distinction is between mentioned locations and impacted ones. In a post about a deadly fire, the Greek town of Mati was impacted; Greece and Athens were only context. The team fine-tuned language models to extract impacts and impacted locations only, including informal or abbreviated place names. Their model scored an F1 of 0.69 on impacts and 0.74 on impacted locations, beating the pretrained baseline. The backing corpus, DILC, covers 19 major natural disasters across 11 countries. Llama models beat conventional named-entity recognition given context-aware prompts and disaster-specific training.
arxiv-2511-21853:
Pineda and colleagues map the magnetic field of YZ Ceti, whose innermost rocky planet may tug on it magnetically. Radio bursts from the star, strongly circularly polarized, repeat at phases matching the planet YZ Ceti b's orbit, which hints at a magnetic star-planet interaction. Confirming it would give a first handle on a close-in rocky planet's magnetic field, but depends on the star's field geometry.

Using a technique called Zeeman Doppler Imaging, which reads magnetic signatures in starlight, the team produced the first measurements of the star's large-scale field topology. The field does not rule out the interaction scenarios, though the authors find evidence both for and against the hypothesis and stress that the field's evolution must be tracked better. They also suggest planet-triggered flares near the magnetic equator, at the Alfvén surface where the stellar wind takes over.
arxiv-2511-21953:
Xu and colleagues design neural network controllers that steer autonomous systems along a planned path while keeping them safe under disturbances. Their test case is a Dubins car, a standard model of a vehicle that moves forward at fixed speed and steers. The method starts with a nominal trajectory, then computes backward reachable sets, zones from which the system is guaranteed to reach its target while obeying all safety constraints.

Those guaranteed-safe zones then shape both the architecture and the training of a neural network tracking controller, which learns to keep the system's state inside them. Unguided networks can behave unsafely, and optimization controllers are too slow for real-time use. After training, formal verification with conformal prediction attaches statistical safety guarantees to the controller. The result is a closed-form controller that evaluates quickly yet carries evidence about how safe it is.
arxiv-2511-22153:
Kristanto and Hakim, computer scientists in Indonesia, build a detector for machine-written text that refuses to trust any single method. Detectors usually pick one paradigm and generalize poorly, flagging innocent academic writing too often. Their hybrid ensemble fuses all three: a RoBERTa classifier for deep semantics, a GPT-2 perturbation detector reading likelihood curvature, and a statistical analyzer of linguistic style. The three are combined by weighted voting whose weights are learned to maximize F1 rather than set by hand.

A bias-variance analysis motivates the design, and the three members indeed correlate only weakly, around 0.35 to 0.42 in error correlation, the condition ensembles need. On a 30,000-document multi-generator corpus the system reaches 94.2 percent accuracy with an AUC of 0.978, and cuts false positives on academic text by 35 percent relative, the property that matters most for fair deployment in education.
arxiv-2511-22253:
Le, Tran, Nguyen, Zhou, and Gurrin retrieve images with almost no training data by changing the target instead of the query. Image-guided retrieval with optional text unifies composed retrieval, where text modifies a reference photo, and sketch-based retrieval. Most research enriches the query representation while targets stay as raw features from a pretrained vision-language model. Their UNION representation fuses each target image's embedding with a null-text prompt, aligning targets with multimodal queries, and demands no architectural changes to the underlying model.

Training uses only 5,000 samples per task, a caption-enriched composed-retrieval set and a sketch set the team built. Even so, UNION reaches a CIRCO mAP at rank 50 of 38.5 and a Sketchy mAP at rank 200 of 82.7, surpassing many heavily supervised baselines that trained on orders of magnitude more data. Lightweight target-side design, they argue, beats brute-force supervision here.
arxiv-2511-22453:
Stone and colleagues examine the galaxies hosting quasars, the brilliant centres powered by feeding supermassive black holes, in the nearby universe. Using the Galaxy and Mass Assembly survey, they study 205 type I quasar host galaxies. They reconstruct their star formation histories and stellar populations. They compare them with ordinary galaxies of the same mass and distance.

About 80 percent of quasar hosts are actively forming stars, on the usual star-forming main sequence. Only about 20 percent are quiescent. That is well below the 54 percent quiescent share among ordinary galaxies. Their average star formation rate rose by a factor of two to three over the past 100 million years, yet the hosts formed stars at all earlier times too. The pattern fits quasar activity switching on alongside a burst of ordinary star formation, so the authors favour gentle triggers such as internal processes and minor mergers.
arxiv-2511-22653:
Sengupta works out how a magnetic field makes sound and lattice vibrations travel differently in opposite directions through a chiral Weyl semimetal. These materials host Weyl fermions, whose band geometry is described by Berry curvature. The work uses a semiclassical Boltzmann framework. It includes Berry curvature, orbital magnetic moments, and node-by-node electronic structure. From it come corrections to the phonon dynamical matrix for both types.

The mechanism is a chiral imbalance between the Weyl nodes. The nodes are inequivalent, with distinct Fermi velocities, energies, and relaxation times. They respond unevenly when phonons propagate along the field, feeding back on the lattice. The acoustic branch shows a subtle frequency shift but enhanced nonreciprocal attenuation, so waves die faster one way than the other. The optical branch develops a magnetochiral splitting that grows linearly with wavevector. The effect thus becomes a non-electronic probe of topological band geometry.
arxiv-2511-22753:
Rantzer derives an adaptive controller as a worst-case game's exact solution. The setting is a multivariable linear system whose matrices are unknown constants, hit by disturbances; the controller chooses inputs from past measurements, while an adversary chooses the disturbances and the parameters themselves. The cost balances state errors against disturbance energy, in the spirit of H-infinity control, and the resulting Bellman equation normally has no closed-form solution.

For fully actuated systems, input matrix the identity up to sign and no control-effort penalty, Rantzer solves the Bellman equation explicitly. The minimising policy is a dual controller: it optimises the tradeoff between exploration, probing to learn the parameters early, and exploitation, using that knowledge later. The solution proves and generalises Vinnicombe's scalar-system conjecture. With large uncertainty, no fixed linear controller can even stabilise all candidate models, while this nonlinear adaptive law stabilises and optimises simultaneously.
arxiv-2511-23153:
Koellermeier and colleagues improve the magnetic rotating shallow water model, a two-dimensional stand-in for thin layers of electrically conducting fluid found in the Sun's tachocline, neutron star atmospheres, and magnetically active exoplanets. Depth-averaging makes the model cheap to run but throws away all vertical structure. So the team instead expands the vertical profiles of both velocity and magnetic field as polynomials of arbitrary order.

Closing the enlarged two-dimensional system with evolution equations for the polynomial coefficients, derived by Galerkin projection, keeps the model's speed while restoring vertical detail for the conducting-fluid case. Earlier moment methods had not covered that case. In numerical experiments with moment systems up to third order, the approximations cut model error at little computational cost. The even-order model reduced the error of every variable by a factor of about four or more in the reported test.
arxiv-2511-23253:
Wen and colleagues build AgriCoT, a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models can actually reason about farming problems. Not just answer questions about farm images. Its 4,535 curated samples pair agricultural images with questions and with human-refined chain-of-thought explanations, step-by-step reasoning written out. So graders can judge the model's logic as well as its final answer, especially in zero-shot use where no examples are given.

Putting 26 representative models, proprietary and open-source, through the benchmark exposed a split result, in that some proprietary systems answered questions impressively while their underlying reasoning lagged far behind. The authors argue this gap is exactly why answer-only benchmarks mislead model selection for precision farming, crop monitoring, and pest detection. And they release the dataset publicly so future models can be compared on the quality of their reasoning, not only their conclusions in the field.
arxiv-2512-00053:
Nikhil Rout and Blaise Tine design a configurable dot product unit for GPU tensor computation. Efficient mixed-precision matrix operations are critical for deep learning workloads on general-purpose GPUs. Open-source designs often use separate arithmetic units, wasting throughput and silicon area.

Their unit fuses floating-point and integer pipelines into one architecture for inner dot products. It is built for the open-source, RISC-V based Vortex GPGPU's tensor core. A fused unit promises better utilization for mixed-precision AI on open hardware. A singular fused architecture replaces discrete arithmetic units, the design choice behind the throughput and utilization gains.
arxiv-2512-00153:
Networks fail, and planners need to know quickly how a failure changes what can flow through them. Mridul Ahi and co-authors design fault-tolerant data structures for maximum-flow and minimum-cut problems in a 2025 study. Their setting is unweighted directed graphs with a fixed source and sink.

Sensitivity oracles answer, after an edge change, how the best flow or smallest cut is affected, without recomputing everything. Fast answers matter for transport, communication, and supply networks that must react to breakdowns. The work is theoretical computer science, aimed at data structures that stay useful when graphs are damaged. Fault tolerance here means the data structure keeps answering after parts of the graph fail.
arxiv-2512-00553:
Reinforcement learning results are notoriously hard to reproduce: rerun the training and the policy changes. Bohan Zhang and co-authors study list replicable reinforcement learning in 2025, inside the probably approximately correct framework. An algorithm must return a near-optimal policy from a small fixed list, across different runs.

List replicability relaxes exact reproducibility to a shortlist: the answer may vary, but only among a few candidates. Formalizing that idea gives practitioners a target between impossible exact replication and anything-goes variance. Reliable learning algorithms are a precondition for deploying reinforcement learning in medicine, robotics, and infrastructure. A shortlist of policies is also easier for auditors to inspect after training. For teams who ship such tools, the gain is calm. A rerun may swap one good plan for a near twin, but it will not leap to a wild new one.
arxiv-2512-01253:
L Cheng and five coauthors study light-induced ferroelectricity in a crystal in a 2025 physics paper. Strontium titanate is a quantum paraelectric: it hovers near becoming ferroelectric, where a lasting electric polarization appears, without quite doing so. Intense terahertz pulses can push it over the edge briefly, breaking its inversion symmetry.

The mechanism behind that effect remains controversial. Using very strong fields, the team reveals second harmonic generation that varies across space in a patchy way. They attribute the pattern to competing lattice and defect dynamics. Sorting out the mechanism matters for fast control of materials with light.
arxiv-2512-01353:
Rongzhe Wei and co-authors show a new way to slip past AI safety guards. Guards block prompts that ask for harmful text. Most past attacks keep clear signs of harm in the prompt. Guards are now trained to spot those signs fast.

The new attack weaves harmful asks into harmless-looking prompts. It then uses a tree search that adapts as it goes. The aim is to hide the harmful sense from the guard. Work like this is shared so guard makers can test and patch the holes before real attackers find them.
arxiv-2512-01553:
Amy Li proves a vanishing result for Hurwitz spaces of marked covers. Hurwitz spaces collect ways one curve can cover another. Fully marked admissible covers add labels at key points. Their first cohomology group holds shape data about the space.

Li shows that group vanishes for covers of degree three. She then draws the same result for classic simply-branched covers. Vanishing results simplify the geometry of these spaces a lot. They help scholars count covers and study families of curves with fixed branching. Degree three is the first hard case, so a clean vanishing there hints the pattern may hold for higher degrees as well.
arxiv-2512-01953:
Long documents strain large language models because the key-value cache, their running memory of past tokens, grows in a straight line with text length. Sai Gokhale and four co-authors study in 2025 how to shrink that memory and the model itself, especially for deployment on small edge devices.

Single tricks are well explored: quantizing the cache, chunking the input, or quantizing the model's weights. What happens when they are combined, and which combination is best, was largely unknown. The authors examine these techniques jointly at the systems level, mapping the trade-offs. Their map helps engineers fit long-context models into tight memory budgets.
arxiv-2512-02053:
Sorting song lyrics by type or theme is a text classification job, and extra structural features can help if they are woven in well. Marco Gameiro's 2025 study builds the SFL Transformer, which feeds auxiliary structural features directly into the attention mechanism of a pre-trained BERT encoder.

Earlier designs fused such features only at the final output layer, after the text had already been processed. Gameiro's contextual gating instead modulates the hidden states inside the encoder stack, letting structure steer reading as it happens. The study also examines calibration, how well the model's confidence matches its accuracy, a trust issue for any classifier.
arxiv-2512-03353:
Six distances among four points reveal the shape of a space. Nina Lebedeva, Anton Petrunin, and Vladimir Zolotov study those relations in this 2025 work. They look at length spaces, where distance is the basic notion, and impose quadratic inequalities on the six distances in every quadruple of points.

Such conditions restrict how a space can bend and branch. The authors study what effects these quadratic comparisons have on the space as a whole. Results of this kind help classify metric spaces in geometry. They may also inform work on data sets viewed as abstract spaces. Quadruples are the smallest sets where such curvature signs first become visible.
arxiv-2512-03853:
Shuttling single electrons along a silicon chip is a promising way to link qubits, but real devices come with rough surfaces and stray charges. Jack J. Turner and colleagues simulate that transport in a 2025 quantum physics preprint. They focus on silicon metal-oxide-semiconductor devices, where conveyor-belt shuttling demonstrations lag behind a related material system.

Their full three-dimensional simulations solve the Poisson and time-dependent Schrödinger equations across shuttling speeds and gate voltages. At low gate voltages, extra screening from multi-layer gates collapses conveyor-belt motion into a bucket-brigade mode, exciting the electron's orbital state. Stronger confinement restores smooth transport, which proved robust against interface roughness, gate misalignment, and defects buried in the oxide. Defects sitting exactly at the silicon interface remain dangerous, though. Some can excite passing electrons or even capture them outright, marking the key challenge for reliable designs.
arxiv-2512-04453:
Debasmita Ghose, Oz Gitelson, Marynel Vazquez, and Brian Scassellati present BALI, a method that helps robots guess what their human partner truly wants. In joint work, goals are often vague, hard to state, or not on any fixed list. Older tools force goals into a preset menu, watch actions only, or demand plain orders. Each shortcut breaks in messy real settings. Their 2025 arXiv paper blends two richer cues.

BALI merges what a person says with what the person does, inside a planning tree that looks ahead a few steps. It asks a clarifying question only when the expected gain beats the cost of the interruption. It then picks support actions that fit the inferred goal. Tests used joint cooking tasks, where goals could be new to the robot. BALI beat baseline tools on helpfulness measures, a step toward robots that assist without constant instruction.
arxiv-2512-04853:
Mauricio Ferreira, Angel Miramontes, and Jose Morgado refine how theory describes the pion, the lightest meson, using dressed quark-gluon interactions. Pions rule low-energy strong-force physics, and their masslessness in the chiral limit is a cornerstone fact any sound framework must keep. A recent framework allows full quark-gluon vertices while respecting core symmetries. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a lean truncation inside it that keeps the key Ward-Takahashi identities intact.

The truncation simplifies the quark-gluon Schwinger-Dyson equation with little loss of accuracy. The Bethe-Salpeter equation shrinks to two one-loop diagrams carrying the full vertex, plus one two-loop diagram that proves vital for the pion's masslessness. Detailed numerics then test the scheme against known pion properties. A tractable yet faithful truncation lets theorists compute meson structure with tools that honor the symmetries of quantum chromodynamics.
arxiv-2512-04953:
Weiting Wang, Lintao Xiao, Bo Zhang, and co-authors demonstrate a scalable chip architecture that links superconducting qubits through sound waves in solid circuits. Quantum acoustics promises compact devices, but past systems were isolated toys with no way to route phonons or join many parts. Their 2025 arXiv paper integrates tunable transmon qubits with suspension-free phononic integrated circuits, waveguides carved into the chip itself.

Two cavity styles join the platform: Fabry-Perot cavities built in one piece, and microring cavities added by flip-chip assembly. Both couple coherently to the qubits. The cavities boost phonon emission sharply, with a Purcell factor near nineteen. These parts are the elementary blocks of phononic circuits. A working, routable acoustic platform could host phonon-based quantum processors and test new ideas in quantum acoustics at a scale single devices cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-05153:
Yuri Antipov develops a new approximation scheme for the electronic structure of single-walled carbon nanotubes. Rolling a graphene sheet into a tube changes how its electrons behave, and for narrow tubes the curvature effects are large enough that standard methods strain. The paper proposes an analogue of Bloch theory and the tight-binding approximation that works for the three tube families — armchair, zigzag, and chiral — on the same footing.

The technique rests on reciprocal nanotubes, mirror constructions in momentum space, and on applying combined translation-rotation moves in both real and momentum space at once. The resulting sums run over two intertwined helices and contain huge numbers of terms, yet the method stays efficient across the full range, from narrow tubes to megatubes. Antipov reports band-structure calculations for sample tubes of each family, showing the approach delivers the electron energy bands that determine a nanotube's electrical behaviour.
arxiv-2512-05253:
Sébastien Gomé and Anna Frishman explain a puzzle in rotating turbulence: energy in a spinning fluid flows two ways. Some energy climbs into large, two-dimensional structures, while some drains into small three-dimensional waves. In turbulence energy and helicity — a measure of the flow's twist — both cascade to small scales, so the split behaviour of rotating flows needed an origin story.

The authors find the traffic is directed by helicity. Fast waves, stirred by the large two-dimensional flow, keep their helicity in sign camps, and that bookkeeping forces their energy backward into the large flow, feeding condensation. Slower modes swap helicity across the sign divide and send energy forward, as in non-rotating turbulence. A mean-wave kinetic theory turns this picture into formulas that predict how the large-scale flow depends on rotation and Reynolds number, matching nonlinear simulations from modest to extreme rotation.
arxiv-2512-05353:
Andrew Irving and Ebrahim Patel analyze the geometry of trochoidal waves through Gerstner's classic model of water waves. Gerstner waves are among the few exact solutions of the water-wave equations. Their profiles are trochoids, the curves traced by a point on a rolling circle. They come in flattened and extended families. The authors study the motion by riding along with the wave, in the reference frame where the pattern stands still.

In that frame they derive the height of each profile's defining feature, be it cusp, inflection point, or self-intersection. They also derive a condition under which the flattened and extended profiles have exactly equal arc length over one wave cycle. They close by examining how switching frames changes particle accelerations and trajectory geometry. The results sharpen a two-century-old model's fine print, of interest wherever exact wave solutions serve as benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-05453:
Luc Moreau, Alfred Rossi, and Sophie Stalla-Bourdillon present Parajudica, an open rule system for judging whether a given use of data complies with the rules that govern it. Organizations rarely answer to one framework: privacy law, sector regulation, and industry standards can apply at once, and whether access is allowed depends on context. Policy-based access control promises to automate judgments, but implementing it across overlapping frameworks is the hard part.

Parajudica is built on web-standard semantic technology, RDF data and SPARQL queries, as a modular rule system with a metamodel for expressing compliance frameworks. The authors apply it to existing legal frameworks and industry standards, showing how the same machinery serves policy enforcement, compliance monitoring, data discovery, and risk assessment. Comparing frameworks inside one system also shows where they agree and clash. The resource is offered as shared infrastructure for a problem every data holder faces.
arxiv-2512-05853:
Shiji Zhao leads a ten author team exposing a way to jailbreak multimodal language models through pictures alone. Safety filters scan text well; the visual channel is checked weakly. Their method, Visual Reasoning Sequential Attack, splits a harmful request into a chain of linked sub-images. Together, and reasoned over in sequence, they reassemble the full harmful intent inside the model's own reasoning.

Three refinements make the chain work. One polishes the scene most relevant to the hidden query. Another rewrites each sub-text with its context, for coherence. Across a series of experiments, the attack succeeded more often than leading rivals, against both open models and closed commercial ones. The warning to defenders: reasoning itself is an attack surface. A model that cheerfully explains a story told in pictures can be walked, step by innocent step, across its own safety lines.
arxiv-2512-05953:
Yunhao Cao, Zubin Bhaumik, Jessie Jia, Xingyi He, and Kuan Fang teach robots tasks by pointing: naming the spots that should move, and where they should go. Their framework, COIL, defines each task through the intended motion of keypoints chosen on objects in the scene, described in three dimensions. A task may use any number of points, spaced however the job demands.

A conditional policy turns those specifications into arm motion. Its spatio-temporal attention fuses images, points, and timing into one decision stream. Training is self supervised: demonstrations come from simulation, with labels filled in afterward, in hindsight. The result generalizes across tasks, objects, and motion patterns, and on real world manipulation it beat prior methods under both sparse and dense task descriptions. Pointing at what should move becomes a robot programming language.
arxiv-2512-06153:
Wesley Quaresma Cota classifies a corner of the algebra world by how fast its identities multiply. The codimension sequence counts an algebra's polynomial identities by degree. That sequence either crawls polynomially or explodes exponentially. Graded algebras have their own codimensions and varieties. Cota pins down the quadratic growth case.

Every such variety is a direct sum of minimal variety generators. Minimal pieces are the atoms. Classification converts a zoo into a grammar. The quadratic building blocks anchor the climb to higher growth. The field throughout has characteristic zero. Growth is measured degree by degree.
arxiv-2512-06253:
Shuainan Liu and four co authors look for a sharper way to hide private data behind added noise. When a result drawn from touchy data is shared, random noise can mask what any one person's record adds. The strength of that shield is summed up by a privacy loss value, which tells how much the noise might give away in the worst case.

Usual setups draw noise from a bell curve in all directions at once. The authors note that such noise looks the same from every angle, so its size and its direction can be split apart and studied on their own. They build noise with that split in mind, then work out the privacy loss in a closed form built from the two parts. A geometric view like this can yield tighter risk bounds for data holders who share results.
arxiv-2512-06353:
Kaicheng Yang and eight co authors present TreeQ, a way to shrink diffusion transformers, the big models behind much of today's image generation. These models give fine images but demand heavy memory and compute, which blocks their use on modest hardware. Mixed precision shrinking, which stores different parts at different bit counts, had pushed older image models below four bits per value, but had barely been tried on transformers of this kind.

TreeQ attacks three snags at once. A tree shaped search walks the design space fast, pruning poor branches by direct comparison. A single dial aligns the goals of the two main shrinking routes, one done after training and one during it. A new branch design, the General Monarch Branch, eases the squeeze that ultra low bit counts put on information flow. Together they aim to keep image quality at sizes small devices can hold.
arxiv-2512-06953:
Himanshu Bora, Debajyoti Dutta, and Abinash Medhi ask whether two future neutrino experiments could together catch a subtle break in the rules of relativity. The break, called Lorentz invariance violation, would tweak how neutrinos change flavor as they fly. The danger is confusion: the violation's effects can mimic shifts in two key neutrino quantities.

Simulations show that mimicry could fool an experiment into picking the wrong value for a mixing angle's range and for a phase tied to matter-antimatter imbalance. Using two ESSnuSB beam distances helps but leaves some confusion standing. Adding DUNE changes the picture. Its beam catches neutrinos at a first peak where matter effects are strong, while ESSnuSB excels at a second peak. Jointly, the pair clears every degeneracy tested and tightens limits on all the violation parameters.
arxiv-2512-07153:
Maatla Sefawe and co-authors review the fixed sensors that scientists use to keep watch over bats. Tracking bat colonies matters for following disease spread, migration, population change, and the toll of a shifting environment. The survey first lays out the bat biology that shapes any monitoring plan. Then walks through four families of instruments that watch from fixed posts: infrared sensors, cameras, radar, and acoustic detectors tuned to bat calls.

Each family is weighed for coverage, typical uses, accuracy, and limits. Sound recorders eavesdrop on echolocation but can miss quiet species, cameras see only so far in the dark, and radar trades fine detail for range. By laying the trade-offs side by side, the review aims to guide researchers choosing equipment for new studies. The synthesis also flags where combining several sensing styles into multimodal setups could cover the blind spots any single instrument leaves.
arxiv-2512-07453:
Van An Nguyen and twelve co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on cooperation among self-interested agents. Groups often pay incentives to push members toward working together. Past research usually chased two goals at once: spend as little as possible while raising cooperation as high as possible.

The authors ask a question that earlier work largely skipped. Does the cheapest path to cooperation also give the best overall social welfare? Their approach drops the twin goals and aims at welfare alone. They build on classic evolutionary game theory models of finite populations. Both well-mixed groups and groups with fixed social structure are covered. An analytical model and agent-based simulations compare reward strategies. Paying for local habits gives different results than paying for global ones. A wide cost gap separates welfare-first plans from cost-first or cooperation-first plans. Incentive design, they argue, should target welfare itself.
arxiv-2512-07753:
Thomas Buc-d'Alché wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on counting maps drawn on surfaces. Maps, in this corner of combinatorics, are graphs embedded on a surface. Their counts hide inside the statistics of random matrix ensembles.

His objects are the cumulants of power sums for a beta-ensemble's particles. A fresh expansion in the ensemble's size and its beta parameter is the goal. The tridiagonal model of Dumitriu and Edelman supplies the route in. Coefficients of the expansion are counted by specially labeled maps. Those labels follow a scheme from Bouttier, Fusy, and Guitter. His expansion differs in nature from LaCroix's earlier one. Only orientable maps appear, where LaCroix's work ranged more widely. A new many-to-one mapping links the two expansions bijectively at first orders. It relates labeled planar maps with two minima to maps on the projective plane. The bridge clarifies how two counting stories describe one phenomenon.
arxiv-2512-07853:
Jinwoo Jeong and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 computing paper on a costly training failure. Deep models for agentic systems keep growing in size and complexity. Their graphics memory needs can exceed the card, killing training with an out-of-memory error.

Such a crash wastes the whole run and the compute behind it. Predicting peak memory before training starts is the obvious defense. Earlier predictors handled only single-mode architectures, like text-only models. Multimodal models, common in agent systems, broke their assumptions. The authors build a predictor designed for those mixed models. It decomposes a model into its layers, one by one. Factorization then estimates how much memory each layer will consume. Summing the parts forecasts the peak for the whole training run. Tests show their estimates land close to the true usage. Training teams can now size jobs before burning expensive hardware time.
arxiv-2512-07953:
Shreya Kumar, Alex E. Jones, Daniel Bhatti, and Stefanie Barz wrote this 2025 quantum optics paper. Photons are bosons, yet specially prepared pairs can misbehave on cue. Entangled photons have shown fermionic and even anyonic exchange character before.

Those tricks were demonstrated with two photons at a time. Three photons open a far richer landscape of exchange symmetries. Each pair among the three can carry its own symmetry type. Bosonic, fermionic, and anyonic behaviors can coexist inside one state. Such mixed-symmetry systems are impossible with a pair alone. The team investigates how these configurations show up in interference. Experiments with three photons track the predicted patterns directly. Tuning a pair's symmetry switches interference effects on and off. Statistics, usually fixed by particle species, become a design variable. Scalable photonic platforms gain a new knob for quantum technologies. Interference-based devices could exploit symmetry engineering deliberately.
arxiv-2512-08053:
Nora Almasi and Maria Axenovich, mathematicians who work in combinatorics, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the online Ramsey turnaround game, a two player game played on a board of vertices with three colors. Builder reveals one new edge at a time and may ban one color for that edge, while Painter colors it and tries to force a single colored copy of a fixed graph.

The authors study how many edges Painter needs before a win is guaranteed, and how large a complete board must be. They give bounds for both quantities. They also show the game connects closely with other ideas in extremal graph theory, including polychromatic colorings and several kinds of Ramsey and Turan numbers. Those links let results from one area inform the other, and they frame the new game as part of a wider family of coloring problems.
arxiv-2512-08353:
Ruo Li, Haoyang Liu, and Jun Yin, numerical analysts in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They design a finite element method for distributed elliptic optimal control, where a control spread through a region steers a system governed by an elliptic equation. Their scheme uses a reconstructed discontinuous approximation, which packs high order accuracy into each element while keeping only one unknown per element.

Both the state and the adjoint variables live in that same lean approximation space. The authors derive error estimates of both kinds: a priori bounds known before computing, and a posteriori bounds read from the solution itself. They also build a discrete system that can actually be solved efficiently, using a projected gradient descent method with proven linear convergence. Numerical tests confirm the predicted convergence order and show the a posteriori estimates are efficient.
arxiv-2512-08753:
Anindya Bhattacharjee and coauthors propose a low cost system to monitor fruit quality using an electronic nose linked through the internet of things. Post harvest losses are high when quality is judged only by eye, a problem that hurts income and food safety, notably in Bangladesh. An objective, science based check could help farmers and sellers make better decisions.

Their system uses an array of gas sensors to track gases given off by fruit, including ethanol, methane, and ammonia, which signal both ripening and decay. Tests use bananas as the sample fruit. Thresholds on gas levels feed a mathematical model that grades quality. Results are shown on a dashboard for quick monitoring and action. The authors argue the design is low power, affordable, and scalable along the supply chain.
arxiv-2512-08953:
Filippo Cenacchi, Longbing Cao, and Deborah Richards present SimClinician, a simulation testbed for collaboration between psychologists and artificial intelligence in mental health diagnosis. In practice, the value of a diagnostic system depends on how clinicians respond to its suggestions, whether they accept, adjust, or reject them. Mental health decisions are gradual and shaped by tone, pauses, word choice, and nonverbal cues.

The platform turns patient data into a collaborative diagnostic setting that can be tested before live studies. A dashboard joins audio, text, and gaze and expression patterns. An avatar module renders de identified patient dynamics for analysis. A decision layer maps model outputs to multimodal evidence, so psychologists can review the reasoning and enter their own diagnosis. Tests built from hundreds of clinical interviews, expanded into many simulations, show a confirmation step raises acceptance notably. Escalations stay low and interaction flow stays smooth throughout the simulated sessions.
arxiv-2512-09253:
Tianyuan Cai and Xiao Zhang study Majorana spinors, particle fields that are their own antiparticles, in Kerr spacetime, around a rotating black hole. They ask which such fields can exist there at all. Their first results are negative: massive Majorana spinors depending on time or on the angle around the hole cannot exist in Kerr or its cosmological cousins.

For massless spinors, the Dirac equation separates into radial and angular parts governed by two complex constants. When at least one constant vanishes, the authors solve the equation explicitly. When both are nonzero, they prove no time-periodic solutions can exist outside the horizon of a non-extreme hole. They then build the Hamiltonian picture. Its self-adjointness forces the spin to zero, reducing the spacetime to the non-rotating Schwarzschild case. There, the field's probability drains from any fixed region over time.
arxiv-2512-09353:
Mordehai Milgrom uses bimetric MOND as a platform for theories in which Newton's gravitational constant, G, is not truly constant. MOND is his long-standing alternative to dark matter for explaining galaxy dynamics. Its rules demand a return to standard dynamics at high acceleration. That automatically gives the standard value of G in places like the solar system, where changes in G are tightly limited.

That split is the point: constraints from high-acceleration systems then say nothing about cosmology. Milgrom explores theory variants where a larger effective G governs the later expansion of the universe. This could do work usually assigned to dark matter, without adding new fields or new constants. He gives examples where G keeps its standard value for all systems below cosmic scale, even deep in the MOND regime. Other examples switch the change on only late in cosmic history, respecting limits from the early universe.
arxiv-2512-09453:
Xiangtong Wang proposes BlockFlex, a routing architecture for mega-constellation networks of thousands of low Earth orbit satellites. Such networks promise global internet coverage, but their topology never sits still: satellite-ground links change constantly and links between satellites fail on and off. Those dynamics create heavy control traffic and leave the network sparse, hurting both efficiency and resilience.

BlockFlex hides the churn behind a robust virtual overlay. Satellites are clustered into unnamed blocks that present a stable topology to the routing layer. Between blocks, convergence-free forwarding carries traffic; inside each block, an isolated routing process runs, keeping control traffic local instead of global. Extra mechanisms add scale and resilience. In tests on current operational constellations, with up to roughly a third of inter-satellite links failing at random, BlockFlex substantially outperformed leading schemes in both routing resilience and efficiency.
arxiv-2512-09853:
Zhaoji Tang sharpens a known statistical result about deep neural network estimators. Earlier work by Farrell and coauthors gave probability bounds for general deep feedforward networks with rectified linear activations. For fully connected networks, though, their convergence rate was below the best possible. Those authors suggested that better approximation results for fully connected networks could close the gap. Tang supplies exactly that, deriving approximation bounds tailored to a narrower class of fully connected deep networks.

With the new bounds in place, the earlier theorem improves to an optimal convergence rate, up to a logarithmic factor. The note also shows briefly why deep network estimators can dodge the curse of dimensionality in two important cases. One case covers functions built by composing simpler pieces. The other covers functions defined on lower dimensional manifolds sitting inside high dimensional space. The contribution is a focused theoretical note rather than a new method.
arxiv-2512-10053:
Tiago Brogueira and Mário A. T. Figueiredo propose a new score for judging binary classifiers. The standard score, the area under the receiver operating curve, is rank based and popular. The authors identify problems where it misleads: tasks unchanged by locally swapping the two classes. They call this property invariance to local exchange of classes, and they build a metric that has it by construction. Their metric is also rank based, intuitive, logically consistent, and always computable. A companion curve gives a more detailed picture of performance across decision rates.

The authors map the metric's relationships to existing ones. It can be read as a symmetrized form of the standard area, as a rank based analogue of accuracy, or as a more interpretable variant of another recent area measure. Their showcase is causal discovery between two variables, where the metric fixes known flaws of current scores. Code is public.
arxiv-2512-10353:
Yiheng Lyu leads a team segmenting medical volumes when only slice level labels exist. Weakly supervised segmentation trains from plane level annotations, far cheaper than voxel by voxel tracing, but most methods use two dimensional encoders that ignore the volume's third dimension. Their model, TranSamba, is a hybrid: a vision transformer backbone augmented with cross plane Mamba blocks. Mamba sequence models run in linear time, and here they shuttle information between neighboring image planes. That cross plane exchange sharpens each plane's attention and improves the attention maps used to localize anatomy, all while keeping time and memory costs flat as volumes get deeper.

Across three datasets spanning different imaging modalities and diseases, TranSamba reached state of the art weakly supervised performance.
arxiv-2512-10453:
Lars Johnsen revisits a classic debate in linguistics: what counts as evidence that grammar has real structure inside the mind? Traditional generative grammar points to sharp contrasts, sentences native speakers accept against near-identical ones they reject, as proof of a hidden hierarchical system. His paper tests whether large language models show the same contrasts.

Johnsen probes GPT-4 and LLaMA-3 with two famous constructions, subject-auxiliary inversion and parasitic gaps, asking for acceptability ratings. The models reliably separated grammatical from ungrammatical versions in both cases, even though they were trained only to predict surface text. He concludes that a working sensitivity to syntax can grow out of prediction training alone, without the structure being built in by hand, which reframes what the classic evidence actually proves.
arxiv-2512-11153:
Saeed Shaebani settles an existence question about a highly regular way of colouring the vertices of a graph. In a FAT colouring, every vertex must see exactly the same pattern of colours among its neighbours, with one proportion for its own colour class and another for every other class. For fixed numbers of colours and fixed proportions, it was unknown whether any graph with no isolated vertices could admit such a colouring.

Shaebani answers yes by explicit construction. He builds an endless sequence of regular graphs, no two of them equivalent under graph homomorphisms, each carrying a FAT colouring with the required parameters. The result shows these rigid colourings are not rare accidents but occur in rich families. That opens the door to studying how such symmetry constrains graph structure more generally.
arxiv-2512-11753:
Agustin Cabrera, David Ziegler, and Markus Schläpfer map where city cyclists suffer most from heat, and how to cool them best. Riders are exposed by design, and heat waves put them at real risk. The team joined a fine scale city weather model with 4.76 million Citi Bike trips in New York during the June 2024 heat wave.

A small share of streets carried most of the heat exposure. Planting trees on just 1.5 percent of the street network cut heat exposed riding distance by 19 percent, worth about 4 degrees of stress relief. Random citywide planting did far worse. Day heat stress also ran higher in lower income areas, a fairness point for planners.
arxiv-2512-11853:
Mitchell Marfinetz lets evolution design the optimizer, the rule that tunes a neural network weights during training. His genetic algorithm encodes optimizers as genomes mixing basic parts: gradient, momentum, RMS scaling, Adam style adaptation, and sign based steps, plus schedules and settings.

Across 50 generations of 50 candidates, judged on several vision tasks, a winner emerged. It beat Adam by 2.6 percent in total fitness and by 7.7 percent on CIFAR-10. The evolved rule pairs sign based steps with adaptive moments, uses lower momentum than Adam, drops bias correction, and adds warmup with cosine decay. The odd recipe hints that hand designed optimizers may not sit at the best spot after all.
arxiv-2512-12253:
Hector Cancio and Pere Masjuan compute pion form factors in a 2025 physics paper. Pions are light particles made of quarks, and a form factor shows how charge spreads inside them. The middle energy range is poorly known, sitting between low and high energy regimes where different methods work.

The authors use a holographic QCD model with two dilaton fields to get a running strong coupling. Data for the neutral pion stray from expected high energy behavior, and the charged pion is less studied. Their results suggest non-perturbative effects matter even at energies once thought safe for simple methods. They also study isospin breaking through the pion mass gap.
arxiv-2512-12553:
Muhammad Hassnain, Anirudh Basu, Ethan Ng, and Caleb Stanford present Cargo Sherlock, a checker for software trust costs, in a 2025 paper. Supply chain attacks hit open source ecosystems by sneaking bad code into trusted packages. Judging a dependency's trust by downloads or author counts is informal, while formal safety proofs ignore those human signals.

Their framework joins both: an SMT based model, checked by automated solvers, combines code analysis data with metadata like downloads and authors. Trust cost is the cheapest set of assumptions that proves the code safe. Cargo Sherlock targets Rust crates. It flagged synthetic supply chain attacks and known incidents, including typosquatted and poorly AI maintained crates, and scaled to many dependencies.
arxiv-2512-12653:
Tatsuru Kikuchi builds a continuous framework for treatment effects with spillovers in a 2025 paper. A policy's effect can spread through space and through economic networks, so treated and untreated units are not independent. Standard discrete models capture parts of that spread, but a unified treatment has been missing.

Kikuchi derives a master equation from three foundations: heterogeneous agent aggregation, market equilibrium, and cost minimization. Classic spatial and network models appear as special cases. One result ties the space network interaction term to the mutual information between geographic and network coordinates. In Monte Carlo tests, standard estimators showed 25 to 38 percent bias when spillovers existed, while his estimator kept correct inference in all cases.
arxiv-2512-12953:
Madhav Sankaranarayanan and co-authors develop methods for regression when the answers must obey straight-line constraints. Their work is driven by genetics: how genes affect diabetes related traits, using outside knowledge about proteins that sit between genes and disease.

They study several candidate estimators and examine how each behaves in theory and in numbers. The setting is high-dimensional, with many more variables than classic methods assume. They look for sharp large-sample optimality, meaning the methods do as well as possible when data are plentiful. The goal is sound inference that uses external protein data without bending the results.
arxiv-2512-13253:
Julian Berger and co-authors argue that human learning is an overlooked lever for making people and AI work better together than either alone. A recent meta-analysis found that human-AI pairs, on average, do not beat the better partner alone. The authors suspect study designs are to blame.

They re-analyzed all 74 studies in that meta-analysis. Most designs lacked features that help people learn, such as outcome feedback. Studies with feedback showed tentatively higher synergy. Feedback plus AI explanations was linked to positive synergy, while explanations without feedback linked to negative synergy. They call for a paradigm shift toward designs that foster learning.
arxiv-2512-13453:
Eugeny Babichev, Sukrti Bansal, Maria Mylova, and Antonio Padilla extend Weinberg's effective field theory of scalar-tensor gravity to sixth order in derivatives. Effective theories collect all interactions allowed by symmetry at a given order, giving a systematic tool to test gravity beyond Einstein's theory. The four-derivative case was built by Weinberg himself.

Their on-shell theory contains five parity-even and three parity-odd independent six-derivative terms, exhausting the changes consistent with general covariance. An independent count using scattering amplitudes in flat spacetime confirms the tally. The framework supports studies of quantum or string corrections, parity violation, and strong curvature in cosmology and black hole physics.
arxiv-2512-13553:
Thomas Mutschler, Greta Villa, and Oded Zilberberg extend a topology frame for nonlinear resonators to cover limit cycles. A limit cycle is a self-sustained loop of motion in phase space. Past flow topology tools were built on fixed points and missed these loops, even though they act as strong organizing centers.

Using a graph-based build, the authors show how periodic attractors change the global links of phase-space flows. They show the idea on a Van der Pol resonator, where limit cycles sit next to fixed points. The result gives one account of steady and periodic phases in bosonic systems. It bears on photonic, superconducting, and optomechanical devices, and on sync and quantum uses.
arxiv-2512-13753:
Mika Sipilä and co-authors add time awareness to deep networks that downscale satellite pollution data. Satellite measures of air pollutants are often coarse, which limits local analysis. Downscaling turns coarse fields into high-resolution maps, here for tropospheric ozone over Italy.

They extend two standard models, a super-resolution deep residual network and a UNet, with a light temporal module. The module encodes observation time with sinusoidal or radial basis encodings and fuses it with spatial features. Against their baseline versions, the time-aware models improved downscaling results and convergence speed. The cost was only a slight rise in computing complexity, making the temporal step a cheap gain for ozone mapping.
arxiv-2512-13853:
Finley Devlin and Jaron Sanders view dropout training of neural networks through the lens of percolation. Dropout, introduced by Hinton and co-authors in 2012, randomly removes connections at each training step and updates what remains. Removing links at random is much like percolation, the statistical physics model of flow through a random network.

If dropout removes so many links that no path joins input to output, the network cannot use the data at all. The authors build percolation models that mimic dropout and link network topology to that path problem. Their theory shows a percolative effect exists in dropout. They argue it can cause training breakdown in networks without biases, and heuristically in networks with biases as well.
arxiv-2512-13953:
Dawid Malarz and co-authors introduce unbranding, a task for removing brand identity from generated images. Text-to-image models often reproduce trademarked content without permission. Past removal work targets general concepts like styles or celebrities, not specific brand markers, which include subtle traits like a car's front grille.
