They build a benchmark data set and an evaluation framework that pairs vision language models with segmentation classifiers trained on human labels for logos and trade dress. Newer, higher-fidelity systems such as SDXL and FLUX synthesize brand markers more readily than older models, raising the urgency. Their results confirm unbranding is a distinct problem that needs specialized techniques, beyond general concept unlearning. A project page hosts the benchmark and details.
arxiv-2512-14053:
Sa Wang and co-authors study groomed jet substructure in heavy-ion collisions as a probe of the quark-gluon plasma. Jets lose energy in that plasma, and grooming strips soft radiation to expose their core structure. They examine both inclusive jets and photon-tagged jets in lead-lead collisions with the SHELL transport model.

Using Dynamical and Soft-Drop grooming, their calculations show suppression at high relative transverse momentum between groomed subjets, matching recent ALICE measurements. They trace that suppression to energy loss of the subleading subjet plus a narrowing of the groomed radius from selection bias. No enhancement appears even without selection bias. Broadening of the radius in photon-tagged jets gives direct evidence of substructure broadening, growing with jet radius.
arxiv-2512-14153:
Michael Mandl, Erhard Seiler, and Denes Sexty review kernel methods for complex Langevin simulations in a 2025 conference paper. Complex Langevin is a sampling method used when standard Monte Carlo fails, for example in some lattice gauge theories, but it can settle on the wrong answer.

The authors show how a kernel, a chosen function that reshapes the process, can fix wrong convergence in a simple toy model. They also discuss a new test for correctness that is both necessary and sufficient, unlike older tests. A machine learning approach for finding good kernels is outlined too. Early results apply it to the heavy dense limit of QCD, the theory of quarks and gluons.
arxiv-2512-14753:
Li Lin and coauthors study how to hide a detectable mark inside code written by large language models, so the code's origin can be proved later. Watermarking code matters because such code often carries valuable ideas and rights. Their 2025 method is called Code Acrostic, named for the way the mark hides in chosen spots.

Older methods fail when an attacker simply deletes the comments, which leaves the code working but strips the mark. Code is also hard to watermark because most of it is low entropy, meaning highly predictable. The authors use a Cue List of words to find the less predictable spots and place the mark there. Tests on HumanEval beat three leading methods on detection while keeping the code usable.
arxiv-2512-14853:
George Georgiou and a coauthor propose a new family of holographic dualities, the links that tie a gravity theory to a quantum field theory without gravity. Their focus is defect conformal field theories, theories with a lower dimensional defect embedded in a larger space. Many known examples rely on supersymmetry, which theirs mostly drops.

Their setup bridges two known cases: the half BPS D3-D3 brane system at one end, and a duality from an earlier 2025 study at the other. On the gravity side, a D5 probe brane sits in AdS5 by S5 space and ends on two D7 branes. That pairing cancels a gauge anomaly through inflow, keeping the system sound. The authors also solve the matching field theory equations and find ranges where no unstable modes appear.
arxiv-2512-15053:
Fanzhe Fu proposes a protocol for turning chatty language models into dependable software parts. Today's prompt engineering is mostly craft and guesswork, with no firm guarantees for critical uses. The Meta-Prompting Protocol instead treats prompts as code in a self optimizing system.

At its center sits an Adversarial Trinity: a Generator that writes, an Auditor that checks, and an Optimizer that revises. Textual critiques act like gradients, the signals that steer learning, inside a semantic computation graph. The author argues this loop curbs hallucination and guards against model collapse. The framework leans on tools like DSPy and TextGrad to show the design can be built. It is offered as a base for what the author calls observable software engineering in an age of probabilistic computing.
arxiv-2512-15453:
Michele Cortinovis, Fabio Lingua, and David Haviland solve an inverse problem for parametric oscillators in a 2025 paper. A parametric oscillator can mix signals at different frequencies when driven by a pump wave. The hard part is working backward: given a desired mixing pattern, what pump shape will produce it?

Their method computes the frequency parts of the pump wave that realize a chosen scattering pattern between modes. Numerical checks confirm it works, and they test how added Gaussian noise affects it. Experiments at microwave frequencies show complex multi mode scattering, including one way circulation of signals. A faster approximate method can also reroute signals quickly between modes.
arxiv-2512-15553:
Krystyna Kolwas models the decay of localized surface plasmons in metal nanoparticles in a 2025 paper, viewing those plasmons as quasi particles. Plasmons are collective electron oscillations that can emit light, and their damping limits sensing and emission control uses. The model links classical electrodynamics with a quantum emitter picture.

Unlike cavity quantum electrodynamics, where emitter and cavity are separate, here the quasi particle sits inside the resonant near field cavity it creates itself. Kolwas extends Fermi's Golden Rule to include that self generated cavity effect. The resulting formulas for total damping rates show a size dependent suppression in higher multipolarity modes. The suppression comes from radiative and non radiative channels acting together, a self quenching effect.
arxiv-2512-15653:
Tamanna Hossain and co authors probe what the Mamba language model family forgets in a 2025 paper. Mamba models use a fixed size memory at run time, unlike transformers, so long inputs must lose some information. Earlier work timed when loss begins, but not which kinds of information go first.

The team trains an autoencoder to rebuild sequences from Mamba's hidden state and compares inputs with rebuilds for models from 130 million to 1.4 billion parameters. Loss falls hardest on math tokens such as numbers and variables, on organization names, and on dialects other than Standard American English. Forgotten tokens tend to be rarer in pretraining data, which points to clear fixes.
arxiv-2512-15853:
Guillermo Barro and co authors map the spectral diversity of Little Red Dots with JWST spectroscopy in a 2025 paper. Little Red Dots are compact early universe sources with blue ultraviolet light, red optical slopes, and broad Balmer lines that challenge standard models. They may be a population of unusual active galactic nuclei.

Using public NIRSpec prism spectra across six deep fields, the team studies 118 Little Red Dots with high signal spectra. Bluer sources show blue ultraviolet slopes and power law optical shapes, while redder ones show Balmer breaks and curvature. Line diagnostics shift from active nucleus dominated to host dominated along the same trend. A two component model, a gas wrapped black hole plus a galaxy host, reproduces the variety.
arxiv-2512-16153:
E F Keane and a large SKA team plan a sky census in their 2025 paper on arXiv. Before astronomers can time pulsars precisely or locate them with linked telescopes, they must first find them. The authors lay out how to run an all-sky blind pulsar survey with the Square Kilometre Array.

They weigh the known pulsar population, the performance of the SKA parts now under construction, and practical limits like radio interference. Their best plan mixes both telescopes: SKA1-Low sweeps as much sky as possible, while SKA1-Mid focuses near the galactic plane. In their most realistic scenario, phase one finds about 10,000 ordinary pulsars and about 800 millisecond pulsars. A larger final array raises the yield by about 20 percent. The census would sharpen knowledge of the whole neutron star population.
arxiv-2512-17253:
Yiren Song and three co-authors present Mitty, a system that turns a video of a person doing a task into a video of a robot doing the same task. Older methods first reduce the human video to key points or paths, and that shortcut loses detail and piles up errors. Mitty skips the shortcut and works end to end.

Built on a pretrained video diffusion model, Mitty squeezes the demo into tokens and blends them with the robot video as it forms. The team also built a pipeline that makes matched human and robot clips from large first-person video sets, easing a shortage of training pairs. On two test sets, Mitty beat prior methods and handled new rooms it had never seen.
arxiv-2512-17653:
Deon Janse van Rensburg and seven co-authors chill rubidium atoms held in laser tweezers down to 4.0 microkelvin, colder than the standard method reaches. Their trick is lambda-enhanced gray molasses, a laser cooling recipe that slows atoms by making them climb light hills, here applied to a rubidium line most labs avoid for this purpose. Colder atoms also hold their quantum state longer: the clock qubit coherence time grew by a factor of 1.5.

The setup needs no careful beam alignment and rides on the same lasers used to trap the atoms, needing only frequency and phase tweaks. A four-level computer model of the forces matched what the lab saw. Colder, longer-lived atoms are direct fuel for quantum computing and precision clocks.
arxiv-2512-17953:
Ellie Zhou, Jihoon Chung, and Olga Russakovsky show that action spotting models often cheat by reading the room instead of the person. A model may call a clip swimming because it sees a pool, not a swimmer. They test this background bias across plain classifiers, image text models, and video chat models.

Every type leaned on the background by default. For classifiers, feeding a cut out view of the person cut the bias by 3.78 percent. For video chat models, tuned prompts steered answers toward the person's motion and raised human focused reasoning by 9.85 percent. The fixes are partial, but they show where honest action reading can start.
arxiv-2512-18153:
Roblêdo Mak's Miranda Sette studies when a repeated map must settle on a point it leaves unchanged. Think of stepping again and again under one rule: if the total path length stays finite, the walk is called summable. Sette builds a score from that total length, summed over every step of a walk.

When that score behaves gently, he proves a settled point exists exactly when some walk is summable. The same test marks the broad Caristi family of maps, and his score is the smallest of its kind. The test covers the classic Banach shrinking rule, yet it stops short of two looser families, and he names the exact case that draws the line.
arxiv-2512-18353:
Maher Boudabra closes the last open case of a probability puzzle posed by R. Gross in 2019. The planar Skorokhod problem asks for a random walk in the plane that stops at a set time and lands with a given spread of outcomes. Gross solved it for spreads with a finite second moment, and later work covered every spread with a moment above one.

The borderline case of moment exactly one stayed open for years. Boudabra shows the embedding works there too, as long as one linked transform of the spread's quantile curve stays integrable. That single extra condition wraps up the whole line of study, a neat end to a six year thread.
arxiv-2512-18453:
Jayant Lohia works on Winograd convolution, a fast method that cuts the arithmetic needed to run neural networks. For 3x3 kernels it cuts the work by 2.25 times. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, targets a weakness: the standard transforms use whole-number points. Their error grows so fast at large tile sizes that low-precision hardware cannot use them. For the F(8,3) setting the condition number reaches 2 x 10^5.

His framework, NOVA, treats point selection as a continuous search. It then snaps the winners to simple fractions and checks them symbolically. The fractional points it finds improve F(8,3) conditioning 415-fold in one dimension. On FP16 ImageNet tests, standard transforms collapse to 4.7 percent accuracy on VGG16. NOVA restores 75 to 78 percent with no retraining. The transforms drop straight into existing pipelines.
arxiv-2512-18953:
Nicolas Caytuiro and Ivan Sipiran audit 3D generative models for a property humans expect automatically: symmetry. Chairs, cars, and animals are mirror-symmetric, yet standard benchmarks never check whether generated shapes keep that symmetry. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, scores generated point clouds with a Chamfer-distance-based symmetry measure and finds a persistent gap hidden by good headline metrics.

The gap is not just inherited from training data. Diagnostics at the sampling and latent levels show reflection symmetry is not reliably encoded in the generative process at all. Their fix is data-centric: train on half-objects and rebuild full shapes by reflection at sampling time. Across model backbones, geometric consistency and plausibility jump while standard scores stay competitive. Symmetry, they argue, deserves its own line in every 3D benchmark.
arxiv-2512-19053:
Asuka Ito, Ryuichiro Kitano, Wakutaka Nakano, and Ryoto Takai propose a detector for very high-frequency gravitational waves. Their sensor is a flat crystal of trapped ions. A passing wave can set the crystal's drumhead modes ringing, in step with the wave.

An optical force links those vibrations to the ions' shared spin, turning motion into a spin rotation that can be read out. The link also squeezes the spin state, which lets the device pass the standard quantum limit. Bigger crystals with more ions do better. The team targets waves from ten kilohertz to ten megahertz, a band few other designs reach.
arxiv-2512-19353:
Xiyun Xu and Ming Xu settle the basic shape of left-invariant complex Finsler metrics on complex Lie groups. Finsler metrics let distance depend on direction, a richer geometry than the Riemannian kind. When the metric is unchanged by left multiplication on the group, symmetry should force strong restrictions.

Using invariant frames, they prove any such metric must be a complex Berwald metric. Its spray extends to a holomorphic field and matches the group's canonical bi-invariant spray. Strongly Kähler, Kähler, and weakly Kähler all turn out to be the same condition here, holding exactly when the group's Lie algebra is Abelian. Holomorphic sectional curvature vanishes outright.
arxiv-2512-19553:
Luke Benz, Rajarshi Mukherjee, Rui Wang, and David Arterburn ask whether bariatric surgery's benefit has drifted over calendar time. Health-record studies usually report one constant effect, yet surgical craft improves and patient mixes shift, so a single number can mislead. Their data come from Kaiser Permanente records on two procedures against standard care.

The framework estimates the average effect separately by the year treatment began, using doubly robust methods. Those estimates are then projected onto structural models that describe how and why effects vary, with a selection step to choose among explanations. Covariate shift in effect modifiers is handled head-on, separating real drift from a changing patient pool.
arxiv-2512-19753:
Yanzhen Wang leads a fourteen-author team introducing QMBench, a benchmark meant to test whether language-model agents can do real quantum materials research. Solving problems in this field demands condensed matter physics knowledge plus working skill with tools such as density functional theory. Existing general benchmarks barely touch that combination, so the team built a standardized evaluation around it.

QMBench spans structural and electronic properties, thermodynamics, symmetry principles, and computational methodology, sampling the main domains of quantum materials work. The stated ambition is to speed development of an AI scientist able to contribute creatively, not merely answer textbook questions. The authors also expect the benchmark to keep evolving, treating it as shared community infrastructure rather than a frozen test.
arxiv-2512-19853:
Marco Ratta, Pavel Mozgunov, Sandrine Boulet, and Moreno Ursino redesign clinical trials that borrow yesterday's control patients. Historical controls help when full randomization is infeasible, but populations, diagnostics, and standards drift over time, inviting bias. Hybrid designs mix a concurrent control arm with historical data, and this proposal adds a mid-trial checkpoint that measures how well the two control sources actually agree.

Agreement is quantified by a Hellinger-distance criterion at the interim analysis. That single measure then steers two decisions: how strongly the historical data shape the prior for the final analysis, and how the second-stage sample size is reassessed. Simulations across continuous and binary endpoints show the design flexing sensibly with the degree of mismatch between old and new controls.
arxiv-2512-19953:
Spencer Rogers, Salman Shahid, and Wenchao Ge gauge how nonclassical a noisy state of light stays. Their gauge is the operational resource theory measure. It is prized for two traits. It behaves well as a resource measure, and it links to metrological gain. But it is hard to compute for mixed states, since it hides an optimization. The paper targets mixed states with photon-number coherence. That is the off-diagonal structure between unlike photon counts.

Exact formulas cover a broad class of rank-two mixed states. Numeric answers cover some higher ranks. The team then compares nonclassicality with metrological power. They show where the power meets the resource bound and where it falls short. Dephasing never lifts either quantity. Both can plateau, in a pattern like entanglement sudden death. Trimming coherence can, at times, yield more useful states.
arxiv-2512-20153:
Grega Šuštar, Jer Pelhan, Alan Lukežič, and Matej Kristan count crowds with almost no examples. Low-shot counting estimates how many instances of a never-seen object category fill an image, given a handful of exemplars or none. Density-based counters tally dense clusters of tiny objects well but localize them poorly; detection-based counters localize precisely yet run out of pretrained queries when objects number in the thousands.

CoDi is the first latent-diffusion counter built for this task, producing high-quality density maps from which object positions are read off by non-maxima suppression. Its core is an exemplar-conditioning module that extracts object prototypes and adjusts them into the denoising network's intermediate layers. On the FSC benchmark it cut counting error by double-digit percentages across few-shot, one-shot, and reference-less settings, and set a new state of the art on MCAC.
arxiv-2512-21353:
Nonlinear diffusion with power-law tails governs systems from plasmas to city populations, and Airton Deppman finds exact solutions for a hard case of it. The Plastino-Plastino equation usually forces approximations, especially with several overlapping modes. His trick is letting each q-exponential mode carry its own moving centre, which decouples the modes entirely.

Transient modes then keep constant width and decay by exact power-law relaxation, while one attractor mode absorbs all the probability and spreads, steering any starting state to the known stationary profile. The solution hierarchy closes with no approximation, and every earlier exact result falls out as a special case. Applications named range from heavy-quark jets in quark-gluon plasma to Lévy flights and urban redistribution.
arxiv-2512-21653:
Liuyang Bai, Weiyi Lu, and Li Guo present SemDAC, a neural speech codec that compresses speech using meaning as well as sound. Ordinary codecs spend bits on acoustic detail that a listener could infer from the words themselves. That wastes bitrate and can hurt speech recognition on the decoded audio.

SemDAC adds hierarchical semantic conditioning to residual vector quantization. Its first quantizer is distilled from HuBERT features, so its tokens carry phonetic content. Later quantizers encode the leftover acoustic detail. The decoder is steered by the semantic tokens through feature-wise linear modulation, pushing reconstruction toward what the semantics cannot explain. At under one kilobit per second, SemDAC matches or beats a baseline codec running at two and a half kilobits on standard quality and intelligibility measures and on recognition error. Listeners also rated it higher than higher-bitrate baselines. Explicit semantic conditioning, not bigger models, drives the gain.
arxiv-2512-21953:
Distributed MIMO systems that both talk and sense must split their access points and power between the two jobs. Venkatesh Tentu and colleagues study phase-coherent distributed MIMO integrated sensing and communication, where synchronized access points serve users while detecting and estimating several static targets.

Their scheme runs in two stages, combining non-coherent and coherent estimation. Two mode-selection plans adapt the array: one maximizes downlink spectral efficiency, the other picks well-spread receive points for coverage. Simulations confirm the trade-off, softened by sensible power splits and larger apertures, reaching millimeter-level precision at high spectral efficiency. An optimal number of receive access points emerges for coverage. The study maps the trade-off in full.
arxiv-2512-22053:
V. S. Shalgin, a mathematician at Saint Petersburg State University, studies when a hidden quantity inside a system of usual differential equations can be pinned down from watching the solution. The hidden quantity here is not a single number but a whole function. Earlier work covered only systems where the parameter and the solution have the same dimension.

Shalgin widens that earlier class of systems and also handles cases where the parameter's dimension is smaller than the solution's. For both settings, the paper derives sufficient conditions under which the parameter function is locally identifiable. Identifiability is judged from observations of the solution at only a finite number of points.
arxiv-2512-22253: Bayaz Daraby, Asghar Rahimi, and Hasan Haddadzadeh write a short mathematics article. It extends the inner product, the construction measuring length and angle in vector spaces, into fuzzy mathematics over ordered intervals. They first define ordered intervals, then introduce an ordered fuzzy inner product built on that notion, and describe some of its traits, including the fuzzy norms that arise from it.
arxiv-2512-22353:
Mihalis Maliakas and Dimitra-Dionysia Stergiopoulou extend a tableau construction that produces the irreducible representations of transformation monoids, algebraic forms describing all ways to map a finite set to itself. Grood built the tableaux for the rook monoid and Steinberg for the full transformation monoid. The new approach works in any characteristic and covers every submonoid of partial transformations that contains the symmetric group.

The engine is a functor carrying rational representations of the matrix monoid into representations of the transformation monoid, from which two branching rules follow. The main results describe graded module forms of orbit harmonics quotients for the rook, partial transformation, and full transformation monoids. These yield analogues of the Cauchy decomposition for polynomial rings in matrix variables.
arxiv-2512-22653:
Amir El-Ghoussani, André Kaup, Nassir Navab, Gustavo Carneiro, and Vasileios Belagiannis estimate depth from a single photograph using an autoregressive image model rather than a diffusion model. They adapt a large text-to-image visual autoregressive model, adding a scale-wise conditional upsampling mechanism with classifier-free guidance. Generation then proceeds coarse to fine in ten fixed stages, mirroring how the image model builds pictures scale by scale.

Remarkably, fine-tuning needed only 74,000 synthetic samples. Under that constrained training budget, the method reached state-of-the-art results on indoor benchmarks and stayed strong outdoors. The authors position autoregressive priors as a complementary family of geometry-aware generative models for depth. Advantages include how little data adaptation requires. The recipe also transfers readily to other 3D vision tasks.
arxiv-2512-23353:
Nilin Abrahamsen introduces ISOPO, a policy optimization method for reinforcement learning that approximates the natural policy gradient in a single step. Proximal methods like GRPO and CISPO approach the same target indirectly, taking multiple gradient steps while clipping importance ratios against a reference policy. ISOPO instead builds the geometry in directly, normalizing each sequence's log-probability gradient in the Fisher metric before combining it with the sequence's advantage.

A second variant reshapes the microbatch advantages using each layer's neural tangent kernel. Either way, the correction is applied layer by layer inside one backward pass, so the overhead over plain REINFORCE is negligible. The note is deliberately compact: its claim is that faithful natural-gradient geometry does not need the old-policy ratios, multiple epochs, and clipping machinery that current proximal methods carry. That simplicity is the selling point for practitioners who find ratio bookkeeping fragile.
arxiv-2512-23453:
Zongsheng Cao and co-authors present CoFi-Dec, a strategy that stops vision-language models from describing things that are not in the picture. Hallucination remains the reliability bottleneck for these models, and retraining is expensive. CoFi-Dec needs no training: it borrows the visual habit of glancing at the scene before inspecting details, generating draft responses from coarse and fine views of the image.

Those drafts are rendered into synthetic images by a text-to-image model, creating multi-level hypotheses that enrich the grounding evidence. A fusion mechanism based on the Wasserstein distance aligns the predictions from all these conditions into one geometrically consistent path. The design aims to keep high-level semantic consistency and fine-grained grounding pulling in the same direction. On six hallucination-focused benchmarks, CoFi-Dec cut both object-level and semantic-level hallucinations and beat decoding strategies, staying model-agnostic.
arxiv-2512-23553:
Members of the COSINUS collaboration, writing with G. Angloher as first author, study defects in sodium iodide crystals used to hunt for dark matter. Sodium iodide scintillators reported a long-debated annual modulation signal, and cryogenic versions aim to test that claim. When a dark matter particle strikes a crystal, it can knock atoms out of place and leave lasting defects behind.

Combining molecular dynamics simulations with density functional theory, the team modeled a collision and catalogued the resulting vacancies and interstitial atoms. They computed the electronic states these defects create inside the band gap, the energy each defect costs, and how the displacement threshold varies with direction. Because defects carry distinctive electronic signatures, the authors propose them as a possible new detection channel for dark matter.
arxiv-2512-23753:
Deep Shankar Pandey, Hyomin Choi, and Qi Yu study evidential deep learning, a technique that makes ordinary neural networks report how uncertain they are. Rooted in subjective logic, these models learn evidence for each class rather than a bare probability. The catch is structural: evidence must be non-negative, forcing special activation functions whose geometry can freeze learning, because gradients nearly vanish for samples mapped into low-evidence regions.

The authors characterize this learning-freeze behavior theoretically and analyze how different evidential activations shape learning dynamics. From that analysis they design a general family of activation functions with matching regularizers that keep evidence updates consistent across regimes. Experiments span four standard image classification benchmarks, two few-shot problems, and blind face restoration, and they support both the theory and the practical gains of the generalized models.
arxiv-2512-23853:
Hussen Abu Hamad and Dan Rosenbaum add flow matching to the neural process family. Neural processes learn a stochastic process from data and can then predict distributions at arbitrary new points, sample from them, or condition on observations. Flow matching, a generative technique that learns a velocity field steering noise into data, has excelled in other modalities, and the authors build it into the neural process framework.

Their model keeps the standard amortized training of neural processes but samples conditionals by solving an ordinary differential equation, with no auxiliary conditioning machinery. The number of solver steps trades accuracy against runtime at the user's discretion. Benchmarks covered synthetic one-dimensional Gaussian process data, two-dimensional images, and real weather records, and the flow matching model outperformed earlier neural process methods across them. The work appeared at NeurIPS 2025, with code released.
arxiv-2512-24153:
Weilong Guo, Lianguo Li, Qingjun Tong, and Ci Li study excitons in atom-thin semiconductors. An exciton is a bound electron-hole pair. The authors examine two sideways effects. One is a Hall effect for excitons. The other is its thermal cousin, the Nernst effect. Their tool is semiclassical transport theory.

They derive the exciton Berry curvature in momentum space. The formula links it to electron and hole properties. Effective masses enter as well. Two materials serve as examples. Both are monolayer systems. In these materials, symmetry forbids a linear Hall current when Berry curvature is present. That matches earlier observations in one compound. Black phosphorus breaks the pattern, though. Its strong anisotropy yields a sizable linear current. The effect resembles an anomalous Hall effect.
arxiv-2512-24253:
Alireza Rafiei and four colleagues aim wearables at early sepsis warning. Sepsis is a runaway immune response to infection. It brings high mortality and heavy healthcare costs. Early intervention depends on early prediction. Most existing models target intensive care patients. Detection outside hospital wards remains a gap.

The team designs four machine learning models for wearable devices. Heart rate signals are the only input. A genetic algorithm refines each model's architecture. The search balances accuracy against computing cost and memory. Those constraints decide whether a wearable can run the model at all. Initial models predict sepsis one hour ahead. Transfer learning extends the window to four hours. Results suggest wearables could flag sepsis beyond wards and intensive care. That prospect motivates the whole design.
arxiv-2512-24353:
Shubhankar Mandal, Avijit Pal, and Bhaskar Paul build functional models for a class of operators. The operators are Gamma-n contractions, objects from multivariable operator theory. A functional model represents an abstract operator as concrete functions and shifts. The first model follows Douglas's model for a single contraction.

Factorization results come next. They clarify how a minimal isometric dilation relates to an arbitrary one. Those results feed two further models. One is of Sz.-Nagy-Foias type for completely non-unitary Gamma-n contractions. The other is of Schäffer type for Gamma-n contractions in general. Models like these let analysts compute with operators through their function-theoretic shadows. The paper extends a classical single-variable theory into the multivariable Gamma-n setting.
arxiv-2512-24453:
William Paul Heath, Sayar Das, and Joaquin Carrasco revisit stability multipliers for Lurye systems. A Lurye system couples linear dynamics with a static nonlinearity. The nonlinearity here has restricted slope. Dynamic multipliers can certify stability of such loops. They said nothing about finite incremental gain, though. This paper closes that gap.

Multipliers do bound the closed-loop power gain, the authors show. The bound is quantifiable. Power is measured about a steady bias point. One condition is needed: the multiplier must not force the nonlinearity to be odd. Noise sensitivity then stays low when other signals settle to constants. Periodic excitation is subtler. Subharmonic or chaotic responses can apparently occur. A class of multipliers guarantees a unique, period-preserving response. The authors re-derive it with classical tools and recheck its assumptions.
arxiv-2512-24553:
Bohm-Jung Yang reviews a new era in measuring quantum geometry in solids. For decades, geometry in band theory meant the Berry phase and Berry curvature. Those quantities reshape how electrons move and underpin topological matter. The full story is richer. One tensor holds both the Berry curvature and the quantum metric. Measuring the whole tensor in real crystals was the challenge.

Resolved photoemission spectroscopy now reaches it. Two approaches succeeded recently. One builds a measurable stand-in that faithfully represents the tensor. The other uses pseudospin tomography in a material with a simple band structure. That route retrieved every component of the quantum metric. Yang explains what the advances mean, where they stop, and what remains open. Direct access turns quantum geometry from theory into measurement.
arxiv-2512-24653:
Chengkai Hou, Kun Wu, Jiaming Liu, Zhengping Che, and co-authors release RoboMIND 2.0, a large real-world dataset for training robots that use two arms and can move around. It holds more than three hundred thousand dual-arm trajectories across six robot types and hundreds of tasks. Tactile episodes and mobile manipulation runs add contact and travel.

Alongside the physical data, the team built digital twins of the real settings and released a simulated set as well. The aim is better generalization to long, two-handed tasks in messy places. Robot learning researchers get scale, variety, and paired real and virtual material in one resource.
arxiv-2512-24753:
Sohan Kumar Jha examines a magnetically charged black hole, shaped by nonlinear electrodynamics, sitting inside a Hernquist dark matter halo. Two influences compete: magnetic charge and the halo's density profile. He tracks the event horizon and the critical impact parameter for light, watching how charge and halo parameters move each quantity.

A recurring pattern is cancellation, where charge and halo effects offset and observables match a plain Schwarzschild black hole. Shadow and related measures show the same tendency. Readers get a warning for black hole observation: different underlying physics can hide behind familiar-looking measurements, so extra care is needed when inferring charge or halo traits.
arxiv-2512-24953:
Yuanchao Xu, Itsushi Sakata, and Isao Ishikawa — evidence title names the entry Resolvent-Based Singular-Value Diagnostics for Data-Driven Koopman Finite Sections — study how to judge Koopman estimates from data. Finite Koopman eigenvalues alone do not show resolvent growth, mainly for non-normal compressions. Their Resolvent Dynamic Mode Decomposition first removes open paths, then builds the compression in a data-based orthonormal basis.

At a chosen spectral value, the inverse of the smallest shifted singular value gives the resolvent norm on the kept space, and singular vectors give a minimum-residual testing. Dynamical systems readers get a sharper test of data-driven models than eigenvalues alone provide.
arxiv-2601-00053:
Yotam Shomroni develops new tools for studying words and subgroups inside free groups, a basic object in algebra. His 2026 paper builds a theory of polymatroids, structures that generalize independence, on special graphs tied to subgroups. That theory yields lower bounds for stable measures of words and subgroups, and upper bounds on how often random maps send them into a chosen subgroup of a finite group.

With those tools, Shomroni settles a gap conjecture about a stable rank measure. He also proves a conjecture about counts of solutions to equation systems in finite group actions. A unified proof covers a rank-one Hanna Neumann result and its higher-rank version. He ends by proposing a field-based analogue of the classic conjecture.
arxiv-2601-00453:
Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Wanda Isnard, Roman Pasechnik, and Anca Preda question a common belief about theories with a fifth dimension. Such theories are usually said to lose predictive power just above the scale where the extra dimension is curled up, because couplings grow too fast. The authors show five-dimensional gauge-Yukawa theories can stay valid to very high energies under two conditions.

Only a finite number of terms may be needed to absorb the fast-growing divergences, and all couplings must flow toward stable ultraviolet fixed points. By computing the relevant divergences directly, they prove the one-loop behavior for interactions that would be well behaved in four dimensions. The result gives a test that separates consistent five-dimensional models from ones describing only a few extra modes.
arxiv-2601-00553:
Rajarshi Roy and a twenty-author team release a large dataset for telling real photographs from AI-generated images. Generators such as Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, and MidJourney now produce pictures that are hard to distinguish from photos, which helps creative work but also spreads misleading media. Detection research needs shared data to make progress.

Their dataset, MS COCOAI, holds ninety-six thousand real and synthetic items built from the MS COCO collection. Synthetic images came from five generators, including two Stable Diffusion versions, SDXL, DALL-E 3, and MidJourney v6. The team defines two tasks on the data: deciding whether an image is real or generated, and naming which model made a synthetic one. The dataset is publicly available for other researchers.
arxiv-2601-00653:
Johannes Hörner and Paula Onuchic model a judge who must decide which of two speakers to trust, knowing only one is a genuine expert. The expert sees the true state perfectly; the other speaker is a quack with no information. Both want to be chosen, and the judge, who has private but imperfect information of their own, wants to find the expert.

They show an equilibrium generally exists where the expert stays honest, yet the judge favors more extreme signals. Surprisingly, that bias toward extremism sustains truthful communication rather than provoking exaggeration. The quack mimics the expert and sometimes panders to the judge's prior. Learning also compounds: better-informed judges identify the expert more often, an information-begets-information pattern with echoes in courts and expert testimony.
arxiv-2601-00753:
Dao Sy Duy Minh and six co-authors study, in 2026, the review load that AI coding agents place on human teams. The agents now file whole code changes, called pull requests, on their own. The team read over thirty-three thousand such requests. About twenty-eight in each hundred merged at once, with no fuss.

The worst cases end in ghosting, where the agent drops the task after hard feedback. That tail of costly requests acts as a hidden tax on staff time. The authors build a guard model that flags costly requests at birth. It uses plain cues, such as file types and the size of the change. At a fifth of the review budget, it caught about sixty-nine in each hundred of the costly ones. Teams could thus fail cheap requests fast and speed the easy wins.
arxiv-2601-00853:
Sameer Rahil, Zain Abdullah Ahmad, and Talha Asif improve federated learning, where many devices train one shared model without sending their data to a center. Devices hold very different data mixes, and that heterogeneity hampers convergence. A technique called sharpness-aware minimization helps by seeking flat, robust optima, but existing federated versions apply the same perturbation size to every client.

Their algorithm, FedSCAM, clusters clients and modulates the training per client. A heterogeneity score is computed for each client, and both the perturbation radius and the aggregation weights adjust in response, with less typical clients perturbed less aggressively. The design aims at robust optimization that respects how different edge devices really are, rather than treating the federation as uniform.
arxiv-2601-01253:
Spencer Rooke, Dmitry Krotov, Vijay Balasubramanian, and David Wolpert ask what it costs, in heat and work, to run a memory network. Dense associative memories are networks that store patterns and recall them from partial cues. The same math underlies Hopfield networks, transformers, and diffusion models, which makes these networks a clean test bed for the physics of computation.

The authors define the entropy produced while such a network operates away from equilibrium and study mid-sized memory loads at large scales. Using mean field theory, they work out how much work recall takes, how long it takes, and how errors creep in when the network is fed corrupted memories. They find a failure mode in higher-order networks that zero-temperature studies had missed, plus trade-offs among heat produced, recall accuracy, and speed. The results link AI performance to basic thermodynamic limits.
arxiv-2601-01753:
Recommenders learn each domain's tastes separately, yet privacy rules often forbid sharing user data between domains, blocking the usual cross-domain methods. Hyunsoo Kim, Jaewan Moon, Seongmin Park, and Jongwuk Lee propose MergeRec, which builds one universal sequential recommender by merging models rather than pooling data.

MergeRec starts from a training-free merge of domain models. It fabricates pseudo-user sequences. Each item is treated as a short virtual history. It then tunes the merging weights with a combined goal. The merged model should recommend well. It should also keep the shared signals of the source models. Experiments show the merged model keeps the strengths of its parts and generalizes to unseen domains, beating conventional merging by up to about seventeen percent in recall. The code is public.
arxiv-2601-01953:
Could a nucleon and an antinucleon bind together into a single state? Aaron Park, Sungtae Cho, and Su Houng Lee examine the nucleon-antinucleon system. Their tool is a constituent quark model. They build wave functions for the pair. The quark part and the antiquark part each respect the Pauli exclusion principle.

With a Hamiltonian combining color-dependent forces, spin-dependent interactions, and three-quark potentials, they search channel by channel for binding. In specific channels the interaction turns strongly attractive. A bound state looks strongly possible there. Such exotic matter-antimatter molecules would be a striking find for hadron study. The calculation tells lab teams which channels deserve the closest look.
arxiv-2601-02153:
Sunspot groups live and die on the far side of the Sun where no telescope sees them, yet global oscillation frequencies feel activity everywhere. William Chaplin and seven co-authors probe how long sunspot groups actually last. They use week-long datasets from the BiSON network. Frequency shifts are fitted with a mix of near-side activity and a far-side proxy.

Simulating spot group evolution shows the solution is sensitive to the assumed lifetime law linking a group's peak area to its lifespan. The best fit implies a proportionality well below the classic Gnevyshev-Waldmeier rule. The average lifetime is near five days. The fitted distribution still includes enough long-lived groups to explain the data, though. The work sharpens a basic input to solar activity modeling.
arxiv-2601-02653:
Ajay Brahmakshatriya, Saman Amarasinghe, and Martin Rinard replace a standard compiler technique with a predictive one. Many optimizations need to know how a program will behave in the future. The usual route builds an intermediate representation of the code. It then runs a backwards analysis that pushes information against the flow of control to the place where a decision is made. Their alternative is prophecy variables, variables that predict future facts inside the program itself.

Prophecy variables are implemented in BuildIt, a lightweight system for building domain specific languages inside C plus plus. BuildIt compiles in stages, running ordinary C plus plus first to generate optimized C, C plus plus, or CUDA code for the second stage. With prophecy variables available during that first run, language parts such as parsers can be removed and changes guided by predicted behavior, without a separate analysis pass.
arxiv-2601-02753:
Yao Shi and four co authors synthesize a voice that matches a face. In face based speech synthesis, the generated voice should sound like someone who looks like the reference photograph. Progress has been limited by the lack of studio quality paired audio and video data, so earlier systems either sounded poor or suffered domain mismatch when knowledge was transferred from elsewhere.

Their approach, Vclip, borrows the facial semantic knowledge of the CLIP image encoder and learns the face voice association directly from noisy audio visual data. Reaching a strong cross modal verification score on the VoxCeleb test set. For generation, a retrieval step proposes likely speakers for a given face, and a mixture model based speaker generator feeds a downstream text to speech system. Experiments show the pipeline bridges much of the gap between face and voice features.
arxiv-2601-02853: Pak Tung Ho constructs a special self-shrinking curve, known as a lambda-Angenent curve, using a modified curve shortening flow. Such curves arise in the study of how shapes evolve and shrink over time, and this one had previously been built only with a shooting method. Ho's flow-based approach gives a second, more dynamic route to the same curve, adding a tool for work on geometric flows.
arxiv-2601-02953:
Anuj Malik and Anees Ahmed study a unitary matrix model whose potential has Fisher-Hartwig singularities, sharp features that shape the model's behavior. Matrix models like this one are simplified stand-ins for hard problems in physics and probability. The authors map out the model's phases, the distinct regimes it passes through as its coupling changes, at both finite and large matrix size.

At finite size, the model shows phase transitions whose order depends on the coupling. At large size, those transitions become third-order Gross-Witten-Wadia transitions between several ungapped phases and a single gapped one, while direct transitions between ungapped phases are forbidden. In both regimes, the phases are pinned down by where the Fisher-Hartwig singularities sit in the complex plane.
arxiv-2601-03053:
Charlie James Paxman and twelve co-authors report a nuclear physics experiment on oxygen-20, performed at the GANIL facility in France. They fired deuterons at oxygen-19 and watched the protons and gamma rays that came out, a transfer reaction that adds one neutron and reveals the energy levels of the product nucleus. States above the neutron separation energy, which fall apart by emitting a neutron, were a special target.

The team observed bound states fed by s-wave and d-wave transfer with improved angular distributions. More notably, several unbound states between about 7.6 and 9.8 million electron volts were reached for the first time through this reaction channel and isolated with particle-gamma spectroscopy. The measurements trace one particular neutron orbital and sharpen the picture of oxygen-20's structure.
arxiv-2601-03353:
Antoine Rignon-Bret and Matthieu Vilatte restate the generalized second law of black hole thermodynamics from the viewpoint of observers at the edge of spacetime. The law says generalized entropy, black hole area plus the entropy of quantum fields outside, never decreases. Standard proofs work on the event horizon itself, using observable algebras and a symmetry-invariant vacuum. Distant observers at future null infinity have no access to the area term, so a dual formulation is needed.

Exploiting how the law depends on the chosen algebra and reference state, the authors analyze several physically motivated vacuum states, including the Hartle-Hawking state and regularized alternatives. They identify the quantity that increases monotonically at null infinity. This first part of a two-part work sets up a version of black hole thermodynamics that asymptotic observers can actually use.
arxiv-2601-03453:
Ioannis Ivrissimtzis and three co-authors propose a new way to measure bias in classifiers, meaning systems that sort cases into groups. Their idea uses sample size: if a bias is real and large, few cases are needed to prove it with statistics. If huge samples are needed, the bias is small. The measure turns that logic into a score.

The team studies two demographic groups and error rates estimated without assuming a fixed data shape. They check that the score behaves sensibly and compare it with the common difference and ratio of error rates. Their score can rank classifiers differently from both older measures. They argue its behavior comes from basic features of the method, not from the rough formula used.
arxiv-2601-03553:
Sangyub Lee, Heedou Kim, and Hyeoncheol Kim argue that police use of language models needs its own testing framework before real deployment. A model's answer may not be flatly illegal, yet unverified advice could still lead to unlawful arrests or mishandled evidence. Their framework, PAS, covers the full evaluation process using police action scenarios.

From more than eight thousand official documents, the team built a question dataset and set metrics checked against police expert judgments. Commercial models struggled on the new tasks, especially when asked for fact-based recommendations. The authors release their data and prompt template so others can extend the tests. The message is caution: high-stakes public safety work needs evidence of reliability first.
arxiv-2601-03653:
Giacomo Micheli and Mihran Papikian connect two distant areas of algebra: Drinfeld modules and rank-metric codes. Rank-metric codes are error-correcting codes where distance is measured by rank, useful in network coding and storage. Drinfeld modules are algebraic objects from function field arithmetic. The authors build codes from spaces of maps acting on parts of a Drinfeld module, focusing on semifield codes.

Inside that framework, a known construction by Sheekey falls out naturally, and one of his main results gains a short conceptual proof. The pair then construct new infinite families of semifield codes from Drinfeld modules over finite fields. Bridges like this matter because each field's hard problems can become the other's construction tools, enlarging the menu of codes engineers can choose from.
arxiv-2601-03953:
Lucas I. Iñigo Gamiz and three co-authors use quantum Monte Carlo integration to predict how many electron-positron pairs appear when two photon beams collide head-on. The process, the linear Breit-Wheeler process, matters for high-energy physics and intense laser-matter experiments. Quantum Monte Carlo is theorized to give a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo, making it attractive inside hybrid quantum-classical supercomputing.

Their quantum simulations matched theoretical predictions with high accuracy. The only limits came from approximations needed to embed polynomials and to initialize the quantum state. The demonstration is small but concrete: a real physics quantity, pair creation from light, computed through a quantum integration routine. Such validated building blocks are how quantum modules will earn places inside larger scientific simulation pipelines.
arxiv-2601-04053:
Pat Lank, writing alone, proves a key result for derived categories on a broad class of stacks. A stack is a space that also tracks the symmetries at each point. Lank assumes the stack is regular and Noetherian. He also assumes its diagonal map is quasi-finite.

He shows that one perfect complex can generate the whole derived category. In the concentrated case, the category is also singly compactly generated. That is a stronger finiteness trait. The proof glues generators along a recollement. It also uses careful filtrations and presentations of the stack. A single generator makes later work much simpler. Every object can then be built from one starting piece.
arxiv-2601-04253:
Sophie Greenwood and Nikhil Garg build and study Paper Skygest, a personalised feed of science posts on the Bluesky social network. Decentralised platforms built on the AT Protocol let anyone create and run a feed for others, a freedom closed platforms rarely grant. Their feed surfaces research posts from each user's own network.

By the authors' account it is the first and largest such academic feed run continuously, with heavy weekly use and a solid daily user base gained without promotion. Usage data show steady use and satisfied readers, and joining the feed raises interaction with research posts. Greenwood and Garg share their full code and system design so others can build feeds that last. They also discuss how custom feeds could support studies of algorithm design and user agency.
arxiv-2601-04353:
Samir Canning and nine co-authors work deep inside algebraic geometry in a 2026 arXiv paper, on the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties. A space that parametrizes certain fundamental geometric objects. Inside its Chow ring of cycles sits a smaller tautological algebra generated by natural classes, and a canonical projection maps every cycle onto that algebra. The open question is whether the projection respects multiplication.

The team computes how the Torelli locus, which marks abelian varieties coming from curves, intersects product loci built from smaller pieces, for the smallest cases, by two independent routes. Direct excess-intersection geometry, and a recasting through Gromov-Witten classes with a wall-crossing formula. The answers support the conjecture that the projection is indeed an algebra homomorphism, at least for special cycles. their machinery produces new classes they conjecture lie in the Gorenstein kernels of related tautological rings.
arxiv-2601-04653:
Zhe Hou reports building a theorem prover almost entirely by asking language models to write it, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The prover, Isabellm, does proof synthesis for the Isabelle/HOL assistant and runs on consumer hardware with a local model or a commercial API. A stepwise engine proposes proof commands that Isabelle itself validates inside a bounded search, while a planner drafts structured proof outlines and tries to fill and repair the gaps.

The system is a small arsenal: beam search over tactics, learned re-rankers, premise selection by small transformers, a retrieval store of archive proofs, and counterexample-guided repair. Every line of code, the author states, was implemented by recent frontier models. The prover can discharge lemmas that defeat Isabelle's own Sledgehammer automation. Yet those same model generations, he finds, cannot reliably implement the intricate fill-and-repair algorithms intended, a candid limit on vibe coding complex designs.
arxiv-2601-04853:
Zhiwei Liu and 6 co-authors introduce RAAR, a retrieval-augmented agentic reasoning framework for spotting misinformation across domains in a 2026 paper. False stories change character between topics such as health, politics, and finance, so detectors trained in one domain often fail in another. Reasoning language models help, but they too are usually limited to data resembling their training distribution.

RAAR retrieves material from multiple perspectives to support its reasoning, aiming for transfer beyond same-distribution assumptions. An agentic design lets the system plan checks rather than judge from surface cues alone. Cross-domain detection matters because misinformation campaigns deliberately move into underrepresented topics where single-perspective detectors are weakest and least tested.
arxiv-2601-04953:
J. I. Katz offers an explanation for puzzling fast radio burst behaviour in a 2026 paper. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of radio energy from deep space, and repeaters and apparent non-repeaters behave oddly differently. Katz proposes that the sources are dynamically triaxial magnetars, neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields and unequal axes, whose bursts are narrowly beamed along open field lines.

In repeaters, the rotation axis, field lines, and rare burst direction happen to point near Earth, so bursts are seen again and again. In non-repeaters those directions wander as the star rotates, cutting the observed duty factor by orders of magnitude. One geometric model uniting both classes would simplify a crowded field of burst theories.
arxiv-2601-05053:
Ziqi Zhao and 11 co-authors aim to make big language models search more widely when they learn by trial and reward in a 2026 paper. In that style of training, a model tries many lines of thought and keeps the ones that end at a checked-right answer. Tree search can grade each step on the way, which is a plus. But the search tends to walk the same few paths and to waste steps.

Their method, ROSE, pushes for search that roams over lines of thought that truly differ in sense. It keeps the fine step-by-step grading, yet steers the hunt toward fresh turns. Wide search could help a model crack a hard task by the one odd path that works, in place of a fresh gloss on the same failed path.
arxiv-2601-05253:
Hadi Hosseini, Debmalya Mandal, and Amrit Puhan release SP-Rank, a dataset for studying ranked preferences together with predictions about other people in a 2026 paper. Each data point carries a personal vote, the first-order signal, plus each person's guess at how others will vote, the second-order signal. Traditional ranking datasets capture only the personal preference, discarding information about social expectations that often shapes real voting and recommendation.

The dataset holds many thousands of human-generated points across geography, movies, and paintings, spread across nine formats for asking, with subset sizes that vary. That structure supports benchmarking algorithms that exploit both signals. Richer preference data could improve social choice systems and recommenders that currently treat every ballot as if cast in isolation.
arxiv-2601-05453:
Yang Li and Yuri Mishin report, in a 2026 materials paper, how stress pointing through a metal surface changes stacking fault energy. Stacking faults are errors in the regular stacking of atomic planes, and they shape how face-centered cubic metals deform and crack. The stress studied acts perpendicular to the close-packed plane.

Using density functional theory calculations on aluminum, nickel, copper, silver, gold, and platinum, the team found a consistent pattern. Compression raised both stable and unstable fault energies, while tension lowered them. Many classical and machine-learning potentials predicted the wrong trend, sometimes the opposite one. The paper discusses how such potentials could be improved to capture this effect.
arxiv-2601-05553:
Luis Fabian Pena and 13 co-authors measure, in a 2026 paper, how cross-hatch strain patterns affect silicon-germanium quantum dots used for spin qubits. These heterostructures are grown on virtual substrates that relax most strain, but a residual cross-hatch pattern survives into the layers above. That unevenness may make qubits vary from device to device.

The team aligned strain maps, surface images, and cross-section microscopy across twenty-five commercially processed wafers. A diffusion model explained the surface roughness and its temperature dependence. Measured strains could shift paired quantum dots noticeably over short distances, while roughness only modestly reduced a key energy splitting. Thicker buffer layers and cooler growth are suggested as remedies.
arxiv-2601-05653:
Phu-Hoa Pham and 4 co-authors build EvoQRE, a 2026 approach for simulating safety-critical traffic with realistically imperfect drivers. Most simulators assume drivers choose optimally, through Nash-style equilibrium or imitation. Human drivers instead show bounded rationality, making roughly good decisions under limited attention and perception.

EvoQRE models traffic interactions as general-sum Markov games solved by quantal response equilibrium, where choices stay probabilistic rather than perfectly optimal. A pretrained generative world model combines with entropy-regularized replicator dynamics to mimic stochastic human behavior. The authors prove convergence to the logit version of the equilibrium with a clear rate. Tests on Waymo and nuPlan data reportedly raised realism and safety metrics. That makes the fake drivers act less like perfect chess players and more like real people on a road.
arxiv-2601-05953:
Colin McDiarmid and 3 co-authors study in 2026 two network quality measures, edge expansion and modularity, inside random preferential attachment graphs. Preferential attachment grows a network by linking new nodes preferentially to already popular ones, mimicking real social and information networks. Expansion measures connectedness, while modularity measures how cleanly a graph splits into communities.

The authors establish new bounds for the likely edge expansion in two standard preferential attachment models where each step adds at least two edges. Bounds for expansion of small vertex subsets then yield new upper bounds on modularity for small numbers of added edges. Both parameters matter for robust network design, random walk analysis, and clustering applications.
arxiv-2601-06253:
Philip F. Hopkins and 2 co-authors use maser and broad-line observations to rule out whole classes of black hole accretion disk models in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Gas spiraling into a supermassive black hole forms a disk whose support could come from heat, radiation, turbulence, or magnetic pressure.

In the outer disk, thermal or radiation pressure models predict disk masses far exceeding the black hole itself and strongly non-Keplerian rotation. Observed maser and broad-line motions immediately exclude those models, along with cosmic-ray pressure versions. Pure turbulence could survive only with implausibly high values. Magnetic pressure-dominated models agree with all constraints, including measured maser magnetic fields. The observations strongly favor hyper-magnetized outer disks.
arxiv-2601-06353:
Some groups act on a space of sums, and a few parts of that space stay fixed under the act. Yongle Jiang and 1 co-author sort all such parts for a wide class of groups in a 2026 math paper. Each group joins a grid of whole points in n ways with the grid's own twist group.

For two ways, the sort gives a new proof of a past result. For three or more ways, these are the first groups of this stiff type whose fixed parts can be fully sorted, though they lack a trait past sorts leaned on. In each case, one part stands out: the sole top fixed part with a mild growth trait. The sort shows order can hold where the old trait fails, which opens new ground for this branch of math.
arxiv-2601-06753:
Yiran Rex Ma charts computational Chinese paleography in 2026 as a position paper. Chinese paleography studies ancient Chinese writing in its earliest forms. The field is undergoing a computational turn powered by AI.

He argues the field is evolving beyond automating isolated visual tasks. It moves toward integrated digital ecosystems for scholarly research, he writes. Reading bronze inscriptions and oracle bones involves many linked steps. Recognition, dating, and interpretation support each other in real scholarship. Digital ecosystems could join those steps into one research environment. His trajectory maps where the field has been and heads next. Digital humanities readers get a roadmap from a field remaking itself. The paper is a position statement, inviting debate and building.
arxiv-2601-07153:
Genta Indra Winata and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with can large language models understand, reason about, and generate Code-Switched text?. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Code-switching is a pervasive phenomenon in multilingual communication, yet the robustness of large language models (LLMs) in mixed-language settings remains insufficiently understood.

The authors present a comprehensive evaluation of LLM capabilities in understanding, reasoning over, and generating code-switched text. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07253:
Li Zheng and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to clean noise out of training data. The data trains Stable Diffusion, a tool that makes images from text. Foes can lace the data with noise that warps what the tool learns. The warped tool then makes poor images. Cleaning the data first is called adversarial purification.

Past cleaning tools were built for sort tasks, like naming what a photo shows. They miss tricks made just for Stable Diffusion. One such trick aims at the part that codes the image, the VAE encoder. A trick can also aim at the UNet, or at both at once. The authors set out a broad form of cleaning based on DDIM, a fast way to run the image tool. A new loss guides the clean-up, for data free of the foe's warp.
arxiv-2601-07353: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Tianyu Liu and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers talon. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Speculative decoding (SD) has become a standard technique for accelerating LLM inference without sacrificing output quality. Recent advances in speculative decoding have shifted from sequential chain-based drafting to tree-structured generation. Where the draft model constructs a tree of candidate tokens to explore multiple possible drafts in parallel. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07553:
Kabir Swain and colleagues introduce VirtualEnv, a simulation platform for embodied AI research, in 2026. VirtualEnv is built on Unreal Engine 5, a game engine known for realistic graphics. It evaluates large language models in interactive, task-oriented settings. Agents receive natural language instructions and must act in a virtual world. The platform also supports multi-agent tasks.

A figure in the paper lays out the full pipeline for multi-agent planning and execution. Users give instructions, and the system coordinates models that plan and carry them out. High-fidelity simulation lets scholars test agents safely and repeatably. Failures cost nothing, unlike tests with real robots. VirtualEnv aims to be shared ground for comparing embodied AI systems.
arxiv-2601-07653:
A large CHEX-MATE collaboration compares two ways of measuring the temperature of galaxy cluster gas. One way uses X-ray observations; the other uses millimetre observations. Both are often compared under simple assumptions: smooth gas with spherical symmetry. The authors note those assumptions create expected differences between the inferred profiles. Their 2026 preprint studies that relationship in CHEX-MATE clusters.

Galaxy clusters hold hot gas whose temperature profile traces the cluster's depth and history. If two methods disagree in a patterned way, the pattern itself teaches something. It can reveal structure in the gas or effects on cosmological estimates. The team works within the CHEX-MATE sample, built for such comparisons. Astrophysicists measuring cluster properties are the readers. The study helps them read method differences as information, not just error.
arxiv-2601-07853:
Zhi Yang and a large team benchmark the safety of AI agents that handle money. Financial agents powered by large language models now support investment analysis, risk assessment, and automated decisions. Their power to plan, call tools, and change mutable state creates new security risks. Finance is high-stakes and highly regulated, so failures are costly. Their 2026 preprint, FinVault, tests agents in execution-grounded environments.

Execution-grounded means agents act in a working system, not a chat simulation. Safety failures then show up as real bad actions, like wrong trades or leaked data. A benchmark built this way exposes risks that static question sets miss. Banks and fintech firms need such evidence before deploying agents. The paper serves AI safety and financial technology scholars. It supplies a testbed for agent safety where money moves.
arxiv-2601-08253: Marius Juston and three co-authors analyze how LDLT Lipschitz network layers behave at initialization. Their 2026 arXiv paper derives the exact output variance for these layers. The setup starts the parameter matrix with independent Gaussian entries of a stated variance. Lipschitz layers bound how much a network can amplify input changes, which aids robustness. Knowing output variance at the start guides scaling choices before training begins. The analysis helps builders set initial weights so signals neither vanish nor explode through deep stacks of such layers.
arxiv-2601-08453: Jakub Gismatullin and Patrick Tardivel link the beta distribution to associated Stirling numbers of the second kind. Their 2026 arXiv paper gives a formula for these numbers based on a moment computation. The moment comes from a sum of independent random variables with a beta distribution. From the formula, probabilistic methods yield lower and upper bounds for the numbers. Stirling numbers count set partitions, so new bounds serve combinatorics and probability alike. The bridge between a continuous distribution and counting numbers is the paper's neat turn.
arxiv-2601-08753:
Rishav Sen and four co-authors work on bus fleets that mix fuel types. Towns add more clean buses that run on stored power. A mixed fleet of clean and diesel buses is hard to run well. The price to charge a clean bus shifts through the day, so a poor plan can waste cash.

The team builds a plan that ties charge times to bus trips. It looks at grid price, bus routes, and charge point use at the same time. The aim is low cost with full service kept in place. A reader who runs a town bus fleet gets a way to cut charge bills. The plan also helps keep clean buses on the road more of the day.
arxiv-2601-09153:
Josue Martinez-Martinez, Olivia Brown, and Giselle Zeno test how to train image tools that hold up when shots go bad. Shots can blur, dim, or fill with rain and snow. A tool trained on clean shots may fail on the first storm. The team studies train plans that use a learned flaw maker. It makes true to life flaws, not just noise dots.

They add mix plans that pair wide flaw reach with sharp foe based fix steps. They also track if a tool knows when it is unsure, and how dear each plan is. A reader who ships sight tools gets a plan for storm proof train. It fits self drive and care scans, where a bad shot must not mean a bad call.
arxiv-2601-09253:
Zehua Liu and three co-authors use bad samples, not just good ones, to tune chat models. Plain tune uses dear expert text. A next path drafts many replies, keeps the best, and tunes on them. That path throws the rest away. Yet a bad reply holds sense: it shows what to shun, and how close a near miss can be.

Their method is called RIFT. A reward score grades all drafts, good and bad. Tune then uses each draft with a weight from its grade. No draft is waste. A reader who tunes models gets a data lean path. It may cut the need for expert text while it lifts the last score.
arxiv-2601-09353:
Ioannis Peridis and five co-authors plan car moves in a road with no lanes by a tree search led by a net. In a lane free road, cars can use the full width. That use can lift flow past lane roads. But each car must plan in a space with no lane rails to cut its picks. The search space is vast and shifts as all cars move at once.

They join Monte Carlo tree search, a look ahead by random tries, with a net that guides which tries to run. The net cuts the vast space to rich lines. A reader in self drive work gets a plan tool for a road form that may come, and that breaks lane based plans.
arxiv-2601-09653:
Balram Singh and five co-authors study a magnetic effect in wires bent through three dimensions. Their 2026 arXiv paper measures how geometry shapes exchange bias in tilted CoFe/IrMn microwires. Exchange bias arises where a ferromagnetic layer meets an antiferromagnetic one, pinning the magnet's preferred direction.

That pinning effect underlies many spintronic functions in use today. Moving it into 3D shapes lets researchers probe coupling on curved, non-planar structures. The tilt of the wire becomes a design variable. Results point toward spintronic parts that use shape itself, not just flat layer stacks, to set their behavior.
arxiv-2601-09953:
Christabel Acquaye, Yi Ting Huang, Marine Carpuat, and Rachel Rudinger ask if AI can judge how hard a math test item is. Test makers now pay for trial runs with real pupils. Those runs set the hard grade of each item. The team tests if open language models can do this grade work.

They find a split result. Models are poor judges when asked to rate an item at once. But when models act as fake pupils and try the item, the grades track real grades more well. The right setup is key. The work hints at a cheaper path to pre test new items.
arxiv-2601-10353:
Bowen Zheng, Minquan Cheng, Kai Wan, and Giuseppe Caire cut the packet cost of cache fed broadcast. A server with many antennas sends files to many users. Each user holds a cache of past files. Smart cache use can cut the load on the air.

Past plans oft split files into a vast count of parts. That split cost is named subpacketization. It can grow too fast to run. The team give a new build with a lean split. It uses a half sum pack of parts that do not clash. The aim is the same gain at a far lower split cost.
arxiv-2601-10453:
Victor Zheleznov, Stefan Bilbao, Alec Wright, and Simon King make modal sound synth that can learn. Modal synth builds sound from the tones of a thing. A string, a bar, or a plate each rings in such tones. Past modal tools are fixed once built. They can be slow to tune by ear.

High swings make the tones link in dense ways. The team give a form that stays firm as it runs. It can also be tuned by a learn step. Slopes flow through it, so a net can fit its terms to a target sound. The work joins old synth craft with new learn tools.
arxiv-2601-10553:
Jianhao Yuan and co authors fix the physics of AI made videos at run time. Top video tools make fine shots. Yet balls pass through walls and drops fall up. Such slips curb their use in real work. Past blame fell on weak physics sense from train.

The team say run time picks share the blame. They treat the fix as an align task at run time. A latent world model grades how true the physics is. That grade, named WMReward, steers the run. The aim is shots that look right and act right, with no fresh train.
arxiv-2601-10753:
Anik Chakraborty and Varinder Kumar build Fredholm theory on a twisted scale of Hilbert spaces. They start with the space of square-integrable functions on the unit interval. A unitary twist operator maps the standard Fourier basis to exponentials at half-integer frequencies. The weighted spaces that result form a scale, ranked by smoothness.

On this scale sits a diagonal operator with compact resolvent. Its spectrum is the set of half-integers. Frame theory, the study of redundant bases, supplies the approach. The work extends Fredholm theory, which governs when equations have solutions, to a setting built for half-integer modes. Such modes arise in problems with antiperiodic boundary rules.
arxiv-2601-10853:
Sandra Chulliparambil Shaju, Maria Azhar, and Karin Everschor-Sitte propose a new route to complex magnetic textures called hopfions. Three-dimensional topological spin textures draw interest for their rich geometry and possible device uses. A hopfion is a knotted swirl of magnetization, tied in a closed loop of twists. Making and keeping such knots is the hard part.

The authors introduce symmetry-transforming magnetic models. The idea is to generate and stabilize rich three-dimensional textures inside any magnetic background. If the method works broadly, hopfions could move from rare curiosities to design elements. They are candidates for dense, robust memory and computing devices that store data in knots of spin.
arxiv-2601-11053:
Qipan Wang, Tianxiang Zhu, Yibo Lin, Runsheng Wang, and Ru Huang present ATSim3.5D, a thermal simulator for 3.5D chip systems. The 3.5D style mixes stacked and side-by-side dies, which creates structures at many scales. Rising temperatures make thermal-aware design essential. Past tools struggle with both the multiscale structures and the nonlinear effects of high heat.

The simulator uses a nonlinear multigrid method, solving the heat problem at nested resolutions. Multigrid speed matters when designers iterate daily. Accurate heat maps for hybrid stacks guide floor plans before tape-out. The work extends the team's ATSim line to the newest packaging style, where heat paths cross dies, interposers, and packages at once.
arxiv-2601-11753:
Yicheng Shi, Jing Su, Anouar Rahmouni, and co-authors report work on quantum links. They send those links through fibre in the air at labs in the United States. Entanglement, a close quantum link, is a base step for quantum nets. Such nets could aid safe talk, sense work, and shared quantum computing.

Links that use light alignment are easy to make and to change. But fibre in use twists that alignment in ways that shift with time. The link must thus be held steady by active means. Their work deals with that steady hold over an aerial fibre line.
arxiv-2601-12053: Maël Donoso argues for a new base for AI: train foundation models on human brain data in a direct way. Today's models learn from text and other human-made data. That data is a filtered trace of a deeper brain process. Training on brain data could skip that filter. It could give models a more rich source of human thought. The claim is bold and raises hard points on data capture, scale, and ethics. The work sets out the case and the path it would need.
arxiv-2601-12153:
Arthur N. dos Santos and Bruno S. Masiero survey more than thirty years of automatic singing assessment and singing information processing. Both fields aim to aid singing teaching, performance study, and vocal training with computers.

One strand grades a singer by firm metrics, from live visual feedback to pitch tracking and spectral checks. The other matches a singer's voice to a target to read fine traits. The survey maps how both strands grew. Teachers and tool builders gain a full view of what works.  The survey spans work from the early days to now.
arxiv-2601-12453:
Amilcar Branquinho, Ana Foulquie-Moreno, and Manuel Manas study banded matrices of infinite size. A banded matrix has non zero entries only near its diagonal. Past theory gave spectral formulas for such matrices in the bounded case. The team push that theory past the bounded setting, into the unbounded case.

Their route uses shifts and factorizations of finite cut offs of the matrix. Each cut off, once shifted, splits into positive bidiagonal factors. That split is the key assumption of the work.
