From it, Favard type spectral formulas can be rebuilt for the full matrix. The results link to mixed type multiple orthogonality, a field with ties to random matrices and approximation.
arxiv-2601-12753:
Ruofan Li and Jiuzhou Zhao study a number theoretic property of prime ideals in number fields. Let K be a number field with ring of integers, and fix an element of that ring. For each prime ideal, they obtain a higher form of the alpha Wieferich property. Wieferich style conditions link exponent patterns to prime divisors in a rigid way.

Their result implies a nonexistence theorem for higher Wieferich unramified prime ideals. The title also ties the work to a conjecture of Erdos. Nonexistence theorems close doors that might otherwise waste search effort. They also sharpen what a conjecture must allow. The work sits in algebraic number theory, where prime ideals extend the role of prime numbers.
arxiv-2601-13253:
Ebubekir Tosun and co-authors give a mixed route to build large sense link sets for tongues with thin data. Their test case is Turkish. Sense links state how words relate, as kin, foes, or part to whole. Such sets feed search, teach tools, and language models.

Their route has three steps. First, fast word maps group words by sense with a cluster rule. Next, a large AI model tags the link in each group. Last, hand made dictionary sources are folded in to clean and grow the set. The mix aims for scale with care. Low resource tongue teams gain a plan they can copy with their own sources.
arxiv-2601-13853:
Kinga Słowik and Robert Wolak bring a classic map idea into the study of foliations in 2026. A foliation splits a space into layers, like pages in a book. For a Riemannian foliation, those layers carry a metric, a way to measure distance. The team defines a basic Albanese map for such spaces.

The map is built from basic 1-forms, which vary in a layer-friendly way. They relate this map to the classical Albanese map of the whole space. The study of its general traits is backed by key examples. New maps give geometers fresh tools to sort foliated spaces.
arxiv-2601-13953:
Gorgi Pavlov tackles a stubborn problem: teaching exact Boolean logic by gradient descent in 2026. Neural networks tend to settle on fuzzy approximations of logic. Those fuzzy forms degrade under quantization, when values are rounded to set steps. Precise logic needs sharp, exact choices at each step.

Pavlov's Hierarchical Spectral Composition selects spectral coefficients from a frozen Boolean Fourier basis. A Sinkhorn-constrained routing step composes them, with column-sign modulation. The design aims for logic that stays exact after training ends. Exact learned logic could serve chips, proofs, and safe control.
arxiv-2601-14353:
Özgür Sevinç, Özgür Ökcü, and Ekrem Aydiner link two ideas from gravity theory in this 2026 paper. One is MOND entropy, from modified Newtonian dynamics. The other is the extended uncertainty principle, which tweaks the basic quantum limit on what can be known at once. They build one unified framework from both.

The team starts from a higher-order version of the extended uncertainty principle. From it, they obtain a modified entropy-area relation. They then derive modified Friedmann equations, the rules for how the universe expands, by three distinct routes. The routes use the first law of thermodynamics, entropic gravity, and the emergence of cosmic space. They also check the generalised second law.
arxiv-2601-14453:
Christian Ferko, James Halverson, and Aaron Mutchler prove a broad claim about neural networks in this 2026 paper. They show that any quantum field theory admits a neural network description with a countable infinity of parameters. The claim extends to any probability distribution over tempered distributions. In short, field theory and neural networks can mirror each other.

As a worked example, they realize the two-dimensional Liouville theory as a neural network. They numerically compute the three-point function of vertex operators in that form. The result agrees with the DOZZ formula, the known exact answer. Readers get a proof of universality plus a numeric check that the mirror holds in practice.
arxiv-2601-14553:
Brian Christian and Matan Mazor study fair judgment in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM FAccT conference. Fair decisions require ignoring irrelevant, potentially biasing information. To do that, decision-makers need to approximate what decision they would have made had they not known certain facts. Examples are the gender or race of a job candidate.

That counterfactual self-simulation is notoriously hard for humans. It leads to biased judgments even by well-meaning actors. The authors test two aids: self-blinding and counterfactual self-simulation. Their title says these mitigate biases and sycophancy in large language models. Readers get methods for making both human-style and machine judgments fairer.
arxiv-2601-14653:
Yuyu Liu and five co-authors fill gaps in single-cell data in this 2026 paper. Missing data in single-cell sequencing datasets pose significant challenges for extracting meaningful biological insights. Existing imputation approaches often assume uniformity and data completeness. They struggle with cases where large patches of data are missing at once.

The team presents CROT, a Cluster-Regularized Optimal Transport method. It is an optimal transport-based imputation algorithm designed for patch-based missing data in tabular formats. Optimal transport fills gaps by matching distributions at the lowest cost. Cluster regularization keeps the filled values true to each cell group. The work is pure math. No new lab run is used, but the end terms feed straight into how the MUSE data will be read. Readers get an imputation tool built for the worst kind of missingness in single-cell studies.
arxiv-2601-14953:
Advaith Arun, Shiv Shankar, and co-authors work on how future wireless systems will gauge their channels. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with massive MIMO arrays, which use many transmit ports at once. More ports can raise spectral efficiency, the data sent per slice of spectrum.

The cost is overhead. Reference signals must be sent across the time-frequency grid, and they eat into data throughput. The team uses port cycling, a way to sound the channel with fewer ports at a time. Deep learning helps them estimate the precoder from that leaner data.
arxiv-2601-15353:
Asim H. Gazi, Yongyi Guo, and co-authors survey why reinforcement learning still struggles outside the lab. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with statistical reinforcement learning in the real world. The field has won in gaming, robotics, online ads, public health, and language tasks.

Yet a wide gap stands between research results and deployed systems. Two recurring challenges underlie much of that gap. The survey names the main obstacles to real use. It then sets out future directions that could one day close the distance between journal papers and daily real-world practice.
arxiv-2601-15553:
Quoc Anh Tran writes a note in non-abelian Hodge theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Earlier work by others built a map between two moduli spaces on a projective log smooth variety. One space collects logarithmic Higgs bundles with nilpotent residues. The other collects logarithmic connections with nilpotent residues. The known map between them is a continuous bijection.

Tran argues the map is in fact a homeomorphism, a stronger claim that also matches the spaces' topology. The note extends the picture to higher-dimensional quasiprojective varieties, per its title. Such correspondences link flat connections with Higgs fields across geometry.
arxiv-2601-16253:
Jay Farihi and coauthors report shifts in gas take up by a dead star with dust. Their 2026 preprint is a short letter on WD 0106-328. The star is a white dwarf with dust and rock waste in fall. Gas lines of two ions show the rate of fall. Six views span a full span of years with two big scopes, VLT and Keck.

The line strengths shift by a clear, firm count through time. Shifts mean the fall rate of waste is not fixed. A shift rate helps read how waste disks feed dead stars. It also tests if bursts of fall drive the change. The letter gives rare long term proof of such shifts.
arxiv-2601-16453:
Daniel Staros and three coauthors test how grain links bend the integer quantum Hall act. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Hall act in a square grid. In that act, flow steps sit at whole count marks. Links twixt grains can shift or blur those steps. The team varies link strength by a push term in the maths.

Runs show how steps move as the push term grows. Clear shift maps help read Hall tests in real stuff. Real stuff always holds some grain links in its grid. A map of link acts firms up the pure Hall tale. The work is a code run study of linked grids.
arxiv-2601-16653:
Jesús Algaba, Esteban Acuña, José Manuel Míguez, Bruno Mendiboure, Iván Zerón, and Felipe Blas study a form of ice that traps gas. Carbon dioxide hydrates form when cold and force squeeze gas and water. These solids matter for climate and for gas stores. How they first form rests on one key value. That value is the pull at the edge where hydrate meets water.

Just two past tests have gauged that edge pull, and both did so in a round-about way. The team's 2026 paper turns to screen models for a fresh gauge. Such models can track each small part of the mix. A sound value would sharpen forecasts of hydrate growth. It would also aid safe gas haul and storage plans.
arxiv-2601-16853:
Ian de Haan, Peter van der Putten, and Max van Duijn test how chatbots read minds in tales. Mind-read tests ask what a tale's folk think or know. Chatbots now score high on such tests. That sparks a row on what the scores mean. Their 2026 preprint asks if deep thought steps make scores more robust.

Thought-trained bots learn by steps with checked rewards. The team pits such bots on mind tests with twists. Twists can break bots that lean on stock cues. Robust scores would mean the bots track minds, not cues. The work helps labs judge social skill in bots with care.
arxiv-2601-16953:
Daniel Iľkovič and Jun Yan count lone point sets in a class of trees. A lone set holds points with no edge twixt them. Trees here branch in an r-way form with no flaws. A star set is all lone sets of a size through one point. Their 2026 preprint works out how those sets spread.

Counts by size and hub point fill the work. Such counts tie to hard sums in graph math. They also feed codes that place guards or hubs on nets. Pure counts on clean trees give base truth. Rough real nets can then be set next to that base.
arxiv-2601-17053:
Shuhao Que and a team of five co-authors keep gait tools true for old adults in rehab. Hip breaks need slow, tracked work to heal well. Wear tools can count steps and pace in that work. Most such tools were tuned on mid-age gaits. Old gaits are slower and less even, so tools slip. Their 2026 preprint uses fake data to pick sound traits.

Fake gait data fills gaps where real data is thin. Trait picks guided by fakes hold up on real old gaits. True counts help docs tune rehab with care. They also flag when a patient's pace slides back.
arxiv-2601-17253:
Yachan Liu and six co-authors ask which made-up zeolite-like materials could be made in real life. Zeolites are crystals full of tiny pores. Labs have made some of them. Computers have proposed vast numbers more. Most of those proposals may never form in fact. The team built ZeoNet-based classifiers to sort real from proposed forms.

They use three-dimensional neural networks on grids of distances inside each form. The abstract reports scores far above older tools. Gains are more than ten times those from shape filters or older learning methods. Such sorting helps labs spend time on forms that can work. It trims huge lists down to strong leads.
arxiv-2601-17353:
Houhao Wang and four co-authors built a catalog of phonon particles in real materials. Phonons are units of lattice vibration in a crystal. Some phonons carry chirality or topology, traits that shape heat and sound flow. Symmetry rules can predict such phonons. Yet no one had mapped the full set across material databases in a system-wide way.

The team set out to close that gap. They classify phonon emergent particles by symmetry. They also hunt for chiral phonons in known materials. A shared catalog helps labs pick materials for tests. It turns scattered case studies into a field map. Future work can start from known hosts, not blind search.
arxiv-2601-17753:
Roberto Crotti, Giovanni Denaro, Zhiqiang Du, and Ricardo Muñoz Martín tackle a gap in writing research. Their 2026 preprint presents Hylog, a tool for logging how people type. Most keyloggers miss the changes made by input method editors, the software that builds characters for scripts that are not based on an alphabet. That blind spot has limited studies of text work in such scripts.

Hylog joins two kinds of logging in one system. One side tracks each key press in fine detail. The other side tracks the text as it grows on screen. Put together, the two views give a fuller record of how a text is built. The tool is meant for researchers who study the mental steps of writing.
arxiv-2601-18253:
Peng Sun, Xiangyu Zhang, and Duan Wu build a scalable way to judge how happy users are with a chat assistant. Their 2026 preprint presents BoRP, short for bootstrapped regression probing. For open-ended assistants, classic A/B testing lacks reliable metrics. Explicit feedback is sparse, since few users bother to rate chats. Implicit metrics are ambiguous, since a long chat can mean delight or confusion. BoRP probes the model in a way that scales to many chats.

A high-fidelity satisfaction signal feeds the loop of product improvement. Without it, teams fly blind between releases. The method aims to give them a gauge they can trust at scale. Conversational AI lives or dies by such feedback.
arxiv-2601-18353:
Tuhin Chakrabarty and Paramveer Dhillon ask whether a machine can learn to write at the level of a skilled human author. For a long time, fine prose was seen as a craft that needs a human voice and a human sense of style. New text systems can now copy the voice of many authors in a few seconds, at almost no cost in work.

Their study tests what comes from training such a system on books of high worth. The claim in the title is that strong, expert level prose can grow out of that kind of training. The work speaks to a live debate for writers and teachers. It also matters for firms that sell text tools. If style can be learned from good books, the line between a human draft and a model draft gets much harder to draw.
arxiv-2601-18553:
Primož Kajdič and three colleagues report a new kind of edge on zones that ride in front of the Earth's bow wave in space. The Sun's wind hits that bow wave and piles up. Chunks of that pile can break off and ride on, with sharp rims of their own. Past work found two kinds of rim on such chunks.

The team found four chunks with a third kind of rim at one end. Two of them were caught by a fleet of craft that fly in a group. The rim is a known hot flow fault that forms when the wind meets a break in the field. A third rim kind shifts the tale of how these chunks form and fade. It also gives crews who watch space weather a new sign to track.
arxiv-2601-19153:
Zexu Pan and six co-authors pull a named sound out of two ear audio and say where it came from. Most sound extraction tools work on single channel audio and only isolate the sound. Real scenes are three dimensional, and two ear, or binaural, audio holds rich clues about where sounds sit.

Their system, LuSeeL, takes a language query, like a plain words request for one kind of sound. It then extracts that event and locates it in space. Hearing aids, robots, and smart glasses all need exactly this: pick one sound from a scene and know its direction.
arxiv-2601-19253:
Pascual Lucas and José Antonio Ortega-Yagües prove that two named surfaces are the only ones with a special line property. On a surface, isogonal lines cross the main curvature lines at matched angles. The pair ask which surfaces have all such lines be both generalized helices and pseudo-geodesic lines.

The answer is a clean pair: helix surfaces and the Enneper surface, and no others. A theorem that ends with a full list is a prized kind of result in surface theory. It closes the question and gives the two named surfaces a new mark of distinction.
arxiv-2601-20253:
Si Chen and five colleagues build a way to generate test benchmarks automatically from domain guidelines. Open-ended question answering tests whether a model can reason in context, not just recall facts. In practice-based fields, knowledge is procedural and rests on professional judgment, yet human exam sets for testing are often missing.

The authors use Bloom's taxonomy, a classic ladder of thinking skills, to shape the questions they generate from guidelines. A reliable generator would let hospitals, firms, and agencies test models on their own rules. That matters where buying or writing an exam by hand is too slow or costly.
arxiv-2601-20453:
The Tuan Hoang, Nhu Phong Tham, and Bao Quoc Tang study the fast reaction limit of a bulk-surface reaction-diffusion system. The system models a reversible chemical reaction with general stoichiometric coefficients. One chemical fills a bounded vessel, while the other lives only on the vessel's boundary, where the reaction takes place.

The authors investigate how the system behaves as the reaction becomes very fast, and at what rate solutions converge to the limiting one. Such limits simplify models of surface chemistry, from catalysis to cell membranes, where reactions at a wall drive everything inside.
arxiv-2601-20653:
Francois Baccelli, Diletta Olliaro, Marco Ajmone Marsan, and Andrea Marin develop a stochastic recurrence equation for multiserver jobs in cloud computing. Data centers face highly variable workloads: jobs may need one core or thousands, and run for milliseconds or for days. This variability limits how fully the infrastructure can be used.

The authors' equation models that queueing behavior for performance evaluation. Predicting delays and utilization under such spread is how operators decide capacity. A tractable model helps cloud providers promise service levels without wasteful overbuilding. With it, a team can test a new center on a screen long before it is built in steel and glass.
arxiv-2601-20753:
Zhiheng Jiang and five co-authors build a test bed for AI that must balance rival goals. Their 2026 paper presents GraphAllocBench, a benchmark for preference-conditioned policy learning. In this setup, one model must serve many users with different trade-offs. The model takes the user's stated preferences as input. It then produces a policy tuned to those weights.

The goal is to cover the Pareto front, the set of best compromises among goals. A single trained model should flex at run time, not need retraining for each taste. The benchmark tests how well policies land on or near that front. It gives researchers a shared yardstick for multi-objective reinforcement learning. Such tools matter wherever one system must serve people who value outcomes in unlike ways.
arxiv-2601-21053:
Thomas Cohen offers a teaching tour of a famous puzzle in quantum chromodynamics. His 2026 article introduces the Silver Blaze problem. The problem is a clash between two views of QCD with a chemical potential. At zero temperature, QCD stays in its ground state, the vacuum. All physical observables remain unchanged while the potential stays below a critical value. That stillness is the Silver Blaze property.

Naive reasoning suggests the system should respond sooner. Reconciling the two views takes care with how the theory is computed. Cohen writes pedagogically, for readers new to the puzzle. The article explains why the vacuum can stay silent under pressure. It is a guide to a subtle point in nuclear theory. Students of dense matter will find a clear entry here.
arxiv-2601-21153:
Liang Hong offers a new strategy to predict future insurance claims with honest guarantees. The 2026 paper treats prediction intervals in the regression setting. The field shows a paucity of finite-sample valid intervals for future claims. Finite-sample validity means the coverage promise holds at any sample size. It does not rest on large-sample math. Most old methods cannot promise that in regression.

Hong's strategy converts a method from one setting to another. It starts from a method built for the plain iid setting. It then turns that method into one for regression. The conversion keeps finite-sample validity. Insurers could quote claim ranges with certified coverage. Both regulators and actuaries value such honesty. The paper fills a noted gap in the field.
arxiv-2601-21253:
Wei Minn and six co-authors tackle a stubborn limit in automatic testing of Android apps. Good testing should visit as much of an app as it can. In practice, even the best current tools reach less than a third of an app's screens in real-world cases.

Their system, CovAgent, uses smart agents plus live changes to the running app. The agents plan what to try next, and the live tools let them get past screens that block simple scripts. The goal is to push coverage well past the old ceiling. Higher coverage means more bugs found before users ever see the app.
arxiv-2601-21353:
Qinhan Tan, Akash Gaonkar, Yu-Wei Fan, Aarti Gupta, and Sharad Malik adapt a classic chip-checking method for security. Formal checks can prove that a chip design keeps secrets from leaking to visible outputs. Both secrecy and integrity come down to whether information flows where it should not.

The underlying method, IC3, is a proven way to check safety properties. The authors tailor it to the flow questions that security checks ask. Off-the-shelf tools often struggle with those questions at real chip scale. A custom version could let designers prove security claims before any chip is built.
arxiv-2601-21553:
Keiya Sakabe, M. Levent Doğan, and Michael Walter settle a question about tensor complexity that has stood open since nineteen ninety-one. Strassen's asymptotic spectrum is a frame for measuring how hard tensors are to compute with. It feeds fields from computer science to quantum information.

A key issue is whether Strassen's support functionals are truly universal points of that spectrum. The authors show that they coincide with the quantum functionals, another candidate family. Settling the equality firms up the whole spectrum picture. It gives complexity theory a cleaner map of the landmarks it navigates by.
arxiv-2601-21653:
Vasileios Sevetlidis and George Pavlidis measure how a network's inner representation twists along a path through its inputs. Deep networks learn features whose geometry shapes both accuracy and robustness. Classic similarity scores compare sets of activations point by point, but they miss how features evolve along a path.

Two models can score as near twins yet react very differently to small nudges. Their gauge-invariant holonomy tracks the twist itself, in a way that does not depend on arbitrary coordinates. Path-aware geometry gives a sharper tool for comparing models and for spotting fragile ones before deployment.
arxiv-2601-21953:
Tathagata Banerjee, Maciej Olszewski, and Valla Fatemi examine the surfaces that limit superconducting devices. Resonators and qubits lose performance through dielectric losses in surface oxides. Labs fight those oxides with metal capping layers, surface passivation, and acid treatments.

The team studies how fabrication steps affect oxidation and contamination in bilayers of niobium with another metal. They use X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, which reads the chemistry of the topmost atomic layers. Their 2026 preprint connects processing choices to the surface states that follow. Quieter surfaces mean longer-lived qubits, so this kind of careful materials bookkeeping is part of how quantum hardware slowly gets better.
arxiv-2601-22053:
Sankha Subhra Bakshi and Gia-Wei Chern simulate what happens when interactions inside a material are suddenly switched. Such interaction quenches are a clean way to probe how strongly correlated electron systems behave far from equilibrium. The test bed here is the Hubbard model, a standard model of interacting electrons on a lattice.

Earlier theory, which treated the system as uniform in space, found coherent oscillations and long-lived transient states after a quench. The authors go beyond that uniform picture and report spatial textures that emerge after the quench. Their 2026 preprint shows the system does not respond evenly. Spatial structure in far-from-equilibrium states matters for experiments on cold atoms and quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-22253:
Katherine Muñoz-Mellado and four co-authors teach a neural net to sort quantum states by their links. Their 2026 preprint uses a type of autoencoder, a net that learns to copy its input through a tight code. The net learns to tell linked states from states that can split apart.

The team train it for pairs of parts, from the smallest size up to a much larger one. The net also learns to spot a second, softer kind of quantum link. It can tell bound links from free ones as well. Such fast sorting can help labs check states they make.
arxiv-2601-22353:
Vladislav Korostelev, Pjotrs Žguns, and Konstantin Klyukin study how hydrogen soaks into a class of oxides called brownmillerite perovskites. These crystals have a neat, layered atomic frame. Their 2026 preprint uses first-principles math to track what the soaked-in hydrogen does.

They work with two iron- and cobalt-based forms of the crystal. The hydrogen shifts the electron layout, the pull between magnetic atoms, and the favored spin paths. Such shifts could let makers tune a material with a gas, not a rebuild. The results give design rules for hydrogen-aware oxides. They suit sensors, cells, and switches.
arxiv-2601-22953:
Wavelet methods give a fresh handle on a classic quantum field theory in this study. The theory, named in the title, is studied in one space and one time dimension using a Hamiltonian approach that avoids small-step approximations. Daubechies wavelets in momentum space supply the building blocks.

Each wavelet carries a resolution and a position index, giving natural cutoffs at both fine and coarse scales. Those cutoffs make hard, nonperturbative problems computable. The setup could help study strong-force-like theories where standard expansion methods fail. Working in momentum space suits the analysis here, since wavelets there separate scales of motion in a natural way.
arxiv-2602-02453:
Andong Chen and 5 co-authors propose comics as a middle path for machine visual reasoning, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Static images cannot show how events unfold over time, while videos carry heavy redundancy and cost. Comics keep temporal structure, embedded text, and narrative coherence at far lower reasoning cost.

The authors systematically study two reasoning paths built on comics. They evaluate them across reasoning tasks and long-context understanding tasks. Comic-based reasoning beat image-based reasoning on multi-step temporal and causal problems. It also stayed substantially cheaper than video-based reasoning. Narrative structure and art style consistently shifted performance across tasks. The findings position comics as an effective intermediate representation: dense like a story, cheap like a picture, and ordered like a film.
arxiv-2602-02653:
A hybrid quantum network joining an atomic source and a solid-state memory, both working directly at telecom wavelengths, is demonstrated by Yuzhou Chai and 6 co-authors in their 2026 paper. Quantum technologies suit different platforms, but spectral mismatches and missing telecom interfaces block long-distance links between them. Frequency conversion is the usual workaround, with its own losses.

The team instead built both nodes natively in the telecom C-band. A neutral-atom single-photon source reached high purity at a strong emission rate. A rare-earth memory stored light with solid efficiency and large multimode capacity. Tunability let the two spectra overlap precisely. Storage and retrieval worked at microsecond scales across thirty-seven temporal modes. Non-classical correlations survived ten kilometers of metropolitan fiber and nearly fifty kilometers in the laboratory. The result sketches a backbone for telecom-native quantum repeaters.
arxiv-2602-02853:
Stefanos Pertigkiozoglou and 3 co-authors study how neural networks should handle symmetry in a 2026 paper. Networks that respect a task's symmetry often generalize better. Forcing perfect symmetry, though, can make training harder when the data is only nearly symmetric.

Their method, RECM, lets each layer learn how much to relax its symmetry rule. The learning uses only the training signal and each layer's own symmetry properties. The authors prove the relaxation settles near a measured symmetry gap. Layers with exact symmetry return to full symmetry. Layers with rough symmetry keep useful flexibility. Tests on exact and approximate symmetry tasks, including molecule generation, favor RECM.
arxiv-2602-02953:
The first stars in the universe may have limited their own growth with jets, according to a 2026 simulation by Yasmine J. Meziani and 5 co-authors. Their run follows one metal-free star forming at very early cosmic times. The simulation includes radiation, magnetic fields, and fluid dynamics together, zooming in on a single forming system.

A rotating disk forms around the protostar, extending to small scales. Magnetic conditions allow jets to launch from the disk. Those jets regulate how much gas the star gains and push back infalling material at larger distances. The star reached a mass a few dozen times the Sun's over tens of thousands of years. The stable disk stayed supported by heat and turbulence.
arxiv-2602-03153:
Backdoor attacks hidden in robot policies are erased at test time by Xuetao Li, with 9 co-authors. Fine-tuning vision-language-action models for robotics can expose them to poisoned pretraining data. Implanted backdoors stay stealthy until a trigger makes the robot act harmfully, while earlier defenses lack insight into multimodal backdoors or demand costly full retraining of the deployed model.

The team uncovers a deep-layer focus grabbing mechanism behind such backdoors. Triggered focus redirects late in the network, forming compact vector clusters. Their system, Bera, detects tokens with anomalous focus, masks suspicious regions, and reconstructs a trigger-free image. No retraining or pipeline changes are needed. Tests across platforms showed nominal results kept and attack success sharply reduced.
arxiv-2602-03253:
Recognizing a place from words alone is benchmarked by Ofer Idan, with 3 co-authors, in a dataset called LaVPR. Visual place recognition fails under extreme environmental change and when other places look alike. Standard systems also cannot localize from a verbal description, a capability that matters for emergency response when no image of the location is available to search against.

LaVPR extends earlier datasets with hundreds of thousands of rich natural-language descriptions. Two paradigms are investigated. Multi-modal fusion improves strength, with language helping most in degraded cases and letting compact models rival much larger vision-only systems. Cross-modal search gets a earlier method that substantially beats standard contrastive methods. Code and data are released.
arxiv-2602-03353:
Causal graphs are recovered from an invariance property by Nang Hung Nguyen, leading 4 other authors, in a system exploiting distributional stability. The spread of an effect, conditioned on its causes, stays invariant when the prior spread of those causes changes. That observation yields a direct test for potential causal relationships. It checks how much the effect-cause conditional spread varies across data subsets. Those subsets reflect other cause priors while keeping the conditional relationship itself.

Combined with the empirical sparsity of most causal graphs, the test becomes an efficient learning method. Its complexity is quadratic in the number of variables, cutting processing time dramatically against leading methods. Tests on a varied benchmark of large-scale datasets showed superior or equivalent results. The authors emphasize scalability to large variable sets as the main advance.
arxiv-2602-03453:
Light traveling through a photonic time crystal can look as if it moves faster than light itself. Kyungmin Lee and 3 co-authors show that this impression is misleading in a 2026 paper. A photonic time crystal changes its optical properties in time rather than space, and its steep dispersion curves are often read as superluminal transport.

By deriving a flux relation for these modulated media, the authors prove the cycle-averaged energy velocity stays strictly bounded. They also establish a product law that ties energy velocity to group velocity through the time-averaged inverse permittivity. The apparent superluminal effect turns out to be geometric drift from the modulation. It is a mismatch of electric and magnetic phase connections, not real energy flow.
arxiv-2602-03553:
Majorana bound states are prized quasiparticles for quantum computing, and light might become a knob for tuning them. Aksel Kobiałka and 3 co-authors study a topological superconductor hosting Majorana states inside a photonic cavity in a 2026 paper. They model the coupled system with exact diagonalization over a finite number of photons.

The Majorana states survive the cavity field, but they appear at finite, tunable energy instead of the usual zero. Photon energy adds a constant shift, while the light-matter coupling makes the energy drift with coupling strength and magnetic field, a kind of pseudo-dispersion. Stronger coupling even calms their energy oscillations without hurting disorder stability. A modified spectral localizer tool completes the topological characterization.
arxiv-2602-03753:
Nicolas Sereyjol-Garros and 4 co-authors steer image generation at test time using features instead of words. Their 2026 paper introduces REPA-G, short for representation-aligned guidance, for diffusion models. Text prompts are often ambiguous and class labels coarse, while the rich features of self-supervised models carry precise semantics.

At inference, REPA-G optimizes a similarity objective that pulls the denoising process toward a target representation from a pretrained feature extractor. Control works at several granularities, from matching a single patch to global semantic guidance with whole-image tokens. Distinct concepts can also be composed faithfully in one image. No extra training is required, and results on ImageNet and COCO show high-quality, diverse generations.
arxiv-2602-04053:
Peeling a cluttered room apart object by object makes 3D reconstruction tractable. Rio Aguina-Kang and 4 co-authors present SeeingThroughClutter in a 2026 paper. Instead of segmenting and estimating depth once on a messy image, their pipeline removes foreground objects one at a time.

Vision-language models orchestrate each round: detect, segment, erase, then fit a 3D model of the removed object. Each removal cleans the view for the next object, even under heavy occlusion. No task-specific training is needed, so the method improves as foundation models improve. Results on 3D-Front and ADE20K show state-of-the-art robustness for structured scene reconstruction.
arxiv-2602-04153:
Less context can forecast better when data are scarce. Zihao Jing and 2 co-authors propose a transfer-oriented framework for forecasting multivariate time series on graphs, such as traffic networks. Their 2026 method prunes the graph context before learning, keeping only structurally informative pieces.

Information-theoretic and correlation criteria select subgraphs and features worth keeping. A spatiotemporal convolutional network then models dynamics on that compact context. On large traffic benchmarks, the pruned model beat baselines specifically in low-data transfer scenarios, where models move to new domains. The moral: explicit pruning is a generalization strategy, not just compression.
arxiv-2602-04553:
Jin Lei shows how neural networks can solve quantum scattering problems in a 2026 paper on physics-informed neural networks. These networks learn solutions to equations while respecting physical laws. Scattering waves, however, oscillate forever instead of fading, which made them hard for such networks.

Lei applies exterior complex scaling, a technique that turns the outgoing waves into decaying ones beyond a chosen region. A driven-equation form keeps the source on the real axis, avoiding hard analytic continuations. Tests covered nucleon scattering from calcium and a heavier lithium-lead system. Phase shifts and scattering matrices matched conventional solvers closely. The approach could later support fitting nuclear potentials directly from data.
arxiv-2602-04653:
Ariel Fogel and 3 co-authors uncover a hidden attack route in a 2026 paper on chat templates, the small programs that format conversations before a language model sees them. Templates run at every inference call and sit between user input and the model in a privileged spot.

The authors show a tampered template shipped with an open-weight model can implant a backdoor. No weight changes, poisoned training data, or runtime control are needed. Triggered attacks crashed factual accuracy and made models emit attacker-chosen links, while normal inputs behaved fine. At agent level, backdoors hijacked tool use and evaded tested defenses. Poisoned files passed platform security scans, exposing an undefended supply-chain risk.
arxiv-2602-04753:
Vishruti Kakkad and 3 co-authors compare how industry professionals and students view adversarial machine learning in a 2026 user-study paper. Adversarial machine learning covers attacks such as poisoning training data, a growing security concern as generative AI spreads.

A survey of professionals found a clear link between cybersecurity schooling and concern about such threats. The team then built two capture-the-flag challenges that teach language and generative AI ideas through a data poisoning attack. Surveys of Carnegie Mellon students at both levels judged them. The challenge format engaged students' interest in adversarial threats well. Based on all responses, the authors urge putting security schooling directly into machine learning curricula rather than treating it as an optional extra.
arxiv-2602-05553:
Trials that randomize treatment across people in a social network face a subtle flaw: networks sampled around each person look separate, but hidden links between them can carry effects across. Bar Weinstein and Daniel Nevo study this contamination in egocentric-network randomized trials, where each sampled person recruits some neighbors and treatment is randomized across the sampled people. Under a design-based framework, they show standard estimators go biased whenever such hidden links exist.

The authors derive bias-corrected estimators for direct and indirect effects. They also build a sensitivity analysis that uses parameters for the chance or count of missing edges, run through both grid checks and probabilistic bias analysis. Applied to a well-known HIV prevention trial study, the method suggests ignoring contamination can understate indirect effects and overstate direct ones. The tools give trial designers a way to test how fragile their conclusions are.
arxiv-2602-05953:
Assigning requests to facilities as they arrive, with no take backs, is the online facility assignment problem. Lamya Alif, Raian Tasnim Saoda, and 4 co-authors study it on discrete grid graphs. Facilities sit fixed with limited capacity, and each unit demand request must go to an available facility at Manhattan distance cost. The question is how grid geometry and capacity exhaustion punish simple rules.

Adversarial request sequences show that a capacity sensitive Voronoi heuristic can suffer cascading region collapse when nearby capacity runs dry. Plain greedy assignment can be driven into repeated long reassignments by an oscillating construction. These are failure modes specific to discrete grids with hard capacities. As a remedy, the authors discuss a semi online variant that may delay assignment briefly and solve each batch optimally with a min cost flow. They delineate the parameters of that batching framework.
arxiv-2602-06153:
Predicting a yes-or-no outcome is usually done with logistic regression, whose curve is trapped between zero and one at its ends. Anthony Almudevar and Jacob Almudevar note that many real responses never reach those extremes. Earlier fixes added parameters to bend the curve, but often ignored linked responses and extra factors.

Their compound logistic model builds the average response from several logistic curves combined. That frees the end levels while keeping the familiar logistic machinery. The model also handles responses that are correlated with each other, and it accepts covariates, the background factors that shift risk. The result is a wider family of models with the old method's practical advantages.
arxiv-2602-06253:
Logic that can talk about propositions themselves, not just things, is called second-order logic. Justus Becker and 3 co-authors develop a second-order version of intuitionistic tense logic, a logic of time that looks both forward and backward. Intuitionistic logic demands constructive proof, which makes the design delicate.

A key payoff of going second-order is that positive connectives can be defined from negative ones. The diamond operator, meaning sometime, is recovered from box operators alone, once both time directions are present. The team gives three definitions of the logic: by axioms, by proof rules, and by models. They prove all three coincide, with a labeled proof system shown complete through a search argument.
arxiv-2602-06553:
Smoothing out the sharp points of shapes remains open in prime-field settings, where arithmetic in prime fields creates quirks. Gergely Bérczi reports trials with a search model, AlphaEvolve, hunting for ranking functions that must strictly decrease along standard blow-up sequences. In characteristic zero, Hironaka solved the problem with such measures.

In the prime-field case, classical measures can stall or even rise, an effect nicknamed the kangaroo effect. Bérczi's test cases are four-dimensional hypersurface sharp points in characteristic three with a special leading term, where naive order measures often fail. After refining the trial design, the search found a five-part ranking rule meeting a bounded-delay descent test with no violations.
arxiv-2602-07253:
Hallucination detectors work well for question answering but falter on thinking tasks, where errors hide in chains of thought.  Litian Liu and four co-authors reframe the problem through out-of-spread detection, treating next-token prediction as classification and adapting vision-style OOD techniques to language models.

The resulting detectors need no training and judge single samples, yet they achieve strong accuracy on thinking hallucinations.  The reframing itself is the contribution: a well-studied detection problem, properly adapted, covers a newer safety problem.  Teams building trustworthy language models get a lightweight detector and a fresh angle on a stubborn failure mode.
arxiv-2602-07553:
Penalty usually targets anyone who defects, but in many real societies penalty flows between distinct groups.  Sinan Feng and four co-authors model a bipartite population where cooperators in a public goods game punish only defectors from the other subset.

They find cooperation can emerge and stay stable under symmetric intergroup penalty. At low penalty intensity with a small enhancement factor, intergroup penalty beats uniform penalty at promoting cooperation.  From ant-acacia mutualism to Inuit conflict resolution, dedicated between-group penalty is widespread, and this model shows why group identity can reshape the evolution of cooperation.
arxiv-2602-07653:
Tensor-train breakdowns compress high-dimensional data, and skeletonized low-rank approximations add interpretability, but they can suffer accuracy loss, fragility, and high cost. Daniel Hayes and two co-authors propose projection-enhanced interpolation methods that refine current approximations.

By oversampling data outside the skeletons to add information and picking pivot subsets for faster projections, the family of methods improves results while keeping cost low. Wide numerical tests, including synthetic tensors up to ten-D, confirm the gains. Data experts working with high-dimensional tensors get a refining step that sharpens ones they already compute.
arxiv-2602-08053:
The Jacquet-Langlands link links codes of GL(2) with those of its inner forms, and Jun Yang gives it a new form through tensor products over Hecke algebras. For a non-split inner form over a number field, the likeness theta link equips a square-tame function space with a two-sided space structure.

Joining that two-sided space over the Hecke algebra gets the full link as a split into basic codes paired with their Jacquet-Langlands transfers. The build is explicit and structural rather than merely mere. Code theorists and number theorists gain a concrete algebra route to a key link, opening the door to analogous realizations elsewhere.
arxiv-2602-08153:
Making series that count curves on sheets often turn out to be modular forms, but log Gromov-Witten constants add sharp fibers that tangle the story. Hülya Argüz studies modular for making series of log Gromov-Witten constants of oval bundles relative to singular fibers.

Spurred by Vafa-Witten theory forecasts, she guesses these series are mock modular forms. She proves it for a large class of constants of the rational oval surface mirror to the shadow plane, beside to a cycle of nine rational curves. The proof routes through a link with Vafa-Witten constants shown with a partner. Enumerative geometers and physics teams gain a proved case of mock modular at the mirror-balance interface.
arxiv-2602-08353:
Forecasting with temporal knowledge graphs sounds like a test of time sense, yet many benchmarks let models score perfectly without using time at all. Jiasheng Zhang and five co-authors trace that shortcut to dataset biases and to task designs that are too simple. Their arXiv paper argues that current tests cannot tell true forecasting skill from bias exploitation.

Their answer is TKGB, a benchmark built around four linked tasks and a pipeline that creates fresh, context-rich graph data with shortcuts under control. Fixed histories, thin context, and unguarded shortcuts are all addressed. Early results show TKGB exposing gaps and failure modes that older tests hide. Readers get both a warning about past scores and a stricter yardstick for future models.
arxiv-2602-08953:
When agents learn from each other in sequence, a small change in order or network shape can wreck the whole crowd's judgment. William Guo and two co-authors study networks that learn the truth when the decision order is random, a property called random-order asymptotic truth learning. They ask which such networks survive tampering, and how to build them.

Networks with the property prove resilient to a bounded number of adversarial changes, and the paper characterizes the conditions they must meet. Several graph constructions learn through different mechanisms, and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm converts any network into a random-order learner with minimal edits. The work offers design tools for sturdier social learning.
arxiv-2602-09053:
Rishabh Mishra and three co-authors build the theory behind the stall-cell simulations of their companion paper. Their analytic model treats the separation vortex and the trailing-edge vortex as finite, counter-rotating tubes. Linear stability analysis of the coupled system yields the growth rate and wavelength of the Crow-type instability that bends the vortex structures into waves.

A weakly nonlinear analysis, via multiple scales, produces a Stuart-Landau amplitude equation giving the saturation level where nonlinearity halts growth and quasi-steady cells settle in. Coupling the separated shear layer through the Birkhoff-Rott equation predicts the vertical vorticity driving alternating spanwise flow. The theory matches spanwise velocity, vorticity spread, and sheet deformation in quantitative terms.
arxiv-2602-10053:
Game theory usually assumes players either know how others reason or hold rigid, simple beliefs about them. A 2026 paper led by Raman Ebrahimi, with four co-authors, offers Connected Minds, a model that joins those views. Agents see not the whole crowd but a sample skewed by their network spot, with a locality factor capturing ranking, homophily, or disclosure.

As networks grow opaque, the model falls back to short-sighted level-by-level reasoning, and when all is visible it recovers the standard hierarchy of reasoning. Opacity also breeds a subtle bias, inflating rivals' perceived depth. The authors derive an escalation rule for games where moves reinforce each other, and a clarity flip for coordination games, making network design a lever on stable outcomes.
arxiv-2602-10153:
Safety rules for untrusted AI often rely on weaker trusted models to monitor stronger ones, but monitoring fails when the watched model's actions exceed the monitor's grasp. A 2026 paper led by Ashwin Sreevatsa, with two co-authors, introduces legibility rules, which nudge the untrusted model toward actions a monitor can evaluate. In coding tests, an adversarial agent tries to plant backdoored code undetected.

The studied rules let the model document its code fully with comments, reversing prior work that stripped comments to prevent deception. Commenting improved safety without costing task performance, and helped honest code most. Honest code usually has a natural explanation, and gains grew with stronger monitors that better separate genuine reasons from surface-plausible ones.
arxiv-2602-10253:
Bayesian Network Structure Learning has drawn wide empirical and theoretical attention, yet its parameterized complexity remains partly unmapped. A 2026 paper by Robert Ganian and Viktoriia Korchemna follows up on superstructure-based analyses of the problem. Where known results suggest the problem is unlikely to be fixed-parameter tractable under vertex-cover size in the superstructure, the authors show a feedback edge set parameterization yields fixed-parameter tractability.

That result strengthens to a localized feedback edge set, with matching lower bounds completing a complexity classification across virtually all well-studied graph parameters. The paper then turns to input representation: where past work assumed a non-zero representation, an additive representation makes the problem fixed-parameter tractable under far milder superstructure restrictions, notably treewidth alone. The results extend to the closely related Polytree Learning problem.
arxiv-2602-10353:
Alloy grain stability has relied on two mechanisms. Heat-based stabilization reduces grain boundary free energy, and motion-based stabilization curbs boundary mobility through solute drag or embedded pins. A 2026 paper by Omar Hussein and Yuri Mishin proposes a third mechanism, self-pinning. There, the segregation cloud of a moving grain boundary breaks on its own into solute-rich clusters giving strong pinning beyond the free energy drop from segregation.

Clusters form from strong solute-solute pull at boundaries, driving a first-order shift between solute-lean and solute-rich boundary phases. Kinetic Monte Carlo runs with segregation thermodynamics, boundary dynamics, and solute diffusion demonstrate the effect. Self-pinning supplies in-built grain-growth control that couples thermodynamics and kinetics, removing any need for old second phase inclusions and refocusing alloy design on boundary phase behavior.
arxiv-2602-10553:
Junichiro Takahashi and three co-authors build a stronger ECG encoder for mixed medical AI in a 2026 paper. Large medical models handle text-based exam questions well, but their ECG results lags, and some leading models do not support ECG data at all. Interpreting heart traces is hard, and scores vary with the reader's experience.

The team trains an encoder on real hospital data using a contrastive model with a sigmoid loss suited to multi-label prediction. They then present a modified loss tailored to the multi-label nature of ECG diagnosis, where one trace can carry several settings at once. Tests reported in the paper show the approach improves ECG grasp, giving mixed medical models a firmer footing in cardiology.
arxiv-2602-10653:
Xu-Hong Ye and seven co-authors test the linking of blazars and radio galaxies in a 2026 paper. Older linking says blazars are radio galaxies viewed down the jet, but accretion state muddles the picture. Optical light-line classes, low- and high-excitation radio galaxies, track accretion better than viewing angle alone.

Pulling Fermi blazars and radio galaxies, the authors analyze accretion traits and high-energy beaming patterns by the numbers. In the gamma-ray brightness versus photon index plane, high-excitation galaxies occupy higher bright levels and softer spectra. The results support a unified accretion-outflow story linking aligned and tilted radio-loud active galaxies, with accretion state, not just angle, shaping what scopes see.
arxiv-2602-10753:
Krzysztof Szczygielski transfers a older result on decomposable maps in a 2026 paper. He proposes countable decomposability for bounded linear maps on C-star algebras. A map counts as countably decomposable when it splits into an endless sum of compositions of completely positive maps and bounded star-maps.

The paper portrays countable decomposability under various assumptions on the part maps. The findings extend a older result of Stormer from 1982, at first formulated for decomposable positive maps, into a broader setting. The work gives rule algebraists a refined sorting tool for maps that resist finite decomposition but yield to countable ones.
arxiv-2602-11153:
A Kondo insulator can hide superconducting hints at short scales. J. E. Ebot and five co-authors run the first large-scale study of the 1D Anderson lattice behind the Kondo necklace. An exact mapping links that lattice to a pairing layer coupled to a metallic reservoir.

Below the scale where insulation sets in, pairing and density links look degenerate and nearly ordered, far beyond any isolated pairing layer. The metallic layer mediates an extended-range coupling that drives the effect. The same physics appears as near-long-range magnet order in Kondo systems, with a strongly renormalized coupling. Tests are proposed in heavy-fermion compounds, adatom chains, and cold atomic gases.
arxiv-2602-11553:
Cleaning noise from a photo usually trades sharpness for smoothness, and the usual error-driven methods smear fine detail when noise is strong or unfamiliar. Nam Nguyen and two co-authors take a different tack: rebuild the image from a compressed code that forces simple structure, then let a generative decoder restore realistic texture. Two versions of the idea are built, one based on a conditional generative adversarial network and one on step-by-step diffusion guided by the compressed code.

The paper also gives hard bounds on how far the rebuilt image and its decoding can stray under Gaussian noise, rather than relying on tests alone. On both made-up and real noisy images, the method keeps perceptual quality high while staying competitive on plain error measures. It points toward denoisers that aim for images that look right, not merely images that score well.
arxiv-2602-11753:
Aligning AI with human values depends heavily on human feedback. Most research targets training algorithms, while the user interface is treated as a mere detail. Danqing Shi argues that omission matters. The paper introduces a reference model, a systematic framework for analyzing where and how UI design can improve the fit between AI and people.

A structured taxonomy organizes the model. Two case studies plus a preliminary investigation across six screens demonstrate how it works in practice. The work highlights openings to advance human-AI fit through interaction design. Screens, in this view, are not decoration around an aligned model but part of the fit mechanism itself.
arxiv-2602-11853:
Reading solar flare conditions is essential for understanding coronal energy release. Tatyana Kaltman and three co-authors reconstruct 3D maps of magnetic field and plasma values in a May 2021 flare, combining radio and X-ray data. Imaging spectra from the Expanded Owens Valley Solar Array yields spatial maps of field strength, thermal and fast electron counts, and the power-law index of fast electrons through gyrosynchrotron modeling.

Joint X-ray views from Hinode and Solar Orbiter, taken from different vantage points, enable a two-view rebuild of the flaring loop. Matching radio and thermal X-ray source positions links 3D coordinates with radio-derived plasma values. The maps of field strength, Alfvén speed, and plasma beta reveal a magnet-ruled setting, guiding models of magnetic reconnection and flare dynamics toward a true-to-life 3D picture of energy release.
arxiv-2602-11953:
Load sharing usually assumes past moves can be forgotten, but most schemes leak that history through their state. Michael A. Bender and three co-authors give a strongly history-independent two-choice balls-and-bins algorithm on n bins that handles both insertions and deletions for up to m balls. It guarantees a maximum load of m over n plus a constant, with high probability, and only a tiny expected number of moves per operation.

To the authors' knowledge, this is the first such solution with real bounds when the average load grows without bound. It is also the first fully dynamic scheme, either way, to achieve constant overload with sublinear moves. For systems where the internal state must reveal nothing about the past, that combination of balance, motion, and independence is new.
arxiv-2602-12053:
One-way patterns resist the usual playbook, and an index theory for them was missing. Kansei Inamura proposes an index of one-way symmetry actions in two-dimensional spacetime. It relates to whether such symmetries can live on tensor products of finite on-site Hilbert spaces. The index extends the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner index for invertible cases represented by quantum cellular automata.

If all fusion channels share the same index, the author shows fusion rules of finite symmetry moves on a tensor product space. They can match, up to QCAs, only those of weakly whole-number fusion sets. The paper also develops topo matrix product operators covering plain, tame fusion category, and Kramers-Wannier cases. It constructs defect spaces and step circuits, with fusion and splitting tensors built by hand for those examples.
arxiv-2602-12153:
Diffusion language models can fill in words at any spot in parallel, which opens a new way to scale up reasoning at test time. Sicheng Feng led this work with four co-authors, proposing dVoting, a voting method that needs no extra training. It starts from several samples for one prompt and looks for where they disagree.

Tokens that stay steady across samples are left alone, while shaky tokens are remade by vote, and the cycle repeats until the text settles. Tests show steady gains on maths, science, and general knowledge sets, with the largest lifts on some science questions. The gain comes at only a modest extra cost, which makes the trick a cheap way to sharpen diffusion models.
arxiv-2602-12353:
Finding carbon dioxide on an Earth-like world will shape how the Habitable Worlds Observatory is built, especially how far into the infrared its coronagraph must reach. Celeste Hagee led this work with five co-authors, using the BARBIE Bayesian method to test CO2 detectability against signal-to-noise ratio, wavelength, and abundance. Twenty-five evenly spaced 20 percent bandpasses from 0.8 to 2.0 microns were tested.

Simulations span Earth epochs and a Venus-like case, tracking how detectability shifts as a rocky planet evolves. Carbon monoxide alone never reaches strong detection, while methane and water play a pivotal role in whether CO2 can be picked out. Weighing those degeneracies, the team concludes the coronagraph's long-wavelength cutoff should sit at 1.68 microns.
arxiv-2602-12453:
Radon transforms add up functions over sheets, and their microlocal traits reveal which singular points can be found. Gaik Ambartsoumian led this work with four co-authors, studying general Radon transforms over quadric sheets whose centres lie on an orientable sheet S. The quadrics are level sets of a second-degree form from a symmetric, invertible matrix A with real entries.

Singular points of the left and right views of the standard link are set by the sign pattern of A and the shape of S. When A gives ellipsoids, with S strictly convex, those points are folds. When A gives saddle shapes, with S convex or cylindrical, cusp, fold, or blowdown points appear. For bowl shapes, the Bolker rule holds, closing a tidy picture.
arxiv-2602-12553:
Topological insulators host surface states with unusual optical responses, and magnetic fields add another tuning knob. Haoyu Li led this work with three co-authors, studying shift current in surface states of Bi2Se3, under an upright quantised magnetic field. Charge states are described as Landau levels.

A small-step approach yields a tiny form for shift current, split into band parts with found choice rules. With C3 point group balance, non-zero parts obey a mirror link, so pure twisted light generates zero shift current. In the clean limit, currents are non-zero only at discrete photon levels, due to discrete Landau levels and energy keeping. They become bell shapes once damping relaxes that rule. Spectra depend on damping, field, and doping level. Shift current proves highly tunable by doping level and field, promising strong, tunable non-linear magneto-optical uses.
arxiv-2602-12753:
The successor representation lets an agent predict future states apart from rewards, so it can adapt fast when goals change. But the classic version depends on the current policy, and policies shift as learning goes on or tasks change, leaving old predictions stale. In maze-like worlds it also smears out, giving dense, overlapping features that scale poorly. Changmin Yu and Máté Lengyel propose a hierarchical version that adds time-scale structure to the predictions.

That hierarchy learns stable state features that survive policy changes. Factored with a non-negative method, it yields a sparse, low-rank map that transfers to new tasks with very few samples in multi-room worlds. The factored map also reveals readable structure of the environment and can drive efficient exploration, bridging the gap between fast model-free habits and flexible model-based planning.
arxiv-2602-12953:
As AI systems outpace humans on many tasks, people are left orchestrating, checking, and deciding, a lopsided division of labour. Yuanrong Tang and seven co-authors propose Human Tool, an interface that treats people as callable tools inside AI-led workflows, borrowing the Model Context Protocol pattern. The word tool here means a coordination abstraction, not a demotion of human authority.

Structured schemas describe what a person can offer, know, and decide, letting agents call on human input when human strengths matter most and fold answers back in through efficient, natural interaction. Controlled studies on decision-making and creative tasks show better performance, lower human workload, and more balanced collaboration than baselines. The framework aims at strong AI leadership that still amplifies distinctly human strengths.
arxiv-2602-13153:
Intermediate polars are magnetic white dwarfs accreting from companions, and V515 And sits inside the period gap where few such systems are well studied. Srinivas Rao and six co-authors combine long-term TESS photometry with spectroscopy from the large Devasthal telescope for a comprehensive analysis. They pin the orbital period at about 2 hours 44 minutes and confirm spin and beat periods near 465 and 489 seconds.

Timing analysis shows accretion geometry changing not only between TESS sectors but within individual sectors, with the dominant mode alternating between disc-fed and stream-fed accretion. Two successive outburst-like episodes, each lasting about a day and peaking near three and two times ten to the thirty-third erg per second, look like micronovae. Strong Balmer and helium-II lines with an inverse Balmer decrement confirm the magnetic nature of the source.
arxiv-2602-13253:
Safety training may mute open bias in language models, but quiet, stereotype-driven links can survive underneath. This study probes that hidden layer for transgender people in two settings. First, word association tests check whether models tie negative words to transgender people and positive words to cisgender people. Second, a mock scheduling task asks models to assign cisgender and transgender patients across medical specialties where stereotypes often bite.

Seven models were tested in English and Spanish, and bias showed up steadily in areas such as looks, risk, and truthfulness. In scheduling, transgender patients were favored for STI and mental health care, while cisgender patients were favored for gynecology and breast care. Micaela Hirsch leads the work with eight co-authors, who call for research that tackles these subtle links so health uses treat people fairly.
arxiv-2602-13353:
Mean-field games shrink huge multi-agent problems to a duel between one representative agent and a population distribution, but classic versions assume a fixed starting distribution and fully rational players. This paper drops both assumptions, adding risk aversion over the starting distribution and bounded rationality for players who deviate from perfect reasoning. The mix yields a new equilibrium concept, the mean-field risk-averse quantal response equilibrium.

Existence is established, and both fixed-point iteration and fictitious play are shown to converge to it. A scalable reinforcement learning method extends the idea to large state-action spaces, and numerical tests show the new policies withstand distributional shifts better than classic mean-field policies. Bhavini Jeloka leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13653:
Graphical interface agents must cope with screens and apps that keep changing, which makes data collection and policy training costly in real deployments. This framework centers on multimodal language models and pairs two components. Agentic-Q estimation learns a Q-model scoring each action's contribution to task completion step by step, and step-wise policy optimization trains the policy by reinforcement learning on those scored steps.

All state-action trajectories come from the policy itself, keeping data costs manageable, and policy updates are decoupled from the environment for stable efficient optimization. The framework gave Ovis2.5-9B strong interface interaction skills, with remarkable results on navigation and grounding benchmarks, even beating larger contenders. Yibo Wang leads the work with nine co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14553:
Qinqi Lin and three co-authors build a 2026 arXiv money setup for checking machine un-learning rule-following. Despite legal rules for the right to be forgotten, AI firms routinely fail to meet data erasure asks. Machine un-learning offers a tech route to wipe personal data sway, but rule-following assurance lags behind tech feasibility, opening a gap between un-learning theory and rule enforcement.

The paper first marks un-learning's built-in check doubt through a guess-testing view of certified un-learning, deriving the checker's spot power. A game-theory model then grasps planned play between checker and firm. Machine un-learning curves in model use and spot odds make tangled planned links. Those links block closed-form answers in old checking setups, so the authors build methods to handle those links and check rule-following in use.
arxiv-2602-14653:
Speakers tend to spread information evenly across an utterance, or so one hypothesis claims. Matteo Gay, with three co-authors, gives the first computational test of uniform information density in visually grounded speech. Earlier tests used text alone, ignoring what speakers can see.

Surprisal is estimated with multilingual vision-and-language models over captions in 30 languages and visual stories in 13 languages. Grounding on perception smooths information flow in both global and local measures. In visual narratives, grounding on image and discourse together cuts surprisal most at discourse-unit starts. The study moves the hypothesis toward realistic multimodal language use.
arxiv-2602-14753:
Joshua Lehman defines a flexible surface in a four-manifold as one where every mapping class of the surface appears as the restriction of a diffeomorphism of the pair. He constructs flexible surfaces in the complex projective plane and in the product of two spheres, within any prescribed non-characteristic homology class.

Inside characteristic classes a spin structure obstructs full flexibility, so Lehman constructs spin-flexible representatives instead, the best available under that obstruction. The paper maps where flexibility holds, where it fails, and what survives in between. Four-manifold topology gains new, explicit examples.
arxiv-2602-15253:
Kendiukhov examines scaling in masked-reconstruction transformers trained with single-cell RNA data. Neural scaling laws link loss, model size, and data, and are known for language and vision transformers, but barely explored in single-cell genomics. From CELLxGENE Census profiles, the team builds two regimes: data-rich, with 512 highly variable genes and 200,000 cells, and data-limited, with 1,024 genes and 10,000 cells.

They fit a scaling law to validation error over seven model sizes that span three orders of magnitude. In the data-rich regime, power-law scaling is clear, with an unbeatable loss floor near one and a half. In the data-limited regime, scaling is negligible, so scarce data, not model size, set the limit. Scaling laws like those in natural language processing thus emerge here when enough data exist, with the data-to-parameter ratio as key.
arxiv-2602-15353:
Fu and colleagues offer NeuroSymActive, a parted setup joining a smooth sign thinking sheet with a live, value-guided search driver for fact web query solving. Large ready word models and brain thinking nets have grown many plain word jobs, yet stay stuck by fact-heavy asks needing exact, ordered multi-hop logic. Fact webs give a tight sign base for true rooting, but joining web structure with brain models is hard.

Bluntly stuffing web bits into cues leads to waste and weakness, while only sign or search-heavy routes can be pricey in fetches and lack slope-based polish. The tool pairs soft-merging style sign parts with a brain path judge and a Monte-Carlo style search rule picking high-value path growth. Observed findings on usual KGQA tests show NeuroSymActive hits high scores while cutting pricey web fetches and model calls versus usual fetch-boosted rivals.
arxiv-2602-15553:
Conte and colleagues argue that personal AI built on vector search is a black box that cannot truly forget. When such a system hallucinates or pulls up sensitive material, the user cannot see why, fix the error, or delete a concept cleanly, since traces linger as probabilistic ghosts in vector space. Their answer, RUVA, grounds personal AI in a personal knowledge graph instead.

With a graph, users can inspect what the system knows and redact single facts with precision, keeping a genuine right to be forgotten. The design puts the user in the editor seat for their own memory store, with human-in-the-loop curation at its core. A project page and demo video accompany the paper, which will interest readers who want personal AI that can show its work and honour deletion.
arxiv-2602-15653:
Craddock and colleagues demonstrate entanglement swapping over real city fibre, a step toward a quantum internet built on repeaters, blind computing, distributed computing, and distributed sensing. Swapping needs photon pairs from separate nodes to be indistinguishable and to survive deployed fibre, which has kept most past demos in labs or forced elaborate stabilisation. The team uses naturally indistinguishable sources based on warm atomic vapour cells.

With no shared lasers or frequency references between nodes and no pulsing of the sources, they reach a swapping rate near 500 pairs per second while keeping the CHSH parameter above two. They hold that quality over 17.6 kilometres of deployed fibre in New York City, using commercial single-photon detectors at spoke nodes, superconducting detectors at the hub, and standard time synchronisation. The work points toward practical hub-and-spoke quantum networks in cities and data centres.
arxiv-2602-15853:
Islam and Surdeanu propose a lightweight explainable guardrail, or LEG, to detect unsafe prompts. LEG runs a multi-task learning setup that learns a prompt classifier together with an explanation classifier, the latter marking prompt words that explain the safe or unsafe overall call. LEG is trained on synthetic explanation data, generated using a novel strategy counteracting confirmation biases of language models. Training also uses a novel loss that takes global explanation signals as weak supervision and weights uncertainty while combining focal and cross-entropy losses.

With a much smaller model than current approaches, LEG matches or beats the state-of-the-art on prompt classification and explainability, in its own domain and in others, across three data sets. The paper offers a compact, interpretable safety tool: a classifier that also points to the words behind its call, trained without relying on large model scale.
arxiv-2602-16053:
Mehrab Beikzadeh leads a team of seven researchers tackling a gap in AI support for mental health care. Over a billion people live with mental health disorders, yet care is scarce and costly. Current AI alignment tends to tune each goal alone rather than balancing patient wishes against clinical safety. The team surveyed 335 people with lived mental health experience to rank therapeutic priorities. They then built reward models for six criteria, including empathy, safety, active listening, trust, and patient autonomy.

Their multi-objective approach, MODPO, balances empathy and safety better than single-objective tuning. Single-objective tuning scores very high on empathy but much lower on safety. Therapeutic criteria also beat general communication principles by a stated margin. Blinded clinician review preferred MODPO, with evaluator agreement near the level seen between clinicians. The paper offers a measured path toward safer, more balanced therapeutic AI.
arxiv-2602-16153:
George Li, Jason Li, and Junkai Zhang solve the single-source shortest paths problem on directed graphs with real-valued edge weights, which may be negative. Their paper refines the shortcutting procedure introduced by Li, Li, Rao, and Zhang in an earlier work, pushing the running time down to just above quadratic in the number of vertices. The abstract states the result crisply, with the refinement itself as the contribution.

For readers in algorithms, the interest lies in that tight bound for a classic problem where negative weights rule out the simplest methods. A near-quadratic algorithm for directed graphs with arbitrary real weights narrows the gap between what is known to be possible and the quadratic barrier that dense graphs suggest. The paper thus offers a cleaner, faster route to shortest paths in a setting where edge weights can pull in both directions.
arxiv-2602-16853:
Inha Cha and co-authors trace four eras of image-based digital sexual violence in South Korea. The span runs from the early internet of the 1990s to deepfake scandals in the mid-2020s. Digital sexual violence has been persistent since internet tools arrived. It has grown in severity and scale alongside digital tools. Public concern is widespread. The paper draws on media coverage, legal texts, and academic work. It maps forms and traits of cases in each era.

The study finds three linked dimensions. First, victims' imagery is collectively framed as obscene in male-dominant networks. Second, violence grows harder for victims to perceive as tools change. Third, abuse is commercialized through decentralized economic infrastructures. The paper traces how entrenched misogyny is reshaped through evolving tools and shifting laws. It suggests next steps for computing research.
arxiv-2602-16953:
Hejia Zhang and co-authors present LLM4Cov, an execution-aware agentic learning frame for high-coverage testbench generation in hardware verification. Execution-aware agents learn from tool feedback, but such feedback can be expensive and slow, making online reinforcement learning less practical in some settings. High-coverage hardware verification exemplifies that challenge, relying on industrial simulators and non-differentiable execution signals.

LLM4Cov models verification as single-step state transitions guided by deterministic evaluators, in an offline agent-learning frame. It brings in execution-validated data curation, policy-aware agentic data synthesis, and worst-state-prioritized sampling to enable scalable learning under execution constraints. A reality-aligned benchmark adapted from an existing verification suite is also curated. A compact four-billion-parameter model reaches strong pass rates and average coverage, beating its teacher and rivaling models an order of magnitude larger.
arxiv-2602-17053:
Yunseok Han led a three-author team asking whether the reasoning that large reasoning models show actually drives their answers. Such models often produce plausible-sounding chains that do not reflect how they chose, which undercuts trust even when the answer is right. The paper sets out a formal test of reasoning faithfulness, split into stance consistency and causal influence of the stated reasoning on the answer.

To run that test, the authors built RFEval, a benchmark of over seven thousand cases across seven tasks using counterfactual output interventions. Twelve open models proved unfaithful in about half their outputs, mostly through stance breaks, with failures worst in brittle fields like math and code. Accuracy proved a weak proxy for faithfulness once model and task were held fixed. The lesson is that trustworthy models need sound reasoning structure, not just right answers.
arxiv-2602-17153: Pradipta Bandyopadhyay led a two-author short note settling a question about Banach spaces. The note proves that the hereditary Mazur intersection property does not imply Frechet smoothness, using an example built by Borwein and Fabian in 1993. The proof is brief and self-contained, and it tells apart two traits that might otherwise be mixed up. Readers get a clean counter-case: a space can inherit the intersection trait at every subspace level while still failing the smoothness test.
arxiv-2602-17453:
Juan A. Cañas led a four-author team on charge and energy transport in graphene with smooth finite-range disorder.
