Covertness means the gap between the Warden's real channel output pattern and the hypothetical output pattern if the transmitter always sent a specific zero symbol stays below a given threshold.

Their capacity result comes in computable form, and numerics show time-sharing is suboptimal in general, with improved rates available through superposition coding. The work extends a line of covert communication research. Reliable communication over memoryless Gaussian channels works when the number of information bits grows with the square root of channel uses.
arxiv-2605-09553:
Aydin and two colleagues introduce prescribed angle surfaces in curved spaces, tied to a pair made of a unit vector field and the angle it makes with the surface normal. The study focuses on the case where the vector field is torse forming, a class with a special derivative form. Prescribed angle surfaces extend constant angle surfaces, a classic topic in surface geometry, by letting the angle vary in a set way.

In the three dimensional case, the authors work out the inner and outer curvatures of these surfaces. Those curvatures are given in terms of the set angle and the potential function of the vector field. From those formulas they sort prescribed angle surfaces under suitable assumptions. The paper thus extends the constant angle theory to a wider, more flexible family of surfaces in curved spaces.
arxiv-2605-09853:
Li and six colleagues address a clash inside modern language-model training: test-time methods work best when the model samples widely, but reinforcement learning sharpens its output distribution and kills that variety. Their fix, Exploration-Driven Optimization, folds reward-biasing exploration goals into standard training objectives, keeping sampled answers diverse so later test-time computation has more to work with. It comes in two forms, built on iterative preference optimization and on group-relative policy optimization.

Both forms raised solution diversity and reasoning scores, especially when paired with self-consistency, a test-time trick that votes across many samples. Gains ran one to one and a third points over the strongest baselines on three in-distribution reasoning tests, plus about one and a half points on average across five out-of-distribution tasks. Training also stayed steadier, with model entropy preserved instead of collapsing.
arxiv-2605-10353:
Carlo Giunti, Yu-Feng Li, and Rong-ping Zhang revisit a long-running neutrino puzzle. The Reactor Antineutrino Anomaly is a deficit between measured reactor antineutrino event rates and theoretical predictions. First spotted in 2011 at 2.5 sigma, it seemed resolved by 2021, falling to about 1 sigma under newer flux calculations. Their 2026 paper applies a flux model never before used for the anomaly.

That model, a 2023 French summation calculation, is the first to include a comprehensive uncertainty budget. With it, the anomaly revives to 2.2 sigma. The authors also test the standard explanation, oscillations into a light sterile neutrino, and find tension of 3.8 sigma with gallium source experiments once solar, KATRIN, reactor spectral-ratio, and Daya Bay bounds are included. Enlarging gallium uncertainties in a global analysis cuts that tension to 1.3 sigma, suggesting underestimated systematics may explain the clash.
arxiv-2605-10453:
Anton Plaksin and three colleagues speed up speculative decoding by shrinking the draft model's LM-head. Speculative decoding speeds up generation: a lightweight draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass. Although the drafter network is small, its LM-head still projects to a large vocabulary. Prior work addressed it via static or dynamic vocabulary truncation, adding complexity. Their 2026 paper proposes SlimSpec.

SlimSpec is a low-rank form of the drafter's LM-head that shrinks the inner representation rather than the output, keeping full vocabulary support. The authors evaluate it with an EAGLE-3 drafter across three target models in latency- and throughput-bound regimes. SlimSpec runs 4 to 5 times faster than the LM-head architecture while keeping a competitive acceptance length, beating existing methods by up to 8 to 9 percent of end-to-end speedup. It needs minimal changes to training and inference pipelines.
arxiv-2605-10653:
Jan-Mou Li and three colleagues report embodied AI insights from the SAE World Congress 2026. Embodied AI is rapidly moving from labs into real systems such as self-driving cars, mobile robots, and factory machines. As these systems grow more capable in changing settings, they introduce new challenges. The challenges cover safety, trust, governance, and uptime. Their 2026 white paper summarizes the panel session Embodied AI in Action.

The discussion treats embodied AI as a systems challenge needing engineering rigor, lifecycle rules, human-centered design, and new standards. The paper gives views for executives, policymakers, and tech leaders adopting embodied AI responsibly. The panel agreed long-term success depends not only on AI gains. It will depend equally on safe and trustworthy deployment. Trust will be earned through clear, explainable, and repeatable work under real operating conditions.
arxiv-2605-11153:
Ramchand Kumaresan decomposes an evolutionary mixture-of-LoRA system on a from-scratch widened-1536 substrate, about 150 million parameters, into three factors. The factors are a router rewrite, a per-domain leave-one-out evaluation scope, and a lifecycle of death plus alpha-blend inheritance plus SVD mutation plus slot reallocation.

A 5-of-8 partial factorial run at three seeds and 25,000 adaptation steps per cell gives a sharp attribution chain on this substrate. The router rewrite alone carries the entire plus 0.0426 nat balanced log-PPL improvement attributed to the full evolutionary system versus the static B3 baseline, while the headline full-system contrast itself is plus 0.015 nats and does not clear the 0.05 significance level. Mixture-of-experts researchers get a caution: the router, not the lifecycle, drives the gain here.
arxiv-2605-11253:
Kemal Atalar and three co-authors investigate low-rank compression of two-electron reduced matrices. Two-body reduced forms encode core two-electron physics. But their quartic storage cost limits daily workflows.

The team studies a simple protocol compressing transition and other 2RDMs into a lower-rank representation. It preserves wedge-product structure and symmetries under truncation. The decomposition links Coulomb and exchange channels via one shared set of low-rank factors, giving a tighter rank-sparse form than single-channel splits. For correlated states, rank scales linearly with system size, achieving about 99 percent savings for octane's coupled-cluster 2RDM while keeping chemical accuracy. Applied to ab initio eigenvector continuation workflows, many-body wave functions get interpolated over nuclear shapes at mean-field cost. The scheme drops memory cost from quartic to quadratic at a fixed error each. Chemistry teams get a compaction method with steering metrics.
arxiv-2605-11453: Ethan Parks and Dalal Alharthi introduce a structural diagnostic for multi-agent language-model communication graphs. Teams now pick among chain, star, mesh and richer layouts with no advance check for drift, agreement or breakage. Their check uses the successor representation, a matrix that sums future visits under the message pattern. Three numbers from that matrix map to three failure modes. The condition number predicts robustness to perturbation perfectly, the spectral gap partly predicts consensus dynamics, and the spectral radius runs perfectly inverted against cumulative error.
arxiv-2605-11653: Gloaguen, Staab, Vero and Vechev propose a binomial multi-bit LLM mark putting every bit everywhere. Commercial marking needs multi-bit payloads like user IDs in made text. Their method uses binomial coding to put every bit at every token, plus a coder shifting pressure to undercoded bits. Against 8 baselines on 64-bit payloads, the scheme beats rivals on accuracy, with gaps widening for large payloads. They challenge prior scoring methods and introduce per-bit confidence scores.
arxiv-2605-11753: Abid Ali, Diego Molla-Aliod, and Usman Naseem build a summarizer that reads text and pictures together instead of bolting shallow visual features onto a language model. Their SPeCTrA-Sum system aligns a visual encoder with the language model layer by layer and picks representative images with a relevance predictor trained from a determinantal point process teacher. Tests show more accurate, visually grounded summaries and better image choices.
arxiv-2605-12453: Narayana and three colleagues publish a real-world data set for AI-driven mobility in next-generation mobile networks. Most mobility research trains on simulated data, which misses real deployment behaviour and traffic patterns. Their data come from a live commercial network across walking, cycling, driving, bus and train travel at varied speeds. The focus is handovers, with timing advance readings at signalling events, aiming to cut handover gaps and keep throughput steady during and just after each handover.
arxiv-2605-12553: Jiang and four colleagues improve channel prediction for fast-moving massive MIMO-OFDM links. Accurate channel state information matters for reliability and spectral efficiency, yet deep models struggle to catch both short local swings and long nonlinear trends in channel sequences. Their ChannelKAN model pairs convolutional nets, which catch local spatial-frequency patterns within a time step, with Kolmogorov-Arnold nets, which fit nonlinear change across steps using learnable Chebyshev activations. Dual-domain expansion and multi-scale frequency enhancement then sharpen the forecast.
arxiv-2605-12653: Go, Deb and Banerjee give trading agents a way to adjust at run time using price guesses. Static policies lack any way to adapt from guesses when deployed, yet under the price-taker rule, holdings actions do not move future prices. Their FinPILOT plugin lets a multi-step price model supply dreamed market paths without step-by-step action-tied rollouts. At each step, the model's given path builds a share-based dreamed return goal, and the ready policy is tuned at run time before one trade step runs.
arxiv-2605-12753: Hoareau and eight colleagues optimise sparse-to-dense weakly supervised learning for multi-label segmentation of ex vivo MRI data. Fully supervised 3D segmentation of ex vivo MRI is limited by costly volumetric annotation, forcing use of sparse 2D slices. A 2D Teacher learns from sparse slices, then generates dense pseudo-labels for a 3D Student. The team evaluates spatial augmentation, human-centric preprocessing and soft-label tuning on both architectures. They analyse divergent regularisation needs for multi-class segmentation of spinal cord MRI from multiple sclerosis cords.
arxiv-2605-12953: Hao and eight colleagues present Seg-Agent, a training-free system that segments image regions from natural-language instructions. Earlier systems reason only in text, but Seg-Agent runs an interactive visual loop of generation, selection and refinement. It draws candidate regions onto the image so the model can see and reason spatially. It matches training-based state-of-the-art methods without any parameter updates. A new benchmark, Various-LangSeg, tests generalisation across segmentation task types.
arxiv-2605-13053: Kostric and Balog retest seven conversational recommender systems on the ReDial dataset under shared rules. Shifting preprocessing and ground-truth definitions have made cross-study comparison shaky, and backbone capacity often drives gains more than architectural ideas. They find fine-grained ranking swings wildly with implementation detail, while nearly half of reported accuracy comes from repetition shortcuts absent in novelty-focused evaluation. Plain recall, they show, often inflates real conversational effectiveness.
arxiv-2605-13353: Sebastian Golat and two colleagues apply a bispinor language to tiny dipolar particles in light fields. Standard formulas for forces, torques and absorbed power are long and hide their common origin. The new language expresses them all through broken symmetries of light and particle. It yields basic inequalities that particle cross-sections must satisfy. It clarifies why pressure forces track momentum differences while recoil forces track helicity cross-sections. The authors present it as a short tool for dipole interactions, including chiral and nonreciprocal particles.
arxiv-2605-13453: Clara Lucia Galimberti and four colleagues propose a way to learn a KKL observer for guessing the hidden state of a nonlinear system. KKL observers place system dynamics into stable latent dynamics, but results hinge on a hand-picked choice. The authors state a rule under which the observer locally acts like a minimum energy estimator, the Mortensen observer. They use deep learning to approximate the KKL map and latent dynamics, with designs that force shrinking. Tests show good results under state and measurement noise.
arxiv-2605-13653: Hong Deng, Liyan Luo and Lei Wu propose a two-scale coupling plan to speed up direct simulation Monte Carlo for chemical reactions. A large-scale synthetic equation joins flow rules for spread, stress and heat flux, plus higher-order rules capturing uneven transport. The large-scale system is solved to steady state, and its result corrects particle spreads in DSMC at times. The coupling holds up, runs fast and cuts noise, easing DSMC jams for near-flow cases by several orders of size.
arxiv-2605-13753: Ashkan Shahbazi and three colleagues propose min General Sliced Gromov-Wasserstein, a sliced form for the Gromov-Wasserstein problem using rich general slicers. The key idea is learning coupled bent slicers assigning matching push-forward values to both inputs. Min-GSGW cuts that cost straight in the original spaces and is rigid-motion steady, a crucial property for shape matching and shape study. The team also builds a shared variant swapping per-case tuning with a learned slicer for unseen input pairs.
arxiv-2605-13953: Van Beekveld and four co-authors set out PanScales final-state showers that weigh quark masses and hit next-to-leading log exactness. Sights where quark mass means nil keep their old scores. Fixed-order tests run to second order in the strong force, and all-order checks match resummed sums for Lund-tree shapes, non-global energy flows and Lund sub-jet counts. Phenomenology tests with LEP data round out the work.
arxiv-2605-14053: Sastre, Moncecchi and Rosa offer Derivation Prompting, a logic-based aid for retrieval-augmented generation in question answering. Language models often hallucinate or reason wrongly on knowledge-heavy, niche tasks. The method derives conclusions from starting hypotheses by applying set rules step by step. The result is a derivation tree that can be read and checked, giving more control over what the model writes. A case study cuts unacceptable answers well below those of plain RAG and long-context methods.
arxiv-2605-14253: Robertshaw and eight co-authors develop a live catheter tip tracking pipeline under fluoroscopy for autonomous navigation. Mechanical thrombectomy improves stroke outcomes but is limited by local treatment access. Reinforcement learning robots could ease this gap, but need live tip tracking. The pipeline handles low contrast, noise and occlusion with frame reading, preprocessing and inference. U-Net, U-Net+Transformer and SegFormer were benchmarked in two-class and three-class forms. Two-class SegFormer reached a mean error of 4.44 mm, beating U-Net and three-class models.
arxiv-2605-14553: Li, Shi, Ou, Shen and Yang treat prompt selection as a multi-objective problem, since one metric cannot capture every facet of prompt quality. Casting it as pure-exploration bandits, they adapt algorithms for recovering Pareto-optimal prompt sets and identifying the best feasible prompt, with theoretical error guarantees in the linear case. Experiments across several language models are claimed to show significant improvements over baselines on both tasks.
arxiv-2605-14753: Gerasimov, Krachkov and Lee calculate next-to-next-to-leading order QED corrections for the C-odd portion of the differential cross section for electron-positron annihilation into muon pairs. This part feeds angular and forward-backward asymmetry. Together with an earlier paper, the work completes the analytical calculation of this differential cross section at next-to-next-to-leading order.
arxiv-2605-15253: Jairo Diaz-Rodriguez argues, in a position paper, that ideas should sit at the center of machine learning research. The field splits between benchmark-driven engineering that prizes metrics over understanding and idealized theory that usually fail to carry over. His Ideas First framework values ideas by the behavior patterns they predict in modern models, tested through tailored experiments rather than leaderboard wins. The shift also promotes equity by dropping the complexity premium that favors researchers with large resources.
arxiv-2605-15353: Ramon Viñas Torné and six colleagues offer PACER, a scalable framework for causal discovery from large-scale interventional data that ensures loop-freedom by build. Old methods lean on soft loop-freedom fines, tuning over invalid cyclic graphs with wobble and poor scaling. PACER maps a distribution over directed acyclic graphs through variable orders plus edge odds. It tunes straight over valid forms. It handles observational and trial data under one likelihood, with closed-form linear-Gaussian expressions, matching or beating leading methods on protein and genetic benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-15453: Paweł Rafał Bieliński and four others prove a result about graph classes forbidding induced subdivisions of H. Such a class has bounded clique-width exactly when H is an induced subgraph of the four-vertex path, the paw, or the diamond. A paw is a four-clique minus two adjacent edges, and a diamond from a four-clique minus one edge. The characterization answers a question of Dabrowski, Johnson, and Paulusma. It pins down precisely which forbidden subdivisions keep clique-width bounded and which let it grow without limit.
arxiv-2605-15653: Benjamin Hamblin, Victor Calo, and Klaus Regenauer-Lieb stretch the Tolman-Ehrenfest effect to linked thermodynamic channels. On the entropy manifold they derive one multi-channel invariant: each channel's holonomy factor times its temperature stays fixed. For a granular volume-stress set, Rowe's dilatancy ratio and energy cap drop out as geometry effects of off-diagonal curvature. A sixty-year puzzle over a state-linked modulus clears up near jamming. Their forecast that one correction times susceptibility stays flat across a shear band can be tested in labs.
arxiv-2605-15853: R. Kord Valeshabadi, S. Rezaie and K. Azizi study unintegrated double parton distributions built from non-factorized inputs. Using GS09 inputs evolved to unequal scales under double DGLAP evolution, checked by sum rules, they test MRW recipes for adding transverse momentum dependence. The DMKMRW, DVO-MRW and matched DVO-MRW recipes apply to the collinear input, avoiding the piecewise LO-MRW build. DMKMRW keeps normalization by design, while DVO-MRW drifts, a flaw matching removes. Effects of non-factorization vary by channel, largest near the kinematic boundary.
arxiv-2605-16853: Wu, Huang and Wang model social-law synthesis as a Bayesian single-parameter auction built on alternating-time logic. They prove any valuation respecting alternating bisimulation can be written in compact form as a feature set of logic formulas. They reduce payment finding to allocation finding in polynomial time, fixing the multi-unit payment problem. They prove allocation finding is FP-NP-complete, so they encode the logic in integer linear constraints for solvers. Their PO-ASL mechanism is incentive-compatible, rational for each player, and profit-optimal.
arxiv-2605-16953: Zhu's team records brain signals from 27 people judging whether image descriptions from a multimodal language model are correct. Mean event-related potentials show distinct patterns for hallucinated versus accurate content across semantic integration, inference, memory retrieval, and cognitive load. Notably, neural responses differ between hallucinations people got wrong and those they got right. The authors conclude wrong items failed to trigger the standard neurocognitive fact-checking pathway.
arxiv-2605-17053: Shin and colleagues complete the 2021 prime-field sweep of a systematic hunt for hidden planets in archived microlensing data. They add seven new planetary systems and three candidates, about a third of that season's prime-field discoveries. The by-eye search still finds most planets, yet the authors argue the systematic sweep stays essential for a fair census of planets across the galaxy. All event data are public.
arxiv-2605-17153: Troxell and colleagues generate neural-network verification problems whose true robustness labels are known by construction, fixing a gap in current benchmarks. Their framework exposed numeric tolerance worries and a bug in popular verifiers. A difficulty profile then maps distinct sources of problem hardness, and tests of five leading verifiers show different problems stress different parts of the checking pipeline.
arxiv-2605-17253: Mirashi and colleagues present resolved hydrogen observations of six dwarf-galaxy candidates thought to hold more ordinary matter than dark matter. Using the uGMRT array they measure shapes, spin speeds and masses more reliably than earlier global spectra allowed. Four galaxies look dark-matter poor, three of them strikingly efficient at gathering baryons, while two fit the dark-matter-dominated picture. The poor ones sit in quiet settings, straining standard expectations.
arxiv-2605-17453: Yan and colleagues study cognitive poisoning in tool-using agents. A malicious tool acts benign during exploration, builds trust, and turns harmful only when hidden state aligns with the final action. Their TRUST-Bench holds 1,970 hidden-trigger compromise episodes with matched safe controls, scored by the asymmetric GuardedJoint metric. Prompt heuristics, scalar features and zero-shot judges fail. Their trajectory-aware VISTA-Guard scores final-action risk strongly in-domain and under distribution shift.
arxiv-2605-17553: Repček and colleagues measure elastic coefficients and thermal diffusivity of a three-micron NiTi film through a thermally induced phase cycle, using transient grating spectroscopy. Elastic values show a shear-modulus crossover between austenite and martensite. Thermal diffusivity changes 450 percent between the R-phase and austenite. With no hysteresis there, the film suits thermal switches. The heat-spread shift traces to anomalous R-phase heat capacity. Temperature-dependent values are supplied for microsystem sims.
arxiv-2605-17653: Xinting Jiang and colleagues present LLMForge, a hardware-aware search for edge models. Sub-billion-parameter edge models gain privacy and latency, yet budgets make architecture cost central. Infinite-Head Attention decouples query heads, KV groups, and per-head dimensions. Forge-DSE pairs Forge-Former with a cost model for GPUs and ring accelerators. On the ring substrate, co-search returns three Pareto variants. The accurate variant has the lowest loss, the energy variant cuts energy per token by 40 percent, and the latency variant cuts TTFT and TPOT by 43 percent.
arxiv-2605-18153: Xin Peng's 2026 paper presents ReasonVul, a vulnerability detection framework in which three language-model agents reason in distinct modes and then debate. Each agent first judges the code alone, then the trio resolves clashes through rounds of rebuttal and revision toward a joint verdict. On the PrimeVul set it reaches 40 percent pair accuracy and an F1 score of 72.52 percent, far above the best baseline on pair accuracy. Of 542 conflict cases studied, 389 were resolved correctly, showing the debate step catching flaws single-mode reasoning missed.
arxiv-2605-18553: Huajian Zeng and five co-authors present StableHand, a 2026 quality-aware flow-matching system for world-space dual-hand motion estimation from egocentric video. Hands often leave view or suffer heavy occlusion during hand-object contact, and current methods ignore per-frame observation quality. It splits observation quality into four channels, wrist shifts and finger bends per hand, predicted by a learned quality network. Using these signals, it keeps good observations while rebuilding poor ones from a two-hand prior. It cuts error 20 to 25 percent on HOT3D and ARCTIC.
arxiv-2605-18753: Yuxiang Huang and seven colleagues offer DashAttention, a 2026 method for long-context language models. Older layered attention picks a fixed number of key-value blocks, which blocks learning between sparse and dense stages. Their design lets each query choose a varying number of blocks, then guides full softmax attention with that choice. The whole chain stays learnable end to end, and tests show it matches full attention while skipping three quarters of the work.
arxiv-2605-18853: Ahmed Šabanović and two colleagues route vision-language inference between edge and cloud by input difficulty. Cloud models answer well but add delay and energy cost, while edge models run fast with less capacity. Static placement wastes both, since image quality and reasoning difficulty vary. Their INAR-VL system reads light image and text complexity signals, keeps simple queries local, and offloads hard ones. Tests show about thirty-six percent of requests stay on the edge, with latency down about twenty-four percent and energy down about twenty-six percent.
arxiv-2605-18953: Conaire Deagan and five colleagues measure how much the Sun's activity wobbles its apparent position, a noise floor for planet hunting by astrometry. Using solar images across nearly a decade and three narrow wavelength bands, they quantify centroid jitter through high and low activity phases. Typical jitter at about 607 nanometers sits well below the roughly three microarcsecond signal an Earth-like planet would imprint on a Sun-like star. Stellar activity thus leaves the detection limit between Mars and one Earth, leaving instrument precision as the binding constraint.
arxiv-2605-19253: Xiaoyan Ma and three colleagues defend over-the-air federated learning against backdoor attacks, where the server cannot see client updates. Non-IID data makes the task harder, since benign drift can look malicious. Their two-stage framework gives each client a trust score, with indicators chosen by data type and design. The server runs trust-based access, sorting clients into trusted, suspicious, and malicious groups, with suspicious clients facing inspection and reputation checks. Tests on several datasets show stealthy backdoors, including Neurotoxin, are suppressed while accuracy stays competitive.
arxiv-2605-19753: Manara, Smirne and Vacchini probe memory effects in a simplified Caldeira-Leggett model, a workhorse picture of a quantum system coupled to its surroundings. The adapted model tracks both system and environment directly, letting the team measure information flowing back from environment to system. Correlations respond mainly to coupling strength, while changes in the environment itself respond more to temperature. The findings back the distinguishability view of non-Markovian behaviour and confirm the model as a sound tool for quantum foundations.
arxiv-2605-20053: Divyasree C-Ramachandran and Amit Hogadi prove a torsion bound for zero cycles on flag varieties. For a central simple algebra with index n, the Chow group of zero cycles on its r-th Severi-Brauer variety has torsion set by d and n divided by d. Here d is the greatest common divisor of r and n. Reducing to division algebras of prime-power index gives vanishing cases and bounds, and for local or global fields the group is zero, with stable birationality extending the results to flag varieties.
arxiv-2605-20153: A. Acharyya and many co-workers report VERITAS and multiwavelength observations of NGC 1275's exceptional 2017 gamma-ray flare. NGC 1275 flared in very high energy gamma rays from December 31, 2016 to January 3, 2017, peaking near one point five Crab units. VERITAS caught the flare on January 2 and 3, 2017, at a flux of zero point five Crab units. Blob-in-jet modelling of those nights' energy distributions supports a two-component model with a ten-degree jet angle and an emission zone near the C3 radio component.
arxiv-2605-20253: E. G. Santos derives a generating function for counting integer compositions of n into k parts with a given number of inversions, and similar results for descents. The method uses a known bijection pairing each composition with a permutation and an integer partition. Inversion counts and descent counts over k-compositions match, respectively, the distribution of major index with inversions and of inversions with descents over permutations of one through k.
arxiv-2605-20453: Payne reviews what is known about curve moduli spaces through their cohomology. Through coniveau forms of the Hodge and Tate conjectures, Hodge structures and l-adic Galois representations connect to algebraic cycles. The boundary stratification's stepwise structure settles the conjectures far more widely than expected. Arithmetic ideas guide the survey, which closes on open problems and future directions.
arxiv-2605-20553: Abdellatif Elgrou, Abdelaziz Rhandi, and Jawad Salhi study how a class of noisy evolution equations behaves over long times. Noise here scales with the state itself, and the setting is a Hilbert space, a kind of infinite-dimensional vector space. They give clear sufficient rules for two kinds of exponential stability, in mean power and almost surely. They link the two notions, show a discrete scheme keeps these traits, and back the theory with simulations.
arxiv-2605-20853: Muhammad Mun'im Ahmad Zabidi and two colleagues present SEABAD, a tropical bird activity detection dataset for passive acoustic listening. Non-stop recording creates vast amounts of uninformative audio, straining storage, power, and long-term edge use. Bird activity spotting filters irrelevant recordings before downstream analysis, but most systems train on temperate data despite tropical soundscapes being denser and richer. SEABAD holds 50,000 picked three-second clips from Southeast Asian soundscapes, split between bird-present and bird-absent samples across 1,677 species.
arxiv-2605-20953: Tangerman studies one standard map that conserves energy in complex 2D, focusing on the edges of Siegel disks. In this example, Siegel disks can be shown and analyzed by computation for edge smoothness. The paper formulates conjectures about those edges and offers computational support for them. It is a focused numerical study of one map, rather than a general theory of Siegel disk edges.
arxiv-2605-21253: Camille Touron and co-authors give a guide for annealed Langevin dynamics in combined simulation-based inference. Score methods approximate a posterior from many observations by pooling learned scores. The combined score matches no spread along the forward path, so reverse sampling carries bias. Annealed Langevin dynamics treats it as the score of bridging densities sampled in turn, giving a bias that can be controlled when tuned well. Tuning choices cover step sizes, steps per level, and level counts.
arxiv-2605-21453: Mohamed Almukhtar, Anwar Ghammam, and Hua Ming study quality and security signals in AI-generated Python refactoring pull requests from the AIDev dataset. As AI agents increasingly contribute to code maintenance, evidence on how agent-authored refactoring edits affect quality and security once merged remains limited. They analyze agentic pull requests with PyQu across five quality attributes, complemented by Pylint and Bandit static analysis before and after each change.
arxiv-2605-21653: Alexander Smirnov argues fine-tuned AI-text detectors amplify a pretrained direction, not an AI-human boundary. Detectors flag formal writing as machine-generated, rating the essay as ninety-nine point five percent AI but clearing hot AI at ten point five percent. Decomposing a detector into an inherited reading and a tuned residual, the inherited part carries cross-generator transfer and drives the flagging, while the residual stays generator-specific. This yields a no-go: no training objective, threshold, erasure, or ensemble tested removes the harm while preserving detection.
arxiv-2605-21753: Sunghyeon Jo gives a deterministic linear-time algorithm for the Erdos-Ginzburg-Ziv problem: from any 2n minus 1 integers, find n whose sum is divisible by n. Earlier methods ran in n log n time, later improved to n log log log n. The core is a prime target subset-sum method built on a compact arithmetic-progression picture of reachable sums. When two progressions meet, a bounded Frobenius interval merges them into a longer one. A standard multiplicative reduction then extends the prime case to arbitrary moduli.
arxiv-2605-21853: Qinghua Ding and Venkat Anantharam study information quantities of edge-reinforced random walks on finite graphs, where each traversed edge gains one unit. On a finite graph such a walk is a random-environment walk, whose law is the magic formula for initial weights. They derive an annealed entropy-rate representation and a closed-form environment-level Kullback-Leibler divergence formula and trajectory-level divergence bounds converging toward that level. They serve two-point testing for trajectories, the Stein exponent, and should matter for identity and closeness testing.
arxiv-2605-22053: Anastasios Papazafeiropoulos proposes a joint model joining stacked intelligent metasurfaces with fluid antenna systems for wireless links. The stacks manipulate signals in the wave domain, while fluid antenna systems move them in space; sending uses such a stack and receiving uses a fluid antenna system. Using a block-diagonal matrix approximation, the author derives a closed-form outage probability formula and tunes metasurface phase shifts to minimize outage. Numerical results validate the analysis and show large gains over standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-22353: Humes and Agarwal test whether sparse multiband survey data can reveal patchy surface colour on asteroids. Their test compares observed light curves against a well-fitting model of a uniformly coloured body. Gaps between the two count as signs of patchy colour. With simulated rocks and Monte Carlo trials, they track hit rates and false alarms against data count, noise and model errors. Hits prove most sensitive to errors in the assumed rotation period. False alarms respond most to errors in band phase functions.
arxiv-2605-22453: Adhikari and colleagues study ferroelectric LaMoN3 under pressure up to 40 GPa, using first-principles methods. The compound stays stable in a single phase across that range. Its indirect bandgap narrows from 2.17 eV at 0 GPa to 1.45 at 40 GPa. Pressure boosts the SLME while lowering exciton binding energy, both good for solar cells. Bulk solar efficiency tracks shift current density, peaking near 15 GPa before falling as nonlinear response weakens. The authors propose a multi-junction device combining absorber layers tuned for linear and nonlinear currents.
arxiv-2605-22553: Gao and team confirm a conjecture proposed by Kühn, Osthus, and Treglown by showing that for any given graph H, there exists a constant C(H) such that the following holds. Let G be a sufficiently large n-vertex graph satisfying d(x) + d(y) ≥ 2(1 - 1/χ_cr(H))n for all nonadjacent vertices x, y in V(G). Then G contains an H-tiling covering all but at most C(H) vertices. Here χ_cr(H) denotes the critical chromatic number of H.
arxiv-2605-22653: Eberle and Lindermayr show that predictions can help online algorithms through timing alone, with no content at all. They study the secretary problem plus a stochastic precursor: a content free signal always beating the best item to arrival, but otherwise randomly timed. In random order, one uniformly timed precursor already lifts success to at least one half, beating the classic one over e benchmark, and later precursors push success toward one. In adversarial order, concentrated precursors restore constant success guarantees where traditional models offer little.
arxiv-2605-22953: Mondal, Pati, and Sinha present an open coupled-top Dicke model for studying quantum scars in a lossy setting. The model maps to a two-species Bose-Josephson junction coupled to a leaky cavity. Photon loss drives spontaneous synchronization through projection onto a dissipation-free subspace, with transient chaos before sync and coherence return. Two scar types appear: one stays protected with persistent revivals, while the superradiant scar decays slowly. Results suit ongoing cavity QED tests.
arxiv-2605-23053: Bor and six coauthors assess multi-hazard risk for the US high-voltage transmission network with one consistent framework. The framework links hazard data, fragility models, and economic impact. Across nine hazards plus a compound freezing rain and wind gust scenario, tropical cyclone wind causes the largest expected daily damage at 137 million dollars. Tornado causes the largest downstream output loss at 4.93 billion dollars per day. A 250-year geomagnetic storm costs 2.07 billion dollars per day. The compound scenario affects 237.4 million people with 85.16 billion dollars per day in losses.
arxiv-2605-23153: Ma and five coauthors present scanning free mid-IR single pixel imaging via two photon optical coding in a silicon device. Standard IR cameras are costly and cold, while current two photon imagers are slow or insensitive. Spatial coding comes from a near-IR structured pump at 7 micrometer resolution, enabling high quality modulation without phase matching. The single element device integrates the modulated response for recovery by computer. Compressed sensing and deep learning recover images at 10 percent compression under photon starved light. Multispectral images across 2.5 to 3.8 micrometers distinguish plastic films.
arxiv-2605-23453: Elvin Somón Sánchez and Miguel Gutiérrez-Naranjo revisit migraine classification work and repair leaked data and skewed scoring. They combine two hemiplegic subtypes under ICHD-3 guidance and pick synthetic data methods per class size, capping growth in proportion instead of forcing full balance. On 400 patients across seven subtypes, their approach beats synthetic data methods across eight classifiers, peaking at 0.914 with FT-Transformer.
arxiv-2605-23653: Papo, Smoller, and Laufer present ExpOS, an explainable framework for assessing open-surgery skills from data instead of expert observation alone. Rather than expert-defined metrics, ExpOS learns discriminative temporal patterns from motion data and flags segments and behaviors most predictive of skill. Trained on 221 videos of medical students doing three surgery tasks, it combines hand poses, tool detections, kinematic descriptors, and global motion statistics. Attention-based pooling then predicts skill and explains its calls. It correlates strongly with expert ratings, best on fascial closure at r equals 0.778.
arxiv-2605-23753: Shirzad and colleagues present SeedER, a Seed-Expand-Retrieve method for knowledge graph retrieval using graph transformers. Knowledge graphs offer relational knowledge, but irregular structure hinders retrieval. Dense embeddings precomputed for nodes can require dimensions comparable to graph size. Query-adaptive embeddings can overcome this, and some graph neural network variants can too, but whole-graph processing costs memory and needs dense labels. SeedER runs on CPU at inference as a retriever, needs feedback on only a few nodes, and competes with fine-tuned large language model methods.
arxiv-2605-24053: Leyva and Smarandache test neutrosophic logic, which treats truth, indeterminacy, and falsity as independent, for modelling uncertainty in language models. Standard probability forces probabilities to sum to one, collapsing ignorance, paradox, and vagueness together. Across GPT models, five phenomena, and three prompting strategies, the neutrosophic approach let truth plus indeterminacy plus falsity exceed one. They call that state hyper-truth, seen in 35 percent of evaluations, mostly under ethical contradiction and paradox. The approach preserves truth values in fuzzy settings and flags conflict, pointing toward more transparent systems.
arxiv-2605-24653: Gunnar Peng and Ory Schnitzer show that charge on a long conducting cylinder evens out only slowly. Extra charge lingers near the ends, and that end boost grows as the square root of the log of the length-to-width ratio. They derive the rule by resumming a perturbation series for the slender-body integral equation. It also covers truncated slender bodies, such as shapes tapered near the ends. Simulations for flat and rounded caps back the rule, which the authors extend to diffusion, plasmonics, and Stokes flow.
arxiv-2605-24753: Avery Gump and others attack internal glare in compact LiDAR, where light from bright surfaces scatters inside the sensor. The artifacts create phantom objects, hide real ones, and threaten safety. The authors model glare as a linear, scene-independent operator on transient measurements, called TGSF. They develop a training-free method on low-level detections before point-cloud formation, weighing each detection for glare. The approach fits existing pipelines and unmodified commercial sensors. Real single-photon hardware tests suppress severe glare while preserving true scene structure.
arxiv-2605-24953: Chengrui Li leads a multi-turn dialog system for running and maintaining industrial assets. Questions there unfold over turns and lean hard on external tools. The usual plan-then-act agent loses track across turns and redoes past work. The new design splits labor between supervisor and specialist agents, adding artifact reuse, dynamic replanning, and parallel tool calls. Tests show better answer quality, with planning and task completion both up sharply. Artifact reuse across turns slashes redundant tool time and makes later turns several times faster.
arxiv-2605-25253: Enzo Erlich, Jérémy Ledent, and Krzysztof Ziemiański characterize the languages of higher-dimensional automata, machines that model events happening at the same time. They prove a language of pomsets, partially ordered words, is regular. It arises exactly as the inverse image of a functor into a finite category. First-order definability matches recognition by an aperiodic category, extending a classic theorem to this setting. Counter-free machines, they show, accept only first-order definable languages, while the converse stays open.
arxiv-2605-25353: Divyam Goel and colleagues fill a gap in machine learning for physics: benchmarks for inverse problems, where the goal is to recover hidden parameters from observed solutions. Their PDEInvBench dataset covers time-dependent and steady partial differential equations across varied physical behaviors and parameters, with splits testing both familiar and shifted settings. The team explores training methods, problem encodings, and scaling in one design study. Two-stage training works best, derivative features consistently help, and diverse starting conditions beat wider parameter ranges. Dataset and code are public.
arxiv-2605-26153: Atiratch Laoharenoo and Chanatip Sujsuntinukul settle exactly when a family of integrals built from powers of cosine differences converge or diverge. For whole-number powers and real-valued shifts, they map every parameter range and give exact values in all cases where the integrals converge. The same method yields a family of counting identities from sine-and-cosine series. It extends to a matching class of integrals built from sine differences.
arxiv-2605-26353: Xinran Liang and five colleagues tackle contextual bias in vision: models learn objects best in common settings. Yet spotting a beach ball on a road may matter more than spotting one on sand. Their DecoupleGen method personalizes text-to-image diffusion models to synthesize coherent images in rare contexts while keeping original visual details. Verification constraints keep the augmented data relevant. On object classification and recognition over complex scenes, the approach consistently beats prior methods, and analysis pins down factors behind the gains.
arxiv-2605-26553: Jia-Peng Wei and six colleagues test FRB 190520B's supernova-remnant origin. Its large dispersion measure and broadening point to a dense environment. The team models a core-collapse remnant expanding into a wind, self-similarly. Observed dispersion and scattering constrain remnant and host parameters. Twenty cases span four ejecta and five scattering prescriptions; only six fit. All six share shallow ejecta, young ages of 79.8 to 169.8 years, and large ejecta mass. Secular dispersion fits better than scattering detail, and up-drift hints at extra inner structure.
arxiv-2605-26853: Bak and Gustavsson introduce a nonabelian surface holonomy built from a one-form gauge potential valued in a loop algebra of the U(N) gauge group. The construction parallel-transports a nonabelian string across a surface. Although invariance is not obvious from the setup, they show the holonomy does not change under reparametrizations of the surface.
arxiv-2605-27153: Zhang and co-authors turn a pile of social experiments into an atlas that shows what is known, what clashes, and what is missing. For a target study, their ExAtlas tool finds close prior studies and asks whether their effects can be combined to predict the target effect. A match links the target to past evidence, a mismatch prompts a search for factors that explain the clash, and a failed combination prompts a bridge experiment. On held-out targets, the tool gets the effect direction right in 98.6% of cases.
arxiv-2605-27253: Kosaku Takanashi and Kenichiro McAlinn study how well competing prediction rules perform for a class of location models. They prove an exact identity linking Kullback-Leibler prediction regret to the energy of a related Markov process. That link turns regret comparisons into a question about recurrence, and yields tail conditions under which a Bayes prediction rule cannot be beaten.
arxiv-2605-27353: Sagnick Mukherjee and colleagues model how clouds change sub-Neptune atmospheres and interiors. Clouds heat deep layers by at least 1000 kelvin and cool shallow layers, leaving most sample planets with a molten atmosphere-mantle boundary. That heating shifts interface chemistry sharply, with oxygen, silane, and silicon monoxide abundances rising by at least a third on TOI-270 d.
arxiv-2605-27453: Iftekher Chowdhury and colleagues study Lifshitz transitions where type-I Weyl fermions turn into type-II. Using the Painleve-Gullstrand metric at a black hole horizon, they draw analogies between the horizon and the Dirac-line transition surface. The transition state acts like a horizon with a Dirac-line Fermi surface, a nontrivial invariant, and a critical chiral anomaly effect.
arxiv-2605-27553: Jurgen Gutekunst and colleagues design low-cost predictive control for microgrids with generator up and down times. Swapping nonlinear power-flow equations for convex quadratic stand-ins turns the problem into a mixed-integer program with quadratic limits, solvable by standard solvers. Added time-linked limits keep the scheme feasible where simple end limits fail, and periodic dissipativity yields stability.
arxiv-2605-27753: Kenneth Benicio and colleagues study where one target sits with group-linked beyond-diagonal smart surfaces in a one-station network. Their nested tensor method models the signal as a third-order nested Tucker tensor, splitting delay-Doppler and angle domains. A two-stage plan finds target-bearing factors first, then pulls out the rest with subspace and closed-form steps.
arxiv-2605-27853: Thao Nguyen and Heng Ji build a multi-agent chemist for early drug design, splitting the work among literature, chemist, and coordinator agents sharing one memory. Molecules are broken into meaningful blocks with plain names, letting the model reason and edit at block level rather than wrestling raw chemical strings. Across four benchmarks it beat frontier models and specialist rivals.
arxiv-2605-28253: Huaman and colleagues build the first dedicated speech resources for Puno Quechua, shaped with its speakers. The release offers the biggest speech collection for one Quechua variety, sixty-six hours with thirty-six transcribed and validated, plus the first systematic speech-recognition benchmark for the variety. All datasets and fine-tuned models are openly released.
arxiv-2605-28553: Matteo Gioele Collu and six colleagues ask whether a language model's refusal can be read from its inner activations before it generates output. Linear probes on residual-stream activations show refusal is decodable well before the final layer. They exploit this with Mechanistic AutoDAN, a probe-guided jailbreak search that swaps full-model fitness checks for partial passes plus probe scoring. Attack success rivals vanilla AutoDAN while cutting per-iteration search time by up to about three quarters, with probe guidance growing more useful at larger model scales.
arxiv-2605-28653: Stef Baas, Judith ter Schure, and Joost van Rosmalen design adaptive single-arm binary trials around e-values, a robust replacement for p-values and Bayes factors. E-values stay valid at any stopping time, allowing interim checks, complex stopping rules, and valid inference despite protocol deviations. The authors build designs maximizing power or minimizing sample size, with or without minimum-power limits, by dynamic programming. Exact calculations show operating traits against standard adaptive designs, and small e-values automatically signal futility, with zero ruling out any efficacy conclusion.
arxiv-2605-28953: Antoine Dierckx, Sébastien Clesse, and Francesca Vidotto ask whether dark matter could be Planck-scale remnants of light primordial black holes in loop quantum gravity. A large early population of holes lighter than a thousand kilograms would overproduce relics. Hawking radiation from heavier holes leaves relics as only a tiny dark-matter share. Near a thousand kilograms, evaporation reheats the universe while remnants supply all of today's dark matter, with no fine tuning. The scenario predicts scalar-induced gravitational waves that detectors can test.
arxiv-2605-29553: Guorui Ma and Zhifei Yan pin the threshold for Hamilton cycles in perturbed sparse graphs. Adding random edges to a sparse graph with smallest degree a vanishing fraction of the vertex count, they prove the union holds a Hamilton cycle with probability tending to one. That happens past a logarithmic threshold scaled by that fraction. That improves the leading constant from six to one. They show the bound is best possible when the degree fraction times the vertex count grows without bound, using robust expansion and sprinkling.
arxiv-2605-29853: Thomas Delépine, Pascal Ochem, and Matthieu Rosenfeld take up Harju's 2019 question on endless three-letter block-free words. They ask for which prime pairs the word stays block-free along steps of each prime, known only for two pairs. They prove only finitely many prime pairs lack such a word, so most admit one. The proof builds words from multi-valued and circular block-free maps, plus square-free transducers, which widen block-free maps. The result closes the question, leaving a finite set of pairs to rule out.
arxiv-2605-29953: Li Yin and five colleagues estimate 3D poses in team sports, where bodies hide each other and kits confuse views. Their training-free MAEM pipeline matches players across views in two epipolar stages from a single-view mesh model. Disjoint-set clustering plus per-joint triangulation lock links and rebuild poses. On two basketball sets it beats rival training-free matchers and RGB-only leaders indoors and out. Scores near sixty and forty-one on one set show mesh shape can carry matching with no target-domain tuning.
arxiv-2605-30053: Philip Cervenjak and four colleagues improve approximation bounds for connected submodular maximization. The task is to pick a fixed-edge tree whose vertices score highest under a diminishing-returns function. It covers wireless deployment, path planning, outbreaks and cancer genome work. Earlier polynomial-time methods were bounded by the square root of tree size or by the radius of the best solution. Their GreedyRadius-based framework gives a stronger radius-based guarantee for plain and directed variants, with a size violation allowed in the rooted directed case.
arxiv-2605-30153: Jingda Wu and Changxiao Cai show score-based diffusion models are near-optimal for learning low-dimensional multi-modal data. Current theory leans on strong regularity assumptions, such as bounded densities or smooth scores, which miss such structure. For distributions on a union of low-dimensional subspaces with subgaussian pieces, diffusion models need sample counts growing only with intrinsic dimension to reach a given error in Wasserstein distance. The rate avoids the curse of dimensionality and needs no smoothness or log-concavity assumptions.
arxiv-2605-30253: Rocco Caprio, Adrien Corenflos and Sam Power study non-asymptotic contraction in Wasserstein distance of coordinate ascent variational inference. This holds under a smoothness condition on optimality maps and a transport inequality at fixed points. Results are sharp and general, and unlike those based on strong log-concavity, they allow local convergence over smooth, non-smooth, and discrete manifolds. Work spans statistical physics and Bayesian statistics, including Ising, Curie-Weiss, Gaussian mixture, Probit Regression and Logistic Regression models. In many models, these are the first convergence results of their kind.
arxiv-2605-30353: Nhat-Minh Nguyen presents a study of a physicist's AI coding agent over 57 sessions to build CLAX-PT, a perturbation theory module in JAX. The agent resolved ten of 15 events against oracle tests, and two more with the physicist's knowledge. The three it could not, evading detection, mistook symptom reduction for root-cause resolution. It spent 33 sessions tuning coefficients within an architecture that could not match the physics. Three supervision practices proved critical: testing, shared changelogs, and a rule against unphysical patches. Supervision design, not capability, determined trustworthiness.
arxiv-2605-30553: Noël offers a unifying view of diffusion models as machines that learn by destroying information and then reconstructing it. Withholding data from a model's input and training it to guess what is missing is a broad family, he argues. Diffusion's destructive version is more flexible than hand-crafted withholding, especially when data are scarce. The paper then probes pitfalls of importing reinforcement-learning exploration tricks into diffusion and sketches more native ways to handle them. A tutorial and a new kind of probabilistic graphical model round out the argument.
arxiv-2605-30653: Huang and colleagues challenge a common belief in multi-agent systems: that agreement means an answer is right. Once agents talk, they can fail together and fake consensus, so the same vote share can mean agreement in one layout but overconfidence in another. Their CAGE-CAL framework compares each query's graph after talk with a what-if graph without talk, capturing pairwise failure links and group ties. Instead of counting agreement, it estimates the what-if shift and sets confidence, improving reliability checks and layout choice on five benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-30753: Li and colleagues treat diffusion language-model decoding as a control problem to cut delay from repeat refinement. Old methods use step-local confidence rules or fixed plans, sensitive to prompt and task change and missing position effects. Their trace-aware design has two parts. Temporal-Spatial Parallel Decoding uses a light controller to fix settled tokens. Confidence Extrapolation, a training-free state-space module, predicts future logit trends with uncertainty. Together, the parts cut needless denoising rounds while keeping output quality.
arxiv-2605-30853: Aolaritei and colleagues introduce a diffusion uncertainty model for robust optimization on directed graphs. Shocks to edge weights spread along neighboring edges and respect node conservation rules, a pattern natural in transport and energy networks. They test shortest path, easy in the setting, and the traveling salesman problem, already hard. For shortest path, propagation depth triggers a sharp jump between tractable and intractable robust versions. For the salesman problem, robustness often adds no extra hardness, because fixed-tour adversarial costs collapse to formulas.
arxiv-2605-30953: Cohen and Hamann study how wiggly primordial spectra evolve beyond the linear regime. Slow-roll inflation predicts a smooth, nearly scale-invariant spectrum, but many non-minimal models predict spectra with wiggles. New surveys will probe spectra with unprecedented accuracy, raising sensitivity to wiggles, but nonlinear growth must be tracked. Using N-body runs, the authors fit a one-value damping model for wiggles in the late spectrum. They show that when the wiggle rate is high, the spectrum can be forecast to within one percent, opening wiggle searches.
arxiv-2605-31053: Chang and colleagues enable music editing that changes traits while keeping rhythm and melody. Steering methods harm structure for edits, while structure adaptors dampen meaning response. Their AnchorSteer couples structure anchoring with found meaning steering. It probes representations to extract clear, unlabeled vectors via a self-taught rebuilding goal, setting traits apart without curated data. During editing, these vectors go into diffusion layers while a structure adaptor keeps structure. Tests on ZoME-Bench show AnchorSteer beats both baselines and gives large meaning changes while keeping structure strong.
arxiv-2605-31253: Amanatidis, Birmpas and Reiffenhäuser study Envy Cycle Elimination when agents play to win. The plain rule gives each agent a share that is envy-free up to one item, for any head count. Little was known about its equilibria, though. When agents chase their own gain, the rule's clear logic falls apart, even with few agents and plain valuations. Small rule details suddenly loom large. Even so, pure Nash equilibria exist for several plain versions, and fairness holds in rough form for best responders with at most three agents.
arxiv-2605-31353: Geng and Zhang study sensing with random signals and time sharing. In known-waveform ISAC settings, the sensor knows the sent waveform. That fails for passive or spread settings, where the sensor knows the rule, not the symbols. They study a symbol-unaware model, measuring sensing by raw mutual information. For no-memory channels, they map the rate region with a sharing variable. The best upper edge is the concave cover of the single edge. Open time sharing is unnecessary for concave edges, but helpful when its cover tops it.
arxiv-2605-31553: Bezuglov and team present a general system for exact numerical work on multivariate hypergeometric functions. These functions solve holonomic partial differential equations. Their approach adapts methods first built for multi-loop Feynman integrals to hypergeometric functions of many variables. They construct Pfaffian systems for these functions by applying Laporta reduction to suitable relations. Then a Frobenius-based scheme computes local power-series answers with set precision and moves them along set paths, tracking how answers change when paths loop around singular points.

arxiv-2606-04053:
Eduardo Terrés-Caballero and Herke van Hoof revisit the Boolean Task Algebra in 2026. This is a scheme that lets learning agents mix goal-reaching tasks with logic steps such as and, or, and not.

The pair show that the algebra's promises hold only under narrow conditions. Under those, mixing the logic steps gives the same end values as policies trained over time. In grid worlds, though, value slicing let the end policy drift to the extremes. Picking which base policies to mix was random, and that broke the shortcut. They argue the algebra works as logic for values, not as a tool that rebuilds policies. So the costly extreme mixing step can be skipped.
arxiv-2606-04253:
Maurício Corrêa builds a theory in 2026 of transversal unfoldings of derived foliations. A foliation splits a space into leaves, like pages in a book. An unfolding lifts the sideways directions into true symmetries across the leaves.

He constructs a single object that governs all such unfoldings. The set of strict unfoldings turns out to be the plain shadow of a richer derived space. In concrete terms, the governing object is described by Lie-type derivations, up to inner ones. When the inner action has a kernel, a crossed version keeps the hidden structure. The theory is then rebuilt from a de Rham algebra, with no need to pick a presentation first. It covers the classical and Poisson cases alike.
arxiv-2606-04753:
Polenakis and coauthors extend the El Farol Bar game, a classic coordination puzzle, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In the puzzle, people choose whether to visit a bar that is pleasant only when it stays uncrowded. No one knows the plans of others in advance, so each person guesses from past attendance. The work joins game theory, the study of strategic choices, with methods for designing rules and prices.

Their version lets each person see only part of the past attendance, not the full record. They also make the bar an active player that learns to set prices as the game repeats. The bar balances income, use of its space, and staying open over the long term. Both sides learn at once, so attendance and prices shape each other as the system evolves. They link the idea to congestion in traffic and other shared systems.
arxiv-2606-04953:
Seeyangnok and Pinsook trace superconductivity and its rival, charge-density-wave order, to the same soft vibrations in a tungsten nitride monolayer family, in a 2026 arXiv condensed matter paper. Both phenomena often spring from electron-phonon coupling, so the authors compute the structural, electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties of monolayer W2N and its halogen-functionalized variants with fluorine and chlorine. Pristine W2N shows pronounced phonon instabilities near key momentum points, driven by exceptionally strong coupling in softened low-frequency phonons, marking a charge-density-wave tendency.

Including van der Waals interactions stabilizes the lattice and yields strong-coupling superconductivity with a transition temperature of 13.2 kelvin. Across the family, softened acoustic phonons near one momentum point govern the low-energy physics, unifying charge-density waves and superconductivity as competing manifestations of one soft-phonon coupling mechanism, tunable by chemistry and strain.
arxiv-2606-05053:
Tian Tian and co-authors build a deep learning system for predicting underwater acoustic channels in this 2026 arXiv paper. Underwater acoustic links carry data for things like subsea sensors. Their channels change fast while feedback takes seconds over kilometer distances, so adapting to reported conditions is often too slow. Their framework, built for OFDM systems that split a signal across many frequencies, forecasts channel state several steps ahead instead.

At its core sits PatchCSI-T, a Transformer model that treats channel features independently and shares parameters to stay light. Paired with a greedy scheme that adapts modulation and power allocation, the forecasts drive link settings before conditions change. On real-world underwater acoustic channel datasets, the approach improved end-to-end bit error rate and spectral efficiency. It also kept prediction latency low, showing that learned forecasting can replace stale feedback in adaptive underwater systems.
arxiv-2606-05253:
Peilong Zhou and colleagues propose test-time training for RTL optimization in this 2026 arXiv paper, with a framework called TTT-RTL under the Alpha-RTL heading. Language models can generate RTL designs that work, but current systems train a generator before deployment or search at test time with a frozen policy. Here the policy keeps learning at test time, adapting to feedback from the automation pipeline for each design.

The loop samples implementations, verifies them by syntax checking and simulation, and scores designs by power-performance-area product. High-reward variants are reused through a design-state pool indexed by a PUCT rule, while a controller steadies updates when rewards are sparse. On the RTLLM v2.0 benchmark the method cut the mean power-performance-area product by 65.1 percent, against 26.1 percent for the best frozen-policy agent. On an industrial floating-point unit it cut the area-delay product by 59.4 percent.
arxiv-2606-05553:
Woojung Song and colleagues test whether role-playing agents grow with their characters in a 2026 arXiv paper. A good role player should not freeze a hero at chapter one. Values and habits shift as a novel's arc unfolds. Older tests check facts chapter by chapter, not this inner trajectory. The team built ArcANE, a benchmark drawn from seventeen novels and eighty lead characters.

Each character's arc is split into phases along a chosen trait. The same scenario is posed in every phase, inside and beyond the book's own events. Six models under six context styles were tested. Giving the model the character arc beat every other context strategy on every model. The edge grew largest on scenes the books never show, where lookup has nothing to find. Fine-tuned versions widened that lead further. Staying in character, the study shows, means tracking the arc, not the facts.
arxiv-2606-05653:
Junhyeok Jeong and a large team settle a long debate about a high-temperature superconductor in a 2026 arXiv paper. In underdoped cuprates, electron maps show broken arcs whose meaning was unclear. They might be scraps of a large surface or whole small pockets. That choice decides whether pairing looks weak and standard or strong and exotic. The team studied a clean four-layer cuprate with two sharp probes.

Photoemission maps and quantum oscillation counts together showed a small Fermi pocket. The same layers held a large superconducting gap at the same time. That pairing of traits is the hallmark of the BCS-BEC crossover, the border between two pairing regimes. Key ratios reached the top values theory allows for flat superconductors. Oddly, the crossover switched on as carrier density rose, inside a doping shift under one percent. The result grounds the pairing story of these materials in direct measurement.
arxiv-2606-05753:
XiuYu Zhang, Fang, and Liang show a trusted score for latent visual reasoning points the wrong way in a 2026 arXiv paper. Some vision-language models think through hidden tokens placed between seeing and answering. Training aligns those tokens with visual targets, using cosine similarity as both loss and quality gauge. The team tested five variants of the design. Better alignment came with worse answers, in a strong negative trend across all five.

Two diagnostics, packaged as PRISM, explain the inversion. A probe asks where the answer becomes readable; a corruption test asks whether the latent carries any load. The supervised latents turned out to be largely bypassed. Scrambling them moved accuracy by at most four points. Answers became readable only downstream of the latent, never at it. The training loss, the authors argue, reshapes the language model through shared weights. The latent it claims to train is mostly a bystander.
arxiv-2606-05953:
Vidal-Rosset uses a proof assistant to settle a philosophical logic dispute in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neil Tennant's Core Logic was advertised as paraconsistent: contradictions would not explode into proving everything. Tennant also claimed his system overlaps minimal logic. Both claims, this paper argues, are false. The argument is not left as prose for referees to eyeball.

Every step is certified in Coq, so a machine checks the proof. The dispute turns on weakening rules, which let irrelevant premises pad a derivation. Core Logic bans weakening, which Tennant took to block the Lewis paradox derivations. Vidal-Rosset shows the claimed antisequents do not hold as advertised. Minimal logic's overlap claim fails alongside the paraconsistency claim. Certified proofs bring unusual certainty to a field used to contested hand arguments. The paper is a case study in formal verification meeting philosophy of logic.
arxiv-2606-06053:
Haoyang Hong, Wang, Gu, and Huazheng Wang prove learning guarantees for agents trained with the wrong model class in a 2026 arXiv paper. KL-regularized bandits and reinforcement learning power modern RLHF pipelines. Their theory assumed realizability: the true environment lives inside the learner's model class. Practice violates that daily, and classical regret bounds can collapse. The authors introduce misspecification-aware formulations for bandits and episodic tasks.

Algorithms with Gibbs policy updates are analyzed under the new lens. The resulting high-probability regret bounds carry explicit misspecification terms. Approximation bias, unavoidable with a too-simple class, appears in the guarantee instead of voiding it. Setting misspecification to zero recovers the standard realizable results as a special case. Post-training of language models is the motivating setting. Stability from the KL penalty and honesty about model error can coexist. Theorists gain bounds that survive contact with real model classes.
arxiv-2606-06453:
Zhuoming Chen and co-authors build a workshop for inventing faster attention in this 2026 arXiv paper on AI systems. Sparse attention lets language models skim long contexts by attending to only some tokens, saving enormous compute. But each new sparse algorithm takes heavy engineering to deploy in a real serving stack, so ideas are tested slowly. Vortex aims to make prototyping nearly as fast as thinking.

The system pairs a Python embedded language for writing attention patterns with a page centric tensor backend wired into modern serving frameworks. Researchers write an algorithm once and immediately measure real throughput. The authors then let AI agents loose in the workshop to generate and refine algorithms on their own. The best agent designed variant reached up to three point four six times the throughput of full attention while preserving accuracy. Vortex also carried sparse attention into newer model architectures and very large contexts.
arxiv-2606-06653:
Hot water sometimes freezes faster than cold water, a puzzle known as the Mpemba effect. Aditya, Murciano, and Turkeshi study its quantum cousin in this 2026 arXiv paper, where a system that starts out breaking a symmetry more strongly can restore that symmetry sooner. They ask whether the effect survives when conservation rules split the system's state space into many sealed off sectors.

Working with circuits and models that conserve both charge and dipole moment, the team found a layered version of the effect. The charge imbalance and the dipole imbalance each showed the telltale crossing behavior, but on clearly different timescales. Sorting states into frozen and active sectors explained the pattern: frozen sectors keep a leftover imbalance forever, while active sectors do the relaxing. Fragmentation, then, does not kill the effect; it reshapes it into stored memory plus active repair.
arxiv-2606-06953:
Humanoid robots learn to move by copying motion capture libraries, and bigger is not better. Guan and co-authors make that case in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework, LIMMT, treats data quality as the main lever. It is the first data centric study of physics based humanoid motion tracking.

Quality has three dimensions in their scheme. Motions must be physically feasible, behaviorally diverse, and dynamically complex. A cleaning pipeline filters, embeds, and samples clips by those measures. The shock result: under three percent of the big AMASS library beat the full set. Curated subsets trained better tracking policies than the whole corpus. Cleaning web sourced motion data helped as well. The gains transferred across trackers and data sets. The moral for robot learning is blunt. Volume alone does not teach; well chosen motion does.
arxiv-2606-07153:
A physics trained network can produce a fine looking reconstruction that is quietly wrong. Katende builds a safety gate for such results in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is inverse problems ruled by partial differential equations, recovering hidden sources from indirect data. His framework certifies a learned answer before trusting it.

Every candidate gets an error radius set by its residuals. Data mismatch, physics violation, edge errors, and leftover slack all feed the radius. The learned result replaces a trusted baseline only if its radius is no worse, within a small margin. Otherwise the system returns the baseline, guaranteeing no harm. Tests covered source recovery, heat imaging, limited angle tomography, and coefficient finding. The gate accepted genuine improvements and rejected shifted or hallucinated candidates. In strongly ill posed regimes it turned conservative, as it should. Certification, not a new architecture, is the contribution.
arxiv-2606-07453:
Faizi and Rafiey approximate a graph deletion problem on graphs avoiding induced paths, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The odd cycle transversal asks for the fewest vertices whose removal makes a graph bipartite, meaning two-colorable, no edge inside a color. It is NP-complete on path-free graphs of modest path length, and general graphs resist such approximation under a conjecture. The authors show the problem becomes polynomial-time solvable on subclasses, notably graphs avoiding a 6-vertex path and a triangle, by splitting them into rings of bipartite pieces.

They give the first constant-factor approximation for the path-free case. The guarantee depends on the forbidden path length: the length minus 2 when it is odd, and minus 3 when even. This fits the expectation that no constant independent of path length should exist if the Unique Games Conjecture holds. The results map where bipartization shifts from tractable to approximable.
arxiv-2606-07553:
Taghavi and a large team build a recommender that tells medical imaging researchers which classifier to use, sparing them wasteful trial and error, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Choosing a model for tasks like skin cancer or tumor classification means training many candidates, burning compute and energy. The team mined 3,000 published articles into a public benchmark dataset of over 5,000 records describing models, tasks, and results across skin, tumor, wound, breast, and MRI classification. Missing values are common because papers under-report details, which the recommender must tolerate.

Their transformer-based recommender, MedicalRec, was evaluated in 4 modes using richer feature sets, from 5 up to 18 features per record. It reached a top-100 hit rate of about 75 percent, meaning the best model appeared in its top 100 suggestions 3 times out of 4. 12 independent base models validated the recommendations. The authors frame model selection as an environmental and efficiency problem worth automating.
arxiv-2606-07753:
Morrissey proposes ReadingMachine, a method for having language models read whole document collections carefully instead of skimming them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Institutions now produce more text than analysts can read, and standard tools retrieve or summarise in part, which risks silent omissions. High-stakes synthesis for research, policy, and law needs coverage that can be inspected afterwards.

ReadingMachine breaks reading into bounded, checkable steps: extracting atomic insights, clustering them, building a theme map, and repeatedly hunting for omissions by tracking orphan insights that fit nowhere. Compression is delayed, step-by-step results are kept, and disagreement between documents is preserved rather than averaged away. In a demonstration on one hundred fifty-two documents about industrial policy, the system produced more than seventeen thousand atomic insights and a structured theme map. Morrissey also reports costs, runtime, and failure modes honestly, noting that formal comparison against rival methods remains future work.
arxiv-2606-07953:
Zekai Zhang and co-authors unify two worlds of industrial inspection in a million-image benchmark, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Factories need detectors for known fault types, a closed-set problem, and for faults described only in words, an open-vocabulary problem. Training data covering both, across many industries, did not exist, and manual prompts inject noise.

Their MMIOC-1M benchmark holds more than one million samples spanning fourteen super-categories, twenty-nine industrial scenes, and three hundred fifty-one defect subcategories, supporting both closed-set and open-vocabulary detection. Alongside it they propose RTVPNet, a network refining text-visual prompts automatically. Its components include an expert-assisted projection that adapts general vision models to industrial domains quickly, and an energy-based sparse sampling strategy for picking informative regions. The pair is pre-training infrastructure: a shared foundation on which industrial detectors, open or closed, can be built and compared.
arxiv-2606-08153:
David Eje and co-authors build a log anomaly detector on a language model with a new reward, in this 2026 arXiv paper. System logs are where failures and intrusions show, but their volume defeats review. The previous best approach coupled GPT-2 with reinforcement learning. Its short context window and crude binary reward limit it.

LogNEO upgrades the base to GPT-Neo, a one point three billion parameter open model. It replaces the reward with a partial-credit scheme. Correct early predictions earn more; late errors are penalised harder. The reward decays exponentially by position. On the HDFS, BGL, and Thunderbird benchmarks it reached F1 scores of about zero point nine three, zero point nine one, and zero point nine eight. Recall improved by up to six points over the earlier system. A deployment showed forty-five millisecond latency at fifteen thousand events per second.
arxiv-2606-08253:
Alessandro Montenegro and co-authors present a learning framework that tells a humanoid robot exactly where to step, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Humanoid robots that walk by following velocity commands are robust, but they cannot control foothold placement precisely, so they may step somewhere unsafe or poorly positioned for a following task. Explicit foothold-tracking policies fix this by accepting target foot poses as commands. Earlier versions assumed unrealistic state information or were welded to one task.

The authors introduce a lightweight, general-purpose framework for training three-dimensional foothold-tracking policies. Their design avoids the fragile state assumptions of prior work and stays independent of any single pipeline. The robot learns to place each foot on commanded targets while balancing in complex surroundings.
arxiv-2606-08453:
