Chun-Wei Liu and colleagues propose a new way to encode qubits in arrays of neutral atoms, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutral-atom arrays combine scalable registers, long coherence times, and strong entangling interactions, making them a promising quantum computing platform. Fault-tolerant error correction, however, demands repeated mid-circuit measurement and reset of helper qubits without disturbing nearby data qubits. Qubit encoding, the choice of which atomic states hold the information, becomes a key architectural decision.

Their dual metastable-state encoding for ytterbium-171 atoms uses two independent qubit subspaces inside different metastable manifolds. One manifold provides a long-coherence nuclear-spin qubit suited to storing data, while the second offers a subspace better suited to the measurement and reset tasks of ancilla qubits. Keeping the two roles in separate subspaces aims to let error correction run its frequent checks without the usual disturbance cost on the data.
arxiv-2606-08753:
Nurowski studies quantum particles hopping across networks built from classic geometric patterns, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The networks are Levi graphs, webs that turn points and lines into nodes and links. His tool is a tight-binding Hamiltonian, an energy rule for a particle sitting on a node or hopping to a neighbor. He computes the allowed energies for the Desargues, Kantor, Schläfli double six, and Cremona-Richmond configurations.

Set flat in ordinary space, the first two patterns lose their symmetry and trap waves in place. A complex version of the plane instead restores free travel. The Schläfli graph gives twenty states at zero energy, a flat band caused purely by geometry. He maps it onto the SU(6) flavor symmetry, where the flat band mirrors ultra-heavy baryons frozen in place. The Cremona-Richmond pattern completes an algebraic symmetry tied to twenty-seven lines.
arxiv-2606-08853:
Arbour and colleagues argue that experimenters can sharpen randomized trials with AI predictions, without inventing any new statistics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language models can forecast human responses from rich inputs like text, acting as digital twins of participants. Rather than trusting those forecasts as data, the authors use them to reduce noise. The recipe is regression adjustment: include the AI prediction as a covariate, as one adjusts for a prognostic score.

The approach carries a do-no-harm guarantee. When predictions are uninformative, the adjusted estimate falls back to the difference in means. Rival methods built on prediction-powered inference lack that property. The paper gives practical guidance on extracting continuous scores from discrete outputs and featurizing unstructured inputs. Simulations and three real applications, a survey mega-study, an email marketing test, and a platform experiment, showed modest gains, largest where studies contain much text.
arxiv-2606-09053:
Belcheva and Zlateva rescue existence for a class of optimization problems by changing the ruler, not the problem, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Variational problems ask for the curve of least action, a quadratic kinetic term plus a potential, in a Banach space. When the potential is lower semicontinuous rather than convex, a minimizer may fail to exist: sequences approach the infimum without attaining it. Their perturbation method replaces the norm with an equivalent one arbitrarily close to the original.

In the perturbed norm, a minimizer exists. The problem's form is preserved; only the norm changes. Since equivalent norms describe the same space, the solution answers the original question. The result extends a theorem of Ivanov and Zlateva from convex potentials to the lower semicontinuous case. Such problems model least-action paths in mechanics and control, where potentials with jumps are natural. A guaranteed minimizer is the prerequisite for computing it.
arxiv-2606-09253:
Stefan Heldmann and colleagues give radiotherapy teams a practical way to carry image-registration uncertainty through to the dose numbers clinicians read, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deformable image registration warps one scan onto another so doses from separate treatment sessions can be added up. The warping is never exact, and its errors flow straight into dose estimates. Their framework models where each voxel, a tiny volume element of the scan, might map to as a random variable.

A transparent local certainty map drives the model, set by safety margins, structure-boundary mismatch, or conservative per-structure values. Out come dose probabilities, expected dose, confidence bounds, and dose-volume histogram envelopes, curves summarizing dose across an organ. In a prostate case study, certainty-map design moved the bounds more than the kernel choice. An optional in-out strategy, restricting mappings to anatomically plausible regions, helped only modestly.
arxiv-2606-09453:
Dasari Naga Raju asks whether microscope images of prostate tumours carry warning signs that standard grading misses in this 2026 arXiv paper. After surgery, a rising PSA level signals this recurrence, and risk scores lean heavily on Gleason grade. Raju builds a strict benchmark from four hundred eighty-seven patients, with out-of-fold scoring throughout.

Earlier comparisons showed the aggregator choice mattered little, the feature extractor mattered most, and no imaging-only model beat a clinical model on grade, stage, and age. His proposed GD-MIL changes that: a gated-attention encoder is trained with a gradient-reversal adversary that stops the slide representation from encoding grade itself. Fused with clinical variables, GD-MIL reached a concordance index of about seventy percent, significantly above both rivals. Its risk split separated patients sharply: roughly twenty versus seventy percent recurrence-free at five years.
arxiv-2606-09553:
David Guzmán and his colleagues release OpenBibleTTS, a large speech resource for languages that speech technology usually ignores, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Text-to-speech systems work well in a few major languages, while most of the world's roughly seven thousand languages lack the paired text and audio data needed to train them.

OpenBibleTTS instead builds a benchmark from Biblical recordings, a domain where genuine low-resource data exists, spanning thirty-seven underrepresented languages. The team compared several synthesis architectures and large speech generation models on both Biblical and out-of-domain text, mixing automatic metrics with human listening judgements. No single system won everywhere. A commercial Gemini system earned the highest listener ratings in most languages, but monolingual models trained on OpenBibleTTS itself were strongest for intelligibility and preferred in several African languages. Open from-scratch systems degraded sharply outside the training domain.
arxiv-2606-09653:
Grégoire Dhimoïla and his co-authors sort out what it means for two AI systems to share the same concepts in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models trained apart often build look-alike internal maps. Sparse autoencoders can unpack those maps into named features, or concepts.

Their frame splits alignment two ways: what is matched, raw maps or concepts, and at what grain, single cases or whole spreads. That yields four traits to check. A new test, InterVenchA, grades extraction, translation, and concept match apart. Trials showed that gains on one trait do not buy the others. Pure unsupervised routes failed to recover case-level match at all. Their joint model, CoSAE, enforces the traits together, and strong alignment showed only there. A tiny sliver of paired data, a tenth of a percent, was enough to anchor the rest.
arxiv-2606-09853:
Konstantinos Kontras and his co-authors aim training straight at synergy, the signal that exists only when senses combine in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal models fuse sight, sound, and text. Much of what they learn is shared or single-sense fare. The joint-only part, the bit no sense holds alone, is the prize, and plain training often skips it.

Their objective, SynIB, adds a twist to the task loss. The model must do well with all senses live. It is then fined for staying sure when one sense is masked off in turn. Surety with a sense gone betrays a single-sense crutch, not joint work. On fake XOR tasks with known synergy, plain training missed the joint rule while SynIB found it. On five real test sets, gains on synergy-hungry items ran up to seven point eight percent.
arxiv-2606-09953:
Cortés-Ferre and colleagues use deep learning to fill in missing slices in head CT scans, in a 2026 arXiv paper on medical imaging. Computed tomography gives fine detail within each slice, but slices sit two to five millimeters apart along the head. That uneven spacing, called anisotropy, degrades three-dimensional reconstructions and volume measures such as hematoma size. Interpolating new slices could restore balance.

Their system synthesizes the slice between two neighboring axial slices, halving the effective spacing, and its outputs also come out visibly denoised in the same pass. The team systematically compared pixel losses, structural similarity losses, and hybrid mixes on a held-out test set. Every trained model beat classical interpolation and pretrained video frame methods on structural measures, with the MS-SSIM plus L1 mix offering the best balance.
arxiv-2606-10053:
Reinman and colleagues analyze what happens when search engines diversify results while publishers compete for ranking, in a 2026 arXiv paper on information retrieval and game theory. In competitive search, publishers strategically edit their documents in response to rankings to climb higher. Diversification, showing varied results instead of near-duplicates, changes those incentives. The authors model the interaction as a game and ask whether the document corpus settles into stability, an equilibrium where nobody gains by editing.

Their analysis reveals an inherent tradeoff between corpus diversity and corpus stability. For two representative diversification methods, they show stability need not be reached, leaving the corpus churning as publishers keep modifying documents in response to rankings. They then present a new approach for designing diversification-based ranking functions that are guaranteed to lead to corpus stability. The result matters for search designers who want diverse results without endless strategic rewriting by publishers.
arxiv-2606-10153:
Morshed and Boddeti address learning how the world's factors combine when data is scattered across isolated owners, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Understanding how factors combine requires seeing interacting factors together, but real data is scattered into silos that each hold only fragments. Their framework, Decentralized Compositional Flow Matching, enforces built-in constraints across the global set of factors without exchanging any raw data.

Novel combinations emerge through peer contact, even when no single source can support the composition alone. In tests, it handily outperforms federated learning and mixture-of-experts baselines on three testbeds: conditional image generation, robotic spatial planning, and medical attribute co-occurrence modeling. The result matters wherever privacy or ownership keeps data apart, from hospitals to robot fleets. Instead of pooling private records, partners can teach a shared model how factors compose, unlocking mixes none of them could show alone.
arxiv-2606-10453:
Bunke and Volpe prove a uniqueness result in this 2026 arXiv paper in higher category theory, a branch of pure mathematics about structures and the maps between them. Their subject is six functor formalisms, frameworks packaging the six standard operations of a cohomology theory, a tool for extracting invariants from spaces. On locally compact Hausdorff spaces, the familiar example is sheaves, assignments of data to open sets that glue consistently.

The answer is no. The authors characterise the sheaf formalism as the unique six functor formalism on these spaces meeting a short list of expected conditions, including canonical descent, being determined by sections, and finitary behaviour. As a direct consequence, every continuous six functor formalism in Zhu's sense is equivalent to sheaves valued in its own coefficients at a point. The result pins sheaves down by their properties, not by construction.
arxiv-2606-10553:
Rossanigo proves kernel theorems in this 2026 arXiv paper in algebraic geometry. The setting is rigidly-compactly generated infinity-categories, stable categories built from compact, dualisable objects, as arise from spectra and sheaves on schemes. Functors between them are often controlled by kernel objects, as integral transforms are by their kernels. The paper proves two finitary kernel theorems for finite objects picked out by a t-structure, coherent and perfect complexes among them.

The first theorem represents contravariant functionals on perfect objects, valued in pseudo-coherent objects, by objects of the same kind. The second represents covariant functionals on coherent objects by perfect objects. The proofs rest on three finiteness notions, compactness, dualisability, and coherence, and their interplay. Applications cover ring spectra modules and quasi-proper maps of schemes, and the paper recasts Grothendieck duality, a cornerstone of the field, in terms of internal left adjoints.
arxiv-2606-10653:
Hailan Zhang and colleagues improve how text-to-image generators follow intricate prompts in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pretrained diffusion models paint fine pictures, yet on complex prompts they often drop requested objects, or attach an attribute, like a colour, to the wrong thing: the semantic alignment problem. Existing fixes lean on costly fine-tuning or layout guidance. STEDiff is training-free and works inside the text-embedding space, the model's internal picture of the prompt.

It uses the end-of-text token to reinforce each sub-sentence's semantics, then swaps the strengthened pieces back into the prompt embedding. A new semantic enhancement loss adds spatial discipline, pushing each entity's meaning toward its proper image region. On T2I-CompBench, evaluations show better semantic consistency and completeness in complex scenes. The hosted text here is truncated, so this description follows the official arXiv abstract.
arxiv-2606-11053:
Allmis, Pin, and Vega Redondo model a puzzle in financial markets in a 2026 arXiv paper. One trader privately knows an asset's future return. Conventional wisdom says she would never share. Communication runs along a social network, and the authors ask when sharing is the smart move in equilibrium, the game's stable outcome.

In the unique equilibrium, the informed trader reveals her information with positive probability. She shares selectively, disclosing only signals inside a critical interval around the average signal. Revealing slightly bad news dampens neighbors' demand and helps her. Good news stays concealed, since it would lift demand and price against her. Very bad news is hidden too, because the price drop would hurt too much. A side effect follows: prices need not fully reveal the asset's return, even with risk-neutral traders. The paper also studies which networks form when traders choose links beforehand.
arxiv-2606-11253:
Hasan surveys two giant telescopes now being built, in a 2026 arXiv review of extremely large telescopes. Ground-based observatories with mirrors over twenty meters across mark a new era in astronomy. This second article in her series focuses on the Giant Magellan Telescope and the Thirty Meter Telescope, and their enabling technology.

Segmented or multi-mirror primary apertures, active optics, adaptive optics, laser guide-star systems, and high-throughput instruments. Together they deliver a major jump in light-collecting area and angular resolution. In diffraction-limited adaptive-optics modes, they will reach image sharpness beyond current space telescopes at comparable wavelengths. Space observatories stay essential for light Earth's atmosphere blocks and for stable, low-background work. Hasan also argues ground and space astronomy are complementary. Satellite interference cannot be solved by moving astronomy into space, and ground sites, upgradeable for decades, will keep a leading role.
arxiv-2606-11353:
Van der Hofstad, Müller, and Riddlesden analyze threshold group testing in a 2026 arXiv paper. In group testing, pooled tests identify a sparse set of defectives; a test is positive when its defective count meets a threshold. Classical group testing is the threshold-one case. They ask how raising the threshold changes the tests needed, in the noiseless, non-adaptive setting.

Their main contribution is a sharp information-theoretic phase transition: a precise constant times k log(n over k) tests are necessary and sufficient under the constant-column design. The constant depends on defective prevalence and the threshold. At low prevalence, threshold testing matches the classical behavior. At higher prevalences the threshold significantly reduces the tests required. Yet when the defective proportion is positive, threshold testing becomes strictly harder, apart from trivial reductions. The upper bound rests on an analytic assumption the authors verify for threshold two.
arxiv-2606-11453: Appearing on arXiv in 2026, this research paper lays out a new study. The title sums up the subject: On phase-space singular surfaces in. The paper lives in science and technology, careful study of how the natural and built world works. New findings are reported here for the research community.
arxiv-2606-11553:
Pradhan, Bahadori, and Amini, of Cisco Systems, build a time-series model native to wireless networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Generic time-series models transfer poorly to wireless telemetry, whose signals are bursty, zero-inflated, and coupled across protocol layers. APEX is a decoder-only transformer pre-trained on telemetry from about 4,500 production networks and one hundred thousand access-point series.

It comes in large cloud and small edge versions; the edge one runs sub-second, privacy-preserving inference on the access point itself. The team evaluates on DHCP degradation, a network task where address assignment falters. On a 192-step, four-day benchmark, APEX-Large cuts mean absolute error by eighteen percent against the strongest baseline and thirty-eight percent against SARIMA, a classical method. Its anomaly-detection F1 reaches 0.93 in the reported evaluation. The authors argue network-native pre-training suits proactive operations, catching failures before users feel them.
arxiv-2606-11753:
Shoumik Debnath and Sudipta Saha design a light absorber that favours one polarisation in this 2026 arXiv paper on photonics. Polarisation describes the direction in which light waves vibrate. Their stack layers a striped grating of rhenium disulfide over a molybdenum oxide spacer on a gold mirror. Both crystal layers are anisotropic, meaning their optical behaviour depends on direction.

Simulations with a tuned geometry show near-perfect absorption at a red wavelength under one polarisation. Over ninety-nine point nine percent of the light is captured. The stripes are two hundred fifty nanometres wide on a five hundred nanometre period. The other polarisation resonates about sixteen nanometres away, giving clean separation. The field hugs the stripe edges. Replacing either crystal layer with a plain equivalent weakens the effect. Rotating the crystal retunes the resonance across about one hundred twenty nanometres without rebuilding the device.
arxiv-2606-11853:
Zhirui Chen, Ziwei Chen and Ling Shao compress the memory of multimodal models in this 2026 arXiv paper. In-context learning lets a model adapt from examples shown in its prompt, but long image-text sequences overflow the context window. Existing compression deletes tokens by rigid rules or by sample-specific importance scores, which biases memory and mangles visual structure.

Their framework, TASM, needs no training. A task vector, a direction summarising what the task cares about, guides which content matters across all demonstrations. Tokens are merged, not pruned, through graph matching that respects semantic structure. Memory is organised into a compact core plus a latent bank that queries can search. Evaluations show memory usage cut by up to eighty-five percent while matching or beating full-context performance across diverse benchmarks. The authors conclude that structuring memory by task relevance and semantic shape beats aggressive deletion.
arxiv-2606-12153:
Pu and co-authors teach one system to animate almost any digital creature from a single video, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Motion capture usually needs species-specific templates, fixed body models such as the human SMPL, or slow hand rigging. Their framework, TopoCap, instead learns motion itself as something separate from body shape. A graph-based encoder compresses any skeleton, from two-legged figures to six-legged ones, into a shared fixed-length motion code.

A second stage predicts those codes from video using flow matching, a generative method that turns noise into data. Training uses Mobjaverse, a dataset the team built with over five thousand distinct skeletal structures and two million frames, about one hundred times the structural variety of earlier sets. TopoCap beats specialist models on human and four-legged benchmarks. It retargets motion onto creatures never seen in training, with no test-time fitting.
arxiv-2606-12253:
Gambacurta and Grasso review a repaired theory of how atomic nuclei ring like bells, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Giant resonances are collective vibrations where many nucleons move together. The random phase approximation models them from a mean-field picture. Its second-order extension, SRPA, adds richer correlations but develops pathologies inside energy density functional theory: instabilities and double counting of effects already in the functional. The subtracted variant, SSRPA, removes the double-counted pieces and restores sanity.

The review walks through the formal properties, then the anomalous SRPA behavior across several nuclear interactions. Pathology-free SSRPA studies cover charge-conserving and charge-exchange excitations, where a proton swaps into a neutron or back. Comparisons with experimental data quantify the improvement over both earlier methods. The authors also estimate how beyond-mean-field correlations in SSRPA affect modeling of the nuclear equation of state, the pressure-density law governing neutron stars.
arxiv-2606-12353:
Bouladiane and co-authors steer electron spin and valley currents by slowing carriers inside a barrier, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Monolayer tungsten diselenide hosts electrons with two labels: spin and valley, the momentum pocket they occupy. Both could carry information in devices. The authors model a barrier where the Fermi velocity, the carriers' speed, and the electric potential are tuned together. Speed changes refract carrier paths, like light bending between materials.

Solving the Dirac equation with current-conserving matching at the interfaces gives transmission and conductance for each spin-valley channel. The results show strong direction effects, with transport depending on incidence angle, plus resonant tunneling features. Barrier speed, potential, angle, energy, and width all act as control knobs. Polarized currents tune smoothly in size and pointing under speed and potential changes. Speed engineering thus joins gating as a design tool for two-dimensional electronics.
arxiv-2606-12653:
Fabricant reflects on a long career building instruments for ground-based telescopes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Writing from experience on major and minor projects with many colleagues, he gathers lessons he says newcomers often learn only by making mistakes. The paper is practical, on work habits, project leadership, and engineering judgement rather than any single instrument design.

Early sections stress understanding the scientific mission first, staying humble and curious, and connecting new knowledge to a bigger picture. Fabricant urges beginners to read widely, contact experts, and use experienced colleagues before trying to reinvent proven approaches. Later sections turn to systems engineering, the discipline of tracking requirements and interfaces across a complex build. Throughout, he argues that designs must leave room to adapt, because instruments are built in varied settings, and that good advice, honestly recorded, can spare the next generation several costly errors.
arxiv-2606-12953:
Gulluk and colleagues present OpenMedQ, a medical vision-language model pretrained on the broadest open medical data mix to date, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most published medical vision-language models rely on a few narrow pretraining sources and withhold their weights, their data, or both, leaving practitioners without an inspectable baseline. OpenMedQ combines a ViT-base vision encoder with a LLaMA-7B language model, trained with next-token prediction on 14 datasets totalling 3.35 million samples spanning pathology, radiology, microscopy, and text-only clinical question answering.

OpenMedQ reaches state-of-the-art BLEU-1 on PathVQA at 75.9, beating Med-PaLM M variants of up to 562 billion parameters, roughly 80 times larger, and matches the best VQA-MED BLEU-1 of 64.5. Its vision encoder, transferred to 8 medical classification benchmarks under a downstream recipe, obtains the highest average macro-F1 of 0.757, ahead of BiomedCLIP and PMC-CLIP at 0.745, PubMedCLIP at 0.746, and a from-scratch baseline at 0.616.
arxiv-2606-13353:
Lallemand and a large collaboration hunt for double asteroids using stellar occultations in this 2026 arXiv paper. An occultation occurs when an asteroid passes in front of a star, briefly dimming its light. The timing and shape of that dip reveal the asteroid's size and silhouette with precision. If the asteroid has a companion, extra dips can betray the second body. Networks of observers, many of them amateurs, record these events from scattered locations, and each chord of timings constrains the objects' shapes.

The team reports the detection and characterisation of binary asteroid candidates through such events. Confirming a companion requires careful modelling of the chords and ruling out single irregular bodies. Binary asteroids matter because their mutual orbits reveal masses and densities that spacecraft visits rarely measure. Occultation campaigns are also cheap compared with radar or imaging from Earth. The paper demonstrates the yield of occultation networks.
arxiv-2606-13453:
Capel and colleagues analyse when Langevin dynamics mixes on curved spaces in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sampling from a Gibbs measure, the canonical law of statistical physics, underlies Bayesian computation and lab simulation. Langevin dynamics, noisy gradient descent on an energy landscape, is the standard sampler. On a Riemannian manifold its speed is governed by a logarithmic Sobolev inequality. The authors identify what makes it hold: the space's curvature, the inverse temperature, the escaping directions from saddle points, and the absence of barren plateaus and fake local minima.

When the conditions hold, mixing times polynomial in the dimension are achievable, a strong guarantee. The proof relates Langevin paths on a space and on its image under a submersion, a structure-preserving projection, a relation of independent interest. Rapid mixing guarantees tell users when a sampler can be trusted to explore a law rather than loiter near its start.
arxiv-2606-14253:
Cao and Zhou use an algebraic assembly trick, the matrix-product construction, to build quantum codes that break records. Quantum states are fragile and cannot be copied, so storage needs strong codes; locally recoverable codes add repairing a lost piece from a few others. The construction combines several classical codes of one length through a defining matrix. Their 2026 arXiv paper works with special defining matrices, called tau-optimal, whose properties transfer to the new codes.

First, they prove a unified decomposition theorem for invertible self-adjoint matrices over finite fields of any characteristic, and build new tau-optimal families in characteristic two. The resulting codes include 222 beating the best-known records in Grassl's database. Second, two schemes produce optimal pure quantum locally recoverable codes, in four new infinite families. Most strikingly, 30 codes are simultaneously optimal locally recoverable codes and record-level codes in the database, a combination never reported before.
arxiv-2606-14453:
McWhorter and co-authors propose a privacy-based redistricting method in a 2026 arXiv paper on election maps. Independent redistricting commissions invite public testimony about communities of interest, neighborhoods people want kept in one district. That openness invites manipulation, since organized groups can flood the process with misleading testimony.

The authors treat each testimony as a data point and sample district plans using differential privacy, a guarantee that no single input can sway the output much. Their marked edge walk sampler targets two score functions across a range of privacy budgets. Tested on Missouri's mid-cycle redistricting with eight hundred eight community testimonies, the method beat both an uninformed baseline and the enacted plan. Attack experiments showed robustness at certain budgets, sometimes better than formal guarantees suggest.
arxiv-2606-14553:
Braun and co-authors boost entangled photon output in ultrathin semiconductors in a 2026 arXiv paper. Entangled photon pairs usually come from bulky crystals. Those crystals need careful phase matching. Atom-thin van der Waals semiconductors work differently. Sheets like transition metal dichalcogenides are nonlinear enough to make pairs natively. The crystal symmetry shapes the entanglement. But output is capped by the material's short coherence length.

The team studies periodically poled versions of these sheets. In them, the sign of the nonlinearity flips at set intervals. Each interval is one coherence length. This trick is called quasi-phase matching. It scales up the pair rate while keeping entanglement nearly perfect. Fidelity stays above ninety-nine percent in their analysis. A detailed theory model explains how symmetry and propagation effects interact. The work opens a route to engineered quantum light in nanophotonic systems.
arxiv-2606-14853:
Barker, Gladwyn, and Zell warn about a shortcut in early-universe simulations in a 2026 arXiv paper. Lattice simulations track violent processes after cosmic inflation. Inflation is the brief burst of rapid expansion just after the Big Bang. Many codes treat the expanding background as a perfectly smooth FLRW spacetime. They drop the small ripples in the metric itself.

The authors show this shortcut breaks a key effect. During inflation, ripples that stretch beyond the horizon should freeze in place. With the smooth background, they do not. In slow roll, the curvature power spectrum decays as the fourth power of the expansion rate. In ultra-slow roll the distortion is stronger still. Measured inflation observables can be badly skewed. Reheating studies seem far less sensitive to the omission. The authors give a practical validity check and add it to the CosmoLattice code.
arxiv-2606-15053:
Chung and coauthors build surrogate models whose latent dynamics obey physical laws by construction in a 2026 study. Fast surrogates help predict and control complex systems. A model can fit training trajectories yet break conservation laws when pushed further. The authors extend the Latent Twin framework so structure is enforced inside the latent space.

An encoder, decoder, and latent flow map are learned together between time-indexed states. The latent flow is constrained to preserve or dissipate chosen structural quantities. A constraint-transfer view links physical structure in the state space to latent conditions that can be enforced. The team proves bounds showing latent enforcement controls defects after decoding. Stated conditions cover maps that preserve linear and quadratic invariants or enforce dissipation. Tests on equation benchmarks show better constraint satisfaction and long-time behavior. Prediction accuracy stays competitive with unconstrained models throughout.
arxiv-2606-15253:
Zhang and coauthors diagnose why detection transformers forget old classes in a 2026 computer vision paper. Incremental object detection teaches a detector new classes in stages without retraining. The authors name the failure gradient dilution: preservation signals weaken as training proceeds. They trace it to background noise swamping foreground gradients, unstable query matching, and shrinking support for old classes. Their framework, FAS, answers with three fixes named focus, align, and sustain.

Prior-injected queries focus learning by filtering background interference at the source. Deterministic anchor distillation aligns query-to-target assignments across stages. Manifold-support replay sustains coverage of the old-class feature space during updates. Together they restore optimization dynamics in experiments. FAS beat leading methods across the incremental settings. The hardest setting, adding ten classes four times, improved by over five AP points. The paper frames continual detection as a gradient health problem, not a memory problem.
arxiv-2606-15553:
Zhang and colleagues work on distilling image generators in 2026, compressing slow diffusion and flow models. Representation autoencoders give these models a richer latent space, built from strongly clustered pretrained features, but that space is sharply curved and uneven, which makes trajectory-based methods unstable. The team argues the space suits a different distillation family, the recently proposed Drifting Models.

They first measure curvature and isotropy across autoencoders, and show in theory that drifting should fail on scattered reconstruction-based spaces while fitting clustered ones. Their method, Drift-RAE, then distills pretrained flow models inside the representation space, with changes that align the drifting field with related frameworks and stabilize training. On ImageNet at 256 resolution it reaches an FID score under two after only ten thousand distillation steps. That beats earlier distillation methods in such spaces and matches the original Drifting Model, without needing the extra feature extractor it required.
arxiv-2606-15653:
Quincozes and colleagues present IoT-Zoo in 2026, a container-based testbed for Internet of Things experiments that prizes device diversity over raw scale. Networking and security tools need realistic, reproducible traffic, yet most platforms scale by cloning a few device types. Built on Containernet, IoT-Zoo instead runs dataset-driven profiles of many different devices at once.

The testbed supports forty-three distinct device profiles, the highest diversity among the platforms the authors compare. It automates multi-domain scenario deployment and traffic capture behind a single-command interface, and speaks real protocols such as MQTT and RTSP. Experiments show varied patterns, from periodic telemetry to bursty human-driven behaviour, reproduced at once with a light footprint on commodity hardware. By bridging static datasets and live emulation, it generates consistent traffic baselines for testing intrusion detection and other tools. That makes results easy for other teams to repeat and check.
arxiv-2606-15753:
Huang and colleagues introduce RoboPIN in 2026, a vision-language model for embodied reasoning whose chain of thought is pinned to the evidence. Standard traces mention objects in text or loose coordinates, so references drift and detach from what the camera sees. Multi-view scenes make the drift worse, since the same object changes appearance between viewpoints.

Their Pinned Chain-of-Thought gives every task-relevant entity a reasoning anchor: a tag with name, unique identity, view index, and spatial grounding, carried through every step. An automated pipeline builds the 170-thousand-example training set, and three training stages add rewards policing anchor localisation and identity consistency. On fourteen reasoning and pointing benchmarks, the four-billion-parameter model beats seven-billion open-source embodied rivals. It beats the strongest seven-billion baseline by twelve percent on average. Grounding each reasoning step visibly, rather than hoping text stays honest, is the core lesson.
arxiv-2606-15853:
Akbiyik and colleagues trace how energy cascades through the lattice of semimetal WTe2 after light excitation in 2026, using ultrafast electron diffraction at its surface. How excited carriers hand energy to phonons, the quantised lattice vibrations, sets the pace of relaxation in quantum materials. WTe2 is strongly anisotropic, its structure threaded by tungsten chains.

Bragg peaks fade in a Debye-Waller pattern showing a two-step rise, the signature of stepwise lattice relaxation. Diffuse scattering builds up parallel to the tungsten-chain axis, showing anisotropic coupling as electrons cool. The intensity then spreads across the surface Brillouin zone and pools near its centre. That stage reflects anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering into low-frequency acoustic modes over thirty to one hundred picoseconds. Energy relaxation runs as a hierarchy: selected finite-momentum phonons are fed first, the lattice bath only later, a pathway hidden from probes lacking momentum resolution.
arxiv-2606-16053:
Paekivi and Karjus use language models in 2026 to code what brand TikTok videos are doing, at a scale hand coding cannot reach. Short-form video mixes sound, image, language, and trends, so meaning is hard to standardize. The authors turn interpretive theories into measurable variables instead, drawn from narratology, rhetoric, and semiotics.

Multimodal models annotate 77 theory-driven variables for about 10,000 videos from Estonian brand and organizational accounts. The variables add modest but consistent gains for predicting likes, comments, shares, and saves, beyond follower count and video age. Human checks show a clear reliability gradient. Perceptual variables can be coded fairly reliably by humans and machines alike. Deeper semiotic constructs prove harder for both. The corpus reveals a repertoire built around promotion, entertainment, and explanation.
arxiv-2606-16353:
Ge and co-authors ask in 2026 what a streaming video model should remember, and answer: only compact evidence. Streaming models must answer questions at any moment under fixed memory and compute budgets. Bolting on ever more history can backfire, diluting the model's view of the current scene. Their framework, SelectStream, frames the problem as budgeted online allocation of latent evidence.

The current observation stays directly visible to a frozen vision-language model, while history enters only through a small, query-conditioned evidence budget. Three mechanisms govern the memory: surprise-driven adaptive windowing, priority-preserving consolidation, and query-conditioned graph reasoning over a fixed-capacity memory graph. Retrieved evidence is calibrated and injected as latent tokens. On OVO-Bench with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, SelectStream raises the real-time and backward-tracing average from 65.13 percent to 70.95 percent, per the report. Backward tracing alone jumps from 51.90 to 61.05 percent.
arxiv-2606-16553:
Peschken and co-authors simulate in 2026 how supernova explosions in the Milky Way's center launch the giant outflows seen as the Fermi and eROSITA bubbles. Cold atomic hydrogen clouds are observed kiloparsecs above the disc. Using the Piernik code, the team models the whole chain at three-parsec resolution, from gas accreting along dust lanes to winds launching.

Star formation runs in cycles, bursts followed by quiet periods, driven mainly by intermittent gas inflows along the dust lanes. The feedback generates hot winds near ten million degrees moving at roughly a thousand kilometers per second from the central zone. Colder hydrogen clouds ride along at about a hundred kilometers per second, reaching heights of one to two kiloparsecs above the mid-plane, per the simulation. Matching both the hot bubbles and the cold clouds in one simulation ties the Galaxy's most dramatic structures to ordinary star formation physics.
arxiv-2606-16753:
Ferreira and colleagues measure variety bias in language models in a 2026 benchmark paper on Portuguese. Portuguese is spoken differently in Europe and Brazil, with distinct words, forms of address and grammar habits. Brazilian Portuguese dominates training data, so models may quietly favor it even when a user writes or requests the European variety.

Their benchmark, P3B3, is an expert-curated set of multi-turn conversational prompts designed to be neutral between the two varieties. An evaluation framework then scores both bias, which variety a model drifts toward, and controllability, whether it can be steered to the requested one. Across several models, most show a strong pull toward Brazilian Portuguese. Steering works to a degree, and larger, newer models are more controllable. European Portuguese output stays less consistent, though. The authors argue training and evaluation must represent varieties more evenly, not treat one national standard as the whole language.
arxiv-2606-16953:
Liu and colleagues benchmark sidewalk navigation in a 2026 robotics paper. Delivery robots and assistive devices increasingly share city sidewalks, where they face cluttered layouts, unpredictable walkers and long routes. Visual guidance models promise to guide them, but no shared benchmark existed for fair comparison.

SidewalkBench fills that gap inside a GPU-accelerated simulator. Its scenes mix generated streets with real-world scanned ones, populated by reactive animated walkers. The test suite spans hundreds of short unit scenarios, hundreds of walker scenarios and about a hundred long routes. Nine current models are evaluated head to head. Two weaknesses stand out: handling walkers and staying robust over long distances. Training on more simulated sidewalk data looks like a promising remedy, the authors find. Until those gaps close, they caution, real-world deployment of current models would be premature.
arxiv-2606-17053:
Xu and colleagues teach language models to find the decisive detail in a 2026 paper on reinforcement learning. Models often fail when an answer hinges on one small piece of evidence buried in a long tool trace or a subtle image detail. Standard training rewards only the final answer, so grounding goes unsupervised.

ContextRL adds an indirect auxiliary task. The model sees a query, an answer and two highly similar contexts, and is rewarded for picking the context that actually supports the pair. Contrastive data comes from coding-agent trajectories filtered into pairs, and image pairs built by editing and similarity search. The method beats the standard GRPO baseline on long-horizon agent benchmarks and a dozen visual question answering sets. Crucially, baselines given the same contrastive data as ordinary examples gain almost nothing. The gain comes from the selection objective itself, a light signal that sharpens grounding.
arxiv-2606-17153:
Eftekhari and colleagues read a fossil galaxy for traces of the first stars in a 2026 astrophysics paper. NGC 1277 is a massive relic: it formed fast and early, then evolved passively, preserving the chemistry of its birth. If the universe's first, Population III stars left fingerprints anywhere, such a galaxy is a place to look.

Deep spectroscopy reveals unusually strong silicon absorption. The silicon-to-iron ratio is strikingly high, and silicon-to-magnesium exceeds what standard models or ordinary supernova yields can produce. Magnesium sits only moderately elevated, so the pattern is silicon-rich. That signature points to very massive, metal-poor progenitors at the earliest times. Yields from pair-instability supernovae, the explosive deaths of the largest first stars, fit the pattern. Rapid formation and little later accretion kept the signal undiluted. The result is rare chemical evidence for enrichment by the first massive stars.
arxiv-2606-17253:
Li and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper benchmarking language and vision-language model agents on chip physical design, the layout stage of making integrated circuits. Models have done well at front-end design tasks, but physical design demands multi-stage optimisation under strict limits, tool use, and repeated refinement. No standard benchmark existed for that agentic work, so the team built one, called PDAgent-Bench, with hundreds of curated problems.

The problems mix concept questions with real industrial artefacts and cover five skills, from basic knowledge to full-flow implementation. Eleven leading models were tested, and they handled conceptual tasks fairly well, with the best score on root-cause analysis coming from a top commercial model. Scores fell sharply on tool-centred execution such as script generation, and on long multi-stage reasoning. Human-skill-guided workflows improved end-to-end results markedly in their studies.
arxiv-2606-17453:
Bai and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper benchmarking map agents on the unspoken needs behind everyday location requests, not just the stated task. People phrase map queries informally, leaving implicit decision factors, such as avoiding stairs or minding timing, buried in their past behaviour. Asking clarifying questions burdens users, so a capable agent should recover those factors from available evidence before answering, and this benchmark tests exactly that recovery skill.

A restore-identify-filter method rebuilds full user needs from behaviour-chain evidence, names the implicit factors, and keeps only those backed by evidence from before the query. The benchmark is built from large-scale anonymised real user data with ground truth annotated across five dimensions. Current agents complete explicit tasks well, the experiments show. They lag on implicit factors and on proactively gathering the evidence satisfaction requires.
arxiv-2606-17753:
Ratnakar and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper resolving a puzzle in fractional quantum Hall colliders, devices that braid anyons in time to read off their exchange statistics. At one filling fraction, experiments found a negative Fano factor where theory expected a positive one, hinting that something in the device physics was missing. The authors study what happens when the edges of a multi-mode collider interact with each other. Earlier treatments of the braiding signal had left that coupling out of their analysis.

Interactions split the anyon beam into correlated and uncorrelated parts with sharply different braiding behaviour. In long junctions the uncorrelated part wins, flipping the tunnelling current's sign and reproducing the observed negative factor. The mechanism needs no exotic new state, just the edges talking to each other. Collider readings of anyon statistics, the work warns, must budget for inter-edge physics before claiming a phase.
arxiv-2606-17953:
Li and colleagues catch multimodal language models in the act of changing a right answer into a wrong one, in a 2026 paper. When an image contradicts the text, these models usually side with the text, even when the picture clearly shows otherwise. Tracing predictions layer by layer, the team finds the models often form the correct visual answer in middle layers, then override it late in favor of the text.

That direction of drift is itself a signal: most failures shift toward text, while most successes shift toward vision. Their fix, CALRD, watches for a confident visual prediction being suppressed and restores it during decoding, with no retraining needed. Across five models of varied design, the method gained up to about nine points on conflict benchmarks while barely touching ordinary performance.
arxiv-2606-18153:
Ramirez de Chanlatte and colleagues explore replacing the classical 3D mapping pipeline of a forest observatory with neural rendering, in a 2026 paper. The Open Forest Observatory, a university collaboration, builds low-cost drone-based forest maps for ecologists, land managers, and the public, feeding uses from reforestation planning to wildfire risk and carbon accounting. Its current maps come from structure-from-motion, which leaves artifacts and detail gaps, especially at the forest floor where overhead views barely reach.

The team examines folding Neural Radiance Fields into the observatory's workflow. NeRFs handle sparse viewpoints more gracefully and can lean on learned priors, promising cleaner geometry where photogrammetry smears or drops trees. Better maps matter downstream, since reconstruction errors flow into wildfire simulations and carbon estimates. The paper scopes the integration and the future tooling needed for state-of-the-art 3D vision in the database.
arxiv-2606-18353:
Sears and colleagues report late-time JWST observations of GRB 250702B, an extremely long gamma-ray burst, and of the galaxy that hosted it, in a 2026 astronomy paper. The team imaged the field about ninety-five days after the burst and modeled the host galaxy's light.

The host proves to be a single galaxy seen nearly edge-on, crossed by a prominent dust lane, with a high stellar mass and heavy dust content. If the burst came from a collapsing massive star, its host would be the brightest and most massive yet known at similar distances. Faint possible detections in two filters hint at a late-time flattening of the fading light, behavior also seen in jetted tidal disruption events, where a star is torn apart. The data also fit a supernova plus afterglow picture, so the team stresses that later template images are needed to settle the origin.
arxiv-2606-18453:
Shomali and colleagues ask whether a language model's mathematical reasoning in different languages runs on the same internal parameters or on separate ones, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Models vary in math performance across languages, and knowing where that ability lives inside the network could explain why.

Using a fine-grained analysis that localizes and compares the parameters supporting math reasoning, they find a middle answer. The extracted math-linked parameter sets overlap only partly across languages, with the strongest sharing concentrated in the model's intermediate layers. English consistently engaged the largest set of math-relevant parameters, while lower-resource languages engaged smaller sets. The authors conclude that mathematical behavior in multilingual models is neither fully language-invariant nor fully language-specific, but a shared core with language-dependent differences on top. That picture matters for anyone building models meant to reason fairly in many tongues.
arxiv-2606-18653:
Shoshi and colleagues present a study of young stars and their planet-forming disks in the Ophiuchus star-forming region, in a 2026 astronomy paper. It follows earlier work that applied two-dimensional super-resolution imaging to archival ALMA observations and resolved seventy-eight disks. Here the team analyzes the sixty-seven systems with robust dust-radius measurements, combining known stellar parameters with disk properties from the sharper images.

Comparing evolutionary stages and disks with and without substructures such as rings and gaps, they found substructures appear preferentially in relatively massive and extended disks. A tight size-luminosity relation links dust radius to millimeter brightness, and Class II disks with substructures follow a distinctly steeper version of that relation than other subsamples. That pattern matches evolution models in which planet-induced pressure bumps trap dust, suggesting substructures shape how disks and their dust evolve.
arxiv-2606-18953:
Kim and colleagues tackle robot arm control in 2026. Vision-language-action models can follow tasks, but they often fail at fine touch and grip. Small errors build up as a task goes on. Fixing the base model in the real world is slow, costly, and unsafe. The team instead trains a small fix-up policy in simulation only, then adds it to the frozen base model on the real robot.

The fix-up policy watches object poses, not raw images. Pose data looks much the same in simulation and in real life, which helps transfer. The team also replays the same human demos in simulation to build a matched base model there. Noise is added in training to build robustness. On five tasks with a real Franka arm, success rose a great deal with no real-world training. Good new runs can then retrain the base model.
arxiv-2606-19053:
Yu and colleagues introduce FG-BMK in 2026, a large benchmark for fine-grained image tasks in vision-language models. Such models do well on broad perception and reasoning, but their grasp of subtle visual detail is poorly known. Fine-grained skill is basic to computer vision, from telling apart bird species to reading small product traits. The benchmark was built to test that skill directly and to diagnose why models fail when they do.

FG-BMK holds about a million questions and a large image set, from common objects to niche domains. It tests both dialogue-level recognition and feature-level discrimination, in human-style and machine-style modes. That split shows whether a failure comes from weak visual features, weak grounding, or thin knowledge. Tests find leading models still inadequate as fine-grained recognizers.
arxiv-2606-19253:
Baranowski and colleagues present OneCanvas in 2026, a panoramic reprojection method for three-dimensional scene understanding in vision-language models. Existing approaches need complex, model-specific geometry encoders or large training budgets to gain spatial reasoning. OneCanvas instead puts patch features from all views onto a single panoramic canvas. Each patch is placed by its depth and camera pose at the angular position of its world point.

A position embedding of each patch's metric coordinates restores the depth lost when the world collapses to angular coordinates. Patches from all frames then share one spatial frame, and the pretrained vision-language model reads the canvas as an ordinary image. The canvas can center on any pose, supporting reasoning from a specific viewpoint for robots. A spatial training curriculum places object patches at chosen world positions on an empty canvas.
arxiv-2606-19553:
Anant Shyam and Brian Bullins set hard limits for optimisation with biased derivative data in 2026. Nonconvex stochastic optimisation seeks points where the gradient nearly vanishes. Real derivative oracles can be both noisy and biased, skewing every step.

In the first-order setting, the pair prove tight lower bounds on achievable stationarity. The bounds match known upper bounds, closing that case. Higher-order derivative access brings bias-dependent lower bounds of a new form. Trust-region methods then match those bounds across certain bias ranges. A higher-order variance reduction scheme improves oracle counts further when bias runs high. Such gains are known to be impossible in unbiased stochastic settings. Biased gradients thus change the rules: extra derivative orders can pay off precisely where noise once ruled them out.
arxiv-2606-20253:
Jan Raisinger and Jan Eliáš test new boundary rules for simulating how cracks localize in concrete-like materials. Their 2026 paper works with mesoscale discrete particle models, where a loaded sample should develop one clean localization band, the seed of a macroscopic crack. Standard periodic rules distort that process. On square models they produce falsely ductile responses with excess energy loss when the band's angle mismatches the grid. On circular models they block proper band crossing altogether.

The authors evaluate two families of fixes, tessellation and percolation-path-aligned conditions, plus a modified spherical rule with an added jump. Square and circular models under tension were compared across loading directions, and in 3D cubes. Percolation-aligned conditions showed major flaws, spawning multiple bands and spurious banding. Tessellation rules produced one well-defined band whose length followed the geometry alone.
arxiv-2606-20553:
Shanghao Shi and eight colleagues show that a malicious server can turn federated fine-tuning adapters into privacy backdoors. Their 2026 paper studies federated learning for language models, where parameter-efficient fine-tuning freezes the base model and trains small adapters. That efficiency, it turns out, creates an attack surface.

A corrupted adapter can be steered to memorize the client's training samples as isolated per-sample parameter updates stored in separate neurons. The backdoor stays stealthy because the adapter still performs its task. Privacy leakage then hides inside the very mechanism meant to keep data local. Federated deployments must audit adapters, not just data flows, before trusting the privacy story.
arxiv-2606-21553:
Sheroz Shaikh dissects agentic retrieval-augmented generation in 2026, testing which parts of a fancy question-answering pipeline actually earn their complexity. Such systems loop through reasoning, decompose questions, and route retrieval adaptively to answer multi-hop questions, but the value of each piece is unclear under tight budgets. Shaikh ablates a full pipeline on five thousand HotpotQA distractor questions using only a local seven-billion-parameter model.

The full pipeline beats a single-pass baseline by about ten points on exact match and F1. Fixed hybrid retrieval with rank fusion beat rule-based adaptive routing, because the router over-fired on named entities. Two retrieval rounds captured ninety-five percent of the gain of five. Decomposition and reranking helped, but modestly. On a local budget, the simpler fixed choices win.
arxiv-2606-21753:
Xiaoyang Liu, Shangzhe Wu, and Kai Han make photorealistic 3D scenes physically playable in 2026. 3D Gaussian Splatting captures scenes beautifully, but physics engines cannot read splats, and earlier physics-for-splats work handled single objects on ideal planes, in isolation. Their framework lets splat-based assets join scene-level simulations alongside meshes and fluids, bumping into real captured collision geometry.

The core is a representation abstraction layer translating every asset, splats, meshes, fluids alike, into one unified physical particle set. A solver-agnostic kernel simulates that set against static scene boundaries, and results map back to each asset's own visuals. The payoff is two-way interaction previously out of reach: deformable splat objects sloshing against fluids, resting on scanned furniture, inside large-scale captured rooms. Capture fidelity and physical interactivity finally coexist.
arxiv-2606-22053:
Poli and Yilmaz argue, in 2026, that machine learning models should be judged by computational effort rather than by peak accuracy alone. They define effort as the total gradient descent steps needed to reach an acceptable accuracy with high probability, extending a notion from genetic programming. Minimizing that count, they show, doubles as a form of automated machine learning, since it selects training settings by cost-effectiveness.

Across eleven diverse models and five standard classification datasets, a consistent pattern emerged: optimal hyperparameters favour unusually large learning rates. The fast, aggressive movement through the loss landscape that large rates enable not only aids generalization, as in superconvergence, but also statistically minimizes expected training effort. The search strategy itself flips with the target: one run suffices for modest accuracy goals, while pushing toward a model's limit demands many short independent restarts. The framework also supports choosing algorithms at a fixed step budget.
arxiv-2606-22453:
A. Zuevsky extends a theory of Hardy spaces in this 2026 mathematics paper. Hardy spaces collect well-behaved analytic functions on a surface, judged by their boundary values. Earlier work treated finite bordered Riemann surfaces, curved surfaces with edges, in an indefinite setting. Zuevsky moves to ramified analytic coverings, maps that wrap one surface over another with branching points.

Given a finite covering between two such surfaces, the paper builds three objects. First, the direct image of a flat vector bundle, extended carefully across the branch locus, where the wrapping folds. Next comes a canonical matrix function encoding the surface's parahermitian structure. Finally comes an explicit isometric isomorphism, a perfect structure-preserving match, between the two surfaces' Hardy-Krein spaces. That match holds under stated conditions on the covering and boundary. The paper then develops operator theory for these objects through vessels and Bezoutian operators.
arxiv-2606-22553:
F. Lorenzi and L. Salasnich simplify the modelling of light beams in thermal media in this 2026 physics paper. Some materials respond to light nonlocally: absorbed light heats the material, heat diffuses, and the refractive index changes far from the beam. In graded-index media this thermal response reshapes how beam modes interact, but the full equations are costly to simulate.

Inspired by the nonpolynomial Schrödinger equation framework, the authors derive a reduced model of lower dimension. They couple the optical field to an equation for the temperature-induced index change. A variational ansatz, a trial shape built from annular Laguerre-Gauss modes, then yields explicit analytic equations for the mode dynamics. The effective model shows how the interaction depends on mode order and degree of nonlocality. It gives a tractable description of thermal nonlocal media without solving the full spatial problem.
arxiv-2606-22953:
Aman Mehta and Anupam Datta ask whether language model agents remember their own plans in a 2026 paper. Long tasks force systems to shrink stored context, the text the model can still see. Old material gets summarized or dropped so the task can continue. Plans are written early and used for many steps, yet they are often the first thing dropped. The authors test what happens inside the model when a plan leaves the visible context.

Mehta and Datta rerun the same task with and without the plan present. They compare internal states between the two runs. The plan signal spikes right after the plan appears, then collapses within one action step. A probe can detect this decay, though it may not read the plan itself. Reasoning models blur the test because their thinking traces restate the plan. Removing a plan outright cut success sharply in a household task benchmark.
arxiv-2606-23053:
Christian Petersen and colleagues map how electric current flows inside nanowires in a 2026 nanophysics paper. The wires grow by selective area growth, where a mask confines crystal growth to chosen patches of a chip. Knowing whether charge travels through the wire's bulk or along its surface is vital for interpreting device behavior. The team uses conductance fluctuation tomography. Tiny interference patterns in electrical conductance shift as a magnetic field changes strength and direction, and those shifts reveal the paths charge actually takes.

Petersen and colleagues study indium arsenide wires in two device layouts, one plain and one joined to a superconductor. The measurements point to a near-surface accumulation layer carrying most of the transport. Plain devices show coherent flow across the wire's top ridge. Hybrid devices with superconducting contacts show more facet-dependent behavior, with flow favoring individual crystal faces.
arxiv-2606-23153:
Yuang Zhang and colleagues teach swarms of four-legged robots to navigate together in a 2026 robotics paper. Animal groups thread cluttered ground through local coordination alone. Robot swarms still struggle to copy that skill in the physical world. Learning perception, robot-to-robot interaction, and legged locomotion together overwhelms standard reinforcement learning sampling. The team's trick is asymmetric physics. During training, a realistic non-differentiable simulator produces true motion and contact, while differentiable surrogate models supply the gradients that steer learning.

Zhang and colleagues scale the setup to as many as five hundred twelve quadrupeds learning shared navigation policies in obstacle-rich worlds. At run time, each robot acts alone from one forward depth camera, with no communication, central planning, or global map. The policies transferred without retraining to six real robots across five settings. Emergent behaviors included predictive avoidance, right-side yielding, and pausing before bottlenecks.
arxiv-2606-23353:
Jing-Zong Zhang and colleagues turn ultra-peripheral collisions into a probe of nuclear structure in a 2026 physics paper. In such collisions, two nuclei pass close without touching, and light from one probes the other. Coherent vector-meson production creates patterns of diffraction and interference. Those patterns encode the nucleus's spatial density directly. Reading them is a hard inverse problem, tangled by deformation, neutron skin effects, and backgrounds. The team builds a multitask deep learning framework that maps momentum data to several nuclear indicators at once.

Zhang and colleagues test the approach on coherent J/psi photoproduction in zirconium collisions. The learned features separate diffraction-led from interference-led information cleanly. The framework also shows which momentum regions drive each call, keeping the physics legible. Its outputs are ready-made observables for future high-luminosity data.
arxiv-2606-23553: This paper studies how skewness tunes the small-drift record rate of random walks and Lévy flights. The studying studies. Their rate is small-drift record. The tuning tunes skewness. It is probability. The studying is random walks Lévy flights.
arxiv-2606-23653:
Farchione, Idoughi, and Wonka estimate the volume and surface area of objects directly from a handful of photos, in a 2026 paper on computer vision. Such measurements serve coral reef monitoring, dietary analysis, and medical body measurement. Older pipelines need special scanners, manual work, or full mesh building, and they degrade badly when views are few or data are noisy.

The proposed framework is fully feed forward, meaning one pass through the network gives the answer. It predicts scale normalized volume and surface area, plus an uncertainty estimate for each, straight from multi view images. A graph based decoder fuses point cloud reconstructions with features aligned to each view, skipping slow iterative optimization. Experiments show it beats current methods, especially with few input images, across coral monitoring, dietary analysis, and anthropometry.
arxiv-2606-23753:
Singh tests an entropy preserving way of breaking video data into binary choices inside a from scratch reimplementation of a standard video coder, in a 2026 paper on data compression. CABAC, the entropy coder in the H.264 video standard, first converts each value into binary decisions, called bins, then compresses them. An alternative, entropy conserving binarization, provably keeps entropy intact when mapping values to binary strings, but had never been tested inside a real coder.

Singh implements four schemes sharing one backend and benchmarks them on synthetic data, image residuals, and the full Kodak photo suite. The entropy conserving scheme overtakes a single context Huffman scheme as data grow sparser, and beats it at every setting on the Kodak images. A Huffman variant with separate contexts per bin position beats it on most test cells, showing context allocation drives the rate gap.
arxiv-2606-23853:
Moss and Pedersen give an exact account of when qualitative majority judgments can be backed by numbers, in a 2026 paper on logic and social choice. Phrases like most and more likely than not sit between pure rankings and full probabilities. The authors study social decision frames: finite sets of voters with designated families of coalitions counted as strict majorities. When can such verdicts be represented by a finitely additive measure, a consistent assignment of weights?

They identify a coherence criterion, stated purely in terms of the frame's structure, and prove it characterizes representability exactly. A minimal natural logic for strict majority reasoning is also shown sound and complete. The framework corrects a classical representation theorem of Patrick Suppes, and yields a May type characterization of strict majority rule.
arxiv-2606-24353:
Choi and colleagues open the wordlist of the top-down maps self-driving cars navigate by. Bird's-eye-view perception fuses camera images into a unified overhead picture. Production systems recognise only a fixed category list, though. They stumble on the wild real world. Their 2026 task, open-vocabulary BEV segmentation, borrows vision-language models to recognise categories never seen in training.

Lifting two-dimensional semantics into three dimensions is ill-posed in geometry. The framework, OVBEVSeg, constrains it in three growing stages. Reliable three-dimensional projection generates pseudo-labels for general use. Joint per-scene tuning enforces structural match between the flat and overhead views. A distillation step restores online speed. On the nuScenes benchmark the system sets the state of the art. It beats closed-set methods by a wide margin on unseen categories. It performs remarkably even with no ground truth for the novel classes.
arxiv-2606-24653:
Yang He and Zhonghan Hu revisit a century old problem in computing crystal forces. Workers who simulate solids and liquids must add up electric forces across an endless lattice of charges. Such Coulomb lattice sums converge only conditionally. The answer can therefore depend on the order in which terms are added. A recent finite lattice sum was built to remove that ambiguity. It describes the lattice by its exact shape and size.

He and Hu analyse this finite formulation in close detail. They compare it with the many earlier derivations found in the literature. The sum splits cleanly into three parts. One part is a periodic bulk term. A second is a boundary term set by shape. A third corrects for finite size. Together the pieces form an effective pairwise formula. The authors also sketch future uses, from oddly shaped crystals to mesh style algorithms for condensed matter work.
arxiv-2606-24853:
Josevany do Amaral and Rute Sofia build a low cost digital twin for industrial networks using only open source tools. Testing network changes and failure cases on live Internet of Things infrastructure risks real disruption. A digital twin offers a safe replica for such experiments. Their twin targets edge deployments in the IoT edge cloud continuum. It is assembled from Containerlab, Open vSwitch, the ONOS controller, and a Prometheus and Grafana monitoring stack. Topology emulation, software defined traffic control, and live telemetry sit in one package.

Validation compares the twin against a physical Raspberry Pi edge wireless network. Round trip time medians nearly match, differing by 0.4 milliseconds. UDP throughput differs by only 0.03 megabits per second. Two measures diverge more: TCP throughput and packet loss. Amaral and Sofia trace those gaps to identifiable virtualisation artifacts. For each they give root causes and remediation paths.
arxiv-2606-24953:
Joachim Stein and Eric Raidl, philosophers of science, argue that the opacity of machine learning has a second, neglected layer. Prediction opacity, not knowing why a model gives an answer, is widely discussed. Learning opacity is different: the training process itself, the time evolution of a network's weights, is poorly understood. Neural network training, they argue, is essentially a complex system. Its opacity follows from dynamical complexity and the epistemic problems complexity creates.

Three properties of training carry the argument. Learning is sensitive to weight initialisation. Gradient based optimisation contains feedback loops. Training is also sensitive to the data fed in. These are not accidental flaws of current tools. Damping or removing them would change what machine learning is. Some opacity in these systems may therefore be irreducible, Stein and Raidl conclude. The claim reframes interpretability work: part of the darkness is structural, not a temporary engineering debt.
arxiv-2606-25653:
Topological phases hide their order in the pattern of quantum entanglement, not in any local marker. Procolo Lucignano studies a monitored Rashba nanowire in 2026. Its ends host Majorana modes, the boundary states prized for quantum computing. The probe is the disconnected entanglement entropy. This combined measure stays nonzero only while the topological pattern survives. Trajectories are followed jump by jump as the surroundings are watched.

The topological value lasts for a time that grows in direct proportion to the chain's length. This holds even when the watching acts at the boundary, right where the Majorana modes live. Watching also flips the system among its topological states, creating and removing a mode in turn. Over time, though, emitted quasiparticles race across the chain. Their poisoning finally destroys the entanglement pattern, and that race sets the linear lifetime.
arxiv-2606-25753:
Chip masks for extreme ultraviolet lithography must be pre distorted. Light diffracting off their three dimensional absorber stacks would otherwise blur the printed pattern. Vasiliy Es'kin and Egor Ivanov present gradient based inverse lithography in 2026. It designs the mask by running the physics backwards. Two engines serve as differentiable forward models. One is the rigorous waveguide method for wave propagation. The other is a neural operator version. It replaces the costliest linear solve with a perceptron and keeps the surrounding physics. Automatic differentiation then adjusts the absorber's permittivity until the wafer field matches the target.

Tests used realistic two and three dimensional absorbers. The materials were tantalum boron nitride, lanthanum, and uranium, at eleven point two nanometres. In each case the optimisation recovered a mask giving the desired wafer field. End to end gradients through a full diffraction model make inverse design practical. No precomputed training sets are needed.
arxiv-2606-26253:
Hooman Davoudiasl asks whether Earth's core glows in dark photons. Dark photons are hypothetical particles that mix faintly with ordinary light. Stellar cores have long been used to bound that mixing, since a hot star would leak energy into dark photons. Earth's core is far cooler and tamer, but it is also close and well studied. Sub-electronvolt dark photons could stream out of it thermally.

Cooling arguments set the first bounds. Earth's core cannot be leaking energy faster than geology allows, which caps the mixing. Direct detection experiments add a second handle. Results from SENSEI and DAMIC-M already cut into fresh parameter space, Davoudiasl estimates. A proposed experiment, Oscura, could go two to three orders of magnitude deeper near a specific light mass. Home-planet physics thus joins stellar physics in the hunt for a hidden sector.
arxiv-2606-26453:
Jiading Gai and eight colleagues present KernelPro, a multi-agent system that optimizes GPU kernels. A kernel is a small program that runs one computing job on a graphics processor. Experts squeeze speed from kernels by profiling hardware counters and rewriting code by hand. KernelPro automates that loop with language models. It generates code, profiles it, and rewrites it again and again.

The system turns raw profiler numbers into plain-language advice. Small tools encode expert rules for spotting bottlenecks. A roofline check, which compares speed against hardware limits, decides which tools run. A search method adapted from game-playing algorithms explores rewrites and remembers dead ends. KernelPro writes code in a modern low-level style used by expert engineers. On the KernelBench suite, it achieved speed gains the authors report as several-fold. Gains grew on the harder levels of the benchmark.
arxiv-2606-26653:
Agrim Dewan studies how to test whether a given polynomial secretly equals the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial. That polynomial sums over all cycles visiting every vertex of a complete directed graph once. It is a central hard object in algebraic complexity theory. Valiant showed it is complete for a large class of polynomials over every field, a distinction few rivals share.

The test problem takes a polynomial given in some compact form. It asks whether the polynomial is exactly the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial. Dewan's work, following Kayal's randomised algorithm for this problem, examines the test's power and limits. The polynomial's role as a universal hard case makes such identity tests important. They anchor attempts to generalise circuit lower bound results to all fields at once.
arxiv-2606-26853:
Mészáros and Osborne design a particle method for mean field games, which model crowds of many small players each chasing personal goals. First-order versions lack random noise, and hard cases allow tangled Hamiltonians plus spiky starting crowds. Their scheme steps time with an implicit Euler rule and samples space with particles that follow the linked characteristic system. Arbitrary time horizons are allowed in the 2026 analysis, which earlier rigorous schemes could not handle together.

Convergence is proved as particle counts grow and time steps shrink together. Crowd distributions converge in a transport-based metric, and value slopes converge along best paths. Extra smoothness of costs yields a further error bound for the value itself along those paths. Sampling choices come with explicit convergence rates. Numerical experiments across starting crowds, horizons, and dimensions illustrate the scheme behaving as the theory promises.
arxiv-2606-27153:
The X Square Robot Team presents DMuon, a distributed version of the Muon optimiser used to train large neural networks. Muon treats each weight matrix as a whole and orthogonalises it, rather than nudging entries one by one like AdamW. Its Newton-Schulz iterations can cost more than twice the normal forward and backward passes. In 2026, DMuon drops into existing pipelines with no framework changes.

Tests span embodied foundation models and large language models. End-to-end step time speeds up by roughly one and a half to three times across those workloads. The optimiser step alone runs many times faster, in the best cases over a hundred times faster. Per-step delay lands near AdamW levels, removing the old penalty for matrix-aware training. Efficient distributed Muon training becomes practical at scale.
arxiv-2606-27553:
Nicolae Strungaru reviews linked questions in aperiodic order. That field studies structures that repeat without forming a regular crystal. His 2026 survey connects three ideas about such structures. One is whether the diffraction spectrum is continuous. A diffraction spectrum is the pattern made when waves scatter off a structure. The second idea concerns Fourier–Bohr coefficients, averaged wave measures that may fade away evenly. The third is a matching rule called the consistent phase property.
