Research on sharp, point-like diffraction grew after quasicrystals were found in the 1980s. Strungaru traces the main answers given since then. Some used almost periodicity, a near-repetition property of the autocorrelation. Others used dynamical spectra or compactness of the hull. Against that settled background, he sets out what is known about continuous spectra. He also explains when vanishing coefficients and the phase condition hold together.
arxiv-2606-27653:
Repeated games reward players who respond to what an opponent just did. Reactive strategies are the simplest such responses. They condition only on the opponent's previous action. Franziska Lesigang, Christian Hilbe, and Nikoleta Glynatsi study these strategies in 2026. Their setting is repeated additive games between two players with finitely many actions. The donation game is one famous member of this class.

For symmetric Nash equilibria under reactive play, the authors prove a reduction. The equilibrium conditions become linear equalities and inequalities. That form lets them characterise all such equilibria. Each non-empty subset of actions gives one equilibrium class. These classes use exactly the actions in their subset against themselves. The well-known equalizer strategies appear as the class using the full action set. Simulations of social learning add an evolutionary view. A class prevails based on how easily it arises and how well it resists invasion.
arxiv-2606-27753:
Daniel Farley studies a family of transformation groups in 2026. Each group consists of piecewise linear homeomorphisms of an interval. The maps preserve orientation and have slopes that are powers of n. Breakpoints fall at n-adic rational points. Every map also fixes a chosen list of points in the interval. The question is whether these groups have a diagram description.

Farley proves that they do. Each group in the family equals a diagram group built from a semigroup presentation and a chosen word. Both ingredients can be computed from the n-ary expansions of the fixed points. Finiteness properties then split sharply on arithmetic. If every fixed point is rational, the group has type F-infinity, a strong finiteness property. If any fixed point is irrational, the group is not even finitely generated. Diagram groups thus capture these homeomorphism groups completely, arithmetic included.
arxiv-2606-27853:
Galaxies at cosmic noon were still assembling their disks. Juan Espejo Salcedo and colleagues present rotation curves for thirty such galaxies in 2026. The data come from the MSA-3D survey, using the JWST/NIRSpec instrument. Redshifts run from about zero point five to one point seven. Ionised-gas motions combine with NIRCam imaging. Forward modelling separates stars and gas from dark matter.

The primary sample of twenty-three galaxies is mostly rotating disks. Their internal motions run from about thirty-one to sixty-five kilometres per second. Dark matter fractions span from about zero point one to zero point nine at the effective radius. The median sits near zero point six three. Among nineteen well-covered galaxies, six rotation curves rise, six stay flat, and seven fall. Systems range from dark-matter-rich disks to baryon-concentrated ones. Stellar masses reach down to about a billion solar masses.
arxiv-2606-28053:
The EM algorithm is a workhorse for fitting mixture models. Its theory is usually developed for Gaussian mixtures. Rajita Chandak and Kathryn Dullerud extend that theory in 2026 to mixtures of exponentials. They show EM fits a mixture of two exponentials at a sub-exponential rate. At most logarithmically many iterations in the sample size are needed. Consistency holds for a balanced two-component mixture under random initialisation.

Standard Gaussian-setting assumptions get new forms in this setting. Mean-separation and signal-to-noise conditions are extended. A simulation study checks performance in practice. Results are promising for such mixtures. The authors conclude that leaving the Gaussian world does not damage EM's statistical performance. The paper is a first step toward theory for non-Gaussian mixtures generally. High-dimensional versions are a named direction. They should follow under independence across dimensions.
arxiv-2606-28153:
Yanchen Yin, Dongqi Han, and Linghui Li ask what actually changes inside a large language model when a jailbreak attack succeeds. Their 2026 study examines attention heads, the model parts that route information between words, and the safety features that make a model refuse harmful requests.

Yin and colleagues find that attacks do not wipe out safety features across the whole model. Instead, they switch off a small set of heads in early layers, which the authors name Adversarially Compromised Heads. Other heads in middle layers, called Safety-Aligned Heads, keep working even when an attack succeeds. Switching off the compromised heads alone made the model accept requests it normally refuses, and reading the surviving safety signals, with no extra training, also detected attacks well.
arxiv-2606-28353:
Qingqing Yang, Haijiang Liu, and Moyan Li connect two paper trails that rarely meet. One trail is the regulatory approvals the Food and Drug Administration grants medical devices. The other is the patents those devices rest on at the patent office. The link matters for recall investigations, intellectual property discovery, and tracking technology, yet the documents share almost no vocabulary.

Yang and colleagues built a benchmark from cardiovascular devices, with hundreds of devices, hundreds of thousands of patents, and hundreds of expert-verified pairs. Their Bridge-MedDevKG system narrows candidates using company ties, meaning-based similarity, and a medical ontology, then reranks them with a boosted classifier. It recovered at least nine tenths of the verified links while cutting noise roughly in half, and produced millions of high-confidence links overall.
arxiv-2606-28853:
De la Cruz-Dombriz, Dunsby and Sarkar test how structure grows in the universe under a modified theory of gravity. The theory changes Einstein's rules by adding a term built from the energy-momentum tensor squared, a quantity summarising matter's energy and pressure. Using a gauge-invariant covariant method, which tracks real physical changes rather than coordinate artefacts, they follow the density contrast, the clumpiness of matter, as the universe expands.

They examine the growth factor, growth index and a weighted growth rate observations can measure, for two coupling strengths. The growth index fell with rising redshift and matched standard behaviour early on, while mild differences appeared late. One choice stayed close to general relativity. The stronger choice departed more clearly. Viable settings stayed within two standard deviations of current growth data, keeping the theory alive.
arxiv-2606-29453:
Federico and four colleagues introduce Resonant Brane Splatting for arbitrary-scale super-resolution, enlarging an image by any continuous factor. Recent methods replace heavy implicit decoders with explicit 2D Gaussian Splatting, which renders a picture from many soft Gaussian blobs. Ordinary Gaussians are smooth, so edges and fine textures need many overlapping splats. That overlap creates a bottleneck during rasterization, the step that turns shapes into pixels.

Their new primitive, the Brane, emits colours that vary across its own footprint. Internal Gaussian-Hermite modes give each Brane several colour values. The lowest mode matches a standard Gaussian, while higher modes capture sharp local contrast. A network predicts Brane parameters straight from low-resolution features. Because one Brane carries richer detail, far fewer shapes must overlap. A rasterizer that can skip negligible regions speeds rendering further. Benchmarks show better quality and a better speed trade-off than earlier Gaussian methods.
arxiv-2606-29553:
Gupta settles a graph theory conjecture produced by TxGraffiti, a conjecturing program. Such programs scan graph collections for inequalities violated by no stored graph, then put the survivors up for proof or refutation. This conjecture lower-bounds the independence number, the size of the largest set of vertices with no edges among them. The bound combines the annihilation number, the residue, and the maximum degree of the graph.

The conjecture was known only for two special families. Gupta proves a degree-sequence inequality linking the annihilation number to the Caro-Wei sum, a known quantity in the area. Combined with known lower bounds, that inequality settles the conjecture for every connected graph whose maximum degree is at least three. An argument handles the maximum-degree-two case. The single edge is the only counterexample. The result also brackets the independence number between two quantities that are quick to compute.
arxiv-2606-29953:
Zhang and three colleagues propose STABLE, a method that designs algorithms with several connected components on its own, using language-model-guided evolutionary search. Earlier search methods either rewrote whole designs, losing good parts, or polished parts inside a few fixed layouts, and both ignored algorithm semantics.

STABLE organises candidate designs into layered, modular structures drawn from domain knowledge. It then evolves two levels together: the high-level layout and the low-level components themselves, so updates stay coordinated. At each level a semantic model records how components link and fit together, and why, guiding the language model as it generates and scores candidates. In experiments, STABLE's designs beat human-designed baselines and leading search methods.
arxiv-2606-30153:
Michael Kühr, Mevlüt Yildirim, and three colleagues attack traffic sign classifiers with light that humans cannot see. Self-driving cars rely on cameras to read road signs. Most physical attacks stick visible patches on signs. This team instead uses near-infrared light and persistence of vision. Rapid flashes paint content that cameras register but people miss.

The display can show dynamic content and be triggered remotely. Digital simulation first finds the best position for the device. Real-world tests then use two different traffic signs. Twelve machine learning models from several families face the attack. Distances reach twenty meters, under varied lighting conditions. Attack success rates run high across the test scenarios. The authors propose defenses on two levels. Near-infrared cutoff filters block the light physically. A software detector spots the attack's traces in images.
arxiv-2606-30253:
Federica Loiacono and a large team of collaborators count little red dots, a puzzling new class of distant objects found by JWST. These compact red sources may be early, fast growing black holes. The team searches a field around a high-redshift quasar. Five broad line emitters qualify as little red dots there. They are red in color and invisible in X-rays.

From five objects among one hundred fifty-four candidates, they derive number densities. Luminosity functions are built at two cosmic epochs. At the later epoch, red dot density nears that of known active nuclei. The earlier estimate agrees with wider-area studies by other groups. Tracking abundance from cosmic dawn to cosmic noon shows no evolution. Their density stays flat for the luminous population studied. Other studies' apparent drop likely reflects sampling only bright ends. Their noon density far exceeds recent model predictions.
arxiv-2606-30353:
Christopher Chong and three colleagues study shock-like waves in a two-dimensional lattice of coupled masses. The Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou lattice is a classic nonlinear wave model. Traveling waves move through it without changing shape. Dispersive shock waves spread as wavy, modulated zones instead. The paper proves results about the first kind. It then explores the second kind.

Variational methods prove periodic and solitary traveling waves exist. Convex interaction potentials suffice for the existence proof. For unimodal profiles, convexity can be dropped entirely. The variational form also yields a computation algorithm. Line dispersive shocks form from jump-like initial data. Their shape depends on the direction of travel. Their speed and amplitude do not, the simulations show. Comparisons with the KdV equation agree well for small jumps. A fitting method matches the numerics even better.
arxiv-2606-30553:
Yilong Zhao and six colleagues tackle a hardware bottleneck for running large language models on phones. Their 2026 framework, COSM, schedules work between a phone's normal processor and processing-in-memory, or PIM, chips that compute inside memory itself. Running both at once inside shared memory promises privacy and speed, but the two can clash over memory banks and clog the data bus.

COSM adds a low-interference control interface that issues as many PIM commands as possible without disturbing processor memory access. Its scheduler also slips PIM commands into idle gaps in the processor's own access pattern, hiding PIM delays and overlapping compute with data transfer. In tests mixing language models with everyday mobile workloads, COSM raised PIM throughput up to about two point eight times over the baseline scheduler. The cost to processor performance stayed under two percent.
arxiv-2606-30653:
Marina Mancoridis and Zoë Hitzig measure whether language models judge their own work by the same standards they used to produce it. Automated pipelines increasingly let a model generate an output and then evaluate it, with no outside check. That only works if the model's grasp of a concept stays stable across both roles. The pair define generator-evaluator self-consistency to test exactly this assumption.

They applied the measure to ten frontier models across nearly five hundred concepts. Self-consistency varied substantially between models. In a clinical test built on thirty-five physician-validated mistakes, a disturbing pattern emerged: models with higher self-consistency were more vulnerable to the mistakes. Consistency, in other words, does not imply correctness, since a model can apply a wrong concept very steadily. The authors call this the consistency dilemma, and warn that self-checking pipelines inherit the risk.
arxiv-2606-31053:
Malewicz and eight colleagues report an experiment that breaks a famous symmetry of quantum optics. In the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect, two identical photons entering a beam splitter always leave together through the same port, because destructive interference cancels the outcome where they split up. The team shows this is only one possibility within a broader family of two-photon interference.

Using a programmable integrated photonic processor, they interfere imbalanced two-photon states on a variable beam splitter and tune the output distribution continuously. At the extreme, destructive interference suppresses bunching at one output port instead: the photons may leave separately or bunch at the other port, but never together at the forbidden one. The result widens the known toolbox for characterizing photon sources and building quantum sensors.
arxiv-2606-31153:
Alsubhi adapts a classic solver to a practical flaw in X-ray computed tomography. CT rebuilds an image from X-ray measurements by solving a huge linear system. Software generates the forward projector and the back projector with different discretizations. The two operators then form an unmatched pair, and the normal equations lose their consistency. The conjugate gradient method, the usual workhorse, stops producing useful solutions.

For matched pairs, Golub-Kahan bidiagonalization works well. It projects the big problem onto a small subspace, where a bidiagonal matrix carries the solution. Alsubhi proposes AB-GKB and BA-GKB, preconditioned forms of that method built for unmatched pairs. Both are simple to implement and allow parameter tuning. He compares their operation counts with existing methods. Numerical tests across several CT problems show the new algorithms resist the noise amplification that plagues many Krylov methods, giving more stable reconstructions.
arxiv-2606-31453:
Azimi-Mousolou introduces a spectral measure of multipartite entanglement, the quantum link shared among many parties at once. Two-party entanglement is well understood, but measures for many parties remain an open problem. The new measure reads the spectrum, the eigenvalue pattern, of an entanglement graph and its entanglement matrix.

The framework scores the links for any split of a composite system into parts, in one computable form. Azimi-Mousolou proves it meets the standard demands placed on such a measure. A general monogamy rule follows. Monogamy says entanglement cannot be shared freely, and the new form extends the residual version past qubit systems to arbitrary states. The result gives many-party quantum systems a single spectral yardstick.
arxiv-2606-31553:
Liang, Xu and Zhou analyze how fast Fisher-KPP equations spread through an almost periodic medium, where the environment repeats in a near-regular pattern. These reaction-diffusion equations model invasions and population growth, and the spreading speed describes how quickly the occupied region expands. The twist is initial data that decay slowly with distance rather than cutting off sharply.

Using a Hamilton-Jacobi approach, the authors build one framework covering two cases: data decaying exponentially, and data decaying more slowly than any exponential. They show the level sets of the solution, the moving fronts where it crosses a fixed level, can be estimated from the generalized principal eigenvalue of the linearized operator. The decay rate of the initial data is used as well.
arxiv-2606-31653:
Melis, Del Rincon and Sharma combine two training styles that usually pull in opposite directions. Adversarial training makes neural networks empirically hard to fool. Certified training makes their robustness formally provable. Bound-based certified methods sacrifice ordinary accuracy, while adversarially trained models resist the verifiers that issue certificates. Their method, AD-CERT, tries to keep both strengths.

Adversarial information is distilled from an empirically robust teacher at the level of output logits, the raw class scores. This provides a stand-in for the lower bound of the worst-case loss. An Interval Bound Propagation term supplies the upper bound. AD-CERT reaches state-of-the-art certified performance on several robustness benchmarks, and logit-level distillation beats a feature-space variant by up to 5.40 percentage points of certified accuracy in a unified setup.
arxiv-2606-31753:
Chen studies distributed quantum state certification, where many separated nodes each hold one copy of an unknown state. A central referee knows the target state completely but receives only limited one-way messages. The question is how many nodes are needed before the referee can tell whether the unknown state matches the target or sits far from it.

Earlier work by Doosti and others gave conditional lower bounds when only quantum messages were allowed. Chen proves unconditional lower bounds that hold when classical and quantum communication are both permitted. The public-coin lower bound is matched by an explicit algorithm, making it tight. For the private-coin setting with quantum-only messages, Chen gives an almost tight upper bound as well.
arxiv-2606-31853:
Aguilera and Massas build a logic that is at once constructive and quantum. Intuitionistic logic drops proof by contradiction, while orthomodular logic captures quantum propositions. Earlier Ex-logic captured their shared implication-free core. The missing piece was a proper implication connective that behaves well in both worlds.

Reading implication as the Sasaki hook, a standard quantum definition, the pair axiomatize iEx-logic. They prove it equals the intersection of full intuitionistic logic and orthomodular logic in the wider language. A structural payoff follows: logics extending iEx-logic form a product of the intermediate-logic lattice with the orthomodular-logic lattice. Extensions with modal operators are also probed to test the algebraic method's reach.
arxiv-2608-00253: Adaptive Hybrid Modeling of Collisionless Plasma Shocks, arXiv 2608-00253. The plasma shocks. Scholars can read the full paper. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
braid-hypnotic-therapeutics-1853:
Cases fill Braid's Hypnotic Therapeutics, printed in 1853 as a record of hypnotic cures. Braid, the founder of hypnotism, reports patients treated by trance in his practice. Pain, palsy, and nervous ills supply the case histories. Each case states the method, the sittings, and the outcome he observed.

An appendix turns to table moving and spirit rapping, then sweeping the parlors. Braid traces those wonders to unconscious muscular action by the sitters. That reading came decades before the SPR studied the same feats. The appendix is the earliest physiological account of such phenomena. The volume joins clinic and controversy in one binding. Both halves show his method.
bronte-villette-1853:
Charlotte Brontë published Villette in 1853, her most psychologically intricate novel of inner life. The book is a landmark of interior narrative and unconsummated desire in Victorian fiction and beyond. It draws on her own years as a teacher in Brussels, thinly masked as Villette.

Lucy Snowe, penniless and alone, teaches English at a girls' school in a foreign town. She watches, hides, and endures while others court, quarrel, and shine around her quiet post there. The fiery Paul Emanuel slowly sees her worth, and a storm clouds their parting at sea. A spectral nun, a drugged night fête, and confessions to a priest crowd Lucy's path. Brontë leaves the end veiled, and readers still argue Lucy's fate with real heat.
cia-0000008853:
Political trends in western Germany drew CIA analysis in June 1948, as the western zones moved toward statehood. Parties were forming, leaders emerging, and a currency reform was about to reset the economy. Across the line, the Soviet zone was hardening into a separate system.

The paper tracks which forces were rising in the west and how stable the new order looked. A democratic West Germany anchored American plans for Europe, so the reading mattered. The Berlin blockade began the same month, raising the stakes further. This file catches the Federal Republic's birth being watched closely from Washington.
cia-0000009053:
Savannakhet province, in Laos, is named in an April 1974 report of an American prisoner of war sighted there. Savannakhet stretches along the Mekong River and the routes of the Ho Chi Minh Trail. Its prisoners belonged to the secret war's hidden ledger.

Laotian sightings were the hardest to settle, since access stayed limited long after 1973. A report from Savannakhet might be the only trace of a man lost over the trail. Analysts kept such traces carefully, matching them against loss records from the air war. This file keeps one late Laotian lead on the record.
cia-0000009253:
Huu Quan village appears again in the files, this time in an August 1967 report of an American prisoner sighted there. The village, in Thuy Nguyen district near Haiphong, surfaces in reports five years apart. In 1967 the war was young enough that rescue and negotiation still seemed possible.

Early sightings set the baseline against which later reports were judged. If the same village produced sightings in 1967 and 1972, analysts had a thread to pull. Whether the thread led anywhere, the file cannot say alone. Together with its later companion, it shows prisoner reporting accumulating around one small place.
cia-0000013953: A prisoner of war facility in Hanoi is the subject of a CIA note dated January 6, 1969. The note concerns a site where captives were held in the northern capital. Each new site report helped map the camp system at its center. The file adds one more Hanoi location to the record built up over years.
cia-0000014653: Requests for clemency for Julius and Ethel Rosenberg fill a CIA file dated May 3, 1955. The title files them under miscellaneous matters, yet the plea was heartfelt. The Rosenbergs had been put to death in 1953 for atomic spying. Pleas and protests in their name ran on for years, and the agency kept clipping them.
cia-0000015353: A briefing of one board on unidentified flying objects fills a CIA file dated January 5, 1953. Which board is left in clipped words in the title. Briefings carried the saucer files to men who set budgets and policy. This one came days before the great panel met to judge the evidence.
cia-0000022653: Three American prisoners of war were sighted in Tan Uyen District, in Bien Hoa Province, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. A sister entry reports two prisoners in the same district a year earlier. Whether the groups overlapped, the titles do not say. Repeated reports from one district drew fresh checks each time they reached the prisoner offices.
cia-0000023353: A Pathet Lao soldier claimed that about two months earlier he had done something the clipped title cuts off, in an untitled CIA record dated in 1975. An older summary fills the gap with a claim about held Americans, but the title itself cannot prove it. So the entry stands as a soldier's claim, partly lost. Even broken reports were kept for the prisoner search.
cia-0000036853:
A French television reporter interviewed American prisoners, including an admiral's son, in an article kept by the CIA on January 3, 1968. The admiral's son was John McCain, whose father commanded American forces in the Pacific. The interview gave the prisoners a rare public voice from inside Hanoi's prisons.

Inside, the reporter sets down what the prisoners said and how they appeared. Such accounts were studied for signs of health, mood, and pressure from captors. The piece remains one of the better known windows into the prisoners' daily reality. The admiral's son drew special notice, since his capture carried weight far beyond one family's grief.
cia-0000037153:
Live American prisoners of war were allegedly seen in the Lao People's Democratic Republic, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1983. A live sighting was the strongest claim in the whole POW and MIA debate. It said, in effect, that men had been left behind and were still held.

The record preserves the allegation as it arrived, for analysts to test against known facts. Such claims drew intense public attention whenever they surfaced in the press. The file captures both the hope these reports raised and the care officials took before treating any of them as proven.
cia-0000045253:
Prensa Latina gave its view of the Ines Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated October 2, 1985. Havana's agency read the crisis through its own commitments. Cuba stood with the rebels in El Salvador's long war.

Inside, the Cuban reading of the case is preserved as published. Foreign verdicts shaped how the crisis looked beyond its borders. They also fed the arguments of both sides at home. Havana's praise or blame could be quoted in San Salvador within the day it was printed abroad. The file holds Havana's version from that October, useful now as a measure of how the same kidnapping could be told as two different stories.
cia-0000049053: A rightist death squad worked inside El Salvador's National Police, and a CIA item from 1983 reports its existence and where it operated. A squad hidden inside a state force was the war's signature evil: murder with an official address. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, naming a structure investigators later had to prove.
cia-0000049253:
The situation in El Salvador is surveyed in a CIA paper from 1989, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. By 1989 the civil war had run nine years, killed tens of thousands, and settled into a stalemate neither army nor guerrillas could break. Situation papers took the whole country as their subject at a single moment.

Inside, the war's parts are weighed together: the fronts, the politics, the economy, and the mood of a tired country. Such surveys were written for readers who needed the whole board before deciding anything. This one catches El Salvador in the year of the great offensive and the Jesuit murders, at the war's turning point.
cia-0000049353: Status of the churchwomen murder case in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049353, dated January 1, 1982. The item, marked for the Truth Commission, follows the case of the murdered churchwomen. Readers get a brief dated update in record form, showing the case still active in the agency's files more than a year after the killings.
cia-0000112353: Take 2 of 2 Tass Reviews Press for 10 Aug is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112353, dated July 3, 1988. The title marks the second of two takes of a TASS press review for August 10. That review date falls after the file's own July date in the record. The brief record is the closing half of a two-part press digest.
cia-0000115453: Cuban Policy Toward Latin America -- National Intelligence Estimate is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000115453, dated May 2, 1981. The title marks a formal estimate on Cuban policy toward one region, Latin America. A second volume with a near matching title followed the next month. The brief record is the first of that estimate pair from 1981.
cia-0000119753: An October 1956 CIA report states that Soviet mechanized units are moving out of Budapest. The withdrawal raised brief hope that Moscow might let the revolution stand. The report tracks the movement of the tanks at the moment that hope peaked. The pullback formed part of a brief Soviet pause that autumn, days when Nagy's government declared neutrality and the world waited for Moscow's answer.
cia-0000132453: A preparatory peace meeting of Latin American communists fills item 11 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated February 2, 1960. The word peace sits in quotation marks in the headline, showing the agency's doubt about the meeting's stated purpose. Such congresses were a standard tool of communist organizing in the region. The short item covers who met and what was planned.
cia-0000132653: Poland working out an aid deal with Cuba fills a CIA paper dated January 1, 1961. Warsaw was the latest bloc capital to sign on that winter. Bloc aid was weaving Cuba into the communist world's trade web, loan by loan. The short paper covers the talks and what Poland was prepared to offer the Castro government.
cia-0000132753:
Chinese communist work across Latin America fills a CIA paper dated January 4, 1961. The split between Moscow and Beijing was going worldwide at that point, and the hemisphere was its newest front. Beijing was building a network of its own far from home that year.

The paper tracks that work country by country, capital by capital. Trade, press, and party contacts all served as tools in the effort. For readers, the entry shows the Cold War becoming a three-sided contest in the Americas. Washington now had to watch two rival communist powers courting the same region at once. That double watch would last for years.
cia-0000134253: Worry in the Honduran government over pro-Castro work fills a CIA paper dated October 2, 1960. Honduras was a quiet front in the region's Cold War, far from the headlines. Tegucigalpa was watching its own left with growing care that fall. The short paper reports the worry and the signs of Cuban-inspired work that fed it.
cia-0000136053: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 3 February 1954 that deals with character assassination aimed at Cruz Wer, reputation used as a weapon, the heading cut off. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136153: A CIA cable dated 4 April 1954 deals with a WSBURNT report of rail explosions, passed to ONTRICH with a copy for SKILLET, in files since declassified. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136253: One CIA cable dated 6 May 1954 handles an ODACID statement, asked for in a cable whose file alone shows what it was to say. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136753: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 2 October 1960 and flags the date as estimated. The brigade was in its buildup that fall, training in secret for Cuba. An estimated date means the timing comes from the declassification record. No subject is named for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, among the brigade's autumn paperwork.
cia-0000136853: An aircraft deal gone sideways is reported to the senior representative at LINCOLN in this February 1954 cable. JUBILIST is in contact with a firm holding eighteen Navy version Spitfire aircraft for sale. He had been approached the previous spring about their availability for alleged anti-Guatemala elements claiming to represent a colonel; JUBILIST grew suspicious the planes might actually be for the Guatemalan government itself. He was willing to scratch the deal if it was not in United States interests.
cia-0000136953: Let events teach STORAX a lesson, headquarters tells LINCOLN in June 1954. Frank Wisner signed the cable. No advance coordination of a STORAX proposal took place. Headquarters is pleased at the turn of events. It will show STORAX that SYNCARP cannot predict American reactions. Headquarters is not dismayed at any weakening of SYNCARP. LINCOLN may pass a hint to BRODFROST. SYNCARP should not look too close to Washington. It should not look too well informed on American decisions either.
cia-03179153: Mid-March 1956 saw this bulletin circulate. The intelligence community's take on world events. The Cold War's spring dispatch. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. This declassified bulletin persists. The record is kept. The file remains. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
cia-03179253: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1960/05/24, a CIA publication. Another May briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-03184153: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1959/10/15, a CIA publication. The October briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06626853: Argentina's junta jailed La Opinion's director Jacobo Timerman in 1977. The agency filed the detention. The press crackdown, noted. The library keeps the document safe. This file preserves that declassified CIA paper. Kept for posterity. The work remains readable.
cia-06628553: WORLDWIDE DEVELOPMENTS RELATED TO THE US STAND ON HUMAN RIGHTS FEBRUARY 1978, a CIA document. The human rights survey. This file preserves that declassified paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06741353: H. RAY LAHR V. NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD, ET AL., a CIA document. The court case file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06779553: SCHEERCASE RAMPARTS REPRESENTATIVES IN LONDON: DANIEL SCHECHTER AND, a CIA document. The London representatives. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
comte-positive-philosophy-martineau-1853:
Auguste Comte's main work reached English readers in 1853, in Harriet Martineau's short version. Comte, a French thinker, held that sound knowledge rests on facts we can observe. His law of three stages says thought moves from gods to abstract ideas to tested science. Volume 1 covers numbers, the stars, and the study of matter in that scheme.

Martineau cut Comte's six French volumes down to two English ones, with his blessing. Her clear text carried his ideas across the English-speaking world. Comte also ranks the fields of study from the most simple to the most complex. His new science of society crowns the scheme in the next volume.
constitution-denmark-1953:
Denmark's Constitutional Act dates from 1953, the latest in a line going back to 1849. Fewer than ninety sections make up the whole charter, and the tone stays short and plain. Opening sections keep the country a monarchy under a constitution. A king or queen heads the country, and the Evangelical Lutheran Church holds a place backed by law.

Real power sits with a prime minister and cabinet that must keep the trust of the Folketing, the single-chamber parliament. Sections cover elections, lawmaking, the courts, and basic rights such as speech, assembly, and property. The 1953 act also let a woman inherit the throne for the first time, which is how Queen Margrethe the Second later came to reign.
copyright-renewals-1953: Copyright Renewals 1953, issued by the Library of Congress Copyright Office, survives in this copy only as a placeholder note. The file states plainly that it is an unused, empty reservation, kept for an ebook in the United States Copyright Renewals series. The renewal records for 1953 were placed instead in two companion files, one covering January to June and one covering July to December. No entries, names, or listings appear here at all. A reader seeking the actual 1953 renewals must use those two companion volumes.
cornelius-nepos-lives-watson-1853:
Cornelius Nepos, a friend of Cicero, wrote short lives of great commanders around 40 BCE, the first such book in Latin. The men are mostly Greeks and Carthaginians, not Romans. The Reverend John Selby Watson translated the lives into English in 1853, with a notice on the life of Nepos himself.

Miltiades, Themistocles, Aristides, and Epaminondas stand beside Hannibal, Cato, and Atticus, each life told in a few plain pages. Nepos cared more for character and fair judgment than for long war reports. His little book set the pattern for biography in the Roman world and was read in schools for centuries after.
davis-present-age-inner-life-1853:
Andrew Jackson Davis surveyed the young spiritualist movement in The Present Age and Inner Life, from 1853. Davis, the Poughkeepsie Seer, wrote as the movement's leading thinker. The book follows his earlier Spiritual Intercourse as a sequel. Five years of rappings, circles, and mediums get sorted under his harmonial philosophy.

He defines spiritualism, describes a spiritual congress, and classifies media and their causes. The phenomena of the spiritual spheres receive their own treatment. His system blends Swedenborg, mesmerism, and reform era hope. The first edition captures the movement taking stock of itself. Historians use it to map early spiritualist thought. Davis writes with a prophet's calm certainty.
dickens-bleak-house-1853:
Charles Dickens published Bleak House in 1853, his great novel of the Court of Chancery. The suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce drags on for years and ruins all it touches. Dickens aimed at a legal system that fed on delay, cost, and human hope.

Esther Summerson tells half the tale, and a grave narrator tells the rest. Lady Dedlock hides a secret that a cold lawyer hunts through fog and law. A crossing sweeper, Jo, spreads disease and shows how all ranks link in London. The suit ends when costs eat the whole estate it fought over for years. Fog, law, and charity give the book its vast and sombre power.
dumas-countess-of-charny-1853:
Alexandre Dumas published The Countess of Charny in 1853, climax of his Marie Antoinette romances in French. Henry Llewellyn Williams made this English version of the Revolution's climax and Louis XVI's end. The vast serial brought Dumas's revolutionary cycle to its scaffold close in Paris at last.

Andrée, now Countess of Charny, and Gilbert move through the monarchy's fall and the Terror's rise. The royal family's flight to Varennes, the Temple prison, and the king's trial fill these pages. Old friends from the earlier romances meet fates of exile, madness, and the guillotine in Paris. Dumas pauses for long views of the crowd, the court, and the Revolution's driving ideas in France. The cycle ends in elegy for a world the Revolution swept wholly away.
europmc-pmc10009953:
Lawrence and colleagues review the roles of reactive astrocytes in brain disease in a 2023 systematic review. Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells in the brain. After injury or during inflammation, signals from other brain cells can push them into a toxic state that harms nearby nerve cells.

The review pulls together studies on this harmful form and on milder reactive forms. It asks when these cells protect the brain and when they drive damage. The paper gives a balanced guide to a debate that shapes research on stroke, infection, and memory loss.
europmc-pmc10253853:
González and co-authors give a critical overview of the links between high blood sugar and oxidative stress in a 2023 review. The body burns glucose using oxygen, mostly in mitochondria, the cell's powerhouses. When sugar stays high, as in diabetes, harmful oxygen byproducts build up and damage tissue, and that damage in turn worsens sugar control.

The review traces this two-way relationship in detail. It covers the main chemical routes and the organs most harmed. It also weighs treatments that target the stress. The paper ties two core problems of diabetes into one account.
europmc-pmc1074353:
Moriyama and co-authors showed in 2005 how swelling chemicals sharpen a pain sensor in mice. The chemicals are prostaglandins, made at sites of injury. Two of them, PGE2 and PGI2, are known pain drivers. Their partner receptors in that role were still in doubt.

The sensor is TRPV1, a channel on pain nerve cells that fires with heat and spice. In lab cells and mouse nerve cells, the two chemicals boosted TRPV1 through receptors EP1 and IP. Moriyama found the boost cut the heat trigger to below 35 degrees Celsius. Body heat alone could then fire the channel. Mice that lacked TRPV1 or EP1 felt far less heat pain from the chemicals.
europmc-pmc10773453:
Revell presented phytools 2.0 in 2024, an updated R software pack for family tree studies in biology. Such studies use a species tree to infer how traits evolve, how fast groups split, and where they lived. The pack has grown over ten years into a core tool for that work. It now holds hundreds of functions.

Version 2.0 adds fresh tools and updates old ones, Revell reports. Tasks span fitting trait change models and rebuilding the states of ancestors. Users can also study how fast lineages branch and draw trees with data laid on top. Sample workflows walk through the most used paths in the pack. The pack stays free for any R user.
europmc-pmc1182353:
Bendtsen and co-authors built a 2005 computer tool called TatP. The tool hunts for a special tag on bacterial proteins. Proteins with that tag leave the cell by their own export route. That route differs from the standard export path most proteins use.

TatP learned from known tagged proteins how to spot the signal. It correctly found most known cases in tests. It also made far fewer false alarms than simple pattern searches. Bendtsen made the tool public so labs can screen genomes. Better tag calls help map how bacteria ship proteins.
europmc-pmc1241553:
Flake, Andersen, and Dixon reviewed uterine fibroids, benign womb tumors, in 2003. Fibroids develop in most American women over a lifetime. About one third develop symptoms from them. They are the top reason for hysterectomy in the United States.

Risk runs higher with age, African-American ancestry, no prior births, and obesity. About 40 percent of tumors show nonrandom chromosome changes. Estrogen and progesterone promote fibroid growth. Growth factors found at high levels in fibroids may carry out that promotion. Flake sums up what triggers remain unknown and what clues exist. The role of hormone-like chemicals from the environment was only just being explored at the time.
europmc-pmc1253653:
Gee and Payne-Sturges built a framework for racial health gaps tied to environment in 2004. Social and environmental factors clearly interact to produce disparities. How they interact stayed vague in past work. The environmental justice movement pointed to higher hazard exposure in poor areas.

Stress from social conditions is their proposed linking factor. Chronic stress alters immune and other body systems. It can also lead straight to illness. Residential segregation shapes who faces community stress and hazards together. Gee merges exposure science with stress biology into one model. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2004. It ran in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2004.
europmc-pmc1475653:
A rare syndrome makes the body attack its own hormone glands. Meager and co-authors studied patients with autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 in 2006. The cause is a faulty gene, AIRE, that teaches the immune system to spare the self. The team tested blood for antibodies that block interferons, proteins that fight viruses.

Every one of 76 patients from Finland and Norway carried strong blocking antibodies to most type I interferons. The antibodies showed up early, even before the yeast infections that often come first. Levels topped those in patients with a related tumor condition. Meager suggests these antibodies could serve as an early marker of the syndrome.
europmc-pmc1654153:
Grape berries resist clean RNA extraction, yet gene studies of ripening depend on it. Reid and co-authors fixed the method in 2006, adjusting for the berries' low pH and high sugar and phenol loads. The tweak improved RNA precipitation from berry skin and seed.

They then validated yardstick genes for Cabernet Sauvignon berry skin, testing 14 candidates with three statistical approaches. Several proved fairly stable, but no single gene won under all three methods. Using several yardsticks together beat using one. Reid also showed the payoff by tracking two genes, for water and sugar transport, across berry development.
europmc-pmc1810553:
Harrow and colleagues described GENCODE in 2006, the reference gene annotation for the ENCODE project regions. Those regions cover one percent of the human genome, chosen for detailed study. GENCODE aimed to find and map every protein-coding gene inside them.

The work combined hand annotation by the HAVANA team with lab validation and then refinement. Gene features fell into eight classes, of which only two count as confidently protein-coding. Of 420 coding loci tested by lab methods, 229 products were sequenced. They supported lengthened gene starts at 30 loci and new splice variants at 50 loci. A further 46 loci without coding evidence were validated as transcripts. The final set held 487 loci, of which 434 were coding.
europmc-pmc1876453:
Proffit, Turvey and Phillips updated in 2007 the stability ranking for jaw surgery that repositions the face bones. Orthognathic surgery moves the jaws to fix bite and facial balance, and metal rigid fixation holds the bones while they heal. Not all movements stay put equally well, so surgeons plan around a known hierarchy.

Two additions join the list: fixing facial asymmetry holds well with rigid fixation, and chin repositioning is very stable. In the first year after surgery, corrections for Class II long-face patterns held better than those for Class III patterns. Between one and five years the picture flips, with Class III patients then more stable. Changes over two millimeters occurred in a surprisingly large share of patients even after healing. Teeth usually adapt, so bite changes lag behind bone changes.
europmc-pmc2008453:
Cole, Jones and Todd reported an early trial in 1971 of a new anti-oestrogen drug, ICI46474, for advanced breast cancer. Anti-oestrogens block oestrogen, a hormone that can fuel some breast cancers. Hormone treatment was standard for late or returning cancer, but only some patients responded. The team treated 46 patients whose cancer was advanced or had come back.

Ten patients showed a good response to the drug. That rate matched what doctors saw with oestrogens and androgens, the older hormone options. The clear advantage was tolerability, meaning how easily patients could bear it. Troublesome side effects were uncommon. The authors present the drug as a useful new option for palliation, care aimed at easing disease rather than curing it.
europmc-pmc2125253: A medical paper with a method for cultivating Treponema pallidum in fluid media. The syphilis germ, grown. This article preserves that bacteriology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128353: A medical paper on antagonistic growth-activating and growth-inhibiting principles in serum. The serum's push-pull. This article preserves that cell biology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131153: Rabbits built their defenses over days, and this paper followed agglutinins and protective antibodies as they rose. Blood samples charted the immune climb. The growing protection, tracked. The article preserves that immunology research. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140653: How fast trypsin digests depends on the conditions around it, which this kinetics paper worked out in detail. The team varied the reaction setup and clocked the enzyme. The protein-cutter's pace, established. The article preserves that biochemistry research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2222953:
Gabriel, Herwig and Klenk showed in 2008 how influenza A adapts to new hosts through its copying machinery. An avian virus strain became mouse-adapted through mutations in its polymerase proteins and nucleocapsid protein. Those changes raised transcription and replication in mammalian cells. The team focused on two mutations, N319K in NP and D701N in PB2, and asked how they help the proteins enter the cell nucleus.

Both mutations strengthened binding to importin alpha1, the mammalian shuttle that carries cargo into the nucleus. Binding was followed by faster nuclear transport of PB2 and NP in mammalian cells. Importin temporarily gathered in the nucleus and drained from the cytoplasm. No such enhancement occurred in avian cells. Adapting to the host's nuclear import machinery is thus a key step in cross-species transmission.
europmc-pmc2329653:
Oren surveyed salt-loving microbes in this 2008 review. Such microbes are called halophiles, meaning salt lovers, and they live in places like salt lakes and salt pans. They appear in all three domains of life, the broad groups named Bacteria, Archaea, and eukaryotes.

Oren described two main ways these cells balance salt. Some fill their insides with potassium chloride, which forces all their proteins to work in near-saturated salt. Their proteins are highly acidic and fall apart in fresh water. Others keep salt out and make harmless organic solutes instead, such as ectoine and glycine betaine. That second group copes with a much wider range of salt levels. One red bacterium, Salinibacter, uses the salt-in plan and shares many genes with salt-loving Archaea.
europmc-pmc2361453:
Cassidy and co-authors built the LLP risk model for lung cancer in 2008. The model estimates a person's chance of developing lung cancer within five years from their risk factors. Such estimates could pick who should get early screening, since lung cancer found late is rarely curable.

They built the model from 579 lung cancer patients and 1,157 matched controls in Liverpool. Smoking, family history, asbestos exposure, and other factors went into the final version. For example, a 77-year-old male non-smoker with early family cases and asbestos exposure scored a risk of 3.17% over five years. Testing showed the model separated future cases from non-cases fairly well, with an accuracy measure of 0.70 on a scale where 1 is perfect. The authors said outside checks should come before clinical use.
europmc-pmc2361853:
Burnet and colleagues argued in 2005 that cancer research money should be judged against years of life lost, not just deaths. Years of life lost adds up how many years each death cuts short. A cancer killing young people scores far higher than one killing mostly the very old.

They compared 17 cancer sites in Britain, where the national research budget was about 250 million pounds. On this measure, cancers of the ovary, cervix, and brain looked much bigger burdens than raw death counts suggest. Brain tumor patients lost the most life each, just over 20 years on average, while prostate cancer lost the least, at 6.1 years per death. Lung cancer stayed underfunded on both measures. Brain, cervix, kidney cancers and melanoma stood out as high-burden but low-spending sites.
europmc-pmc2395253:
Henegar and a large team profiled fat tissue from obese people in 2008. Obesity research often focuses on fat cells themselves, but the tissue around them, the extracellular matrix, also changes. This matrix is the scaffold of proteins that holds cells in place.

Comparing white fat from obese and lean subjects, they found a clear gene activity signature in obesity. The obese tissue showed more interstitial fibrosis, meaning extra scar-like scaffold laid down between cells. It also held more infiltrating inflammatory cells, immune cells drawn into the tissue. The authors argued the stiffened matrix is not a side detail but part of the disease process in human obesity. A tight scaffold can squeeze fat cells and fuel the inflammation that drives obesity's complications.
europmc-pmc2569153:
de Vries, Ramrattan, Smorenburg, Gouma, and Boermeester systematically reviewed in 2008 how often hospital patients are harmed by their care. Adverse events, unintended injuries caused by treatment rather than disease, were recognised as a grave problem, but no pooled picture existed. The authors searched the major medical databases and selected studies that reviewed patient records for such events.

Eight studies covering 74,485 records qualified. The median rate of in-hospital adverse events came to 9.2 percent, so nearly one patient in ten was affected, and a median of 43.5 percent of events were judged preventable. Most patients suffered no or minor disability, but 7.4 percent of events were lethal. Operations accounted for 39.6 percent of events and medications for 15.1 percent, marking where prevention efforts should concentrate.
europmc-pmc2648953:
Lyons and colleagues described in 2009 a Welsh databank that links health and social care records for research while hiding who people are. Services collect huge amounts of data on patients every day. Joining those records up could improve care and science, but privacy rules demand strong safeguards.

Their system, called SAIL, had already loaded over 500 million records from many providers. The team built a matching program that gives each person a coded tag, so records join without names attached. They tested how well the national health number works as the matching key. The method proved right more than 99 times in 100 at spotting true matches, while missed matches stayed low. Care records, hospital records, and social service files were then tied to one register with the same approach.
europmc-pmc2654153:
Merabishvili and co-authors described in 2009 how they made a small batch of bacteria-killing viruses, called bacteriophages, pure enough to test in burn patients. Phages infect and burst specific bacteria. The mix aimed at two germs that often infect burns, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, in a Brussels military hospital.

From a starting pool of 90 phages, three rounds of selection left just three winners. The team grew them, stripped out bacterial toxins, and ran strict checks: shelf life, sterility, heat-causing impurities, and safety on human cells. Gene and protein scans confirmed the phages kill rather than hide inside their hosts, and carry no toxin genes. Electron microscope images showed the right virus shapes attacking the right bacteria. A pilot trial in patients was already cleared to begin.
europmc-pmc2667253:
Cureton and co-authors filmed in 2009 how a rod-shaped virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, sneaks into cells through a doorway built for much smaller loads. Cells swallow surface material in bubbles coated with a protein called clathrin. The virus is longer than a normal bubble is wide, so full coating looks impossible.

High-resolution movies of single viruses entering lit-up cells showed the answer: part coating is enough. Virus bubbles carried more clathrin than usual, but never a full shell. The missing help came from actin, the cell's moving scaffold, whose parts gathered at the virus bubbles. Blocking actin froze the viruses at the surface, trapped in half-made bubbles. The team also showed the virus triggers its own doorway rather than waiting for a random one to form.
europmc-pmc2669153:
Korolchuk and co-authors showed in 2009 that the cell's two garbage systems back each other up in unexpected ways. One system, the proteasome, shreds proteins tagged with a marker called ubiquitin. The other, autophagy, wraps larger loads and digests them in acid sacs. The two were long thought to serve separate clients.

When the team blocked autophagy in cells, proteasome targets piled up anyway. The cause was a helper protein, p62, which itself builds up when autophagy stops. Extra p62 gums up delivery of tagged proteins to the proteasome, delaying their destruction. Short-lived control proteins such as p53, and clump-prone proteins linked to brain disease, rose as a result. Blocking one system, the authors warn, quietly weakens the other, a fact that matters for drugs aiming at either route.
europmc-pmc2671453:
Meijer and the European Influenza Surveillance Scheme group reported in 2009 that flu viruses able to resist the main flu drug had spread across Europe in the 2007–08 season. The drug, oseltamivir, sold as Tamiflu, was a front-line treatment and preventive for influenza A H1N1. Resistant viruses had once been rare curiosities.

That season they were anything but rare. The scheme ties the spread to two helpers: a heavy season of virus circulation, and the arrival of a changed virus variant in a population with little immunity to it. Resistant strains could ride that wave even though few Europeans took the drug. The report warned health agencies that resistance can take hold without drug pressure, changing how stockpiles and treatment guides should be planned for future seasons and pandemics.
europmc-pmc2699053:
Ma and a large team read in 2009 the genome of Rhizopus oryzae, the fungus behind mucormycosis, a fast, often fatal infection that invades blood vessels. It kills over half its victims. The fungus also serves science as a model of the early-branching fungi, a group whose history was sketchy.

The genome spans 45.3 million letters, about a fifth of it jumping DNA repeats. Among its 13,895 genes, many sit in matched pairs. Their arrangement and shared ancestry point to one ancient event: the whole genome doubled. The doubling copied nearly every part of the cell's energy and waste systems. Gene families for growth signals and for secreted cutting enzymes, known weapons of fungal infection, expanded too. One doubled target of antifungal drugs may explain the species' uneven response to those drugs. The cell wall recipes, absent from human cells, offer clean targets for new ones.
europmc-pmc2706953:
Hewitson, Grainger, and Maizels reviewed in 2009 how helminths, parasitic worms, calm the host immune system with proteins they secrete. Worm infection usually drives a Th2 response, one arm of immunity, while also raising cells that damp immunity down. That mix lets worms live for a long time inside a host.

Clearing worms with drugs reverses the calming effect, which proves live worms actively hold immunity down. Their review surveys single secreted proteins that block host signals at many steps, from first sensing to final attack. Targets include immune messengers and receptors, the docking sites on cells, plus proteins that break down or shield against host defenses.
europmc-pmc2775953:
Liao and co-authors showed in 2009 that cancer-associated fibroblasts drive tumor growth and spread by shaping the immune setting around a tumor, in a mouse model of metastatic breast cancer. Fibroblasts make up most cells in tumor stroma, the supporting tissue, and are tempting drug targets. The team removed them in living mice with a DNA vaccine aimed at fibroblast activation protein, a marker on these cells.

Removing the fibroblasts flipped the local immune balance from a Th2 pattern to a Th1 pattern, the kind that attacks tumors. Protein levels of two immune signals rose, while suppressive cells and new blood and lymph vessels fell. The vaccine also boosted the anti-metastasis effect of doxorubicin chemotherapy and drew in more dendritic cells and killer T cells. Fibroblasts, they conclude, are valid treatment targets in metastatic breast cancer.
europmc-pmc2794253:
Wu and colleagues presented a faster way in 2009 to free living plant cells from their walls, using the small weed Arabidopsis. Such wall-free cells, called protoplasts, let researchers test genes and watch proteins interact inside a living cell. The older method cut leaves into thin slivers, which was slow and often damaged the cells.

Their Tape-Arabidopsis Sandwich sticks one tape to the leaf top and another tape to the underside. Peeling the lower tape strips off the bottom skin, so enzymes can reach the inner cells and digest their walls. Ready protoplasts take under an hour, and gene tests can run within two hours, with less skill and gear needed.
europmc-pmc2798753:
Löffler and colleagues tested in 2010 how strongly a staph toxin called Panton-Valentine leukocidin, or PVL, harms human neutrophils. Neutrophils are white blood cells that rush in first against infection. PVL's role in severe tissue-killing disease was disputed, since mouse studies gave mixed answers.

PVL works by punching pores in the cell membrane. PVL triggered fast activation and death in human and rabbit neutrophils, but left mouse and monkey cells unharmed. Strains releasing PVL killed the cells early and fast, unlike the slower, normal death that follows germ eating. Another staph toxin group hit all species alike. The species gap means mouse and primate models can mislead work on this toxin, the authors warn.
europmc-pmc2829053:
Netea and colleagues reviewed in 2010 how the immune signal IL-1beta gets switched on during infection. IL-1beta and its cousin IL-18 rouse front-line defense cells and steer later adaptive responses, but both are made as inactive precursors that a cutting enzyme must trim. The best-known cutter, caspase-1, is itself switched on by platforms called inflammasomes.

Mice missing caspase-1 or inflammasome parts fall prey to several infections more easily, the review notes. Yet in other infections and in sterile inflammation, caspase-1 matters little. There, enzymes from neutrophils, the first-responder white cells, or even from the germs themselves do the trimming. The authors conclude the inflammasome is one activation route among several, not the whole story.
europmc-pmc2873753:
Chan and co-authors reported in 2003 on Singapore's large 2000 epidemic of hand, foot and mouth disease, a mostly mild childhood illness that can turn deadly. Case reports from doctors and childcare centers showed cases climbing through September and falling by late October. Nearly three thousand eight hundred cases were notified, almost all in children under four years old.

Cultures from patients grew human enterovirus 71 more often than any other virus, in both patients with the illness and patients with other complaints. Five children died, and autopsies on the fatal illness cases showed inflammation of the brain, lungs, and heart muscle. Virus was confirmed in most of the deaths. The account ends with the outbreak plan Singapore built for fast, coordinated control of severe recurrences.
europmc-pmc2913853:
Piccinini and Midwood reviewed in 2010 how the body's own debris, called DAMPs, can keep inflammation burning through the same receptors that detect germs. DAMPs are molecules released by damaged or dying cells, plus matrix fragments freed when tissue is torn. They trip Toll-like receptors, the immune system's alarm sensors, launching repair programs that normally shut off once healing starts.

In rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, and cancer, the alarm instead feeds itself: inflammation damages tissue, damage releases more DAMPs, and the loop becomes chronic. The review distinguishes the signaling routes used by different self-activators, since they are not all equal. Blocking specific DAMPs could calm disease inflammation while leaving germ defense intact, a precision that broad immune suppression cannot offer.
europmc-pmc2914753:
Guerra and colleagues mapped in 2010 the worldwide limits of Plasmodium vivax malaria, the second great human malaria parasite, and counted who lives at risk. Vivax had long been overshadowed by its deadlier cousin, so its true range was fuzzy. They assembled the newest case reports from every endemic country and graded each area as malaria-free, unstable, or stable transmission.

Temperature and aridity layers trimmed the map where the parasite or its mosquitoes cannot persist, and local intelligence erased risk from big cities and free islands inside endemic borders. Overlaying a detailed 2009 population surface gave at-risk headcounts by risk class. The result is a contemporary baseline for the relapsing parasite, whose hidden liver stage makes elimination harder than case counts suggest.
europmc-pmc2923753:
Lenardon, Munro, and Gow reviewed in 2010 chitin synthesis in fungi, the process that builds the skeleton of the fungal cell wall. Chitin is a tough carbohydrate mesh absent from humans and other vertebrates, which makes its machinery an inviting drug target. Fungi place chitin precisely through the cell cycle, reinforcing buds, branches, and the cross-walls that divide cells, and they remodel it fast when the wall is stressed or attacked.

The review assembles how the synthase enzymes are made, shipped, switched on, and restrained, and how those controls fail or adapt during infection of animals and plants. Chitin also talks to the immune system, provoking and at other doses calming responses. Drugs and farm fungicides that jam chitin placement could disarm many pathogens at once, a prospect the authors develop.
europmc-pmc2950153:
Wauquier and colleagues studied blood samples from Ebola patients in Gabon and Congo outbreaks between 1996 and 2003, comparing those who died with those who survived, in a 2010 study. Human immune data on this virus were scarce because outbreaks strike remote areas.

Fatal cases showed floods of inflammatory signalling molecules and growth factors, yet almost none of one key antiviral signal. Their infection-fighting T cells also crashed in number, with death markers rising on the remaining cells, and helper molecules from T cells stayed low. Survivors showed a calmer, better balanced pattern. The profile links death to a misfiring early defence plus immune cell loss.
europmc-pmc3012653:
Hinderliter and colleagues built ISDD, a computer model predicting how many lab-grown cells particles in culture fluid actually reach, in a 2010 article. Toxicity tests usually report dose as what was added to the dish, not what lands on cells, skewing comparisons.

The model combines sinking under gravity with random diffusion for round particles and their clumps. Checked against measured transport for plastic beads of many sizes, silica, and iron oxide clumps, predictions landed close to measurements without any tuning. The authors then chart how particle size, density, and fluid depth change the true cellular dose.
europmc-pmc3035253:
Auch, von Jan, Klenk, and Göker tested in 2010 whether computers can replace a slow lab test used to decide if two microbes belong to one species. The old test mixes DNA from two strains and measures how well it sticks together, but it is tedious, error prone, and cannot build a shared database. Genome sequencing offered a faster path, if the math could match the old results.

The team compared methods that find long matching DNA stretches between two genomes and turn them into a distance score. Their best formulas tracked the old test closely, handled shrunken and repetitive genomes, and stayed steady when parts of a genome were missing. The scores also matched a standard gene based family tree better than the old test did. The methods were released as a web service for naming new species.
europmc-pmc3037053:
Sundar and Chakravarty reviewed in 2010 the harms of antimony, a metal used both in industry and as a medicine. Workers can breathe it in, causing lung irritation, skin spots, and stomach trouble, and one form may cause cancer. As a drug, antimony compounds have long treated two parasitic diseases, leishmaniasis and schistosomiasis.

During treatment, the main dangers are heart rhythm damage, seen in roughly one in eleven patients, and inflammation of the pancreas. The pancreas problem is especially common when patients also carry HIV and visceral leishmaniasis together. Safer workplaces have cut job related cases sharply. For patients, the authors stress checking each drug batch for quality and watching closely for side effects throughout treatment. Careful monitoring keeps a useful old drug acceptably safe.
europmc-pmc3057953:
Philippe and coauthors argued in 2011 that simply gathering more DNA sequences will not settle the hardest questions about the tree of life. Their essay responds to genome scale studies of early animal evolution that reached strongly conflicting trees despite huge datasets. Each rival tree tells a very different story about how simple or complex the first animals were.

The trouble, they argue, is not a lack of data but systematic error inside it. Fast evolving lineages, poor models, and contaminated or misaligned sequences can pull a tree the wrong way with great statistical confidence. More data then makes a wrong answer look more certain, not less. The authors urge better models, careful data selection, and slower thinking over brute volume. Their piece is a caution to a field dazzled by sequencing speed.
europmc-pmc3063653:
Bouvier and Lowen reviewed in 2010 the animal models used to study how influenza viruses cause disease and spread. Human flu ranges from silent infection to fatal pneumonia, depending on the strain and on the person's age, immunity, and past exposures. Not every strain that can infect people can pass between them, which is the property that decides pandemic risk.

Ferrets, mice, guinea pigs, hamsters, cotton rats, and monkeys each copy part of the human picture. Ferrets sneeze and spread virus much like people, while mice allow deep genetic work but spread virus poorly. The review weighs each model's strengths and limits for testing drugs and vaccines before human use. Choosing the right animal for each question, the authors argue, is what turns lab results into reliable warnings about real strains.
europmc-pmc3093253:
Jiao, Yu, Zhang, and Ewart reviewed in 2011 the chemistry and medical promise of sulfated sugars from seaweeds. These long sugar chains, decorated with sulfate groups, are made by red, green, and brown algae and include familiar materials such as carrageenan and agar relatives. Cut into shorter pieces, they show a striking range of biological effects in lab studies.

The review first updates the detailed structures of the main families, which differ by algae type and sugar building blocks. It then surveys their actions: thinning blood and blocking clots, fighting viruses, calming inflammation, lowering blood lipids, and mopping up damaging oxygen radicals. Several effects are strong enough to interest drug developers, though the molecules are complex and hard to standardize. The authors present them as a rich, renewable source of candidate medicines from the sea.
europmc-pmc3120753:
Sven Bocklandt and colleagues built a way to guess age from chemical marks on DNA in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Marks called methylation change steadily across life and affect how genes behave. The team scanned saliva DNA from male identical twins and found dozens of sites whose marking tracked closely with age.

Three sites, near genes involved in growth and nerve signalling, rose or fell in a straight line across five decades of life. Using just two of the sites, the team predicted age with an average error of only a few years. Such a test could help forensic work when only a body sample exists, and could one day flag people ageing faster than their years suggest.
europmc-pmc3175453:
Irene Winkler, Stefan Haufe, and Michael Tangermann built an automatic cleaner for brain-wave recordings in a 2011 paper in Behavioral and Brain Functions. Recordings are polluted by eye, muscle, and device artefacts, and the standard fix, hand-picking bad components after a mathematical separation, is slow and varies by person. Their classifier learns from expert-labelled components instead.

Using just six features spanning frequency, space, and time patterns, the linear classifier matched expert disagreement levels on its training study. It held up well on a new listening study with different equipment. On motor-imagery data it preserved the brain signals a brain-computer interface needs, even while discarding the worst three fifths of components. The method works across headsets and subjects without per-person artefact recordings.
europmc-pmc3218953:
Jennifer Patnaik and colleagues asked what older women with breast cancer actually die of, in this 2011 retrospective study in Breast Cancer Research. Many survivors die of unrelated causes, so the team used a linked cancer-registry and Medicare database. They followed more than sixty thousand women diagnosed at age sixty-six or older between 1992 and 2000.

After a median follow-up of about nine years, just under half the women were still alive. Heart and blood-vessel disease was the single largest cause of death, edging out breast cancer itself. Age and other illnesses at diagnosis drove deaths from other causes most strongly, and conditions such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes also raised breast-cancer mortality somewhat. The authors urge priority for heart-health care in long-term follow-up.
europmc-pmc3221353:
David Mohr, Pim Cuijpers, and Kenneth Lehman proposed a model called Supportive Accountability in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Online health programs work better when a human supports the user, but that support was rarely described or guided by theory. The authors built their model from organizational psychology, motivation research, and studies of computer-mediated communication.

In their account, support works through accountability: users stick with a program when answerable to a coach they see as trustworthy, kind, and expert. Expectations should be clear, focused on process, and set with the patient's input, and the benefits of the relationship should be mutual. Intrinsic motivation reduces how much support a person needs, and the communication channel, phone, email, or messaging, shapes the process. Each part of the model is offered as a testable claim.
europmc-pmc3315253:
Li and Siegrist combined long term studies to measure how physical activity protects the heart, reporting in 2012. They searched three decades of research and kept only large, high quality studies that followed adults free of heart disease for at least five years. Twenty one studies qualified, covering more than six hundred fifty thousand people and about twenty thousand new cases of disease.

People with the most active leisure time had roughly a quarter lower risk of heart and blood vessel disease than the least active, in both men and women. More activity brought steadily more protection. A moderate amount of physical work on the job also helped, cutting risk by a smaller margin. The authors say the pattern supports prevention efforts in rich and developing countries alike.
europmc-pmc3366753:
Keiser and Utzinger warned in 2005 that foodborne trematodiasis — infection with liver, lung, and intestinal flukes — was emerging as a public health problem. People acquire these parasites by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish, crustaceans, or aquatic plants, and the diseases they cause range from liver damage to chronic intestinal illness.

The authors linked the rise chiefly to booming freshwater aquaculture, which expands habitats and distribution routes for the parasites. In China, infections with the liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis had more than tripled in a decade, reaching roughly fifteen million people. They urged that aquaculture expansion in endemic regions be monitored so food production gains do not come with more disease.
europmc-pmc3379953:
Rizzardi and colleagues tested in 2012 whether computers can score tissue staining as reliably as pathologists do by eye. Such staining, called immunohistochemistry, validates markers found by gene studies, but visual scoring is costly and subjective. The team used tissue arrays built from more than two hundred ovarian cancer specimens stained for one protein.

Software first outlined the cancer areas, then measured how much staining they held. Its outlines matched the pathologists' hand-drawn ones closely. Staining scores from pixel analysis tracked the visual scores very tightly on both measures used. The study shows digital scoring can turn a judged grade into a continuous, repeatable number.
europmc-pmc3430553:
Hayes, Hayes, and Mikedis pooled brain-scan studies of posttraumatic stress disorder in 2012 to find the neural pattern that survives across study designs. Scans had implicated many regions, but results varied widely. Their meta-analysis gathered data from several hundred patients and matched controls across dozens of studies published before 2011.

Two zones stood out as overactive in patients: parts of the anterior cingulate and, in targeted studies, the amygdala on both sides. Underactivity spread widely, especially in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and a frontal region nearby. The quieter that prefrontal zone ran, the hotter the amygdala burned, a coupling the authors verified directly. The pattern supports a model of PTSD as a broken balance between salience detection and emotion control.
europmc-pmc3433453:
Pendleton led a team that produced the first global estimate in 2012 of carbon emissions from wrecking vegetated coasts. Marshes, mangroves, and seagrasses lock away huge carbon stores in their sediments, the so-called blue carbon. Earlier counts tallied only the uptake lost when these places vanish, missing the stored carbon that escapes.
