Combining world area data, conversion rates, and near-surface carbon stocks, the team estimated yearly releases spanning a wide range, several times the older figures. The total rivals a noticeable share of global deforestation emissions, with yearly damages in the tens of billions of dollars. These emissions sit outside current carbon accounting and markets. Protecting coasts, they conclude, is climate policy hiding in plain sight.

europmc-pmc3491353: Feedback learning got a brain-wave review. This 2012 review surveys brain-wave studies of feedback learning. The author maps the studies. Their overview guides neuroscience. San Martín's review is a classic. The paper is widely cited. It is widely taught. The review shaped decision research.

europmc-pmc3834153: Cryo-EM got a self-fooling check. This 2013 paper checks self-fooling in cryo-EM maps. The authors reveal the check. Their work guides structural biology. Chen's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped microscopy.

europmc-pmc3989053: MRSA got a new-bad-strain review. This 2014 paper reviews a new MRSA strain. The authors map the strain. Their review guides microbiology. Paterson's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped infection control. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc4028053: Bees got the lost-genes-found study. This 2014 paper finds lost bee genes. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides genomics. Elsik's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It is a landmark. It shaped bee genomics.
europmc-pmc4073853: Pigs got a new-pig-virus-found study. This 2014 paper finds a new pig virus. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides veterinary science. Wang's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Vets rely on it.
europmc-pmc4106453: Seniors got a word-list-tasks review. This 2014 paper asks what word lists measure. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides psychology. Shao's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped aging research. The review is widely taught. Clinicians rely on it.

Antimicrobial resistance (germs beating drugs) represents one of the most crucial threats to public health and modern health care. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
europmc-pmc9848053: This 2023 research paper covers yahs: yet another hi-c scaffolding tool. Summary we present yahs, a user-friendly command-line tool for the building of chromosome-scale scaffolds from hi-c data. A tested new tool like this gives doctors a steadier way to measure what they see in patients.
europmc-pmc9857053: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on obesity and cancer: a current survey of epidemiology (how diseases spread in populations), pathogenesis (how the disease develops), results, and care. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc9936053: Doctors and scientists took on the use of delphi in health sciences research: a narrative review in this 2023 review paper. It walks through what the field currently knows, study by study. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc9979453: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on CD39/CD73/A2AR pathway and cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
eutropius-abridgment-watson-1853:
Eutropius wrote his Breviarium, a short history of Rome, around 369 CE for the emperor Valens, who wanted the past in brief. John Selby Watson translated it into English in 1853, adding a notice on the author's life. In ten slim books the story runs from Romulus to the emperor Jovian.

Each reign gets a few crisp lines: wars won, lands gained, emperors made and unmade. The plain style made the book a school text for a thousand years, the most copied Roman history of the Middle Ages. Readers who want the whole arc of Rome in one short read still start here.
filmer-advertisement-to-jury-men-english:
Robert Filmer, the royalist thinker, published his Advertisement to the Jury-Men of England in 1653. The tract warns jurors against convicting witches on rotten evidence. Filmer also draws a neat line between the witch of English law and the witch of Hebrew Scripture, arguing the two are not the same.

His caution is legal rather than tender. Bad proofs, he insists, make bad verdicts, whatever the crime. Coming from a defender of kings, the skepticism surprises. The law here questions itself in a quiet voice. Filmer's pamphlet belongs to the slow English retreat from witch convictions, led as much by lawyers' doubts about evidence as by any change of heart.
frus-1861-d153:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 September 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 153 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The crossing habit of the Paris file appears once more in September. Each man wrote from his own week's facts, not the other's. The record gains from it: two honest views of one bond, neither trimmed to fit the last letter. Neither view was trimmed to please the other, which gives the file its force. Force of that kind is why scholars still read this file with close care.
frus-1861-d253:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands, dated 18 September 1861. Congress received it as Document 253 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d53:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 June 1861. It is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams and Seward wrote to each other on the same day more than once that summer. Neither could answer the other's latest word for at least two weeks. Their letters form two lines that cross but never quite meet, a true picture of rule by mail across an ocean. Their crossed letters of June show a bond of trust that distance could not fray. Trust that survives slow mails is the strongest kind a service can build.
frus-1862-d153:
A dispatch of 26 September 1862 from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, as Document 153 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of many Seward letters sent across the Atlantic that fall.

London and Washington were ten days or more apart by mail steamer, so each side often answered news the other had already moved past. That gap shaped the tone of the whole exchange. Short, frequent dispatches like this one kept the envoy supplied with fresh orders and fresh facts as the British cabinet weighed its course. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d253:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 19 February 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 253 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter joined the regular flow between the Department and the Paris legation.

Mid-February 1862 brought the surrender of Fort Donelson, a Union triumph that impressed foreign watchers. Seward could write to Europe from a stronger hand than he had held in months. His letters to Dayton in this season worked that advantage, pressing France to keep its distance from the Confederacy while Union arms advanced. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d353:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to Henri Mercier on 10 January 1862. In a letter printed as Document 353 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier served as the French minister in Washington.

Early January was a settling time after the Trent settlement, with both Britain and France recalculating their American course. French forces were ashore in Mexico, and Washington wanted French aims stated plainly. Seward's letters to Mercier in this season kept the channel warm while harder questions formed behind it. French citizens and ships caught by the war gave the legation a steady stream of case work.
frus-1862-d453:
Six days after his last order to Vienna, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to John Lothrop Motley on 10 March 1862. The dispatch is Document 453 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The quick follow-up is typical of Seward's style: when news moved, instructions moved with it. That week the ironclads Monitor and Merrimack had just fought in Hampton Roads, an event every naval power in Europe studied closely. Motley needed Washington's account of such events before Vienna's court formed its own. Short orders like this one kept American ministers current, and they make the printed file read like the working log of a government at war.
frus-1862-d53:
By the date of 26 April 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 53 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d553:
The Belgian file opens on 17 March 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Brussels. It is Document 553 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Belgium was a small, industrial kingdom whose king, Leopold I, was uncle and adviser to half the courts of Europe. Sanford, a wealthy and energetic Connecticut man, made Brussels a listening post as much as a legation. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Belgian court. The letter begins a file in which a minor post punches above its weight, because Sanford reported everything and knew everyone.
frus-1862-d653:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Townsend Harris in Japan on 7 October 1861. Harris was nearing the end of his time as the first American minister there. The letter is document 653 in the Foreign Relations volume covering 1862.

By the fall of 1861 the Civil War filled Seward's desk, yet the Japan file still drew his care. Letters of this kind kept the legation in line with Washington's plans and told Harris what news from home might mean for his work. It is one piece of the steady stream that held a new and fragile link between the two lands.
frus-1863p1-d153:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 10 April 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 153 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a Seward letter often added the point that had just ripened at home. In April 1863 the ripening news was of the war and of Congress's mood. Adams had to know both to speak well in London. This letter is the second half of the day's work from Washington. Filed with its twin, it keeps the exchange's pace into mid-April.
frus-1863p1-d253:
The State Department's mail for London dated 29 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 253 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d353:
A formal note dated 7 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 353 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Trade bound the countries tightly, from Southern cotton to British mills. Both sides had much to lose from a break, and the notes reflect that caution. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d453:
Document 453 in the volume is a letter of 9 April 1863 from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d53:
Stephen R. Mallory wrote to James M. Mason on 30 October 1862. Mallory was the Confederate secretary of the navy; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 53 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mallory wrote to London twice in this file within the week, a sign of how much of his navy was being built in British yards. Mason was his man on the spot, facing the builders and the British law. This letter is part of that traffic. Read against the Adams mail in the same volume, it shows both sides of one fight. One side sought ships for the South. The other drove to stop them.
frus-1863p1-d553:
Secretary William H. Seward addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 6 June 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d653:
F. W. Seward, the Assistant Secretary of State sent an official note to Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London on 2 November 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d153: On November 21, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, and two more Churchill notes of the same date follow in the volume. This one is Document 153 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three notes in a day, on the eve of a conference both men were attending in person, shows how much still ran on paper. The record gives the date and the names. The text is in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d253:
President Roosevelt's morning calls at Cairo on 23 November 1943 are reconstructed by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The Log lists the visitors: Vyshinsky, Mountbatten, Churchill with his daughter, the Chiangs, and three Chinese generals. No memoranda of the talks were made, so the editors rely on letters from Harriman and Bohlen.

The fullest account concerns Andrey Vyshinsky, who was passing through on his way to serve as the Soviet member of the Advisory Council for Italy. Roosevelt urged close three-power cooperation on that council, aired his troubles with de Gaulle, and floated trusteeship for immature countries, naming Morocco. Vyshinsky agreed in general terms and seemed struck by the President's frankness. The note also weighs when Tehran lodging invitations from Russia and Britain reached Roosevelt.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d353:
The Log of the President's trip continues with the Tehran chapter, covering 27 November to 2 December 1943. Kept hour by hour by Lieutenant William Rigdon, it opens with a fog-delayed departure from Cairo on the morning of 27 November.

The President's plane took off at seven minutes past seven. It flew 1,310 miles in about six and a half hours. The route passed over the Suez Canal and circled Jerusalem for the view. It then followed the Lend-Lease road and rail lines across Iraq and Iran. Trainloads of supplies bound for Russia could be seen from the air. The party landed at Gale Morghe airport, a Russian army field south of Tehran, with no honors, by request, for security. General Connolly met the President, who drove straight to the American Legation.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d453: Inserted at Document 453, an editorial note carries the historians' voice. The Cairo-Tehran volume collects papers from the 1943 summit conferences. Its editors added notes where context was missing from the file. A note might explain an earlier decision or cite a parallel record. Cairo hosted talks before and after the Tehran meeting with Stalin. Keeping those stages straight is part of the note's work here.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d53: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on October 22, 1943, the day after their previous exchange in this series. The letter is Document 53 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Replies at a day's turn were the rhythm of their wartime partnership. The record states sender, receiver, and date, and offers no subject line. In the published volume it sits with the other papers written while the foreign ministers met in Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d553:
President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin on February 23, 1944, keeping up the direct correspondence the two men had begun before they ever met. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume, in its follow-up section.

By February the Red Army was advancing fast, and the questions between Washington and Moscow mixed military coordination with the first hard problems of Poland and the postwar map. Roosevelt's letters to Stalin worked to hold the partnership steady through those strains. For readers, this message belongs to the testing season of the alliance, when Tehran's goodwill met the realities of armies moving west.
frus-1944-quebec-d153:
British strategy for the war against Japan is set out in this chiefs of staff memorandum of August 23, 1944. Since the Sextant Conference, American forces had raced across the Pacific, Japan had reinforced Burma to ten divisions, and Germany's possible collapse might soon free troops. London had studied how British forces could best help finish the Pacific war.

The paper rejects continuing the slog in North Burma, where sickness alone cost 282,000 casualties in early 1944. Instead it backs Mountbatten's Vanguard plan: seize Rangoon by airborne assault and cut Japan's communications in Burma. It also offers a strong British fleet, built around new battleships and carriers, to serve under American command in the main operations against Japan by mid-1945.
frus-1944-quebec-d253:
Roosevelt answered Stettinius from Quebec on September 15, 1944, and the compromise voting formula found no favor. Neither he nor Churchill was inclined to approve the proposed amendment. Roosevelt's own thought was to record the subject in the Dumbarton Oaks agreement as discussed but undecided, leaving it to the meeting of the United Nations.

Churchill feared that course would be unacceptable to the Russians. They would know they faced overwhelming defeat in a United Nations meeting, grow sore, and take it out on the allies on some other point. Roosevelt counseled keeping on trying. Failing agreement, he preferred silence about the disagreement, or a general statement that certain points remained open. The editors note both London and Moscow soon rejected the formula officially.
frus-1944-quebec-d53:
Lester B. Pearson, Canada's ambassador in Washington, wrote to Harry Hopkins on September 3, 1944. Pearson, later Canada's prime minister, was then his country's chief envoy to the United States. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Canada was host to the coming conference and a full partner in the war, and Pearson's channel to Hopkins handled the Canadian side of the arrangements from Washington. A message in this channel shows the host country working quietly inside the alliance's machinery. For readers, it adds a diplomat of future fame to the conference's supporting cast.
frus-1945-50-intel-d153:
A memorandum dated 6 June 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Langer). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Staff Committee. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 153 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d253:
Dated 9 December 1947, this memorandum runs from the Executive Secretary (Souers) to the Members of the National Security Council. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 253, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d353:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached Allen W. Dulles on 17 November 1948. Readers meet it as document 353 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles survey team was checking how well the CIA worked, and agencies across Washington were stating their views on the record.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d53:
Rear Admiral Thomas Inglis, chief of naval intelligence, wrote to Admiral King, chief of naval operations, on 30 November 1945. The paper moved inside the Navy's own chain. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Naval intelligence had won great victories in the war, above all in code-breaking, and its chief meant to keep its strength and secrets. Inglis reported to the one man whose backing he most needed. Readers meet the Navy thinking as a service here, distinct from Forrestal's cabinet-level maneuvering. The two levels, the uniformed chief and the secretary, worked the same cause from different chairs, and the volume lets readers watch both at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d153:
From Warm Springs on 15 December 1944, Roosevelt asked Churchill what to do next about Poland. His top secret telegram, number 674, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the prime minister's Commons statement on the Polish question.

Roosevelt wants Churchill's judgment on two things. First, can Mikolajczyk come back into power with enough authority to carry out his plans? Second, what should the allies do if the Lublin Committee declares itself Poland's provisional government and Stalin recognizes it? He wonders whether to ask Stalin to hold off any firm step until the three leaders meet. Pressure at home, he adds, may force him to publish the policy points of his letter to Mikolajczyk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d253:
Stalin argued for an invasion through Switzerland at a Moscow military conference, Harriman reported on 15 October 1944. His account to the President, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, covers the previous night's session. General Brooke, backed by Churchill, had laid out the allied plans.

Stalin called the attack on the Ruhr the knockout blow for Germany, yet again urged turning the Siegfried Line from the south, through Switzerland. Churchill explained why that move would not work, and voiced confidence in the drive in the north. On Italy, Stalin showed keen interest in landings on the Istrian peninsula, and in allied and Soviet forces joining hands in Austria. General Antonov then gave the Red Army's position, starting with an offensive in the far north, two miles from Petsamo.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d353:
Alger Hiss filled pages with pencil notes during the February 6, 1945 plenary at Livadia Palace. His jottings open with errands — a note to the President, pictures to be sent, a redraft on voting — then list who sat where. The three delegations are named man by man, down to the interpreters standing behind the chairs.

The substance follows in shorthand bursts. Stettinius reported that "and the dismemberment" would be added to Article XII of the surrender terms. Molotov withdrew a further proposal of his own. Churchill said his Cabinet had not approved the instrument, yet he welcomed the agreement. Hiss shows the session as a staffer lived it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d453:
Hiss's jottings of February 10, 1945, follow Eden's report on Poland to the plenary. Agreement had been reached, Eden said, with two questions outstanding. He read the draft as it then stood. It carried changes agreed by Churchill and Stettinius in a private meeting before the session, plus Molotov's noon amendment.

A new amendment appears in the notes: the powers would exchange ambassadors, by whose reports their governments would keep informed about Poland. Churchill then spoke on frontiers. All were agreed on the eastern frontier, and in principle on the western. The Poles were to have East Prussia and freedom to go to the Oder line. Hiss shows the formula closing, clause by clause.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d53: Roosevelt closed this opening run of papers with a message to Churchill on 12 January 1945. It is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Days later the president sailed for the Mediterranean, and the written preparation in these fifty-three documents gave way to the conferences themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d153:
Secretary of State Stettinius raised the idea of a joint surrender demand on Japan in a telegram from San Francisco dated June 15, 1945. The message to Grew is document 153 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Joint Chiefs had reported that Japan might seek to end the war on certain terms.

Stettinius asks whether the demand for unconditional surrender should be made a three- or four-power demand, issued at or after the Big Three meeting. It might be paired with some assurances to the Japanese about their future. Getting Russia to join such a demand would be worth a real effort, he argues. If a demand is needed when the Okinawa fighting ends, the President should issue it alone, in a way that does not block later Big Three action. The idea led toward the Potsdam Declaration issued that July.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d253:
A briefing paper laid out Korea's future in three stages, dated July 4, 1945. The paper is document 253 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is a companion to the paper on interim administration printed just before it in the volume.

The first stage is an Allied military government, with Allied representation in the occupation army and its administration so far as practicable. The second is an interim international supervisory administration, running Korea until the Koreans can govern themselves. The third is a free and independent Korea, as the Cairo Declaration promised. The Department's recommendations are stated in three short paragraphs, one for each stage. In the event, the middle stage never came: Korea was divided at the 38th parallel instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d353:
How the Reparations Commission and the Control Council should share power is mapped in a Joint Civil Affairs Committee memorandum. American policy, set down for Pauley's guidance in Moscow, made the occupation authorities responsible for carrying out the reparations plan inside Germany. The two bodies were not to work at cross purposes.

Within that rule, the Control Council could hold back specific items from transfer as reparations. It could act when removal would cut Germany's means below the least level the occupation's other aims required. If the Council split, a zone commander who believed an item should stay could carry the question higher. The memo guards German recovery against reparations demands.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d453:
Hayter, secretary general of the British delegation, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945, with news on the Greek elections. Since his letter of the night before, the Foreign Office had heard that the Greek government agreed to the proposals put to it in Athens. The way was therefore open for invitations.

Invitations could now go to the Soviet and French governments. The Foreign Office suggested the invitation to the Russians be made to their representatives at the conference on July 17 or 18. That timing should allow a Soviet reply before the conference, called Terminal, ended. The invitation to France could be made in Paris on the same day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d53:
Churchill gave in on the meeting date in telegram number 75 to President Truman, sent from London on June 6, 1945. The printed extract is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. For days Churchill had argued that July 15 was too late for the Big Three to meet near Berlin.

The whole surviving text is one line: Churchill accepts July 15 and is telling Stalin. Truman had told him a day earlier that no earlier date was possible, and the Prime Minister dropped his push for June or early July. With that, the last of the three leaders fell into line, and planning for the Potsdam Conference could go forward on an agreed date.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d553:
Harold Shantz, the U.S. charge in Belgrade, wired the Acting Secretary of State on July 7, 1945. His secret report is document 553 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the state of politics inside Yugoslavia that summer.

Shantz says there is no free press and no free political life. The secret police act as they please, so freedom from fear is lacking too. He reports that Ivan Subasic, the deputy premier, is glad that civil courts are starting. Yet Subasic fears the leaders have lost grip on their own men below. Subasic had asked that Tito be told the Tito-Subasic deal was not being kept. He hoped the Big Three meeting would say so in public.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d653:
The British Embassy in Washington delivered an aide-memoire on Tangier on June 20, 1945. It is document 653 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its subject is how and when to tell the Soviet government about the coming Tangier talks.

London agrees with Washington that the time to inform Moscow has now come. Tangier, it notes, has lately drawn much press attention. Britain holds that France should be joined with any message to the Soviets on the talks. It proposes that the British and U.S. embassies in Paris approach the French foreign ministry together. A draft cable is attached, setting out the lines the message to Moscow should follow. The short paper shows the care taken to keep Moscow informed, but at arm's length.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1053: Secretary of War Henry Stimson included this passage in his memorandum to President Truman of July 16, 1945. The printed text is an extract; the rest appears elsewhere in the volume. Stimson says he would grant Poland some areas on her western border. They would offset the territory Poland is to cede to Russia in the east. His condition concerns the Germans living in those western areas. Russia, he insists, must show that proper care will be made for those millions. They must not be shunted onto American responsibility.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1153:
James Clement Dunn, an assistant secretary of state on the American team, wrote this memorandum on 31 July 1945. Dunn was a career diplomat of long service. His papers summed up staff judgment for the team's leaders in the summit's last round.

A note written two days before the close belongs to the work of finishing: fixing stands, noting what remained open, and preparing the record. Dunn's view is the trained envoy's, not the politician's. His memoranda across the volume show how the American machine thought as it worked. This one catches it at the finish line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1253:
The Secretary of State wrote to Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov on 26 July 1945. Byrnes to Molotov was the working channel between the American and Soviet chiefs at Potsdam. The two men handled much of the summit's hardest business between themselves.

A letter on this channel could press a point, propose a text, or register a stand for the record. This one went out the day the Allied terms to Japan were issued and Britain changed leaders. It shows the American chief tending the Soviet tie on the summit's fullest day. The paper joins the set of Byrnes-Molotov exchanges that carried the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1353:
Joseph Grew, the acting secretary of state, wrote to Secretary Byrnes at Potsdam on 19 July 1945. Grew's letters crossed the Atlantic throughout the conference, keeping the secretary tied to his department. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

These home-office letters did quiet but vital work: they told the men abroad what Congress, the press, and other agencies were doing in Washington. A secretary cut off from that flow would have bargained half blind. This second Grew letter in the run shows the channel in steady use. It rounds out the picture of a department split between two cities for a month.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-153:
Another delegation memorandum bears the date July 31, 1945, the eve of the Potsdam close. The volume holds a cluster of staff papers from that day. Each one moved a small piece of the ending into place. This memo was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Clustered papers reveal the division of labor at the end. While leaders met, officers chased the details that made agreement real. The memorandum preserves one such chase in writing. Readers studying the final protocol can use papers like this to see its roots. They show the settlement as work, not just words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-53:
An editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers covers a visit by Secretary Stimson to Churchill on July 21, 1945. No official record of the conversation has been found, the editors say. In its place they print Stimson's diary entry for that day.

Stimson writes that he left the Little White House and picked up Harvey Bundy on the way. At the prime minister's house they conferred with Churchill and Lord Cherwell. Stimson turned over a paper to Churchill, who began reading it on the spot. A few minutes before five, Churchill was interrupted and had to hurry to the Big Three conference. He asked Stimson to return the following morning to finish up the report. The paper is identified by the editors as document 1305, the fuller report in the atomic series printed later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d753:
Artemus Gates, Under Secretary of the Navy, wrote to a senior fleet plans officer on July 21, 1945. Document 753 is a Navy house paper from the Potsdam week. It passed between the Navy's civilian head and the staff of the Commander in Chief, United States Fleet. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

Service papers like this one show the war machine's inner mail. Civilian chiefs and uniformed planners traded views in plain terms. Readers see naval concerns carried at a high level while the summit sat. The document widens the volume beyond diplomats: fleets, too, had a stake in what Potsdam decided.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d853:
Document 853 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 18, 1945. Staff drafted it on the conference's second day. Early working papers turned briefing books into live texts. This one stayed in the delegation files and entered the second Potsdam volume.

Second-day drafts show a team settling to its work. The writers now had the other sides' tones in their ears. Readers can look for early adjustments in the paper's lines. The document belongs to the foundation layer of the talks. Before the famous clashes came days of quiet drafting, and this paper is a piece of that groundwork.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d953:
Soviet delegates handed this reparations proposal to Secretary Byrnes on July 30, 1945, though the paper itself is undated. Each government would take one-time removals from its own zone within two years of the surrender. The removals should speed rebuilding in countries that suffered under German occupation, and cut Germany's war potential.

Because Soviet heavy industry suffered huge losses, the USSR also claims 5.5 to 6 million tons of listed equipment from the western zones, mainly the Ruhr. It further claims company shares worth 500 million dollars. Yearly deliveries of current goods would total 8 billion dollars over ten years, half going to the USSR.
frus-1961-63v11-d53: Another 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the Missile Crisis volume. The crisis papers. This document holds that memo. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. The text survives intact.
frus-1969-76v02-d53: A 1969-1976 FRUS memorandum from President Nixon to the Secretary. The president wrote. This document preserves that memo. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
galileo-sidereus-nuncius-1653:
Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius, The Starry Messenger, appears here in the 1653 London Latin printing. Galileo published the work in Latin in 1610, reporting what his improved telescope showed. No public-domain English translation exists for this line, so the text stands in Latin, as early readers across Europe read it.

Galileo reported mountains on the Moon, four moons circling Jupiter, and crowds of stars inside the Milky Way. Each sight struck the old picture of perfect, unchanging heavens. News of the book raced across Europe and made Galileo famous and suspect at once. The slim 1610 report, kept here in its 1653 London form, is one of the founding documents of modern astronomy.
gao-gaoreports-b-297553: Bio-Rad Laboratories took its February 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Lab giants get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297853: The Castle Group took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-306353: The Capitol architect's contract ratification got a fiscal ruling in this October 2005 GAO call, which tests the ratification. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the ratification was legal. The law had the final word. The ratification had to be legal.
gao-gaoreports-b-310553: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Comprehensive Health Services, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-311453: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by L-3 Communications EOTech, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-400153: This 2008 GAO ruling is about agency Tender Official at Gary M. Williamson. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-253: Freshwater funding got a GAO map in 2005, and the report covers federal dollars at home and abroad. The review follows the water money. The rivers deserved the accounting. The map was drawn. The dollars were followed. The water money was followed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-753: Tax compliance needed better data in 2005, and GAO's report says improved compliance figures and long-term goals would support strategy. The findings demand the information. The report warns that the cheating deserved chasing. The data had to be better. The cheating deserved chasing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-953: Fund-raising stamp sales factors got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the Postal Service's charity stamp lessons were learned. The findings take the measure. The report shows the cause stamps' sales were studied. The lessons had to be learned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-353: Forest pest invasions offered lessons in 2006, and GAO's report says three recent infestations could guide future management. The findings extract the wisdom. The report warns that the tiny invaders threatened the mighty woods. The lessons had to be learned. The woods' tiny enemies needed studying.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-53: Youth Opportunity Grants offered lessons in 2006, and GAO's report says the program taught lessons, though Labor needed to release the data. The findings balance the wisdom and the secrecy. The report warns that the young workers' program deserved sunlight. The data had to be available.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-753: Olympic security planning needed improving in 2006, and GAO's report says better planning could enhance U.S. support to future games. The findings prescribe the preparation. The report warns that the world's stage deserved American readiness. The planning had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1053: The SEC was retooling its exams in 2007 — aiming at risk, opening the curtains — and GAO's report grades the effort. The findings track the shift from box-checking to hunting where the danger lives. For investors, the payoff of smarter exams is a watchdog that bites before the scandal, not after.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1153: This 2007 GAO report finds State Department staff planning blind to the aid mission. The department was taking on bigger foreign-aid jobs without lining up the people to do them, GAO said. The report warns that plans drawn without the real workload leave the diplomacy-and-development bench thin where it counts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-153: Donating federal cars to youth programs got a GAO look in 2007, and the report examines the effects of giving vehicles to YouthBuild. The findings measure the benefits. The report shows the old sedans were driving new opportunities. The donations had to do good.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-253: Bank capital rules needed sunlight in 2007, and GAO's report says regulators had to improve transparency and finish the job. The findings press for completion. The report's timing proved prophetic: the crash was a year away. The banks' cushions were thinner than claimed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-353: Air ambulances needed better watching in 2007, and GAO's report says improved data collection was essential for overseeing the industry. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the flying ERs should not fly blind to regulators. The patients in the air deserved oversight on the ground.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-53: Food stamp fraud at shady stores needed targeting in 2007, and GAO's report says better targeting of likely traffickers would strengthen integrity. The findings demand the focus. The report warns that the corner-store scams were stealing from the hungry. The cheats had to be caught.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-653: Taxpayer-funded science was going dark in 2007 — GAO's report says the rules for sharing federal research needed clarifying. The findings press selected agencies to open up. The report's creed: the public paid for the discoveries, so the public should get to read them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-153: GAO published its findings on iraq Reconstruction: Better Data Needed to Assess Iraq's Budget Execution in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-53: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report telling the Department of the Navy it needs a real management structure and defined policies for its business-system investments. Like the Air Force, the Navy was buying financial and logistics software without institutional discipline. GAO's findings press the service to treat billion-dollar IT spending with the same rigor it applies to ships and aircraft.
guicciardini-history-of-italy-goddard-vo:
Francesco Guicciardini, a Florentine statesman, wrote his Storia d'Italia between 1537 and 1540, and it was first printed in 1561. Volume one here opens Austin Parke Goddard's English translation, issued from 1753 to 1761 in ten volumes. Guicciardini had served popes and governed cities, and he wrote Italy's recent past as an insider.

His subject is the Italian wars, the long invasion and struggle that began in 1494. France, Spain, and the empire fought across a peninsula split into rival states. Guicciardini traces how that split invited ruin, with a cool, probing mind. His work is often called the first modern analytical history, and volume one shows why.

Volume two continues Goddard's English version of Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy, the translation of 1753 to 1761. Guicciardini wrote the Storia d'Italia in 1537 to 1540, after a career at the top of Florentine and papal politics. It reached print in 1561, after his death, and Europe read it as a revelation.

The history follows the Italian wars year by year, siege by siege, treaty by broken treaty. Guicciardini refuses simple blame: ambition, fear, and chance share the guilt in his pages. His divided Italy stands as a warning of what disunion costs a rich land. Volume two keeps his clear, severe analysis moving through the storm.

Goddard's translation of Guicciardini's History of Italy reaches volume three of ten. Francesco Guicciardini composed the work between 1537 and 1540, drawing on state papers and his own years in high office. The Storia d'Italia was first printed in 1561 and soon ranked with the great histories of the age.

Its theme is tragedy at national scale: a brilliant, wealthy peninsula torn by its own rivalries. Foreign kings marched in, and Italian states called them in against each other. Guicciardini weighs each prince and republic with the same unsparing hand. Later historians learned from his method of close, causal analysis. Volume three carries that method deeper into the wars.

Volume four of Goddard's English Guicciardini, from the ten-volume translation of 1753 to 1761, continues the History of Italy. Francesco Guicciardini wrote the original in 1537 to 1540, and it was printed in 1561. He had governed Modena and the Romagna for the pope, and negotiated with kings, before turning to history in forced retirement.

Retirement gave him distance, and distance gave the book its cool, dissecting power. The Italian wars unfold in his pages as a chain of choices, each one narrowing the next. No hero escapes his scrutiny, and no folly lacks its cause. Volume four holds the middle of that chain, link by hard link.

Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy reaches its fifth volume in Goddard's translation, the English set of 1753 to 1761. The Italian work, written in 1537 to 1540 and printed in 1561, covers the decades when Italy became the battleground of Europe. Guicciardini knew the courts he describes from the inside.

At the midpoint of the set, his great argument stands fully visible. Italy's states, rich and cultured, lacked union, and so fell prey to France, Spain, and the empire in turn. Guicciardini tells the story with a statesman's grasp of motive and money. His history founded a cooler, modern way of explaining events. Volume five keeps that explanation at full strength.

Volume six continues Goddard's ten-volume English Guicciardini, translated between 1753 and 1761. Francesco Guicciardini's Storia d'Italia, written in 1537 to 1540 and first printed in 1561, narrates the Italian wars from 1494 onward. The author had served as ambassador to Spain and as a papal governor, and his history breathes that experience.

Campaigns, leagues, and betrayals fill these pages, each traced to the interests that drove it. Guicciardini trusted no slogan and no hero, only the record and the motive behind it. That habit made his book the first truly analytical history of the modern kind. Volume six advances the long tragedy of a divided peninsula, told by one of its ablest sons.

Goddard's English History of Italy by Francesco Guicciardini moves into volume seven of ten. The translation ran from 1753 to 1761; the Italian original was written in 1537 to 1540 and printed in 1561. Guicciardini, once a power in Florence and the papal states, wrote the wars of his age as a man who had helped to wage them.

The seventh volume keeps his steady gaze on the struggle for Italy. Great powers clash, small states scheme, and the peninsula pays for every bargain. Guicciardini's genius lies in showing how each disaster grew from choices men praised at the time. His cool method still teaches historians how to argue from evidence. The tragedy deepens here.

Volume eight of Goddard's translation continues Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy toward its later books. The English set ran to ten volumes between 1753 and 1761. Guicciardini's Italian text, composed in 1537 to 1540 and printed in 1561, had long been a classic before Goddard Englished it.

The wars roll on in these pages: France and the empire fighting over Italian soil, Italian states shifting sides to survive. Guicciardini anatomizes each shift with a surgeon's patience. He shows a peninsula whose disunion turned its wealth into a prize for others. Readers rank the work as the first modern analytical history for good reason. Volume eight sustains that rank, campaign by campaign.

The ninth volume of Goddard's English Guicciardini stands one step from the end of the ten-volume set. Francesco Guicciardini wrote his History of Italy in 1537 to 1540; it was printed in 1561, after his death. Goddard's translation, 1753 to 1761, brought the Florentine's masterpiece to English readers entire.

Near the close, the Italian wars have consumed a generation, and Guicciardini's verdict has only hardened. Division invited invasion; invasion fed on division; and Italy's states learned too late. His analysis stays close to councils, purses, and armies, where causes truly live. Volume nine carries the great history to the edge of its somber end, with its method undimmed.

Volume ten completes Goddard's English translation of Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy, the set of 1753 to 1761. Guicciardini wrote the Storia d'Italia in 1537 to 1540, and it was first printed in 1561. With this volume, his account of the Italian wars and of Italy's fall from freedom stands whole in English.

The final books gather the harvest of fifty years of invasion and rivalry. Guicciardini ends as he began, a statesman explaining power to anyone wise enough to listen. His work taught Europe a new, analytical way to write history, cool and causal. To finish volume ten is to close one of the founding books of modern historiography.
hawthorne-tanglewood-tales-1853:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Tanglewood Tales in 1853, his second volume of Greek myths for children. With A Wonder-Book, it forms the canon of children's classical mythology in English for the young. Eustace Bright returns to Tanglewood with six more tales for his troop of child listeners there.

Theseus threads the labyrinth, Jason seeks the Golden Fleece, and Circe turns men to swine. Hawthorne keeps the marvels and trims the blood, though his Ulysses still outwits monsters and storms. The children interrupt, doubt, and delight, giving the old myths a living fireside air in Massachusetts. His prose makes Greek names feel like household words to readers meeting them for the first time. Generations met the classical world first in these two friendly, golden volumes of tales.
henry-huntingdon-chronicle-forester-1853:
Henry, archdeacon of Huntingdon, wrote his Historia Anglorum at the order of his bishop, and carried it to the year 1154. Thomas Forester translated the chronicle into English in 1853. Henry tells the story of England from the Roman landing to the death of King Stephen.

He frames the tale as five great plagues of invasion sent for the sins of the land. They are the Romans, the Picts and Scots, the Saxons, the Danes, and the Normans. Battle pieces, speeches, and verses of his own stud the prose. Henry knew the court of Henry I and wrote of men his elders had seen. His chronicle is a key voice of the twelfth century.
instrument-of-government-1653:
England gained its first written constitution in December 1653, when the Council of Officers adopted the Instrument of Government. John Lambert did much of the drafting. The plan replaced the Rump Parliament after the Civil War and named Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector, the country's single head of state.

Power was split three ways: the Protector ruled with a Council of State, and a Parliament chosen every three years held the purse and made laws. The text also promised freedom of worship to most Protestants and set rules for votes and seats. It worked for less than four years, yet later constitution writers still study its design.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-rudo:
Rudolf Löwenstein (1819–1891) was a German author born at Breslau and baptized at age nine, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman tells his story. He studied at Breslau and Berlin, earning his doctorate in 1843. His children’s songs, “Der Kindergarten” (1846), first made his name.

In 1848 Löwenstein helped found the famous comic paper “Kladderadatsch” and became one of its chief editors. A liberal during the revolution of 1848, he was expelled from Prussia in 1849, returned in 1850, and edited the paper for thirty-seven years. The article also notes his later newspaper work, his retirement in 1887, and the political poems of 1860 to 1880 that won him wide fame. It preserves a lively record of a poet who shaped German humor and politics in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magazin-fur-die:
Magazin für die Wissenschaft des Judenthums, a German journal of Jewish scholarship, is described in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Abraham Berliner founded it on January 1, 1874. It first appeared every two months under a title about Jewish history and literature. Early issues carried Berliner's studies of Hebrew manuscripts in Italian libraries.

The article traces the journal's growth and its end. With the third volume in 1876 it became a quarterly of larger format. Stricter scholarly articles were welcomed, and a Hebrew supplement presented unpublished manuscripts. David Hoffmann joined Berliner as co-editor. Contributors included Steinschneider, Kaufmann, Bacher, and Harkavy, among the leading scholars of the age. The standard held for twenty years. In 1893 the editors suspended publication under pressure of other duties. The entry preserves the record of a journal central to the science of Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandelstamm-ben:
Benjamin ben Joseph Mandelstamm, a Russian Hebraist, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Zhagory at the end of the eighteenth century, he received a liberal education. For over forty years, with some breaks, he worked for the Gunzburg family. From 1864 he was their representative at Simferopol. He died there in 1886.

The article centers on his three-part book, Hazon la-Mo'ed, printed at Vienna in 1877. Its first part describes his journey from Zhagory to Moscow about 1835. The second prints his Wilna letters on Lilienthal's education mission in Russia. Once enthusiastic, he turned against the mission's results and methods. The third part describes the Crimea and plans to better Russia's Jews. He also wrote a Hebrew description of Paris after visiting in 1875. Critics rank him among the best Hebrew prose writers, though too florid for modern taste.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-roger-1045:
Roger Marx was a French art critic. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Nancy on August 28, 1859. He moved to Paris in 1878 and wrote for theater and art journals. By 1883 he was art critic, and then literary critic, of the newspaper Voltaire.

His career ran through the art administration of France. He served as secretary and then inspector of the Academy of Fine Arts. In 1886 the government sent him to Spain to study design schools, and from 1889 he was assistant inspector-general of museums. He organized the centennial display of French art at the Paris Exposition of 1900. The entry lists his many books, above all his histories of the French medal, and notes his strongly individual style as a writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menander-10653:
Menander, in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, is first of all a puzzle of attribution, examined by Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss. A Syriac manuscript in the British Museum, printed by Land in 1862, carries a book of proverbs headed "The sage Menander said." Was he a real Hellenistic Jew? Do his Greek sayings survive only in Syriac? Or is the famous comic poet's name a borrowed label, as Schürer supposed? Frankenberg, the article reports, settled the substance if not the name. The sentences are Jewish work, kin throughout to the Book of Proverbs and to Ecclesiasticus.

The entry then quotes the evidence in a string of parallels. Rejoice in your children. Wrong your maidservant, and God's vengeance finds you. A quarrelsome wife is hell. Never show a full purse at another man's table. Each saying is printed beside its biblical cousins. The printing lets the reader judge the family resemblance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-ernst-107:
Ernst Meyer, a Danish genre painter born at Altona on May 11, 1797, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer, published in 1906. He trained in Copenhagen at the Academy of Arts and won two silver medals as a young pupil. An early Gretchen painting, shown in 1818, drew warm notice.

Meyer hoped to paint history but gave that up after a failed attempt, spent three years in Munich, and settled in Rome among Danish artists around the sculptor Thorwaldsen. His best-known canvas, Sailors Landing Travelers at Capri, shown at Copenhagen in 1837, grew so popular that he painted several copies of it. He died in Rome in 1861.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minir-10853:
Minir was a family of scholars from Tudela in Spain. Its members turn up later in the East and in Italy. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling record them in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry is a set of short notices rather than a story. Four members were prominent in Tudela's community in 1363. The rest fan out across two more centuries.

Isaac ben Joseph Minir was a commentator and liturgical poet. He studied under Yom-Ṭob of Seville. He wrote a Talmudic commentary called Be'erot Yiẓḥaḳ. His son Joseph became rabbi at Constantine. Joseph spent ten years as a pupil of Isaac ben Sheshet, who prized his scholarship. A Moses Minir was editing Hebrew books at Venice in 1593. A Shem-Ṭob Minir surfaces at Constantinople in 1569.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montagu-hyman-1:
Hyman Montagu, who died in London on February 18, 1895, was an English lawyer whose real fame was coins, as Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind recount in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Trained at the City of London School, he became an expert in bankruptcy law. Collecting came first as beetles, then as coins pursued with enterprising industry until he ranked among the highest numismatists.

He gave a valuable collection to the British Museum and catalogued the coins of the Anglo-Jewish Historical Exhibition of 1887. His books cover England's milled coinage from George I to Victoria and its copper, tin, and bronze issues from Elizabeth on. His Greek coins were his glory: their sale catalogue became the standard work on the subject.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-aaron:
Moses ben Aaron, also called Moses Lwow or Lemberger, was a Moravian and German rabbi born at Lemberg about 1705. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. After study at Nikolsburg he became rabbi of Leipnik at about twenty.

In 1729 King Frederick William the First ordered the Berlin community to make the young man its chief rabbi. The elders protested that he was too young, accepted him under pressure, and within a year paid to have him dismissed. Moses then served at Frankfort on the Oder until 1743 and rose at last to chief rabbi of Moravia. He died at Nikolsburg in 1757.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-netter-eugene-1:
Eugene Netter rose from Alsatian emigrant to Manila's archbishop. Richard Gottheil wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1840 at Bergheim, near Colmar. At fourteen he sailed to New York with his brother. Gabriel joined the Union army and died at Louisville.

Eugene went at sixteen to Porto Rico. Yellow fever there brought him near death. A priest's promise of cure led him to baptism. He recovered and was sent to study at Salamanca. In one year he passed both baccalaureates there. Rome made him a papal gentleman after ten months. Posts in Porto Rico and Spain followed in turn. About 1898 he became archbishop at Manila.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nish-nissa-1155:
Nish is a city of Servia on the Nissava. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish community dates from the early 1700s. Gershon, its first chief rabbi, was elected in 1728. He wrote to Salonica about spelling the town's name.

By the 1700s' end Nish held a fine rabbinical school. Its cemetery keeps the tombs of its tribunal rabbis. Chief Rabbi Alkala'i later held great sway with the Turks. Midhat Pasha ruled the district on his reports. Governors lodged their first days at Alkala'i's house. The sultan gave him the Medjidie order in 1873. Some 700 Jews live there, with one synagogue. Four charities care for its sick, widows, and orphans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orange-11753:
Orange is the chief town of Vaucluse, in France. Gotthard Deutsch and Jules Bauer wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was a small realm of its own till 1702. The first texts on Jews there date from the thirteen hundreds. Those texts show a hard lot for the Jews.

Jews at Orange were charged with greed in loans. They were barred from proof in court against Christians. They could not hold office in the town at all. They paid heavy tax and fed six men for the guard. In 1477 they were shut out of the wheat trade. The town pressed more than once for their casting out. The prince held back, for they paid him well each year. In 1505 the Jews of Orange were cast out at last.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paiva-payba-de-:
De Paiva was a Spanish Marano family of Amsterdam. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Some of its men lived in far off Mexico too. A Marano was a Jew forced to hide his faith. Three men of the name stand out in the entry.

Abraham de Paiva was a poet at Amsterdam about 1687. A Spanish sonnet of his stands in a tract by Barrios. Jacob Ribero de Paiva wrote a Spanish book on sums. Moses Pereyra de Paiva was a merchant of Portuguese stock. He roamed to Malabar and lived at Cochin, in India. He put out a tale of the Jews of those parts. He paid for that book from his own purse in 1687. It came out in more than one tongue in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paulli-holger-o:
Holger Paulli was a Danish merchant who declared himself the Messiah. He was born in Copenhagen in 1644 and died there in 1714. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He first made a fortune in the slave trade.

In 1694 Paulli said God had chosen him to convert the Jews. He left his wife and six children behind. In Amsterdam he printed tracts calling Israel to wake up. He promised a new Jewish kingdom in Palestine by 1720. Dutch officials jailed him in 1701 for his wild claims. Denmark's king later shut down his meetings at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesah-sheni-120:
Pesah Sheni is the second Passover sacrifice of the year. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was also called the lesser Passover. It fell on the fourteenth of Iyyar. Its warrant stands in the Book of Numbers.

The rite served those who missed the first date. Some had been far from the Holy City. Others had been ritually unclean in Nisan. Most rules of the first sacrifice still applied. But the people were not split into three groups. No festal offering joined it, and leaven was allowed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pilpul-12153:
Pilpul is a sharp method of studying the Talmud. The Executive Committee and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word comes from a verb meaning to spice. Study, like food, is seasoned by dispute.

The method pins down each concept in a saying. It then draws out every consequence that follows. Two sayings that seem to agree get tested. If their results clash, the agreement was only skin deep. Two sayings that seem to clash get redefined. Fine limits can melt the clash away.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollonais-ameli:
Amélie Pollonais was a French giver to good causes, born at Marseilles in 1835. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was the daughter of Joseph Jonas Cohen. She wed Désiré Pollonais and made her home in the south of France.

In 1868 she set out a full plan for teaching young children. A second book gave a way for children to teach themselves. For her care of the wounded in the war of 1870 she won a Red Cross medal. Her best known book grew out of visits to poor homes and schools. She helped found a paper for children. In 1898 she set up a society to aid prisoners. Two streets at Villefranche took her name after her death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prey-birds-of-1:
Birds of prey in the Bible are listed by Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz. Their article appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Few clean birds are named in the Old Testament, they note. Unclean birds of prey get two full lists instead. One list stands in Leviticus and one in Deuteronomy. The first names twenty birds and the second names twenty-one.

The common Hebrew name for such birds is ayit. It shows up in Genesis, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Job. The sheer count of names tells its own story. So do the many sayings drawn from these birds' ways. Jews knew these hunters well, the writers say. Yet their flesh was banned as food by the Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pygarg-12453: Pygarg is the name of a clean beast in the book of Deuteronomy. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name stands in the fifth verse of the fourteenth chapter. It follows the Greek form of the text there. Which beast is truly meant has not been settled. The writers give the one source they cite for more. That source is a book on the beasts of the Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reich-moritz-12:
Moritz Reich was a German writer born on April 20, 1831. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Rokitnitz in Bohemia. He died there on March 26, 1857.

The article says his father was a poor ritual slaughterer and cantor. Reich attended schools at Reichenau and at Prague. In 1853 he went to Vienna to write. He devoted himself to literature there. His life was short, ending at age twenty five. After his death his friend Alfred Meissner collected his sketches. They appeared in 1858 as An der Grenze. The book came from Reich's literary remains. The entry preserves a writer cut off very young.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rieti-12753:
Rieti is an Italian family named for the city of Rieti. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The city lay in the Pontifical States. Family members appear there by the late fourteenth century.

The article traces the family to Rome, Sienna, and Bologna. Several members worked as physicians across generations. Michael practiced at Terni in the late 1400s. Solomon practiced at Rome in 1510. Ishmael hosted the false Messiah David Reubeni at Sienna. Yet he refused Reubeni any large financial help. Reubeni bitterly criticized him for that refusal. Ishmael's son Moses funded a mission to Rome. It won a papal decree for Jews at Empoli. The entry shows one family in medicine and public defense.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenhain-georg:
George Rosenhain was a German mathematician born at Königsberg, Prussia, on June 10, 1816. Isidore Singer and S. Gundelfinger wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He taught at Breslau and Vienna before becoming associate professor at Königsberg in 1857.

Rosenhain won fame through a prize essay honored by the Paris Academy in 1846. It treated functions of two variables that reverse certain hard integrals. He proved that the Abel functions defined by Jacobi really exist. That step, from functions of one variable to functions of two, mattered greatly. It helped push higher mathematics forward in the nineteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saadia-b-joseph:
Saadia b. Joseph, called Sa'id al-Fayyumi, was Gaon of Sura and founder of scientific Judaism. Wilhelm Bacher wrote his long entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He was born in Upper Egypt in 892 and died at Sura in 942.

Saadia was the first known bearer of that Hebrew name. His enemies spread base stories about his father's low calling and origin. He answered by claiming descent from Shelah, son of Judah, of the Bible. Among his claimed ancestors stood Hanina b. Dosa, the famed ascetic. The entry opens a life that reshaped Jewish thought for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sama-b-rabba-13: Sama b. Rabba was a Babylonian amora, the last head of the Pumbedita Academy. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He succeeded Rahumai II and officiated about twenty years, from 456 to 476. Tradition says the prayers of Sama and Mar b. Ashi caused a dragon to devour King Yezdegerd II in his bed, ending a persecution of the Jews. Sama is mentioned only three times in the Talmud, and nothing else is known of him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-isaa:
Samuel ben Isaac of Uceda was a Talmudist of Safed in the sixteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His family came from Uceda, and settled at Safed after Spain's banishment.

At Safed Samuel headed a Talmud school kept up by a rich patron. When Solomon di Shiraz died, the school lost its support entirely. Samuel then became an itinerant preacher, traveling to earn his bread. At Constantinople a friend paid to print his last book for him. His works comment on Pirke Abot, on Lamentations, and on Ruth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schechter-solom:
Cyrus Adler and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Solomon Schechter. He leads the Jewish Theological Seminary of America as president of its faculty. Schechter was born in Rumania in 1847. His youth went wholly to rabbinical study. He then trained at Vienna and Berlin. In 1882 he moved to England as tutor to Claude Montefiore.

At Cambridge, Schechter rose from lecturer to reader in rabbinics. His Studies in Judaism appeared in 1896. On May 13 that year, he found the first leaf of Ben Sira in Hebrew. In December he sailed for Egypt and Palestine. He returned from Cairo laden with genizah treasures. That hoard became the Taylor-Schechter collection at Cambridge. From it came The Wisdom of Ben Sira in 1899. The article traces a scholar who remade his field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scott-charles-a:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Charles Alexander Scott. He was born Karl Blumenthal. Scott was an English author. He was born in London in 1803. He died at Venice in November 1866. As a young man he went to Italy for a long stay. He mastered several languages and traveled widely.

In 1848 Scott joined Italy's revolution against Austria. He fought bravely before Venice fell. Later he served as a soldier of fortune under Garibaldi. In 1860 he sought leave to kidnap young Mortara from Rome. His plan had him enter the city disguised as a monk. The attempt was abandoned. That year Lord Seymour had him publicly horsewhipped after a quarrel. Scott won 500 pounds in damages at law. He never truly recovered from the beating. He left large sums to Jewish charities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemaiah-of-soi:
Shemaiah of Soissons, also called ha-Shoshani, was a twelfth-century scholar and pupil of Rashi. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His notes on the Tabernacle's building survive from Exodus chapters. Berliner edited that work from a Munich manuscript in 1864.

Other works by Shemaiah stay in manuscript, the entry notes. They include readings of Deuteronomy and notes on the prayer book. He glossed the Pentateuch and commented on the Song of Solomon. Writers often confuse him with Shemaiah of Troyes, another Rashi pupil. The entry sorts his works out carefully. Readers meet a quiet French scholar whose notes still served synagogues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-signature-13653:
Signature treats how names were placed on writings in the ancient Hebrew world. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the topic. Today a writer signs at the end of a piece. That signing certifies authorship or accepts sponsorship.

Ancient Hebrews apparently did not follow that custom, the entry says. A literary work put its author's name at the start. The Proverbs of Solomon opens one famous example. The vision of Isaiah begins another such book. Usually the full name includes the father's name too. A line closing Psalms' second book ends David's prayers. That reads like a compiler's note, not David's signature. The entry then turns to royal edicts and letters. It shows naming customs that differ sharply from modern practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simonias-modern:
Simonias, now called Samuniyyah, was a city in Galilee. Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lay about two hours southwest of Sepphoris. The Talmud identifies it with the Shimron of Joshua. That older name gave way to Simonias in Greek times.

Josephus calls the place a village in his writings. He tells how Roman cavalry attacked him there at night. The horsemen failed because the ground did not suit cavalry. A story shows the town's Jewish spirit in another way. Its people once asked the patriarch Judah I for a scholar. They wanted a teacher sent to instruct them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-speyer-jacob-sa:
Jacob Samuel Speyer was a Dutch philologist born at Amsterdam in 1849. Isidore Singer and E Slijper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on December 20 of that year. He studied at Amsterdam and at Leyden, graduating in 1872. He taught at Hoorn and at the Amsterdam gymnasium for years.

In 1877 he became lecturer in Sanskrit at Amsterdam. In 1888 he was called to Gröningen as professor of Latin. In 1903 he succeeded his teacher Kern at Leyden in Sanskrit. His works include Sanskrit Syntax and Vedische- und Sanskritsyntax. He translated the Sanskrit Jatakamala into English for scholars. He also edited the Museum journal from 1893 to 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stilling-jakob-:
Jakob Stilling was a German eye doctor born at Cassel on September 22, 1842. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was the son of Benedikt Stilling, the surgeon. He studied at Marburg, Würzburg, Berlin, and Paris. He earned his medical degree in 1865.

In 1867 Stilling set up as an eye specialist in Cassel. He later taught eye medicine at the University of Strasburg. He became assistant professor there in 1884. His books study color sense and color blindness in depth. He also examined how the eye's central organs are built. Later works ask why short sight develops in people. The entry follows a second-generation doctor into his own field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-syene-14153:
