Rolling bearings support nearly every rotating machine, and their faults hide under noise and shifting speeds. Their network reads vibration signals at several scales at once. Then it applies two kinds of attention. One reweights which signal channels matter. The other spotlights the brief fault impulses in the stream. Only then does it classify the fault type.

On the standard public bearing dataset, the system reached accuracy above ninety-nine percent in the hardest cross condition tests, where the machine's speed and load change between training and testing. Under heavy added noise it still held above ninety-two percent. It beat three recent rival methods on accuracy and related scores while running cheaper and faster. For factory maintenance teams, that combination promises earlier warnings from the sensors they already own.
plos-pone-0358353:
Juan-José Gallego led a team of eight authors testing eye movement checks in liver patients, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cirrhosis can cloud the brain in a subtle condition called minimal hepatic encephalopathy. The standard psychometric score misses some early cases. The team asked whether tracking eye movements catches changes the score labels as absent.

Gallego's study found that eye movement analysis does detect early neurological changes in those patients. Eyes are easy to test, cheap, and hard to fake or practice, unlike paper tests. Earlier detection lets doctors adjust treatment and warn about driving safety sooner. The work offers clinics a practical add-on test for a complication that quietly affects daily life.
plos-pone-0358453:
Ming Fei Li, Lavania Nagendran, Christopher Kiru, Lauren Schroeder, and David Samson published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It asks a playful question with real science behind it: who is disrupting whom at night, humans or their dogs? The authors examine nighttime activity patterns of both.

People often blame dogs for broken sleep, but human schedules may disturb dogs just as much. Recording activity for both sides of the bed gives an even-handed picture of shared nights. Sleep researchers and pet behavior specialists can use this two-way view to advise households where restless nights are blamed on the dog by default.
plos-pone-0358553: Sharafi and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on bull sperm and water movement across cell walls. They measured how well sperm handle water that is too strong or too weak in salts. Age, breed, and which collection round the sperm came from all played a role. The findings matter for freezing sperm, since ice damage depends on how water leaves and enters cells.
plos-pone-0358753:
Tingting Zhu and Yuhuan Wang study how live streamed shopping affects young buyers' loyalty to old, heritage brands, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Brands with long histories carry craft traditions but must win over shoppers who buy through video streams. The authors asked which parts of a live session actually build that bond, focusing on excitement and the feeling of a real relationship with the brand.

They surveyed just over four hundred consumers aged eighteen to forty who had watched heritage brand streams. Both chatting with the host and engaging with products raised viewers' sense of social presence and belief that the brand was genuine. Those feelings fed emotional excitement, which in turn strengthened identification with the brand. The chain gives heritage sellers a practical map for designing streams that younger audiences trust.
plos-pone-0358953:
Xu Li and Yufeng Qiao use public gene data to hunt for shared markers between two rare autoimmune diseases, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. One condition inflames and scars the kidneys under attack from the immune system's own antibodies. The other swells glands and organs with immune cells. Case reports hint the two overlap, but nobody had compared their gene activity across tissues.

Working from a kidney dataset for the first disease and a salivary gland dataset for the second, they screened hundreds of altered genes and used machine learning to narrow the field. Two genes, ITGAM and CXCL1, emerged as candidate markers common to both, and immune pathways dominated the shared signal. The authors frame the pair as leads for diagnosis research, noting the small samples behind the second dataset.
plos-pone-0359153:
Hongyi Yuan and four colleagues present a software method, published in PLOS ONE in 2026, for sorting huge collections of single cells by their gene activity. Modern sequencing can profile hundreds of thousands of cells at once, but grouping those cells into types gets slow and unreliable at that scale. Their framework, called scLTF, is built to handle the volume.

The method first makes rough groups with a fast graph based algorithm, then picks the most typical cells from each group. A transformer model, the kind of network behind modern language tools, then refines the groups step by step. On several real datasets it matched or beat leading deep learning methods on accuracy while using only a fraction of their running time.
plos-pone-0359353: Ju and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on forecasting how long freeway incidents last. Crashes and breakdowns tie up traffic, and crews must guess when lanes will clear. The team applied machine learning to predict incident duration. Sharper guesses help traffic centers warn drivers, set detours, and send the right crews to the scene.
plos-pone-0359553: de Goede and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a new interview for moral injury in soldiers. Moral injury is the lasting pain from acts that clash with a person's values. The team built a military version of a clinical interview and tested whether it can be used in practice. A workable interview is a first step toward care for a wound that standard trauma checks may miss.
plos-pone-0359653:
Vaishaali Gunalan and co-authors set out a study protocol in 2026 for testing whether color vision checks can catch early diabetic retinopathy. This eye disease, a complication of diabetes, damages the retina and is a leading cause of blindness in working age adults. It usually causes no symptoms until the damage is advanced, so screening decides who keeps their sight.

Their project, shortened to CODER, proposes color vision assessment as the screening tool, since color perception can falter early in the disease. A protocol paper fixes the design, measures, and analysis plan before results exist, keeping the eventual findings honest. A cheap, quick test that community clinics could run would widen screening far beyond specialist eye centers.
plos-pone-0359853:
Yi Zhang, Li Zhang, Jihui Hu, Meng Zhang, and Xiapei Peng published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study of stroke survivors in middle and older age. The authors examine pre-stroke social participation, how active a person was socially before the stroke, and its association with current physical resilience.

The comparison runs across frailty levels, from robust survivors to very frail ones. Physical resilience is the body's ability to bounce back after stress, and it may rest partly on a person's earlier social life. Rehabilitation teams planning recovery support are the readers who could use social history this way.
pmc-13122053:
Imtiaz Wani is first author on a 2026 retrospective case series of subareolar breast abscess in males, an infection pocket under the nipple area. The condition is extremely rare in men, with few cases in print. The authors reviewed eleven men treated at their center from April twenty fourteen to July twenty twenty-four.

Nine cases were uncomplicated abscesses with no clear cause. One man had diabetes and another had underlying breast cancer. Pus cultures mainly grew Staphylococcus, a common skin bacterium. Treatment ranged from antibiotics alone to needle drainage and surgical drainage. For uncomplicated cases, the authors name incision and drainage, cutting open and emptying the pocket, as the treatment of choice.
pmc-13162553:
Subhadip Choudhuri leads a 2026 mouse study of a new immunotherapy for Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. The standard drug, benznidazole, cures adults poorly and causes notable side effects. The team tested a low-dose, two-gene immunotherapy, with and without an immune booster, against the standard drug in infected adult mice.

All three treatments controlled parasite burden by over ninety-five percent. The unboosted therapy cut inflammation and tissue damage markers throughout infection, while the boosted therapy and standard drug protected mainly in the chronic phase. Heart wall changes and pumping problems were eased more by the new therapies. The authors present them as promising alternatives for preventing Chagas heart damage.
pmc-13197453:
Björn Boshof and colleagues evaluate a new cell growth vessel called CellScrew in 2026. Growing surface-loving cells at large scale is key for making proteins, gene therapy vectors, and vaccines. Stacked flasks need much hand work and lack process control, so a rotating vessel could help.

The vessel turns its growth surface in a steady roll, which improves mixing and oxygen flow. The team tested three cell types, including human kidney cells used in production. Cell yields and survival matched stacked flasks. Pulling cells off the surface worked well and used far less release fluid. The authors see a scalable, lower-waste swap for classic flask stacks, pending wider tests.
pmc-13197653:
Yong Zhang and colleagues used genetic methods in 2026 to untangle fatty acids, immune cells, and artery clogging. Coronary atherosclerosis means fatty buildup in heart arteries. Watch studies link blood fatty acids to the disease, but cause and effect stayed murky.

Their method uses gene variants as natural experiments, a design called Mendelian randomization. Across 731 immune cell traits, thirty showed causal links to artery disease. Blood fatty acid levels also raised disease risk in the genetic tests. One immune cell type, dendritic cells, carried part of the fatty acid effect. Dendritic cells alert the immune system to threats. The work points to new targets where diet and immunity meet.
pmc-13198053:
Michael Mutz and Johannes Müller analyzed what people mean when they rate their own health in a 2026 study. Self-rated health is a single survey question used worldwide, yet its meaning is murky. The team paired that question with an open follow-up asking people to explain their rating in their own words.

Answers showed a weighted judgment, not a pure medical score. Current aches and long-term diseases dominated among people in poor health. People rating their health very good pointed more to mood, social ties, and daily function. Older adults stressed disease burden and physical capacity. Women weighted feelings and caregiving duties more. Income also shifted the mix.
pmc-13199853:
Yoko Kanamitsu and colleagues present a 2026 autopsy case report on fatal adrenal gland failure in intensive care. Adrenal glands make stress hormones. In critical illness, low output can cause shock that defies blood pressure drugs, but hormone shortage from gland damage looks just like a milder functional dip.

Their patient was a 70-year-old man with heart and kidney failure and no known immune weakness. Two shock episodes during a long ICU stay briefly eased with steroid treatment. After steroids stopped, shock returned and he died despite sepsis care. Autopsy found both adrenal glands destroyed by bleeding. Microscope signs proved cytomegalovirus infection of the glands. Hidden virus revival can wreck the glands, they warn.
pmc-13201253:
Bastian Abarca-Rozas and colleagues present a 2026 case report on recurring heart tumors in a teen with Carney complex. Carney complex is a rare inherited syndrome causing tumors in the heart, glands, and skin, with spotty pigmentation. Its heart myxomas start young, span several chambers, and return often after removal.

Their patient was diagnosed at fourteen with myxomas in both upper chambers and the right lower chamber, all surgically removed. Skin pigment signs and a small pituitary tumor confirmed the syndrome despite negative gene testing. New masses were first read as clots and treated with blood thinners. Richer imaging proved tumor return, prompting a second full removal with good recovery. Heart MRI proved decisive.
pmc-13202153:
Vaping around the time of surgery is poorly understood, and a 2026 protocol led by Suzanne R Harrogate plans a scoping review to map what evidence exists. The protocol covers e-cigarette use in the perioperative setting, where tobacco smoking is already a proven risk factor for complications.

Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, the team will search major medical databases and grey literature from 2003, when commercial e-cigarettes appeared, through early 2026. Studies of any design, across all surgical specialties, will be screened and extracted by two independent reviewers. The synthesis will show how vaping is defined and measured, which patients were studied, and where research gaps remain.
pmc-13203353:
Light-activated cancer treatment needs molecules that find tumor DNA, and a 2026 study by Çetin Çelik tests porphyrins built to grip a special DNA shape. The research article synthesizes three water-soluble porphyrins with positively charged imidazolium groups and measures their binding to human telomeric guanine-quadruplex DNA.

Titration and energy-transfer experiments showed the porphyrins bound quadruplex DNA about ten times more stably than ordinary DNA in the reported tests. Under deep red light they generated singlet oxygen, the toxic species behind photodynamic therapy, and quadruplex DNA boosted that output further. The compounds entered cells and killed cancer cells more strongly than normal cells under illumination.
pmc-13212753:
Jiří Borovec and colleagues survey in 2026 public knowledge about surgical removal of wisdom teeth, one of the commonest oral operations. They compared people who had already had the surgery with people who had never faced it.

Questionnaires from 584 respondents showed the experienced group knew more, yet both groups scored worst on pain medication and post-surgery diet. Complications and pain relief were the topics people most wanted explained. Fear eased after a first extraction and ran lower in men and regular dental attenders. Leaflets paired with spoken instructions worked best, and the authors urge clinics to close the pain-control knowledge gap.
pmc-13215153:
Danielmartin Arogyasami, writing alone in 2026, introduces an open-source artificial intelligence pipeline that assembles treatment option dossiers for rare solid tumours. Rare cancers draw a quarter of diagnoses yet lack the precision-medicine infrastructure built for common cancers, and soft-tissue sarcomas show the gap starkly.

Six modules chain together variant interpretation, immune target prediction, drug matching across four databases, trial searching that surfaces basket studies, and evidence write-ups steered by a language-model agent with fixed guardrails. Run on 260 sarcoma patients from a public atlas, the pipeline finished every case. Three in ten patients received at least one top-tier drug match, approved or genomically matched. Cloud and local deployment options cover privacy rules.
pmc-13217453:
Jie Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 study hunting diagnostic genes for renal interstitial fibrosis, the scarring process that carries chronic kidney disease toward failure. Standard blood markers rise only after heavy damage, so the team mined gene data for earlier signals tied to inflammation and low oxygen.

Three public datasets, with 76 fibrosis and 142 control samples, were merged and screened. Five hub genes emerged: EDN1, HLA-G, MYC, HIF1A, and TLR2. A model built on them separated fibrosis from control tissue respectably, with areas under the curve between 0.7 and 0.9, and the genes tracked closely with immune cell patterns. Two molecular subtypes of fibrosis appeared. Rat experiments confirmed all five genes switched on more strongly in scarred kidney, supporting their candidacy as biomarkers and drug targets.
pmc-13218453:
Claude Mambo Muvunyi and colleagues review the state of cholera in Africa in a 2026 article on trends, challenges, and the path to elimination. Cholera is preventable and treatable, and vaccines exist, yet outbreaks keep returning across the continent. The authors trace that persistence to failing water and sanitation systems, weak surveillance, poverty, and conflict rather than to any gap in knowledge.

Cases across Africa more than doubled between 2014 and 2024, reaching roughly a quarter of a million cases and several thousand deaths in twenty countries. The review highlights limited diagnostic capacity, patchy data, and infrastructure deficits as barriers that let outbreaks grow before they are contained. Against that picture, the authors argue for integrated strategies: stronger surveillance, vaccination campaigns aimed at hotspots, investment in clean water and hygiene, and action on poverty and displacement. They close by calling for political commitment, more funding, and solutions fitted to each community's circumstances.
pmc-13221753:
Mirkka Söderman, Carl Johansson, and Lena-Karin Gustafsson run a 2026 Swedish panel study on support for older people living in their own homes. More older adults now stay home with varied, growing needs, which demands coordinated municipal care. Twenty stakeholders and decision makers rated 45 statements across three mail rounds to find consensus.

Every statement reached some consensus. Panelists agreed that today's care recipients are older and frailer, family members need recovery time, and many homes are not adapted to greater needs. Communication and collaboration between services fell short. The authors urge planning that covers both individual wishes and organizational conditions, with digital tools fitted to what older people actually want.
pmc-13222353:
Ji Yeon Kim and co-authors examine why industrial biomanufacturing still lags its laboratory promise, in a 2026 review. Engineered microbes can turn renewable feedstocks into chemicals and materials, guided by systems metabolic engineering. Commercial scale-up, though, remains rare, and the authors probe that gap through two near-mature products: succinic acid and polyhydroxyalkanoates, a family of bioplastics.

Each case shows where strain performance, process costs, and robustness break down outside the lab. The review then considers how artificial intelligence joined with systems engineering could speed strain design and process control. Closing the scale gap matters because these factories could displace petrochemical production across many everyday products.
pmc-13222553:
Shanguang Lyu and co-authors treat stubborn warts around the nails with heated needle puncture plus a Chinese herbal soak, in a 2026 two-case report. Warts beside the nail are hard to treat because drugs penetrate poorly and standard methods risk nail damage. Both patients, a 38-year-old man and a 60-year-old woman, had failed repeated freezing, topical antivirals, and oral medication.

A fine needle heated until glowing punctured each wart core every two weeks, paired with daily warm herbal soaks. The man's wart shed fully after three sessions, the woman's after four. Neither suffered nail damage or infection, and six-month follow-up is reported. The pairing offers a gentler route worth testing more widely.
pmc-13222853:
Di Cui, Xiang Wang, and Xiaoling Shang examine how brain support cells and opioid receptors shape cancer spread to the brain, in a 2026 review. Tumor cells crossing into the brain face a defensive wall built around reactive astrocytes and microglia. Most arrivals die at that bottleneck. Survivors reprogram the defenders toward a supportive state.

Reprogrammed glia amplify inflammation, suppress immunity, and rewire metabolism, building a niche where metastases grow while neurons suffer collateral injury. Opioid receptors on these glial cells act as control nodes that reset their responses, indirectly favoring tumor colonization. The authors map this selection process to find treatment points that protect both brain tissue and its guard cells.
pmc-13223653:
Thuy Trinh Nguyen and co-authors combine two engineered immune drugs against pancreatic cancer in mouse tumors, in a 2026 study. Pancreatic tumors are famously cold, with few T cells inside and a suppressive surroundings. One drug activates dendritic cells at tumor fibroblast markers, while the other pairs a checkpoint target with a modified interleukin to grow T cells.

Together, the pair built dense clusters where helper and killer T cells sat alongside a key dendritic cell type, right inside the tumor. Those clusters tracked with tumor regression, which needed both T cell types. Treated T cells also produced more attack signals and leaned toward a helper-one profile. Forming fresh immune clusters in place may warm cold tumors.
pmc-13223853:
Nicola Pegoraro and co-authors recount a fruit pit that impersonated gallstone ileus on imaging, in a 2026 case report. A 49-year-old Italian woman with a previous bowel resection arrived with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. Scans showed small bowel obstruction above her old surgical join, with three dense masses in the ileum and real gallstones sitting in her gallbladder.

No air in the bile ducts and no fistula appeared, which argued against a migrated gallstone. Colonoscopy found the masses were hard foreign bodies stuck at a narrowed join. Two were nudged into the colon, and the last, removed after balloon widening, proved to be an apricot pit she recalled swallowing. Swallowed pits belong on the obstruction checklist.
pmc-13225153:
Hailing Zeng and Qiongfang Zhang assemble a 2026 evidence atlas for laboratory diagnosis of tuberculosis in the urinary and genital tracts. The disease hides well: symptoms are nonspecific, bacteria are scarce, and test performance swings with method and specimen type. Reviewing three databases, the authors mapped what is known into matrices and flow diagrams rather than a single pooled number.

Twenty-one studies qualified, most of them using urine specimens. Molecular tests, especially Xpert MTB/RIF and other DNA amplification methods, were the most studied on urine samples. Reported sensitivity ranges were wide for every method, showing how much setting matters. Combined urine sampling with molecular testing formed the most evidence-rich pathway the atlas could identify.
pmc-13227353:
Xiaonan Wang and colleagues compare a 2026 pair of surgical approaches for repairing holes between the heart's chambers in very small infants. One route opens the breastbone; the other slips in beneath the right armpit, sparing the sternum. Eighty matched infants under five kilograms and six months old were split evenly between the approaches, and breathing measures around surgery were compared.

Oxygen levels, airway pressures, and blood gases showed no significant differences between groups, and nobody died in either arm. Complication rates were low and similar. Operating time was actually shorter through the armpit route. The authors conclude the side approach does not raise the risk of breathing failure after surgery in fragile, low-weight infants.
pmc-13227553:
Alghalya Khalid Almaawali and colleagues report a 2026 newborn case from Muscat, Oman. A two-week-old girl had a swollen abdomen and feeding intolerance caused by the rarest form of sacrococcygeal teratoma, a tumour at the base of the spine. Type IV tumours grow entirely inside the pelvis, with no external lump to give them away, and hers was purely fluid-filled, which made it look deceptively harmless on imaging.

Surgeons removed the cyst with keyhole assistance and took the tailbone as well, the standard safeguard against recurrence. Tissue study confirmed a mature cystic tumour. Her recovery was smooth apart from a minor wound separation that healed with simple care, and follow-up showed no return of the lesion.
pmc-13233353:
Yaxuan Xu and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of acupuncture for trigeminal neuralgia, a disorder causing episodes of severe facial pain. Earlier reviews suggested benefit, so the team updated the evidence by searching eight English and Chinese databases through December 2025. They pooled 38 randomized trials covering 2,836 patients and graded the certainty of the findings.

Patients receiving acupuncture had higher overall response rates and lower pain scores than control groups. Pain episodes came less often, facial pain ratings fell, and adverse events were fewer than with comparison care. Much of the benefit appeared when acupuncture was combined with medication. The authors caution that trial quality is low and call for rigorous multicenter trials with standard protocols.
pmc-13233853:
Fawzi, Asker, and Yousef test how deep concrete beams stand up to twisting. Their beams use high-strength concrete and cross-inclined stirrups, the steel ties set at a slant inside the beam. Nine beams were built and loaded under pure torsion, a twisting force that deep beams in bridges and buildings must sometimes carry.

The team measured strength and how much each beam deformed before failing. Slanted ties may grip twisting cracks better than straight ones, but proof needs tests, not theory. Their results give designers the grounding for safer and cheaper deep beams, where guessing at torsion strength risks either waste or failure.
pmc-13234053:
Marwan Abdelnasser Ragab, Waleed A Elmahy, and Marihan Elgayar published a 2026 randomized trial of tooth filling materials that set without a curing light. Bulk-fill composites let dentists fill deep back-tooth cavities in one layer, and newer versions harden chemically, by dual curing, or by light. Twenty patients received sixty back-tooth fillings, split evenly among the three types, and returned for scoring over a year.

Every filling survived the year with acceptable scores, and the three materials matched on function and biological criteria. Looks differed: the light-cure material kept the best surface shine, one self-cure product matched its color best alongside it, and the dual-cure product scored lowest on color match. Nothing changed significantly over time. The authors endorse the light-free options where appearance matters less.
pmc-13235053:
Lingfei Shangguan and a large team reported in 2026 a genome for the Pinot Noir grape that keeps its two parental copies separate. Grapevines carry large differences between their paired chromosomes, and clonal propagation preserves that complexity. Single merged assemblies hide many genes that exist on only one copy. The team assembled both haplotypes plus a merged version for the famous wine variety.

Both haplotypes exceeded five hundred million DNA letters with high completeness in quality checks. Comparison showed about a thousand genes hidden by the merged assembly, many tied to metabolism. Variation in gene density and function appeared between corresponding chromosomes in the maps. Separate measurement of gene activity showed many gene pairs expressed equally, while others favoured one copy strongly. The resource links DNA differences to traits shaped by growing environment, known as terroir.
pmc-13235253:
Saskia-Linda Stämmler, Nina Viberg, and Louise Bengtsson assessed in 2026 how open European Union health teamwork with Africa really is. Team Europe Programs are a main vehicle for joint European development action and claim open partnership as a founding principle. The study mapped where health programs sit by region and interviewed twenty-three leaders in Europe and Africa. Interviews ran during the first months of 2024.

Health programs cluster heavily in Africa, with uneven taking part among European member states. Leaders mostly praised the model for building trust, teamwork, and steadier engagement that might draw funding. Limited local voice in choices, lasting power gap, and teamwork strain drew repeated pushback in interviews. Both sides agreed taking part must widen beyond European bodies to reflect local aims. The authors urge a stronger role for partner-country actors when programs are built and run.
pmc-13235453:
S.-A. Im and a large trial team analysed in 2026 side effects of a three-drug combination for advanced breast cancer. The INAVO120 trial added inavolisib to two established medicines for tumours carrying a specific gene mutation and resisting hormone therapy. Earlier results showed longer survival without progression and longer overall survival for the combination. Safety analysis focused on high blood sugar, mouth inflammation, rash, and diarrhoea.

High blood sugar appeared within about a week for many patients and most often led to dose pauses among the four problems. Standard supportive medicines managed each side effect, from metformin for blood sugar to a steroid mouthwash for mouth sores. Very few patients stopped the new drug permanently because of any single side effect listed. Patterns looked broadly similar across regions and age groups in the trial. The authors judge the safety profile consistent with longer-term experience and manageable in practice.
pmc-13236753:
Masashi Higashino and co-authors followed in 2026 patients with a rare brain tumour called intracranial germinoma treated at one centre over forty years. Forty-three patients were tracked for a median of eleven years after treatment. Survival and freedom from progression were worked out at ten and fifteen years. Treatment records, mainly treatment fields, were rechecked for patients whose disease came back.

Survival stayed very high at ten years, with disease-free rates only a little lower over the same span. Eight patients had recurrence, three of them in the spine after quiet spans lasting many years. Tumours in unusual sites and partial first response raised recurrence risk in simple checks. Radiation covering the whole ventricular system of the brain sharply lowered recurrence risk in the full model. Some older treatment plans had missed full ventricular cover, the review showed. The authors urge field review and life-long careful watching.
pmc-13236853:
Yang Zhao and colleagues examined in 2026 whether Guangxi, a multi-ethnic region of China, should pool its basic medical insurance at the provincial level. City-level funds have ended up uneven: some hold large surpluses while patients and money drain toward cities with richer hospitals. The authors compared two pooling models using official 2023 figures.

They recommend starting with an adjustment fund, where a shared pot smooths differences between local funds, because it faces less resistance than full unified collection and spending. Dual-track adjustment funds, clear rules for contributions, and stronger digital systems form the suggested package. Over time the region could move toward unified revenue and spending. The goal is a fairer, more durable insurance system across town and country.
pmc-13236953:
Narayanan Narayanan and colleagues engineered cassava plants in 2026 that poison the whitefly Bemisia tabaci, the insect spreading two viral diseases that can infect every cassava field in East Africa. Gene-silencing constructs in the plants target fifteen whitefly genes covering water balance, sugar handling, partner bacteria, and toxin cleanup. The team produced 140 transformed plant lines from a local variety.

Feeding trials showed the plants killed about 58 percent of adult whiteflies within a week and most nymphs within 25 days, while the target genes quieted inside the insects. Population modeling suggested the approach could hold whiteflies down under field conditions. The authors frame the work as a durable, plant-based defense for a staple food crop.
pmc-13238053:
Aksyniia Tsaruk and colleagues compared lactate dehydrogenase enzymes from fungi, bacteria, a protist, and mammals inside the heat-tolerant yeast Ogataea polymorpha in 2026, aiming to brew L-lactic acid for bioplastics and medicines. Each borrowed enzyme redirects the yeast's metabolism toward lactic acid. The engineered strains were fed glucose, xylose, glycerol, or methanol under varied shaking and acidity conditions.

The bovine enzyme won on glucose, reaching about 73 grams per liter when acidity was neutralized with chalk. A fungal enzyme led on xylose, while methanol gave only small yields for every strain. Ethanol stayed negligible despite the yeast's intact alcohol pathway. The authors conclude that enzyme origin and sugar choice jointly govern success, with redox balance the main bottleneck on poorer feeds.
pmc-13239253:

From nearly ten thousand records spanning 2010 to 2025, the eligible studies had to integrate at least two data layers or tackle the governance and equity questions around clinical use. The caveats are heavy: two-thirds of the AI models showed ancestry bias, few used explainability tools, and only about a fifth of biomarkers reached real-world evaluation. Das closes with a roadmap for fairer global rollout.
pmc-13239953:
Yusuke Ito presents a 2026 clinical image case about air that showed around a lung after fluid was drained. An 84-year-old woman had fluid around her right lung. She felt chest pain during the drainage, and the next film showed air plus fluid. That first raised fear the needle had nicked the lung.

Films from before and after told a subtler tale. The chest on that side had shrunk, and the airway had shifted toward the drained side. That pattern marks pneumothorax ex vacuo, where a lung that cannot stretch leaves a vacuum space. A tumour blocking the airway explained the trapped lung. She was cared for safely with no further procedure.
pmc-13240253:
Nadine Nolan and co-authors check the genetic health of an endangered Australian frog in a 2026 conservation study. The population of Rawlinsonia littlejohni lives with a dam, built ponds, and swings between drought and flood, and the team measured diversity, inbreeding, and mixing to judge how it is coping.

Two subpopulations sat only a short distance apart yet exchanged few genes. Heavy rain in 2021 briefly loosened that separation, while drought in 2023 tightened it again. The northern group, mixing built ponds with natural creek pools, stayed genetically healthier. The pond-only southern group lost diversity and inbred sharply. The authors suggest extra ponds as stepping stones between the groups.
pmc-13240353:
Mingjun Han, Fan Yu, and Huanhuan Li test a plant compound against the injury that follows restored blood flow to the heart in a 2026 study. When a blocked heart artery reopens, stressed internal cell machinery can trigger further muscle cell death, and imperatorin, found in several medicinal plants, had known heart-protective hints.

In heart cells stressed by oxygen loss and return, and in mice with tied then released coronary arteries, the compound cut cell death and calmed the stressed machinery. Calcium overload and two death-linked proteins fell, while a protective signalling pathway switched on. A pathway activator strengthened the benefit and a blocker erased it, confirming the route of action.
pmc-13241353:
Kang's team at Anhui published this correction to their review of crop resistance to stalk rot. The first article surveyed genetic and molecular pathways behind resistance. One co-author's name appeared with the wrong spelling. The notice fixes the byline and the credit list.

The name changes from Xinhan Hu to Qinhan Hu. Both spellings render the same Chinese mark in Pinyin, the notice explains. Hu's credited task, gathering papers and revising the draft, stays unchanged. The journal has updated the first article to match. No science content of the review was altered.
pmc-13241453:
Bai and colleagues in Shenyang traced a molecular chain that drives hypertrophic scars after burns and wounds. The long noncoding RNA TUG1 runs high in scar tissue. Levels of its partner microRNA run correspondingly low. Expression assays, cell experiments, and a rabbit ear model tested the axis.

TUG1 sponges the microRNA, freeing the growth receptor IGF1R from repression. Freed fibroblasts then proliferate and migrate faster, laying down more collagen. Adding the microRNA back reversed these effects in cells and animals alike. Bai nominates the axis as a drug target for fibrotic skin disease.
pmc-13241553:
Diociasi and an Italian-Swiss team trained a neural network to outline the entire anterior visual pathway on brain MRI automatically. Training used high-resolution scans from healthy volunteers and multiple sclerosis patients.

Eighty scans in total, split between thirty-four healthy controls and forty-six patients, tested the system. Agreement with expert tracings was strong for the whole pathway, reaching a Dice score of 0.86 overall. Optic nerves and the chiasm scored nearly as well. The thinner optic tracts proved harder, scoring somewhat lower, which the authors flag for future biomarker work.
pmc-13241653:

Under the best settings, results for zinc, copper, and iron matched the design predictions. A decision tree model confirmed the same optimum. The authors present the approach as a promising, lower-impact route for food element analysis.
pmc-13241853:
Rory J. Piper and Martin M. Tisdall offer a 2026 review of clinical trials for implanted stimulation therapies in epilepsy. About a third of people with epilepsy keep having seizures on medication. Some cannot have the seizure source removed by surgery, which leaves stimulation as an alternative.

Options now include deep brain stimulation, a responsive system that reacts to seizure signals, vagus nerve stimulation, and a newer under-scalp device. The review walks through the milestone trials that shaped current practice for each option. Ongoing trials are summarized, and the authors look ahead to how future studies should be designed. Readers gain a single map of an expanding treatment field for drug-resistant epilepsy.
pmc-13242753:
Javad Momenisoroshk and co-authors present a 2026 trial comparing two simple ways to ease injection pain in newborns. Healthy babies receive a vitamin K shot soon after birth, and pain control matters even for brief procedures. Babies in Rafsanjan, Iran, were assigned to flick massage, local warmth, or no intervention.

A trained scale scored pain during the injection. Both treated groups scored significantly lower than the control group. Babies warmed before the shot fared somewhat better than massaged babies during the injection, though the two methods tied afterward. The warming used a hair dryer to bring the skin to a set temperature. The authors say either technique can be used in practice, depending on conditions at hand.
pmc-13242853:
Lorvens Decosma and co-authors present a 2026 case of reduced brain glucose uptake that fully reversed. A 40-year-old man had stubborn B-cell lymphoma, treated with many regimens including engineered cell therapy, and was in remission. Brain imaging during a lung inflammation illness linked to COVID showed global low glucose uptake, matching his cognitive symptoms.

His thinking recovered quickly after treatment brought on steroid-driven high blood sugar, alongside care for the lung condition. Repeat imaging two months later showed the brain pattern completely normalized. The authors use the case to argue this imaging pattern can be temporary when driven by body-wide illness. They call for research into how systemic disease suppresses brain energy use and what treatments can reverse it.
pmc-13243753:
Limin Chen and colleagues describe a Chinese man caught between two immune diseases that pulled his treatment in opposite directions. Their case report appeared in the Journal of International Medical Research in 2026. He had lived for years with ankylosing spondylitis, a spinal arthritis, then arrived with recurrent joint swelling, fever, and tender red nodules on his limbs. Together with swollen chest lymph nodes, the picture fit Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis.

Steroids calmed the new syndrome well. Reviewing his course, the team suspected the biologic drug adalimumab, taken for his spine over the previous year, had triggered the Löfgren relapse. Their literature comparison adds a population twist. Asian patients with this syndrome tend to be diagnosed later and need longer steroid courses than Western patients, whose illness often fades alone. Genes shaping the immune response may explain the difference, the authors suggest.
pmc-13243853:
Hyungwoo Lee and co-authors pool evidence on blood thinner pairs after stroke in a 2026 meta-analysis. Some stroke patients have both a heart rhythm problem and hardened large arteries. Doctors must choose between a strong anticoagulant alone or adding an antiplatelet drug.

The team combined eight cohort studies found in two major databases through mid-2025. Adding the second drug seemed to cut repeat stroke in the first three months, though the signal weakened under stricter checks. Over a year or more, the pair raised major bleeding and death without cutting repeat stroke. The authors advise brief paired use only for selected patients, if at all.
pmc-13244253:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes issued a safety opinion on subtilisin, a protein-cutting enzyme made by an engineered bacterium. The opinion appeared in the EFSA Journal in 2026. The enzyme comes from a Bacillus licheniformis strain developed by Novozymes and is destined for processing grain into distilled alcohol. Because distilling removes the enzyme traces, the panel did not even need to calculate how much consumers might swallow.

The production strain passed Europe's presumption of safety route, and the finished enzyme carries no living cells or strain DNA. Sequence checks did flag look-alikes among known allergens, mostly respiratory ones, but the panel judged dietary allergy risk excludable here. Toxicity testing was waived given the safety status, clean manufacturing, and negligible exposure. The verdict: no safety concern under the intended conditions. The document is a worked example of how the European system clears industrial food enzymes.
pmc-13244353:
Ana Flores and colleagues interviewed bereaved caregivers of Latinx immigrants who chose to go home to die. Their study appeared in Palliative and Supportive Care in 2026. Nineteen caregivers described patients treated at a United States urban hospital between 2013 and 2020 who requested repatriation after a terminal diagnosis. Most families came from the Dominican Republic. The team asked about the journey, symptom control, care received, and how the death itself was judged.

Only two patients hit logistical trouble on the trip home, and none needed feeding tubes or breathing support en route. Symptoms were mostly well controlled, including pain in nearly every case where it occurred. Caregivers' accounts let the authors rate these deaths and map where the system strained. The wish is hard to grant but deeply valued when granted. Their findings give hospitals a practical base for building repatriation pathways instead of improvising them.
pmc-13245753:
Mullin, Plascak, and Tan tracked HPV vaccination among American teenagers in this 2026 PLOS One study. The vaccine prevents several cancers, yet too few adolescents finish the series. Using the National Immunization Survey–Teen, the authors examined provider-verified records for more than one hundred twenty-six thousand adolescents aged thirteen to seventeen, from 2021 through 2023.

Completion of the series barely moved across the three years, holding near sixty-three percent, while roughly fifteen percent of teens started but never finished and about twenty-two percent never started at all. Older teens and girls completed at higher rates than younger teens and boys. The authors urge earlier vaccination and stronger provider recommendations to close the gap.
pmc-13245853:

pmc-13249753:

pmc-13249953:

pmc-13251853:

pmc-13252853:

pmc-13252953:

pmc-13253653:

pmc-13254853:
Eszter Balla and colleagues sound the alarm over a surge of congenital syphilis in Hungary in a 2026 public health report. pmc-13254953:

pmc-13255053:

pmc-13256253:

pmc-13256853:

pmc-13257253:

pmc-13257353:

pmc-13258653:

pmc-13258753:

pmc-13259953:

pmc-13260453:

pmc-13261353:

pmc-13262153:

pmc-13266853:

pmc-13267653:

pmc-13268053:

pmc-13268153:

pmc-13268353:

pmc-13269553:
Ruhi Bhanap, Klaus Oberauer, and Agnes Rosner published a journal article in 2026 on the 'looking at nothing' effect. In that effect, people glance back at empty spots where items once appeared, while remembering them. Earlier work hinted that such glances, or hidden shifts of attention, might aid memory. Two experiments tested this in short-term memory.

Participants learned three word pairs shown at distinct screen spots, then recalled them after a sound cue, at once or after a delay. During recall, gaze or hidden attention was steered toward the matching spot, a wrong spot, or the center. Memory scores did not differ between these conditions. The authors conclude that restoring the original place does not boost word-pair recall in either memory store.
pmc-13270253:
Ayalew Zewdie and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on children injured in road traffic crashes seen at a trauma hospital in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Records for 279 patients aged up to 18, treated from December 2021 to December 2023, were reviewed with a standard checklist. The study describes who was hurt and where they went next.

The median age was 13 years, and fifty-four point one percent were male. Children aged 15 to 18 made up forty point nine percent. Pedestrians formed seventy-four point six percent of cases, and 48 percent were hurt traveling to work or school. Limb and pelvis injuries led at forty-eight point four percent, with head injuries at forty-one point nine percent. Most patients, ninety-one point four percent, went home from the emergency department, and deaths there were zero point seven percent.
pmc-13270853:
Karim A Elhaw and co-authors test in 2026 whether a dental laser cuts bone more gently than rotary drills during removal of impacted lower wisdom teeth. Twenty-four patients were randomized evenly between Er:YAG laser osteotomy and conventional rotary cutting. Cone-beam scans before surgery and at three months measured bone density, while pain, swelling, and jaw opening were tracked clinically.

Bone density rose over time in both groups, but the laser group finished significantly higher at three months and reported less pain on day two. Swelling and jaw stiffness improved equally, with no significant difference between techniques, while laser operations took longer. The authors conclude the laser may ease early discomfort and support denser bone healing, though larger studies must confirm the long-term benefit.
pmc-13271053:
Dandan Wu is lead author of a 2026 journal article testing four large language models, the kind of AI behind chatbots, on infectious disease decision-making. The models were DeepSeek-R1, ChatGPT-5, Grok 3, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, and their answers were compared with those of trainee infectious disease doctors.

On examination questions, the models matched the residents on accuracy and scores, doing somewhat better on fact-based questions and worse on simple case questions. On ten real clinical cases, expert reviewers rated model answers highly for accuracy, completeness, and safety. Doctors aided by a model scored higher on completeness than either doctors alone or models alone, the clearest gain found.
pmc-13271153:
Francesco Antonio Mallus is lead author of a 2026 review tracing normative modelling in brain electrophysiology, the study of the brain's electrical signals. Normative modelling charts typical brain function so that one person's deviation can be measured, much like a growth chart for height.

The review follows the field from early 1970s work through a period of neglect to a recent revival driven by machine learning and large data sets. Models grew from small, single-site, age-only charts to harmonised approaches combining many kinds of data. Remaining problems include no standard practice and poor comparability between studies. The authors argue scale, shared pipelines, and international teamwork can turn demonstrations into precise individual brain mapping.
pmc-13271953:
Alessandra Landi and coauthors study in 2026 grassroots circular economy projects in Bologna, Italy. City policy on reuse tends to favor industry and technology, while community groups practice repair, sharing, and regeneration on the ground. The study asks what these groups contribute and what blocks them.

Working with 17 organizations in a participatory project, the researchers mapped actors, practices, and business models through workshops and co-design sessions. Their circular work centered on social value rather than recycling tonnage alone. Barriers appeared at organization, community, and institutional levels, including gaps in support structures that policy could close.
pmc-13272153:
San San Tay and coauthors develop in 2026 a prototype smartwatch that verifies the harder exercises used in cancer prehabilitation, the training patients do before treatment. Home exercise is hard to monitor, and shop-bought watches track mainly walking and cycling. Strength, compound, and jumping moves central to prehabilitation go uncounted.

Built on a small development board, the watch scores seven standard exercises with an error-height algorithm. Six health workers supplied reference movements, and twenty healthy volunteers then tested the device under watch and at home for four days. Counted repetitions matched human counts closely, and reported compliance ran high.
pmc-13272253:
Soňa Brestovičová is lead author of a 2026 journal article proposing a new salt-loving bacterium species, Idiomarina solivarensis. It was isolated from brine in the former underground salt mine at Solivar, near Prešov in Slovakia. The strain grew best at mild warmth, neutral acidity, and three to six percent salt.

Gene comparisons placed the strain inside the genus Idiomarina, closest to two known species, but whole-genome similarity scores fell well below species thresholds. Its fatty acid profile was distinctive: hydroxyl-bearing fatty acids dominated, a pattern never seen in this genus or other salt-loving bacteria, the authors say. The genome spans 2.8 million DNA letters. The strain is deposited in two public culture collections as the type strain.
pmc-13272353:
Oguzhan Tokur and coauthors benchmark in 2026 three commercial AI tools that find and judge lung nodules spotted incidentally on CT scans. Such nodules are common, and management usually hangs on size alone. Software that also estimates malignancy risk could focus follow-up where it matters, but real-world accuracy was unproven.

The study drew 374 patients from a larger chest CT cohort spanning 2015 to 2024, with cancer status settled by tissue diagnosis or two years of stability. All three tools were scored on detection and risk prediction against radiology reports. Agreement statistics and accuracy curves showed how far the tools can be trusted in routine reading.
pmc-13272553:
Su-jin Yum and colleagues tested a targeted antimicrobial treatment to extend lettuce shelf life in a 2026 study. A bacterium called Sphingomonas paucimobilis spoils plant foods and can also harm people. Normal preservation cannot easily remove one species without disturbing the rest.

Their approach uses short nucleic acid strands that block key genes in the target bacterium, joined to peptides that carry them into cells. The best carrier killed the bacterium at low doses by silencing genes it needs to copy DNA and make proteins. Mismatched strands had no effect, which showed precise targeting. Spraying the treatment on lettuce at a low dose cut discoloration and slowed bacterial growth. The authors propose such tools for safer fresh produce.
pmc-13272853:
Orla Hennessy leads a 2026 study of the learning curve when a hospital unit switched to a cemented composite beam stem for half hip replacement after fracture. Such stems have low fracture rates during surgery, but concern about learning a new implant can slow adoption. The team reviewed the first 140 cases at one center.

Early cases were more often misaligned than with the older stem used for over ten years, at an odds ratio of 2.19. Misalignment fell from 32 percent in the first 46 cases to 4.34 percent in cases 93 to 138, matching the old stem. No higher risk of fracture around the implant was found during adoption.
pmc-13273553:
Yanxing Wei and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their protocol for deriving human trophoblast stem cells from primed pluripotent stem cells. Trophoblast cells form the outer layer of the early embryo and later the placenta. The original protocol appeared in 2022, and the correction fixes errors in its materials tables.

Several stock solutions were printed with the wrong strength unit, micro where milli was meant, a thousand fold gap. The affected chemicals span the stem cell medium and two media used to grow later cell types. One chemical also had its volume corrected downward tenfold. The authors apologize for the errors and any confusion. Anyone repeating the work should use the corrected values, since the wrong strength would change how cells behave.
pmc-13273853:
Dickson Akankwatsa and co-authors described a virtual One Health community in Uganda's West Nile sub-region in a 2026 report. The area sits near the Congo Basin and faces repeated health threats that cross human, animal, and environmental lines. A formal risk exercise had ranked nine priority hazards.

Organizers chose online meetings as the cheapest and most scalable way to build cross sector habits. Between April 2023 and September 2024 they held eleven of eighteen planned sessions, with a median attendance of thirty-three people. Human health workers dominated, making up nearly all participants, which limited the One Health balance. The authors call the model practical and low cost, while urging better digital skills, stronger incentives, mixed formats, and real institutional backing to draw other sectors in.
pmc-13274153:
Ana Luiza Bierrenbach and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on early effects of HPV vaccination in Brazil. Brazil added the quadrivalent HPV vaccine to its national program in 2014. The team tracked first clinic visits for high-grade cervical cell changes, a warning stage before cancer, in national outpatient records.

Among girls and women aged fifteen to nineteen, visit rates rose from 5.5 per 100,000 in 2011 to a peak of 7.1 in 2015, then fell to 1.8 by 2023, below pre-vaccine levels. Older age groups showed no such drop. Visits for other sexually transmitted infections kept rising at all ages, which argues the fall was tied to vaccination, not changed care seeking.
pmc-13275153:
Laura De Pellegrin and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of flow couplers, devices that both join and monitor veins in free flap surgery. In this surgery, tissue is moved with its blood vessels reattached, and a silent vein clot can kill the flap. The team searched three databases through November 2025 for studies of coupler monitoring.

Eleven studies covering 1,775 flaps met criteria, 876 of them coupler-monitored. Pooled accuracy for detecting flap compromise was high: ninety-six point five percent sensitivity and ninety point nine percent specificity. Flap failure ran slightly lower with couplers, two point two versus three point one percent. False alarms were common and usually technical rather than true clots, and couplers cannot spot arterial failure, so the authors advise combined monitoring.
pmc-13275253:
Natalia Nöllenburg and co-authors tested a fermented herbal extract in pigs on working farms in a 2026 study. Breathing problems and tail biting are common welfare issues in pig rearing. A fermented mix of herbs with lactobacilli and yeasts might calm both without drugs.

Two Austrian welfare label farms raised pigs with intact tails across three batches spanning all seasons, with matched pens on plain or supplemented feed. At the end of rearing, supplemented pigs had far fewer shortened tails, which hints at less tail biting. During fattening they also coughed and sneezed less in farm observations, though slaughter checks of the airways showed no difference. Growth measures were recorded throughout. The authors see promise worth further study.
pmc-13275653:
Huan Zeng and colleagues present a 2026 gene analysis of repeated pregnancy loss linked with antiphospholipid syndrome. In that syndrome, the immune system produces antibodies that raise clotting and pregnancy risks. The shared biology behind both conditions remains unclear, which limits diagnosis and care.

Public gene datasets for both conditions were compared, and ten shared altered genes emerged. Machine learning narrowed the list to three hub genes: NAA30, ARHGAP44, and SUGT1. A prediction model built on these genes was checked with standard accuracy curves. Follow-up cell tests supported the findings, and immune imbalance appeared as a common thread across both conditions.
pmc-13276053:
Palina Bartashevich and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how a giant Amazon fish breathes in groups. Arapaima gigas must surface to gulp air, and youngsters often rise together at the same moment. Such teamwork is odd because each fish's need for air builds at its own pace.

Alone, individual fish kept consistent personal surfacing rhythms that differed from each other. In a shoal of about two hundred young fish, though, a large share surfaced within the same second. Computer models of the group pointed to a simple social rule behind the timing. Fish that respond to neighbors in a matching way can sync up without ignoring their own body needs. The authors call this pattern cluster synchrony.
pmc-13276253:
Yulia Tyurina and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on which membrane fats feed a type of cell death called ferroptosis. In ferroptosis, iron drives damage to fatty molecules until the cell dies. One fat family, the ether lipids, was thought to protect against this death, but the evidence was mixed.

Using detailed fat analysis, lab tests, gene tools, and computer models, the team studied an enzyme called 15-LOX. Both forms of the enzyme eagerly oxidized one class of ether fat, turning it into a death signal. The step once thought protective ran about five hundred times slower, ruling it out here. The death signal also appeared as a harmful factor in asthma, cancer, brain trauma, and sunburn-like skin injury. The authors name the enzyme's bias as a possible drug target.
pmc-13276753:
Alberto Rizzo and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on diagnosing fever in travelers returning from an Ebola outbreak zone. The current outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus in Congo and Uganda, will send worried, febrile travelers to specialist centers abroad. Ruling out Ebola, they argue, must not end the workup.

Early Ebola symptoms overlap with malaria, dengue-like viruses, typhoid, and chest infections, most of them treatable. The authors propose traveler-centered pathways that run broad test panels in parallel with Ebola testing, not after it. A recent imported bird flu case in Italy shows the value: an odd flu result triggered sequencing, treatment, notification, and contact tracing. Fast parallel testing, they say, keeps rare deadly diseases from delaying recognition of common ones.
pmc-13277253: Fangfang Zhu and colleagues are named on a 2026 retraction note for a review of the gut-lung axis and microbe imbalance in non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections. The journal's editor-in-chief retracted the review after concerns about undeclared use of artificial intelligence tools, plus errors in a figure and in the text. Asked to explain, the authors could not give a satisfactory account or supporting data, and the editor lost confidence in the article. One author stated that the authors disagree with the retraction.
pmc-13277353:
Camila Moraes Garollo Piran leads a 2026 Brazilian case-control study of young people living with HIV who return to treatment after dropping out. Staying on daily HIV drugs is hard for teens and young adults, and gaps can breed drug resistance. The study, described as the first of its kind in Brazil, compared factors tied to returning for retreatment.

Lack of a religious affiliation was tied to higher odds of retreatment. Sex, alcohol use, and living in an institution also showed links. Diagnosis at the testing center and missed appointments lowered the odds. Knowing what brings young people back, or keeps them away, can help services prevent permanent dropout, the authors argue.
pmc-13278053:
A O'Kane leads a 2026 study of clotting risks after a treatment used to reverse blood thinners during serious bleeding. The treatment, prothrombin complex concentrate, restores clotting factors. The team reviewed 682 patients treated in the Belfast Health and Social Care Trust from 2015 to 2021, grouped by which blood thinner they took.

Brain bleeding was the most common event in every group. Clotting events within thirty days ran higher in patients on newer direct blood thinners, at about nine percent overall, than in warfarin patients, at five percent. Thirty-day death rates ranged from thirteen to twenty-three percent. Few patients restarted blood thinners afterward. Planned pathways for restarting treatment are needed, the authors say.
pmc-13278453:
Sudha Rani Unnam and Kareemulla Shaik present a 2026 study of a deep learning system that detects routing attacks in Internet of Things networks. Such networks link many small devices, and their low-power routing protocol is a target for attacks such as blackhole and flooding. The framework first selects the most useful data features with an optimization algorithm, then classifies attacks with a memory-based neural network.

On a standard attack dataset covering four attack types, the system reached about ninety-nine percent accuracy with a low false discovery rate. It beat baseline models in comparison tests. The authors note two limits: the evaluation rests on simulated data, and training adds computing cost that may hinder real-time use on small devices.
pmc-13279153:
Meriem Boui and colleagues report a 2026 case of joint infection that looked like a belly emergency. The joint is the pubic symphysis, the front joint of the pelvis. Infection there is rare and is most often seen after surgery. Their patient was a fifty nine year old woman with no past surgery or illness.

She had fever with deep pain low in the belly, which first pointed to gut or womb causes. Scans showed worn bone and a fluid pocket near the joint. Magnetic resonance imaging, a detailed scan, mapped the spread best. A needle sample drew pus that grew Staphylococcus aureus, a common germ. Targeted drugs brought fast relief, and later scans showed clear shrinkage.
pmc-13280453:
Dan Liu and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study that adds phosphonate groups to azaarenes, nitrogen bearing ring compounds prized in drug research. Adding the group by direct C-H functionalization, editing a carbon hydrogen bond, is a formidable challenge. Their route runs an intermolecular cyclizative rearrangement, a ring forming shuffle between molecules. A cascade joins a dipolar ring step, a sigmatropic shift and selective carbon bond cuts.

A zinc bromide catalyst proved crucial to the transformation. It not only gave high conversion but also controlled which site reacted first, which in turn set the selectivity of the whole process. The protocol serves late stage functionalization of diverse pharmaceuticals and ligands, drug building blocks. Further product diversification was shown as well. The authors claim the first example of C-H methylenephosphonylation of arenes.
pmc-13282353:
Mohammad Valibeknejad and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on sodium silicate grouting, a method that injects a glass-like chemical into soil to block water flow and strengthen loose ground. The technique has been used for decades, yet field results vary widely. Soil differences, groundwater chemistry, and pollutants all change how the gel forms and lasts. Risks include grout leaking into groundwater and gels breaking down over time.

The review is the first full synthesis since the nineteen nineties, drawing on research, field cases, and industry practice. It traces the processes from injection through gelling to later change, at micro, pore, and field scales. Sand-gel contact, pore blocking, and strength gains get close attention. The authors also weigh environmental impact and a resistivity imaging method for checking grout spread. They call for better predictive models and design rules for safer, greener use.
pmc-13282453:
Nicolas Riveros-Neira and co-authors present a 2026 case of spinal disc and bone infection caused by a drug-resistant gut bacterium in a healthy woman. Discitis and vertebral osteomyelitis are rare infections of the disc space and spine bone, hard to diagnose because symptoms are vague. Their patient was a sixty-two-year-old woman with returning lower back pain and scans suggesting infection at the base of her spine. Her immune system was normal.

Early cultures and a biopsy gave no clear answer. Surgery finally confirmed bone infection by an Escherichia coli strain producing enzymes that defeat many antibiotics. She responded well to a powerful carbapenem antibiotic. Long-term suppressive treatment with another antibiotic followed. The authors highlight two lessons: diagnosis may need surgical sampling when early tests fail, and resistant gut bacteria should be considered even in low-risk patients without immune weakness or hospital exposure.
pmc-13282553:
Zihang Wang and co-authors wrote a 2026 review that sorts out naming for long-term cough that resists standard care. Clinicians use three labels, idiopathic, unexplained, and refractory chronic cough, often as if they mean the same thing. The review sets out how each label is defined and how the labels relate.

The authors also weigh cough hypersensitivity syndrome as a shared frame for why such cough persists. That frame treats an over-sensitive cough reflex as the core problem behind many cases. Clearer terms should help studies enrol more alike groups of patients, so results guide care with less confusion. The review notes open questions about testing and treatment that still need work.
pmc-13282953:
Primary care charts across Qatar reveal how often blood pressure targets are met, in a 2026 review assembled by Nada Abdelkader's group. Uncontrolled pressure raises risk of heart disease and early death. The review asks how many patients reach target levels and which traits predict control.

Charts from 2017 to 2020 covered more than two thousand selected patients. Over 60 percent of patients reached target pressure in each study year. Patients with diabetes or kidney disease also passed 60 percent in most years. Sex, nationality, and other health conditions shaped control rates. The authors find broad success but clear gaps for some patient groups that need attention.
pmc-13283153:
Carlota F Galán-Plana and colleagues brought fresh evidence in 2026 that wild western chimpanzees in Dindefelo, Senegal, pound open baobab fruit. This hard-shelled fruit feeding was known from only two other areas, in Senegal and Mali. The team gathered signs during the peak fruit season of late 2021 and early 2022.

Camera traps filmed the apes, smeared anvils and cracked empty shells were found, and droppings were checked for baobab traces. Apes of all ages tried pounding, on the ground against rocks or roots and in trees against branches, though only adolescents and adults broke the fruit open. One further technique needed no striking at all. Seed re-swallowing also looked common, widening the known range of this behaviour.
pmc-13283453:
A third of Vietnamese arthritis patients also meet fibromyalgia criteria, inflating activity scores, Ngan Tran Thi's clinic study finds in 2026. Fibromyalgia can inflate symptom scores without true joint inflammation. Data from low- and middle-income countries on this overlap remain scarce.

A total of 187 patients with rheumatoid arthritis were checked with 2016 criteria. Just over a third also met criteria for fibromyalgia in the study. Those patients had higher joint activity scores driven mainly by subjective parts. Objective inflammation markers differed only modestly between the two groups. Adjusted models kept fibromyalgia linked to higher activity scores on its own. Quality of life was worse, and steroid use was more common.
pmc-13283553:
Chuan Meng and colleagues traced in 2026 why tetraploid Chinese cabbage seeds lose vigour faster in storage than normal diploid seeds. Tetraploid plants carry four sets of chromosomes and offer useful farm traits, yet their seeds fade sooner, which costs growers money. The team profiled genes and chemicals in seeds across a long storage time span.

Viability fell most steeply across a seventeen-year gradient, so deep profiling focused on the oldest seed lots. Tetraploid seeds switched on a shared signalling hub joining two plant hormones, auxin and salicylic acid, while helpful flavonoid compounds drained away. Energy pathways, mainly starch, sugar, and membrane fat handling, showed the earliest imbalance. The authors offer the hub and energy markers as breeding targets for hardier tetraploid seed.
pmc-13284453: Max Trauernicht and co-authors publish a short correction, dated 2026, to a protocol for measuring transcription factor activity with barcoded reporters. One primer sequence in the key resources table was printed in error. The notice gives the correct sequence for the indexed Illumina barcode primer and states that the right primers were used throughout, so results and conclusions stand. The authors apologize for the oversight.
pmc-13284753:
Charles Garcia da Cunha and co-authors test light-driven glycerol oxidation in a 2026 materials study. Splitting water for hydrogen could gain value if paired with turning biomass waste such as glycerol into useful products. The team coated varied carbon nitrides onto glass, then grew bismuth vanadate on top to form paired light absorbers.

All paired films kept a bandgap close to plain bismuth vanadate, and imaging showed mixed zones rich in each part, the authors report. Adding glycerol raised photocurrent fourfold for the base material at a set voltage. One polymeric nitride pairing worked best of those tested. Rankings show nitride choice matters for designing solar fuel and chemical systems.
pmc-13285353:
Fast tech growth in forensic work can outrun the rules that keep it fair, warns Sarah P. Chu in a 2026 framework article. New AI, automation, and data-heavy tools promise much, yet labs often adopt them before proof and guardrails catch up, a pattern long seen in criminal justice tech. Chu reads the risk through the Gartner Hype Cycle.

Adopting tools at the hype peak invites harm when validity, due process, and public trust lag behind. The framework urges labs to weigh proof first, center justice in each rollout, and build ways to repair harm when tools mislead. Moving fast, Chu argues, should mean strengthening justice at the same speed, not after damage is done.
pmc-13286353:
Irina Kolotuev and colleagues combine two electron microscopy methods to picture the tiny bridges that connect developing egg cells in fruit flies. These ring canals let nurse cells feed the growing egg, yet their small size inside a large tissue makes them hard to image in three dimensions. The 2026 study pairs array tomography with focused ion beam scanning.

The combined views measured how bridge size and thickness vary within and between cell clusters. Finger-like folds of membrane near the bridges appeared earlier in development than previously reported. Reconstructions showed how these extensive contacts sit in space. A new membrane structure lining the inside of the bridge channel was also found. The imaging approach could serve other hard-to-reach structures.
pmc-13286753:
Katharina Kreiger, Elisabeth Weiss, and Felix Fluri ask what makes some stroke patients respond to rehabilitation while others do not. Their 2026 study reviews 100 patients aged 65 and older treated after ischemic stroke. The idea of cognitive reserve, the brain's cushion against damage, is usually guessed from schooling, which may miss how the mind actually works.

Enjoying cognitive leisure activities predicted responder status far better than education did. Responders were defined as patients improving in at least two functional areas. Baseline test scores alone did not separate the groups. Network analysis told a different story: responders' thinking and movement measures formed a denser, more connected web. Reserve, the authors argue, may live in that integration rather than in any single score.
pmc-13286953:
Jingwei Li and co-authors hunt for gene markers of dilated cardiomyopathy, the common non-ischemic heart muscle disease that often ends in heart failure. Their 2026 study starts from heart tissue gene data, intersects two gene-finding methods, and then lets four machine learning algorithms vote on the strongest candidates. Seven genes survived the process.

Models built on those genes separated disease from healthy tissue almost perfectly in the discovery data, though the authors warn those scores are likely optimistic. Checks in outside datasets supported four of the seven genes consistently. Tissue atlases placed some candidates in heart muscle cells and others in fibroblasts. Genetic and network analyses suggest the genes respond to disease rather than cause it, framing them as markers for future validation.
pmc-13287153:
Jenifer Caroline Moreira Campos led a 2026 laboratory study of how seeds of the endangered orchid Vanilla lindmaniana begin to grow. Mature seeds were cleaned, treated, and placed on a nutrient medium in darkness at a steady warm temperature, then examined under ordinary and electron microscopes.

Growth began after about three months. The authors report that 61.8% of seeds germinated, and most young structures later formed roots. Opening started with a split in one seed-coat layer, described as clam-like, while starch built up inside. Roots appeared at a later stage and grew strongly. The method may support propagation work for protecting and cultivating the species.
pmc-13287753: Editors of Scientific Reports retracted an article in 2026, published that same March, claiming that a plant compound called flavokawain C slows a childhood kidney tumour. After publication, editors learned that the cell line used as the tumour model, G401, in fact comes from a different childhood kidney tumour type, a rhabdoid tumour. The claims about the named disease are therefore unsupported. All authors agreed to the retraction. The short notice reports no new experiments.
pmc-13288053:
Humaira Mustafa and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a year of care for 60 children given breathing support. Ages ran from one month to eighteen years. Support came through a soft nasal tube in a paediatric intensive care unit. Support avoided a breathing tube in the windpipe. Records covered January to December 2024.

Support succeeded for 44 children, which is 73.3%. Most admissions were for lung illness. Failure clustered in children with other health problems, higher severity scores, and higher pressure and oxygen needs. Failed cases had more lung air leaks, longer stays, and half died. No deaths occurred among successes. Better oxygen levels at start marked likely success.
pmc-13288753:
Clara Gallay and co-authors ask if childbearing shapes Alzheimer's harm in 2026. Their data come from the ALFA+ cohort in Barcelona. It held 254 women past menopause. None had symptoms at entry. Spinal fluid and brain scans were taken. Thinking tests ran at one or two visits.

Child count and amyloid status joined forces. Memory decline split by both. Hippocampus size split by both too. Among amyloid-positive women, more children meant steeper decline. Their hippocampi were also smaller. No such pattern showed in amyloid-negative women. Parity may shape brain reserve against early change, they suggest.
pmc-13289053:
Mohammad Ismail Zubair and colleagues study polio after regime change in Afghanistan in 2026. Their study asks if the 2021 shift hurt polio control. Afghanistan is one of two last polio nations. Many feared outbreaks after US forces left. The team also checked the 2001 shift for comparison.

No outbreak came after the 2021 withdrawal. Patterns near 2001 and 2021 looked alike. Vaccine work did not drop after 2021. In fact, polio infections fell a lot. Vaccine rates shifted up at the same time. The study urges work on why control held. Such lessons could aid endgame plans elsewhere. Other nations still fighting polio may gain.
pmc-13290853:
A coffee-derived acid packed into a double-network gel speeds infected wound closure, Mengwei Zhang and colleagues show in a biomaterials study from 2026. Infected wounds stall under bacterial load, runaway inflammation, and oxidative stress, so the team loaded caffeic acid into a dressing meant to fight all three.

The hydrogel's porous structure soaked up fluid and released the acid steadily. In vitro it proved gentle on cells and blood, strongly inhibited Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, and scavenged free radicals. It also nudged macrophages toward the healing M2 state and raised collagen production in fibroblasts. In the animal wound model, treatment improved infection control, sped closure, and boosted skin regrowth and collagen deposition. Zhang and colleagues present the gel as a template for dressings that combine infection control with repair.
pmc-13290953:
Health needs more than body, mind, and society, Nazanin Abbaspour and colleagues argue in a framework paper from 2026. Engel's 1977 biopsychosocial model reshaped care. But it stays vague on food, lifestyle, money, surroundings, and politics. So the authors build a nine-part model of health determinants. It adds cultural, environmental, economic, political, spiritual, and lifestyle domains.

Each part splits into categories and measurable elements. Clinicians apply only the subsets a case needs. Obesity is the test case. Four factors, activity frequency, caloric intake, dietary fiber, and insulin sensitivity, feed a Bayesian network and a rule-based scorer. On NHANES data they reached about 85% predictive accuracy and about 80% agreement. The authors stress this is proof of concept on simplified factors, not a validated clinical tool.
pmc-13291053:
Heating fat under facial skin without burning skin is the goal for Dong-Min Lee and colleagues in 2026. Normal heat devices reach too shallow or burn the surface. The team built a small antenna with a cavity back. It works in the 2.4 to 2.5 GHz band.

Sharp contrast at the skin-fat border helps push energy deep. Computer models guided pulse length and power. Tests ran on pig tissue first. A first human check used 10 W of power. Warming hit the target depth in a repeatable way. No skin harm was seen. Wide coverage and lasting benefit still need trials.
pmc-13291153:
