Nursing care around a cold plasma eye treatment is reviewed in a 2026 study by Dan Hu, Yuan Lin, and Huping Wu. The method treats surface disorders of the cornea. The team looked at healing, pain, and patient satisfaction. They also split cases by cause.

Records covered 38 patients treated from mid 2022 to early 2024. Thirty cases were structural or refractive. Eight were due to infection. Infected eyes healed more slowly and hurt more. Their condition also came back more often within three months. Satisfaction ran lower in that group. The authors use these gaps to shape closer nursing watch for infected cases.
pmc-13291753:
Timothy R Smith and Janet Koprivnikar report a 2026 behavioral study asking whether red flour beetles steer clear of places carrying parasite risk. Beetles chose among foraging options involving two natural enemies: Beauveria bassiana, a fungus, and Steinernema carpocapsae, a nematode. Trials mixed single and paired threats, live infective stages, and dead beetles that had been killed by infection or put down another way.

Contrary to expectation, the beetles mostly failed to avoid either parasite or the parasite-killed bodies, and they were drawn toward corpses infected by the nematode. Mixed danger cues also failed to change their choices. The authors say the result questions how widely avoidance works as an antiparasite defense, and it matters for using fungi and nematodes as pest control agents.
pmc-13291853:
Joseph M Unger reviews how completely cancer trial reports describe who took part, in a 2026 systematic review. Place and money shape cancer outcomes in the United States, from screening access to travel burdens. Trial papers, though, may not say where participants lived or what they earned. Unger examined 441 primary reports of United States randomized oncology trials. He tallied which geographic, socioeconomic, and demographic traits each paper reported.

Age and sex appeared in most reports, as expected. Reporting of race and ethnicity has grown substantially over time, the review found. By contrast, rurality was rarely reported at all. Income, education, insurance status, and area-level deprivation were rare or wholly absent across the set. Without those details, readers cannot judge whether results travel to poorer or rural populations. Unger argues that journals should expect fuller cohort description. Such reporting would sharpen debates about fairness in cancer research.
pmc-13292053:
Yu-Hao Huang and co-authors examine a 2026 study of BCLAF1, a transcription factor tied to the BCL2 family, in radioresistant triple-negative breast cancer. Such tumors shrug off radiation and harbor stem-like cells that drive relapse. Working with the Cancer Genome Atlas data and a radioresistant MDA-MB-231 cell line, the team varied BCLAF1 and SRC levels and tested the drug dasatinib.

High BCLAF1 matched more advanced stages and shorter survival. Radiation-resistant cells carried extra BCLAF1, and SRC overexpression raised BCLAF1 while lowering radiation sensitivity. Knocking BCLAF1 down shrank tumorsphere growth, a sign of weaker stemness, and dasatinib lowered BCLAF1, HIF-1α, and stemness proteins together. Blocking HIF-1α erased the sphere-forming boost from BCLAF1. The authors nominate BCLAF1 as a target for beating radioresistance.
pmc-13292553:
Ruiheng Jing and co-authors publish a 2026 laboratory protocol for making ultrapure full-length Tau protein, the microtubule protein whose deposits mark Alzheimer's disease. Tau2N4R, the isoform they target, aggregates heavily in diseased brains, and sloppy preparations have hampered precise structural work. Their workflow combines affinity chromatography with preparative HPLC for a cleaner finish.

Steps cover building the construct with an N-terminal hexahistidine tag joined through a cleavable SUMO tag, expressing it in E. coli, and polishing the product. The payoff is homogeneous Tau that forms fibrils in vitro both with heparin and without any cofactor. The authors contrast their yield with older routes plagued by truncations and leftover tag fragments, and with chemical synthesis, which is pure but slow and equipment-hungry.
pmc-13292653:
Daniela Morales Hermosilla and co-authors share a 2026 letter on three patients whose alopecia areata had resisted standard care, treated instead with 308-nanometer excimer light. The autoimmune hair loss had shrugged off corticosteroids and other standbys. Excimer light delivers narrow-band ultraviolet in a targeted beam, needing fewer sessions and lower total dose than whole-scalp phototherapy.

One woman with a SALT severity score of 46 cleared completely to zero after sixteen weekly sessions, without side effects. A 12-year-old boy with alopecia totalis regrew hair across stubborn patches after sixteen twice-weekly sessions, showing only prolonged redness twice. The first case involved a 43-year-old woman with a SALT score of 54 who had failed a year and a half of drug combinations. The authors present the light as a safe salvage option, while noting it fails in total scalp and body hair loss.
pmc-13292853:
Cong Chen and co-authors review, in 2026, how astragaloside IV may act against diabetes. The compound comes from Astragalus membranaceus, a plant used in traditional care, and diabetes involves tangled signals for sugar, fat, and inflammation.

Across lab studies, the compound is reported to aid insulin action, calm inflammatory signals, and cut oxidative harm through several pathways acting together. It also shapes cell survival, self-cleanup, and energy centers, which may protect kidneys, heart, eyes, and nerves. Most proof still comes from animal and cell work, and poor absorption in the body limits use. The authors call for better dosing and human trials.
pmc-13292953:
Yuka Kondo presents a 2026 case report on a kidney tumor in a 25-year-old woman that was hard to name at first look. The 4.5-cm mass looked like kidney cancer, since tests showed strong TFE3 staining and no pigment marker signal.

After surgery, the tumor shape and a negative PAX8 test pointed instead to a rare growth called epithelioid angiomyolipoma, part of the PEComa family. Gene testing confirmed a fusion joining ASPSCR1 and TFE3, matching a newly noted tumor type. Even without pigment markers, this tumor can occur. Marker and gene tests help split it from look-alike cancers and guide care.
pmc-13293453:
Samantha Schofield and colleagues measure, in a 2026 study, how young blacklegged ticks breathe in bursts rather than steadily. Ticks spend most of life off hosts and must trade air intake against water loss through open breathing tubes.

Carbon dioxide output of nymph ticks was tracked in a flow-through system, giving the first such measures for this Ixodes group. Burst cycles were confirmed, and both burst rate and burst size varied with how the nymphs had developed. Lab-raised and wild-caught ticks differed in pattern. Comparing with relatives may show how this disease-carrying tick balances water and air across settings.
pmc-13293653:
Cynthia Imtiaz, Changsoo Kim, and Dong-Guk Paeng test, in a 2026 mouse study, whether focused ultrasound can ferry ginseng nanoparticles across the blood-brain barrier in Parkinson disease. The barrier blocks most brain drugs, and the ginseng compound Rg3 protects nerve cells but enters poorly.

Sound pulses briefly opened the barrier in a rotenone-based mouse model, then labeled particles were injected. Imaging showed far more particles reached the brain after opening. Combined care gave the best energy and enzyme values in brain cells and better movement than either part alone, though group gaps were trends. More work is needed to firm the claim.
pmc-13293753:
Mild heat therapy delivered by light gets a rat test from Kaiping Bai and colleagues in 2026 for bladder failure after lower spinal cord injury. Such injury brings leakage, infections, and kidney harm, and current care mostly manages symptoms rather than fixing the bladder.

Treated rats showed better bladder shape and pressure measures, with stronger gains when care began early. Heat care cut bladder scarring, calmed long-term inflammation, and restored the balance between cell growth and death. It also boosted useful vessel growth and repaired bladder nerve fibers. The authors argue for early, repeated sessions and offer a base for human trials.
pmc-13293853:
Tara Peña and colleagues shrink transistors built from atom-thin semiconductors down to ribbon widths in a 2026 electronics study. Future chips need channels that are short, narrow, and extremely thin, and single-layer materials such as molybdenum disulfide offer the thinnest possible body. Earlier devices worked well only at widths far larger than future designs allow, so the team patterned ribbons with a top-down process and anchored contacts to keep the fragile strips from peeling.

Channels reached lengths and widths of twenty-five to thirty nanometers, with little edge damage confirmed by light-based inspection. Devices of both electron and hole types delivered strong currents for their size, and one material improved on earlier ribbon results by more than a hundredfold. The results position patterned two-dimensional ribbons as candidates for the next transistor generation.
pmc-13294353:
Lars Vogt introduces the Semantic Units Framework in a 2026 manuscript on knowledge infrastructure. Standard knowledge graphs store lone triples, which scatter meaning and hide whether a claim is rare, typical, or universal. Vogt treats whole statements and compound structures as first-class units with clear borders, identity, and epistemic status, plus resource classes for some, most, every, and all cases.

Negations, hedges, and higher-order claims about other claims fit the same scheme. No new graph engine is proposed: the concepts can ride on current tools for FAIR and CLEAR data goals. Human readers and machines both gain statements that carry their own context.
pmc-13294653:
Chantas Mahaisavariya and colleagues test a web application called Wellhealth for osteoporosis care in a 2026 feasibility study. The work took place at the Golden Jubilee Medical Center of Mahidol University. Older adults often start osteoporosis treatment late or stop early, raising their later fracture risk.

Thirty-two patients, averaging 71 years old, used the system and its liaison support service for one year. Weekly logging averaged about 62 percent for bone medicines and higher for calcium and vitamin D. Satisfaction was mostly high or good, and steady calcium logging was the one factor linked to steadier logging of bone medicines.
pmc-13294853:
Xiaodong Xie and co-authors examine faster emergency care plus health teaching for stroke patients in a 2026 study. Acute ischaemic stroke demands rapid treatment, and anxiety and low mood can slow recovery. Their centre compared routine care in early 2023 with an improved pathway used later that year.

Each group held 57 patients, for a total of 114 people treated across the year. Waiting, diagnosis, and vessel-opening times all shortened under the improved pathway. Neurological recovery was greater, anxiety and depression scores fell further, and patients and families reported higher satisfaction, suggesting combined process and education changes benefit both care speed and mood.
pmc-13294953:
TJ FitzGerald and co-authors argue for strong quality checks in radiation cancer trials in a 2026 editorial. Clinical trials now drive improvements in cancer care, but they must run the same way across many hospitals and countries. Patients, equipment, and local habits vary widely between sites.

A sound quality programme, the authors explain, rests on five parts, from qualifying and credentialing sites to reviewing treatment and imaging data. Sites must show they hold the staff and services a given trial demands before joining. Keeping care uniform for every enrolled patient is what lets trial answers be trusted and turned into better routine practice.
pmc-13295053:
Jan Pawlas introduces a greener way to join peptide fragments in a 2026 methods article. Drug makers build large peptide medicines, including diabetes and obesity treatments, by linking protected fragments. Standard release from resin supports relies on a harsh fluorinated acid and a suspect solvent, with lengthy clean-up steps.

The new route uses a common coupling helper, Oxyma, in ethyl acetate to free fragments from their support resin. Freed material goes straight into the next joining step without isolation, reusing the same helper as a coupling aid. A ring-closed, sulphur-bridged fragment shows the method can build complex shapes and support modular production.
pmc-13295753:
Andreas Glantz and colleagues study leaders rolling out shared activity time in psychiatric wards in a 2026 article. Time Together sets one hour on five days each week when nurses and patients do joint activities. Earlier work hinted at rollout trouble, but leaders' views on the process were unstudied.

Interviews with 11 mid-level leaders and rollout leads across three wards in northern Sweden fed the analysis. Leaders saw the idea as fitting ward aims, yet some frontline staff viewed joint activities as not proper work. Thin information and a fuzzy reason for change slowed uptake. The authors call for clearer purpose and fuller staff involvement next time.
pmc-13295853:
Robert Muni-Lofra and a large co-author group assess care for adults with spinal muscular atrophy in the United Kingdom in 2026. Care guidance was written largely around children, so the team checked how far adult services match those standards using registry data.

Data from 426 adults with confirmed disease showed common breathing weakness, swallowing problems, joint contractures and heavy limits on daily life. Yet support often fell short of guidance, with clear gaps in breathing help, physiotherapy and nutrition care. The authors call for adult services to apply the standards more evenly across the lifespan.
pmc-13296053:
Xueyu Zhu and colleagues probe how cadmium and copper together stress the larvae of a cuttlefish, Sepia esculenta, in a 2026 study. The species is a prized catch on China's east coast, and the two metals, common in the sea, slow its growth. The team paired stress gauges with gene activity reads to trace how the pair harms the young.

Joint exposure plainly harmed the larvae and stirred oxidative stress. Gene maps showed transport, cell work, and DNA copying held back. A network study pulled out twenty key genes, among them ones that glue cells to their matrix, ones that keep that matrix whole, and ones that ferry metals across cell walls. The authors sketch how the two metals together poison the larvae's basic upkeep.
pmc-13296153:
How wording and tactics in assault accounts shift blame onto victims is tested in 2026 by Pantxika Victoire Morlat and co-authors. Two hundred two adults read short stories varying the coercion used, whether the telling sounded active or passive, and answered questions on rape myths.

Older participants blamed victims more, and men scored higher on myth acceptance and blame than women. Active wording made readers in both tactic conditions less likely to call the event sexual assault. People low in myth acceptance blamed less throughout. The authors stress that language choices in policing, courts and media shape recognition of assault.
pmc-13296253:
Yang Du, Kui Deng, and Ziyang Liu study what pulls shoppers back to buy again, focusing on fear of missing out, in a 2026 survey. The data came from 518 Chinese consumers who had bought Pop Mart goods, a market shaped by social media, scarce drops, and show-off posts. The team modeled how materialism, envy, and scarcity feed the fear, and how the fear feeds snap buying and the wish to return.

All three traits fed the fear, with scarcity the strongest. The fear fed snap buying, and snap buying fed the wish to buy again. Three chain paths held, with fear and snap buying carrying each trait's pull in turn. The authors extend fear-of-missing-out work into cultural and creative goods and show how market cues turn feeling into lasting buying habits.
pmc-13296653:
Kun Bi, Zhuoyi Chen and Tianran He design, in 2026, a compact high-torque magnet motor for humanoid robots that must push and feel contact rather than just hold positions. Their layout puts the rotor outside and tucks a planetary reducer inside the stator to save space and boost torque.

Different slot and pole pairings are compared by computer modelling for peak torque, torque per weight and overload headroom. One pairing is optimised and built, and bench tests confirm the predictions. The authors say the verified design suits force-controlled joints in interactive robots.
pmc-13296753:
Jerome Clatot and co-authors study, in 2026, a faulty potassium channel variant tied to epilepsy. The channel, KV3.1, lets certain neurons fire very fast, and one recurring change switches the channel off when tested alone.

When the faulty subunit was mixed with normal ones, as in patients, the combined channels instead gained function, a dominant-positive twist. That reversal shows single-subunit tests can mislead about real biology. The authors say understanding such partner effects matters for matching treatments to variant type in this gene's wide spectrum of brain and movement disorders.
pmc-13297153:
Fang Duan, Xiongping Cao, Zheng Yan, and Jianming Chen compare brain responses to three kinds of oddball sounds in a 2026 EEG study. In oddball tasks, a rare deviant sound interrupts a steady stream. Thirty-eight healthy volunteers heard deviants that were a plain tone, reversed speech, or their own name.

Hearing one's own name produced the strongest electrical responses at the scalp. Source analysis showed a wide network lighting up, covering salience and self-reference regions of the brain. Tone and reversed-speech deviants engaged smaller, more localised sets of areas. Name responses could be classified with about eighty percent accuracy. The authors suggest name-based tasks for brain-computer interfaces and clinical assessment research.
pmc-13297253:
Ann Morcos and co-authors review, in 2026, tiny parcels shed by diffuse midline glioma, a fatal childhood brain tumour where radiation is the only standard help and relapse is near certain. The parcels carry RNA and proteins between cells and may shape how tumours answer radiation.

The review gathers evidence that the vesicles help tumour cells communicate, adapt and resist treatment. Because they reach blood and spinal fluid, they could also let doctors watch the tumour without surgery. Loading them with drugs is floated as a delivery route. The authors map open questions for diagnosis and therapy.
pmc-13297453:
Should allergy shots aim higher than symptom relief? Fabiana Furci and co-authors argue in a 2026 review that allergen immunotherapy should be judged by whether it can deliver lasting clinical remission. They trace how the field's goals have shifted from control toward changing the disease itself.

Immunotherapy remains the only treatment that modifies IgE-mediated allergic disease rather than masking it. The authors review definitions of remission in allergic rhinitis and asthma, where remission includes freedom from symptoms, no systemic steroid use, and stable lung function. They weigh the evidence that treatment can hold benefits after it stops and discuss tools clinics could use to recognize remission in everyday practice.
pmc-13297553:
Light bouncing off a thin metal film can report what living cells are doing, and Petia Genova-Kalou with colleagues chart how that trick matured in a 2026 review. Surface plasmon resonance began as a way to measure molecular binding outside cells; over the past 20 to 25 years it has moved into cell-based assays.

The review traces that chronology and the pressures that drove each new variant, giving special attention to grating-coupled designs used with cells. Strengths and weaknesses of competing techniques are weighed against results from real biological samples. The authors close with forecasts of which approaches look most promising and where notable results are likely to appear next.
pmc-13299353:
Norman Nkuzi Khoza and others survey silica dust safety among mineworkers in four Southern African countries, in a 2026 occupational health study. Structured surveys reached 1,440 exposed workers, gauging knowledge, attitudes, and practices about a dust that causes fatal lung disease. Most workers showed sound knowledge and decent practices.

Yet half held negative safety attitudes. Company training correlated with knowledge, but mandatory in-house training predicted lower practice scores in the regression model, which the authors call a training paradox. External training and higher education predicted better compliance. Technicians and younger workers looked higher risk. Participatory, role-specific programmes are recommended over top-down compliance.
pmc-13299553:
Jason Reece, Jee Young Lee, and Rachel Kleit examine a housing mobility programme that pairs three years of rental help with life coaching, in a 2026 case study. Low-income children in the United States disproportionately live in distressed housing, and the pathways from moving to better health were poorly spelled out. Surveys, interviews, and records traced participating families over time.

Families reported wide health gains driven by safer housing, cleaner indoor air, lower stress, coaching support, better finances, and stronger schools. Physical gains appeared early, and mental health followed as stability grew. Improved health then fed educational and economic progress. A three-year subsidy looked sufficient here.
pmc-13299753:
A platelet-boosting pill helped cancer patients get back on chemotherapy in a 2026 real-world study led by Mehmet Baysal. Chemotherapy often crushes platelet counts, forcing delays, yet no drug is formally approved for that problem; the multicenter team reviewed 31 adults with solid tumors given eltrombopag.

Median platelet counts climbed from 33 at baseline to 99.5 by week twelve, in the units reported. Within three weeks, 58.1% of patients had resumed chemotherapy, and 48.4% finished their planned regimens by week six. Side effects were limited to mild, temporary liver enzyme rises in three patients, with no major bleeding or clots. The authors stress the uncontrolled design and call for proper trials.
pmc-13300253:
Reliable gene-expression work needs yardstick genes that stay steady, and Xinan Li and colleagues set out to find them for the teak defoliator Hyblaea puera in a 2026 study. This invasive moth threatens teak plantations and coastal mangroves, yet its molecular toolkit is thin. The team tested ten common candidate reference genes for RT-qPCR.

Candidates including actin, GAPDH, and several ribosomal protein genes were checked across temperatures, larval stages, adult sexes, developmental stages, and tissues. Stability tools such as geNorm, NormFinder, and RefFinder ranked the genes under each condition. A longevity-pathway gene then served to verify the rankings. The resulting gene sets give future studies of host shifts and stress responses a firmer measurement base.
pmc-13300653:
M Ragagnin and a multidisciplinary team describe their Pregnancy Heart Team's first experience with arrhythmias in pregnancy, in a 2026 report. Carrying a child stresses the heart and blood vessels and can spark new rhythm problems or worsen old ones, so European guidelines endorse teams. Their registry gathered forty-two women seen between 2023 and 2025, before conception, while pregnant, and after birth. Risk was classed by the updated modified World Health Organization scale.

Cases spanned heart muscle diseases, heart muscle inflammation, channelopathies, and ventricular and supraventricular rhythm disorders. Just over half the women sat in the higher risk classes. Care combined delivery planning, rhythm monitoring, and pregnancy-compatible drugs, with beta-blockers and flecainide favored for ventricular problems. Two devices were implanted without fluoroscopy. Treatment worked in all but one case, which settled after delivery, and every completed pregnancy ended well. The authors credit the team model for those results.
pmc-13301353:
Roberta Lo Nano and co-authors ask which electrical measurements predict a positive heart muscle biopsy in a 2026 multicenter study. Fifty-four patients suspected of myocarditis, inflammatory cardiomyopathy, or arrhythmogenic dysplasia had biopsies steered by 3D electroanatomic maps. The forceps were wired into the mapping system, so tissue came from electrically abnormal ground. Samples ran three to six per patient across both ventricles.

Where histology confirmed disease, unipolar and bipolar voltages and conduction speed all ran clearly lower than in healthy samples. A visible electrical scar at the right side of the septum predicted a diagnosis for cardiomyopathy. The tissue's electrical impedance separated diseased from healthy samples, with an area under the curve of about 0.87. The authors argue impedance earns a place beside voltage and conduction in guiding where to bite. That points to fewer blind samples and answers for diseases that hide in patches in the muscle.
pmc-13301453:
Believing you can cope with pain may quietly steer whether dialysis patients keep their regimen, Ioanna Mitsia and colleagues explore in a 2026 cross-sectional study from Athens, Greece. One hundred ninety-nine hemodialysis patients at a single private hospital filled in a pain self-efficacy scale and a dialysis adherence questionnaire, alongside clinical and social details.

Scores landed mid-range on both tools, and the simple correlation between confidence and adherence fell short of significance. Once other factors entered the model, though, self-efficacy emerged as a small independent predictor of sticking with treatment. Longer illness and heavier pill loads dragged adherence down, while marriage lifted it, hinting at the weight of daily support.
pmc-13302153:
Chaeeun Park and co-authors develop, in a 2026 methods paper, two mass spectrometry workflows for measuring short-chain fatty acids in microbiome research. These small molecules, made by gut microbes, influence immunity, energy balance, and inflammation. Measuring them reliably across very different materials has lacked standard methods.

One workflow reads vapour above the material directly, needing little preparation and suiting high throughput. The second extracts and chemically tags the acids first, gaining sensitivity for tiny or dilute materials such as liver tissue. Both were tested on pure microbe cultures, animal faeces and liver, and a standard simulated human faecal material. Together the protocols give laboratories a matched pair of options for profiling these metabolites.
pmc-13303453:
Aidos Omarov and colleagues present a 2026 methods study on rating the natural resource potential of farm landscapes. Such ratings must combine climate, soil, biology, land, and water measures that use very different units and scales.

Working with long-term data for the Ayagoz District in Kazakhstan, the team built a layered model around Harrington's generalized desirability function. Twenty indicators were converted onto one scale from zero to one and combined with geometric averaging. Unlike simple added scores, this approach lets one critically weak resource pull the whole rating down. The output is maps and numbers that planners can compare across zones and districts.
pmc-13305353:
Emma Stirling, Olivia Thomas, and Sharon Croxford build a skills framework for cooking-based nutrition and medicine in a 2026 expert consultation study. Teaching kitchens are spreading in health care, yet shared skill lists for mixed professional teams barely exist.

Nine existing standards from related fields shaped a draft framework of domains and elements. Ten international experts then debated and refined the draft in a guided online group method. The outcome is an early framework meant to prompt wide thinking about team skills. Later steps include outside checking, field-specific standards, and agreement building for training programs.
pmc-13305853:
Junyu Lu asked what the glucose-sensing factor ChREBP does inside skeletal muscle in a 2026 mouse and cell study. The team removed the factor only from muscle, then checked exercise ability, energy use, fibre makeup and repair after injury.

Loss of the factor left fibre type, general metabolism and responses to low oxygen or high-fructose feeding largely unchanged in the reported tests. In dishes, extra ChREBP helped muscle precursor cells mature, and virus-delivered ChREBP supported repair in living muscle. The authors conclude the factor is not needed for fibre switching but does help regeneration after damage.
pmc-13306353:
Ahmed Alsaedawy A Albeshlawy and Hazem A Osman recount in 2026 a finger tumour that went undiagnosed for ten years. Their patient, a thirty-nine-year-old man, had severe pain under the nail of his right ring finger across many specialist visits. Scans finally showed a small, well-defined lesion typical of a glomus tumour.

Surgeons removed the growth through the nail while preserving the whole nail apparatus. Tissue testing confirmed a benign glomus tumour with smooth muscle features. Six months later the man remained pain-free with no sign of return. Classic clues involve pinpoint tenderness and cold sensitivity, which bedside tests can confirm before magnetic resonance imaging. The authors argue that earlier suspicion would have spared years of suffering and delivered the same good surgical outcome.
pmc-13306553:
Francisca Acevedo and a Chilean team build antibacterial silver nanoparticle fibres for wound care in a 2026 study. Four particle coatings were compared: citrate, cysteine, and two common anti-inflammatory drugs. Particles were checked for size behaviour, killing power, and safety with several cell types.

Diclofenac-coated particles performed best, stopping Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa at modest levels and Candida albicans at still lower levels. Irritation in a membrane assay was negligible up to fairly high doses, although fibroblasts responded more sensitively than other cells. Spun into polymer fibres, the particles cut one oral streptococcus sharply and other microbes modestly. The authors argue that coating choice tunes both strength and safety. Such fibres, they suggest, could tackle infected wounds where biofilms resist antibiotics.
pmc-13307453:
Abdulaziz Alqarni, Ahmad Imam, and Thamer Marghalani test in 2026 how much curing light travels through the sides of dental fibre posts. Resin cement under a post hardens only if enough light energy reaches it. Four commercial post systems plus a glass control rod were measured at millimetre steps.

Transmitted energy differed sharply between systems and fell steadily as post length grew. Only a small single-digit share of the light at the top reached deep surfaces overall. One system, iLumi, kept energy above a useful threshold along its whole length. Microscopy showed surface design differences between smooth and serrated posts that matched the optical behaviour. The authors advise choosing post type and length together. Weak curing deep in the root, they note, threatens how long the restoration lasts.
pmc-13308153:
Yushuo Liu, Chengjin Li, and Fan Yang compare exercise programmes in 2026 for patellar tendinopathy, the jumper's knee that plagues jumping sports. Seventeen randomised trials entered their review, and a cleaned network of ten trials with 313 people anchored the main comparison. Heavy slow resistance training served as the reference treatment.

No programme beat heavy slow resistance with statistical confidence in the main network. Eccentric overload training posted the most favourable point estimate, followed by blood flow restriction work, yet intervals were wide. Flywheel, step-based eccentric, and concentric programmes looked worse than the reference. Most trials carried some bias concerns, especially around adherence and extra treatments. The authors warn that the sparse network cannot support a firm ranking. Clinicians, they suggest, should treat heavy slow resistance as a sound default while evidence matures.
pmc-13308753:
Jia Min Yen and co-authors present findings in 2026 from a case series on a wearable electro suit that gives bodywide pulses to ease spasticity after stroke or spinal cord injury. Seven people who could walk with little or no aid wore the suit for one hour, with goal led tasks in two blocks split by rest.

Spasticity scores clearly eased in only two of the seven people in this single session test. Four walked faster, and six showed more even stride patterns in the motion capture checks. Goal success was positive in four people overall. Small size and no control group bar firm claims, so larger trials with repeat sessions must come next.
pmc-13308953:
Johann Paulo Guzman and co-authors detail a 2026 case of a Phrygian cap gallbladder fold in a girl aged 15 years, first taken for a bile duct cyst at surgery. Her first keyhole gallbladder removal was called off mid run when the shape looked wrong and the work grew hard.

Later scans hinted at a rare duct cyst type, yet a duct scope run named the true fold shape in the end. A standard keyhole removal then cured the case with no need for wider cuts. Odd gallbladder shape calls for extra imaging first, since the fold is harmless in itself but can mask true bile duct ills.
pmc-13309453:
Mohammad Sharif Ullah presents a 2026 modeling study on how human choices shape the early control of an outbreak. People weigh the cost and risk of shots, testing, and care, while health agencies adjust testing as cases rise. The model joins those choices to disease spread in one shared population.

Math results and computer runs show that cheaper shots and tests widen the zone where disease dies out on its own. False negative tests weaken the value of more testing by delaying care and letting spread continue. Treatment cuts spread most when paired with fast testing. The author uses the results to argue for low-cost, prompt programs at the start of an outbreak.
pmc-13309553:
David Melching and colleagues publish a curated data set of crack growth measurements in a 2026 article. Full-field image methods tracked how metal surfaces shift as fatigue cracks grow in lab tests. Such data can train and check computer models of fracture, but shared sets with careful labels are rare.

Eight tests on aerospace aluminum alloys cover varied shapes, grain directions, and load setups. Crack tip spots were marked with a repeated correction routine, and fracture values were added as labels. The set holds 8,794 measured fields, expanded to 70,352 samples by standard processing at three grid sizes. A Python tool helps users filter and load the data for machine learning or fracture studies.
pmc-13310053:
Wanyu Sun and co-authors report a hair loss case that resisted one targeted drug but answered another in a 2026 article. The condition, alopecia areata, causes patchy hair loss without scarring and weighs heavily on patients. Immune-targeted drugs in the JAK family offer options when standard care fails.

The patient had lived with the condition for two years and gained little from traditional Chinese medicine approaches tried first. The drug ritlecitinib also failed to restore hair. Switching to upadacitinib brought clear regrowth, and by the 24-week follow-up the hair loss signs had largely normalized in the report. The authors link the difference to JAK1 pathway roles and argue for care matched to each patient.
pmc-13310153:
Thea Difesa and co-authors weigh surgical timing in 2026 for two kinds of hip fracture, asking whether operating sooner saves lives. A systematic review and meta-analysis combined prior studies on neck-of-femur and between-trochanter fractures, with death at thirty days and during admission as the primary outcomes. Complications and hospital stay length were secondary measures.

Most patients in the underlying studies had experienced some surgical delay. Pooled analysis showed a nonsignificant trend toward fewer inpatient deaths with earlier surgery, while the narrative synthesis gave mixed answers. Complication and stay outcomes also varied between reports. The authors argue that optimising a patient's medical state before surgery may matter as much as speed itself. Hip fractures strike an ageing population with thirty-day mortality already reported around five to ten percent.
pmc-13310253:
Zahra Haider writes a 2026 letter on blood-based tracking of Hodgkin lymphoma during treatment. Most patients are cured, but some fail first treatment while others suffer late harm from excess therapy. A mid-treatment scan now guides care, yet its accuracy limits leave room for a sharper blood tool.

Floating tumor DNA in blood allows sensitive checks for leftover disease and live tracking of response. Two lab routes dominate: sequencing-based assays and digital PCR counting. The letter compares baseline-informed versions of both for repeated monitoring, weighing sensitivity tricks such as error correction and paired variant signals. The author argues the comparison matters for sparing patients both relapse and overtreatment.
pmc-13311153:
Thibaud Damy and colleagues survey French cardiac physicians on the emotional toll of patient death in a 2026 study. Death is frequent in cardiac care, yet its effect on doctors is little studied. A poll measured death impact beside anxiety, low mood, trauma stress, and burnout scales.

Among 6,080 invited doctors, 747 replied in full. One quarter scored in the top impact band, and that band showed far higher rates of anxiety, depression, trauma stress, and severe burnout. The high band also reported more team conflict and more use of calming or addictive substances. Female sex, heart surgery specialty, and past personal trauma raised risk.
pmc-13311253:
Benthe H. Doeve and co-authors present their 2026 study of blood markers tied to the scar-like tissue around stomach and food pipe cancers. One marker, a building piece of type V collagen, is the focus.

Eleven stromal markers were measured in stored blood from 78 patients and 11 healthy people. The type V collagen piece ran high in patients, and high levels tied to survival patterns and to a normal form of tumor scarring. Tumor gene data from matched biopsies and a second group of 100 biopsies backed the link. A blood test of this kind could one day help sort patients by outlook.
pmc-13311353:
Ibrahim Fadl Mahmoud, Saud M Erwi, and Ali M Alfageeh review in 2026 how intensive care should handle acute kidney injury, arguing the syndrome is far more than a creatinine number. Between thirty and sixty percent of critically ill adults develop it, with consequences from dialysis dependence to incomplete recovery. The review gathers evolving definitions, injury biomarkers, and bedside ultrasound into one practice picture.

Key advice runs against reflex habits: low urine output should not trigger automatic fluid loading. Blood pressure targets should be read alongside cardiac output, venous pressure, right-heart function, and abdominal pressure, since venous congestion itself injures kidneys. Biomarkers earn their place only when a result would change management. Dialysis timing should follow urgent indications and trajectory rather than a creatinine threshold alone. Recovery planning after intensive care closes the loop. The authors frame precision nephrology as aligning phenotype, risk, and trajectory at the right moment.
pmc-13311953:
Claire Palles and colleagues investigate, in a 2025 study, how inherited and acquired mutations in the gene RNF43 contribute to colorectal cancer. Inherited loss-of-function variants were thought to cause a syndrome of many serrated polyps and early cancer. That picture came from selected families. The team examined nearly 49,823 cancer or polyp cases against 165,250 controls from large British cohorts. They compared them with tumor-acquired mutations in 2,722 cancers.

One multigenerational family did show the classic early-onset pattern. Most carriers, though, lacked multiple polyps or a striking family history. Some cancers clearly arose independently of the inherited variant. Inherited variants raised risk moderately, with an odds ratio of 2.696. The catch was position: risk rose only when the change sat in the gene's first half. Tumor-acquired changes in the second half still proved harmful, aided by partner mutations. Testing and counseling, the authors argue, should reflect this uneven risk.
pmc-13312053:
Ke Feng and co-authors report a 2026 chemistry study describing a light-driven reaction that builds benzylamides from alkenes in a single step. Their method joins three components at once: an alkene, a nitrile with water, and an aryl thianthrenium salt, forming a carbon-carbon bond and a carbon-nitrogen bond in sequence.

The reaction runs under neutral, mild conditions with visible light and tolerates many functional groups across a wide range of starting materials. The team also modified drug-like structures at a late stage, showing the method's reach. Tests pointed to a single-electron transfer route in which an excited iridium catalyst passes an electron along until an aryl radical forms. The work widens what thianthrenium salts can do in synthesis.
pmc-13312153:
Faizan Uddin and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for preparing single-nuclei multiome libraries from small clinical tissue samples. Profiling tumor biopsies this way is often blocked by tiny tumor mass and heavy debris, a problem the team faced with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma samples.

Their workflow combines mechanical and enzymatic steps to break down tumor and matched normal tissue gently. Red blood cell lysis and an enzyme treatment reduce stray nucleic acid background, and density gradient spinning clears debris before intact nuclei are isolated. The protocol then adjusts the indexing steps for both chromatin accessibility and gene expression assays to squeeze the most library complexity from limited material. The authors aim it at costly, sensitive assays where losing sample quality wastes the whole run.
pmc-13312353:
Anthony Mark offers a 2026 poem, 'Dementia and the hands of time', about a couple whose shared life is being erased by memory loss. The speaker watches his partner hold the hands she has known for fifty years, reading their knuckles, nails, and an old burn mark as chapters her mind can no longer name.

She no longer turns at her own name, and her gaze drifts past him toward somewhere beyond the window, yet her grip stays firm. The poem's center is the body's memory outlasting the mind's: his thumb circling hers as it did when the children slept. Her humming of an old tune, scattered but still hers, moves him to tears. The closing image leaves the hands as the last part of her to forget.
pmc-13312553:
Mostafa Saeed and colleagues trace, in a 2026 study, how the aroma chemistry of Chinese bayberry changes from fresh juice to fermented juice to distilled liquor. The fruit spoils quickly after harvest, and its juice's distinctive scent makes it a candidate for a signature spirit. Nobody had mapped the volatile compounds stage by stage and variety by variety.

The team profiled three varieties, 'Biqi', 'Dongkui', and 'Xiazhihong', by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Terpenoids and esters shifted most across processing: fermentation mainly rearranged the terpenoids, while distillation concentrated volatile esters. Smell-strength analysis found fruity and green notes ruling the fermented juice, with woody and sweet tones taking over in the liquor. 'Biqi' carried more of several key aroma compounds and won the best sensory scores, giving producers a variety-specific fingerprint to work from.
pmc-13312953:
Hatice Bozkurt and a large collaborative team report a 2026 study testing two ultra-sensitive blood assay platforms for motor neuron disease biomarkers. The disease is hard to diagnose, varies widely between patients, and lacks accessible blood tests that could speed diagnosis or track progression. The researchers ran serum from 48 patients and 38 controls through a multiplexed NULISA panel and, in parallel, a single-molecule array measuring two established markers.

Several proteins ran significantly higher in patients, including neurofilament light and heavy chains, multiple tau forms, and two amyloid beta fragments. Where the platforms overlapped, their readings agreed strongly, with correlations above 0.90 for the shared markers. The multiplex panel reproduced the well-known neurofilament elevation and matched other recent findings, which the authors take as validation. Beyond diagnosis, the pattern of elevations offers clues about the disease's underlying biology and its uneven presentation.
pmc-13313053:
Tommy Dharmawan and co-authors report, in a 2026 paper, two cases plus a systematic review of lung cancer masquerading as empyema, a pocket of infected fluid around the lung. Both patients, a woman and a man in their forties, were first treated for tuberculosis-related pleural disease. Her fluid kept draining and leaking air despite therapy, and repeated fluid tests stayed negative until chest surgery biopsy revealed adenocarcinoma. His empyema persisted through surgery, and later imaging showed chest wall and spinal spread from squamous cell carcinoma.

Their literature search through May 2026 found only eight comparable published cases. Symptoms and routine laboratory results rarely separated cancer from infection, though bleeding, weight loss, and appetite loss appeared as warning signs, and scans often betrayed a mass or blocked airway. In every case, final diagnosis required tissue. The authors warn clinicians in tuberculosis-endemic regions to biopsy early when empyema refuses to resolve.
pmc-13313153:
Ari Pereira de Araújo and colleagues test, in a 2026 small first study, whether an AI chatbot can support breastfeeding inside Brazil's public health system. Thirteen mothers at a university hospital human milk bank chatted with the assistant, named Lhia 2.0, over WhatsApp for fifteen days. They filled in confidence and attitude surveys before and after.

The mothers rated the chatbot excellent on plain and fun measures of ease of use, and use ran high, at 92 minutes each on average. Breastfeeding confidence scores rose clearly after the trial, as did attitudes on an infant feeding scale. The authors judge the chatbot feasible and warmly accepted, and propose folding such chatbots into efforts to promote breastfeeding within the national health system. They treat this small first test as early evidence.
pmc-13313253:
Yi Xiang and colleagues use gene data in a 2026 study to find which lining cells mark unstable plaques in the carotid artery. Fatty plaques that crack can trigger stroke, and the cells lining the vessel play a part, yet which cell groups drive instability was not clear.

The team merged single-cell RNA data with bulk RNA data from carotid plaques and grouped the lining cells by their gene patterns. Three subsets, numbered 9, 10, and 11, were far more common in unstable plaques and had switched on many inflammation genes. One subset stood out for high PGF, a growth factor, and the groups tied to the PI3K-Akt path and other inflammation paths. Picking out these cells gives new targets for tests that flag risky plaques and for drugs that might calm them.
pmc-13314353:
Elisa Martello and colleagues run, in a 2026 multicentric study, a probiotic trial measuring something disarmingly basic: rabbit droppings. Intensive rabbit farming stresses the gut, antibiotics are banned or discouraged, and fecal traits offer a window on digestive health. Three trials of thirty rabbits each compared an oral paste containing Lactobacillus acidophilus against no treatment over forty-five days, recording fecal weight, dry matter, acidity, and consistency weekly.

Both groups produced heavier feces over time, but the treated rabbits diverged in quality. Their droppings grew steadily less acidic, drier, and harder, every trend reaching strong statistical significance, while controls showed no such pattern. The authors interpret firmer, drier feces as improved nutrient capture through the rabbits' re-ingestion cycle, and thus better nutrient uptake. They position the probiotic as a sustainable gut-support tool for an industry hunting antibiotic alternatives, with growth trials the logical next step.
pmc-13315453:
Guisheng Zhong and co-authors studied in 2026 how sound-driven bubbles carve a porous texture into aluminum grooves. During ultrasonic cavitation treatment the groove surface changes a lot under bubble impact, and the team wanted to know why the tiny pores form where they do.

Tests varied treatment time and the gap between the sound source and the metal, for two groove types, while a coupled sound-and-fluid model mapped pressure and flow speed. Pores began at the groove bottom and spread toward the peak with longer treatment. Sharp bottom corners, with small curve radius and faster flow, took the strongest impact, while the gap size shaped pore spread at the peak.
pmc-13316053:
Lifeng Luo and co-authors made chemotherapy liposomes more flexible in 2026 so they can push deeper into tumors. Cationic liposomes stick strongly to vessel walls and tumor stroma, so they pile up at the edge and barely reach the core, wasting their promise as drug carriers.

Adding sodium cholate softened the particles carrying cabazitaxel, raising membrane fluidity and bendability. Entry into cells shifted from engulfment to direct membrane fusion, delivering drug straight to the cell interior and skipping lysosome breakdown. In animals the flexible version crossed vessel walls better, penetrated deeper, killed more tumor cells, and improved anti-tumor effect.
pmc-13316453:
Zimeng Qin and co-authors, reporting in 2026, test whether a blood inflammation score predicts liver injury in adults with sepsis. That liver complication can be fatal and lacks reliable early markers. The score, called the systemic immune-inflammation index, is calculated from routine blood counts.

Records from 231 intensive care patients at Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital between 2020 and 2024 were analysed. Fifty-three patients developed liver injury during their stay and died in hospital far more often than others. A high index at admission was strongly linked to later injury and remained an independent risk factor after adjustment. Its predictive accuracy was good, suggesting a cheap early warning tool for intensive care teams.
pmc-13316653:
Yubo Zhao, Yi Feng, and Liang Wu built a 2026 computer model of dual-frequency focused ultrasound paired with phase-change droplets, a method meant to cook tumors more precisely. Two sound pitches together can pop droplets into bubbles, but how that reshapes the burn zone was unclear.

Their model chains sound travel, droplet popping, bubble cloud growth, and tissue heating, then checks shapes against gel experiments with a combined 1 and 5 megahertz device. Single pitch burns came late and teardrop shaped, while dual pitch sparked bubbles at many spots at once and left a triangular zone. More low-pitch power or more droplets moved the burn in predictable ways, giving engineers levers to shape treatment.
pmc-13316753:
Xixiang Shuai and co-authors show, in a 2026 food study, how joining rice protein with macadamia protein fixes rice protein's poor solubility. Plant proteins are prized for sustainability, yet rice protein alone mixes badly and foams weakly, limiting its food uses.

Co-assembly let the two unfolded proteins grip each other through water-shy surfaces, forming even particles. A one-to-one blend worked best, reaching 94 percent water dispersibility in the reported tests, with emulsifying power about 120 times that of rice protein alone and foaming over three times stronger. The blends held oil droplets evenly and balanced amino acids better than either protein solo. Pairing unlike plant proteins looks like a general fix for stubborn ingredients.
pmc-13316853:
Asmita Ghosh and Richard A. Register study, in 2026, whether different grades of a barrier plastic can melt and crystallise together. Ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymers block oxygen well and are used in multilayer packaging. Whether mixed grades can be recycled together depends on how well they mix.

Equal-weight blends were made from grades whose ethylene content differed by up to a set range. Microscopy showed smooth melts for compatible pairs and rough surfaces where blends separated. Calorimetry gave single narrow melting peaks when crystals formed jointly. Even separated blends showed partial joint crystallisation, helped by fast cooling. The allowed composition gap was not fixed. It widened or narrowed with the average composition, matching predictions from earlier pressure, volume and temperature data.
pmc-13316953:
Naser Amirjannati and co-authors asked, in a 2026 matched study, whether taking a small piece of testicle to harvest sperm harms later semen quality. Their men still produced sperm in their ejaculate. The procedure is offered after repeated embryo transfer failures or when sperm DNA damage runs high.

Between 2021 and 2024, eighty men who had the limited extraction were matched with eighty similar men who did not, all with at least three failed treatment cycles. Three to six months later, sperm count, shape, movement, and DNA fragmentation had shifted no differently between groups, and the gaps were tiny. The findings reassure on short-term safety, though the authors want longer, prospective proof.
pmc-13317453:
Zhuo Yang and colleagues write, in 2026, about a weakness of water-based zinc batteries that appears when they rest rather than cycle. Such batteries are cheap and safe candidates for storing solar and wind power. Yet capacity fades quickly during idle periods, a process called calendar ageing, and strategies against it have been scarce.

The commentary discusses research that used a molecular property, topological polar surface area, to screen additives. Water and acid accumulate at the zinc surface during storage and corrode it. Additives scoring high on that property reshaped the ionic layer at the interface. One additive, a phosphine oxide compound, gave zinc anodes much longer calendar life and higher efficiency, pointing to a practical fix for grid storage.
pmc-13317953:
Sameh Gabr and co-authors report a 2026 surgical first: fixing a deadly graft-to-bowel leak by keyhole surgery while keeping the graft. Their patient, a 59-year-old man, was bleeding heavily nine months after aorta bypass surgery. Such fistulas usually force open surgery and graft removal, with heavy complications.

Colonoscopy found the graft poking into the sigmoid colon, and CT confirmed the penetration without abscess. Through small ports, the team removed that colon segment, covered the graft with abdominal lining, rejoined the bowel, and added a temporary stoma. He went home on day seven, took six weeks of targeted antibiotics, and at six months stayed well with an open, trouble-free graft. Careful selection, they argue, can spare some patients the standard drastic operation.
pmc-13318253:
Langchao Liang and co-workers offer a 2026 mouse study of how skeletal muscle fibres mature after birth, combining single-cell methods with a spatial technique that works at the level of single fibres. Material came from five hind limb muscles of five-week-old mice.

Merging cell and nucleus sequencing built an atlas of muscle cell types and traced a steady path from type I toward type IIB fibres. One late subtype stood out for running both oxygen-based energy production and sugar breakdown at high levels, unlike the mostly sugar-based pattern seen in adults. Spatial mapping confirmed that mixed pattern and showed uneven zones inside single fibres, with fibre-type proteins richest near fibre ends.
pmc-13318553:
Hyunju Kim and co-authors deliver a 2026 safety evaluation of DW2009, a probiotic product pairing the bacterium Lactiplantibacillus plantarum C29 with fermented soybean powder, ahead of possible use in functional foods. Safety can vary by strain, so they ran a broad battery of checks.

Laboratory tests found the strain sensitive to all antibiotics tried, with no blood-breaking activity, toxin output, or other warning traits detected. Rats fed the product daily for 90 days showed no harmful effects even at 3,000 mg/kg body weight per day, the highest dose tested in the study. Tests for genetic damage all came back negative, supporting a favourable safety picture for food use.
pmc-13318653:
Dandan Geng and colleagues present a 2026 mediation analysis of stroke recovery. They study patients treated with mechanical thrombectomy, a procedure that removes brain clots. The question is whether high blood sugar on arrival worsens long-term outcome. They also ask whether kidney function after treatment carries part of that effect.

The sample held 397 patients treated between February 2018 and June 2024. All had six-month follow-up data. A good outcome came for 151 patients, or 38.0 percent of the group studied. High admission sugar clearly linked to a lower chance of good recovery. Lower kidney filtration after treatment linked the same way. Mediation analysis credited kidney function with 25.57 percent of the sugar effect in their model.
pmc-13318953:
Joel Novak offers a 2026 narrative review of pressure setting in blood flow restriction training. The method uses cuffs to partly limit limb blood flow during exercise. Setting pressure as a share of each person's full occlusion pressure is the standard recipe. Novak questions whether that resting measure captures the real exercise stimulus.

Occlusion pressure shifts with cuff design, limb shape, body position, and blood vessel responses. Resting values may misrepresent conditions during actual training. Across studies, AOP-based dosing has not shown consistent superiority. Good adaptations occur across a range of tolerated pressures. Novak argues individual occlusion testing is not always required. Pressure choice should sit inside a broader, outcome-focused programme with proper oversight.
pmc-13319053:
Dongmei Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 cohort study testing ultrasound elasticity of the cervix to predict early birth. Cervical length alone predicts poorly in women without symptoms. The study enrolled 275 singleton pregnancies at one centre. Scans ran between weeks 18 and 24 of pregnancy.

Early birth before 37 weeks occurred in 37 women, or 13.5 percent of the cohort. A stiffness measure at the inner opening predicted best alone, with an AUC of 0.797 in their analysis. Combining length with an inner-to-outer strain ratio lifted the AUC to 0.828 overall. That pairing beat either measure alone and gave better decision value. Sensitivity was 73 percent and specificity 82 percent at the chosen cut-off. Outside validation is still needed.
pmc-13319953:
Yujun Zhang and co-authors pair two natural compounds to rescue weak sperm in a 2026 study of male fertility. One plant compound glows more when it clumps, a trait that lets it be tracked in the body while it also acts as a drug. Tiny fat bubbles from cells were used to carry it plus a vitamin like compound into the testis.

Once there, the plant compound fought a rust like cell death path by raising two guard proteins and cutting fat damage. The partner compound lifted cell fuel levels and restored energy output. Together they raised sperm count, speed, and forward motion in live tests. The glowing drug idea may suit other ills where tracking care in the body matters.
pmc-13320253:
Yiqi Su and co-authors test stem like cells grown from embryo cells for joint cartilage repair in a 2026 study of joint wear disease. Worn cartilage in this disease rarely heals into its smooth glass like form, and standard stem cell care often yields rough scar like tissue instead. Their special cells both calm swelling and steer tissue building, which may yield a truer repair.

Tests ran from flat cell dishes through lab grown joint tissue models and animal joint samples to a live rat disease model. Treated tissue formed more glass like filler and showed less swelling, vessel growth, and scarring than untreated tissue. Part of the gain ran through an enzyme that reshapes tissue filler. The lab joint model also gives drug hunters a lifelike test bed.
pmc-13320353:
Yu Wang and co-authors map drug target proteins on a salivary gland cancer in a 2026 study to guide missile style drug care. The cancer spreads along nerves, jumps far, and answers standard drugs poorly, with no approved body wide drug for stubborn cases. Five target proteins that guided drugs can latch onto were stained and scored against tumor type and patient outcomes in a large case set.

Two targets ran high in the less solid, slower tumor form, while two others ran high in the solid, faster form. High levels of the latter pair also tracked with shorter survival in the counts reported. Early care hints from the set may help pick which guided drug fits which tumor form, a step toward matched care for this rare cancer.
pmc-13320453:
Afnan Alsunaidi and co-authors describe a child treated in 2026 with bladder washed antibiotics as a guard against repeat infections linked to a nerve based bladder fault. A 9 year old girl with weak bladder control, early kidney disease, and swollen kidneys had three hospital stays in six months for drug proof urine infections despite daily preventive pills. Her germ proved open only to a few strong drugs.

After a two week vein drug course cleared the bout, a guard plan washed the drug into the bladder through her self catheter on a fading schedule over months. A pill guard was later added back at a check visit. Across about eighteen months of follow up she stayed free of symptoms with no new infections, a hopeful sign for kidney sparing guard plans.
pmc-13320553:
Simone Coluccia and a large team share field data from a 2026 study of oats grown under upright solar panels in Sweden. Pairing crops with solar power on one field can change light, warmth, and water around plants. The trial ran in 2024 at Kärrbo Prästgård near Västerås and compared panel rows with open field ground.

Leaf area was tracked through the season to follow crop growth. At harvest the team weighed grain and straw and checked kernel weight plus protein and fat content. Yield varied a lot within the panel field, while mean total biomass there topped both the open reference and a standard ground panel field. The data help planners judge site fit.
pmc-13320653:
Kaoutar Zirhirhi and colleagues survey, in 2026, physical restraint use in intensive care units at a Moroccan teaching hospital in Casablanca. Restraint prevents self-injury and protects tubes and lines, yet it can damage skin, prolong immobility and leave psychological scars, raising ethical tension. Moroccan data were scarce.

Sixty doctors and nurses across four units completed a questionnaire in 2024. Formal training on restraint was rare in both professions. Most respondents had witnessed complications, with skin injury almost universal among those reporting harm. Despite that experience, large majorities in both groups supported keeping restraint available, and most reported using it on sedated patients. The authors call this a training-use paradox and argue for structured education and clearer rules.
pmc-13321753:
Yuta Tsubouchi and co-authors follow walking recovery for a year after childhood stroke in a 2026 case report. Young stroke can leave lasting movement problems, yet detailed recovery paths are rarely charted. Sensors and force platforms were used to measure gait and balance with precision over time.

The patient was an 11-year-old Japanese girl, healthy before her illness, with left side weakness after an ischemic stroke tied to reversible vessel narrowing. Tests at five points across 12 months tracked trunk sway, step symmetry, rhythm steadiness, and balance. Trunk sway and balance improved most in the first six months, symmetry kept gaining to nine months, and rhythm settled by month twelve.
pmc-13323253:
Binghan Yan and co-authors review natural products that push osteosarcoma cells toward programmed death, in a 2026 article. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in children and teens, and survival stays poor when disease spreads or returns despite surgery and chemotherapy.

Cancer cells survive partly by dodging death programmes such as apoptosis, autophagy, ferroptosis, pyroptosis and necroptosis. Compounds from medicinal plants and foods can reset those programmes through varied molecular routes, with low cost and mild side effects as claimed strengths. The authors sort the evidence by death type and mechanism, aiming to guide targeted strategies that might improve outcomes for young patients.
pmc-13324653:
Ricardo Lara-Ramírez and co-authors chart myelin growth in turtle peripheral nerves, working with Trachemys scripta, in a 2026 study. Myelin, the fatty wrap that speeds nerve signals, is well mapped in mammals but barely studied in reptiles.

The team combined gene tests, RNA sequencing, staining, and electron microscopy across growth stages. Wrapping began late in embryo life and kept building after hatching. Key myelin genes such as Mpz, Mbp, and Pmp22 switched on in a pattern much like that of mammals. Microscopy showed rings on a few axons at stage 21, far more by stage 24, and most adult axons wrapped. The study is the first of its kind for a reptile.
pmc-13324753:
Salai Thanihaivel E and team mapped bicuspid aortic valve disease with newer dual-source CT in an Indian population. Their 2026 forward-looking cross-sectional study took in 100 adults with that valve between July 2022 and November 2023, checking the aorta at multiple levels including annulus and sinus. That valve affects 0.5% to 2% of people and drives growing aortic widening, and scaling aortic size to body surface area may improve risk grouping.

The team derived a cohort-specific aortic size index threshold of 23.8 mm per square meter for CT-defined ascending aortic dilatation above 40 mm, with 84% sensitivity and 90% specificity. CT measures ran larger than echocardiography by a mean 11.72 mm, a gap the authors attribute largely to measure sites and conventions rather than simple underestimation. They present the threshold as preliminary, requiring validation in independent multicenter cohorts with longitudinal results.
pmc-13325353:
Fredrik Petersson, Vittorio Longo, and Mats Jonsson test how boric acid changes hydrogen peroxide breakdown in water in a 2026 chemistry study. Peroxide forms under radiation in reactors, and its fate shapes corrosion of fuel cladding.

Three breakdown routes were compared, with zirconium oxide as a solid catalyst in one arm. Boric acid slowed peroxide loss on the catalyst surface by crowding the binding sites. In plain solution the effect flipped: heat and radiation broke peroxide faster with boric acid present. The team blames peroxoborate forms that react keenly with superoxide and feed a chain reaction. Reactor models may need to drop the old view of boric acid as inert.
pmc-13325453:
Tumay Uludag Yanaral adds a new cause to the debate over moral injury in medicine. The comment is on a 2026 piece that recast doctor distress as system failure rather than own burnout. The letter puts forward stakes-tied being unseen: staff, patients, symptoms, or harms go unseen or missed because of power rankings, high-stakes settings, or test limits. Most sleep doctors, the author argues, will recognize the pattern at once.

The comment applies the idea to surgery-time care, where sleep doctors often remain invisible partners despite decisive contributions. It puts forward remedies such as naming all contributors and positioning that doctor as a visible partner before, during, and after surgery. Professional bodies, it suggests, should set explicit attribution standards. The hypothesis is testable, the author notes, through a prospective multicenter study of the contribution-recognition gap across surgical complexity tiers.
pmc-13327353:
Jiawei Li and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on a gene switch that helps breast cancer grow. The factor SALL2 appears at high levels in breast tumors, yet its role there was unclear. The team traced how a chemical mark on its RNA, placed by the enzyme NSUN2, keeps SALL2 active.

Lowering SALL2 slowed cell growth and spread in dishes and in animals, while the NSUN2 mark, read by the protein YBX1, steadied SALL2 RNA. SALL2 in turn switched off ACSL4, a gene that promotes an iron-driven form of cell death called ferroptosis, and blocking that death route restored growth. The chain points to new drug targets for hard-to-treat breast cancer subtypes.
pmc-13327853:
Xi Ye and a large team study links between smoking and early ovarian failure in a 2026 article. Premature ovarian insufficiency ends fertility early, and tobacco smoke holds many compounds that could harm ovaries. The team joined literature mining with a clinical study of Chinese patients who had infrequent periods between May 2020 and May 2025.

Mining singled out six smoke components tied to ovarian harm, including nicotine, benzo[a]pyrene, and acrolein, and network mapping placed them near core protein targets. In the clinic arm, urine cotinine levels were measured and compared between women with and without the condition under standard criteria. The authors caution that network rank alone cannot prove a leading biological role.
pmc-13327953:
Aiping Gu and co-authors build a risk tool for fast-worsening diabetic eye disease in a 2026 study. Rapidly progressive retinopathy varies greatly between people with type 2 diabetes, so a personal forecast could guide watch intensity. Records covered 342 patients, split into 240 for building and 102 for checking the tool.

Six factors survived screening: diabetes duration, HbA1c, urinary protein over 24 hours, the marker GDF15, disease grade, and the size of the central no-flow zone in the retina. All six were woven into a nomogram, a point-based chart, and compared against forest and boosting models. The chart aims to sort patients into risk bands so eye checks and treatment can be timed earlier for those most likely to worsen fast.
pmc-13328253:
Junjie Shen offers a practitioner's guide to reading the QS Citations per Faculty score in a 2026 article. The indicator carries 20 percent of the QS World University Rankings score and is often read as research intensity, yet its path from raw data to final number is hard to see. Shen walks through each building stage.

QS pulls Scopus citations early each year, applies paper and citation exclusions, normalizes by field, divides by faculty size, then damps big jumps and rescales the result. Each step can shift a score away from what a university expects from its own records. Clearer design and reporting would let institutions verify their numbers and use the metric with open eyes, Shen argues.
pmc-13329853:
Marie A-C Neumann and co-authors review how indirect comparisons of CAR-T therapies handle patient differences in a 2026 article. No head-to-head trials compare these cell therapies for large B-cell lymphoma, so indirect methods fill the gap. Such methods can mislead if key traits are not balanced.

Searches in November 2025 across three databases yielded 27 included publications. Most used matching-adjusted indirect comparisons, then score-based methods and network pooling. Adjustment ranged from none to 19 factors, most often covering age, disease severity, health status, and past treatment. Benefit outcomes were common, while harm outcomes were seldom adjusted. No study gave a full rule for picking factors, the authors note. Shared standards would aid fair comparisons.
pmc-13330253:
Gechang Zhang and colleagues study jaw joint balance in people with one overgrown wisdom tooth in a 2026 report. Thirty patients with growth on one side were compared with 30 people with aligned teeth and no wisdom teeth. Cone-beam scans measured front, top, and back spaces in each jaw joint, and back tooth wear was scored.

Joint space gaps between sides differed clearly between the groups in the reported tests. The overgrowth group also showed higher and more uneven back tooth wear scores than controls. The authors link one-sided overgrowth to joint imbalance and wear. Early removal of the long tooth may prevent bite imbalance and harms such as tooth cracks, they suggest.
pmc-13330653:
Zilin Wang and colleagues study how ultrasound and ultra-high pressure reshape fermented coffee flavour in a 2026 report. Fermentation strips the sticky layer from beans and builds flavour precursors through microbe action. Physical pre-treatments may steer that process, so the team paired them with fermentation of degummed beans.

Metabolomic and volatile profiling tracked how the two treatments shifted bean chemistry and scent makeup. Compounds from microbe activity, such as alcohols, esters, and aldehydes, feed the aroma formed later in roasting. Flavour parts may sit unevenly in the bean, near the surface or in leftover mucilage. Mapping those shifts could help makers tune fruit and acid notes while cutting bitter, burnt tones.
pmc-13331453:
Devi Nair, editor in chief, opens the June 2026 issue of The Journal of Innovations in Cardiac Rhythm Management with a letter to colleagues. She frames June as a month of thresholds, when training years turn over across heart rhythm medicine.

Graduating fellows get counsel on knowing their limits and keeping mentors close, while incoming fellows are urged to master basic anatomy before chasing new tools. New residents are told to treat careful tracing reading and bedside questions as the seed of future work. Nair then previews the issue, which ranges from a comparison of two ablation methods to device problem solving, a poisoning emergency, a tracing puzzle, and a genetic diagnosis missed for decades.
pmc-13332253:
Chris Greiner and colleagues report a 2026 cat case in which a local antibiotic carrier triggered severe high blood calcium. A 3-year-old spayed domestic shorthair had seven months of deep skin inflammation and a positive culture for Actinomyces species. Standard clindamycin courses had not cleared it, so surgeons removed the diseased tissue and placed calcium sulfate carrier loaded with ampicillin-sulbactam for local antibiotic delivery. After surgery the cat developed severe hypercalcemia.

Seven days of saline diuresis plus a bisphosphonate drug brought calcium back down. pmc-13332353:

The condition pairs an abscess under the scalp covering with infection of the frontal bone itself. Infection or trauma usually starts it, and it appears most often in late childhood and adolescence. Left untreated, it can spread inward to cause abscesses around the brain or meningitis.

pmc-13333353:
Yang Liu and a large team examined whether falls push older adults into frailty, in a 2026 analysis of a Chinese aging survey. Frailty is known to cause falls, but whether falls speed the slide into frailty and death was far less charted.

They sorted them as robust, pre-frail, or frail, with death as the final state. pmc-13333453:

Flooding and salt studies in oak, antioxidant enzyme patterns in sweet potato breeding lines, and a genome-wide map of detox genes in blueberry all point one way. Hormone signaling and stress gene regulation round out the picture. The editors argue the combined physiological, biochemical, and genomic views move the field toward crops bred for real-world stress.
pmc-13334953: Xu-xiang Wang and co-authors issued this 2026 correction notice for their article on microvascular proliferation and functional recovery in experimental cervical spondylotic myelopathy. The notice contains no new data. It repairs two citation errors: a methods reference that should have pointed to Li et al. 2022 was printed as Mattucci et al. 2019, and a discussion reference printed as Li et al. 2022 should have been Basso et al. 1996, with both corrected entries given in full.
pmc-13336353:

pmc-13336453:

pmc-13336553:

pmc-13336753:
Huizhou Luo and co-authors solve a materials trade-off in a 2026 study of heat-storing fabrics. Phase change materials soak up and release heat, but strong versions usually store little, and high-storage ones leak or tear. It survived 500 heating cycles without clear loss in the study runs. Spun into fiber mats, it held surfaces 3°C–4°C cooler than cotton under heating. Leak-free, flexible heat storage suits wearable comfort gear.
pmc-13336853:
Zhou-Hang Zhang and colleagues report that stem cells from human urine ease lung scarring in a 2026 study. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis steadily destroys lung tissue with no good cure. Lab co-cultures showed the cells act through released factors, chiefly DKK1, which damps the Wnt and beta-catenin pathway in macrophages. A waste-fluid cell source could become a practical therapy for a fatal lung disease.
pmc-13337453:
Xuehan Zhao and co-authors pool trials of whey protein after weight-loss surgery in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Bariatric surgery treats severe obesity well, but keeping muscle while losing fat afterward is a nutritional challenge. Following PRISMA 2020 guidance, the team searched major databases and grey literature for randomized trials published before August 2025.

That pattern ties to losing fat mass while preserving fat-free mass in the body composition data. The authors rate the evidence cautiously, and the findings support protein support as part of post-surgical care plans.
pmc-13338753:
Manu Priya and colleagues report an unusual eye infection in a young woman with lupus, in a 2026 case report. The 21-year-old, on immune-suppressing therapy for systemic lupus erythematosus, came in with 15 days of blurred vision in her right eye. Eye infection in lupus can mimic sterile inflammation, so the diagnosis is easy to miss.

Blood tests were positive for Toxoplasma IgG and negative for IgM, fitting reactivated disease. The case shows why lupus patients with new eye inflammation need a prompt infectious workup before vision is lost.
pmc-13339653:
Lily McKenna and colleagues map the copper click reaction energy landscape in a 2026 theory study. The azide-alkyne cycloaddition is a workhorse joining reaction, and one versus two copper centers has long been debated. A reaction valley method plus local vibration analysis compared both paths.

The picture gives catalyst designers concrete steps to target for faster click chemistry.
pmc-13341653:
