LED devices outperformed fluorescent tube systems. Between-study variation was very high, yet the direction of benefit never wavered. The authors conclude properly delivered phototherapy remains a reliable, safe mainstay for term jaundice.
pmc-13342053:
Heart muscle cells die in several distinct ways after a heart attack, in a 2026 review by Zhixin Wang and colleagues. Beyond classic necrosis and apoptosis, iron-driven ferroptosis and inflammatory pyroptosis help drive the ventricular remodeling that ends in heart failure.

Ferroptosis surges after blood flow returns, and weakening its guardian enzyme GPX4 worsens membrane rupture, wall thinning, and chamber dilation. Pyroptosis runs through the NLRP3, caspase-1, and gasdermin D pathway, spilling cytokines that fuel scarring and electrical instability. The review maps how these death modes interact and where drugs might interrupt the network.
pmc-13342253:
Hengsheng Wang and colleagues report a 2026 field study of soil microbes around alpine grass roots near Qinghai Lake after heavy rain. Moisture-driven changes in food supply, the authors argue, push each soil zone toward its own survival plan.
pmc-13343153:
Kirika Karppinen and co-authors map the genetics of oral disease in 2026, running genome-wide association studies on 67 mouth and face conditions. Genetic links ran deep: 378 correlations among oral traits and 419 between oral and systemic diseases, including gum disease with chronic laryngitis. Shared immune and structural pathways seem to bind mouth health to whole-body health.
pmc-13343353:
Jörn Nielsen and co-authors study counseling needs of couples living with multiple sclerosis in 2026, using a participatory design where patients helped run the research. Both sides prized couple-oriented help near diagnosis, with relationship worries outweighing disease facts. Communication strain, balancing shared and personal needs, and uncertainty about the future dominated. Folding couple counseling into outpatient and rehab services could strengthen shared coping, the authors argue.
pmc-13343853:
Jenny N. Ijoma, Andoni Gomez-Moreno, Samer Ayoub, and Alexander Ploss review what blocks hepatitis B virus from infecting other species in 2026. Over 250 million people live with chronic infection, yet the virus naturally infects only humans and chimpanzees, a narrowness that has blocked good animal models for decades.

Each model teaches something, but none copies chronic infection in a fully immune host. Cracking the species barrier, the authors argue, is the key step toward models that can speed a true cure.
pmc-13344853:
Kunaraj Perumalu and co-authors describe a 2026 case of device therapy for an extremely rare heart shape defect. A 54-year-old man had a year of fading exercise tolerance. He carried isolated left ventricular apical hypoplasia, where the right ventricle wraps around a stunted left tip. His ejection fraction was just 14 percent.

Despite full guideline drug therapy, symptoms stayed at class II, so he received a resynchronization defibrillator with leads placed through the coronary sinus. Follow-up visits across a year tuned his doses upward, and he had been counseled on genetic testing for the condition.
pmc-13346853:
Berk Bilgen, Berk Kaffaf, and Olcay Şakar survey problems and patient views for metal clasp partial dentures, in a cross-sectional study from 2026. Older dentures brought more mechanical trouble, while some plate and strap designs were tied to pain and poorer speech ratings. More rests and clasps went with lower overall problem scores.
pmc-13346953:
Bilal Aladerah and co-authors used quantum maths in 2026 to test an earth-abundant Heusler alloy, CoMnFeSi, as a catalyst for splitting water into hydrogen gas. pmc-13347153:
Francesco Salis and colleagues validate a two-question depression screen for older adults, in a study from 2026. pmc-13347353:

pmc-13348053:

pmc-13348453:

pmc-13349353:

pmc-13349953:

pmc-13350253:

pmc-13350553:

pmc-13351653:

pmc-13351953:

pmc-13354353:

pmc-13354453:

pmc-13354953:

pmc-13355253:

pmc-13355853:

pmc-13356753:

pmc-13358853:

pmc-13358953:

pmc-13360453:

pmc-13361253:

pmc-13362353:

pmc-13362753:

pmc-13363253:

pmc-13364053:

pmc-13364353:

pmc-13367053:

pmc-13367553:

pmc-13371253:
Xiuye Xing and colleagues test whether mouth bacteria can cause female reproductive disease in a 2026 genetic study. Observational links between oral microbes and body-wide illness exist, but cause has been unclear. Using Mendelian randomisation, a method that uses gene variants as natural experiments, the team tested 44 saliva microbe traits against six reproductive diseases in large European data sets.

Several microbes showed nominal links, including Bacilli and Veillonella with fibroids, and Veillonellaceae with tubal infertility in a protective direction. Most links were modest and need replication before any clinical claim. The study frames the mouth as a possible distant driver of reproductive health and sets out which microbes deserve closer study in trials.
pmc-13374353:
Jenice Dumlao and colleagues devised a gentle way to seed young mouse guts with a beneficial bacterium, in a 2026 study. Akkermansia muciniphila, a mucus-loving gut microbe, carries many reported health benefits, but placing it into intact gut communities without tubes or force was tricky. The team offered the bacterium in food that mice ate willingly after weaning.

Mice took the human strain MucT/BAA-835 quickly and reliably, and colonization lasted at least to 8 weeks of age. Even mice whose gut communities lacked the bacterium natively were colonized just as fast and durably, in both sexes. The feeding protocol gives researchers a stress-free tool for probing how early gut microbes shape health.
pmc-13377153:
Veronika Zámbó and co-authors profile a fat-shaping enzyme in a 2026 review. The enzyme puts a bend in fat chains, which sets how cell walls flow and how cells talk. Of two human forms, one is found in most parts and one in just brain, pancreas, and seed parts.

The rare form lacks the wear tag that makes its kin short-lived, so it lasts in a next way. Its acts bend wall mix, pouch flow, and growth paths. Brain and pancreas roles put it in tales of nerve loss and sugar ills. A full map of its levers may open drug aims its famed kin can't give.
pmc-13379153:
Keisuke Sumii and Takumi Yamamoto report a 2026 case where a heart scan during surgery changed the treatment plan. Their patient, a 73-year-old woman, received a new aortic valve made from animal tissue, plus bypass surgery. Just after, a scan suggested the new valve was moderately narrowed.

Such a finding can mean a faulty valve or a valve too small for the patient, both serious problems. Closer checks with the same scan, which passes a probe down the throat, showed a normal opening size and fast blood flow start. The team concluded the heart was simply pumping unusually hard at that moment. No further action on the valve was needed.
pmc-13380653:
Aron Krause and colleagues wrote a 2026 reply letter about two systems that clean the blood of patients whose liver is failing. The systems perform a form of dialysis that uses albumin, a blood protein, to pull out toxins. Their earlier study was the first to compare the two systems, called OPAL and ALBUNIQUE, in critically ill patients.

In the letter the authors accept some concerns raised about clinical impact and study methods. They note that most evidence for this treatment comes from an older system, and that the newer one may work better partly through longer treatment times. They also explain that decisions to start treatment at their hospital follow international recommendations.
pmc-13382053:
Yu and colleagues review premature atrial contractions, extra early heartbeats from the upper chambers, in children, in a 2026 pediatric cardiology synthesis. These beats are among the commonest findings from fetal life through adolescence. The review gathers epidemiology, causes, diagnosis, and management from meta-analyses, observational studies, and guidelines. It aims to give clinicians limits and risk protocols, since the same finding can be harmless in a normal heart yet serious alongside congenital heart disease or inherited muscle disorders.

In healthy children, prevalence ranges from 0.11 percent to 0.515 percent, with higher rates in newborns. Meta-analysis sets 24-hour monitor limits at 150 beats per day for infants under one year and 50 for older children. Fetal cases resolve on their own, though blocked beats can trigger sustained fast rhythms or a misleadingly slow pulse reading. Diagnosis rests on electrocardiograms and Holter monitoring; drugs such as propafenone enter when beats suppress the pulse.
pmc-13383253:
Rutter and colleagues report a catalyst that builds nitrogen-containing ring molecules in a single mirror-image form, in 2026 organic chemistry research. The reaction is an intramolecular aza-Michael addition, where a sulfonamide nitrogen attacks a tethered unsaturated ester to close a ring. Esters are stubborn partners for this reaction. The team's bifunctional iminophosphorane catalyst, which activates reacting partners, coaxes the closure to form pyrrolidines, piperidines, and indolines. These ring systems are common in drugs, and the method controls the three-dimensional handedness of the products.

Products formed in yields up to 99 percent and enantiomeric ratios up to 97.5 to 2.5, meaning the desired form dominated almost fully. The method tolerated variation in the sulfonamide group, the acceptor, and the tether between them. Gram-scale reactions ran at reduced catalyst loadings without losing selectivity. Rutter converted several pure products onward, positioning the catalyst as a tool for chiral amine building blocks.
pmc-13384953:
Zhengzhao Lu and colleagues measure chronic hepatitis B across the Asia-Pacific region using 2023 burden data in 2026 work. The region held 63 percent of world cases in 2023, some 178 million people living with the infection. Deaths and disability shares were similarly outsized compared with the global picture.

East Asia carried the largest raw case count, while South Asia had the most cases in young children. Trends since 1990 diverged, with some subregions falling and others seeing mortality rise. Projections leave the region off track for World Health Organization 2030 elimination targets, the authors warn.
pmc-13386953:
Chloe R. Koon and Megan Culler Freeman shift focus from neurons to glial cells in viral brain disease in a 2026 review. Neurons make up only half the cells of the human central nervous system, yet most infection studies center on them. Glia, including astrocytes, microglia, and progenitor cells, guard and maintain the tissue around them.

The review gathers what is known about acute viral infection of those non-neuronal cells across human pathogens. New single-cell tools and richer human brain models now let researchers watch infection cell by cell. The authors argue that glial roles may hide fresh treatment targets for severe brain infections.
pmc-13389153:
Liangrui Pan's team built DAEM, a machine intelligence model. It detects spread through air spaces in lung cancer tissue slides, a pattern that changes surgery and follow-up choices. Manual slide reading is slow and misses cases, so the model learns multi-scale traits from frozen and wax sections with a spread focus design.

Internal testing separated cases well on both section types. Checks across eight outside centres held up with clear outputs. Using tumour-setting traits, the model also tracked on its own how far spread cells sat from the main tumour, yielding lead biomarkers that could sharpen risk sorting after surgery.
pmc-13391053:
Khanda F M Amin and colleagues develop, in 2026, a greener ultraviolet method for measuring three blood pressure drugs in a single sample. Candesartan, chlorthalidone, and amlodipine are often combined, but their ultraviolet spectra overlap so heavily that simple measurement cannot separate them.

The team built maths-based models to unmix the signals. The models were tested on lab-made mixes and on shop-bought tablets. Drug analysts gain a low-solvent way to check triple tablets. The study shows which model copes best with the overlap of the three drugs. All three drugs sit in one pill, so a fast joint test saves time and cost.
pmc-13392253:
Hao Du's team better protein-protein interaction forecast by pre-training on pseudo-dimers built from abundant monomeric proteins, addressing the scarcity of dimer shapes that limits models such as AlphaFold-Multimer and AlphaFold3. Collecting true dimer shapes is expensive and slow.

Their split-and-merge proxy splits monomers into pseudo-sensor and pseudo-ligand halves and trains models to rejoin them by predicting contacts or docking, enabling large-scale pre-training at no extra cost. Fine-tuned models beat strong baselines across benchmarks and surpassed both AlphaFold systems on several CASP15 dimer targets.
pmc-13393053:
Jorge P B Batista and colleagues report how an international project to build biomedical ethics and oversight capacity played out in São Tomé and Príncipe, a small Portuguese-speaking island nation. The BERC-Luso project worked across Lusophone Africa to align laws with good practice, grow regulators and ethics committees, and train local experts. At the start the country had almost no framework in this field and no dedicated bodies.

Despite the thin starting point, political backing and stakeholder engagement carried real change. The country created a national ethics committee for scientific research with authority over clinical studies, and advanced the legal blueprint for a national regulatory authority. The authors present those steps as the foundation blocks future clinical trials will need, and as a model other resource-limited countries might follow.
pmc-13393653:
Yu Zhang leads an twelve-author study of how a microRNA called miR-34a sharpens the leukaemia drug ATRA in acute promyelocytic leukaemia. That drug already transformed the cancer by forcing immature cells to mature. Patient samples showed both forms of miR-34a climbing when remission was reached compared with diagnosis. Adding extra miR-34a in cells and mouse grafts deepened ATRA-driven maturation.

Each form attacks a different brake: one lowers a cell-cycle driver, the other silences a metabolic gene called ISOC1, whose low levels mark patients whose blood lineage programmes run stronger. Silencing ISOC1 alone mimicked the microRNA's help, and blocking the ERK signalling pathway cut the whole effect, placing ERK upstream as the promoter of the axis. The authors propose targeting this chain to squeeze more from ATRA therapy.
pmc-13393753:
Reza Azizi Malamiri and coauthors report a rare lupus presentation in a teenager in a 2026 case report. Systemic lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease with varied symptoms, and brain involvement is fairly common, but isolated slurred speech as the main sign is exceedingly rare.

A 14-year-old girl arrived with fatigue, weakness, joint pain, and worsening slurred speech that hurt her schoolwork. Examination showed the classic butterfly rash, mouth ulcers, hair loss, and arthritis, while labs confirmed strong autoimmune markers. The case urges clinicians to consider lupus when a young patient develops unexplained speech difficulty alongside systemic signs.
pmc-13393853:
Samrat Kumar Dev Sharma and colleagues build machine learning models to predict low birth weight in Bangladesh in a 2026 study. Low birth weight drives newborn death and lasting illness in low- and middle-income countries, and early prediction could target scarce care.

Using the 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey, the team analyzed 3,400 mother-child pairs with survey weights and cluster-aware splitting. Seven classifiers were tested, with class imbalance handled by weighting rather than synthetic oversampling to preserve representativeness. The paper distinguishes prediction from causation and offers a tool for flagging at-risk pregnancies.
pmc-13394153:
Caleb A Massimi and others test a two-step screen for a dream-enacting sleep disorder in a 2026 multi-site study. This sleep disorder flags early Parkinson-type disease, yet most cases stay missed since short forms guess poorly and night sleep labs are scarce.

A brief form on dream-enacting signs and other early signs went to 289 people aged 40 to 80, and 236 wore wrist motion trackers for at least fourteen nights. A wrist-based rule built on four motion traits was weighed against night-lab sleep proof. Doctors gain a cheap, scalable screen for catching early brain disease before it moves far.
pmc-13394553:
Bach and co-authors validate, in 2026, two wireless skin temperature sensors against a wired reference probe during exercise in the heat. Skin temperature underpins research on how humans regulate body heat, but wired probes restrict movement. Twenty-six adults rested, cycled at a fixed heat production, and recovered in a chamber held at 35.0 degrees Celsius, wearing the new eTemp Performance sensor, the widely used iButton, and the reference thermocouple.

The eTemp showed a small negative bias of 0.04 degrees and met every acceptability threshold the team set in advance, including agreement limits within half a degree. Its concordance with the reference reached 0.986 across all periods of the protocol. The iButton read slightly high, with a bias of 0.11 degrees, and its agreement interval marginally exceeded the half-degree limit during exercise and recovery. Both devices performed well enough for most research, with the eTemp closer overall.
pmc-13395353:
Takeshi Uchikura and co-authors explore, in 2026, whether phone movement data can hint at who ends up in hospital. Anonymised location records came from phone users in two Tokyo wards over eleven months. The team guessed eating-out habits and clinic visits from movement paths. Hospital stays of two days or more marked the outcome.

Of 647 people, 67 had a hospital stay. Only the most frequent diners-out, past eight times a month, showed higher odds of a stay. Other dining bands showed no clear link. People with both frequent clinic visits and frequent dining out clustered in the hospital group. The authors urge caution, since age and sex were unknown.
pmc-13395553:
Rebecca Jean DeCarlo and colleagues present, in 2026, a five-year-old boy with a huge fatty growth inside his spinal cord. Such growths, called intramedullary lipomas, are rare in children when the spine closed normally at birth. Fewer than two dozen child cases sit in the record. Most span short stretches, while this one ran the whole back length of the cord.

Size and length raise the stakes of surgery, since no clean plane splits growth from cord. Full removal is often unsafe, so partial clearing is favoured. Timely surgery in children with symptoms can halt decline and allow real recovery. The authors add the case to guide diagnosis and long-term planning.
pmc-13396053:
Lorenzo Palombi and co-authors describe a sharper way to watch leaves rebalance light between their two photosystems, in a 2026 methods paper. This shift, called a state transition, keeps energy supply even when light quality changes, but older ways of measuring it blur the two systems' signals together.

Their approach uses pattern analysis of the glow leaves give off, called fluorescence, to separate the signal of photosystem I from that of photosystem II at normal leaf temperature. In tobacco leaves the shift from one state to the other took about one minute, roughly twice as fast as older methods suggested. The work was done in tobacco lines that differ in isoprene release.
pmc-13396153:
Amina H. Rhaman and co-authors systematically review how mouse studies of heat exposure are designed, since housing conditions can distort results meant to inform human health. Mice are nocturnal and standard housing sits below their thermoneutral zone, the temperature range where they need no extra energy to stay warm. Their 2026 review covers studies from 2020 to January 2025.

Of 170 included studies, 83 percent housed control mice below the thermoneutral zone, effectively comparing heat-exposed animals with cold-stressed controls. Only seven studies kept controls in the neutral zone. Heat exposures ranged from 30 to 45 degrees and usually ran during the light phase, against the mice's night-active pattern. Most studies used males only, and sex often went unreported. Outcomes focused on digestion, inflammation, and the nervous system. The authors urge designs that account for mouse biology to improve translation.
pmc-13396453:
Simona Coniac and co-authors looked for blood clues that warn which lung cancer patients on immunotherapy will develop hormone side effects, in a 2026 study from a Romanian hospital. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have lengthened survival in lung cancer, but they can also turn the immune system against glands such as the thyroid.

The cohort held 173 people with non-small cell lung cancer treated with at least three cycles between November 2017 and August 2024. Routine blood values were grouped by hierarchical clustering, a method that lets similar patients gather into families, and those groupings were tested against hormone-related side effects. The hope is earlier warning and closer monitoring for patients at risk.
pmc-13396553:
Inês Agostinho and co-authors describe therapy for a 56-year-old man whose arm stayed weak after a stroke, in a 2026 case report from rehabilitation nursing. Arm weakness after stroke is a leading cause of dependence, and one aid is a squishy viscoelastic material that the hand presses and shapes during sensorimotor exercises.

The man had suffered strokes in several brain areas, leaving his left arm impaired. Over 21 days he completed eight sessions mixing standard arm exercises with stimulation using the viscoelastic product. Nurses tracked strength on a standard scale, independence on the Barthel Index, and further function measures, adding one more account to a thin evidence base for this material.
pmc-13397653:
Marjolaine Willems and others profile tear proteins in congenital aniridia in a 2026 protein study. This rare whole-eye malformation, often from PAX6 variants, is worsened by progressive cornea disease, yet tear-film paths behind that cornea disease were uncharted.

Tears from four genetically confirmed patients and four matched healthy volunteers were read by high-performance mass reads, naming off-balance immune, epithelial, and vascular paths behind tear fluid defects. The small but deeply charted comparison points to routes of corneal decline. Eye specialists gain protein-level aims for guarding aniridic corneas.
pmc-13398053:
Aidong Qiu and colleagues build tiny antibody carriers that hitch a ride across the airway lining, aiming to deliver inhaled biologic drugs. Their 2026 study targets a stem part of the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, a shuttle that normally ferries antibodies across mucosal walls. Big protein drugs usually cannot cross such barriers, forcing injections with higher side-effect risk.

From phage display screening came four strong nanobodies, with two leads moving cargo from the air side to the blood side in lab layers and in living mice. Fused to the asthma antibody reslizumab, the carriers worked by inhalation in mice at a tenth of the injected dose. The route could widen what inhalers can deliver beyond small molecules.
pmc-13398353:
Xiaoyan Zhang and Wenya Han write a 2026 letter challenging how a study ranked body-measure indices for predicting diabetes and hypertension. The study under discussion, by Pezeshki and colleagues, compared 19 traditional and new indices in an Iranian group at raised heart risk. Simple tape-and-scale measures matter for screening where lab testing is scarce, so crowning the right index carries weight.

Two faults anchor the letter: rival indices were declared better than BMI by eyeballing AUC gaps without formal DeLong tests, and heavily overlapping indices were thrown into one regression as if independent. Correlation between indices ran high (ICC values near 0.84 in men in the table cited), which can warp such models. The writers urge proper curve tests and collinearity handling before clinics swap tools.
pmc-13398553:
Maoxin Lv and colleagues survey how Chinese hospitals are putting a home-grown language model to work. Their 2026 study focuses on DeepSeek-R1, a large model prized for strong performance at modest cost, now spreading through hospitals as a base for clinical tools. Generative AI promises decision support and smarter resource use, yet hospitals lack guidance on deployment shapes and computing bills.

Data came from the top 20 hospitals, regional centres and township hospitals, gathered through their official WeChat platforms. The survey weighs national policy against ground reality: which units run the model locally, which rent capacity and what each choice costs. Findings aim to give the next wave of hospitals a data-backed deployment map.
pmc-13398753:
Alice Melekian and co-authors dissect the jaw muscles of South American opossums and compute how hard each species can bite. Their 2026 study covers several species never described before, including Caenolestes fuliginosus, Dromiciops gliroides and Monodelphis touan. Opossums are hard to watch or collect, so their chewing machinery and diets remain sketchy compared with other marsupials.

Muscle attachment positions and sizes varied between species, as did how chewing force spreads across the jaw muscles. Bite estimates came from both hand dissection and digital dissection of scans, and the two routes were compared measure by measure. Checking method against method matters, since fossil and rare-species work increasingly leans on digital anatomy alone.
pmc-13398853:
Fong, Hosokawa, and Essen present, in 2026, a method for time-resolved femtosecond crystallography, the technique that films proteins mid-reaction using X-ray laser pulses. The hard part: each dataset mixes the starting protein with a few reacting intermediates, so fitting atomic coordinates to difference density maps invites bias. Their dFoCC method instead matches observed and calculated difference maps through a correlation coefficient, giving reproducible positions and a quality metric.

The method was exercised on side-chain rotations in an animal-like cryptochrome from the alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Their example used an estimated intermediate occupancy of 18.2 percent, a scaling factor of 11 applied to the calculated maps. The authors argue dFoCC simplifies extracting intermediate structures from mixed-state data, with quality judged by the map correlation rather than by eye. They note the approach shares some costs of simulation-based methods, but with less human steering.
pmc-13399653:
Yi-Nan Zhu and colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about breast cancer that returned, a decade later, as a lone lump on the scalp. Their patient, a 47-year-old woman, had undergone surgery for breast cancer ten years earlier. She noticed a scalp mass that grew slowly over nine months from soybean size to peanut size.

Biopsy settled what the eye could not. Tumor cells crowded the dermis with enlarged, dark nuclei, and the staining panel pointed firmly to breast origin. TRPS-1, GATA-3, and CK7 all stained diffusely positive, estrogen and progesterone receptors were strongly positive above 90 percent, and HER-2 scored 2+. Whole-body imaging found no other deposits. The authors note that scalp metastases are easily mistaken for cysts or lipomas, and that tissue examination remains the gold standard when a cancer survivor presents with a scalp lump.
pmc-13399753:
Valeria Vismara and colleagues describe a mini-invasive elbow ligament reconstruction that restores both main bundles of the ulnar collateral ligament. Their 2026 technical paper targets valgus instability, the elbow opening under outward stress, common in overhead throwers and after dislocations. Earlier techniques often focused on one bundle or required bone tunnels on both sides.

The method uses a small open approach and knotless suture anchors placed onlay, meaning fixed onto bone surface, to rebuild the anterior and posterior bundles. The anterior bundle stabilizes the elbow through most of its bending range, while the posterior bundle helps at higher flexion. The paper gives elbow surgeons a less invasive blueprint, while return-to-sport and durability outcomes for this construct still need reporting.
pmc-13400253:
Riyad Mroueh and colleagues saved a toddler's leg with a vein borrowed from his mother, in a 2026 case report from Lebanon. Exploration found both the superficial femoral artery and vein transected, with twelve to fifteen centimeters simply gone. His own saphenous veins, the usual graft material, measured about half a millimeter, far too small to use.

The team harvested a fresh great saphenous vein from the boy's mother and used it as an arterial allograft, ligating the femoral vein instead of reconstructing it, and gave no immunosuppression. Perfusion returned and the limb survived. Four years later the leg remains viable and functional. The authors present parent-derived fresh vein allograft as a viable salvage option when a small child's own conduits cannot serve.
pmc-13400453:
Ying Yang and colleagues follow, in 2026, teenagers with scoliosis to see whether low mood before spine surgery shapes quality of life two years later. The condition twists the spine in three dimensions during puberty. Beyond body effects, it can fuel anxiety, low mood and poor self-image.

The study covered 112 patients who had posterior spinal correction surgery in 2023 and completed two-year follow-up. Mood was scored on arrival with a standard hospital scale, and quality of life was measured before surgery and again at two years with spine and general health questionnaires. Groups started alike on basic traits, setting up a test of whether early negative emotions cast a long shadow after technically successful surgery.
pmc-13400653:
Wasim Akhtar and colleagues made zinc oxide nanoparticles using extracts of the moss Rhodobryum roseum and tested them for medical and farm uses. Their 2026 paper uses green synthesis, a plant-based route that avoids harsh chemicals, then characterizes the particles by spectroscopy, diffraction, and microscopy. Nanoparticles are prized for broad activity, but safer production routes remain in demand.

The particles killed four bacteria, most strongly Staphylococcus aureus, and showed antioxidant activity near that of vitamin C, at 75.2 percent versus 79 percent. Maize seeds primed with the particles grew best at 200 parts per million, with greater fresh and dry weight, more leaves, longer roots and shoots, and higher chlorophyll. The paper presents a multifunctional candidate for antimicrobials and seed treatment, pending toxicity and field trials.
pmc-13401153:
Xiaojuan Zhang and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on how tuberculosis develops. It centers on the long contest between the human immune system and Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium that causes the disease. Tuberculosis still kills more people than any other single infectious agent, even though drug treatment and the BCG vaccine exist.

Inside, the review follows the infection stage by stage, from early innate immune cell arrival and granuloma formation through lasting infection, granuloma breakdown, and active disease. It also covers metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, trained immunity, tissue-resident immunity, and myeloid networks that damp the immune response. The authors close by asking how these processes could guide new vaccines and add-on treatments.
pmc-13401553:
Neal Shore and co-authors published a 2026 real-world study of what happens when men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer stop second-line taxane chemotherapy early. Side effects often force discontinuation, and the team measured the survival and cost consequences using two large United States databases.

Survival came from the Flatiron Health records covering 2012 to 2020, while side effects and costs came from IQVIA claims for 2013 to 2021. Patients given a second androgen receptor drug instead lived a median of about 15 months versus about 14 months on taxane therapy. Among taxane patients, those completing more than eight cycles, 48 people, lived longer than the 166 who stopped at eight or fewer. The study pairs those outcome gaps with the adverse events and spending that early stopping involves.
pmc-13401653:
Mastrangelo and co-authors report, in 2026, the first use of the tyrosine kinase inhibitor toceranib for suspected chronic eosinophilic leukemia in a cat. Their patient was a 16-year-old spayed female shorthair cat with chronic, worsening eosinophilia, vomiting, and weight loss despite eating normally. She had thickening of the small gut, liver changes, and enlarged spleen on ultrasound, after negative viral and heartworm screening.

Therapy with prednisolone and chlorambucil, given for possible gut lymphoma, failed to control signs or eosinophil counts. Switching to toceranib alongside prednisolone produced a response by day 39. That meant resolved signs and a 30 percent drop in blood eosinophils, with no side effects blamed on the drug. A four-week progression-free interval followed before disease advanced on day 75. The cat was put to sleep on day 89 as quality of life declined. The authors present the drug pairing as an option for this rare disease.
pmc-13402353:
Guangyuan Li and co-authors identify a lipid transfer protein, SEC14L2, as a guard of the microtubule network that keeps cells in shape and cargo moving. Microtubules constantly grow and shrink, and a protein called Stathmin 1 breaks them down. The team shows Stathmin 1 is cleared by chaperone-mediated autophagy, a selective disposal path that feeds single proteins into lysosomes, and that SEC14L2 is needed for that clearance to run well.

When SEC14L2 was lost, disposal slowed, Stathmin 1 piled up, the microtubule network collapsed, and organelles clustered around the nucleus. In breast cancer cell models, disturbing this chain changed how cells answered drugs that target microtubules. The work ties a lipid handling protein to protein disposal and to the skeleton of the cell, opening a fresh angle on why some cancer cells resist microtubule drugs.
pmc-13402653:
Haoyu Yin and colleagues design a battery-like cell that makes hydrogen while generating its own power, using a new layered membrane to keep acid and alkali apart without wasting their energy. The setup oxidizes formaldehyde at one electrode, releasing hydrogen at low voltage, while the acid-alkali pairing itself yields electricity. Older membranes either resisted current through peeling layers or let acid and alkali cancel each other out.

Their composite pairs a through-pore anion exchange membrane with a cation exchange membrane. The cell reached a Faradaic efficiency for hydrogen of 198 percent, possible because both electrodes produce hydrogen, and a peak power density of 142 milliwatts per square centimeter. Modeling showed the porous layer steers charge carriers with low resistance and better use of the acid-alkali store. The authors pitch the design as a cleaner route to hydrogen from chemical energy.
pmc-13402853:
Chen and colleagues assemble the first picture of a rare brain lymphoma, the low grade B-cell form that starts in the central nervous system. They use two decades of registry data. The disease is so uncommon that treatment has run on habit more than evidence. Their 2026 study pulls 267 adults diagnosed between 2000 and 2021 from the SEER registry and compares treatment patterns and survival across two eras.

Survival improved. The later era's median survival had not been reached when the data were cut, while the earlier era's sat near eleven years. The death hazard halved. Chemotherapy plus radiation fell out of favor, dropping by half, while single modality held steady. Surgery stood out, with operated patients at about half the death hazard. In the MALT subtype, by contrast, no treatment approach beat another. Registry numbers cannot replace trials, the authors note, but they give this disease its map.
pmc-13403053:
Mohsin Kamran and co-authors review how artificial intelligence and mathematical modeling are joining forces against tumors, with a focus on brain tumor surgery. Solid tumors grow through cell division tangled with neighbor interactions that breed therapy resistance, and drugs that disrupt growth often injure healthy tissue too. Learning systems now aid early detection, surgical planning, and outcome prediction, while equations simulate how a tumor answers each possible intervention.

Combined and hybrid techniques sharpened detection and treatment optimization across the studies surveyed. Persistent weaknesses temper the optimism: thin data, models that cannot explain themselves, and results that fail to travel between hospitals. The authors close with a call for explainable, robust, individualized tools, arguing the merger of data-driven and equation-driven thinking is where safer cancer care will come from.
pmc-13403453:
Ying Zhang, Jing Xie, and Minhui Wang asked in 2026 whether soy protein could ease kidney damage linked to diabetes. Public gene data first pointed to two pathways that cross-talk in sore kidneys. One drives swelling signals, and the other, PPAR-gamma, helps calm them.

In diabetic mice, soy protein lowered blood sugar, waste levels in blood, and kidney harm in step with dose. In human kidney cells, a soy compound cut stress and swelling signals while raising cell survival. Drugs that flipped either pathway removed the benefit. The chain supports soy-based plans as an aid, pending human trials.
pmc-13403553:
Tatsuhiro Amano and colleagues reported in 2026 a teen whose chest pain after choir class came from air leaked into the center of his chest. The 15-year-old, tall and lean with asthma, had pain that grew worse when he breathed in. His vital signs stayed steady and no collapsed lung was found.

An X-ray showed faint lines of air tracing the heart and a large vessel, plus air under neck skin. A CT scan confirmed air spread from around the heart up to the neck. Singing likely spiked chest pressure and popped tiny air sacs. He healed with rest alone, and a day-ten film looked nearly clear.
pmc-13403653:
Selcan Cesur and Berrin Yalinbas-Kaya tested in 2026 whether a plant compound called spinosin can guard the stomach lining. Spinosin comes from healing plants and is better known for calming the brain. Male mice got a harsh acid and alcohol mix poured into the stomach to cause ulcers.

Mice given spinosin by mouth showed far less lining damage than untreated mice. Swelling signals fell, cell-death marks dropped, and natural defense enzymes rose. A standard ulcer drug served as the comparison arm. Two protective proteins, Nrf2 and HO-1, also rose with treatment. The pair link the benefit to calmer stress chemistry in the stomach.
pmc-13403853:
Ayele Emnetu and co-authors measured malaria in 2026 among sick visitors to a primary hospital in northwest Ethiopia. Their group held 385 people with symptoms that pointed to malaria, seen from April to November 2024. Blood from each person was checked under a microscope for the parasite.

Nearly half, at 46.2 percent of those tested, carried malaria. One species caused about 56 percent of the positive cases. People with no formal schooling faced about twice the odds of infection. Living near mosquito breeding water and skipping bed nets or home spraying also raised odds. Teaching and steady access to prevention tools are the clear needs.
pmc-13404853:
Ricardo Salgado and co-authors outline a 2026 pilot trial of a digital self-management tool for people with COPD, a long-term lung disease. Fewer than 2 percent of patients join pulmonary rehabilitation, and about 40 percent of those who start drop out. Breathlessness, travel problems and low motivation all play a part.

Twenty patients at a Swiss lung centre will be assigned by chance to the Respir'air BPCO programme or usual care. The digital tool builds daily self-management skills and aims to keep people physically active. As a pilot, the study mainly tests whether patients accept the tool and whether the trial runs smoothly. Early effects on activity and symptoms are recorded for planning a larger trial.
pmc-13405053:
Anna E Garcia Whitlock and co-authors use maps to place bleeding-control training where shootings cluster, in a 2026 study. The Stop the Bleed campaign teaches bystanders to stop life-threatening bleeding. Training often misses the neighbourhoods most likely to witness a shooting.

Shooting locations in a large city with high violent crime were mapped in ArcGIS to find hot spots. Eight high-risk community sites were identified, two agreed to host a course and one was chosen. Fifteen community members trained there showed clear skill gains after the course in the reported checks. Knowledge, attitudes and real tourniquet use were revisited at one and twelve months.
pmc-13405153:
Murat Ay and colleagues check two blood markers against organ failure scores among intensive care patients sick with COVID-19 sepsis, in 2026 work. Ferritin and procalcitonin are often read as severity clues, and the SOFA-2 score grades organ dysfunction. The question was whether day five marker levels predict that grade or death.

Patients were split into mild and severe groups by a SOFA-2 cut-off of five. Day five procalcitonin showed no link to severity in the reported analysis. Ferritin above 1191 nanograms per millilitre flagged severe disease with modest accuracy, but lost independent value once other inflammation markers entered the model. Neither marker predicted intensive care death on its own.
pmc-13405453:
Dorothea Sze Min Ong and co-authors lay out a practical approach to facial pain in a 2026 clinical article. Pain between the eyes and the lower jaw, including the mouth, can spring from muscle, nerve, vessel, dental or psychological causes. A structured method helps clinicians sort that crowded field.

An opening case sets the scene: a 49-year-old man with sudden, excruciating sharp pain along one side of his jaw. Attacks lasted seconds, came in waves and were triggered by chewing or talking, with normal findings between episodes. The article builds from such presentations toward examination and cause-by-cause reasoning. Cranial nerve checks and the pattern of attacks steer the first decisions.
pmc-13405553:
Leandro Cesar Pompeu and Fredi Alexander Diaz-Quijano propose a way to estimate missed dengue cases in São Paulo State, Brazil, in 2026 work. Pregnant women see health services often, so their dengue is more likely to be counted. Comparing other women's rates against theirs exposes under-reporting.

Data cover probable dengue cases from January to June 2024 across 645 municipalities. Evidence of under-reporting appeared in 108 towns, ranging from 1 to 95 percent in the reported estimates. About 8,624 missed cases were calculated among women aged 18 to 45 who were not pregnant. Local service coverage, clinic density and urbanisation showed no clear link to the size of the gap.
pmc-13407453:
Meletios P. Nigdelis and co-authors, in 2026, checked whether a phone app for endometriosis keeps helping outside the tidy world of trials. Endometriosis causes chronic pain when womb-like tissue grows elsewhere in the pelvis. Trial evidence already suggested specialised apps can ease symptoms. The team therefore surveyed real users of the Endo-App in everyday practice.

Users answered a short optional survey at sign-up, after three months, and again at six to seven months; 143 responded at the first follow-up and 55 at the second. Average pain and days needing medical help fell significantly by both later points compared with sign-up, and sick days dropped by the final check. The authors caution that the survey was not standardised and numbers thinned over time, so larger real-world studies should confirm the pattern.
pmc-13407853:
B S Niveditha and team tied a blood marker of glial activation to acting-out behavior and brain connectivity in young people. Their 2026 cross-sectional work draws 144 people from the Indian cVEDA group, matched into acting-out and healthy control groups, gauging plasma GFAP and neurofilament light chain alongside resting-state brain imaging. Acting-out disorders, marked by impulsivity and aggression, lack clear biological fingerprints.

A clear age-by-group interaction showed for GFAP, with acting-out youth showing higher levels only under age 14, while neurofilament showed no clear effect. A five-feature connectivity fingerprint tracked with GFAP, featuring stronger sensorimotor-limbic and attention-default links and weaker within-default-mode links. The work proposes an age-bound glial fingerprint for early acting-out pathology, pending long-term proof.
pmc-13408053:
Jing Zhang and co-authors evaluate, in 2026, a single-port endoscope-assisted spinal fusion for slipped vertebrae. Seventy-three patients with low-grade degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis, where one backbone slides forward on the next, had surgery between September 2023 and December 2024. The operation combined arthroscopic assistance with transforaminal fusion. The team reviewed short-term outcomes retrospectively.

The study's stated aim is the technique's early clinical efficacy and technical advantages over more open approaches for this single-segment, low-grade group. Pairing endoscopic visualisation with a single portal aims to limit tissue damage while still stabilising the slipped segment with a fusion cage. As a retrospective cohort from one programme, the work positions itself as early evidence for the method's feasibility, with longer follow-up needed to judge durability.
pmc-13408253:
Gawaz and colleagues look for SARS-CoV-2 spike protein lingering in skin blood vessels long after infection or vaccination, in a 2026 retrospective dermatology study. Vasculitic skin lesions, where small vessels become inflamed, have been reported after both COVID-19 illness and mRNA vaccination. The team examined skin biopsies from 9 patients with persistent or late-appearing lesions: 4 followed infection and 5 followed vaccination, with pre-pandemic vasculitis samples and healthy skin as controls.

Immunofluorescence staining detected spike protein in the vessel lining cells of all 9 patients. The finding places viral protein inside the very vessels driving the skin inflammation, months beyond the acute event in these cases. Control tissues served to check the staining was specific rather than background noise. Gawaz argues persistent spike protein in vessel walls deserves study as a possible contributor to these delayed skin reactions, while the small design limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13408353:
Won Hee Lee and colleagues sequenced single tumour cells in 2026 to watch metastatic bowel cancer evolve under treatment. Bulk sequencing averages millions of cells and hides the subclones that survive therapy and seed relapse. The team grew tumour organoids from individual cells taken from six patients.

Fifty-eight single-cell-derived cultures and matched bulk tumours yielded family trees of the cancers at fine resolution. Chemotherapy left its own mutation signatures, unevenly: faster-dividing lineages collected more drug-linked mutations, and burden differed sharply between and within patients. Later stages brought dramatic changes, including tangled structural rearrangements, loops of DNA outside chromosomes carrying driver genes, and jumping genetic elements switching on. The atlas gives researchers a foundation for studying how late-stage cancers keep reinventing themselves under pressure.
pmc-13408653:
Jingrui Fan and co-authors report in 2026 a membrane that can sieve gases differing by mere angstroms, built from graphdiyne, a carbon sheet pierced by regular in-plane pores. Graphdiyne's built-in holes make it a natural molecular sieve, yet making a continuous film whose pores actually face the gas flow had defeated earlier attempts. The team's answer was to grow the sheet inside the aligned channels of a porous crystal template.

The confined film separated three-angstrom gases such as hydrogen and helium from larger molecules with high selectivity. Calculations credit a double effect: strict size exclusion at the pore plus an amplified electronic polarisation unique to the graphdiyne framework. Because the wider graphyne family offers tunable pore sizes, the templating strategy could yield a whole shelf of precision gas-separation membranes.
pmc-13408953:
Xia Huang, Thomas Alter, Roswitha Merle, and Vanessa Szott deliver a blunt result in 2026 for anyone predicting bacterial behaviour from gene activity. Vibrio parahaemolyticus, a marine bacterium behind seafood poisoning, swims, sticks, and builds biofilms depending on conditions. Researchers often read its genes while it floats freely and assume the reading forecasts those surface behaviours. Across a diverse panel of strains, that assumption failed.

Traits and gene expression both varied widely by strain. Once multiple-testing corrections were applied, no robust links tied expression levels to surface phenotypes, and predictive models performed worse than guessing the average. Family-tree style analysis confirmed strain identity dominating the variation. The authors argue that studies pooling strains or reading the wrong growth condition will keep making false confidence, and that a strain-level, condition-matched measure is the honest route.
pmc-13410453:
Qian Cheng and colleagues built a battery separator in 2026 that copies the way living cells move charged particles. Their design places crown ether molecules inside a porous metal framework, forming channels that guide lithium ions evenly while steadying the surface where the electrode meets the liquid inside the cell.

Lab tests showed the new separator held back the spiky lithium growth that shortens battery life, and test cells kept running for more than 1500 hours in one setup. Full cells kept 86 percent of their charge capacity after 1200 cycles, a result that points toward longer lasting batteries for cars and portable devices.
pmc-13410553:
Nicola Frericks and a large team pinpoint in 2026 where hepatitis E virus fails when it tries to infect mouse liver cells. The virus normally infects many species, yet ordinary mice resist it, which hampers lab study. A related rat virus also poses a spillover risk to people.

Mouse liver cell lines could copy the virus and release new particles once its genetic material was placed inside directly. Immune defenses inside the cells were not the block, the team found. Particles stuck to mouse cells, yet they never opened up to release their cargo. The barrier therefore sits at entry, after attachment and before copying starts, which focuses the search for what human cells provide.
pmc-13411153:
Lujun Shao and colleagues set out in 2026 a bedside plan for treating severe lung infection from Chlamydia psittaci, a bacterium caught mainly from birds. Standard penicillin-type drugs barely touch this germ, yet ward practice varies widely. Modern DNA scanning now names the culprit fast, which sharpens drug choices.

Drawing on six multicenter cohorts, the review splits care into phases: first-guess treatment, then targeted treatment at the two-to-three-day decision point. Doxycycline stands as the preferred backbone once diagnosis is confirmed in non-pregnant adults. Switching drug classes is needless when a patient already improves on the first-guess option, the authors argue. Severity, organ support, and drug stewardship all feed each decision.
pmc-13414153:
Chaofeng Yu and colleagues field-test in 2026 a designer microbial consortium, SynCom-SASW01, meant to help wheat survive drought. Two trial sites, Hohhot and Hulunbuir, compared inoculated and plain plots under dry conditions while the team tracked yield, root chemistry, soil moisture, and which microbes took up residence inside roots.

Grain yield rose 10.42 percent at one site and 8.52 percent at the other in the inoculated fields. Extra tillers and livelier roots drove the gain, while roots stockpiled proline and glutathione and dialled down damage markers. The consortium secreted slime that held soil water like a micro-reservoir and freed nitrogen and phosphorus. Inside roots it arrived early and crowded the community toward helpful genera such as Pseudomonas, a priority effect the authors stress.
pmc-13415253:
Wen Jin and colleagues mine single-cell data to explain why some estrogen driven breast cancers stop responding to tamoxifen, in 2026. Their dataset held sixteen tumors, thirteen untreated primaries and three resistant recurrences. Careful filtering and clustering resolved eleven major cell populations in the tumor setting.

One malignant subgroup stood out, marked by the long RNA called GAS5, and it expanded sharply in resistant tumors. Those cells burned energy at a higher rate and sat at a late stage of the inferred cell family tree. A regulator named SPDEF was unusually active in them. In a large public cancer cohort, high SPDEF levels matched worse survival.
pmc-13415753:
Julhan Irfandi and a large team analyze adolescent obesity in Indonesia using a national health survey from 2018, in a 2026 study. Data covered 75,800 teenagers aged thirteen to eighteen. Obesity prevalence came out at about six percent. Regression models weighed fatty food habits, disease history, activity, family traits, and place of residence.

Parental history of overweight was the strongest predictor, raising odds more than fourfold. Frequent fatty food eating, past disease, and moderate activity levels also mattered, alongside age and sex. Cutting high calorie foods and raising activity deserve priority, especially for teenagers whose parents carry excess weight, the authors conclude.
pmc-13415853:
Simran Khutan and colleagues study what shapes outdoor time and screen time for preschool children, in a 2026 mixed methods project in Leicestershire, England. Outdoor time protects against short sightedness, while screens raise risk. A focus group met in January 2025, then parents of one to four year olds answered a survey that spring.

Fifty-two of 153 invited parents responded. Only five children, under ten percent, reached two hours outdoors daily, the recommended level. Most parents still called outdoor time important and realistic, yet few knew it guards against myopia. Screen exposure was common, with about 78 percent of children reported as screen users in the results shown.
pmc-13416153:
Youngsun Lee and colleagues trace a hereditary nerve disease to a jumping gene deletion that also starves cells of zinc control, in 2026. Repeats called Alu cut exon 17 from the SPAST gene, a cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia with dementia. Brain organoids grown from human stem cells, plus grafts, modeled the cut.

The cut fused SPAST notes with a nearby gene, lowering ZnT6, a Golgi zinc carrier. Zinc piled up in the cytosol, the Golgi fragmented, and amyloid plus ubiquitin clumped. A zinc chelator drug or an antibody that blocks Golgi breakup brought back shape and lowered amyloid. Like fused notes turned up in one sporadic Alzheimer's brain.
pmc-13416653:
Ana Gomes and colleagues ran a family-screening program in 2026 for Alport syndrome, an inherited kidney disease, at a center in Gaia and Espinho, Portugal. Finding relatives early matters because kidney-protecting treatment can slow decline, so the team sent letters inviting first-degree relatives of known patients for kidney checks and genetic counseling.

Of 93 relatives assessed, 76 took genetic testing and 52 carried the family variant, while 24 were cleared and a few declined or faced delays. The paper shows cascade screening finds many new patients in time for protective care, with counseling easing a difficult family conversation.
pmc-13416753:
Zhibin Song and colleagues survey fish along a huge water transfer canal in China, in a 2026 study of the middle route of China's South to North water project. They use environmental DNA, traces of genetic material left in water, plus trait data to map how fish communities change along the canal. The channel is uniform and built by people.

Surveys found 39 fish taxa, with clear shifts from place to place. Communities grew smaller bodied toward higher latitudes, and feeding habits shifted as well. Distance and space explained more of the pattern than local water conditions. The authors advise biosecurity checks and habitat support at key points.
pmc-13418053:
Peixoto and colleagues report a 2026 study of tiny ring structures in liquid crystals that can be written with voltage and set with light. Liquid crystals of this twisted type form finger-like loops whose patterns are hard to place precisely. The team used pre-designed voltage patterns to guide how the loops relax, producing neat concentric rings with chosen sizes.

 Heating the film then raises castle-like surface features, a central pillar ringed by walls, and cooling reverses the change. Models of the physics backed the design rules. Because the rings form on demand over large areas, the method offers a scalable way to print surfaces whose texture switches with heat. Switchable skins could serve in optics, sensors, or soft machines.
pmc-13418553:
Tran and colleagues report a 2026 study from two hospitals in Vietnam on risk soon after heart failure care. They built a simple score, called SAGE-HF, to flag patients likely to die or return to hospital within 30 days of discharge. The score uses three items: a blood marker named sST2, age, and a standard measure of kidney function.

Within 30 days, 47 of the 218 patients died or were readmitted. Each score item linked to events on its own, and sST2 levels ran higher in patients than in people without heart failure. The score split patients into clear bands, with predicted event rates rising from low single digits to about six in ten at the top. Its accuracy held up under resampling checks. Clinics could use it to plan closer follow-up for high-risk patients.
pmc-13418953:
Buckenmaier and co-authors rebuilt a fast magnetic resonance imaging sequence for use with Overhauser enhancement. That method boosts the weak signals from low-field scanners. The standard fast sequence is efficient, but it makes banding artifacts, dark stripes across images. The stripes appear when the magnetic field is uneven or drifts during scanning.

Their changed sequence, called bSSFP180, mixes the boost step with image taking instead of running them apart. In tests, the new sequence wiped out the banding artifacts. It kept working well under uneven field setups made on purpose, where the standard sequence fell apart. The group concludes that stripe-free imaging of this kind is a useful step forward. It points toward sound low-field scanners built from light, cheap permanent magnets for medical use.
pmc-13420053:
Nairi Strauch and colleagues survey patients on fertility counseling during yearly general gynecology visits, as more women delay childbearing. Many women of reproductive age lack clear teaching on how fertility falls with age, even at routine visits. The survey ran in an academic generalist clinic, recruited through posters in eight exam rooms.

Posters carried a code linking to the approved online survey, open from April 1 to August 30, 2024, with a small gift card offered for taking part. Answers show what patients recall being told, what they wish they had heard, and when they want the talk to happen. Yearly visits may be the one reliable slot for that conversation. Clinics can use the stated preferences to shape visit scripts rather than guessing.
pmc-13420153:
Mwalungali and colleagues studied in 2026 social and lifestyle risk factors for cardiovascular complications among adults with high blood pressure in Lusaka, Zambia. Records of 384 patients at the University Teaching Hospital supplied data on income status, salt intake, smoking, drinking, activity, and complications such as heart failure and heart wall thickening. A penalty-adjusted statistical model handled quirks in the data.

Mwalungali found each added year of age raised the odds of complications, while sex showed no firm link after adjustment. Low income status came with about four times the odds, though the result sat on the edge of significance. Smoking roughly tripled the odds, and drinking raised them too. Physical activity was strongly protective, cutting odds to a small fraction, and higher education also protected. The authors urge prevention that pairs lifestyle change with action on social gaps.
pmc-13420253:
Mobini and colleagues use computer simulations in 2026 to study how progesterone slips inside cyclodextrins. Progesterone is a hormone drug that barely dissolves in water, and cyclodextrins are ring-shaped sugar molecules used to carry such drugs. The shape of the ring's chemical decorations may decide how well loading works.

The team built twenty simulated host and guest systems covering the plain ring and three decorated versions, then mapped the energy landscape as the hormone entered from different directions. Decorations strongly changed which entry path the hormone preferred and how deep the energy well holding it became. The hydroxypropyl and sulfobutylether versions showed especially deep wells along certain paths. Binding also squeezed water out of the ring and reshaped it into a rounder, more symmetric form, while weak van der Waals forces dominated the direct grip on the hormone.
pmc-13420353:
Luz and colleagues followed in 2026 adults who had worn fixed braces to see if neck-of-tooth wear lesions appeared over time. The study covered 41 patients at three points: before braces, right after removal, and years later.

Premolars and molars, the chewing teeth toward the back, were hit most often. Teeth stayed as straight as right after treatment, so the gain from braces held. pmc-13420853:
Yizhen Wang and colleagues survey early-years medical students in the United Kingdom on which online learning resources they prefer at each stage of study. A self-completed questionnaire fed statistical comparisons across learning stages, while free-text answers were read thematically. The most preferred resources changed with stage, the headline result, rather than one winner serving all purposes. Cognitive load theory frames the reading: each stage burdens memory differently, so the right tool differs too. Course designers can match resource menus to the week of term instead of offering one flat list.
pmc-13421253:
Rogerio Lopes Vieites and Andres Felipe Gaona Acevedo profile seven pitaya varieties grown in Brazil in a 2026 paper, measuring what the pulp and peel of this dragon fruit contain. Pitaya is gaining commercial interest, and the peel — usually discarded — may hold value of its own.

Statistical grouping separated the varieties by their profiles. The authors present the fruit and its by-products as promising for food use.
pmc-13421453:
Jignesh Chauhan and co-workers built a part-order outbreak model in 2026 for childhood disease spread under shots. Standard models forget the past, yet real outbreaks carry memory effects, so the team generalized the susceptible-infected-recovered framework with a Caputo part-order derivative.

They proved the model has unique solutions, analyzed stability of disease-free and endemic states through the reproduction number, and solved it with a part-order predictor-corrector scheme. Simulations showed higher shot coverage lowering the spread number and steadying the disease-free state. That gives modelers a memory-aware tool for childhood shot planning in future outbreaks.
pmc-13421653:
Pallavi Bhardwaj, Caitlin Jones, Lasse Dierich and Aleksandar Vučković introduce TabularQGAN in a 2026 paper, a quantum generative model that fabricates realistic spreadsheet-like data. Their quantum adversarial network uses a flexible encoding and a new circuit design for mixed data. The team tested the model on a hospital dataset and a census dataset. It ran on a noiseless simulator with reduced feature sets. It matched or beat leading classical generators on a standard similarity score. The authors present it as a proof of concept for quantum data synthesis.
pmc-13422353:
Muhammad Daud and four colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a first drought teaches wheat to survive a second one. Crops increasingly meet drought repeatedly, and the warning value of an early dry spell was unproven.

Added nitrogen lifted growth and hydraulics, and partial root-zone watering further protected water transport while trimming oxidative damage. The pairing emerges as the resilient strategy.
pmc-13423453:
Kohei Suzuki and nine colleagues test how well ordinary abdominal CT scans, done for gut symptoms rather than cancer hunting, catch advanced colorectal cancer. Colonoscopy confirmed 46 advanced cancers. Radiologists had suspected 45 of them on CT, giving a sensitivity of 97.8%; the one miss hid behind a large stomach tumour. Among 304 patients without advanced cancer, 292 were correctly cleared, for 96.1% specificity. Routine CT, the authors conclude, rarely misses advanced disease, though colonoscopy remains the confirming test.
pmc-13424453:
Zoe Behrman and Muhamed Abubacker describe a kidney transplant patient whose infection by the uncommon bacterium Mycobacterium haemophilum convincingly imitated two other diseases at once. A lingering positive fungal blood test added confusion and brought antifungal treatment. Joint fluid then revealed both gout crystals and acid-fast bacteria, and skin biopsy showed rod-shaped organisms of the same type. Routine cultures missed the culprit, which needs special growth conditions; gene tests at two reference laboratories named it. The authors warn that transplant recipients with stubborn skin and joint disease deserve this organism on the list.
pmc-13424653:
Matthew Webster and four colleagues borrow a self-teaching trick from image AI, masked autoencoder pretraining, to outline peripheral nerves in ultrasound scans, a task starved of labelled examples. Most earlier work covered only the median nerve, so the team assembled 10,603 images spanning eight nerves and more than 1,500 patients with normal nerve tests.

A segmentation model first studied unlabelled scans by hiding and reconstructing patches, then fine-tuned on labelled nerves. Pretraining lifted accuracy for every nerve. Gains were dramatic where labels were scarcest: the sural nerve's overlap score rose from 14% to 40%, and another small nerve's from 28% to 55%. pmc-13426053:
Kamel and colleagues built a 2026 microsensor that measures tetracaine, a local anesthetic used in eye medicines, quickly and cheaply for quality checks. They compared it against an identical sensor without the graphene layer.

It also held its signal steadier, repeated better between sensors, and resisted the water film that degrades such devices. It ignored common salts, related drugs, and filler ingredients, and worked across the acidity range of eye products. In commercial eye formulations it recovered between about ninety-nine and one hundred two percent of the known content.
pmc-13426353:
Shiyu Chen and coauthors evaluated a chemotherapy-based conditioning sequence before donor transplant for acute leukemia still in non-remission in a 2026 case series. They received CLAG chemotherapy, combining cladribine, cytarabine, and growth factor, as part of sequential conditioning before donor transplantation between January 2021 and July 2023. No control group was available, so outcomes are descriptive.

All nine patients achieved engraftment in the reported results, and the series tracks transplant complications, non-relapse death, relapse, and survival. For patients with no proven bridge to transplant, even small series inform feasibility. Nine sick men and women is a slim base, so the team keeps claims small and frames the run as a test of what can be done.
pmc-13426953:
Eline Meireson and colleagues tested how repeatable a fetal heart measure is when different experts read the same single heartbeat. The measure, global longitudinal strain, tracks how much the heart wall shortens, using speckle patterns in ultrasound clips.

Healthy women with single pregnancies gave heart clips every four weeks from the second trimester until delivery. The study gathered 632 clips from 124 women, each clip read twice by one expert and once by another. One expert reading the same clip twice agreed only poorly to moderately with herself. Two experts agreed moderately to well, with the left heart chamber steadier than the right and best results before 32 weeks.
pmc-13427253:

They promise privacy-safe sharing and more data for rare heart conditions. The authors warn that rules and checks have not kept pace with use.

Current privacy laws in Europe and America leave gaps for these risks. Fit-for-purpose checks should gate any use as stand-alone evidence, they urge. Rare conditions stand to gain most if the safeguards hold firm.
pmc-13427353:
Nedim Kaban comments on immune polarization when rheumatoid arthritis and asthma coexist in a 2026 letter discussing a cytokine study with twenty-five patients per group. Specific signals differed by comparison: interleukin-5 was higher in asthma than arthritis, interleukin-4 higher in the combined group, and interleukin-10 raised in both asthma groups.

Such nuance matters because overall similarity between asthma and combined disease could hide unresolved confounding in a small cross-sectional sample. Kaban urges caution before treating Th2 dominance as settled biology for overlap patients. Group size was just two dozen and five in each arm, so chance and mix ups in who had what could bend the tale the counts tell here.
pmc-13427853:
Ziersen and Martinussen published a 2026 methods paper on counting life years lost to one cause. When several risks compete, plain death rates can blur what one cause costs. The paper builds estimators that pair flexible machine learning with sound math. Test runs showed the estimators behave as theory predicts under set conditions. They also rank which patient traits change the cost most strongly. The team applied the method to Danish records on antidepressant response. Registry data on switching drugs or hospital return supplied the test case. Simulations backed the method before the registry test case ran.
pmc-13429253:
Newton and colleagues described in 2026 how Delaware's public colleges and universities work together to support healthy aging in a state growing older fast. Chronic disease, inactivity, and memory decline strain care systems built for a younger state.

Three institutions divide the work: Delaware State University, Delaware Technical Community College, and the University of Delaware. Their programs span research, workforce training, proven community programs, policy advice, and outreach across rural, suburban, and city areas. The authors stress that partnerships among campuses, health providers, agencies, and community groups multiply what each can do alone. They propose shared courses, joint research, and a statewide aging summit to tighten the network.
pmc-13430253:
Astrid Berner-Rodoreda and a large group of health and trade scholars examine, in a 2026 commentary, the health stakes of the new free trade agreement between the European Union and India. The deal joins nearly two billion people and about a quarter of world output, and both sides call it their largest ever. Health goods sit at its center: Europe ships medical equipment and medicines to India, while India supplies Europe with pharmaceuticals worth billions.

A European push for patent rules beyond global norms was negotiated out, which the authors credit with protecting fast access to Indian generic medicines. Regulatory standards stay unchanged, a possible bottleneck for some Indian exporters. The commentary holds the deal up as a template for aligning trade with health goals.
pmc-13430853:
Miyuki Toda and colleagues explore how midwives care for pregnant adolescents in Northern Malawi, where teen pregnancy brings risks for mother and baby. Youth-friendly programs exist, yet evidence on quality, context-specific care for this group was thin.

A descriptive qualitative study ran six focus groups with 38 midwives recruited from three hospitals in the region. Midwives, as frontline providers, described their views and routines for adolescent pregnancy care. The findings aim to ground future interventions in local reality, so teen mothers get care that fits their age, fears, and social pressures.
pmc-13430953:
Koh and colleagues reviewed in 2026 nearly a decade of research on Pokémon GO, the phone game that sends players walking outdoors to catch virtual creatures, asking whether its health effects last. This scoping review gathered 186 sources published through late 2025, covering the game's whole lifespan.

Twenty-nine studies found players walked more, though gains often faded fast. Older adults kept the gains longest. Players reported better mood, less loneliness, and stronger community ties. Starting motives were nostalgia and novelty. Risks included distracted walking and play from the couch, which cancels the walking. The authors judge the game a real but uneven public health tool.
pmc-13431253:
Mohammed Al Ghafari and co-authors surveyed pharmacy staff across Oman in 2026 on what they know, feel, and do about germ resistance to antibiotics and careful drug use. The national survey reached 333 staff in primary care clinics in early 2025. It also set clinics with a past record of heavy antibiotic use beside clinics with standard use, to hunt for wider causes behind gaps.

pmc-13432853:

pmc-13434653:

pmc-13434753:

pmc-13434853:

pmc-13435153:

pmc-13437153:

pmc-13437453:

pmc-13437853:

pmc-13438153:

pmc-13439053:
Lorena Niggli and co-authors report 2026 work on the shifting magnetic patterns inside the metal neodymium. Neodymium can settle into a self-made spin glass state, where tiny magnetic regions form patterns that change over time. Fast and slow patches sat side by side, tied to distinct pattern sizes in the metal. A wavelet method, which sorts patterns by scale, helped match local order with its pace of change. pmc-13439153:
Bae and colleagues follow children after bilateral lung transplantation in this 2026 single-center study. Long-term data on how young recipients recover function, grow, and adapt their new lungs are limited. The team reviewed sixteen children who received deceased-donor lungs. Seven were aged ten and under, and nine were older. The review tracked lung function, scan-measured lung volume, growth, and survival.

Scans showed the transplanted lungs progressively expanding after surgery, with similar patterns for lobar grafts, which are trimmed to fit, and whole lungs. pmc-13439253:
Jinfeng Miao and a large team test whether depression moves between older married partners, comparing China, the United States, and England in 2026 work. Low mood in later life often spreads within a household, yet the strength and direction of that sharing across cultures was murky. Partners' symptom scores moved together in every country, most strongly in China. In the Chinese cohort, one partner's mood predicted the other's chiefly through lasting likeness between couples. In England, within-person spillover held up under the strictest checks. Limits in daily living and depression fed each other over time, mainly in the Western cohorts. The authors caution that couple-level sameness, not contagion, explains much of the pattern.
pmc-13440253: Qiong Li and co-authors publish a correction to their multicentre cohort study linking a blood-fat index in early pregnancy to preeclampsia risk. The notice is a correction only, with no new data or findings. One funder, a Baoshan District health youth program, had been left out of the funding statement, and the notice prints the full corrected list of supporting grants. The published article has been updated to match.
pmc-13440453:
Rajesh Ranjan, Jayashree Sunil Bhat, and Mohan Kumar Kalaiah compare a brain-wave marker of working memory in younger and older teenagers, reporting in 2026. The P300 wave rises about three hundred milliseconds after a notable sound and reflects attention and memory updating. An auditory N-back task, where listeners judge whether a sound matches one heard steps earlier, separates holding information from reshaping it. Forty-eight adolescents, half early and half late teens, completed zero, one, and two-back versions.

Older teens showed faster waves and larger amplitudes overall, signs of maturing processing. Holding demands produced the largest amplitudes at every electrode site, above reshaping demands. Group differences across task levels, though, never reached statistical significance. The authors conclude that P300 size alone does not separate early from late adolescents across these memory conditions.
pmc-13440753:
Kunal Singla and colleagues report a giant nerve sheath cancer on the scalp and review the handful of like cases in print, publishing in 2026. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours are rare sarcomas arising from nerve coverings, expected in about one person per million yearly. Scalp sites are rarer still, with only twenty-six cases published before theirs. Their patient, a 50-year-old man, carried a firm mass on his crown for eight months.

Recovery ran smoothly, with discharge on the seventh day. The review favours full removal plus skull repair, radiation after surgery, and chemotherapy held for high-grade or spread disease, while warning that five-year survival sits near thirty percent.
pmc-13441253:
Bailey and colleagues published a 2026 guide to a cheap training model for ear care. A blood pocket on the outer ear, called an auricular hematoma, needs fast drainage. Left alone, it can scar the ear into the lumped cauliflower shape. Trainees rarely get to practice this drainage before facing a real patient.

Learners practice finding landmarks, numbing, cutting, draining, and dressing the ear. The steps mirror the full care routine used in emergency rooms. The authors aim to lift trainee confidence before the first real case arrives. The trainer can be built again cheaply whenever a program needs more.
pmc-13441353:
Jessica Gasparello's team mapped mixed-type bile-sac cancer in 2026 in twenty-five White cases, a rare subtype with worse outlook than ordinary adenocarcinoma. Tumors with over a quarter squamous component were studied by immune staining and gene mapping, including PD-L1, mismatch repair, HER2, and claudin 18.2, plus gene changes. pmc-13442453:
Daniel Medina-Gil and colleagues profile the immune crowd inside B-cell lymphoma tissue in a 2026 study. pmc-13442853:
Liuqin Yan and colleagues grade disaster readiness in mountain villages of Zhangzha Town in a 2026 study. pmc-13443053:

pmc-13443153:

pmc-13445853:

pmc-13447053:

pmc-13447353:

pmc-13448253:

pmc-13448653:

pmc-13448953:

pmc-13449353:

pmc-13449653:

pmc-13451153:

pmc-13451553:

pmc-13452153:

That measure spiked in the seconds before each event, held high for a stretch after, and dipped right at onset. Peaks sat near the balance point in most channels. The authors call the work a single-case, idea-forming study, and they tie the wave pattern to what meditators report feeling.
pmc-13452353:
