pmc-13453753:
Bartłomiej Ptaszek and four co-authors test whether adding blood flow restriction and cooling to interval training shifts blood fats in young healthy people. pmc-13454053:

pmc-13454453:

pmc-13454653:
Yuta Nakaya, Masanori Akamatsu, Akiyoshi Ogimoto, and Hiroaki Kitaoka study, in 2026, whether changes during a hospital stay predict what happens to older patients after sudden heart failure. Their focus is a combined blood index and how it shifts from admission to discharge, alongside shifts in walking distance. The question is whether patients whose numbers improve leave with better prospects than those whose numbers stall or worsen. Pairing a blood trend with a function trend, the authors argue, gives a cheap picture of recovery that any ward can collect.
pmc-13457353:
You and Simonsson test whether early tuberculosis trial data can predict later success in this 2026 study. Phase 2a tuberculosis trials run about two weeks. pmc-13457453:
Shuai Teng, Fengfeng Teng, Yuguang Zhuang, Chenyan Zhao, Saisai Zhao and Yiqin Yao published this 2026 review on nutrition literacy in women living with or beyond breast and gynaecological cancers. They add symptom-led meal plans, family involvement and digital follow-up, judged on outcomes such as diet quality and weight.
pmc-13457853:
Shaonan Zhong and colleagues build a two-stage deep learning system that measures lung cancer burden on FDG PET/CT scans. Automated volumes tracked the human references closely, correlating at 0.984 for metabolic tumor volume and 0.998 for total lesion glycolysis. The authors pitch the system as a reliable way to quantify tumor burden for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning, cutting radiologist workload while keeping numbers trustworthy.
pmc-13458253:

pmc-13458353:
Anne J Maheux and colleagues take a naturalistic look at what American young people type to AI chatbots, using keystroke data from the Aura parental monitoring app. Their 2026 study covers 3,363 users aged 1 to 17 who opted into the keyboard, coding 42,355 user-app-days with a language model checked by human reviewers. pmc-13458653:

Adding silica nanoparticles cut tension further to 0.69 mN per metre and flipped mineral surfaces from oil-wet to water-wet, with glass contact angle falling from 114 to 47 degrees after 14 days. The authors present the work as initial screening for alkaline-nanoparticle recovery, pending core flood tests.
pmc-13459353:
Xinyi Wang and co-authors searched for genes that connect aging with degeneration of the temporomandibular joint, the hinge that moves the jaw. Aging is a major risk factor for this painful joint disease, yet the shared molecular machinery was unmapped. Their 2026 study compared jaw joint tissue from young and old mice. It overlapped the results with joint disease datasets while excluding purely mechanical effects. Network analysis plus machine learning distilled a shortlist of signature genes, checked in aged mouse joints.

The overlap produced fifty two candidate genes tied to both aging and joint degeneration, concentrated in daily rhythm regulation and programmed cell death pathways. Machine learning narrowed these to eight hub genes. The team then verified expression changes for key hub genes by tissue staining in an aged mouse model sorted by imaging and cartilage scores. The signature is a starting point for early diagnosis research.
pmc-13459653:
Charlene Thompson and co-authors mapped what helps and what blocks childhood vaccination across Canada, where coverage still falls short of the 95 percent national target after pandemic disruption. Their 2026 scoping review searched seven databases for studies on families with children up to age six. It screened the literature with established review frameworks and analyzed themes qualitatively. The team also asked whether the balance of factors shifted between the periods before and after COVID-19 arrived.

Thirty one studies made the final set. Five themes played a double role, helping some families and hindering others. They covered access to health services, parents' reasoning about risk, emotional influences on decisions, outside influences such as community voices, and information quality. Two barriers stood alone without a helpful flip side: use of alternative medicine and the colonial character of health institutions for Indigenous families.
pmc-13459753:
Yushan Luo and co-authors describe anesthetic care for kidney surgery in a woman whose windpipe was dangerously narrowed by a rare bone growth disease, tracheobronchopathia osteoplastica. The condition studs the airway with bony nodules, and her narrowest tracheal segment measured about 0.40 centimeters across, too tight for a standard breathing tube. In their 2026 case report, a previous operation at another hospital had been abandoned when intubation failed. The team planned around a formal difficult airway protocol before attempting her partial kidney removal.

A team evaluation produced a tailored plan using a narrow gauge breathing tube placed under video laryngoscope guidance. General anesthesia then proceeded uneventfully, and the surgery on her kidney tumor, a benign angiomyolipoma, went smoothly. The 43 year old patient came through with her airway intact. Careful imaging before surgery and a rehearsed airway strategy turn a potentially catastrophic induction into a routine, survivable operation, the authors stress.
pmc-13459953:
Rachel Berry and co-authors listed what pharmacists and their teams actually do during disease outbreaks, beyond the COVID-19 experience that fills recent memory. Their 2026 global rapid review searched three databases for studies from 2014 to early 2025. It organized every pharmacy role against the World Health Organization's emergency cycle: prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery. Roles were classed at individual, organizational, and national levels. One reviewer screened with a ten percent second check, fitting the rapid timeline.

From 161 articles spanning all WHO regions, the team drew 145 distinct role categories. Response dominated at 46 percent of roles, followed by prevention at 29 percent, preparedness at 15 percent, and recovery at just 10 percent in the sorting. Most roles sat at organizational and individual levels, with national level roles least common at 28 percent. Pharmacy's outbreak value is concentrated in the crisis itself, the authors argue, and preparedness and recovery are where the profession is most underused.
pmc-13460053:
Takashi Sakai and colleagues examined in 2026 whether simple blood and nutrition scores taken before surgery can predict recurrence after complete removal of non-small cell lung cancer. Their retrospective study covered 789 patients operated on between 2012 and 2022, excluding anyone with infection or prior treatment. Four immune and nutritional indices were compared, centered on the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, a balance between two white blood cell types.

Recurrence struck about 23 percent of patients. A high ratio meant clearly worse five-year recurrence-free survival in the whole group and in stage one patients alone. Only in stage one disease did the ratio stay independently predictive after adjustment, beating the three rival indices there. The authors propose it for refining follow-up plans in early disease.
pmc-13461253:
Himel Mallick and seven co-editors introduce in 2026 a research collection on methods for imaging and omics data science, the third and final volume of a Frontiers in Genetics trilogy. Earlier volumes tackled microbiome statistics and then single-cell methods, while this collection widens the lens to images combined with molecular data. It gives special weight to patterns across space and time.

The editors argue the timing is critical: foundation models pretrained across sequences, single-cell profiles, and tissue images now learn shared representations across data types. Yet such models are only as trustworthy as the statistics, benchmarks, and domain knowledge beneath them. The collected papers offer purpose-built methods for representing, integrating, and drawing conclusions from modern multimodal biomedical data, setting standards the editors want the artificial intelligence wave to meet.
pmc-13461553:
Yang, Zhang, and Wang studied in 2026 whether heavier social media use goes with more sports activity among young people in China. Drawing on the 2021 China General Social Survey, they screened 1,709 adults aged 18 to 35 years. A statistical model suited to ordered outcomes tested the link, and extra checks varied the measures and model to probe robustness.

Yang found stronger social media use was significantly tied to more frequent sports participation. The authors read this as consistent with a peer effect, where seeing peers play sports makes it more visible and rewarding. The survey could not measure that path directly, though, or prove cause. A hoped-for twist, that health information searching would reshape the link in a curve, was not supported. Schooling level and gender also tied to participation. The authors urge care in reading a one-time survey as evidence of direction.
pmc-13461853:
Qiulin Liang and colleagues search, in a 2026 data and lab study, for gene markers tied to a chemical-sensing protein in cancer of the nasopharynx, the upper throat. That sensing protein, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, can drive cancer when switched on. Gene data were mined with statistical screening and machine learning to single out markers linked to the receptor. The team then checked the markers in lab tests and mapped their immune links.

Three genes passed the screen: CHRNB2, ADCY4, and CDC6. The first and third ran high in the cancer; ADCY4 ran low. Each marker tied to different immune cell patterns in tumors, some positive and some negative. Small molecules that fine-tune the markers were predicted, forming a wider control network. Drug response differed by marker level for a common drug. The authors offer the three genes as candidate markers to guide later treatment research for this cancer.
pmc-13462153:
Hisashi Ishida and colleagues analyse stem cell transplant outcomes in Down syndrome-linked acute lymph blood cancer in a 2026 study. Down syndrome blood cancer fares worse than other blood cancer, yet transplant data were scarce. Country-wide Japanese data covered patients under 30 with B-cell early blood cancer receiving first donor transplant between 2000 and 2022, comparing 56 Down syndrome cases with 3,873 others.

Take and graft-versus-host disease rates matched between groups, but four-year event-free survival ran lower in Down syndrome cases, 40.3 versus 55.2 percent, narrowing when split by disease status. Return, not no-return death, drove failure, and strong prep trended better than gentler prep in early lull. Doctors gain guidance: patients unable to stand strong prep suit novel cures better than gentler transplant.
pmc-13462453:
Rami A Al-Horani and Amanuel F Tadesse review, in a 2026 article, how to keep artificial intelligence tools for clinical decisions under continuous check. Hospitals are weaving adaptive AI into care processes. Such tools promise sharp prediction, combined data, and real-time help. They also bring system-wide risks that audit methods built for fixed software cannot handle, since the tools keep learning and shifting.

 Audit scope is widening from the model alone to the ecosystem of workflow, staff-machine teamwork, and organizational learning. Explanation after the fact is giving way to tracing the tool's reasoning and sense-making with clinicians. Fixed compliance checks are yielding to monitoring for resilience, graceful failure, and safe change. The authors propose a framework joining technical strength, human-machine safeguards, adaptive governance, and transparency. They admit a stubborn gap between published frameworks and hospital practice.
pmc-13462653:
Li Li and co-authors ask, in a 2026 records study, whether low vitamin D before surgery raises the risk of delirium after anesthesia in children. Delirium after operations, a confused and agitated state, is common in children and slows recovery. The center reviewed 320 children who had keyhole surgery under general anesthesia, measuring their vitamin D form 25(OH)D3 before the operation.

Delirium was common, recorded in about eighty percent of children by a pediatric scale across the first week. Children who developed it had lower vitamin D levels. After adjustment, shortage before surgery stood as a risk factor with an odds ratio, though the estimate carried uncertainty. The link held when sleep quality after surgery was added to the model. Vitamin D alone sorted cases only modestly. The authors suggest screening before surgery to flag at-risk children, and call for trials of vitamin D top-ups.
pmc-13463053:
Franziska K Kaiser leads a 2026 animal study of how the clade Ia monkeypox virus spreads through genital contact, using prairie dogs as the model. Mpox has shifted from rare animal spillovers to sustained human spread, with sexual contact a suspected driver, yet transmission factors were poorly pinned down. Every route produced a full-body infection.

Genital routes gave the highest virus shedding and the most severe illness. In simulated sexual contact, every exposed sentinel animal caught the virus, a hundred percent transmission rate. Sentinels shed high virus amounts from day one, before any visible signs appeared. That early silent shedding helps explain how the virus moves efficiently between partners. The authors say the work backs the central role of anogenital mucosal infection in mpox spread. They urge that vaccines and countermeasures be judged by how well they block mucosal entry, not only by blood measures.
pmc-13463553:
Garrosa-Miró and colleagues built tree-shaped antibacterial molecules in 2026 by loading a biodegradable dendrimer scaffold, a branching polymer, with copper and zinc complexes. Drug-resistant bacteria demand agents that kill fast and last. The team tested the metal-bearing dendrimers for killing power, harm to human cells, speed of action, and whether bacteria could learn resistance.

The compounds stopped a broad range of bacteria at very low doses, with the strongest effect near the lowest tested levels. Keeping more than 70 percent of skin and connective cells alive and sparing red blood cells at killing doses. Second-generation versions wiped out one test species within a day and suppressed a harder species within four hours, beating a standard antibiotic there, with no resistance appearing. The authors present the scaffold as a flexible base for next-generation antibacterial treatments.
pmc-13463653:
Ssentongo and co-authors measured in 2026 how often adults living with HIV in Katakwi District, Uganda, interrupt their treatment. An interruption means missing care for at least 28 days after an expected visit or refill. The team surveyed patients at three antiretroviral therapy clinics. Statistical models built for clustered clinic data then found what predicts an interruption.

Interruption proved strikingly common. It affected about 68 of every 100 patients in care. Risk ran higher for adults aged 25 to 49. It ran higher for people lacking support from family and friends. Those in their first year on treatment were also at higher risk, as were patients whose virus was not suppressed. Living within five kilometers of the clinic lowered interruption rates. The authors urge stronger client-tracking systems and better coaching on staying in care.
pmc-13463853:
Elgin Akin and a large team trace a late-season surge of influenza B at Johns Hopkins hospitals in spring 2025. The surge strain, named C.3.1/re, mixed genes from two flu B lines and picked up a key surface change. That change restored a sugar shield over a spot that antibodies target.

The strain hit children more than adults, yet illness severity looked much the same as before. Blood from vaccinated people barely blocked the new strain in lab tests. Removing the sugar shield restored antibody blocking, which pins the escape on that one change. The mismatch also clouds vaccine strain choice for the next two seasons, the authors warn.
pmc-13464053:
Gaspare Saltarelli and six co-authors compare four store-bought AI tools that measure brain volumes from MRI scans. Clinics lean on such tools in workups for tremor and memory disease, yet each tool may draw its borders differently. All four tools read the same scans from forty-seven adults scanned for tremor review.

Every region showed tool-linked offsets, often twenty to forty percent apart. One tool gave the largest volumes across the board, while another gave the lowest. Agreement ran strongest for the fluid spaces beside the brain and weakest for the frontal lobe. A volume from one tool, the authors warn, cannot be swapped for a volume from another.
pmc-13464253:
Vivek Mehta and three co-authors report late clotting after surgery for a rare heart artery fistula. A fistula is an abnormal channel, here running from the left main artery to the right atrium. The patient, a sixty-year-old woman, also carried factor VII deficiency, a bleeding disorder that ruled out bold surgery.

Surgeons closed the channel exit with a patch and tied the channel mid-course, sparing deep dissection. The gentler repair left a bulge in the left main artery that later clotted and cut blood flow. A bolder first repair might have dodged that risk, the authors concede. The case frames a hard trade between bleeding safety now and durability later.
pmc-13464353:
Xu and colleagues profiled in 2026 which patients carry the dangerous pairing of high blood pressure with abnormal blood lipids. Records came from 5,018 hypertensive patients at 110 hospitals across China. Patients were split by whether their lipids also met the dyslipidemia definition. A model then weighed which traits independently traveled with the combined condition.

Patients with both conditions carried heavier burdens across the board. They had more strokes, chest-pain syndromes, and atrial fibrillation. They used more blood-pressure and anti-clotting medicines. Family history of hypertension, heart disease, and diabetes was also commoner. The final model singled out body mass index and family histories of hypertension and coronary disease as core correlates. Personal histories of stroke, angina, atrial fibrillation, and obstructive sleep apnea joined them. The authors frame these as screening flags for early intervention, pending confirmation in forward-looking studies.
pmc-13464953:
Yifan Wu and seven co-authors rank infant-gut Bifidobacterium strains by how well they stick and fight off rival germs. Sticking to the gut wall decides how long a probiotic stays and works. Twelve strains that feed on human milk sugars were tested against two known reference strains.

Two strains, BB_Y10 and BB_Y22, clumped fastest, shed water best, and clung hardest to gut cells and mucus. Surface coats, slime layers, and wall acids each lent a hand, in mixes that changed by strain. The top pair also beat germs in head-to-head, blocking, and push-out contests in dishes. Both earn a place as lead candidates for animal trials aimed at keeping harmful germs from settling in infant guts.
pmc-13465653:
Wang and co-authors reviewed 100 robot-assisted heart defect repairs in 2026 to ask whether body weight changes the outcome. The operation closes an atrial septal defect, a hole between the heart's upper chambers, using the Da Vinci system. Patients treated at one Qingdao hospital between 2014 and 2025 were split into four weight groups. The groups ran from nine underweight patients to thirteen with obesity, with 52 of normal weight.

The groups matched on heart scans before surgery. Operation length, bypass time, breathing support, and intensive care stay showed no significant differences across weights. No operation converted to open surgery, and nobody died early. Patients with obesity did show higher wound infection and readmission rates in simple comparisons, about 15 and 23 percent. Once other factors were counted, weight itself was not an independent predictor. The authors credit the minimally invasive approach, while noting the small subgroups limit certainty.
pmc-13466553:
Alper Tuna Güven and a large team study potassium safety when patients with diabetic kidney disease start the drug finerenone despite already high potassium, in a 2026 multicenter study. Trials usually exclude such patients, leaving real-world evidence thin. The group covered 166 adults across Turkish centers whose starting potassium sat at or above a raised threshold.

Within three months about one fifth reached a clearly high potassium level, and a small share rose higher still. Most needed no action; some started potassium-binding drugs, and only a small minority stopped finerenone. Models hunted for traits that predict trouble, giving prescribers a practical risk picture for a group trials left out.
pmc-13466853:
Yeojin Kim and Sung-Joon Lee review the three-way conversation between gut, brain, and skin, and how food ingredients might steer it toward healthier skin aging, in a 2026 article. Microbes in the gut release compounds that reach the brain through nerve, hormone, and immune routes. Brain signals in turn shape skin inflammation, barrier strength, and collagen renewal.

Three ingredient families recur across the studies: polyphenols from plants, live probiotic bacteria, and omega-3 fats. Each seems to work partly by reshaping gut communities and calming oxidative stress. Hormone circuits tied to stress, plus the balance of nerve messengers, provide the middle leg of the pathway. Early clinical findings are encouraging, though the authors present the field as young.
pmc-13466953:
Mercier-Guery and colleagues tested in 2026 whether blood levels of periostin, a protein that helps build and remodel bone, mark disease severity in osteogenesis imperfecta, the brittle bone disorder. Severity varies widely in this genetic condition and gene results predict it poorly. The team compared serum periostin in 61 adults with the disorder against 61 matched controls and related levels to clinical features.

Periostin ran significantly higher in patients than controls. Among patients, higher levels went with female sex, spinal curvature, and the severe type III form, and tracked with a measure of trunk distortion. In adjusted analysis, the count of severe fractures, breaks of major bones, independently tracked higher periostin, while smoking tracked lower levels. The authors report the first such finding in adults with the disorder and propose periostin as a candidate severity marker for clinic and research.
pmc-13467153:
Łukasz Boguszewicz and colleagues map how blood chemistry, nutrition, and body reserves move together in men treated for advanced head and neck cancer, in a 2026 preliminary analysis. Sixty-seven patients gave 536 serum samples, drawn weekly during radiation or combined chemoradiation. Magnetic resonance profiling read the small molecules in each sample.

Men who stayed disease-free for three years showed tighter links between blood fats, certain nutrients, and standard nutrition markers such as albumin. In men whose cancer returned, those internal connections broke apart, a pattern the authors call metabolic decoupling. The survival value of body fat, they argue, may lie in this coordination rather than in fat itself, a hopeful lead for supportive care.
pmc-13467253:
Xiaoyun Li and colleagues compute, from first principles, how molybdenum content steadies the high-temperature crystal form of titanium alloys, in a 2026 study. Four alloy strengths were modeled by embedding a small cluster inside a repeated crystal block. Energy comparisons between the two crystal forms showed stability rising steadily with more molybdenum.

The richest alloy favored the single body-centered form outright. One middling alloy showed a negative stiffness value on a key shear path, a sign of a lattice ready to soften, which eases certain deformation routes. The authors propose that stiffness measure as a simple descriptor linking phase stability to how the metal will bend and transform under load.
pmc-13467553:
Yang and colleagues review flexible neuromorphic memristors, devices that mimic brain synapses and can bend, in 2026 materials research. A memristor's conductance can be tuned and held, copying how synapses strengthen or weaken. Mounting that function on bendable materials opens wearable electronics and smart sensing skins. The review sorts the field by switching mechanism: conductive filaments, interface effects, ferroelectricity, and phase change, and by material family.

Natural and bio-derived materials, synthetic polymers, and inorganic films each get a section, plus device shapes from sandwich stacks to crossbar arrays and fiber textiles woven into cloth. Low-heat making methods that flexible bases can survive receive special attention. Uses span brain-like computing and medical wearables. Yang flags stability and device-to-device uniformity as the chief obstacles, pointing toward self-healing materials and combined sensing-storage systems.
pmc-13467653:
Yassin T. H. Mehdar and colleagues present in 2026 a sponge-like silica material designed to pull trace amounts of nickel and cadmium out of water. The team grafted a vanillin-derived chelator, a claw-like molecule that binds metals, onto fibrous mesoporous silica known as KCC-1, whose radial fibers keep its surface open and reachable.

Standard structural and surface analyses confirmed the chelator was attached as intended. The fibrous channels stay accessible even after the chemical modification, which should help metal ions reach the binding sites quickly. A sorbent that is both selective and regenerable would let treatment plants and labs concentrate toxic metals from large water volumes into a small, manageable residue. That concentration is the practical promise tested here.
pmc-13467753:
Qian You, Ying Li, Lin Lei and Hongtao Hu published this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, a cheap inflammation marker from blood counts. They asked whether it tracks cerebral small vessel disease, the vessel damage behind many strokes and much vascular dementia. Earlier studies disagreed. Searching three databases to August 2025, the authors pooled fifteen studies covering 62,961 people and examined the ratio against the disease's presence, burden and signs.

A higher ratio was associated with small vessel disease, with odds 1.43 times greater, and with greater burden, at 1.55. The signal concentrated in the ischemic signs: white matter hyperintensities and lacunes rose with the ratio, the lacune association being consistent. No association appeared with cerebral microbleeds, the hemorrhagic marker, and data on enlarged perivascular spaces were too thin to judge. The authors infer the ratio reflects ischemic rather than bleeding pathways, while calling for longitudinal proof.
pmc-13469153:
Chen and colleagues upgrade a popular object-detection model to spot tiny strawberry diseases and pests in greenhouses, in 2026 agricultural computer vision research. Early lesions are small, half-hidden by leaves, and lost against cluttered backgrounds. Their model, YOLOv8n-DSLW, adds dense feature-reuse blocks and shuffle attention to preserve faint lesion textures, plus a high-resolution detection layer for small targets. It also prunes redundant parts to stay fast enough for real-time farm monitoring.

On a self-collected greenhouse dataset, the model reached a mean average precision of 94.3 percent at the standard overlap threshold, and 77.5 percent across stricter thresholds, beating the plain YOLOv8n baseline. The finished network holds 4.386 million parameters and runs at 45 frames per second on the test workstation. Chen cautions that imaging equipment limits and dataset coverage mean field validation is still needed before growers rely on it.
pmc-13469453:
David Goldman and a team at a Bronx children's hospital report a survey study, published in 2026. It covers lasting health effects in children hospitalised during the COVID-19 pandemic. Families of 176 children took part. Infected and uninfected children were included. Admissions fell in the early variant waves or the Omicron wave. Families reported recovery times and lingering symptoms. Family stress and mental health outcomes were also reported.

About twenty-two percent of children hospitalised with COVID needed months to recover. Several months or more were typical for them. Roughly a third of the earliest wave group recovered slowly. Under ten percent of the Omicron group did. Some children reported symptoms lasting months. The authors compare this with other post-infectious syndromes.
pmc-13469653:
Kang Seo and colleagues examine in 2026 how social networking habits relate to loneliness among adults in Seoul, Korea. They drew on the 2024 Seoul Survey, which covered more than thirty four thousand adults with an average age near fifty two. Loneliness was judged from two questions about feeling cut off inside and outside the family. Five kinds of online behavior were tracked, from active posting to comparing oneself with others.

Any use of social networks came with slightly lower odds of loneliness than no use at all. Specific habits told the opposite story: active use, putting messaging first, social comparison, and feeling left out each raised the odds. Stacking three such habits tripled them. Links were strongest among adults over sixty and among confident digital users.
pmc-13470353:
Lisa Greer tracked at-risk corals in 2026 at Coral Gardens, Belize, after mass die-off in 2023. Staghorn and elkhorn corals have fallen over 90% across the Caribbean, and this long-term site was thought a refuge. A guided Random Tree sorter mapped live coral across 25 square km of space images from 2011 to 2023 against field data from 2012 to 2025.

Mapped live coral fell over 90% by 2023, matching total loss at the field site. June 2025 field checks found live or lately dead corals at 28 of 42 tipped sites, including live groups at 16 before-unmapped spots. Space sorting thus locates living corals for saving, while showing even lasting refugia can collapse.
pmc-13470953:
Alonso Martínez and co-authors adapted a six-question Sexual Risk Behaviour Scale for Spanish speakers in 2026 and checked it measures what it claims. The scale targets adolescents, young adults, and future health and education workers in training. Altogether, 478 students aged from 13 to 48 took part, recruited through schools and universities, and clinicians reviewed the wording. Statistical analyses tested structure, consistency, and links with six related sexuality measures.

The Spanish version held together well, its reliability score reaching an acceptable level for research use. Scores averaged about 10 on a scale from 6 to 24, and factor analysis confirmed all six items tap one dimension of risk. Scores patterned sensibly: they varied with age, gender, education, and dating app use. Risk scores also rose alongside heavy social media use, pornography use, and attitudes excusing sexual violence. The authors offer the scale as a validated tool for Spanish-language prevention research and practice.
pmc-13471453:
Chen and colleagues asked whether a torn shoulder tendon changes sleep itself, using a mouse model of rotator cuff injury with brain-wave monitoring. Their 2026 study recorded 24 hours of EEG and muscle signals in injured and sham-operated mice, scoring deep sleep, dream sleep, and wakefulness across light and dark phases.

Injured mice lost deep NREM sleep and spent more time awake, but only during the light phase, the rest period for mice, while total REM sleep barely changed. Their sleep also broke into more fragments, with more frequent switching between states and altered brain-wave power within each stage. The authors say the pattern mirrors the night pain complaints of human patients and points to sleep maintenance, not just sleep amount, as the casualty.
pmc-13471553:
Zhihe Chen triple-checked GLP-1 dock level effects in 2026 on heart-kidney-body-chem ills. Dock drugs help patients with high blood sugar or obesity, yet effects in non-obese, non-sugar-ill people were unclear. Mendel lottery with pancreas-only dock-level tools, gene-score scores, and watch-based reviews tested chronic kidney disease, heart failure, and body-chem liver disease.

In most people, dock levels lowered odds of all three ills, each near 0.96, with robust checks. Among non-sugar-ill and non-obese people, gene-score and watch-based reviews found little evidence of link. Trials should therefore test drugs in fairly healthy groups before stretching heart-kidney-body-chem claims beyond high blood sugar and obesity.
pmc-13471653:
Hou and co-authors asked whether a slightly tight inner side of an artificial knee, usually treated as an imperfection, might actually suit Chinese patients with bow-legged arthritis. Their 2026 retrospective study grouped 252 replaced knees by the post-operative gap difference between the medial and lateral sides, scoring outcomes at an average of 1.70 years.

Knees left medially tight by 1.0 to 1.5 millimeters improved more on total and functional scores than evenly balanced knees. The advantage was clearest in patients over 70 years old and survived adjustment for age, alignment, sex, and body mass index. A computer stress model, built by thinning the medial insert 1.25 millimeters, backed the clinical pattern. Context: 15 to 20% of knee replacement patients still report pain or tightness despite good alignment.
pmc-13473053:
Zhao and co-authors built a two-headed imaging probe that can latch onto either of two breast cancer markers, aiming to light up tumors that express only one of them. Their 2026 experimental study attached a HER2-binding piece and an RGD piece, which targets a vessel integrin, to a gallium-68 label for PET scanning. They tested it in three mouse tumor models.

The probe was synthesized and labeled at radiochemical purity above 95%. Cell uptake followed the receptor map: the double-high cell line took up the most probe, ahead of single-high and double-low lines. Because HER2-negative tumors make up 70 to 85% of breast cancers, a dual-target agent could rescue scans that single-target tracers miss. The authors say the probe semi-quantitatively reports receptor levels, a candidate for clinical translation.
pmc-13473453:
Huynh Huy Nguyen and Trong Nghia Le modelled in 2026 how uneven jet-grouted soil moves a deep excavation wall in a crowded city. Jet grouting stiffens ground at the base of a dig to limit wall bending, but designers usually treat treated soil as uniform, ignoring its natural patchiness. The team built a probabilistic model in which the soil's stiffness varied across space as a lognormal random field, based on laboratory tests giving a mean stiffness of about 1,337 megapascals.

Forty Monte Carlo simulations showed that spatial variation shifted both the size and spread of wall movement, with maximum displacement generally about 11 to 12 millimetres. For a limit near 11.4 millimetres, the chance of exceeding it fell from about 58 percent at low variation to about 35 percent at high variation. Vertical correlation mattered slightly more than horizontal. The lesson for engineers is that uniform-ground designs can understate the true range of wall movement.
pmc-13473553:
Mingzhi Jiang and five colleagues modelled in 2026 a heating system that pairs an air-source heat pump with a tank storing heat in phase-change material. Such systems can use cheap off-peak electricity and store energy efficiently, but in real industrial buildings many interacting factors shape heat demand, and single-factor models miss dynamics. The team collected operating data from a working system, then built a stacking ensemble called XMS, combining XGBoost and a multi-layer perceptron under a meta-learner.

Compared with a traditional perceptron model alone, the ensemble cut root mean square error by 22.5 percent and raised the coefficient of determination by 10.1 percent, capturing the system's nonlinear, coupled behaviour far better. The authors present the model as a reliable tool for forecasting heating load and tuning controls in heat-pump storage systems. Wider testing across climates and building types remains the next step.
pmc-13473653:
Jia-Xin Li and eleven colleagues introduced in 2026 a single sequencing method that maps two safety risks of gene-editing therapies. Tag polarity limits capture. AviTag-seq repurposes the hairpin ends of adeno-associated virus vectors, called inverted terminal repeats, as tags.

In mouse liver it outperformed a method at profiling Pcsk9 off-targets while mapping virus integration sites. Unlike laboratory results, virus vectors in living liver preferred active gene promoters, a risk for liver-directed therapies. The authors offer the platform as a regulatory-grade safety check.
pmc-13473853:
Tim Johnson and six colleagues published this 2026 systematic test of how consistently AI models answer preventive care questions in line with US Preventive Services Task Force recommendations. Model raters scored agreement against the official guidance.

Performance varied widely. The best model matched the Task Force in 66.9 percent of tests in wave one and 87.8 percent in wave two, while the weakest managed only about 45 and 50 percent. Most mismatches were not factual errors but equivocation: models hedged or pushed for more information even where the guidance was clear. Newer models did better, and chain-of-thought prompting improved consistency, while dropping the questions' hypothetical framing changed little. The authors conclude that model choice and prompting style shape the preventive advice the public receives.
pmc-13474353:
Sirilak Wangngae and four colleagues built in 2026 a metal-free polymer sensor that detects arginine in saliva, a marker tied to metabolic and kidney disorders. They made coumarin-tyrosine polymers whose shape governs how they recognise the target and glow, aiming at noninvasive testing without blood draws.

Binding shifted the absorption spectrum and changed fluorescence in two modes, with detection limits near 33 nanomolar in artificial saliva for both polymer forms. Tests confirmed a one-to-one interaction driven by hydrogen bonding, and saliva proved the best medium because other substances barely interfered. The platform offers a sensitive, needle-free route to tracking metabolic health.
pmc-13474753:
Vidona and co-authors tested whether organizing cadaver dissection as team-based learning beats the traditional watch-and-follow approach for anatomy students short on cadavers. Their 2026 quasi-experimental study at Ambrose Alli University in Nigeria assigned 155 second-year students to team-based dissection (78 students) or traditional learning (77), then compared examination scores and student perceptions.

The team group won clearly on paper: mean examination scores of 84.6 against 74.2 for traditional learners, a gap significant with a t statistic of 8.12 across the groups. Self-reports aligned: enhanced collaboration was reported by 88% of team students versus 52% of controls. Motivation came in at 90% versus 60%, and better use of the scarce cadaver material by 85% versus 38% across the comparison. The authors caution that without randomization, causality stays unproven.
pmc-13474853:
Comini and co-authors reviewed treatment results in 2026 for vagal paragangliomas, rare nerve-related tumors of the neck that usually grow slowly but can invade nearby tissue. Care is contested, since removing the tumor often damages the vagus nerve it grows on, while watching it risks unchecked growth. The team gathered every usable published series to compare surgery, radiotherapy, combined care, and observation.

Across 41 articles covering 501 patients, 325 had surgery, 101 had radiotherapy, 9 had both, and 66 were simply observed over time. Surgery removed tumors reliably but almost always injured the vagus nerve, causing voice and swallowing problems, and impairment of at least one more nerve rose 2.6-fold after operations in the data. Radiation methods controlled tumors well with milder side effects, and the authors stress that the evidence base stays weak and low in quality.
pmc-13474953:
Farzi and co-authors interviewed nurses at an Iranian surgical and trauma center in 2026 about working alongside a specialist wound care nurse. General nurses often report thin training and support for wound care, a daily part of their work. The team spoke in depth with 10 people, including staff nurses, head nurses, the specialist herself, and a nursing instructor, with interviews averaging 35 minutes during 2024 and 2025.

Four main categories organized the accounts, covering specialist care itself, continuity of care, nurse empowerment, and challenges needing improvement. Nurses said the specialist sped healing, cut complications, and made decisions more evidence-based, while also teaching colleagues through hands-on coaching across the wards. Barriers were practical rather than clinical, since staff shortages, an undefined formal post for the role, and patchy management backing all limited what the specialist could achieve.
pmc-13478153:

Apps are cheap and always at hand, but whether their benefit lasts was unclear. The team searched for controlled trials, then used multilevel models with bias corrections to estimate weight change at six months and beyond.

The search found 23 qualifying studies, and app users lost more weight than people on waiting lists by a mean difference of 2.07 kilograms at six months. Against other non-app programs the advantage was 1.64 kilograms at the same point in the trials pooled here. Weight loss inside app groups ranged from 0.63 to 3.87 kilograms at six months and averaged 2.64 kilograms at longer follow-ups, while features like calorie counting or social support did not change the effect.
pmc-13479253:
Womack-Martenson and colleagues survey in 2026 how often recovering newborns are moved from intensive care back to lower-level nurseries, a practice called back-transport, and what blocks it. Such moves free intensive care beds for the sickest infants.

The team analyzed a spring 2025 national survey of United States health professionals, keeping 256 pediatricians and nurse practitioners who care only for children. Just one in five said back-transport often happens when it is medically appropriate. The largest group said it happens only occasionally, and nearly a quarter said rarely or never. The barriers named most often were payment and reimbursement problems, parent preference, and missing transfer agreements between hospitals. A quarter of providers were unsure what the barriers even were, which the authors read as a gap in awareness.
pmc-13479453:
Bander M. Almohayya and Khalid N. Alasim published a 2026 validation of the Arabic version of the fifteen-item Quality-of-Life Scale among teachers. The sample held 401 teachers in Saudi Arabia, split between 235 general education and 166 special education staff. Sound Arabic measurement tools are needed before wellbeing research can guide school policy.

Reliability was excellent, with internal consistency coefficients above 0.9. Scores correlated strongly with an established World Health Organization quality of life measure and moderately in the opposite direction with a health and suffering scale. Confirmatory analysis showed acceptable fit, supporting the translation for use with Arab teaching staff.
pmc-13480253:
Yin Wu and co-authors describe a 2026 method for spotting plant food shortages in greenhouse chrysanthemums by leaf light patterns. Growers often face mixed shortages that look alike to the eye. The team grew four flower types under single and paired element shortages across five growth stages and three trials, building 615 data points confirmed by classic shortage signs.

Light scans split shortages apart even where leaf looks matched. After balancing the dataset with a synthetic sampling trick, a boosted tree model gave the steadiest results, with test accuracy in the mid-eighties to low nineties across tasks. Scanning leaves harms nothing, so staff could check whole houses fast. The authors note that new flower types, seasons, and houses still need testing before the tool can claim wide use.
pmc-13480853:
Ba and Song asked in 2026 whether a cheap blood test, lactate, can warn which grave stroke patients will die within a year. Lactate is a waste product that climbs when tissue lacks air or the body is in deep stress. The team drew on a big intensive care data bank from the United States. They took the first lactate read of each stay for adults with acute ischemic stroke, a blocked vessel stroke, and tracked deaths for a full year.

Of the two thousand patients who fit, fewer than half had a lactate read at all, and that group was more ill. A third of the tested group died in the year. Each step up in lactate came with a step up in death risk, and the top quarter by lactate died at twice the low group's rate. The authors call lactate a side gauge, not a lone seer.
pmc-13481953:
Nitin Kumar Singh and co-authors present a 2026 computer study of genes that shield pancreatic cancer from an iron-driven death called ferroptosis. The team gathered 196 shield genes from a curated database and scanned alterations across 21 pancreatic cancer studies holding 5,189 samples. Seven genes changed in at least three percent of samples, with alteration patterns that mostly teamed up rather than clashed.

Patients whose tumours carried shield gene changes died sooner overall, with four genes showing the sharpest harm. No like pattern appeared in gullet or stomach cancers, which marks the link as pancreas-specific. The wider shield set fed into energy sensing, self-eating, low-oxygen response, and growth pathways. Shield genes may serve as warning markers and as targets for drugs that force the iron death route.
pmc-13482153:
Pang and colleagues set benchmark scores in 2026 for the Chinese Reading Acuity Test in Cantonese-speaking Hong Kong primary school children, giving clinicians a yardstick for spotting reading trouble. The test adapts a standard reading chart to traditional Chinese characters, with 17 sentences per chart shrinking across a wide size range. They recruited 188 children from grades 1 to 6 with no developmental delays or known reading difficulties.

Children read aloud as fast as they could at 40 centimeters until the print grew too small, yielding scores for top speed, the smallest print read at that speed, and reading acuity. Top reading speed rose steeply with age and grade, correlating at 0.72, while acuity improved too, shown by its correlation of minus 0.47 with age and grade level. Near vision scores also tracked all three reading measures, and the authors publish grade-by-grade norms for clinics and schools to use.
pmc-13483053:
İlker Demir and others compare three physiotherapy approaches for people whose low back pain has lasted at least twelve weeks. In 2026, the trial assigns patients at random to standard conservative care alone, conservative care plus elastic kinesiology taping, or conservative care plus blood-starved compression, a method that presses tender muscle points. Pain and spinal movement are measured before treatment and after three weeks.

All three groups improved in pain during movement, at rest, and at night, and in forward and backward bending. Taping added no clear advantage over conservative care alone in the between-group comparison. Blood-starved compression, by contrast, produced larger gains on nearly every measure except sideways bending. Doctors and patients weighing added therapies get a direct, head-to-head comparison rather than separate claims for each method.
pmc-13483153:
Haoteng Chen and co-authors report a 2026 imaging study of a dreaded arm weakness after front-of-neck spine surgery. The C5 nerve root palsy strikes one to five percent of patients after decompression and fusion. The team reviewed one hundred patients operated on between 2019 and 2023 for worn neck discs squeezing the cord, all with scans before and soon after surgery read blind by two radiologists.

Ten patients developed the palsy. Their cords had drifted backward at one key level by a far wider margin than in unaffected patients. After other factors were weighed, each extra stretch of drift raised palsy odds near threefold, and a cut-off near three millimetres sorted cases with fair accuracy. Ten events make for shaky maths, and one centre's records limit reach, so the cut-off needs outside testing before guiding care.
pmc-13483653:
Kanana Naghizade heads a large 2026 multicenter study of anemia in kidney filter diseases, with special attention to IgA nephropathy. Data come from a national Turkish registry covering 5,500 patients with biopsy-proven primary glomerular disease, including 1,571 cases of IgA nephropathy. Anemia was defined by World Health Organization cutoffs and linked to clinical, laboratory, and tissue findings.

Anemia affected roughly 35 percent of patients in both the full group and the IgA subgroup. Patients with the lowest hemoglobin were older and showed worse kidney function, lower protein levels, and higher inflammation markers. Tissue scarring in the kidney's support spaces was especially common in that group. Older age, female sex, and reduced kidney function independently predicted anemia, which the authors say deserves routine attention.
pmc-13483853:
Anna Marcinkiewicz and co-workers ask if a blood level checked before heart bypass surgery can warn of kidney harm after it. Their 2026 study follows 66 patients who had planned bypass surgery with a heart-lung machine. The group holds 27 patients with type 2 diabetes and 39 without it. The blood mark is homocysteine, an amino acid tied to vessel harm.

Starting levels were near the same in patients with and without diabetes. In the whole group, high levels went with high blood fats and high signs of body-wide swelling. High levels went with low levels of the good form of blood fat. Full kidney results sit past the part of the text in hand here. Even so, the early links show why a cheap blood test draws such strong interest.
pmc-13488153:
Zhou and colleagues assembled an evidence summary in 2026 on making urodynamic studies, bladder pressure tests that can be uncomfortable and embarrassing, easier for adult patients. Nurses lacked a single consolidated guide to comfort strategies. Following the Fudan University evidence-based nursing framework, the team searched guidelines, databases, and trial literature up to the end of 2025 and graded what they found.

From 968 records, twenty-one articles met their criteria, including two systematic reviews, one expert consensus, fifteen randomized trials, and three qualitative studies. They distilled eighteen evidence items across four domains: communication and information support, environmental and sensory modulation, local and pharmacological interventions, and privacy and dignity preservation. Eleven items were rated at the highest evidence level. The authors present the summary as a foundation for standardized, personalized comfort care during these tests.
pmc-13491053:
Tørring and colleagues described in 2026 the daily movement patterns of children with cerebral palsy compared with typically developing peers. Twenty-three ambulatory children with cerebral palsy and twenty-three peers wore two movement sensors for seven days. A validated model classified walking, running, cycling, jumping, standing, sitting, and lying from the sensor data.

Both groups built up about five hours of daily activity, mostly standing for roughly two hundred minutes and walking for about one hundred. Children with cerebral palsy were on average ten to seventeen minutes less active per day. They also made about fifteen percent fewer switches between activity and rest, though differences were not statistically significant. The authors say pattern detail, not just totals, should guide activity advice for children with cerebral palsy.
pmc-13491853:
Masahiro Asami leads a thirteen-author team piloting in 2026 a simplified brain-wave monitor that nurses can run for patients with severe head injury. Silent seizures are common after such injuries but hard to catch without specialist continuous monitoring, which many intensive care units cannot staff. The patch device uses three preset channels and goes on quickly at the bedside.

Monitoring succeeded in twenty-one of twenty-four enrolled patients, and sixteen also had a special MRI scan that maps blood flow without contrast dye. Electrical seizures appeared in a quarter of those fully assessed patients, and every one matched a bright patch of increased blood flow on imaging. The authors call the approach feasible and ask for larger studies on whether it changes care.
pmc-13493853:
Alfred Lok-Hang Lee and others revisit the line between extra-strong and standard Klebsiella pneumoniae using genes and disease patterns. In 2026, the study reads 273 germ samples from deep ills at three Hong Kong care sites between 2019 and 2023, calling gene-based extra strength by five markers. It compares looks, drug weakness, and results.

Gene-based extra-strong strains made up about twenty-one percent of germ samples, were more drug-weak, and were not linked to higher death, harm, or spread illness. Nearly half of liver abscess cases were standard strains, and the gene-based test caught liver abscess or spread illness with only forty-six percent hit rate. Genome work names three extra possible genes, showing large overlap between groups.
pmc-13493953:
Kala and colleagues tackle a surgical problem in epilepsy. Removing the patch of malformed cortex that triggers seizures, called focal cortical dysplasia, works only if surgeons find its true edges, and ordinary MRI often shows less than the full extent. Their 2026 study covered 19 patients whose dysplasia was confirmed under the microscope after surgery. The team combined fourteen measures from diffusion MRI, which tracks how water moves through tissue, into one combined score.

The combined score separated diseased from healthy tissue better than any single measure did, with the improvement reaching statistical significance. It also flagged abnormal tissue beyond the borders visible on standard scans. Its map matched metabolic scan cold spots and electrical seizure activity in nine of ten patients. Using the score to plan surgery increased agreement with the tissue actually removed and left less suspicious tissue behind.
pmc-13494553:
Wenxuan Zhao, Kayvan Samimi, Melissa C Skala, and Rupsa Datta present FLIM Playground in a 2026 article, a free interactive program for studying single cells with fluorescence lifetime imaging. That imaging method times how long a dye glows after a flash, which reveals the cell's chemical setting. Turning raw timing data into findings once took many split steps across unlike tools, a burden for new and seasoned users alike.

The program joins the whole workflow in one screen. It checks image details, pulls lifetime values for each cell region, adds shape and texture measures, merges data sets, and shows live charts for hands-on study. The team checked its lifetime math against trade software and past results, then showed the full flow on a cancer cell line data set. They built it to spread shared good practice and to grow toward new imaging types over time.
pmc-13495153:
Yuxiao Wu and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, an MRI model to predict where a glioblastoma has crept into the swollen tissue around it. Glioblastoma is a fast, invasive brain cancer, and the swelling, called peritumoral edema, often hides stray tumor cells that standard scans cannot show. Knowing where they hide would help aim radiation after surgery.

The team mined texture measures from three scan types in training cases of glioblastoma and brain metastasis, then built rival models with three machine learning methods. A random forest model using measures from contrast and diffusion scans within set belts around the tumor sorted the cases best. A check group with other tumor types confirmed the skill, and in ten extra cases the model's calls matched biopsy truth at most sampled points. The authors offer the model as a practical aid for radiation planning.
pmc-13495253:
Chenyang Li and a team ask, in a 2026 registry study from China, whether steady use of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors helps patients with a leaking mitral valve. These inhibitors are a class of heart drugs. The leak, called mitral regurgitation, worsens outcomes, and the drugs' place in its care was unsettled. Patients were classed as always, never, or sometimes users across follow-up. Steady users died least over two years in cause groups, while never and sometimes users faced several-fold higher death risk. Steady use went with the leak easing, above all in the heart-born group and in those not bound for valve repair. Matched analyses agreed. The authors say the drugs may earn a place in tuned medical care, while calling for trials to prove cause.
pmc-13498653:
Constanza Vargas and others ask Australian adults what they value in assessment pathways for funding rare disease drugs. In 2026, the discrete choice experiment gives 1,099 respondents eight choices each as hypothetical government advisors, trading attributes such as evidence completeness, stakeholder input, and waiting time. Different countries use different pathways, creating inequities in access.

Latent class analysis found three groups, including a majority with no strong preferences. Policymakers gain guidance for designing pathways the public sees as legitimate, even at the cost of delay.
pmc-13499853:

The two technologies differ in cost, storage, and side-effect profiles. Their 2026 matched study paired about sixty-nine thousand mRNA recipients with half as many protein-vaccine recipients, balancing age and health factors, then followed both groups for up to six months.

Medically attended COVID-19 occurred in just over one percent of the mRNA group, with the protein group faring worse on both infections needing care and hospitalisations in the adjusted comparison. The authors conclude the mRNA vaccine was more effective over the season in this insured population. They add an honest caveat: the two products also targeted slightly different variant mixes, so the study cannot separate the platform's strength from the strain choice.
pmc-13500853:
Fatemeh Shakeri leads a five-author team with a 2026 double-blind randomized trial of a high-power sperm selection method for couples facing severe teratozoospermia, a condition where most sperm are abnormally shaped. The team also measured sperm DNA fragmentation and relative telomere length in raw, processed, and selected sperm.

Fertilization rates were 67.46 percent for ICSI and 63.67 percent for IMSI, and live birth rates were 30.23 percent against 15.55 percent, a gap short of proof. Chemical, clinical, and ongoing pregnancy rates likewise overlapped, as did miscarriage rates. DNA fragmentation and telomere length in the selected sperm also matched, so the trial found no confirmed advantage for the high-power technique.
pmc-13501653:

Low-risk patients lived longer, on progression-free and overall survival, than the high-risk group across training and test splits. Risk groups differed in immune cell makeup and tumour mutation burden. A sensitivity algorithm predicted the high-risk group would respond differently to immunotherapy and drugs. qPCR checks verified the expression patterns. The authors offer the six-RNA signature as a grouping tool.
pmc-13501853:

Fifteen in vitro studies covering 1,015 teeth qualified, and bias was checked with the QUIN tool; eleven studies rated low risk and four moderate.

Success depended on the adhesive family, the timing of the contamination, and the exact cleaning protocol, so the authors advise prevention first.
pmc-13502853:

The genetic analysis supported links between twenty-one gut microbial groups, thirty-one immune cell traits, and coronary events, and the results held up under sensitivity checks. Mediation analysis suggested part of the microbes' effect on the heart may travel through immune cells, which sit between gut and artery in the pathway. The authors present the immune traits as targets needing confirmation.
pmc-13503453:

Aortic release fell sharply after vessel lining removal or blocking NOX1/4 enzymes, but not after nitric oxide synthase or sodium channel blockade. The compound itself did not contract vessels, yet potentiated alert signal and alarm signal contractions, and relaxed endothelin-contracted rings through nitric oxide and soluble guanylyl cyclase pathways. It emerges as a dual tuner of vessel tone.
pmc-13504053:

The team trained YOLOv5 and YOLOv8 on 2,620 digitized film scans from a public database, covering healthy, benign, and cancer cases with proven diagnoses. The paper weighs speed and accuracy for clinic use, where catching cancer early saves lives. Older segmentation tools are reviewed and set aside for their heavy compute needs and long training times. The authors aim to name the better fit for real screening work.
pmc-13505153:
Valentina Tsartsianidou and co-authors mapped the genetics of Greek local sheep and set them beside breeds from Asia and Europe. Analyses separated Greek breeds clearly from one another while showing mixed European and Asian ancestry. Mainland Greek sheep sat closest to Italian Zackel-type sheep, and the wider pattern ran east to west across the Mediterranean. Greek sheep showed the most signs of recent mixing among regional groups, and some breeds carried higher inbreeding tied to long selection or conservation breeding. The authors offer the results to national conservation work aimed at stopping genetic loss in local flocks.
pmc-13505753:

The tin and copper pair worked together to grip a key intermediate, called *OCHO, at two points at once. That two-point binding steered the reaction step toward methanol along a six-electron pathway, while suppressing the rival *COOH intermediate that leads away from methanol. Potassium ions in the water aided carbon dioxide activation in the simulations. The authors distil a design rule: enforce joint two-point binding to lock in the methanol route. They present it as guidance for building selective real catalysts.
pmc-13507153:

Routine tumor profiling could host this guide.
pmc-13507253:

A unified, process-aware architecture could simplify forecasting centers that now maintain many single-purpose models. Flood warning and reservoir planning both depend on exactly these paired predictions.
pmc-13508353:

pmc-13508453:

Lab tests fed the parcels to insulin cells and measured sugar-driven insulin release and cell death. A census of the RNA messages inside singled out one that rose sharply in diabetes.

pmc-13508553:

The team compared the fairer competing-risk count with the classic estimate, and hunted predictors with matching models.

The fair count put transformation at about forty-seven percent by one year and about seventy-four percent by three years. Classic math overshot each figure by roughly five to six percent in relative terms. pmc-13508653:

The audit found leaflets at only about a quarter of trusts, reading at a level for fourteen to fifteen year olds, and few in other languages. None was fully inclusive. The team built a plainer, more inclusive leaflet with language model help, reaching a reading age near twelve to thirteen.
pmc-13512753:
Jinglan Liu introduces a special issue on clinical cytogenetics and cytogenomics, the study of chromosomes in diagnosis and precision therapy, in 2026 work. Methods have climbed from banded karyotypes through targeted probes, microarrays, and optical mapping to long-read sequencing, each step sharpening sight.

Nine manuscripts in the first edition span that range. The editor notes that copying the landmark success of a targeted leukemia drug has proved hard, because tumors shift, split into clones, and rewire. Most cancers blend large structural change with sequence change, so care has to weigh both layers at once. pmc-13512853:
Dongqing Cao, Yiting Hao, and Wenhao Gui study why green transition policies in Chinese provinces may fail to cut local carbon output, using panel data from 2012 to 2021, in 2026 work. Richer neighbors raised local carbon intensity, with the effect growing stronger across the range. Green-focused forces showed the best cut potential, while digital infrastructure produced rebound. The authors recommend cross-region carbon compensation and longer judging windows for technology shifts.
pmc-13514553:

Standard photographs at one week and three months were measured with image software.

Starting symmetry was similar in both groups. By three months, the retainer group's overall nostril area symmetry had improved significantly more than the control group's. Height and width measures, taken separately, showed no clear difference between groups. Yaşar's team suggests the device helps most where it counts visually, in the whole opening rather than single dimensions.
pmc-13517553:

Well-known hubs included RAF1 and two partners, and known tagging sites on viral proteins matched several candidate kinases. Docking suggested stable fits with the viral polymerase, helicase, and a secreted protein. The authors offer the network as a starting map for host-directed antiviral drug research.
pmc-13518853:
Tomoki Yoshikawa leads a twelve-author team reporting long-term results in 2026 after endoscopic removal of two related stomach growths, fundic gland type adenocarcinoma and oxyntic gland adenoma. These recently recognized tumors arise from acid-making stomach lining, and their behavior years after treatment was poorly defined. The multicenter review covered 72 patients.

Mean follow-up reached 68 months, with no deaths from the disease and no local recurrences among patients checked by scope. New lesions appeared at separate stomach sites in 3 patients, about 4.5 percent, and each was removed endoscopically. Yoshikawa and colleagues call the tumors slow-moving yet urge long surveillance because fresh growths can emerge elsewhere in the lining.
pmc-13518953:
De-Zhi Jin and five colleagues ask in 2026 how the brain's stable network hierarchy emerges from moment-to-moment fluctuations in activity. Brain regions rise and fall together in fMRI signals, and networks arrange along an axis from sensory and motor areas to association areas. Earlier dynamic studies mostly examined only the loudest fluctuations.

Sorting co-fluctuations by strength uncovered a layered pattern aligned with that axis. Strong fluctuations favored sensorimotor networks, mid-strength ones favored association systems, and quiet states engaged the limbic system. The layering sharpened from childhood to adulthood and reshaped itself during movie watching. Replicated across four datasets, the pattern suggests the hierarchy is actively maintained by an amplitude-ordered cascade.
pmc-13520353:
Teng Long and colleagues propose in 2026 a new computer method for inferring cause-and-effect links between long non-coding RNAs and their target genes. Learning such networks as directed graphs without cycles is hard when links are curved or data are discrete.

Their system blends neural networks, attention weighting and reinforcement learning inside a generative model that proposes graph structures. Tests on artificial data and on Alzheimer disease data showed better recovery of true structures than older methods, especially with complex patterns. The authors position the approach as a general tool for causal discovery, with gene regulation as the driving application.
pmc-13521953:
B Sendhil Nathan and colleagues propose in 2026 a feature-building method called SHOS for forecasting spare-parts demand that arrives in rare, irregular bursts. Standard models drown in zeros, while fancy architectures often ignore careful input design.

Demand is split into chance of an order occurring and expected size when one occurs, smoothed with sparsity-aware weighting to preserve real events. Testing used about 56,000 dealer-part series from automotive aftermarket data with rolling checks. Tree models fed with the new features beat raw-feature versions on accuracy and stability across varied demand segments. Signal preservation analyses support the design choice.
pmc-13522353:
Chenconghai Yang and colleagues map in 2026 soil carbon stocks in tidal wetlands world-wide across two time spans, 2009 to 2014 and 2015 to 2020. Data held over 42,000 records and dozens of predictors. Mangroves, salt marshes and tidal flats hold major blue carbon stores.

Total stock fell by about six percent between spans. Deep layers lost the most carbon. Low-latitude zones formed loss hotspots, led by South Asia and Africa. Mangroves lost most through falling carbon density. Salt marshes gained in both area and density. Drivers split by wetland type. Climate and height drove mangrove shifts, while ocean factors ruled flats.
pmc-13523153:
Hirohiko Aikawa and co-authors use a specialized heart scan to guide diagnosis after cardiac arrest in a 2026 case report. A fifty-one-year-old man developed chest pain during exercise, then a dangerous rhythm that caused an out-of-hospital arrest. Emergency artery imaging after resuscitation showed no major narrowing, leaving the cause uncertain and the value of invasive spasm testing unclear.

A BMIPP scan, which captures a lingering metabolic trace of recent reduced blood flow, showed reduced uptake across several heart regions. Provocation testing then triggered near-blockage of a major artery, confirming exercise-induced artery spasm as the cause. Heart magnetic resonance imaging found no muscle disease or clot. The authors propose the scan as a noninvasive guide for deciding on invasive spasm testing in arrest survivors.
pmc-13523253:
Mary Beth McCullough and Gail N Kemp evaluate a training program in psychological therapy for chronic pain in a 2026 study. Chronic pain affects about one fifth of United States adults, and trained providers of cognitive behavioral therapy for pain are scarce. Sixteen clinical psychology doctoral students completed a competence scale before and after a structured pain management training program.

The scale proved internally consistent across its parts. After training, students reported significantly higher knowledge and experience in delivering the therapy, with very large effect sizes. Their beliefs about how effective the therapy is did not change, which the authors attribute to attitudes being slower to move or to limits of that subscale. The program is presented as evidence that structured interdisciplinary training can expand the pain treatment workforce.
pmc-13523353:
Anteneh D Teklemariam leads a team reviewing outcomes of bacterial meningitis in children at a hospital in Hawassa, Ethiopia, in a 2026 retrospective study. Charts covered two hundred three children aged one month to fourteen years treated over five years, from 2020 to 2024. Outcomes were classed as good or poor, with death, acute nerve complications, and discharge against advice counted as poor.

One third of the children had a poor outcome, including about one in seven who died. Five factors clearly raised the odds: male sex, malnutrition, missed vaccine shots, aspiration pneumonia during illness, and coma on arrival. Malnutrition carried the largest effect. The authors recommend stronger nutrition programs and vaccine coverage to cut death and disability from childhood meningitis in the setting.
pmc-13523753:
Chu and Lin used computer simulations to ask how the connectivity of pores inside metal-organic frameworks changes their ability to harvest water from air. These frameworks are sponge-like crystals built from metal nodes and organic links. Their 2026 study compares frameworks with connected cages against ones with separate channels, and also blocks pores deliberately to vary connectivity without changing the local chemistry that attracts water.

Chu ran advanced Monte Carlo simulations, a random-sampling computational method. Chu found that better-connected pores fill cooperatively at lower humidity, because water inside them forms more complete hydrogen-bond networks and a more stable condensed phase. Even fully separate channels showed weak long-range electrical coupling between neighboring pores that shifted uptake. Tests with nonpolar gases confirmed the effect is special to strongly bonding molecules like water, giving designers a new structural lever for air-water harvesters.
pmc-13524853:
Guo, Liu, and Ding reply in 2026 to commentators on their earlier article about a grey-zone decision in knee surgery. A patient's worn knee can qualify for both a partial replacement, called unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, and a bone-reshaping operation, high tibial osteotomy, that preserves the joint. Commentators urged more weight on mechanical factors and on patient-centred thinking. The authors accept the thrust of both points while clarifying their framework.

Their central distinction separates general outcome factors, which predict outcomes after either operation, from factors that on their own steer the choice between operations. Only the second kind belongs in selection criteria, they argue. Traditional checklists no longer deliver personal decisions, so they propose expanding the evaluation dimensions and eventually weighting the factors into a formal scoring system for grey-zone patients.
pmc-13524953:
Wang Hongyue, Wang Bida, and Li Xuerong measure resilience from 2008 to 2022 across 286 Chinese prefecture-level cities. Their 2026 study spans years of financial shocks, a pandemic, and natural disasters. Their scoring combined a weighting method with a ranking method, and spatial models traced how resilience differed by place and what drove it.

Resilience rose overall, with a clear ladder that favored large cities while small cities lagged. Resistance led the subdimensions, followed by recovery and innovation, although new ideas grew fastest. Eastern and central cities formed gradients, while western and northeast cities split apart. Digital tools, medical care, and transport helped more strongly toward the west, city growth helped most in the east and center, and factory growth held cities back, notably in resource-dependent cities.
pmc-13526053:
Loewenstein and colleagues look below the cortex for the signature of dementia with Lewy bodies, a disease whose scan diagnosis leans on a few regions. Many of its symptoms, from parkinsonism to hallucinations, point at deep brain structures, yet glucose PET studies rarely map them. Their 2026 analysis pooled 76 patients from a regional database and the international ADNI collection. It compared their brain metabolism against 19 people with normal scans using statistical mapping software.

Alongside the known cortical cold spots, which validated the method, deep structures ran hot: the dentate nucleus in the cerebellum, part of the thalamus, and a brainstem relay all showed increased metabolism. The pattern intensified with disease stage. The midbrain's visual tectum also lit up. The authors single out the dentate-to-thalamus pathway as a structure of interest that might explain motor and cognitive features.
pmc-13526753:
Xiaoxin Wang and colleagues study, in a 2026 mouse investigation, why lipid handling fails after spinal cord injury and whether a drug can restart cholesterol clearance. Injury releases masses of myelin lipid, turning macrophages into foam cells that sustain inflammation and block repair. Reverse cholesterol transport normally ships such lipid out, yet its behavior at the lesion was unclear.

In a mid-back contusion model, two transport components rose persistently, but one sat mainly in astrocytes rather than macrophages. A third component, ABCG1, fell at protein level despite rising message, a bottleneck favoring foam cells. An LXR-activating drug raised the first component, partly restored the third, cut foam-cell accumulation, lowered an inflammatory signal, and improved movement scores. Full restoration eluded the drug, pointing to protein instability as the next target.
pmc-13527053:
Bar Eilat Yogev and colleagues test, in a 2026 rat study, whether drinking alcohol shortly before a traumatic event worsens later post-traumatic stress symptoms, and whether early ketamine can reverse that effect. Alcohol use before trauma is common yet understudied as a risk factor. Rats received ethanol or saline before a predator scent stress exposure.

Timing mattered. Ethanol given four hours before stress, but not thirty minutes before, raised the share of rats showing a PTSD-like pattern a week later and deepened shrinkage of dendrites in a hippocampal region. Combined exposure lowered two protective molecules, raised a channel protein, and erased a neuropeptide receptor signal. A single early nasal dose of ketamine in lipid vesicles after stress reduced fear freezing and dendritic loss, giving a more resilient profile.
pmc-13527953:
Rui Li and eleven colleagues report a 2026 proteomic study of ovaries from Jining Grey goats, a Chinese breed valued for meat, skin, and high fertility. The team compared ovarian tissue from four goats that bear single kids with four that bear multiples, measuring thousands of proteins with a labeling technique called iTRAQ.

They found 468 proteins differing between the groups, with 255 more abundant in one group and 213 in the other. The differing proteins clustered around cell structure, calcium binding, and pathways involving oxytocin signaling and fat metabolism. Five proteins, including CAV1 and FLNA, stood out as hub candidates, and follow-up blotting matched the main measurements. The results offer leads for breeding more fertile goats.
pmc-13528153:
Emina Masuda and five colleagues map home-visit dental care across Japan's prefectures in a 2026 study. Aging has raised demand for dentists who treat people at home. Use varies widely by region. The team used national claims data for one year to March 2023. They built a standardized use ratio for each prefecture. Workforce traits were then compared against it.

Use ratios ranged from about twenty-five to about one hundred sixty-nine. The median sat near seventy-one. Regions with older dentists used home dental care less. Regions with more clinics and more hospital-based dentists used it more. Adjusted models kept the dentist age and clinic count effects. The authors caution these are region-level links, not proof about single dentists. A younger, denser workforce seems to travel with better home care reach.
pmc-13530253:
Huiliang Xue and colleagues track seasonal breeding shutdown in striped hamsters during 2026 field and lab work. Thirty-two females, eight per season, supplied ovary tissue, blood, and droppings for hormone measurement. Winter brings short days and cold that pause reproduction in many small mammals, and one gene switch drew focus.

Early-stage follicle counts peaked in winter while later stages bottomed out, and the switch gene NR5A2 fell to its yearly low. All five measured reproductive hormones also sank in winter. Gene and hormone levels tracked follicle stage closely, linking the switch to stalled egg development.
pmc-13530453:
Docters and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 64, a systematic review of pie-crusting the medial collateral ligament.
