Pie-crusting is a series of small needle punctures that loosens the knee's inner ligament so surgeons can see and work inside a tight joint during arthroscopy. The open question was safety.

Sixteen studies covering 775 knees met the criteria. The technique widened the medial joint space by roughly three to eight millimeters during surgery, a gain that faded on X-rays over the following year. Only ten of 264 tested patients kept residual looseness under stress testing. Functional scores improved substantially, and complications were rare. There were no cartilage injuries caused by the maneuver and five saphenous nerve injuries, while soreness at the puncture site was frequent but short-lived, usually resolving within two weeks.
pmc-13530753:
Buza and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 125, a study of how much bone surgeons should shave during hip arthroscopy. The patients studied have hip sockets that are borderline shallow, a condition called borderline dysplasia. Removing too little leaves the painful bump; too much may destabilize the joint.

The study tracked 101 patients, 107 hips, aged 14 to 50 who had the reshaping procedure, femoroplasty. Average resection depth was about seven percent of the femoral head's diameter. Deeper resection predicted worse improvement on a standard hip score at one year. It also predicted lower odds of reaching every patient-centered success threshold at that point, from meaningful improvement to an acceptable symptom state. By two years the depth penalty had faded from the results. Neither the final bump angle nor the resection's position angle predicted outcomes at any point.
pmc-13531553:
Frénois and colleagues pool primary care trials in this 2026 literature review and meta-analysis on a prescribing dilemma: flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are routinely given antibiotics, though many are viral. They asked whether bedside biomarker tests, chiefly C-reactive protein measured in the practice, help doctors withhold antibiotics safely.

Seven studies qualified, five on C-reactive protein point-of-care testing and two on laboratory procalcitonin. The protein test meta-analysis found a statistically significant prescribing reduction, with an odds ratio of 0.41 against usual care in the pooled estimate, at low certainty of evidence and no sign of added patient harm in the included work. Too few procalcitonin studies existed to pool, leaving that marker unresolved. The authors support the bedside protein test as an adjunct to clinical judgment, not a replacement for it.
pmc-13531753:
Wujia Wang and co-authors review in 2026 the lipid messenger ceramide and its grip on female reproductive health. Ceramide sits at the hub of fat signaling in cells and tends to promote cell cleanup and death, balanced by a survival-promoting partner molecule. Levels shift across life and in several disorders.

Altered ceramide appears in polycystic ovary syndrome, early ovarian failure, and endometriosis. The review traces effects on hormone release, follicle growth, egg quality, and the uterine setting. Tuning ceramide balance emerges as a possible route to protect fertility, with molecule variety complicating any single fix.
pmc-13531953:
Wei Li, Lirong Wu, and Jing Chen present a 2026 case where laughing gas abuse and hidden syphilis together damaged a young woman spinal cord. The 23-year-old had inhaled nitrous oxide for six months and arrived with three months of limb numbness and unsteady walking. Cord scans showed the classic inverted V sign of vitamin B12-related degeneration.

Further tests confirmed silent neurosyphilis beside severe B12 deficiency and a related blood marker surge. Combined standard treatment improved her nerve function markedly, with no relapse on follow-up. Young cord cases warrant triple screening for gas abuse, B12, and syphilis.
pmc-13533253:
Baliyan and colleagues recreate a trick of biology: persuading an iron-sulfur cluster, one of nature's oldest electron-shuttling cofactors, to behave inside a synthetic cage the way it behaves inside a protein. Enzymes tune these clusters through their surroundings, the outer sphere, which synthetic chemistry struggles to imitate. Their 2026 host-guest strategy slips a standard four-iron cluster inside tetrahedral molecular cages built from nickel, iron, or zinc corners, confirming the capture with magnetic resonance and mass spectrometry.

Binding proved exceptionally tight in the titration studies, and a battery of spectroscopies showed the cage shifting the cluster's iron-sulfur bonding and electron density toward the values seen in genuine protein-bound cofactors. Control experiments with a cluster that only loiters outside the cage separated the causes. The cage corners' electric field does most of the tuning, while stacking and hydrogen bonding inside add finer adjustment.
pmc-13536553:
Wei Zhao and colleagues build in 2026 DICL, a hand-curated database of ion channels and their ligands for drug discovery. Ion channels are major drug targets, yet scattered and uneven data slow both classic and AI design work. The team gathered structure and activity records from over 6,000 papers, patents, and other databases.

The resource holds over 464,000 records and adds binding site details, channel disease links, and test conditions for the first time in one place. A friendly web interface supports searching and browsing without charge. Researchers gain the largest dedicated collection of its kind for channel drug hunts.
pmc-13536653:
Hongqin Li and colleagues pool in 2026 studies comparing two hip fracture nails, the bionic PFBN and the InterTAN, in older patients with thigh bone breaks near the hip. Six studies with 683 patients fed the pooled comparison of surgery and recovery measures. Quality checks used a standard bias tool for non-randomised studies.

The bionic nail group left hospital sooner and had fewer implant-linked complications, though surgery itself took longer. Blood loss, weight-bearing timing, and hip function scores matched between the two nails. Since all studies were observational, the authors urge care in reading the gains.
pmc-13536853:
Yuyou Deng and colleagues build a survival model for clear cell kidney cancer from cell death and immune genes in a 2026 study. Reliable markers for outlook remain limited despite better surgery and drug options. Gene data from large cancer collections were screened to find a compact gene set tied to survival. Lab tests then checked two suspected master switches and their control of a death receptor gene.

Seven genes formed a score that predicted survival well in the main collection and held up in an outside collection. Higher scores tracked with cell death, immune control, and growth pathways. Two switches, RELA and STAT3, were shown in cells to drive the death receptor gene and its killing signal. The authors propose the score and switch pathway for personal risk sorting and drug work.
pmc-13539953:
Sandrine Bujaldon and colleagues revisit two algal mutants in a 2026 study. Labs have used these mutants for twenty years to study state transitions. That process moves light-harvesting proteins between the two photosystems. One mutant could barely breed. The other leaked the trait it was meant to lack.

Long-read sequencing rebuilt the genomes of the Chlamydomonas strains. The near-sterile strain held big chromosome rearrangements. It also carried extra chromosome copies, larger cells, and faulty reproduction. The team bred and gene-edited two clean replacement mutants. Their warning is plain. Old genetic tools need rechecking before results built on them are trusted.
pmc-13540453:
Shi and colleagues uncover a chain reaction by which immune cell debris worsens brain damage after traumatic injury, in 2026 neuroscience research. Neutrophils, first-responder immune cells, can eject their DNA as webs called neutrophil extracellular traps. In injured patients, these traps accumulated alongside markers of ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of neuron death, and tracked with injury severity. The team used a mouse injury model to test whether the traps cause the neuron death rather than accompany it.

Removing the traps, either by disabling the enzyme PAD4 that builds them or by digesting their DNA, sharply reduced lipid damage in neurons and improved recovery in mice. The trap DNA switched on a sensor called STING inside neurons, which suppressed antioxidant defenses and let peroxidation run. Blocking STING, or activating the AMPK pathway, counteracted the damage and preserved neurons. Shi names neutrophil-driven oxidative stress a promising treatment target.
pmc-13540853:
Hsueh-Han Yeh leads a 2026 validation study asking whether a self-harm prediction model built from health records can spot risk among people recently held in jail. After release, people die by their own hand at roughly nine times the rate seen in the wider public, while brief questionnaires in custody are patchy and blunt.

Records covered 4,154 Medicaid-enrolled people incarcerated in Michigan jails. The existing Mental Health Research Network model sorted risk well, catching about two thirds of later self-harm while correctly clearing most low-risk people. Its negative predictions were right ninety-nine percent of the time. Performance improved further for short jail stays. The authors support records-based screening as a scalable aid to prevention.
pmc-13540953:
Fatma Yılmaz Fındık and Meltem Akbas test, in a 2026 randomised trial, whether motivational interviewing helps pregnant women with gestational diabetes feel more capable of managing their health. The condition demands daily discipline around food, activity, weight, and blood sugar checks.

Sixty women at two hospitals in southern Türkiye were split evenly between four interviewing sessions and routine care, with follow-up after the sessions ended. Beforehand the groups matched on self-rated health abilities and quality of life. Afterwards the interviewed group scored far higher on health practice confidence at both the post-test and the follow-up, with a sizeable gap over controls. The authors support the counselling style as practical antenatal support.
pmc-13541853:
Janssen and colleagues chase the mechanism behind a common complaint of leukaemia treatment: sore, weak muscles in patients on tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the targeted pills that transformed chronic myeloid leukaemia survival. Suspicion centres on mitochondria. Their 2026 study took muscle biopsies from twenty patients and ten healthy controls, and measured drug levels inside the muscle. It dosed lab-grown muscle tubes with the same drugs to watch energy metabolism shift.

Drug concentrations inside patients' muscles matched the levels that harmed muscle tubes in the dish. Patients whose muscles held relatively more drug tended to report worse complaints, a dose clue inside the body. In the tubes, the drugs pushed energy production from sugar-burning toward oxygen-burning pathways. Among patients, those without complaints showed higher mitochondrial capacity and reached their first breathing threshold later in exercise, as if better mitochondria buffered the drug's insult.
pmc-13543453:
Wei Zhu and colleagues published a 2026 case report of rescuing a lung operation after a major vein was cut by mistake. During keyhole surgery for left lower lobe cancer in a 76-year-old man with poor lung function, a stapler completely severed the left superior pulmonary vein. The upper lobe began to congest with blood. The remaining vein stump was too short for direct reconnection, and removing the upper lobe as well would have left almost no left lung.

The team converted to open surgery and fashioned a tube from the patient's own pericardium, the heart's sac, to rebuild the vein. They also trimmed the planned resection to spare tissue. Scans afterward showed congestion clearing and good blood flow, with a three-month scan confirming resolution. A homemade pericardial conduit, the authors propose, is a viable salvage when standard repair is impossible.
pmc-13543553:
Maliha Naz, Jawad Hassan, and Neelum Mansoor published a 2026 case report of a chromosome rearrangement never before reported in blood cancer. It was a translocation joining chromosomes 14 and 15 in a child with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The four-year-old boy from Karachi arrived with months of low fever, lethargy, poor intake, and body aches after several hospital visits that brought only brief relief. Blood tests showed anaemia, low platelets, and a white count crowded with blast cells.

Bone marrow testing confirmed the leukaemia type by immune markers. Chromosome analysis then revealed the swap, written t(14;15)(q32;q11.2), and a fluorescent probe technique confirmed it on dividing cells. Single unusual rearrangements matter in leukaemia because chromosome findings guide risk grouping and treatment intensity. Recording a first-of-its-kind translocation extends the catalogue clinicians check when a child's karyotype does not match any known pattern.
pmc-13543653:
Iokieng Iao and colleagues published a 2026 case report of long-term platelet-rich plasma injections for a 57-year-old Chinese man. He had moderate-to-severe osteoarthritis in both knees, a stage where this blood-derived treatment is usually considered weak. Over fifteen months he received thirty-four ultrasound-guided injections into the two joints. Pain and function scores were tracked, and follow-up MRI examined the joint structures.

By the final visit, both his pain ratings and his standardised knee scores had improved significantly, with better function and quality of life. Scans showed tidier meniscus shape and clear reductions in bone marrow swelling, fluid, fat-pad swelling, and lining inflammation. One case cannot prove a therapy, but the pairing of symptom relief with visible structural improvement, the authors argue, justifies proper trials of sustained PRP in advanced disease.
pmc-13545453:
Andrea Elizabeth Pisesky led a 2026 systematic review of how inflammatory signaling proteins behave in children after heart surgery that uses a bypass machine. Bypass triggers a body-wide inflammatory response that can injure organs and slow recovery in children born with heart defects. Earlier attempts to calm that response broadly have given mixed results, so the authors looked for reliable patterns over time.

Following standard review methods, they gathered studies of patients under 18 that measured at least one cytokine after bypass for congenital heart repair, spanning publications from 2000 to 2022. The goal was to chart which signals rise and fall in set windows after surgery. Such anchor markers could guide the timing of targeted anti-inflammatory trials.
pmc-13545753:
Qi Yao and co-authors measure four blood biomarkers against bone mineral density in 315 postmenopausal women, looking for circulating signals tied to bone loss. The women were classed as having normal bone mass, osteopenia, or osteoporosis by standard scanning criteria. Their 2026 study covers pathways involving fat tissue signals, bone-building Wnt signalling, gut hormones, and energy balance.

Both spine and hip density were lowest in the osteoporosis group. Two markers fell steadily across the groups: apelin-13, linked to fat tissue signalling, and beta-catenin, a core part of the Wnt pathway. After full adjustment, apelin-13 was independently tied to density at both spine and hip, and beta-catenin to hip density. Exploratory analyses suggested strong discrimination between groups, but the authors caution that the near-perfect scores need external validation before either marker can be considered clinically useful.
pmc-13547353:
Souleiman El Balkhi and colleagues proposed in 2026 that the changing shape of albumin, the liver's main blood protein, can stage chronic liver disease without a biopsy. As the liver fails, albumin accumulates chemical modifications. The team used high-resolution mass spectrometry to measure the native protein and nine modified forms in 172 patients across all scarring stages, plus 82 healthy controls.

Native albumin fell steeply with disease severity, dropping to roughly a third of healthy levels in the worst stage, while modified forms followed stage-specific patterns. A learning classifier reading the whole profile staged patients with about 82 percent accuracy, comfortably beating a standard blood score. Results repeated on a second manufacturer's instrument, which the authors say supports wider clinical use.
pmc-13547753:
Yohan Choi and colleagues mapped in 2026 where the sodium-potassium pump's parts are switched on at the interface between a pregnant pig's womb and her developing litter. The pump keeps salt and potassium balanced and helps move nutrients, yet its pregnancy behavior in pigs was poorly charted. Tissues were collected across the cycle, early pregnancy, and the placenta-like membranes of later pregnancy.

Several pump subunits rose and fell in a timed pattern, with some higher in early pregnancy than in non-pregnant tissue. The lining cells of both mother and conceptus were the main sites. Signals from the embryo itself, including estrogen and immune messengers, plus a calcium-raising chemical, switched many subunits up. The authors credit the pump with supporting nutrient flow for pregnancy.
pmc-13548553:
Qin Zou and colleagues trace how skin cells talk to each other during the early repair that follows laser treatment, in a 2026 single-cell study. Lasers rejuvenate skin by causing controlled injury, but the first cellular steps were poorly mapped. Sequencing individual cells from treated and untreated skin showed surface keratinocytes and deeper fibroblasts changing the most in number and gene activity.

Co-culture experiments revealed the conversation runs through exosomes, tiny parcels released by laser-treated keratinocytes and loaded with a protein called CEBPA. These parcels sped up keratinocyte growth through a growth pathway while temporarily quieting fibroblasts by raising another protein, IGFBP3. The authors suggest this timed push and pause helps organize early remodeling. They also point to exosome-based treatments as a possible route to better skin regeneration.
pmc-13548653:
Haoran Zhang and colleagues design an injectable gel that fills oddly shaped bone defects and coaxes the body to rebuild bone, in a 2026 biomaterials study. Irregular defects are hard to fit with solid implants, so a gel that sets in place and hosts growing cells is attractive. Their recipe mixes chitosan sugars, a magnesium salt, a four-armed polymer, and porous polydopamine particles carrying a bone growth factor.

The gel injected easily, healed its own cuts, stuck to tissue, and carried moderate load. It slowly released the growth factor and magnesium over time. The gel also fought bacteria and oxidative damage. It encouraged cells to multiply, migrate, form bone, and grow blood vessels, while steering the local immune response toward repair. Bench and animal experiments backed these effects. The authors present the gel as a minimally invasive route to natural bone regeneration.
pmc-13549953:
Sarah C Johnson and colleagues surveyed digital tools for tracking period health across life. Published in 2026, the scoping review pulled 40 original studies of wrist devices and phone apps. Hormone-driven shifts shape symptoms, health, and output, yet symptom handling know-how lags.

The studies echoed lab findings, backing trust in digital tools, and added fresh insights on body workings, habits, and symptoms through cycles and change-of-life shifts. The review also rates wearable hit rates for period-linked body measures against gold standards. Gaps remain on midlife change body workings and how habits ease symptoms. Readers get a field map plus a research agenda for women's health tech.
pmc-13550453:
Wenyue Wang and colleagues predict which bank customers will sign up for term deposits using an ensemble model that also explains itself, in a 2026 study. Marketing data are lopsided and shift between settings, which trips ordinary models. Their approach trains five varied versions of a gradient boosting method. They are weighted by validation performance. A layered explanation system then reads their decisions, scaling from single customers to the whole portfolio.

On public data the system reached a discrimination score of zero point nine five. The real test came at a Chinese city commercial bank, where a pre-deployment fine-tuning strategy lifted performance from zero point eight four to zero point nine three on the new population. Explanation analysis surfaced sensible drivers such as call duration. The authors offer the package as a balance of accuracy, transparency, and portability for bank marketing.
pmc-13550653:
Dilara Long, leading ten colleagues, published a 2026 imaging study of collagen layout in the uterotubal junction, the narrow segment where uterus meets fallopian tube. Abnormal structure there is suspected in endometriosis and infertility, yet collagen direction had not been measured by depth. Tissue from nine people having surgery was opened and scanned with optical coherence tomography, a light-based imaging method.

The team extracted fiber directions from image gradients and sorted them into longitudinal, oblique, and circumferential bands across three segments. A clear inner longitudinal layer appeared near the uterus and thinned toward the tube, while the outer layer shifted from oblique to mixed alignment. The authors offer the measurements as a baseline framework for linking structure to function and disease.
pmc-13551753:
Qihang Fang, with eight colleagues, published a 2026 trial plan for a severe shoulder injury. The injury splits the joint at the top of the shoulder. It strikes young adults in contact sports. Two operations compete: a hook plate and a ligament rebuild. The trial will assign 72 patients evenly to one or the other. It runs at China's national orthopedic center and partner sites.

The main outcome is a standard score of arm and shoulder function at one year. At that point only the analysts will be blind to who got what. Other measures cover repeat dislocation, life quality, and pain. A shoulder function score and complications count too. The team expects the work to take about two years.
pmc-13551853:
Hejing Bao, Chaofeng Wu, Yanna Wu, Nemin Liu, and Canjian Chen published a 2026 case report of torn eardrums during a lung scope exam. A 77-year-old man came in with cough and short breath. Tests showed a large pool of fluid by one lung, pneumonia in both lungs, and lung failure. In intensive care, doctors passed a scope into his airways to find the germ. Mid-procedure he felt sharp pain in both ears, and both ears bled.

Ear doctors confirmed tears in the centers of both eardrums. The tears were small, so the team chose watchful care over surgery. Treatment for a mixed lung infection steadied the man, and he went home. Both eardrums healed on their own with no hearing loss. The team blames cough-driven pressure surges and advises stronger sedation for frail patients.
pmc-13551953:
Melaku Birhanu Alemu, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 qualitative study of sexual and reproductive health services for young people in Ethiopia's Sidama region. Nine focus groups gathered 56 adolescents and young adults from schools, communities, and a nonprofit, plus seven officials, clinicians, and experts, with discussions held in Amharic and analyzed thematically.

Four themes organized the findings: the health system and its policy backdrop, how services are reached and delivered, what users experience, and background social, cultural, and money factors. When participants ranked what sways uptake most, quality of care, cost, and privacy came out on top. Stigma, religious beliefs, poverty, and migration for work also blocked access, leading the authors to argue that delivery-side fixes matter most where they ranked highest.
pmc-13554053:
D Anil Kumar leads a six-author team unveiling a compact power inverter for medium-voltage use in a 2026 report. Inverters turn direct current into alternating current, and stacked designs give cleaner output with less stress on parts. Many such designs need lots of switches, which raises cost and bulk. Their layout uses just ten switches and three separate power sources to make thirteen voltage steps.

Computer models, heat tests, and a working bench unit all backed the design. Heat tests showed top efficiency close to ninety-seven percent at the best point. Voltage stress on switches stayed low, and the stepped output cut distortion. The team sees the unit serving green power systems and other medium-voltage jobs where clean, steady power matters.
pmc-13554153:
Nakul Ganju leads a seven-author team studying weight-loss drugs of the GLP-1 family in adults who have both Crohn's disease and obesity in a 2026 database study. Crohn's inflames the gut, and extra weight makes its course worse. Records from 162 health groups between 2015 and 2024 supplied new drug users and matched non-users. Close to ten thousand pairs were compared at one year and five years.

Drug starters died far less often in the first year than matched non-users. They also entered hospital less, visited emergency rooms less, and needed fewer strong gut drugs. Steroid use matched at first, then dipped slightly by year five. The authors note that healthier-user bias could inflate the gains, so trials should test the drugs directly in this group.
pmc-13554253:
K N Jakir Hussain leads a six-author team judging whether groundwater in a Karnataka watershed suits irrigation in a 2026 study. Thirteen sites supplied water samples for a battery of chemical tests. Maps and classic diagrams sorted the water by salt load, sodium risk, and mineral family. Depths to water ran from about ten to seventeen metres below ground.

Most water leaned mildly alkaline, typical of dry-region aquifers. About a quarter of samples fell into the saline class, and nearly half carried moderate sodium risk. No sample showed a carbonate hazard. By a combined quality index, most water rated excellent or good, with a small share poor. Salt and hardness drove most of the differences between sites.
pmc-13554353:
Helder Miguel R. O. Carreira offers a framework for writing better ethical opinions in research review, publishing the narrative review in 2026. Research ethics committees guard human participants, yet their written opinions often lack reasons and clear communication, which can feel like arbitrary gatekeeping and wear down trust. The author searched major databases and drew on guidance from the WHO, CIOMS, and the World Medical Association.

Opinion quality, he argues, rests on three linked pillars: grounding in principles, integrity of group deliberation, and honest, readable reasoning in the document itself. The weakest spots are usually informed consent and weighing risks against benefits. Rather than rigid checklists, he defends structured judgement, blending communicative rationality with practical wisdom, as the route to opinions researchers can understand and respect.
pmc-13554453:
Ji-Hun Kim leads a eight-author team reporting a new family of fatty compounds, named Reglid, found in Korean red ginseng leftovers in a 2026 study. Ginseng is famous for saponins, yet other active parts keep surfacing. The leftovers after red ginseng making, called marc, proved rich in this group. The compounds dissolve in water and carry two fatty ingredients plus sugars.

White and American ginseng lacked the group entirely. In skin cell tests, Reglid sped cell growth and wound closing. It also boosted the cells' recycling activity, a sign of healthy upkeep. In pigment cells it cut melanin output by blocking a key enzyme. The authors see cosmetic uses for skin health, turning a waste stream into a product source.
pmc-13554753:
Mingxiao Li leads a large team studying takotsubo syndrome patients whose illness does not mimic a heart attack in a 2026 registry study. Takotsubo, a sudden weakening of the heart often triggered by stress, is frequently mistaken for a blocked artery. Data came from eighteen Chinese hospitals covering 421 patients. Most patients, about three in five, lacked the classic heart-attack picture.

That group held more men, more physical triggers, and breathlessness as the lead symptom. Their heart pumping power ran lower and shock struck more often. Despite gentler blood markers, their death risk ran more than double, both at thirty days and long term. They needed stronger support in hospital yet received fewer of the heart drugs tied to survival.
pmc-13555853:
Wenbin Tang leads a seven-author team mapping how maize seedlings rewire genes and DNA access under cold stress in a 2026 study. Cold at the seedling stage slashes maize growth and yield. Two inbred lines faced off: one cold-tolerant, one cold-sensitive. Gene activity and DNA openness were tracked across time in both lines.

Tolerant seedlings leaked less cell fluid and showed less leaf damage. Their gene activity swung widely with cold, with a big shift at twenty-four hours. Defence pathways lit up, covering energy making and protective chemistry. A family of transporter genes rose together, and DNA near gene start sites opened in step with activity. The linked gene set gives breeders leads for hardier maize.
pmc-13555953:
Tianshuai He leads a thirteen-author team linking lung microbes to early lung cancer behaviour in a 2026 study. Their cohort held 106 Chinese patients with early-stage lung adenocarcinoma, sorted by how malignant their tissue patterns looked. Lung tissue microbes, blood metabolites, and host gene activity were profiled together. Correlation maps tied specific microbes to gene activity through their chemical products.

Four microbe genera stood out as likely influencers of cancer progression. Genetic causal checks suggested two metabolites, serotonin and uric acid, may lower lung cancer risk. Tissue images themselves carried hints of clinical differences between patient groups. The authors frame the microbe-metabolite-gene links as candidate levers on early disease, while noting the findings stay suggestive rather than proven.
pmc-13558053:
Colin Carlson and co-authors examine in 2026 whether human-caused climate change has already changed childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa. Malaria spread depends strongly on temperature and heavy rain, yet experts have argued for decades about the net effect of warming so far.

Using more than a century of clinical records, the team linked malaria rates in children to temperature and extreme rainfall. Warming likely added cases in East and southern Africa but prevented a similar number in West Africa, leaving a small net rise. Their projections suggest warming could speed malaria's decline in West and central Africa, while limiting warming below two degrees would spare highland East Africa and the south extra cases by 2100.
pmc-13558653:
Nur Ashiqen and five colleagues tested in 2026 whether the blood monocytes of patients with loose joint implants are primed to home in on inflamed tissue around the implant. Aseptic loosening, the top cause of implant failure, is fed by these immune cells gathering where wear particles inflame tissue. Human periprosthetic tissue and healthy joint tissue were implanted on opposite sides of immune-deficient mice, and labelled monocytes from healthy donors, first-time implant patients, and loosening patients were injected.

Monocytes from every group preferred the diseased tissue, yet loosening patients' cells migrated most and earliest, followed by first-time patients and then healthy donors. Patient group and years with the implant independently predicted migration strength. The authors conclude that the tissue calls cells in, and that loosening patients' circulating cells are systemically primed to answer, a two-sided mechanism that may yield early warning tests.
pmc-13558753:
Han Liu and six colleagues unveiled in 2026 a vision-language model named Lingjian, built to read the microscope work of clinical laboratories at expert level. Morphology reading is slow, scarce expertise, and variable between observers. The model was adapted in stages on more than four hundred thousand laboratory images paired with text and location labels. Training taught it to understand images, name cells, describe shapes, explain findings, and point at targets within one system.

On five years of national external quality assessment material, the model scored ninety-three percent overall accuracy, beating a human expert panel and strong general-purpose models. In a reader study of 120 cases, junior readers assisted by the model caught far more abnormal cases while their accuracy on normal cases held steady. Weights and evaluation resources were released for others to verify and build on.
pmc-13560153:
Han Byeol Mun and colleagues build a three-dimensional co-culture platform pairing gastric cancer organoids with pooled immune cells from healthy donors. Their 2026 study targets peritoneal metastatic gastric cancer, a form with poor outlook and uneven response to checkpoint immunotherapy. Organoids grown from patients were embedded so donor T cells could infiltrate them realistically.

Activated T cells did penetrate the organoid structures over time. Organoids split into two susceptibility styles: some were killed by immune attack and others resisted, regardless of tissue-type matching. Proteomic profiling showed the killable lines leaned on metabolic pathways, while resistant lines leaned on immune signaling. Pembrolizumab response varied even among organoids with high PD-L1. Nonresponders carried extra amounts of alternative checkpoint ligands tied to TIGIT and TIM-3 pathways. The authors offer the platform as a working testbed for predicting immunotherapy response.
pmc-13560253:
Valeriia A. Kovalskaia and colleagues characterize a novel splice mutation in the CEP290 gene behind Joubert syndrome in two siblings. Their 2026 study follows an eleven-year-old boy and his five-year-old sister, both showing the syndrome's hallmark molar tooth sign and developmental features. Their parents reported distant consanguinity. An earlier genome scan had found nothing.

Reanalysis of the raw genome data, prompted by a geneticist's fresh phenotype review, surfaced a homozygous intronic variant never described before. Both affected children carried two copies inherited from carrier parents, while their healthy sister carried none. Deep RNA sequencing proved the variant wrecks splicing completely: the main transcript skips an exon or swallows intron pieces, and no normal message survives. Reclassified as likely pathogenic, the finding let the family pursue IVF with embryo testing. The authors stress pairing sequencing with functional RNA studies.
pmc-13560453:
Jie-Lin Wang and colleagues identify a small RNA, piR-26681, that suppresses ovarian cancer by sabotaging the tumor's DNA repair. Their 2026 study screens piRNAs differing between early- and advanced-stage tumors, then tests the candidate in cell lines, mouse xenografts, and patient-derived organoids. Repair-proficient ovarian cancers resist PARP inhibitor drugs, so a new lever matters.

The piRNA was scarce in advanced tumors and its presence predicted better outcomes. Restoring it slowed cancer growth across all three model systems. Mechanistically, it grips the two methylation enzymes METTL3 and METTL14, stabilizing both and raising global m6A marking. That marking stabilizes the message of FBXO16, a protein that tags the repair factor MORF4L1 for destruction. With repair impaired, damage piled up and cells grew sensitive to the PARP drug niraparib. The authors propose the axis as a way to crack resistant tumors.
pmc-13562353:
Kota Tanaka and eleven colleagues sort adenomyosis, a condition where womb lining tissue grows into the muscle wall, into scan-based subtypes and ask what drives fertility treatment and live birth in each. Their 2026 multicentre study covered 199 women aged 32 to 49 who had pelvic scans and surgery between 2010 and 2023. Cases fell into intrinsic, extrinsic, and indeterminate groups. The team tested age, past fertility treatment, lesion thickness, and related findings within each group.

Women with the extrinsic pattern more often had a history of assisted reproduction than the intrinsic group, at 32.8 against 8.6 percent. Live birth was lowest in the indeterminate group. Thicker lesions lowered the odds of a baby in extrinsic cases, while an ovarian endometrioma hurt chances in indeterminate cases. Counselling, the authors say, should follow the subtype rather than treat all patients alike.
pmc-13562453:
Arman Shamani-Aminian and two colleagues compare eye disease caused by the Toxoplasma parasite in patients of Latin American and European origin. The infection is the commonest cause of inflammation at the back of the eye worldwide. Their 2026 review covers 144 patients treated at a referral centre in Barcelona, Spain. Seventy-three patients came from Latin America and 71 from Europe. Charts supplied details on symptoms, blood tests, recurrences, and final vision.

Latin American patients more often showed unusual disease patterns, suffered repeated flare-ups, and ended with worse vision. Their antibody levels ran higher, and they more often needed steroid drugs alongside anti-parasite treatment. Infection present from birth and damage in the central retinal zone also predicted poor sight. The authors read the pattern as a harsher form of disease in that group, calling for closer follow-up and care matched to each patient's risk.
pmc-13562553:
Qing Zhu and two colleagues check whether the water collection troughs inside tall cooling towers can withstand extreme wind. These troughs gather cooled water high inside high-level towers at power plants. Wind pressing on the structure could lift or shove them, so the 2026 team tested a model built at 1:363 scale in a wind tunnel. Pressure sensors mapped the inside and underside of the trough across wind directions, with and without windbreak partition walls.

Without the walls, wind barely changed the internal pressure pattern but shifted loads underneath, with a peak pressure-difference value of 0.45. Adding walls raised that peak to 0.68, a jump of about half. At the extreme design wind speed of 46 metres per second, upward pressure reached 2100 pascals and sideways pressure 850 pascals. The authors urge designers in storm-prone regions to verify trough strength and their fixings, and to confirm the findings in the field.
pmc-13562653:
Fengwei Zhang and two colleagues teach a neural network to spot where fishery research and technology are heading next. Funding bodies must bet on promising lines early, and older foresight methods miss how research networks shift over time. Their 2026 model, DTH-GNN, builds a changing knowledge graph from 2010 to 2024 sources: 32,847 publications, 8,956 patents, and 1,856 projects. A graph encoder reads the mixed node types, while a memory module follows how links evolve year by year.

The system predicted future links with a score of 0.934, clearly beating three rival graph methods after leakage checks. Timing information carried about as much predictive weight as network structure, at 31.8 against 29.1 percent of the shared information. Three rising pathways passed expert review with strong agreement: smart aquaculture, a green seed industry, and ecological fisheries. The authors offer the rankings as evidence for where fishery investment may pay off.
pmc-13563753:
Xiaomei Lei and four colleagues reconstruct how childhood respiratory infections reshaped themselves in one Chinese city after the pandemic. A single hospital in Chenzhou kept swabbing through the whole period, giving a consistent lens. Their 2026 review covers 42,505 nasopharyngeal samples from January 2021 to December 2025, each tested for thirteen pathogens at once. Age-layered rates and adjusted models sorted which germs rose, fell, or changed their seasons.

Rhinovirus never left, averaging 33.65 percent positivity across the years. Flu A climbed back toward pre-pandemic peaks, sharing autumn and winter with RSV and parainfluenza. Mycoplasma pneumoniae spiked hard in 2023 at 16.03 percent, then collapsed to 0.56 percent by 2025. Age sorted the pathogens neatly: RSV in infants, several viruses peaking in preschoolers, and mycoplasma risk rising with age. Local timing differed from Western reports, a caution against importing other regions' calendars.
pmc-13563853:
Sonja Lackner and eleven colleagues map every objective in a medical degree to find the nutrition teaching hiding inside it. Nutrition matters to nearly every specialty, yet it sits fragmented across courses instead of standing as a subject of its own. Their 2026 study combed 3,423 objectives from preclinical and clinical phases, with staff across disciplines and a student survey alongside. 574 objectives, 16.8 percent, touched nutrition, scattered but never gathered into a coherent domain.

From that raw material the team built a framework of three domains: nutrition fundamentals, applied nutrition and public health, and clinical nutrition. The trick was alignment, not addition: teaching was relabelled and sequenced rather than new hours being bolted on. Students, meanwhile, rated their general knowledge as middling and their clinical confidence as poor, with about 79.1 percent calling their clinical knowledge weak. The authors offer the mapping route to any school carrying a cross-cutting topic.
pmc-13569453:
Samuele Cortese leads a 2026 analysis of the Global Burden of Disease 2021 data on attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in people under twenty across 204 countries, covering three decades. New cases, total cases, and years of life lived with disability were estimated from 1990 to 2021.

In 2021 the condition affected an estimated forty-seven million young people worldwide, with a global prevalence near two percent. Rates ran highest in Australia and were higher in boys than girls and in richer regions. Overall rates eased slightly since 1990. Policymakers get the most complete country-by-country picture available for planning child mental health services.
pmc-13569553:
Nanbin Liu and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 pan-cancer study, a gene called KANSL2 that helps control which genes are switched on. They ask how it behaves across cancers and especially in liver cancer. Public data on expression, outcomes, mutations, and immune patterns were combined with laboratory tests that silenced the gene in liver cancer cells.

The gene was switched on more strongly across many cancers and linked to worse outlook, most clearly in liver cancer. Its partners clustered around cell division, and immune signals in tumors shifted alongside it. Silencing slowed cell growth, movement, and invasion and stalled division. The gene looks like a useful marker and a possible drug target in liver cancer.
pmc-13570353:
Xu Liu and co-authors study, in a 2026 cell study, a fat-handling protein called FABP4 in liver cells taken from Xupu geese. Goose fatty liver is unusual because severe fat build-up causes no inflammation, so the team raised and lowered the protein's levels and sequenced the responding genes.

Extra FABP4 quieted several inflammatory signals and a fat-export protein, while removing it raised those signals plus fat-uptake genes. Blocking a partner pathway partly undid the calming effect, placing FABP4 downstream of that switch. The results help explain how goose liver stays peaceful under fat loads that would inflame a human liver, a puzzle with lessons for human fatty liver disease.
pmc-13571253:
del Moral-Trinidad and colleagues described in 2026 the hospital burden of measles during the large 2025 to 2026 outbreak in Jalisco, Mexico, based on 609 confirmed cases at one referral hospital. Measles has resurged as vaccination coverage slipped, and recent reports focused on surveillance or on children alone. This cohort covered children and adults together.

About a third of confirmed cases were admitted, 186 people in all. Pneumonia was the leading complication among those admitted, and more than half of inpatients needed extra oxygen. Low oxygen levels and fast breathing at arrival marked the patients most likely to be admitted. Most cases were in people never vaccinated or too young to be eligible, yet vaccinated patients also appeared among admissions and were described separately. Front-door breathing measures best flagged who needed a hospital bed.
pmc-13572453:
Na Li, with seven colleagues, presents a 2026 method for rebuilding an ancient river system in the Junggar Basin of China. The rocks are Lower Jurassic river deposits on the east side of the Chepaizi Uplift. Such deposits can store oil, gas, or carbon dioxide, so their shape matters for drilling plans.

The team joined 3D seismic data with map tools and a modern river area in Inner Mongolia as a guide. Their model sorts the rock pile into source, transport, and sink zones and gauges channel width, length, and spread. Valley shape carried a signal: V-shaped valleys marked strong flow and erosion, while U and W shapes marked calm settings. The rebuild gives planners a numeric map of where old channels ran and how big they were.
pmc-13572553:
Kavitha Premkumar, with three colleagues, ran a 2026 study of immune cells that help tumours by calming other immune cells. These regulatory B cells make a signal, TGF-β, that mutes T cell attack. What pushes B cells into that role inside a tumour was not known.

In mouse fibrosarcoma, removing these B cells slowed tumour growth, and putting B cells back restored it. A fat-like signal from the tumour, PGE2, drove their formation through a STAT3 route. Only the TGF-β-making subset truly suppressed T cells. A COX-2 blocker stopped their formation, shrank tumours, and freed T cell responses. In human data, cancers high in the PGE2-making gene PTGS2 carried the same B cell pattern and worse survival. The authors propose blocking that route in care.
pmc-13572953:
Muhammed Oğuzhan Doğan, with six colleagues, reports the design and lab tests of new compounds aimed at Alzheimer's disease. The illness steadily damages memory, and one drug target is an enzyme that breaks down a key brain signal. The team used a heart drug, trimetazidine, as a cheap starting frame and shaped it toward a known drug's features.

Twenty new hydrazone compounds were built and their structures confirmed by spectral checks. Tests in dishes gauged how well each blocked the target enzyme and a sister enzyme, with donepezil and tacrine as benchmarks. Several compounds blocked the target strongly. Most barely touched the sister enzyme, a selective pattern the team wants. Computer docking then modelled how the best compounds sit in the enzyme's pocket. The set offers leads for later rounds of design.
pmc-13575153:
Matthew Ivory and three colleagues test whether skill at spotting fake faces also helps with fake voices, in a preregistered 2026 study. AI tools now make synthetic faces and voices that look and sound real, raising risks of fraud and false stories. Whether detection skill crosses between senses was unknown.

Volunteers sorted real and AI-made faces and voices. Accuracy beat chance for both tasks. Yet people who did well on faces showed no matching edge on voices, pointing to separate, sense-specific skills. Confidence matched accuracy for faces but not for voices. The authors warn that training or talent in one format should not be assumed to carry over, a point that matters for jobs that screen media for fakes.
pmc-13575253:
Chen Chen leads a 2026 study on judging the cultural value shoppers see in creative products sold online. Buyers judge such goods mostly from photos and text on a page, yet sellers lacked a structured way to score that perceived value. The team built a scoring framework and a ranking model to fill the gap.

Their framework covers three domains: how a product looks, what buyers infer about its use, and the meaning it carries. A combined decision model weighs the indicators and ranks rival products from several angles. A case study used cultural aromatherapy burners. Expert judges disagreed widely, so the authors warn the scores structure opinion rather than measure true quality. Shopper surveys matched the model rankings closely, which supports the method as a design aid.
pmc-13576353:
Mahmut Tankuş and Tülin Ufuk Toygar Memikoğlu study enamel damage when braces come off teeth that have white spot lesions, in a 2026 laboratory study. White spots are early decay marks that often form around brackets. Removing brackets and cleaning off glue can pit the enamel further, especially where lesions are severe.

Forty healthy premolars carried metal or ceramic brackets, with mild or severe lesions created around them. Ceramic brackets left significantly more glue on the tooth after removal than metal ones. Pitting grew sharply during the finishing step when lesions were severe, in both bracket groups. With mild lesions, finishing added no clear damage. The authors warn that a lesion ringing the whole bracket risks cratering during clean-up, so residue removal on such teeth needs extra care.
pmc-13578253:
Weimin Zhong and co-authors ask which male kiwifruit plants make the best pollen partners for the Hongyang type, in a 2026 orchard study. Pollen choice can shift fruit size, sweetness, and seed count, an effect growers call xenia. Fruit from vines dusted with pollen from twelve male plants of two species were compared with fruit from a store-bought pollen control.

Male plants of one species bloomed later yet gave more pollen, while six males of the other species bloomed in step with Hongyang. Three of those males scored best as orchard partners on fruit quality and bloom timing combined. Two later blooming males suited hand pollination of stored fruit instead. The scoring weighed fruit weight, sugar balance, vitamin C, flesh color, and seed traits.
pmc-13578353:
Heng Zhang and co-authors build a tiny drug carrier for prostate cancer that attacks on several fronts at once, in a 2026 study. The carrier is a hollow ball of manganese oxide loaded with a chemo drug and a light activated dye. Chemo alone can work, yet its side effects grow with dose, so the team sought a smarter package.

Inside a tumor the shell turns excess peroxide into oxygen, easing the low oxygen state that shields cancer. Near infrared light then heats the dye and sparks reactive oxygen for two light based attacks. Shell breakdown also drains a key cell shield and frees manganese for a chemical attack. Cell and animal tests showed cancer cells dying by two routes, with low harm to normal cells.
pmc-13578653:
Mercy Ombogo and colleagues build a design tool that predicts how far a replaced shoulder can move before parts collide, in a 2026 study. Reverse shoulder implants swap the ball and socket to help worn joints, yet bone and implant edges can clash and cap motion. Older math checks used rough overlap guesses that lose fine shape detail.

Their pipeline moves solid design models into a motion simulator and seeds clouds of points on key bone edges. Contact at a millimeter of overlap marks the limit during motion sweeps. Lowering the implant neck angle widened free motion by up to twenty three degrees. Printed test parts on a lab frame matched the forecasts almost exactly. Point placement on bone edges proved key to accuracy.
pmc-13578753:
Mehmet Latif Candemir and colleagues split sexual violence against women in Türkiye into three forms and ask what drives each, in a 2026 study. Past work often lumped all sexual violence into one outcome. National survey data from 2014 covered more than six thousand women aged 15 to 59 who had been married or partnered.

Partner behavior dominated every model. Emotional abuse, physical abuse, cheating, money control, living in fear of the partner, and past sexual abuse each tracked with higher odds across the forms. More schooling and higher household welfare generally went with lower risk, with a university degree standing out. The three forms shared much, yet their risk profiles were not identical. The authors call for prevention that tackles several abuse forms at once.
pmc-13578853:
Janna Cousijn and colleagues build a shared photo library for studies of cannabis craving, in a 2026 project. Labs that test how drug cues stir craving each used their own pictures, which made results hard to compare. Their set pairs ninety three cannabis photos with matched neutral photos of like brightness and detail, covering products, gear, and use actions.

Close to seven hundred monthly to daily users across three countries rated sample pairs for craving, arousal, mood, and tobacco craving. Cannabis photos stirred clearly more craving than the neutral set, and the ratings proved highly consistent. A trimmed set of seventy eight photos was kept for the final library. Heavier problem use tracked with stronger cue craving, and mixing tobacco with cannabis shaped tobacco craving in ways the team maps for future users of the set.
pmc-13579953:
Yanyan Li and colleagues read chest CT scans from sixty nine patients with parrot fever pneumonia to see which patterns predict intensive care, in a 2026 study. The bird linked infection is rare yet can turn severe. Cases came from one hospital's records between 2022 and 2025, and nearly all patients recalled contact with birds or poultry. Two radiologists scored each scan two ways, by lobe and by finer segments.

Twenty two patients needed intensive care. Their scans showed wider lung involvement on both scoring systems. The lobe score sorted intensive care need fairly, about matching a standard bedside pneumonia score, and it was the only one whose signal held up firmly in the tests. Most survivors healed fully, and repeat scans cleared or nearly cleared, backing the view that the lung changes pass.
pmc-13580453:
Jean Ikanga and colleagues profile a new dementia cohort in Kinshasa, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the first large-scale study of its kind in French-speaking sub-Saharan Africa. Dementia is rising fastest in low- and middle-income countries, yet data from Central Africa are scarce. Launched in 2024, the EVCD-RDC study aims to recruit 1,000 adults aged 65 and older across four groups, from unimpaired to Alzheimer's and other dementias, with follow-up every two years.

So far 506 people have enrolled, averaging 73.4 years, with 70 unimpaired, 136 mildly impaired, 120 with Alzheimer's, and 180 with other dementias. Dementia cases showed more hypertension, smoking, alcohol use, pollution, conflict, trauma, and poverty, and less education, weight, and resilience. The authors present the cohort as a platform for studying modifiable risks in the region.
pmc-13584453:
Meiyu Liu, Peishan Peng, Jie Chen, and Wei Lu study heart valve hardening in people on long-term dialysis in this 2026 paper. Dialysis cleans the blood when kidneys fail, yet calcium still builds up on heart valves in many patients, a sign of wider vessel disease. The team tested whether a combined blood score, called the CALLY index, could flag that buildup better than single measures.

Their clinic study covered 203 dialysis patients sorted by heart scans into no, single-valve, or double-valve calcium groups. Two thirds of patients had some valve calcium. Lower CALLY scores went with worse buildup even after other risks were counted, and the index beat rival scores at sorting patients. The authors propose adding it to routine checks to catch multi-valve disease early.
pmc-13585553:
Robyn V Bell and colleagues give a lung-tropic gene delivery virus through the vein in mice in this 2026 study. The carrier, a lentivirus dressed in coat proteins from Sendai virus, was built by a British consortium to place working genes into airways for lasting effect. Here the team asked what happens when the same carrier goes into the blood instead, for diseases that need a protein made body-wide.

Both vein delivery and a nose dose sent a test protein into the blood for at least a year. The vein route spread expression across many organs, but it also raised strong antibodies against the carrier, which would block a second dose. The airway route stayed local and left repeat dosing open. The authors favor the airway path for body-wide protein supply on that basis.
pmc-13588753:
Sophia Weis and Johann Maierl map the eye socket of the Huacaya alpaca for veterinarians who treat these animals. Alpacas sport strikingly large eyes on small heads and suffer plenty of eye injuries and infections, yet their orbital anatomy had gaps. The pair examined nine donated alpaca heads, studying two skulls directly and dissecting or sawing through six more to trace every muscle, nerve, and passage in the socket.

The orbit proved to be a complete bony cup, with the eye muscles arising mostly around the optic canal. One muscle, the lower oblique, anchors instead on the tear bone. Nearly all eye muscles take orders from a single nerve, with two exceptions split between two other nerves. New details surfaced, including a fork in the trochlear nerve and fine connecting branches from a neighboring nerve. Otherwise the alpaca matches other farm animals.
pmc-13590453:
Eleanor R Moore and four colleagues test, in 2026, how well wild guppies think and plan, and whether a drug pollutant dulls that skill. Executive function covers holding facts in mind, switching tack, and holding back rash acts. The team used a Y shaped maze that let fish roam freely, and exposed some fish to amitriptyline, a mood drug found in waterways, at two low levels seen in nature.

Working memory and flexible switching clearly guided how the guppies explored the maze. Exposure to the drug, though, did not blunt those skills in this test. Moore and the team say the null result calls for more work, not comfort: such drugs are spreading in rivers, and sharp thinking helps wild animals survive.
pmc-13591653:
Zhang and co-authors show a 2026 way to control terahertz phonon emission from a layered ferroelectric crystal called NbOI2 using a simple mirror. Phonons are lattice vibrations, and their radiative behaviour had rarely been tuned through the optical setting. Placing a mirror nearby changes which light modes the crystal can use.

Changing that photonic environment tuned the phonon's quality factor, peak frequency, linewidth, and emission intensity in a reversible way. Zhang reports modulation near an order of magnitude, meaning nearly ten fold swings, across those traits. The response mirrors the Purcell effect known for light sources, with the phonon radiative rate enhanced or suppressed by the mirror. Near unity radiative efficiency in the crystal makes the effect strong, opening routes to compact tunable terahertz sources.
pmc-13593553:
Matteo Castrichini and colleagues used whole genome sequencing to solve a heart muscle disease that standard gene panels had missed. Their 2026 report concerns a patient with a non-dilated left ventricle prone to dangerous rhythms, whose heart scans showed a ring-like pattern of scarring under the outer wall of the muscle.

Sequencing found two altered copies of GNPTAB, a gene normally tied to mucolipidosis type III, a storage disorder that usually affects many organs. Here the disease appeared in a weakened form that struck mainly the heart, with only faint signs elsewhere. The authors argue that the ring-shaped scar pattern on magnetic resonance imaging should prompt doctors to consider storage disorders. Genome sequencing, they add, can find rare, treatable causes hiding behind a negative panel result.
pmc-13593653:
L. S. van der Knaap-Kind and colleagues compared dental outcomes for children with cleft lip or palate under two Dutch care strategies. The Amsterdam team referred all such children at age one to specialized dental care, while most Rotterdam patients saw a general dentist between team visits. Decayed, missing, and filled teeth in the primary dentition were compared, adjusting for age, sex, and cleft type.

Overall decay experience was similar between teams, but restorative care reached 51.50 percent under specialized care against 29.31 percent under general care. Specialized-care patients also lost fewer teeth to decay. Early referral to specialized dental care therefore improves how completely decay is treated, even when total decay levels look alike.
pmc-13594253:
Sarah Hug and colleagues reviewed what has been tried in primary care. The goal was to get more patients with chronic lung disease referred to pulmonary rehabilitation. That program pairs exercise and education to help breathing and daily life. Their 2026 review found thirteen studies and catalogued each intervention against a standard taxonomy of seventy-three implementation strategies.

Programs typically bundled about a dozen strategies, most often staff education and training, hands-on help, clinician support, and feedback on referral numbers. Despite that effort, pooling the three randomized trials showed essentially no change in referral rates. Study quality was middling overall. The authors argue that counting strategies misses the point: how a strategy is actually delivered, and whether it changes the thinking behind a referral decision, matters more than piling on components.
pmc-13594353:
Nicolae Sanda and a team of co-authors examined the retinas of thirteen elderly donors. The donors spanned normal cognition to Alzheimer's disease. The team focused on the special ganglion cells that sense light for the body clock rather than for vision. Sleep and rhythm problems are among the earliest Alzheimer's complaints, and these cells drive them, so the team recorded electrical responses from freshly harvested retinas.

Ordinary light-sensing rods and cones worked normally, but the clock-related cells were severely depleted in Alzheimer's donors. Survivors looked structurally altered, fired too easily, and could not sustain strong activation. The pattern varied between donors, possibly by cell subtype and disease stage. The authors propose that measuring these cells' light responses might one day help flag or track Alzheimer's changes in the brain, while their failure helps explain the disease's rhythm disruption.
pmc-13594453:
Steven Zweibel and colleagues built a life-long cost model for a new shock-cutting pace tool for fast, risky heart rhythms in people with shock devices. Old pace tools can cut shocks, but wins vary. The new tool, known as iATP, aims to stop fast rhythms more surely while cutting shocks.

In a model from a United States care-system view, the new tool added 0.18 good-life years at added life costs, for a price of 13,114 dollars per good-life year. That price sits far under the 120,000-dollar bar for worth, and it held in all what-if tests. Fewer shocks, with less care use and less life-quality loss, drove the worth.
pmc-13595753:
Yaokang Xue and colleagues report a survey study, published in 2026. It covers second victim experiences among junior nurses in China. Second victims are clinicians who suffer distress after a patient is harmed. The event is an adverse event in care. They surveyed 387 nurses at three Jilin hospitals. All had five years' experience or less. All reported an adverse event in the past year. Distress, support, resilience, and coping were measured.

Profiling split the nurses into three groups. The smallest covered about nineteen percent. One group had low support and high distress. It had the worst scores on both counts. Rule-mining mapped which combinations characterised each profile. Support and personal factors were combined. The authors drafted matched care-bundle prototypes. Hospitals could support each group with them.
pmc-13612253:
Lolwa S Alabdelmuhsin leads a six-author team reporting real-world outcomes for the blood thinner apixaban in Saudi patients with both cancer and atrial fibrillation. These patients sit between clotting and bleeding risks, and trial data in Middle Eastern populations are thin. The retrospective study covered 72 adults with active cancer or a cancer history treated at one tertiary center between August 2016 and October 2020. Events were tracked for six months after starting the drug.

Thrombotic events struck 9.7 percent of patients, including three strokes and three deep vein clots. Bleeding was far commoner, at 36.1 percent, with major bleeding in 9.7 percent. Nearly 29 percent of patients died during follow-up, chiefly from cancer. About a quarter stopped apixaban for clinical reasons such as bleeding or breakthrough clots. The authors read the numbers as a portrait of how precarious anticoagulation is in this group. They argue for close monitoring plus prospective studies.
pmc-13613253:
Bai and the TRUST Working Group present in 2026 a new tool, TRUST, for rating how good a service standard is. Standards govern services from health care to education, yet their own quality varies widely and is rarely judged the same way twice.

The group built a candidate item pool from sixteen existing evaluation frameworks, refined it through an expert survey, and weighted the items by a structured priority method. The finished tool holds 17 items across five dimensions. Quality management carries the largest share of the total score, and collaboration the next largest part of the weighting the panel assigned. A pilot applying TRUST to 51 published standards produced a total score with excellent agreement between independent raters. Agreement on single items, though, ranged from moderate to strong.
pmc-13613353:
An Buckinx and colleagues report a 2026 pilot from Switzerland that tested whether local pharmacies could steer higher-risk people toward free skin cancer screening. Free screening days often draw health-aware people with low risk. Pharmacists and technicians in five cantons took an hour of online training from skin doctors. They learned warning signs such as sun-damaged skin, odd moles, and prior skin cancers. Trained staff then referred people they judged at higher risk to a screening day, where examining doctors did not know who had referred each person.

Of 523 people examined, 50 came through pharmacies and 473 came on their own. Suspicious lesions turned up in 12 percent of the pharmacy group against about 4 percent of the self-referred group. The pharmacy group also carried more sun-damaged skin and needed follow-up more often. The pharmacy route was far smaller than planned, since some self-referred people took reserved slots.
pmc-13613553:
Mark Andrachuk led a 2026 survey of community-run coastal care across five nations in the southwest Indian Ocean region of Africa. Local groups there manage nearby seas for both nature and livelihoods. The team used a shared assessment tool to ask how traits of local rule lined up with how people judged social and ecological results. Traits included clear boundaries, property rights, openness, and day-to-day capacity. Many communities still struggle to build and sustain such systems.

Progress proved uneven across places and across traits. Some areas had firm boundaries and rights. Others lagged on matching rules to local needs, openness, accountability, and staffing. Better ecological results tracked with stronger property rights and local rule. Better social results tracked with local rule and capacity. Rule tended to strengthen in the first five to ten years, then level off or slip, a pattern that matches typical funding cycles.
pmc-13618553:
Elisa M. R. B. Coelho and six colleagues report a pyogenic granuloma on a child's tongue, an unusual spot for this benign reactive growth, and review the published pediatric cases. Their patient, a seven-year-old girl, developed a painless ulcerated nodule on the front left of her tongue after some local injury whose exact nature was never pinned down. An excisional biopsy removed the lesion and tissue examination confirmed the diagnosis.

Healing was complete with no recurrence at three months. The accompanying review searched three databases for oral cases in children up to age twelve and found thirty-six reports. Most growths sat on the gums, with the tongue, lips, and palate as the less common sites, and conventional surgical excision was the usual first treatment. The authors stress that this growth can appear at atypical places in children, so careful examination plus tissue confirmation matters for diagnosis.
pmc-13618953:
Weihong Wang and seven colleagues characterize the volatile organic compounds hanging over Qingyang, an industrial city in western China where regional industry and geography shape a distinctive pollution mix. Air samples from three urban sites and one rural site were analyzed for composition, ozone-forming potential, sources, and health risk, using principal component analysis to separate where the chemicals come from.

They detected one hundred twelve distinct compounds, with total levels averaging about forty-eight parts per billion by volume. Oxygenated compounds and alkanes together made up over half the mix, followed by halogenated hydrocarbons, aromatics, and alkenes. Urban air carried significantly more of these compounds, and more photochemically reactive ones, than rural air. Acrolein stood out as the main driver of non-cancer health risk. The authors advise that controlling alkenes and oxygenated compounds is the critical lever for cutting both pollution and smog-forming potential locally.
pmc-13619353:
Zafer Goren and Yasar Kalip report a rare cause of blocked small bowel in a seventy-two-year-old man who had never had abdominal surgery or trauma. He arrived with belly pain, nausea, and vomiting, and blood tests showed raised white cells. A contrast CT scan showed a clear transition point between swollen and collapsed bowel, which hinted at an internal hernia.

After two days without improvement, surgeons opened the abdomen and found a loop of bowel slipped through a small round hole in the greater omentum, the fatty sheet inside the belly. The loop was still alive, so they freed it and removed the faulty patch of tissue without cutting any bowel. He recovered smoothly and left the hospital on the third day. The authors note this hernia type is the rarest of internal hernias and can turn dangerous when diagnosis lags.
pmc-13619553:
Floor van Meer and five colleagues review how artificial intelligence is being used to keep food safe, in a 2026 article. Food systems generate huge amounts of data, from farm production to processing and retail. The reviewers used an active-learning screening tool to work through the literature in a systematic way and covered more than 150 peer-reviewed publications.

Each study was sorted by research domain, setting, how its data were collected, and which AI technique it used. That structure lets readers see where machine learning is already common and where it is barely tried. The review closes with the main hurdles, such as data quality and trust, and with future chances for AI across the food chain. It serves as a map for researchers and regulators entering a fast-growing field.
pmc-13619653:
Yagmur Inalkac Gemici and five colleagues tracked eye and vision changes in severe sleep apnea before and after airway pressure therapy, in a 2026 prospective study. Thirty-eight patients with confirmed severe disease were compared with nineteen controls. Scans measured the retina's nerve fiber layer and its tiny blood vessels, and visual field tests checked side and central vision.

At the start, differences between patients and controls faded once body weight and multiple testing were taken into account. Thirty patients who used the therapy well were checked again after six months. Nerve fiber thickness around the optic disc grew, and several visual field scores improved, while vessel measures did not hold up after correction. Sleep measures and daytime sleepiness also improved. The authors suggest combined scan and field testing can follow treatment effects on the eye.
pmc-13620053:
Dylan Henssen and three colleagues present brain scans from a forty-six-year-old woman with a rare inherited movement disorder. Over five years she developed frequent falls, stiff legs, unsteady gait, swallowing problems, bladder urgency, low mood, and a mild one-sided parkinsonian picture, plus drooping lids and abnormal vertical eye movements. Genetic testing later found two variants in the SPG7 gene, which causes spastic paraplegia type 7.

A glucose-based PET scan showed a nonspecific pattern of low activity in parts of the cortex and, more strongly, in the striatum, a deep movement center. A second scan targeting dopamine transporters showed a complete absence of binding where signal should appear. She improved modestly on levodopa. The authors read the scans as evidence of profound loss of dopamine-producing nerve endings in this condition, a finding that can confuse diagnosis with Parkinson's disease.
pmc-13620253:
Tshimogo Sathekge led a 2026 record review of psychiatric conditions alongside ADHD in South African children aged seven to twelve, a group with little local data. ADHD often travels with other conditions that complicate diagnosis and care, yet most evidence comes from wealthier countries. The team reviewed records from a specialist child and family unit in Johannesburg for children seen between January 2020 and December 2022, keeping 108 of 573 screened records.

Nearly all children, 95.5 percent, had at least one additional condition. Generalized anxiety affected 52.8 percent, intellectual disability 38.9 percent, and oppositional defiant disorder 29.6 percent, with girls more likely to show defiance and boys more likely to show autism spectrum features. Family violence, drug use by parents, and parents' own psychiatric history were also common. Clinicians get a case for broad, trauma-aware assessment in this setting, where comorbidity runs higher than international figures suggest.
pmc-13620353:
Hiroshi Kiyomatsu and nine colleagues tested a handheld light probe that reads the chemistry of joint cartilage without cutting tissue out. The probe uses Raman spectroscopy, which identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light, delivered through a hollow-core fiber slim enough for future use inside a joint scope. Cartilage came from twelve patients having knee or shoulder joint replacements, plus several joints from a single body donor.

Spectra from the probe separated mildly worn cartilage from badly degenerated areas, with the cleanest separation in knee tissue. The readings also picked up baseline differences between shoulder, hip, and knee cartilage from the same donor, a reminder that each joint starts from its own chemistry. Measurements happened outside the body on preserved tissue, so live use remains ahead. The authors present the probe as a step toward objective, real-time grading of cartilage damage during surgery.
pmc-13620453:
Seung-seob Kim and colleagues validated an ultrasound score for spotting at-risk fatty-liver inflammation against an established rival. Noninvasive scores aim to find patients who may benefit from drug therapy, yet the new LAD-NASH score needed biopsy-backed validation. Their study enrolled 70 patients with biopsy-proven fatty liver disease, testing LAD-NASH, built from sound attenuation, dispersion slope, and liver stiffness, against the FAST score.

Both scores performed near-identically, with accuracy areas of 0.740 and 0.739, a statistical dead heat. At its rule-out cutoff, LAD-NASH caught every at-risk case with no false all-clears. Kim and colleagues present LAD-NASH, needing ultrasound alone, as a handy rule-out tool for at-risk disease.
pmc-13620853:
Siqi Wang and fourteen colleagues tackled a practical question in lung cancer care: how long should immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment run for each patient? Nobody knows the ideal duration for these drugs in non-small cell lung cancer. Their multicenter study gathered 1,054 patients from hospitals in China and the United States. The team built a decision tree on a training group, using a counterfactual method to estimate what each duration would have done.

The tree sorted patients into seven subgroups with distinct patterns. Roughly two fifths of patients fared better in survival terms with short courses, while a similar share fared better with long courses. A smaller slice seemed to gain little from dragging treatment out. Because the tree uses ordinary clinical data and shows its reasoning openly, the authors offer it as a planning aid that prospective trials should now test.
pmc-13621653:
Jakob Stögbauer led a team asking what B-cell-depleting therapy does to the immune memory of Epstein-Barr virus in multiple sclerosis patients. The virus is now seen as central to triggering MS. Anti-CD20 drugs that wipe out B cells are highly effective treatments, yet their effect on virus-specific T cells was murky. The study enrolled 183 people: treated patients, untreated newly diagnosed patients, and matched healthy controls.

Treated patients carried far fewer EBV-specific T cells, both killer and helper types, than controls. Their general T-cell responses stayed intact, and the remaining cells still worked on several fronts at once. Longer treatment meant fewer such cells, and one drug preserved more than another. Antibodies against the virus ran higher in patients despite the B-cell wipeout. The authors suggest trimming such T cells may quietly explain why these drugs work so well.
pmc-13621953:
Ibrahim M Ibrahim and co-authors turn a factory waste problem into a water treatment idea. Sulfuric acid plants discard large amounts of spent vanadium catalyst and pay to bury it. The team tested this used material, without any pretreatment, as a trap for crystal violet, a toxic purple dye released by textile and other industries.

Lab tests with an experimental design showed the waste removed most of the dye from water, with the amount of material and contact time mattering most. Studies of the surface pointed to weak physical attraction rather than a chemical change, working through several forces at once. Cleaning with acid and heat let the material be reused many times while keeping most of its power. Safety checks found little vanadium leaking at normal water conditions, though acid water raised the leak sharply, so the authors limit use to near-neutral water with monitoring.
pmc-13623153:
Xu Chen and colleagues chart the cytokine pattern inside early-stage kidney tumours, a chemical weather report of the tumour's neighbourhood. Cytokines are signalling proteins that steer immune cells, and renal cell carcinoma is known for heavy immune presence that does not always help. The team measured 174 tumour-related cytokines in tissue from twenty patients.

Antibody arrays compared tumour tissue with nearby and normal tissue, and follow-up tests confirmed the biggest shifts. Tumours showed less of several immune-stimulating signals and more of signals tied to blood vessel growth and inflammation. Some of the shifted proteins also appeared at changed levels in blood and urine, and one, called ErbB3 in urine, stood out as a possible painless test marker. Several cytokine genes tracked with survival and with the mix of immune cells in the tumour. The authors say the pattern fits a tumour that quiets defenders while feeding itself.
pmc-13624253:
Beatriz Marín-Díaz and colleagues test whether a sensing protein better known for handling pollutants, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, also helps liver cells repair damaged DNA.
