The team injured the livers of normal mice and of mice lacking the receptor using a cancer-causing chemical, then tracked markers of DNA damage response and cell growth.

Mice without the receptor leaned harder on emergency responses: more programmed cell death and more frantic replacement growth, while the repair work itself ran less faithfully than in normal mice. That sloppier repair threatens the stability of the genome over time. The team also mapped the receptor's partner proteins and found new contacts tied to both repair and proliferation. The authors argue the receptor quietly coordinates rebuilding after injury, a role that could matter in cancer development, where failed repair and runaway growth meet.
pmc-13624753:
Biswa Ranjan Patra and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, report a single endoscopy session that treated two swallowing disorders at once. Their patient, a 59-year-old man, had struggled for six years to swallow solids and liquids, with food sticking, regurgitation hours after meals, and chest pain. Years earlier he had surgery for a throat pouch called Zenker's diverticulum, yet the pouch had returned.

Pressure testing also showed jackhammer esophagus, a disorder where the food pipe squeezes far too hard. Through a scope passed by mouth, the team cut the overactive muscle along nearly the whole esophagus and dealt with the pouch in the same session. Combining both fixes spared the man separate operations and shows how flexible scope surgery can be.
pmc-13626353:
Natascha Kallerhoff and colleagues soak polymer-treated clay for thirty-two weeks to see whether microbes eat the treatment away. Bentonite clay, boosted with polyacrylamide polymers, lines waste sites and steadies tunnels, yet the polymers are organic and might feed soil bacteria. The team modified a standard clay with a positive and a negative polymer, ran water through both, and tracked chemistry, microbes, flow, and thickness before and after.

Pseudomonas species emerged as the main polymer degraders, and the positively charged version drew more microbial attack. Surprisingly, performance hinged less on how much polymer was lost than on how it grips the clay: surface-bound positive polymer stayed robust, while the bridging negative system weakened more. For engineers, charge choice may matter more than dose in keeping liners tight for decades.
pmc-13628053:
Kunal Gharat and Janine Kirstein review how helper proteins called chaperones handle the faulty huntingtin protein behind Huntington's disease. A repeated stretch of code leaves huntingtin with an extra-long tail of one building block. That makes the protein prone to fold wrongly and clump.

The review gathers lab and animal work on chaperones at every step. They help the protein fold right and block harmful sheet shapes. They send bad copies off for disposal. They can even pull apart clumps that have already formed. The authors also show how chaperones team up with the cell's cutting and clearing paths. Their summary maps where this folding machinery might be pushed for new treatments.
pmc-13629253:
Young-Hoon Kim and six colleagues achieved a clean, bonded join between two twisted oxide membranes. The membranes hold a volatile element. Their study appeared in 2026. Twisted layers create moiré patterns that can yield new quantum behaviours. Yet oxide versions usually suffer a messy dead layer at the join. Heating to fix it risks losing ingredients such as sodium to the air.

The team used sodium niobate membranes and a careful oxygen bake. They produced true chemical bonding with orderly atomic registry. Fine imaging confirmed it. The rebuilt join shrank slightly and carried strain unevenly. The bottom membrane stayed relaxed while the top took the shear. The authors present the method as a route to coherent oxide moiré materials. Their strain can be tuned.
pmc-13630553:
James Crabb and two colleagues test whether public facilities in Spokane County, Washington, are placed fairly as well as efficiently. Planners usually optimise network centrality, being well connected, yet neighbourhoods differ sharply in wealth and need, so a central site can still serve residents unequally. Published in 2026, the study clusters census tracts by many social and economic variables.

The team then scored existing facilities with a novel fairness metric, with centrality, and with both combined. Undesirable facilities such as waste sites were not fairly placed under their measure, while hospitals and parks scored as ideally located on fairness and centrality alike. The authors offer the method as transferable to any region with similar public data.
pmc-13630853:
Laveniya Satgunaseelan and colleagues set out resource-tiered testing guidance for ependymomas, rare brain and spine tumours. Gene-based typing sharpened diagnosis and outlook, yet best-practice tests are too costly or out of reach in many low- and lower-middle-income countries. Their ADAPTR guidance adapts WHO tumour guidance to routine lab work under varied budgets.

The guidance tiers testing by lab resources, preserving testing sharpness where gene tools are scarce. The guidance covers tumour types defined by site, methyl-tag patterns, and gene fusions. The authors present the tiers as a hands-on bridge between ideal and doable testing.
pmc-13632853:
Carlos López-Vila and eight colleagues published this 2026 review of survival in rare syndromes that speed up aging. These conditions stem from faults in genes for the cell nucleus envelope. The group covers classic progeria, two forms of mandibuloacral dysplasia, and restrictive dermopathy. The team gathered published cases plus two of their own, keeping only cases confirmed by genetic testing for the main analysis. That left one hundred fifty-eight patients with known outcomes.

Survival differed sharply by subtype. Classic progeria patients lived a median of about sixteen years, while one dysplasia form saw no deaths at all in its group. The most severe restrictive forms took lives in infancy. Causes of death also split by subtype: breathing failure in restrictive disease, heart and vessel causes in progeria, and kidney problems in one dysplasia form. The authors offer these numbers for family counseling and trial planning.
pmc-13646153:
Ramazan Erol sorts eighth-grade students in Türkiye into attitude profiles toward mathematics, using data from the TIMSS 2023 international study. Nearly five thousand students were grouped by how much they liked mathematics, how confident they felt, and how much they valued the subject. Five profiles emerged, running from a low group with very weak confidence to a highly positive group. Erol then tested which factors tracked with profile membership.

Feeling a sense of belonging at school was the steadiest correlate, ahead of educational resources at home, while gender showed a smaller link. Bullying victimization did not separate the profiles once the other factors were counted together. When belonging was left out of a check model, bullying did separate them, a nuance Erol says cannot by itself prove cause or order. The study suggests schools that strengthen belonging may lift mathematics attitudes most.
pmc-13646653:
Renoult and colleagues published a 2026 study on how mountain climate shapes willow chemistry. Willows brew many compounds, from bitter defenses to basic cell fuel. The team sampled four willow species along a steep mountain slope in Europe. Heights ran from about 950 to 2,250 meters above sea level.

Harsher high sites pushed willows to brew stronger defense compounds overall. Bitter salicinoids, the aspirin-like group, rose most clearly with height. Yet the range of one defense group, flavonoids, narrowed at high sites. Climate drove most of the shifts, with soil playing a smaller part. Tree DNA barely differed by height, so flexible responses explain the pattern. Such plastic responses may help willows cope as climates keep shifting.
pmc-13646753:
Ananya Sukhija and three colleagues report a man in his mid-thirties with a progressive nerve disorder that weakened his limbs unevenly and dulled sensation. The illness began in 2022 and fluctuated while steadily limiting daily life. Electrical tests showed a patchy pattern of insulation damage with signal blocks at unusual sites. That picture fits a variant of chronic inflammatory nerve disease called MADSAM, which is uncommon and easy to confuse with other neuropathies.

Steroid treatment brought no clinical response. Infusions of donor antibodies, called intravenous immunoglobulin, then produced significant improvement. The authors use the case to underline two lessons: this variant should be suspected when weakness is strikingly one-sided and patchy, and failure on steroids does not close the door on treatment. Their report adds a documented responder to the small literature on this variant's management.
pmc-13646853:
Fatich Memet and six colleagues review real-world results of a medicated gel for early-stage mycosis fungoides, the most common skin T-cell lymphoma, in a 2026 study. The gel, topical bexarotene, is approved for stubborn early disease, yet everyday evidence and data on continued use after clearance were thin. Records covered fifty-six previously treated patients seen from 2009 to 2022. Response, biopsy checks, side effects, and relapse were tracked.

About six in ten patients responded, and complete clearance arrived for roughly a third. Limited patch-stage disease answered far better than wider disease. Side effects stayed local and manageable. Among complete responders, relapse was common, though patients who kept using the gel as maintenance relapsed later than those who stopped. The authors call that maintenance signal exploratory and in need of prospective testing, while judging the gel effective and well tolerated overall.
pmc-13647353:
Kirsty E Krieg and four colleagues interview ten people with bronchiectasis, a chronic widening of the airways, about a clinic that treats their personal mix of problems rather than the disease alone. The treatable traits approach hunts measurable, relevant traits in each patient and builds a tailored plan. This regional Australian clinic was run by a physiotherapist and respiratory nurses. Patients aged thirty-seven to eighty-two described the experience against a standard acceptability framework.

Three themes came out of the interviews. Patients called the tailored, many-sided care a tool kit that genuinely improved their breathing health. Better breathing spilled into better overall life, the second theme. Yet a third theme admitted that some burdens of the disease did not budge. Overall the group rated the clinic highly and felt life had become easier. The authors say such acceptability evidence should sit beside outcome data when clinics are judged.
pmc-13649053:
Emirhan Ozkul and Mehmet Serhat Mangan review Müller muscle-conjunctival resection, a posterior eyelid operation for drooping upper eyelids, and argue its modern role is wider than tradition allowed. It was long reserved for mild to moderate droop in patients who responded to a phenylephrine test and kept good muscle function.

Recent evidence supports selected use in more severe droop, poor test responders, leftover asymmetry, and certain congenital or nerve-related cases. Refinements include tissue-sparing approaches, simpler suturing, and comfort measures, while the operation's true mechanism and the best dosing rule remain unsettled. The authors urge judging success by contour, symmetry, eye-surface health, and patient-reported benefit, not height alone.
pmc-13649653:
Xiaoli Zhang and three colleagues, in a 2026 study, pack a plant compound into nano carriers to spark heat burn in fat, aimed at severe obesity in kids. The compound is ferulic acid, drawn from plants. The team mixed computer models, cell tests, mouse work, and blood checks in children.

The loaded bits latched onto a heat protein in fat cells, with two master switches above it. In dishes, the bits pushed fat cells to a heat-burning beige form and raised cell breath. In fat mice, they raised energy burn, eased insulin woes, and browned white fat. Muting the heat protein wiped most of those gains out. Kids with severe obesity showed low blood marks tied to browning.
pmc-13650153:
Zezhi Shan and fifteen co-authors, in 2026, test whether a concentrate made from yacon can fight colon inflammation and colorectal cancer through the gut microbiome. Yacon is a root crop rich in fructans and plant antioxidants. Chronic gut inflammation feeds several cancers, so a food that calms the gut while shifting its microbes could help on two fronts.

In mouse models, the concentrate eased chemically induced colitis, with less weight loss and less colon shortening, and it slowed colorectal tumors while lowering their number and total burden. A laboratory gut simulator fed with the concentrate grew more beneficial bacteria and fewer bacteria linked to treatment resistance, with stronger production of helpful fatty acids. Transplanting that reshaped community into mice improved the tumor environment and restrained growth. The findings support yacon as a candidate dietary strategy, pending direct trials in people.
pmc-13651153:
Tadele Amente and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, examine the safety and nutrition of five traditional fermented foods and drinks in Nekemte Town, western Ethiopia. Fermentation preserves food and enriches diets in the region, and the team tested household staples including a cereal beverage, a fermented cabbage dish, and a tuber preparation.

Thirty samples of each food were analyzed for nutrient content, minerals, vitamins, and microbial quality. The cereal drink carried the highest counts of helpful lactic acid bacteria and total aerobic bacteria. Vegetable and tuber foods delivered strong vitamin A and C plus calcium, potassium, and magnesium, while one dish led on iron, zinc, and B vitamins and another on protein. The authors conclude the foods are nutritionally diverse and microbiologically safe, with fermentation cutting antinutrients, which matters most for children and women of reproductive age.
pmc-13651453:
Alexander Muacevic and eleven colleagues test whether muscle wasting predicts a rougher recovery after liver resection for cancer in Bangladesh, where evidence on the question was missing. Sarcopenia, the loss of skeletal muscle mass, is measurable on scans taken before surgery and increasingly blamed for postoperative complications.

The prospective study ran for a year at a university surgical department. Twenty-seven patients were analyzed, and over half qualified as sarcopenic by sex-specific cutoffs on a standard scan level. Sarcopenic patients stayed in hospital roughly twice as long in median terms and suffered infections far more often, affecting three fifths of them against a small minority of the others. Operating time and blood loss did not differ, and no deaths, bleeding, or liver failure occurred in either group. The authors recommend routine muscle assessment so high-risk patients can receive nutrition and exercise preparation before surgery.
pmc-3035253:
Auch, von Jan, Klenk, and co-authors present digital DNA-DNA pairing for drawing species lines among microbes. Naming species rests, in practice, on overall genome likeness. The classic lab test for that likeness is tedious and prone to error.

Their digital method gives the same likeness by comparing genome sequences directly. It offers a faster, repeatable stand-in that name experts can run on a computer. Reliable species lines matter for medicine and industry, since names guide how new microbes are classified, reported, and regulated.  Reference databases of named species now store these digital values alongside type strains.
pmc-4228153:
Salter, Cox, Turek, and their co-authors warned in 2014 about contamination in microbiome studies. New culture-free methods, such as gene sequencing and metagenomics, had transformed the study of microbial communities. These methods read DNA straight from a sample without growing the microbes first.

The team showed that DNA from reagents and the lab itself can enter samples and skew results. The risk is worst for samples with very few microbes of their own. Their findings pushed labs to run blank controls and treat low-level signals with doubt. Clean practice of this kind keeps microbiome claims about health and disease trustworthy.
pmc-4489253:
Yang and Zhang described new developments for the I-TASSER server in 2015. I-TASSER is an online resource that predicts protein structure and adds structure-based notes on function. It works in an automated way from a user's amino acid sequence.

The server first finds structural templates in the Protein Data Bank using several threading methods. It then builds a model and suggests what the protein does. Predicted structures help when no measured structure exists, which is still the case for most proteins. The update kept one of the most used prediction services in step with growing demand.
pmc-6997353:
Jie Li, Feng Cao, He-liang Yin, and coauthors reviewed ferroptosis past, present, and future in 2020. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death discovered in recent years. It features heavy iron build-up and oxidation of membrane fats.

The review traces the concept from early hints to its naming and core machinery. Inducers and blockers of the process are cataloged with their targets. Links to cancer, brain disease, and organ injury are weighed. The authors look ahead to biomarkers and drugs, while noting how much of the pathway map is still blank.
pmc-7619453:
Brian T. Nguyen led a 2026 survey of willingness to use new male contraceptives among men and their female partners in Colombia, Ghana, Morocco, and Togo. Male-controlled options today are mostly condoms, withdrawal, and vasectomy, yet hormonal pills, injections, and gels that suppress sperm production are advancing, and population surveys already show broad willingness despite unproven products. The team surveyed about two thousand sexually active adults aged eighteen to fifty, recruited from clinics and communities in mid-2023.

Nearly three-quarters of respondents, 72.3 percent of men and 76.2 percent of female partners, said they would use new male contraceptives, ranging from 69.4 percent in Togo to 82.2 percent in Colombia. Among men, multiple current partners and a past unintended pregnancy predicted willingness, while among women, wanting to avoid pregnancy and current or desired contraceptive use mattered. For both, more gender-equitable attitudes predicted willingness.
pmc-9848053:
Cheng Zhou, Shane McCarthy, and Richard Durbin presented YaHS in 2022, a tool that assembles genome fragments into chromosome scale scaffolds using Hi-C data. Hi-C measures which pieces of DNA sit near each other in the cell, and those contacts reveal the order and orientation of fragments along a chromosome. Building those scaffolds is a required step before a genome counts as reference quality.

YaHS runs from a single command and asks little of the user beyond an assembly file and an alignment file. The authors designed it to be compatible with similar tools and easy to slot into existing pipelines. Friendly tooling matters in genomics, where small teams assemble genomes for thousands of species.
postel-de-originibus-1553:
Guillaume Postel, the wandering French scholar, published De Originibus at Basel in 1553, with the printer Oporinus. The text is in Latin. Postel had traveled the Ottoman world, learned Arabic, Hebrew, and more, and come home preaching the concord of all peoples under one faith. His book treats the origins of languages, letters, and nations after the flood.

He derives the peoples of the earth from the sons of Noah and argues that Hebrew stands at the root of the tongues. Christian Kabbalah, Greek myth, and travelers' reports blend in his pages. Postel's dream of world concord made him famous and got him locked up as a madman and a heretic. The book is his map of that dream.
ramesey-astrologia-restaurata-1653:
William Ramesey was a physician and astrologer under the Commonwealth whose Astrologia Restaurata appeared in 1653. The title promises astrology restored, purged of error and set in order. Ramesey served great households and wrote for students of the art alike.

He rebuilds the system from Ptolemy and the Arab masters, covering nativities, elections, and the weather in one scheme. His pages mix medical practice with star lore, since his patients expected both from the same man. The book preserves the Commonwealth astrologer's full system at the height of the art's English power. He writes with the confidence of a man whose art still had patrons.
robertson-panel-report-1953:
In January 1953, a panel of scientists met for the CIA to judge the flood of UFO reports. Chaired by physicist H. P. Robertson, it produced the report later called the Durant Report. The file here includes the main report and its three added tabs.

The panel found no proof of craft from other worlds and no direct threat. But it feared mass reports could clog defense channels in a crisis. It urged a public teaching campaign to calm sightings, and quiet watch on civilian saucer groups. The plan shaped official UFO policy for years.
rung-ho-a-novel-pg5153:
Talbot Mundy wrote Rung Ho, a novel whose first chapter opens under verses on Howrah City bowing the knee to masters three: King, and Prince, and Siva. Howrah City, the verse says, pays in pain the taxes the royal twain give to priests, to give again to Siva. The prose begins with a warning in all but words. That was no time or place, the narrator says, for any girl of twenty to be wandering unguarded. Rosemary McClean knows it, and so does the old sweeper woman who follows her.

The old woman, of a caste that is no caste at all, trots in the girl's wake like a dog and growls a stream of warnings. Half of them are things she has seen. Half are things she fears. As Rosemary rides through the loud, many-hued bazaar, trading and gambling pause, then resume.
ruskin-stones-venice-vol-2-1853:
John Ruskin continued The Stones of Venice with Volume 2 in 1853, subtitled The Sea-Stories. This volume reads Venetian history through the city's churches and palaces. The Byzantine and Gothic periods receive the richest treatment. St. Mark's and the Doge's Palace stand as lessons in stone.

Ruskin links each style to the faith and freedom of its age. Gothic, for him, joins nature, variety, and the worker's liberty. The famous chapter on the nature of Gothic influenced William Morris and the labor movement. The volume is the core of Ruskin's moral aesthetics. It teaches readers to see buildings as history made visible.
ruskin-stones-venice-vol-3-1853:
John Ruskin completed The Stones of Venice with Volume 3 in 1853, subtitled The Fall. The volume turns to the Renaissance and the decline of Venice. Ruskin blames pride, luxury, and cold classical rules for the decay of Venetian art. Churches and tombs of the later period show, to his eye, skill without soul.

He ends with warnings to England, which he feared was following Venice's path. The argument is severe, yet the descriptions of light, water, and stone are glorious. The three volumes together form a parable of rise and fall. They changed how Britain thought about architecture. The work remains Ruskin's masterpiece.
stowe-key-utc-1853:
Stowe answered her critics in 1853 with A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin. The full title promises the facts and records on which the story was founded. Her first chapter concedes that doubt had been raised about whether the novel fairly showed slavery as it then stood.

Court cases, runaway ads, and firsthand accounts back scene after scene of the fiction. Stowe argued that the plain truth was worse than anything she had invented. The book works both as a research file and as a weapon for the cause. It stands as a striking early case of an author fact-checking her own famous novel in public.
sunderland-book-psychology-1853:
La Roy Sunderland led the American movement known as mesmerism, the belief that one mind can sway another. His Book of Psychology, subtitled Pathetism, came out in 1853. In it he set down his full system after years of lectures and debate.

Sunderland taught that minds act on each other through sympathy, at a distance and without touch. He used that claim to explain trance, healing, and strong feelings between people. The book came before psychology had labs or degrees of its own. It shows an early American try at a science of the mind, bold and strange at once.
the-complete-angler-1653:
Isaak Walton's Complete Angler, or the Contemplative Man's Recreation, appears here as a facsimile reprint of the first edition, published in 1653. Richard Le Gallienne supplies a preface. He begins by granting the scorn aimed at first-edition worship and calling the first edition, in a modern poet's gibe, also the worst.

Against that scorn he sets his own case. He owns a copy of one of Walton's Lives, that of Bishop Sanderson, with the author's gift inscription to a friend on the title page. He has gone hungry and cold, he says, rather than part with it. Yet visitors often view the treasure with undilating eyes and cold, unenvious hearts. He confesses he has looked the same way at a friend's superb first edition of Pickwick.
the-gamester-1753: Edward Moore wrote The Gamester in 1753, and this copy is a 1948 reprint from the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by Charles H. Peake and a note on the text by Philip R. Wikelund. Only the front matter of the reprint is present here: the series page and the long list of the society's editors and advisers. No cast list, scene, or speech from Moore's play appears in these opening pages.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
Dated November 11, 1897, No. 53 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item praises the British soldiers on the Indian frontier. The past week saw some of the war's hardest fighting. The Afridis held rising ground called the Dargai Ridge, across the British line of advance. A detachment was sent forward to clear it.

The first attack went too easily. The enemy was driven off and Dargai village left in flames. No pains were taken to hold the ridge. Then, on Wednesday morning, the tribesmen reappeared in greatly increased numbers. They reoccupied the ridge in a much stronger position. Their main body held a steep hill about a thousand feet high. It overlooked the road the army had to advance by. The work of dislodging them had to be done all over again.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Military Career, part of the Venetian Years in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, uses Arthur Machen's English rendering of the 1894 London edition, supplemented by chapters Arthur Symons discovered. Chapter Thirteen opens in Bologna, where Casanova resolves to abandon the clerical profession. Having passed through two armies where only the uniform commanded respect, he decides to become an officer himself. He feels answerable to no one for the choice.

A tailor named Morte, an ominous name Casanova notes, measures him for a uniform of his own design. Within a day he walks Bologna in a long sword, brushed hat with black cockade, and false pigtail. He moves to the best inn and admires himself full length in a large mirror. The chapter summary promises an ensign's appointment and embarkation for Corfu. Readers watch a young man's vanity turn a career change into pure theatre.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
A curious chimney-piece from the bishop's palace at Exeter opens volume 19, No. 554, dated June 30, 1832. The engraving shows the kind of rich sculptural decoration used in great houses three centuries earlier. Peter Courtenay, consecrated Bishop of Exeter in 1477 and moved to Winchester in 1486, had it erected.

Heraldry covers the piece. At the centre, Courtenay's arms are joined with those of the see of Exeter, supported by two chained swans. To one side his father's arms appear, and to the other his mother's Hungerford arms, held up by two boars. Mitre, portcullis, foliage, royal arms, and Courtenay's initials fill the mouldings described in detail.
tob-0153:
Crowley launched The Equinox in 1909 as a review of scientific illuminism, part journal, part manifesto for his new magical order. Volume one, number one opens the series. Manifestos, rituals, and the first statements of his system fill its large pages.

Poems, essays, and book reviews stand beside formal instruction, since Crowley meant the review to shape taste as well as practice. The production was lavish for an occult journal. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 edition. Later numbers grew more notorious, but the program of the whole venture is set here: magic presented as a public, printed discipline.
tob-13153:
Manly P. Hall wrote The Lost Keys of Freemasonry in 1923, when he was twenty-two, years before his fame as an occult lecturer. The short book reads Masonry as a spiritual teaching hidden in symbols. It became a beloved primer inside and outside the lodges.

Hall treats the lodge, the degrees, and the lost word of the master mason as signs of man's search for light and truth. The true lost key, he argues, is within the Mason himself. Masons have handed the book to new members for a century, and it shows the symbolic reading of the craft at its most earnest.
tob-13753:
Moses Maimonides, the twelfth-century rabbi and physician of Cairo, wrote the Guide for the Perplexed, in M. Friedländer's translation, for a reader caught between Aristotle and the Torah. The perplexed student knew philosophy well enough to be troubled by Scripture's plain sense. Maimonides argues, with unmatched rigor, that the conflict can be resolved.

Creation, prophecy, providence, and the divine attributes all receive long, careful analysis, including his famous teaching that God is best described by what God is not. The Guide became the major work of medieval Jewish thought and influenced Christian and Muslim philosophy as well. It rewards slow reading and punishes skimming.
tob-4053:
E. A. Wallis Budge's translation of the Book of the Dead rests on the Papyrus of Ani, the most complete surviving copy of the Egyptian funerary text. Ani was a royal scribe, and his scroll follows his passage through the underworld step by step, illustrated vignette by vignette. The famous judgment scene, heart weighed against the feather of truth, comes from this very manuscript.

Spells, hymns, and confessions accompany the pictures, giving readers the text as one Egyptian actually owned it rather than as a composite. Budge's edition made Ani's papyrus world famous. For ancient Egypt's afterlife in its finest surviving manuscript, no other single scroll compares.
tob-4153:
Eliphas Levi's Transcendental Magic, first published in French in the 1850s, effectively invented modern occultism. Waite's 1896 English translation divides the work into doctrine and ritual. Levi names the astral light as the great agent behind magic, and links the tarot, the pentagram, and Kabbalah into one system.

His pages swagger with confidence, mixing real learning with grand showmanship. Every magician since, from the Golden Dawn to Crowley, stands in Levi's debt or in his shadow. Verified from the 1919 edition, Waite's version remains the standard English Levi. Few occult books have been so often quoted, or so seldom read whole.
tob-4253:
Thomas M. N. Owen collected Southern folk-magic tales in Old Rabbit, the Voodoo, and Other Sorcerers, published in 1893. Br'er Rabbit's trickster kin, conjure workers, and root doctors move through his dialect stories. Owen wrote down what he heard from Black storytellers of the South, in their narrative manner.

Spells, haunts, and cunning escapes fill the pages, along with humor that cuts as deep as the fear. The collection preserves a living tradition of conjure and tale-telling that print was already changing. Verified from the 1919 edition, Owen's volume remains a vivid early record of Southern folk magic in story form.
un-doc-atoms-for-peace-speech-president-:
President Dwight D. Eisenhower of the United States gave his Atoms for Peace speech to the United Nations General Assembly on 8 December 1953. The Soviet Union had the bomb, and the hydrogen bomb had just been tested. He had flown in from talks with British and French leaders in Bermuda.

He lays out the awful math of the atomic stockpiles. No shield, he says, can keep a surprise attack from wrecking cities. His way out is a shared pool. The atomic powers should give uranium and fission fuel from their stores to a world atomic energy agency under the United Nations. That agency would turn the atom to farms, medicine, and power. The plan seeded the atomic agency born in 1957.
un-ga-res-2353:
Talks over Gibraltar had stalled by the time the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 2353 in December 1967. Britain and Spain had been urged in 1964 to start talks on the colony's future, and past votes in 1965 and 1966 had kept the push alive. The Assembly now notes a harder line: a colonial state of affairs that breaks a country's unity and land claims clashes with the Charter.

The text regrets the break in the talks. It also faults the referendum Britain held in Gibraltar on 10 September 1967, in which the people of the rock voted to stay British. For the Assembly, the vote cut across its call for a deal struck between the two states.
un-ga-res-a-69-53:
Poison gas and germ warfare are the target of Resolution A/69/53, taken up by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the long will of states to ban the making, storing, and use of chemical and biological arms in full. It gives fresh support to the Geneva Protocol of 1925, the pact that bars the use in war of poison gases and of germ methods of warfare.

The Assembly renews its call to all states to keep strictly to the aims of the 1925 pact. The note of the Secretary-General on the subject is taken on board. In an age of far deadlier arms than those of 1925, the old pact is held up as a rule still worth guarding.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2353 (XXII), from the twenty-second session in 1967, concerned Gibraltar. The Assembly regretted that the talks between Spain and the United Kingdom had broken off. The talks had been urged in its 1965 and 1966 resolutions. It held that a colonial state of affairs harming a country's unity and land wholeness clashed with the Charter.

The text declared that the vote held by the ruling power on 10 September 1967 broke the terms of resolution 2231 (XXI). Both governments were invited to resume talks without delay. The talks were to end the colonial state of affairs in Gibraltar while guarding the people's interests. They were to do so with the Secretary-General's help.

Resolution 69/53 of the General Assembly works to uphold the authority of the 1925 Geneva Protocol. The Protocol is the treaty banning the use in war of poisonous gases and bacteriological methods of warfare. The Assembly renews its call on all states to observe the protocol's principles and objectives strictly. It reaffirms that upholding its provisions is vitally necessary. It calls on states that still keep reservations to the protocol to withdraw them. The Secretary-General is asked to report at the seventy-first session.
un-sc-res-1353: The library catalogues Resolution 1353, a Security Council decision, under the year 2001. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1453:
Afghanistan and its six neighbors signed a good-neighbor pledge in Kabul in December 2002. On 24 December 2002 the Council backed that deal. The signers were the Afghan government and the states around it. China, Iran, and Pakistan signed. So did Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. The Council took the Kabul team as the lawful government until polls in 2004.

All states were called on to respect the deal. They should help put its pledges into practice. The Secretary-General had to report on its use in his regular reports. The signers would supply facts for those reports. The deal aimed to calm a region long troubled by meddling across borders.
un-sc-res-1553:
UNIFIL, the force in southern Lebanon, was renewed in the summer of 2004. On 29 July 2004 the Security Council extended its mandate until 31 January 2005. The Secretary-General had recommended exactly that term. His report noted that Israel had completed its 2000 withdrawal. Lebanon was slowly sending its own army south. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and borders in strong terms.

Lebanon had to keep extending its authority across the south. Deploying its armed forces there was central to that task. The Council also repeated the terms set when the force was created in 1978. All parties had to cooperate with UNIFIL in full. The renewal was routine, but the border stayed armed and tense.
un-sc-res-1653: Security Council Resolution 1653 survives in this collection as a transcription of the United Nations official record. The heading number is its permanent address in the sequence, the form by which officials cite it. Inside that address sits a complete decision: stated grounds first, then the operative clauses through which the Council acts.
un-sc-res-1753:
Liberia's diamond sanctions were lifted by the Security Council on 27 April 2007. Liberia had worked with the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme to control its rough diamond trade. Its government had sent the committee a detailed certificate of origin plan on 4 April. The Panel of Experts had reported on the progress made toward the conditions set in resolution 1521 (2003).

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminated the diamond measures imposed by resolution 1521 (2003) and renewed in 2006. It judged that enough progress had been made toward meeting the stated conditions. The Kimberley Process was asked to report within ninety days on Liberia's application to join the scheme. Liberia was called to carry out the expert mission's advice for the period after admission. The Council would review the lifting once it had the experts' final report, due by 6 June 2007, and the Kimberley report.
un-sc-res-1853: From 2008, Resolution 1853 adds a Council decision to this run of record texts, kept through a copy made by English Wikisource. The act is built in the usual way: first the shared facts, then the steps the members chose. For readers who want to check what the Council truly ordered, that full build is what counts, and it is kept here whole.
un-sc-res-253: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 253, catalogued here at 1966. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-353:
Cyprus came under formal Council review in Resolution 353, adopted unanimously on 20 July 1974. A coup backed from Athens had toppled the island's government five days earlier. Turkish troops landed that morning. Fighting and bloodshed spread across the island, and the whole eastern Mediterranean felt explosive.

The Council calls on all states to respect Cyprus's sovereignty and unity of territory. Every party must cease fire at once as a first step. Foreign military action against the island must end without delay. Troops present outside treaty rights must pull out. Greece, Turkey, and the United Kingdom are told to open talks at once. The aim is peace and a return to lawful government.
un-sc-res-453: The Council considered Saint Lucia in Resolution 453, adopted unanimously on 12 September 1979. The Caribbean island had applied to join the United Nations. The Council studied the application as the Charter requires. It then gave its answer in a single line. The Council recommends to the General Assembly that Saint Lucia be admitted as a member. Such votes are the gate every new state must pass. The Assembly acted on the advice days later, and the island took its seat.
un-sc-res-53: The matter of Palestine was settled in Resolution 53, adopted on 7 July 1948 by eight votes to none, with three abstentions. A first truce in the fighting was about to run out. The UN mediator on the ground had wired the Council on 5 July. The Council sends an urgent appeal to the parties. It asks them to accept in principle a longer truce. The length would be set in talks with the mediator. The text is a single sentence, sent to buy time for peace work.
un-sc-res-853:
Armenia and Azerbaijan are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 853, adopted on 29 July 1993. Fighting over Nagorno-Karabakh had grown worse. The district of Agdam in Azerbaijan had just been seized. Large numbers of civilians had fled, and a grave relief emergency was building in the region.

The Council condemns the seizure of Agdam and all other land taken in recent fighting. It demands an end to the fighting at once. The occupying forces must pull out fully and without conditions. The text backs the Minsk Group's peace work and urges Armenia to press the Karabakh Armenians to comply. States should stop sending weapons that could feed the conflict.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1253, adopted on 28 July 1999, is the Security Council's short response to a membership application. Having examined the request from the Kingdom of Tonga, a Pacific island kingdom, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that Tonga be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That recommendation is the step the UN Charter requires before the Assembly can vote a new member in.

Countries that supply troops to peacekeeping missions carry the risk on the ground, yet they had little say when mandates were written. That imbalance is the subject of this text of 13 June 2001. It follows a Council debate held that January on giving troop contributors a stronger voice.

New ways of consulting those countries before and during missions are set out, including private meetings and regular reports on the talks. The Council promised to weigh their views when deciding on peacekeeping operations. It also backed better planning support, including joint mission teams, and asked its peacekeeping working group to keep improving how the United Nations runs operations.

Just before Christmas 2002, Kabul hosted a rare show of regional goodwill. The Afghan cabinet signed a pact with six neighbors. The six were China, Iran, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. All pledged to live as good neighbors. None would meddle in Afghan affairs. Resolution 1453, passed on 24 December 2002, cheered the deal.

The Council backed the Kabul pact in full. It called on all states to keep its terms. The Secretary-General had to track how well the pact held. His notes would form part of his routine reports on the country. The deal fit the Bonn plan, the road map for rebuilding the Afghan state after the Taliban fell.

Gabon became independent from France on 17 August 1960. Its application for UN membership reached New York within days. Resolution 153 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The decision came at the packed 891st meeting. That single session recommended several African states for admission.

The Council advised the General Assembly to admit the Gabon Republic. The Assembly did so in September. Gabon's oil wealth was still mostly undiscovered or untapped. Politically, the country joined the francophone African group at the UN. The resolution is one line long. Behind it stood the rapid unwinding of France's African empire during the summer of 1960.

South Lebanon, not the Golan Heights, is the stage here. The force there, UNIFIL, had stood since 1978. Beirut asked on 9 July 2004 for six more months of the watch. The chief's report of 21 July warned of strain along the border. Resolution 1553 passed with no dissent on 29 July 2004.

UNIFIL's term now ran to 31 January 2005. The Council backed Lebanon's claim to its full land. It urged Beirut to send its own troops south in force. Both sides had to let UN patrols move freely. Breaches of the Blue Line, by sea, land, and air, drew sharp blame. Mine clearing by the force won praise, as did gifts of mine maps.

Peace and security in Africa's Great Lakes region are taken up in a wide statement of 27 January 2006. The region had suffered a decade of wars, and the 1994 genocide in Rwanda is recalled with condemnation. Growing cooperation among the region's states, the African Union, and the United Nations is welcomed.

Great Lakes countries are urged to deepen their cooperation, agree confidence-building measures, and respect each other's borders and independence. Those guilty of grave crimes in the region are to be brought to justice, with an end to impunity. The world community, aid groups, and donors are also asked to support the region's recovery. That support covers disarmament efforts and the return of refugees, so the recent peace deals in Congo and Burundi will hold.

Resolution 1753, adopted on 27 April 2007, lifts the ban on Liberian diamonds. The embargo had been imposed in 2003, when rough diamonds helped fund Liberia's war. Since then Liberia had joined the Kimberley Process, the certification scheme designed to keep conflict diamonds off world markets, and had proposed a certificate-of-origin system that UN experts reviewed in April.

Having judged that enough progress had been made, and acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminated the diamond measures first set in resolution 1521. It encouraged the Kimberley Process to report back within ninety days on how Liberia was doing. For a country rebuilding under President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, legal diamond exports meant revenue the war economy had stolen.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is extended once more on 19 December 2008. The text again spells out the embargo's exemptions for the African Union mission and for help building up Somalia's own security forces. A separate resolution the month before had added targeted sanctions on people blocking peace in Somalia.

The group's mandate is extended so it can keep investigating violations and reporting through the sanctions committee. The committee is asked to act on the group's findings, including by visiting the region and pressing states to enforce the rules. The renewal kept the monitors in place as the interim government's hold weakened and the insurgency around Mogadishu grew.

Cyprus peace talks set the scene for Resolution 1953, adopted on 14 December 2010. Full negotiations had made progress since 2008, but the pace had slowed and the status quo was called unsustainable. A Limnitis crossing point had opened in October 2010. Demining was advancing, and the Committee on Missing Persons kept working.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 June 2011. It calls on the two leaders to speed up the talks and draw up a practical plan to settle the main disagreements before a January 2011 meeting with the Secretary-General. It urges public messaging focused on common ground and more civil-society involvement. It again asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. A report, including settlement contingency planning, is due by 1 June 2011.

Sanctions on Southern Rhodesia became much wider on 29 May 1968, when the Council adopted Resolution 253 unanimously. Earlier and narrower measures had failed to end the white minority rebellion. The illegal regime had also carried out fresh executions, which brought sharp condemnation.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council ordered all member states to cut off nearly all trade with Rhodesia. Funds and investment had to be blocked. Airlines had to stop flying there, and emigration to the colony was to be prevented. The Council condemned political repression in Rhodesia. Arrests, detentions, trials, and executions were all named. Britain, as the ruling power, was again pressed to end the rebellion and let the people of Rhodesia win their rights.

Turkish troops landed in Cyprus on 20 July 1974, days after a coup backed by Greece. That same day the Council adopted Resolution 353 unanimously. Cyprus's president, Archbishop Makarios, had already asked for foreign forces to leave. The members called the violence a grave threat to peace in the eastern Mediterranean.

Every side was told to stop firing at once. The Council demanded an end to foreign military intervention. Soldiers present without treaty rights had to withdraw without delay. Greece, Turkey, and Britain were urged to negotiate quickly. Talks would aim to restore peace and constitutional rule. The UN peacekeeping force in Cyprus won full backing.

Saint Lucia, a small Caribbean island, became independent from Britain in February 1979. Admission to the United Nations was a natural next step. Its application reached New York as document S/13530. Resolution 453 was adopted unanimously on 12 September 1979. The Council examined the bid at its 2167th meeting.

Members recommended that Saint Lucia be admitted. The General Assembly followed the advice that same month. For a microstate, a UN seat carries real weight. It brings a vote equal to any large power's. It also opens doors to aid agencies and treaties. Saint Lucia's smooth admission shows the routine, welcoming side of the Council's work.

A fragile truce paused the first Arab-Israeli war in the summer of 1948. The UN Mediator worked to stretch that pause. His telegram of 5 July 1948 reached the Council with an urgent request. Resolution 53 followed on 7 July 1948. Eight members voted yes. Syria, the Ukrainian republic, and the Soviet Union abstained.

The whole text is one appeal. Interested parties were urged to accept, in principle, a longer truce. The length would be settled in talks with the Mediator. The resolution is tiny, yet it shows the Council learning peacekeeping by improvisation. Every extra week of truce was meant to save lives and keep diplomacy alive.

Croatia had declared independence as Yugoslavia fell apart. War was already burning across the young republic. Still, its government applied to join the United Nations. Resolution 753, adopted without a vote on 18 May 1992, handled that application. The Council examined the request at its 3076th meeting.

The answer was a recommendation. Members advised the General Assembly to admit the Republic of Croatia. Under the Charter, the Assembly makes the final call on new members. It did so days later. Croatia's admission gave its independence a firm legal footing. It also signaled that Yugoslavia's breakup was being accepted, state by state, in New York.

The seizure of Agdam escalates the Nagorno-Karabakh war in Resolution 853, adopted on 29 July 1993. Relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan had worsened further since Resolution 822 in April. The parties had accepted a timetable of urgent steps, but fighting grew and the district of Agdam in Azerbaijan was taken. Large numbers of civilians were displaced.

The Council condemns the seizure of Agdam and all other recently occupied areas of Azerbaijan, and condemns attacks on civilians and shelling of inhabited areas. It demands an immediate end to hostilities and the complete, unconditional withdrawal of the occupying forces from Agdam and the other areas. It urges Armenia's government to press the Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh to comply, and urges all states to supply no weapons or munitions that could deepen the conflict. It backs the CSCE Minsk Group's peace efforts and its planned monitor mission, and calls for unimpeded relief access.
whewell-plurality-worlds-1853:
William Whewell was a master of many fields at Cambridge. In 1853 he put out a bold tract with no name on it. The tract argues that Earth may stand alone as a home of life. It struck at the claim of a host of lived-in worlds.

Whewell weighs heat, light, and the size of each planet. He holds that most worlds are too hot, too cold, or too wild for life. The tract drew a sharp reply from David Brewster. The clash set off ten years of print debate on the worlds.
william-newburgh-history-stevenson-1853:
William of Newburgh, an Augustinian canon in Yorkshire, wrote his History of English Affairs in the 1190s. It covers the years from the Norman Conquest to 1198. Joseph Stevenson translated the work in 1853. William is often called the most critical of the English historians of the twelfth century, and he earns the praise.

He weighs his sources, mocks Geoffrey of Monmouth's tales of Arthur as lies, and tells even wonders with a raised brow. The reigns of Stephen, Henry II, and Richard pass under his cool judgment. His tale of the civil war of Stephen's time is a chief source for the anarchy. Northern voices are rare in this age, and his is the best.
zoist-vol-11-1853:
Volume eleven of The Zoist spans April 1853 to January 1854. Elliotson edits on, his journal of cerebral physiology and mesmerism in its eleventh year. Case reports of trance cures and painless procedures keep arriving. The somnambulist reports now share an age with table turning and spirit circles.

Mesmerists in these pages claim prior right to the new wonders. Critics answer that trance and fraud explain them all. The thirteen volumes of the run form the movement's archive entire. Volume eleven belongs to its final stretch. The writing stays earnest, detailed, and combative by turns. It records a world of practice that official journals scorned.
